14615-the-sable-cloud-a-southern-tale-wi:
The Sable Cloud, published in Boston in 1861 by the author of A South-Side View of Slavery, defends Southern slavery in fictional form, with Northern comments answering it. The title quotes Milton's Comus.

Chapters open with the death and burial of a slave's infant, then debate Northern conscience, ownership in man, Old Testament slavery, and church discussions of Philemon. A tall Black man urging boys to school appears among the scenes. The book is a proslavery document of the secession crisis, valuable today as evidence of the arguments Americans made for slavery.
24972-reminiscences-of-forts-sumter-and-:
Abner Doubleday's reminiscences, published by Harper and Brothers in 1876, record the first conflict of the Rebellion from inside Forts Sumter and Moultrie in 1860 and 1861. Of the eleven officers in the events, only four survived when he wrote, and he drew on letters, memoranda, and documents in his possession before memory faded. Anderson's little band unfolding the Union flag against a united South in arms gives the narrative its emotional center.

Doubleday writes in the spirit of Lincoln's sentiment, 'With malice toward none; with charity for all,' even when giving opinions that might wound. One homely episode shows his wife in Moultrieville smuggling matches by the gross and a box of candles aboard a boat under a rebel sentinel's stare, for delivery by old soldier M'Narhamy. The memoir stays close, detailed, and humane.
28649-the-letters-of-queen-victoria-vol-:
The third volume of The Letters of Queen Victoria, covering 1854 to 1861, was published by John Murray of London in 1908. Edited by Arthur Christopher Benson and Viscount Esher, the selection comes from the Queen's correspondence between 1837 and 1861, published by authority of the King. A Winterhalter frontispiece shows the Queen, the Prince Consort, and their children.

Chapter 23 follows 1854 through the Eastern Question, the French alliance, war declared, and the Crimea. Alma, Inkerman, the attack on Sebastopol, and Miss Nightingale's mission fill its pages. Chapter 24 turns to 1855, peace proposals, Lord Palmerston as leader, and ministry defeats. Readers get a monarch's view of war and government.
31353-personal-recollections-of-the-war-:
Charles A. Fuller's 1906 recollections, printed at Sherburne, New York, tell his service as private, sergeant, and lieutenant in the Sixty-First New York Volunteer Infantry. They were prepared from letters written from the field to people at home. On March 1, 1861, Fuller went to Cleveland to study law with Boardman and Ingersoll, and he was there at Lincoln's inauguration when Sumter was fired on.

Trouble with his eyes postponed enlistment until the call for three hundred thousand more troops, when he joined Lieutenant K. Oscar Broady's company of Hamilton and Sherburne men, leaving Cleveland on September 5, 1861. Plain, direct, and grounded in letters written at the time, the book is a soldier's own record of the Civil War's opening years.
4127-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-10-apr:
April 1661 brings Pepys's waiting at the Privy Seal round again, with early mornings among his workmen and dinners at home. He dines with Sir William Batten, then walks to the Goat tavern by Charing Cross to meet Dr. Castle.

There the two drink a pint of wine and talk Privy Seal business, in the diary's familiar blend of work and sociability. Spring 1661 shows Pepys settled in office, building his house and his standing at once. Readers get two months of Restoration London in miniature, from tavern talk to the seals of state.
4128-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-11-jun:
June 1661 sends Pepys by water to Woolwich, after taking leave of Sir William Batten and his lady, gone to keep Whitsuntide. With Sir William Pen and Mr. Gauden, he goes from ship to ship, giving orders and noting how forward each vessel is to sail.

Deptford follows, with yards, stores, and captains filling the summer days. The volume shows the Navy Office in motion, fitting a fleet in the first full summer of the Restoration. Readers who like ships and administration will enjoy Pepys among hulls, rigging, and orders. Woolwich and Deptford yards anchor the summer, with ships as the real subject.
4129-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-12-sep:
September 1661 opens on a Lord's day after a rainy night broke into Pepys's house, the stopped gutter spoiling almost all his ceilings. He goes to church in the morning, dines at home with his wife, and walks after dinner to Sir William Batten's.

There he finds Sir William Pen and Captain Holmes, and the talk turns to Navy men and their doings. The volume mixes house repairs, church, and company with office cares, in Pepys's plain daily manner. Readers see how a rising official lived when rain, not war, was the day's chief enemy.
4130-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-13-nov:
November 1661 takes Pepys by coach with Sir William Pen to Westminster, to business at Mr. Montagu's, then back to Whitehall. From there the two walk to the Three Tun Tavern at Charing Cross, where they send for the master's dinner and dine very well.

Tavern dinners, coach rides, and office errands fill these late autumn entries, with Pepys noting each meal and meeting. The volume shows a Navy clerk growing into a man of the town, at ease in taverns and antechambers alike. Readers get London's winter social round in diary form.
4806-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic reaches 1560 to 1561 in this sixth volume, dated 1855. Chapter two opens with agitation in the Netherlands, as ancient charters are resorted to as barriers against government measures. The joyous entrance of Brabant and the constitution of Holland frame the resistance, while Antony Perrenot, archbishop of Mechlin, grows unpopular.

Opposition to new bishoprics by Orange, Egmont, and other nobles joins fury at continued foreign soldiery. Orange resigns command of the legion, the troops are recalled, and Philip attends personally to details of persecution. Perrenot becomes Cardinal de Granvelle, with all power of government in his hands and increasing unpopularity. Animosity and violence of Egmont towards the cardinal, and relations between Orange and Granvelle, whose ancient friendship now strains, carry the volume on. Readers get Motley's account of the Netherlands on the edge of revolt.
6961-military-reminiscences-of-the-civil:
Jacob Dolson Cox aims in this first volume to reproduce his own Civil War experience, from April 1861 to November 1863. Readers grasp how duties and problems struck one man in turn. He served from the beginning to the end. He valued the personal view of men who had served in this or other wars above general or formal history. Soon after peace returned, he set out to write such a narrative of his own army life.

His ties to many prominent officers and civilians gave him a close view of command and counsel. Only this volume's span is told here, from the war's first months through the campaigns that led toward Grant's rise. Cox writes plainly, as a soldier remembering what orders, marches, and councils felt like at the time.
arxiv-2412-00261:
João Mattos, Zexi Huang, Mert Kosan, Ambuj Singh, and Arlei Silva challenged graph neural networks on link prediction in twenty twenty-four. Link prediction guesses which missing connections a network will form. Neural methods report strong scores, but they train and test on balanced samples, while real networks are extremely sparse.

The authors show those scores do not carry over to the realistic imbalanced setting, where simple topology-based heuristics often win. Their method, Gelato, boosts a topological heuristic with node attributes learned from the graph. A ranking loss handles the imbalance, and a partition-based sampler picks hard negative examples efficiently. Experiments show Gelato beats the neural alternatives it was tested against. The paper urges more honest evaluation of link prediction under true sparsity.
arxiv-2412-00361:
Rafee Adnan and a large team of co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, how a galaxy's setting relates to its inner structure. They use strong lensing, where a massive galaxy bends light from a farther one. That bending maps the galaxy's mass, both lit and dark. The sample holds fifteen lens systems. The team modeled each lens with a standard tool to pin down mass and light profiles. They measured local galaxy density as the mark of setting, and tested other definitions too.

They robustly find no link between the offset of mass and light centers and local density. That supports using such offsets to test dark matter theories, since setting can be ignored. A link between mass and light angles and density was moderate, but weakened under other definitions.
arxiv-2412-01561:
Martin Emons and colleagues argue that classic spatial statistics is a ready toolkit for spatial omics. New assays map molecules inside tissue while keeping each cell's place. Two technology families produce two data shapes: point patterns from imaging, grids from sequencing. Spatial statistics has handled both shapes for decades.

The paper walks through what those tools offer biology, with honest notes on friction and nuance. A companion vignette, pasta, runs real examples through several R packages. It shows how clustering, spread, and neighborhood measures read out of tissue maps. The authors aim to save biologists from reinventing methods that already exist. Their message is simple: the spatial toolbox is deep, tested, and waiting. Using it well can sharpen what omics maps actually prove.
arxiv-2412-02861:
Amaury Gouverneur, Borja Rodríguez-Gálvez, Tobias Oechtering, and Mikael Skoglund analyze an exploration algorithm, in a 2024 preprint, for decision problems with yes-or-no rewards. The setting is the logistic bandit: each action pays a binary reward with a chance set by a logistic curve. Thompson Sampling picks actions by sampling from what it believes about the world. Judging how well it learns is the aim, using an information-based yardstick from earlier work.

That yardstick, the information ratio, weighs each step's loss against what the step teaches. They bound it by a quantity that depends on dimension and on how well the action and parameter spaces align. The bound no longer grows with the logistic slope. From it they derive total regret over time. The regret grows slowly with the slope and not at all with the number of actions, a first for this setting.
arxiv-2412-03461:
Baibhav and Kalogera rethink how black holes in lone pairs get their spin in this twenty twenty-four paper. The stock view held that spins of such holes line up with the pair's own spin. That view rests on holes taking spin from the stars that made them.

Inside, the pair loosens that claim and maps routes that can spin a hole up at birth or near it. Some routes scatter spin in all ways, some line it with the birth kick, and some set it crosswise to the kick. Each route leaves its own marks on spin size, tilt, and the joint spin seen as pairs merge. Lone pairs can thus precess and spin back, traits once tied to crowd-born pairs.
arxiv-2412-04761: Xiaotian Xu, Pei Sun, Xin Zhang, Junpeng Cao, and Tao Yang give an exact solution of the Izergin-Korepin Gaudin model. They treat both periodic bounds and open integrable bounds. Gaudin models describe quantum systems with novel long-range forces. With the Bethe ansatz, the team finds the eigenvalues of the Gaudin operators. They also find the Bethe ansatz equations that go with them. The 2024 paper adds the open-boundary case to the solved theory of these models.
arxiv-2412-05061:
Marina Masson and Johan Bregeon hunt for the fading glow of gamma-ray bursts whose jets point away from Earth. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. These orphan glows hide in plain sight among other changing sky objects. Finding them would teach us about burst physics and help pair sky events with gravitational wave signals.

The team built a fake set of short bursts from a real catalog and modeled their off-axis glows. They then simulated how the Rubin Observatory's big survey would see them. From each light curve they drew a set of shape measures. The same measures were computed for a large simulated alert stream. A learning filter, run inside the Fink alert broker, learns to flag orphan-like events. The paper reports how well that filter performs on both test sets.
arxiv-2412-09061:
Shuangshuang Chen, Zijun Wan, and Xiaohua Yao estimate how vibrations fade over time in a beam equation with a potential, in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-four. Such decay bounds underpin the study of nonlinear wave problems. A real, decaying potential sits along the line, and a mass term can be switched on or off.

With no mass term, solutions spread and shrink at a set rate between two natural function spaces. With mass, the decay splits: low-energy parts fade more slowly than high-energy parts. Both results match the potential-free case, whether or not zero energy is a special resonance point. As a payoff, the paper derives the Strichartz estimates used to attack nonlinear beam problems.
arxiv-2412-11061:
Rahul Nair, Gabriel Tseng, Esther Rolf, Bhanu Tokas, and Hannah Kerner investigate geographic bias in driving scene models in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Earlier work showed that geographically narrow image datasets bias simple recognition models. The team asked whether the same holds for the harder task of instance segmentation, using models trained on European driving scenes. They separated two possible sources of error: misclassifying objects versus failing to localize them.

Consistent with earlier work, the European-trained models were geographically biased. Surprisingly, the bias came almost entirely from classification errors, which accounted for most of the geographic gap in both segmentation and detection. Localization proved geographically robust. The authors also show that grouping fine classes into coarser ones, such as treating cars, buses, and trucks as one category, can significantly reduce the bias.
arxiv-2412-12961:
Fatiha Ait Kbir and colleagues test ways to let people query the Land Matrix database in plain words. The Land Matrix gathers data on large land deals across the world. Its aim is to inform debate and action on farming, mining, and energy. Its data are prized in study but little used in policy. Access calls for tech skill and for knowledge of how the database is built.

The team compares large language models and mixes of tuning steps. The steps include prompt work, retrieval-augmented generation, and agents. The systems answer queries through GraphQL and REST links to distinct database systems. Tests can be run again by others, and a demo is online. The broad aim is to ease access to data in many such systems.
arxiv-2412-15961:
Silja Pohjolainen, writing solo, compares two solar radio events that each came in two parts. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Type II bursts trace shock waves driven by coronal mass ejections. In both events, a diffuse wide-band burst came first. A sharper burst followed, singing at the plasma frequency and its harmonic. Both storms were fast, halo-type ejections.

The first burst most likely came from the bow shock at the ejection's front. The second burst allows more than one reading. In the earlier event, the ejection met a streamer, shifting the shock to its flank. In the later event, seen from three angles, a separate shock front showed in white light. The study sharpens how burst pairs are read.
arxiv-2412-16061:
Dario Di Dario, Stefano Lambiase, Fabio Palomba, and Carmine Gravino propose an experiment on whether virtual reality helps students read a software project's health. Repository metrics such as pull requests and issues guide real decisions, and immersive three-dimensional displays might make them click for learners. Evidence in educational settings, though, is thin.

As a registered report, the paper lays out a controlled experiment comparing VR and non-VR presentations of the same metrics. The hypothesis is that immersion builds the analytical skills industry expects, improving both the learning experience and process comprehension. The design is specified in advance, including its aims and context. Results will test whether the headset earns its place in the classroom.
arxiv-2412-17061:
Hai Ye and co-authors study how a team of language models can make training data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Sampling from many models at once can beat one model alone, but the team must be run well. Fixed work plans waste effort and miss good paths.

Their method treats each step as a choice and searches a tree of options as work goes on. A reward model gives quick feedback to guide the search. Tests on translation, chat quality, and math showed strong gains as more compute was used. Data made this way also trained a model that beat strong rivals.
arxiv-2412-19961:
Lu, Supriya, Shaked, Simmons, and Kusenko test two supports for physics students in twenty twenty-four. Gaps in trigonometry and calculus track with race and income, and they affect physics grades. The team built supplemental math assignments with scaled extra credit. They also added AI generated hints to physics homework.

Extra credit was worth more to students with lower exam scores, raising its value where need was greatest. Hints cut the time and social cost of seeking help. Both interventions linked to higher exam scores in their data. Scaled credit also reduced gaps in who completed the math assignments. The design draws on a theory of motivation based on expectancy and value. The authors call the steps simple for any instructor to adopt.
arxiv-2501-00061:
Zhengqi Xu, Han Zheng, Jie Song, Li Sun, and Mingli Song wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It merges separately trained neural networks into one model without any retraining, even when the networks differ in depth and width.

Merging is a cheap way to fuse skills from specialist models, but most recipes assume identical shapes. For depth mismatch, the authors align layers by grouping stretches of layers that behave alike in the deeper model. For width mismatch, their zipping method projects neurons of different sizes into a shared space. Tests across vision tasks showed merged mixed-shape models performing on par with merged same-shape ones. The framework widens the pool of models that can be combined, a practical gain as public model libraries grow.
arxiv-2501-03661:
Günzler and eleven co-authors probe a qubit's magnetic neighborhood in twenty twenty-five. Their device is a granular aluminum nanojunction fluxonium qubit, nicknamed gralmonium. Superconducting qubits with feedback can act as sensors of their microscopic environment. Spin systems are prime targets, but the needed magnetic fields threaten superconductors.

The qubit's spectrum and coherence survive fields beyond one tesla. Sweeping the field reveals a paramagnetic ensemble of spin-half defects. When electron spin resonance matches the qubit, that ensemble becomes the dominant loss channel. Fast flux noise in the megahertz range is also suppressed by the field, suggesting surface spins freeze out. Readers get a qubit that works where spins live, and a map of what limits it there.
arxiv-2501-04661:
Wesley Scivetti and a team of co-authors test whether language models truly grasp phrase meanings or merely recall them. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Huge training sets blur the line between competence and memory, so fair tests need cases rarely seen in training.

The team built a test from construction grammar, which ties sentence patterns to abstract meanings. People easily extend familiar patterns to fresh, creative uses. Models faced two tasks: understand rare but natural uses, and assign the right meaning when the same pattern carries two. Top models, including a leading reasoning system, dropped over forty percent on the second task. Humans split such twins with ease. The gap exposes a limit in how models generalize meaning.
arxiv-2501-05261:
Hanfeng Li and Klaus Schmidt study restricted permutations of infinite amenable groups in two thousand twenty five. Permutations must move each element within a fixed finite set. Those permutations form a shift of finite type over the group. Entropy and pressure of such shifts are the focus.

For amenable groups, entropy becomes a growth rate of permanents. The matrices come from Følner sequences in the group. They define a permanent for elements of the real group ring. It compares with the Fuglede-Kadison determinant of the same element. The permanent also reads as topological pressure of the shift.
arxiv-2501-06161:
Farzana Kabir, David Megías, and Krzysztof Cabaj wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It guards smart meter data as it is summed for the grid, with watermarking and encryption woven into one protocol.

Smart meters spill fine detail about how homes use power, which invites theft and snooping. The design hides the sum's parts with reversible watermarks and AES locks. Slow meters use one watermark form, fast meters a second, matched to their rate. Secrecy, wholeness, and proof of source are all kept. The team built the scheme on real Nucleo boards under the RIOT system. Tests there weigh it against past schemes and find the privacy stronger.
arxiv-2501-07861:
Zhongxiang Sun and a team of co-authors present ReARTeR, a way to make search-aided language models reason better. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with systems that look up facts and then think step by step. Such systems are strong on hard tasks but can go wrong mid-chain.

ReARTeR scores each step with a reward model and adds a second model that explains the score in plain words. Steps can then be fixed as the search goes. For training, the team used tree search to gather good step-level data and tuned the model in rounds. They fix three flaws in past reward models, and tests on multi-step tasks show clear gains.
arxiv-2501-08261:
Cecilio García-Quirós, Shubhanshu Tiwari, and Stanislav Babak ran the first full Bayesian analysis of mock LISA signals entirely in the time domain in a 2025 paper. LISA, the planned space gravity-based-wave observatory, will hear massive black hole binaries for months. Extracting their settings demands waveforms with subdominant harmonics and precessing spins passed through the sensor's response, a heavy math work. The team implemented the IMRPhenomT waveform family and the LISA response in Python on graphics processors to carry the load.

Analyzing zero-noise injections of aligned and precessing binaries over roughly two-month signals, they matched harmonics content, equal versus unequal sensor arms, and interference configurations. Working in the time domain sidesteps per-system rate-domain approximations and allows true to life orbits, a step toward analysis pipelines for real LISA data.
arxiv-2501-09361:
Parinita Nema and Vinod Kurmi improve how vision models learn new classes from few examples in two thousand twenty-five. Such models must add new classes over time without forgetting old ones. Most past setups freeze the old parts, which leaves old classes poorly spread out and prone to clash with new ones.

Their fix pads the feature space with tweaked copies of old class features, each given a stand-in label. That spread leaves room for new classes to land without crowding. A self-supervised contrast loss also pulls old classes further apart. On three standard test sets, the method beat past approaches by a clear margin.
arxiv-2501-12261:
Waldo Gálvez and five co-authors give a framework for diverse solution algorithms in two thousand twenty-five. Many tasks want not one best answer but a set of distinct good ones. Diverse sets add choice, security, and strength against doubt. For hard problems, past diverse methods run in steep time.

Their frame yields fast bi-criteria approximations for planar graph cases. Problems span knapsack, independent set, and vertex cover in weighted form. Sets meet a near best quality bar and near best diversity at once. They also prove plain approximations of that grade cannot exist for two cases. The frame thus marks both reach and limits.
arxiv-2501-16661:
Huichen Will Wang, Larry Birnbaum, and Vidya Setlur present Jupybara, an AI helper for data work, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The hard task they target is exploratory data analysis: digging in complex data and telling a clear story about what matters. Good stories need exact facts, strong framing, and clear relevance.

The team first maps a design space for such work, drawn from theory and talks with experts. Jupybara, built as an add-on for Jupyter Notebook, turns that map into prompts and a team of agents. Expert tests found it easy to use, steer, and fix, and found the design map a sound base for the tool.
arxiv-2501-18361:
Bhargav Ghanekar, Lianne Johnson, Jacob Laughlin, Marcia O'Malley, and Ashok Veeraraghavan track the keypoints of surgical tools in robotic surgery videos. Automated tracking of tool tips and bases underpins downstream uses such as skill assessment, expertise assessment, and delineating safety zones. Deep learning has produced many instrument segmentation systems, but tracking specific keypoints received less attention.

The authors propose a multi-frame, context-driven deep learning framework that localizes and tracks keypoints across video frames rather than treating each frame alone. Trained and tested on annotated frames from the twenty fifteen EndoVis Challenge dataset, it reaches state-of-the-art performance, with high detection accuracy and pixel-level localization error. On a self-annotated surgical skills dataset with more challenging scenarios, the multi-frame models again tracked tool-tip and tool-base keypoints accurately. Temporal context is key: an occluded tool remains findable from neighboring frames.
arxiv-2501-18761:
Zijun Deng and colleagues added uncertainty estimates to underground carbon dioxide monitoring in 2025. Carbon capture and storage can deliver net-negative emissions, but operators must watch the injected plume spread through rock they cannot see, and both plume behavior and reservoir properties are uncertain. Seismic surveys image the plume, and the established joint recovery method combines surveys into one picture, yet it returns a single answer with no measure of doubt.

Their probabilistic joint recovery method instead estimates a full posterior distribution for the plume across surveys, using a generative model shared between them. The output is not just a map but a map with credible ranges, which feeds directly into risk assessment: how sure are we the plume stays where it should. The authors present the method as the uncertainty-aware upgrade carbon storage projects need for defensible decisions.
arxiv-2502-01761:
Stephan Weis wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025, about states on matrix algebras, the averaging rules used across matrix theory and quantum information. It proves a clean topological fact about how those states restrict to smaller structures inside the big algebra.

Every state on the algebra of square matrices also counts as a state on any operator system inside it. The map that restricts a state in this way is generally not open, which complicates topological arguments. Weis proves the map is always open when the smaller structure is a subalgebra closed under the star operation. That single result streamlines a range of topology problems. The paper is short and technical, aimed at specialists in operator algebras and quantum information theory.
arxiv-2502-02961:
Masashi Wakamatsu explored a strange consequence of the quantum vacuum inside protons and neutrons in a 2025 paper. The nucleon scalar charge, tied to the celebrated sigma term, measures how the particle couples to a scalar field with the same quantum numbers as empty space itself. Because the vacuum is not truly empty, the scalar density inside a nucleon should not fade to zero far from its center, but settle to the vacuum's own quark condensate value.

In momentum space that tail becomes a parton distribution with, Wakamatsu argues, a spike concentrated exactly at zero momentum fraction. Such a singularity in the chiral-odd distribution would be a direct fingerprint of the nontrivial vacuum structure of the strong force.
arxiv-2502-03161:
Bołbotowski, Czarnecki, and Lewiński extend isotropic material design with cost measured by L-p norms, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The method minimizes structural compliance by distributing bulk and shear moduli. Both moduli are non-negative fields over the design domain. Cost is capped by L-p norms of the moduli fields.

The original method corresponds to the p equals one case. Each norm choice reduces to a dual pair of elasticity problems. The dual problems involve nonlinear power-law material behavior. Stress states determine the optimal modulus layouts directly. New methods upper-bound the compliance predicted by the original approach.
arxiv-2502-03561:
Jessica Lopez-Sanchez, Erick Munive-Villa, Constantinos Skordis, and Federico Urban simulate ultralight dark matter with different spins to see how spin changes small galactic structures. Their paper came out in 2025. Ultralight dark matter is a candidate form of matter made of extremely light particles that behave partly like waves.

The team merged identical starting blobs, called solitons, and studied the halos that formed. Higher spin produced broader, less dense halos with more prominent outer tails, no matter how many blobs merged. Higher spin also lengthened the time scale for dynamical heating by about tenfold. They found scaling relations that describe halo shape for any number of starting blobs. Satellite disruption tests then showed that the outcome depends on whether halos are matched by density, mass, or core size.
arxiv-2502-04161:
Geetha reviews YOLOv4 for real time object detection in twenty twenty-five. YOLOv4 is a detection model built on the Darknet framework. It jointly handles box placement and object classification in one pass. The review sums up the techniques behind its speed and accuracy.

Methods include cross mini batch normalization and cross stage partial connections. Self adversarial training and weighted residual connections add robustness. A CIoU loss, mosaic data augmentation, and DropBlock regularization further improve results. Multi resolution training with mosaic augmentation aids varied scenes. On the COCO data set, the model reached a reported average precision at high speed on a Tesla V100. The author stresses its efficiency and low cost for real world use.
arxiv-2502-06361:
Arman Goshtasbi and co-authors wrote this robotics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a faster way to make inflatable fabric actuators. These soft air-filled muscles power wearable robots that help people recover movement or lift heavy loads.

Making them by hand is slow: layers are fused in a heat press, then masking layers that shape the air chambers must be peeled away, a fiddly step that invites errors. The team's Weld n'Cut platform joins two machines in one flow. An ultrasonic welder fuses the textile layers, and a vibrating knife cuts the outlines with care. The process is automated and open-source, so other labs can build it. Tests across materials and shapes, including intricate ones, show it holds up. The authors aim to make custom soft actuators cheap enough for wide use.
arxiv-2502-07161:
Fady Ibrahim, Guangjun Liu, and Guanghui Wang survey a new model family for vision tasks, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Transformer models lead in vision but their cost grows fast with image size. The Mamba family uses state-space math to grow in a straight line instead.

The survey covers vision builds that scan images in both directions and pick what to keep. Video builds add time handling for moving scenes. Extra parts, such as position marks and cross-scan paths, sharpen both local and global features. The authors judge the family a strong bet for future vision work.
arxiv-2502-07661:
Tobias Fuchs and Florian Kalinke present a study from twenty twenty-five on learning from data where each case has a set of maybe labels. Human tags often clash, so the true class hides in a set of candidates. Classifiers for this case exist, and add-on tricks can lift them. Most add-ons rest on hunches, not proofs.

Their add-on trims the candidate sets bit by bit with conformal prediction, a tool that gives sound sets. No tagged check set is at hand, so they swap roles: train, tag the check set, trim, and repeat. They prove the trim keeps its soundness for the true labels. Tests on fake and real data lift top classifiers by clear gaps.
arxiv-2502-10161:
Bhadane and three colleagues revisit the famous Berkeley admissions case with causal tests in twenty twenty-five. In nineteen seventy-three data, men seemed favored overall, yet the gap vanished inside each department. That twist is the classic Simpson's paradox. The team asks what fairness means when causes, not just counts, are the lens.

They build a test from Pearl's instrument inequalities that runs on plain records. Several fairness notions, from graph based to what if based, are set side by side. The notions differ in logic, yet their tests agree on this case. The authors pitch case based causal care as a path to principled fairness checks.
arxiv-2502-12961:
Wenjun Li and eight co-authors present MeCo, a plan that lets large language models call outside tools only when they truly need them. Tools like code runners and search help on hard tasks, but models often call them by reflex. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Needless calls slow replies and can add errors from bad tool use. MeCo reads a self gauge score from high level signals in the model's inner space, which tracks the model's sense of its own limits. That score guides each call choice, with no fine tuning and low cost. Tests across models and sets show MeCo reads those inner signals well and sharpens tool use choices.
arxiv-2502-13261:
Khan and a team including Das engineer a two dimensional electrode for light detection in twenty twenty-five. Low contact resistance is a key hurdle for advanced quantum devices. The electrode material is a Weyl semimetal form of tungsten ditelluride. It was grown at wafer scale by molecular beam epitaxy.

Used as a contact for indium selenide, it halves the interface barrier height. Contact resistance fell by a factor of twenty-one versus standard metals. Photodetectors built this way responded strongly from near infrared to deep ultraviolet light. Their response was about sixty times higher than with metal contacts. Rise and fall times were also about four times faster. The authors propose the material for next generation nanoelectronics.
arxiv-2502-14461:
Bilata-Woldeyes, Perea, and Solanes study faint light between galaxies in twenty twenty-five. Deep images show a diffuse glow filling space inside many galaxy groups. This intragroup light comes from stars torn from their home galaxies. Those stars now drift freely, bound to no single galaxy.

The authors ran controlled simulations of one hundred low-mass galaxy groups. Groups varied in mass and in how many galaxies they held. The team tracked how the ex-situ light grows during early group assembly. They also checked which group traits link to that growth. A further question was whether the glow can trace the group's total mass. That use matters most for groups far from settled, where other tracers fail.
arxiv-2502-14961:
Roy Zhao and seven co-authors map the magnetic field in the Sagittarius C cloud complex near the Milky Way's core. Their paper from twenty twenty-five is the fifth in a survey series using the airborne SOFIA observatory. Far-infrared polarization data from the HAWC+ camera trace field lines inside cold clouds. Hundreds of field marks were read across the region.

A tuned Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi study sets field strengths cloud by cloud. Calm zones with even fields run strong; turbulent zones run weak, by a wide spread. Polarization share grows toward cloud edges, as elsewhere in the central zone. Outflows from star-forming spots stir their neighborhoods. The field hugs the skin of a nearby ionized region, in line with twin emission cavities there. Radio filaments and an X-ray glow nearby are weighed against the field map.
arxiv-2502-15261:
Jingheng Ye and co-authors join grammar correction with explanation in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Correction tools for language learners should say why a fix is right, not just give the fix. Past work explained errors found in advance and ignored the tie between the fix and its reason.

Their framework, called EXGEC, generates corrections and explanations together so each can improve the other. They test it on a human-labeled data set of about twenty thousand samples. Finding heavy noise in that set, they build a cleaned version for fairer training and testing. Across three model families, the joint approach beat single-task versions on both tasks.
arxiv-2502-18061:
A team including M. Morbey studied how deuterium is retained in lithium-treated samples inside the DIII-D tokamak, reporting in twenty twenty-five. Liquid lithium divertor designs have been proposed as alternatives to solid designs. Lithium's strong affinity for tritium, however, threatens the fuel cycle of future reactors. The study compares two ways lithium meets the plasma.

Samples were exposed to H-mode plasmas in the far scrape-off layer. Some carried pre-deposited lithium films, while lithium powder was injected during other runs to form co-deposits. Below lithium's melting point, retention did not depend on the thickness of pre-deposited layers. Co-deposits were the main driver of fuel retention instead. Both lithium forms also eroded less than sputtering calculations predicted. The authors conclude that in-situ injection beats pre-deposited films for flatter temperature profiles.
arxiv-2502-18461:
Ziheng Ouyang, Zhen Li, and Qibin Hou join two add-on patches for shot-making tools with no new train run. The work came out in 2025. One patch holds a theme. One patch holds a style. The patches are LoRAs, small tuned add-ons for spread-based shot tools. Users want a learned face drawn in a learned style, time and time again.

Rival join ways drop the theme or the style. Or they call for a fresh train run. The team says the build of LoRA itself hints at the fix. In each watch tier, their way, K-LoRA, weighs the top K bits of each LoRA. The LoRA that rules that spot gives that part of the math. This pick keeps the best traits of both parts in fair share. Tests show the joined tool keeps theme face and style marks side by side.
arxiv-2502-20961:
Gianluca Allinson, Lucy Downes, Stuart Adams, and Kevin Weatherill gauge two deep traits of the cesium atom from the tones of its high, loose states. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

They read the tones at which a warm cesium gas jumps between such states, with waves in two bands: a very high one and a radio one. A twist in the line shape, as the drive is tuned off the mark, lets them pull out the true tone. A joint fit of all reads gives the flaw terms for nine state kinds. Reads between high-spin states give how the core bends in a field, in two forms.
arxiv-2503-05661:
Feodor Dragan and Ekkehard Köhler map in 2025 a family of graph measures that track one another closely. The central measure, path-length, asks how wide the clusters must be when a graph is laid out along a path. Measures within constant factors of each other on all graphs count as coarsely the same.

The authors present several such measures and prove they match path-length in this loose sense. Small path-length turns out to equal several plain conditions. The graph may fit near a simple caterpillar tree. Or one vertex's small disk may cut all paths between two others. Or a short path may dominate the graph. The equivalences give graph theorists new handles on a basic shape property.
arxiv-2503-06161:
Li, Wang, Han, and Zhao build in twenty twenty-five a real-time system that rebuilds moving surgical scenes in three dimensions and labels their parts at once. Keyhole surgery needs crisp live views of soft, low-texture tissue that shifts as tools work. Their method grows a cloud of soft blobs whose shapes track the tissue, enriched with meaning features distilled from a pretrained image model, so labels deform along with the tissue.

One rendering pass yields both the colour view and the label view. It runs at real-time frame rates with a compact footprint. On standard surgery datasets it set top marks for image fidelity and matched strong two-dimensional tools on labelling. The authors pitch it for safer surgical guidance.
arxiv-2503-07861:
H. Yilmaz and co-workers grew crystals of a nickelate cousin under high oxygen pressure in a 2025 paper. Since pressurized lanthanum nickelates superconduct, strontium nickel oxides in the same Ruddlesden-Popper family tempt as other choices. The pure strontium compounds block charge stubbornly. Adding yttrium and aluminum on chosen sites, the team grew a substituted variant by optical floating zone at ten bar of oxygen. Exploring a narrow mix window and checking the pure system's stability with density working math work.

Diffraction, spectroscopy, transport, and magnet strength readings map the crystals' form and actions. Yttrium doping overcame the charge-blocking ground state, cutting resistivity sharply into semiconducting territory. The growth recipe yields large, high-quality crystals for the nickelate hunt.
arxiv-2503-08461:
Jianian Zhu, Hang Wu, Haojie Wang, Yinghui Li, Biao Hou, Ruixuan Li, and Jidong Zhai wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It speeds up serving of multimodal large language models, whose memory cache for past text and image tokens grows huge.

Squeezing that cache saves memory but adds delay, above all when many users call at once. Their frame, FastCache, pairs a smart batching plan across the fill, squeeze, and decode stages with a cache pool that ends memory waste. Tests on two data sets show first-token waits cut by a large factor and throughput up many times over top baselines. It holds steady at high call rates while using less memory on average.
arxiv-2503-10261:
Misa Kawaguchi and five co-authors refine a light-based method for seeing stress inside flowing fluids. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Flow birefringence turns stress patterns into optical signals. Their test flow spreads radially in a thin Hele-Shaw cell. Stress points mostly along the gap in that geometry. The classic stress-optic law, read along the gap, then fails.

Measurements at varied flow rates confirm the failure. A second-order version of the law succeeds instead. It accounts for stress along the viewing direction itself. Rheometer runs cross-check the cell results. Coefficients for the refined law are extracted. Stress imaging in thin gaps gains quantitative footing.
arxiv-2503-10361:
Anastasios Avgoustidis, Edmund Copeland, Adam Moss, and Juhan Raidal test whether cosmic superstrings, in a 2025 preprint, explain a hum of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing teams have reported a background signal at very low frequencies. One candidate source is a network of cosmic strings left from the early universe. In superstring versions, the network holds several string types with different tensions. Ignoring the heavier types warps the predicted spectrum. The authors include them across a wide band, from nanohertz to kilohertz.

They evolve the network with a multi-tension model and fit it to fifteen years of NANOGrav data. The fits give values for the base string tension, the string coupling, and the size of extra dimensions. Cosmic superstrings fit about as well as the favored black hole explanation. Upper bounds on the coupling also emerge. The authors discuss what future detectors could see if the string picture is right.
arxiv-2503-11361:
Swetha Nair, Guillaume Jeanmairet, and Benjamin Rotenberg study ions at electrochemical interfaces, from explicit to implicit solvent pictures. The focus is how metal screening and solvent screening jointly shape the charge an ion induces. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Atom level electrodes follow a Thomas-Fermi screening model. The solvent is treated two ways: full molecular dynamics, or a density functional shortcut. Sodium and chloride ions meet water and acetonitrile in turn. The screening length strongly sways charge spread inside the metal, yet leaves solvent layout at the face much the same. The shortcut method matches fine solvent detail at a sliver of the cost.
arxiv-2503-12261:
Gnana Praveen, Jahangir Alam, and Eric Charton sort feelings from sound and video even when the two channels do not back each other up. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets emotion scores on the valence-arousal plane. Audio and visual cues are expected to complement, but at times they clash or one goes weak. A fixed fusion then drags the score down.

Their GRJCA model adds gates to a recursive joint cross-attention design. Each gate weighs attended features against raw ones by how strongly the channels agree. A second, higher gate then weighs the rounds against each other. On the hard AffWild2 set, scores for valence and arousal beat the ungated base model. Test and validation marks both rose. The design suits wild video, where one channel often falters.
arxiv-2503-13661:
Ha presents Pensez, showing small curated data can strengthen French language model reasoning, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Strong reasoning in non-English languages usually demands massive training data. Only two thousand bilingual samples are fine-tuned in this study. Samples are chosen carefully in English and French.

Math reasoning accuracy rises up to twenty percent on a hard benchmark. A French math benchmark gains twelve percent as well. Quality curation beats raw scale in this comparison. Resource-constrained teams can build capable multilingual models cheaply. The assumption that scale is mandatory is challenged directly.
arxiv-2503-14861:
Tibebe Birhanu and Hang-Hyun Jo build a way to read the hidden rule that joins bursts of events into larger bursts as the time scale grows. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Many real series are bursty: events crowd into short bursts, split by long quiet spans. As the scale that marks a burst grows, small bursts merge step by step into one. That merge path forms a tree. A kernel rule says which bursts merge at each step. The team gives a best-fit way to read that rule from a series. It worked on fake series with known rules. They then use it on real series from varied fields.
arxiv-2503-16961:
F. Valentini, T. M. O'Neil, and D. H. Dubin dissected the death of a stubborn plasma wave in 2025. Electron acoustic waves survive because electrons trapped inside them switch off the usual Landau damping. Yet how such waves are born and how they decay has stayed unsettled. That open question dates from their forecast in the nineteen nineties. The team modeled the plasma with a Vlasov-Poisson code that follows the electron spread.

They first grew stable waves with a resonant outer drive, then nudged them with a small disturbance and watched. The decay followed a two-to-one pattern: a shorter wave merged into a longer one as the phase-space vortices trapping its electrons merged. The trigger was a small group of particles able to hop between nearby trapping wells, exchanging energy between two phase-space holes. While paths near the edge between trapped and free motion turned chaotic.
arxiv-2503-17961:
Wu-Hsiung Huang studies singularities and topological change for deforming domains in two thousand twenty-five. Domains slide inside a manifold and may change their topology en route. The question is when analysis on them stays continuous through that jump. A strongly elliptic self adjoint operator stands in for past stability tools.

Quasi-Lipschitz domains, made by gluing boundary points, allow the change. For monotone deformations of such domains, Sobolev and eigenvalue continuity hold. A global Morse index theorem falls out of that steadiness. He also builds a deformation from a small ball to any such domain. The needed continuity holds all along that path.
arxiv-2503-18261:
Christian Covington and Jeffrey Miller propose a new way to check Bayesian models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In practice, models are often wrong in part. A good check should show not just that a model fails, but where it fails. Their method rests on a neat fact. If data truly came from the assumed model, then a draw from the posterior should look like a draw from the prior.

They rewrite every random part of the model in terms of plain uniform values. These u-values can be grouped and tested in many ways. A group that strays from uniform points at the flawed part of the model. The checks are cheap to run and rest on firm statistics. The paper gives Bayesian analysts a sharper tool for model criticism.
arxiv-2503-21261:
Seonggon Kim and three co-authors cut the cost of training neural networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets backpropagation, the step that tunes a net after each pass. Matrix products eat the largest share of that cost. The team read the backward math in detail to find light tricks with the best pay off. They kept training quality while they cut memory and compute.

Their method, called HOT, leans on Hadamard based tricks. It uses short code forms and low rank fills, each placed on the backward path it suits. Two add ons squeeze the stored signals and tune the steps layer by layer. Readers who train large models get a way to shrink the bill with less loss of quality.
arxiv-2503-21761:
David Yifan Yao, Albert Zhai, and Shenlong Wang built a frame to model moving scenes in four dimensions from one video. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with dynamic scene reading from casual clips. Big pretrained vision models each do a slice of this well: depth, motion, masks, and text links. But one model trained for the whole task stays out of reach. Their frame, Uni4D, chains those models in a staged fit scheme.

It needs no retraining or tuning of the parts it joins. Output covers rebuild of still and moving parts, camera path, and dense three dimensional motion tracks. Scores top past work with strong visual quality. Readers in vision get proof that off the shelf models can be fused for rich scene reads.
arxiv-2503-22661:
Khan builds in twenty twenty-five a new recipe for computing molecule energies that avoids fitted parameters. Energy recipes in this field often mix exact theory with tuned constants, which can fail for strongly interacting electrons. His recipe links two limits exactly: the weak-interaction limit from perturbation theory and the strong limit from a trusted semi-local method.

The result beat its parent method on atom energies and on a large reaction benchmark. It handled weak bonds between molecules better than standard hybrid recipes, without added correction terms. It also showed smaller self-interaction errors in charged test cases. Bond-breaking curves for two test molecules improved over conventional recipes as well.
arxiv-2503-23561:
Niall OSullivan, Licio Romao, and Kostas Margellos connect two frameworks that both promise safe decisions from limited data. Conformal prediction builds sets that contain the true outcome with a stated confidence. Scenario optimization solves a decision problem using sampled cases and bounds the chance that a hidden rule is broken. The two literatures grew apart, and their similar-looking guarantees were never cleanly tied together. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors start from the basic form of conformal prediction and choose its scoring and set-building pieces in a pointed way.

With those choices, the classic scenario bounds on rule-breaking probability come back exactly. The bookkeeping of ranked scores is itself shown to be a small scenario problem with some constraints thrown away, which returns the conformal guarantee from the other side. The bridge also lets the authors analyze a conditional form of conformal prediction with scenario tools.
arxiv-2503-24161:
Enrico Le Donne, Luca Nalon, Nicola Paddeu, and Simone Verzellesi spell out a special class of Carnot groups in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. Carnot groups are the tangent models of sub-Riemannian geometry, where motion is restricted to certain directions.

The question is which stratified groups have the property that hypersurface boundaries with locally constant normal are locally flat. The authors call such groups hypergenerated and prove an algebraic characterization of them. These turn out to be exactly the groups where embeddings of non-characteristic hypersurfaces are locally bi-Lipschitz. The results then extend from hypersurfaces to submanifolds of arbitrary codimension, tying algebraic structure to geometric regularity.
arxiv-2504-04661:
Suyash Vardhan Singh and five co-authors present N-TORC, an optimizer that compiles neural networks into custom hardware under strict latency budgets, in a two thousand twenty-five computer engineering paper. Direct dataflow compilation gives low latency but unpredictable area and slow design cycles.

N-TORC builds data-driven performance and resource models for individual layers, then solves a mixed integer program to choose architectures meeting real-time constraints while trading accuracy against cost. Its models beat earlier HLS4ML estimates in accuracy, and its solver matches stochastic search quality a thousand times faster. The demonstration application, DROPBEAR, reproduces projectile dynamics for a cyber-physical testbed, showing the framework on a real constrained problem.
arxiv-2504-05061:
Song and co-authors sort the round orbits of charged particles near black holes. They use a topological current method based on phi-mapping. The work covers flat, anti-de Sitter, and de Sitter space at large range. Both light-like and time-like orbits are treated in one frame. Charge changes the class of an orbit in clear ways.

For black holes with more than one horizon, the team proves a firm rule. If an orbit with fixed charge and spin sits between two horizons, at least one unstable light orbit and one unstable time orbit must exist. Outside the last horizon, the charge ratio helps set the total topological charge. Tests use the Reissner-Nordstrom family of black holes.
arxiv-2504-06361:
Torrejón and co-authors simulate how hydroquinone behaves where liquid meets vapor in two thousand twenty-five. Hydroquinone is a ring-shaped chemical used in industry and photo work. Its surface traits, density balance, and vapor pressure matter for design, yet are hard to measure directly.

Five molecular models were raced in a single box holding both phases side by side. Two came from the TraPPE force field family, one atom-by-atom and one new grouped version. Two drew on the OPLS family, and a fifth was a coarse-grained model built on a fluid theory. Density profiles, phase densities, vapor pressure, and layer thickness were read for each. The contest shows which shortcuts keep the physics honest.
arxiv-2504-07361: Yongjie Shi and Chengjie Yu extend a known lower bound for Steklov eigenvalues from plain graphs to weighted ones, and pin down exactly when the bound is tight. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Steklov eigenvalues describe how a shape or network vibrates with its boundary free. Perrin's earlier estimate covered only unit-weighted graphs.
arxiv-2504-07561:
V. Vertogradov and A. Övgün explored black hole formation in 2025 under extreme conditions where normal matter turns into quark matter. Standard collapse models always end in a central singularity, a point where classic relativity breaks down. The authors ask whether the change from baryonic matter to a quark-gluon plasma during collapse could avoid that result.

By giving the shift an uneven rate that varies through the collapsing substance. They show with study and numeric work that a regular black hole can form, with a smooth core resembling de Sitter space instead of a singularity. They also look at the size of the black hole's shadow, since telescope readings of shadows could test whether such models match real black holes.
arxiv-2504-12161:
Danyer Perez Adan searches open data from the CMS detector for a rare decay of the Higgs boson into two light new particles. The study appeared in twenty twenty-five and uses proton hits from twenty sixteen. Each new particle would split in turn, one path giving two muons and the other giving two charm quarks. No past search at the collider had used this exact mix.

The hunt covers light particle masses from four to eleven units, where the split parts tend to overlap. No clear excess over the known background was seen. Adan sets upper bounds on how often the decay could occur. The bounds beat past limits in some models where the new particle links strongly to up-type quarks.
arxiv-2504-13361:
Linh Van Ma, Shoaib Azam, Farzeen Munir, and Moongu Jeon describe a booking system for driverless taxis in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In conventional taxi services, drivers make most operational decisions, which unmanned vehicles cannot do. Their system lets an autonomous vehicle accept and serve ride requests on its own. A customer books through a mobile application; the system allocates a vehicle and plans its service trip.

A central server monitors customers and vehicles and brokers communication between a customer and the vehicle assigned to pick them up. The team demonstrated the setup with their own autonomous vehicle serving a real request placed through the app. The work covers the full loop from request to pickup coordination. It is a systems paper aimed at making robotaxi operations practical rather than a study of routing algorithms.
arxiv-2504-13861:
Ivan Sviridov and co-authors present 3MDBench in 2025, a test bed for AI doctors that chat with patients. Models that read images and text are being tried in telemedicine, but running a full consultation takes more than a good diagnosis. It takes the right questions in the right tone.

The framework runs fake consultations with a patient agent whose temperament varies, and an assessor agent grades the visit. It holds close to three thousand cases across thirty-four diagnoses, drawn from real telemedicine records with images. Chatting with reasoning beat one-shot diagnosis, and feeding in a specialist model's guess lifted scores a lot. The code is open for other teams to use.
arxiv-2504-14561:
Riesco and five co-authors survey proof scores, a method to outline formal proofs in the same language as system specs, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Proof scores have long served the OBJ family of specification languages. Their chief perk is that spec writers need no second language to prove traits. Many systems and protocols have been verified this way.

The survey lays out the theory behind proof scores. It reviews systems that adopt them and their newest advances. It catalogs verified system classes and the main proving tricks used. It also explains why wider adoption stalled despite clear wins. The authors close with future work that could fix those barriers and spread the method further.
arxiv-2504-16261:
Krinos Li, Xianglu Xiao, Zijun Zhong, and Guang Yang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It forecasts how strongly a drug-like molecule will bind to a protein, with a geometric deep learning method called IPBind.

Binding strength guides drug design, but past tools sag when the protein is new and unseen. IPBind leans on the push and pull between atoms in the bound and unbound states of the pair. On wide benchmark sets it scores well and holds up on fresh proteins. It also gives atom-level clues for each call. The work shows machine-learned atomic forces as a sound base for this gauge.
arxiv-2504-16361:
Qizhao Chen compares transformer designs for forecasting stock indexes in a 2025 finance study. Many studies report that transformers forecast prices well, yet they treat the architecture as a black box. Which internal structure helps, and which merely adds cost, stays unclear, even though the answer decides what practitioners should build.

Five transformer structures are evaluated head to head on stock prediction. Holding the task fixed isolates the effect of design choices such as attention patterns and layer layout. The comparison aims to name the variant best suited to financial series. Clearer guidance can save trading and research teams from copying designs tuned for language instead of markets.
arxiv-2504-17061:
Leandro Nascimento asks how close a group choice rule stays to a simple weighted sum when fairness rules hold only roughly, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The setting joins personal value scores into one group score. A classic theorem says exact fairness forces the weighted sum form.

Nascimento shows that small breaks from the fairness rules mark rules that sit near the weighted sum form. The gap from the sum is at most half the size of the fairness break. In plain terms, near fairness means near the classic result, with a clear bound. Readers in social choice get proof that the classic theorem is stable, not brittle.
arxiv-2504-17861:
Malihe Nobakht Kooshkghazi, Salman Ahmadi-Asl, and Hamidreza Afshin give iterative methods for tensor equations in two thousand twenty-five. The equations use the T-product, a way to multiply tensors. One class has a symmetric positive definite form. For it they build a conjugate gradient style method.

The method makes residual and direction steps with clean orthogonal traits. It ends in a finite count of steps, with proof. For general systems they pass through a normal equation form. Uneven systems are cast as least squares problems. Tests on fake data, images, and video show high precision at low cost.
arxiv-2504-17961:
Anan Lu and a large collaboration examine eight galaxies and galaxy bulges that hold plenty of cold gas yet form stars poorly. About a quarter of these galaxies have rich molecular reservoirs, a puzzle since gas is the raw material of stars. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team combined an imaging spectrograph at a Hawaii telescope with millimeter array observations of the cold molecular gas. The spectrograph maps glowing ionized gas line by line, and both data sets sit at fine spatial resolution. Emission line ratios reveal what ionizes the gas in each region.

Nowhere in the sample did star formation dominate the ionization, despite the abundant cold gas; old stars ruled. Gas amounts paired with star formation rates or their upper limits pin down how long the gas would take to be used up. The study is one installment of a long-running survey of nearby galaxy centers.
arxiv-2504-18161:
Gramoz Goranci, Adam Karczmarz, Ali Momeni, and Nikos Parotsidis built the first full dynamic tools for transitive reduction. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with directed graphs. A transitive reduction is the smallest subgraph that keeps the reach facts between all pairs of points. Graphs in real use change edge by edge, so the reduction must keep up. Past work lagged in that live setting.

Their first tool updates in near best time for sparse graphs. It can even take in bursts of edges at one point, or cut sets of edges at once. A second tool leans on fast matrix math for dense cases. Readers in algorithms get live upkeep of a base graph form.
arxiv-2504-19661:
Annika Burmester and Ulf Kühn study post-Lie structures on free Lie algebras, a topic in pure algebra. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five also treats the Grossman-Larson product on the algebras' enveloping forms. They give an abstract formula for the product's dual coproduct, of use for the wider theory of post-Hopf algebras.

With a magmatic approach, the pair link post-Lie algebras to multiple zeta values and their q-analogues. For zeta values, the frame gives an algebraic read of the Goncharov coproduct. They also match Ecalle's ari bracket to a post-Lie structure on a free Lie algebra. A like match for the uri bracket is put forward as a conjecture.
arxiv-2504-20361:
Jewel Kumar Ghosh, Francisco Pena-Benitez, and Patricio Salgado-Rebolledo study equilibrium in materials whose quasiparticles disperse at uneven rates in a 2025 physics study. Multi-Weyl semimetals host particle-like modes that are linear along one axis and power-law along the others, breaking the usual spacetime symmetry down to a smaller group. Hydrostatic equilibrium, the balance that fixes density and heat profiles, needs to be worked out anew without Lorentz invariance.

The authors propose a covariant formulation of the low-energy theory with minimal coupling to background fields. From it, equilibrium conditions and response coefficients follow in step. Such matter could show unusual thermoelectric behavior.
arxiv-2504-20861:
Raisinger, Zhang, Bolander, and Eliáš compared two ways of building unevenness into computer models of materials in twenty twenty-five. Such models break a material into rigid blocks joined by contacts, and real materials are never perfectly uniform.

In the standard approach, the unevenness comes from the shapes and layout of the blocks themselves. In the second approach, the layout stays regular but each contact gets a randomly varied strength. The team compared both styles in stretch tests and in breaking tests. The random version could match the overall response after tuning, but the stress patterns inside and the way cracks formed stayed clearly different. The wavy stress pattern of the shaped layout could not be copied by random strengths. The authors say experiments on real materials are needed to judge which view is right.
arxiv-2505-00661:
Andrew Lampinen and nine co-authors compare two ways language models learn new facts in a two thousand twenty-five controlled study. Models often generalize narrowly from fine-tuning, failing even simple reversals of relations they were taught.

In-context learning shows different inductive biases, so the team built clean data sets isolating new knowledge from pretraining. Models absorbed controlled information either through context or through finetuning, then faced tests demanding several kinds of generalization. Data-matched, in-context learning generalized more flexibly in most cases, with some qualifications. Adding in-context thinking traces to finetuning data improved fine-tuning's generalization across splits and benchmarks, a useful takeaway.
arxiv-2505-02461:
Hua Chen studies interacting electrons on a honeycomb lattice in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. The lattice hosts Dirac fermions, particles that move as if massless near two valley points. Chen adds p-orbital states and interactions at half filling. In weak coupling, interactions open a gap by ordering the orbitals. The system becomes a quantum anomalous Hall insulator, a phase that conducts along its edges.

At mid-strength coupling, a surprise appears: coherence between the two valleys, with a tripled repeating pattern. This phase links to an orbital exchange model of the strong-coupling Mott state. Quantum fluctuations around it birth new excitations the author calls orbitons. The paper maps how one lattice can host several exotic phases.
arxiv-2505-07061:
Wenbin Lu reviews how disks of gas evolve after a black hole tears a star apart. His review, from twenty twenty-five, covers tidal disruption events. The shredded star's gas falls back and forms a disk around the hole. That disk's life sets the light curve that telescopes watch.

One focus is a heat-driven flip that makes the disk switch between thick and thin states. It may flip back and forth more than once. A second focus is how fresh falling gas crashes into the disk already there. Late X-ray data clash with the standard story in places. Lu weighs fixes that might save the model.
arxiv-2505-07461:
Onur Ayberk Çakmak and Özgür Sarıoğlu give a method to find Chern-Simons potentials in two thousand twenty-five. The potentials come from Pontryagin densities, which are tied to Chern characters. The work holds in any even dimension. They use a general link rule that allows twist and stretch in the geometry.

Such freedom lets the Chern characters be non-zero, so the densities do not vanish. The authors lay out steps that take a density as input and give the potential as output. They also supply code that runs the steps. The result is a clean, general way to do a task that was once done case by case.
arxiv-2505-07561:
Liu, Milić, Castellanos Durán, Borrero, van Noort, and Kuckein wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names shown as initials in the byline. It maps the fine magnetic weave of a solar plage, a patch of strong upright field on the Sun.

A new integral field unit on a Swedish solar scope caught the patch at fine scale, fast pace, and high spectral truth in two iron lines. An inversion that respects magnetohydrostatic balance rebuilt the field in three dimensions. The main field is strong and spreads wide with height. Beneath it sit weak, tiny loops of the opposed sign, rooted in the surface. The picture reshapes how such patches are thought to convect.
arxiv-2505-07861:
Harry Dong, Bilge Acun, Beidi Chen, and Yuejie Chi present Caprese in 2025, a fix for AI models slowed down by long math reasoning. Tricks that speed up these models often wreck their math skill. Their fix teaches the fast model to regain what it lost, a process called distillation.

Caprese adds only about one percent of new parts and trains them on a small set of made-up examples. The original weights stay untouched. In tests on well-known models, math skill came back almost in full, while word tasks stayed sound. The models also ran with far fewer active parts and answered a bit faster and shorter. The authors offer it as a cheap way to keep reasoning strong at lower cost.
arxiv-2505-08361:
Xinyue Wang and Biwei Huang present WM3C, a reinforcement learning setup that generalizes to unseen environments by recombining causal components, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Agents usually fail when new environments change the dynamics they trained on.

People handle novelty by reconfiguring known parts, and WM3C copies that plan. Language guides the decomposition of the latent space into meaningful, composable causal components, with theoretical guarantees for finding them under mild assumptions. The use uses a masked autoencoder with mutual information constraints and adaptive sparsity. In model runs and real robotic manipulation tasks, WM3C finds latent processes better, learns stronger policies, and transfers to unseen tasks more reliably than prior methods.
arxiv-2505-09761:
Temfack and Wyse tracked epidemics in real time in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Health officials need estimates that update as case counts arrive, not after the fact. Their method runs a squared sequential Monte Carlo scheme in online form. A particle filter updates parameters using only a recent window of data.

A Metropolis-Hastings kernel keeps the target distribution intact while the window slides. Simulated outbreaks first confirmed the method's accuracy. The team then applied it to Ireland's COVID-19 records. It followed the epidemic's course and estimated the time-varying reproduction number well. Costs fell sharply versus processing the full history each time. The authors pitch it for live surveillance.
arxiv-2505-10561:
Zehan Wang and ten co-authors improve text-to-audio generation by scoring its basic skills with automated feedback. Current models handle simple sounds but often miss events in complex prompts or produce poor acoustic quality. Human preference tuning is hard to gather at scale for audio.

Their scoring pipelines check three things: whether every named event actually occurs, whether events arrive in the described order, and overall sound quality. These scores matched human judgments better than existing metrics. With them, the team built a preference dataset of tens of thousands of prompts and hundreds of thousands of clips. Training on that feedback targets prompt-following and fidelity together.
arxiv-2505-12261:
Hanchen Wang and a large team present OpenPros in two thousand twenty-five. OpenPros is a data set for prostate ultrasound computed tomography. The method rebuilds tissue traits like speed of sound from waves. Few angle views and bone warps make prostate scans hard.

Models come from clinical scans and dozens of real specimens. Hundreds of thousands of paired maps and wave records fill the set. Wave runs use set clinical layouts and open solvers. Learning methods beat physics routes on speed and accuracy in tests. Broad skill and fine detail still lag, the team notes. The set is public.
arxiv-2505-13061:
Chengtang Yao and five colleagues show that machines, like people, fall for 3D visual illusions. Painted perspective can make a flat surface look deep to human eyes. The team asks whether depth-estimating software gets fooled the same way. That matters for robots and cars that must judge real distances.

They built a large test set of illusion scenes, with hundreds of thousands of images. Top methods for one-eye, two-eye, and multi-view depth all failed on it. Each read painted depth as real depth in case after case. The authors then built a fix that borrows common sense from a vision-language model. It blends the two eyes' depth with one eye's reading, weighted by plausibility. Their method topped the field on the new benchmark. The work gives vision research a shared yardstick for illusion robustness.
arxiv-2505-13161:
Kyosuke Sato and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on the star birth past of the Ursa Minor dwarf galaxy. Deep wide shots from a big telescope on Hawaii feed the work. A new algorithm fits the color and brightness chart of the stars. It blends a genetic search with a cooling based fit to match fake charts built from star models.

Two star groups show up, spread far from the galaxy's heart. One is richer in iron and began to form stars later than the poor one. Both groups shift in mix with span from the center, but not in age. The past was more tangled than the plain tale told for dwarf galaxies.
arxiv-2505-13561:
Rothschild wrote an essay in two thousand twenty-five on what language models reveal about language and thought. Daniel Dennett once speculated that adding language to a mind changes it so deeply that mind with and without language may differ in kind. Modern AI, the essay argues, amounts to a test of that thesis.

Language models trained on text alone show real, if limited, skill at inference across many domains. Rothschild credits the abstract, compact way language encodes information, which makes inference cheap enough to run. In his slogan, language makes inference computationally tractable. He then asks what that implies for human minds.
arxiv-2505-15561:
Florin Cuconasu and four co-authors asked in twenty twenty-five whether retrieval-augmented AI systems truly suffer from position bias. Such systems fetch text passages and place them in a prompt for a language model. Models are known to weigh text near the start or end of a prompt more than text in the middle, which could skew answers.

Across three benchmarks, the team found a different problem dominates. Top retrieval tools pull in highly distracting passages for most queries, placing them near the top. Since good and bad passages alike get shuffled by position effects, the net harm from position bias is small in real use. Rearranging passages to suit the model's bias did no better than random order. The fix, they imply, lies in better retrieval, not better ordering.
arxiv-2505-17461:
Kazuki Hayashi and four co-authors test vision-language models on color blindness in a 2025 paper. These models are entering navigation, education, and accessibility work, where users see the world differently. The team used the classic dotted-plate test for color vision deficiency as a controlled probe. They checked what models generate, how confident they are, and what their internal features encode.

Models knew facts about the deficiency and could describe the test well. Yet they failed to reproduce what affected people actually see, defaulting to normal color perception instead. The authors warn that current systems cannot represent alternative visual experience, which matters for inclusive deployment.
arxiv-2505-18561:
Shiu-hong Kao, Yu-Wing Tai, and Chi-Keung Tang present a study from twenty twenty-five on picking out objects in video from veiled text prompts. A user may name a thing in a roundabout way that shifts with time. Past tools fine-tune big vision language models, yet they trip on such time bound prompts. Their frame, CoT-RVS, uses step by step thought at test time.

For each frame, the frame names things that could fit the prompt in sense. It then picks a key frame where each thing shows most clear. No training is needed, so closed models can drive it. The frame can swap its target mid stream when a better one shows. Tests on plain and veiled prompts beat past tools by clear gaps.
arxiv-2505-18761:
Minglai Yang and five co-authors ask how irrelevant context distracts language model reasoning in two thousand twenty-five. Their benchmark, GSM-DC, grows grade school math with planted distractors. Symbolic reasoning graphs let each distractor land in a set spot. Tests can thus be strict and repeatable across models.

Models proved sensitive to the planted noise in their tests. Both path choice and arithmetic accuracy took hits. Training with strong distractors lifted scores in and out of distribution. A stepwise tree search with a process reward helped more. Out of distribution strength gained the most from that search.
arxiv-2505-20161:
Jaehun Jung and colleagues measure training data diversity by what it does to the model, not by how varied it looks. Diversity drives generalization, yet surface heuristics for it miss the mark. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran hundreds of controlled training runs. Diversity proved a strong predictor of performance on unseen reasoning tests. Their new metric scores a data set by the entropy of the gradients it induces in a small proxy model. It correlated tightly with out-of-distribution success on inference and math tasks, beating alternative measures.

The companion framework generates synthetic data aimed at underrepresented regions of that gradient space. Models trained on the prismatic output kept improving as synthetic data scaled. Gains showed on familiar tests and on unseen ones. The paper reframes data curation as gradient coverage.
arxiv-2505-20961:
Yiyuan Yang, Shitong Xu, Niki Trigoni, and Andrew Markham present a framework for locating sound sources in three dimensions with fewer microphones and less computation. Their paper came out in 2025. Finding where a sound comes from matters for robots and smart spaces, but current methods are costly and need precise calibration.

Their design uses sparse cross-attention, pre-training, and adaptive measures of how well signals agree across microphones. It can even use microphones whose positions are unknown, estimating those positions alongside the source. Early experiments show it scales to several sources at once without extra hardware.
