The authors aim for a better balance between accuracy, efficiency, and robustness in messy real-world settings.
arxiv-2505-22761:
Sophiya, Nair, Maleki, and Krishnababu present a survey from twenty twenty-five on physics-informed neural networks. Such networks solve differential equations by baking physics laws into training. The field is young and lacks shared standards for wider uptake. Prior surveys cover only slices, like single uses or shallow overviews. This survey spans architecture, variants, uses, and challenges in one place. It adds performance analysis across equations and application domains. Real-world use cases illustrate where the method stands today.

The authors detail current implementation hurdles in depth. They close with future research directions for the field. Their stated aim is to bridge gaps in the existing survey literature. The overview targets both newcomers and active researchers in the area.
arxiv-2506-00761:
Jack Lawless, Andrew Hazel, and Anne Juel wrote a physics paper in 2025 on the oscillatory dynamics of a Saffman-Taylor finger with a bubble at its tip. In the experiments, air is driven into a thin channel filled with liquid, and a finger of air grows into the fluid. The researchers placed a small air bubble at the tip of the finger, extending earlier laboratory work with a systematic investigation.

The system can behave steadily or oscillate from side to side, depending on flow rate and bubble size. Oscillations begin when the bubble grows large enough that the curvature of its tip matches the curvature of the finger tip. At that point the driving pressure fades, and sideways disturbances can grow. At high flow rates, the oscillations give way to disordered meandering of the tip. A large enough bubble can take over as the tip and end the oscillations.
arxiv-2506-00861:
Parismita Gogoi and eight co-authors detect dementia from speech by analyzing its long-term rhythm. Their paper came out in 2025. Speech rhythm changes as dementia progresses, and rhythm formant analysis extracts slow patterns of loudness and frequency movement over whole utterances.

The team turned those patterns into rhythm spectrograms, picture-like summaries they fed to classifiers in two ways. Hand-crafted summary features beat a standard speech feature set by a clear margin on classification accuracy. A second approach fused the rhythm pictures with image and language models. It also improved on the baselines, with rhythm pictures outperforming ordinary sound spectrograms. The work suggests the slow rhythm of speech carries real diagnostic signal.
arxiv-2506-04261:
Cédric Simenel reviews, in a fresh second form, the quantum many-body theory of how atomic nuclei move and crash. The review is from two thousand twenty-five.

Since the first form, more compute has opened new uses of mean-field ways and past them. Pair links can now be treated as they move, which has fed work on swap, fusion, and split reactions. A new part treats how nuclei split in two. The review sums up fresh work with true micro quantum tools. It draws the core mean-field equation from a classic rule of least cost. A stretch of it adds small quantum swings, in a form kin to a known wave method.
arxiv-2506-05061:
Anh Le, Thanh Lam, and Dung Nguyen surveyed Vietnamese document recognition in a 2025 paper. Reading Vietnamese text by machine is unusually hard: stacked diacritics and tone marks crowd each syllable, large labeled datasets are scarce, and real documents vary wildly in layout and quality. Classic optical character recognition falters on those marks, while deep learning models hunger for the very data that is missing.

The survey reviews existing methods, catalogs their limits, and examines how large language and vision-language models could change the field. Future directions include building datasets, adapting models across domains, fusing text with layout and image cues, and cutting computation cost. Better Vietnamese document tools would speed digitization across government and business.
arxiv-2506-05661:
Aguiló-Vidal, Arenas-Carmona, and Saavedra-Lagos wrote in twenty twenty-five about a hard counting problem in pure math. They study maps that show how a finite group acts, using whole numbers from a number field. Their tool is the Bruhat-Tits tree, a branching graph used to organize such problems. Earlier work by Arenas-Carmona and others built a theory of branches on that tree.

The authors turn that branch theory into a general plan for doing the counts step by step. They also give clear formulas for some named families of cases. Readers in number theory get both a method they can follow and worked forms they can check. The work links a graph picture to concrete results about group actions.
arxiv-2506-05761:
The BESIII Collaboration reports new results on how D mesons decay with a lepton in the final state. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. It rests on a large sample of electron-positron collision data. Semileptonic decays, where a lepton and a neutrino appear, probe the weak force cleanly. The team studies decays into a neutral kaon, a neutral pion, and a lepton.

One headline result is the first observation of the muon version of this decay. Comparing electron and muon rates tests lepton flavor universality. That principle says the weak force treats both leptons alike. The paper also gives the first angular analysis of a related decay through an excited kaon state. Such checks can expose cracks in the standard model.
arxiv-2506-05861:
Krystal Guo and Gordon Royle list every cubic graph that dodges a spectral window in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A cubic graph links each of its points to exactly three others. Its eigenvalues, read from its connection table, shape how waves and walks behave on it. The authors seek all such graphs with no eigenvalue strictly between minus two and zero. The answer is short: one thin endless family plus five lone examples.

The famous Petersen graph and the dodecahedron are among the five. The proof constrains the local shape near the shortest cycle, then splits by cycle length. One case needed computer help. Spectral graph theorists are the audience.
arxiv-2506-06661:
Zhichen Pu and Qiming Sun share ways to speed up a popular chemistry software package in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The package, PySCF, is an open-source platform for quantum chemistry. Its speed depends heavily on how tasks are set up and what hardware runs them. The authors survey practical boosts at three levels. First, they offload select modules to graphics processors.

Second, they tune key algorithms, such as starting guesses and integral handling, to cut wasted steps. Third, they apply modern Python tools, like just-in-time compiling and automatic differentiation. Together these changes raise both computing speed and researcher output. The paper is a field guide for chemists who run heavy electronic structure jobs. It shows where the biggest gains hide.
arxiv-2506-07161:
Jiancheng Wu, Qingwen Wu, and colleagues dissect the glowing gas around a quiet black hole in a 2025 astronomy study. Broad emission lines from an active galaxy's core encode the shape and motion of the gas that emits them, and in turn the mass of the central black hole. In this low-luminosity galaxy the line profiles need two pieces at once: a double-peaked part from a rotating disk and a smooth Gaussian part from less ordered gas.

A composite broad-line region explains profiles that neither piece fits alone. Getting the geometry right matters because black hole masses across surveys rest on exactly such line reading.
arxiv-2506-10161:
Yi Wang and Max Kreminski grade language models as storytellers by setting them narrative planning tasks. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that story quality is hard to score. Automatic gauges are weak, and human panels are slow and subjective. Narrative planning, a symbolic craft, names what a good story needs: sound causes, willed acts, and real conflict.

Their benchmark draws cases from literature examples. Top-tier models write causally sound tales at small scales. Intentional acts and dramatic conflict trip them up, even at those scales. Models trained with reinforcement for hard reasoning fare better there. The authors map the size where each trait breaks. Game worlds, where planned stories must hold together, are a named use for the findings.
arxiv-2506-11261:
Shizhe Chen, Ricardo Garcia, Paul Pacaud, and Cordelia Schmid introduce Gondola, a planning model for robot manipulation, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Vision-language-action models often map images and instructions straight to motor commands, which limits interpretability and robustness. Gondola instead separates high-level planning from low-level control. Given several camera views and the planning history, it predicts the next step as text instructions interleaved with segmentation masks marking target objects and goal locations.

Synthetic datasets trained the model on short-horizon grounded planning, multi-view referring expressions, and long-horizon compositional reasoning. Paired with a three-dimensional execution policy, the system reached state-of-the-art results on the GemBench benchmark and showed promising transfer to real robots. Ablations confirmed that pixel-level grounding and the planning-focused supervision drive the gains.
arxiv-2506-11861:
Devitt and co-authors build a MEMS switch screen that blocks back-flow of sound. The screen aims to aid self-noise cuts in sub-sea sound nets. Iron ring parts can't work at sub-sea sound pitch in that role. That gap leaves space cuts and code cuts as the lone paths. Their screen bends in time and space in a set beat. Small MEMS switches, tough and tight, drive that beat in the build.

The screen is a pass-band sift that runs sub-MHz in pitch. Board builds match grid sims of its wave traits well. Peak split from back flow hit 15.99 dB in the board tests. With code cuts, it could back full two-way sub-sea talk. Sense and shot work at sea stand as more use paths.
arxiv-2506-11961:
O'Donovan, Bustamante, Devauchelle, and Benham studied in twenty twenty-five how a bobbing body can ride its own waves to move. A body that bobs at the water top makes waves fore and aft. If those waves are not the same on both sides, their push can drive the body on.

They use a thin-water set-up where a pulsing press patch plays the body role. They get a rule for the push from the fore-aft wave gap. They then find best pulse shapes when the patch strength or its power is capped. Speed bands split the task in three, and they give best states for each.
arxiv-2506-12761:
Joon Soo Yoo, Taeho Kim, and Ji Won Yoon protect location privacy while answering location queries in a 2025 cryptography study. Location services need user coordinates, yet handing them to an untrusted server invites tracking and misuse. Private information retrieval lets a user fetch data without revealing what was asked, and fully homomorphic encryption lets servers compute on sealed values.

Their system, VeLoPIR, supports three modes: checking intervals, validating coordinates, and matching identifiers. Those modes cover tasks from nearby information lookup to emergency alerts. Strong encryption over a torus structure keeps the scheme fast enough for real services, the authors argue.
arxiv-2506-14961:
Griffith, Rufo, Ribeiro, and Chesi study dissipative chaos in the steady state in two thousand twenty-five. Their model is an SU(3) Bose-Hubbard trimer, open to its surroundings. Exact quantum work pairs with semiclassical Langevin dynamics in the study. Classic paths sort into fixed points, cycles, and chaos.

The sign of the Lyapunov exponent rules the quantum steady state. Calm dynamics yield Poisson level statistics in that state. Chaotic dynamics yield Wigner-Dyson statistics instead. Strong symmetries squash chaos, weak ones let it live. A phase space gauge ties entropy to the classic regime.
arxiv-2506-15061:
Wang and seven co-authors built a machine learning potential for twisted multilayer graphene in twenty twenty-five. Graphene is a one-atom-thick carbon sheet. Stacking sheets with a slight twist creates moiré patterns, large repeating designs that host rich quantum behavior.

Simulating such stacks needs fast, accurate models of atomic forces. The team created training data cleverly: they built small repeating cells fit for quantum calculations, then added twist and shift inside them. This captures all possible misalignments while keeping datasets small. An active learning loop picked the most useful new cases. Their fitted Atomic Cluster Expansion potential was tested for accuracy and robustness across simulation tasks. The authors aim to make large twisted-graphene studies practical.
arxiv-2506-16161:
Salg, Romero-López, and Jay present a Bayesian route from lattice QCD data to scattering amplitudes at real and complex energies. Lattice work gives spectra in a finite box, not amplitudes directly. Their method first rebuilds the amplitude on the real energy axis. A Nevanlinna interpolation then extends it into the complex plane. The approach avoids fixing one formula form in advance. Uncertainty from that choice folds into the result itself.

Tests used both toy data and real lattice datasets. Resonant systems from two collaborations served as proving grounds. The method suits multi-hadron scattering, where resonances hide off the real axis. It gives lattice teams a less biased bridge to physics.
arxiv-2506-16961:
Haina Qin and seven co-authors restore damaged images by running decay backwards in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Diffusion models fix photos by wandering through noise, which is slow and complex. Their method, ResFlow, treats damage as a smooth, fixed path instead of random steps. An extra helper process clears up the guesswork about the lost detail. The flow keeps entropy steady along its route.

The model learns by matching the speed field of that path. Restoration finishes in under four sampling steps, far fewer than rivals. Quality rises while compute falls. Fast, sharp restoration matters for phones, archives, and medical scans alike. The paper serves the image processing community. Its core idea may transfer to other inverse problems.
arxiv-2506-17161:
Pérez-Maroto and co-authors measure neutron capture rates on two chromium isotopes at a CERN facility, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Reactor safety benchmarks lean on these rates, yet past evaluations disagreed by up to thirty percent. Time-of-flight runs with low-noise detectors and thin enriched samples covered the key energy band.

Dozens of resonances were resolved for each isotope, with accuracy inside the target range set by an international request list. Cross sections were compared against earlier data and models. The new values do not back a recent proposed rise in both rates. The authors call for fresh evaluations built on their data.
arxiv-2506-20061:
Zhang and co-authors teach task-follow acts by re-tags from big word tools. Task-follow skill in play-learn needs vast hand-tagged task sets. Thin prize marks add more strain to that learn path. Their way lets big word tools tag past paths with new tasks. Tools look back at failed runs and name sub-tasks the aide did. Those names turn flops in rich train facts for the aide.

Re-tags thus cut the need for hand marks by a wide span. One joint act plan learns to heed a wide task range. Tests run in Craftax, a hard play world for such aides. Gains show in pace, task span, and whole act scores. Those gains beat top peer plans in the same world runs. The work backs re-tags as a cheap path to broad skill.
arxiv-2506-21961:
Junho Myung and co-workers at KAIST built a benchmark probing the motivational values of large text models in a 2025 paper. Their PapersPlease test casts each model as an immigration inspector deciding whether to approve or deny entry to people described in short personal narratives. The stories are built from the Existence, Relatedness, and Growth theory of human needs. Ranks needs from basic survival up through relationships to personal growth, across some three thousand seven hundred moral dilemmas.

Six models showed statistically large patterns in their approvals, evidence they encode implicit priority orderings among needs. Weaving social identities into the stories shifted outcomes unevenly, with some models denying marginalized identities more often. The data set is public for further probing.
arxiv-2506-22461:
Chuan Li and Ruoxuan Yang build a machine learning system in 2025 for managing groundwater. Groundwater feeds farms, ecosystems, and drinking water, yet monitoring is hard due to sparse data and slow traditional methods. Their system predicts water level classes from climate data, weather and water records, and land features.

The team trained the system on a large French data set with over three million records from more than fifteen hundred wells. Scores were strong on validation data and lower on later test data, which reflects how conditions change over time. Scenario tests showed the system could support early warnings and decisions about water allocation. The code is open source for wider use.
arxiv-2506-23761:
Nazarenko maps the states of a dark matter model in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The model treats ultralight dark matter as a self-gravitating Bose-Einstein condensate with an axionlike self-interaction. Phase diagrams sort the states as stable, metastable, or unstable, across a range of amplitudes. The interaction proves to destabilize low amplitudes, giving an imaginary speed of sound there.

In one high-amplitude band, the dark matter rests in a stable state that can form a dense solitonic core and calm quantum fluctuations in the halo round it. Thermodynamic sums for the dwarf galaxy NGC 2366 back the picture. So do sums for made-up cases, which show a first-order phase shift in part of the range. Once a dense core hits about twelve percent of the mass, gravity makes the halo stable. In NGC 2366, that part is put at about nineteen percent of the mass.
arxiv-2507-01461:
Kyrama and Gounaris wrote in twenty twenty-five about event processing systems that must handle events arriving out of order. Complex event processing scans streams for patterns in real time. Late, duplicate, and disordered events are common at the edge, where small devices gather mixed data. Their system, LimeCEP, mixes three strategies: lazy, buffering, and speculative processing. A messaging platform helps order events and remove duplicates. Users can tune settings to trade accuracy, delay, and resource use.

Tests compared LimeCEP with two leading systems under heavy disorder. It answered with far lower delay, in some cases by orders of magnitude. Memory and processor use were also several times lower. Accuracy stayed near perfect on precision and recall measures. The authors present it as a fit for non-cloud deployments. Edge analytics need exactly that mix of speed and frugality.
arxiv-2507-03761:
Celso França and five co-authors improve extreme multi-label text classification by fusing the rankings of different retrievers. Assigning labels from a huge vocabulary runs into a long tail: a few head labels cover most documents, while countless tail labels appear rarely. Any single method tends to serve one end of that split.

Sparse retrievers like BM25 match words precisely, while dense retrievers over embeddings capture meaning and generalize to rare labels. Rank-based fusion merges their ordered lists, keeping exact-match strength for head labels and semantic reach for the tail. The authors develop fusion algorithms aimed at lifting effectiveness across both groups at once. The work targets applications from product tagging to document indexing.
arxiv-2507-04161:
Martin Mosny, Joseph Conlon, and Edmund Copeland study scalar fields that roll on a slope whose pull fades in a set way, with no other fluid in the cosmos. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

They show such a field can track itself: its own small waves act as a bath of light-like stuff in the back. Clean math and grid runs both back the claim. The team turns to string-based cosmos tales, where the field roams far in the span from first growth to the birth of light atoms. They work out how big the first waves must be to keep the field from overshooting its mark.
arxiv-2507-05061:
Jena and nine co-authors report a spin liquid candidate in twenty twenty-five. The material is a frustrated magnet where chromium ions sit on a pyrochlore-like network. Competing interactions prevent the spins from settling into order. Such systems can host exotic low-energy excitations instead of frozen magnetism.

The team used thermodynamics, resonance, muon, and neutron scattering probes. No magnetic order or spin freezing appeared down to a tiny fraction of a kelvin. That is striking given the strong exchange coupling between the spins. Below that coupling's energy scale, short-range antiferromagnetic correlations emerged in every probe. Diffuse neutron scattering confirmed the pattern. Readers meet a three-dimensional quantum magnet that refuses to order, as spin liquids promise.
arxiv-2507-06461:
Risi Jaiswal, Supriyo Datta, and Joseph Makin wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It trains neural networks with a forward-forward method built for binary, coin-flipping units, aiming to slash the energy cost of learning.

The standard training method, backpropagation, is awkward for custom hardware because it stores every step and runs backward. Forward-forward training avoids that, but its heavy step is matrix multiplication. Making units binary turns those multiplications into simple table lookups. Randomness in the units, plus shared weights with varied biases, restores the information flow that binary units would choke. The authors note that probabilistic bits, tiny unstable magnets, can do the random sampling almost for free. On image benchmarks, accuracy neared the full-precision version while estimated energy fell about tenfold.
arxiv-2507-08261:
Ivolgina, Fletcher, and Vemuri applied Stein shrinkage to batch normalization in neural networks in twenty twenty-five. Batch normalization rescales each layer's values using the batch mean and spread, steadying training. Shrinkage estimators, which pull estimates slightly toward a center, can beat raw sample values in accuracy.

The authors prove the shrinkage versions of mean and variance dominate the standard ones even under adversarial attacks modeled with light-tailed noise. Their James-Stein version also has a smaller sensitivity constant, implying smoother, more robust behavior. Tests covered image classification on CIFAR-10, a 3D network on brain imaging data, and segmentation on city scenes, with and without attacks. They report top performance, supporting shrinkage as a drop-in improvement.
arxiv-2507-10361:
Jan Krause and Nino Walenta refined the counting model for single-photon detectors in a 2025 paper. These diodes click when one photon arrives, then go blind briefly while they recover. Standard models assume sensitivity snaps back instantly after the blind time, which overstates how many photons the device catches at high rates and skews measurements in bright conditions.

Their model lets sensitivity recover gradually, following an exponential curve with one extra parameter, framed through non-homogeneous Poisson statistics. It predicts counts deep into saturation far better than the step model, and an extension covers extreme flux where the detector stalls. One timing histogram now yields sensitivity, blind time, and recovery time together, simplifying lab calibration.
arxiv-2507-11961:
Pascal Kettmann, Jesse Heyninck, and Hannes Strass showed in twenty twenty-five that two core meanings of fuzzy logic programs fit inside one known framework. Fuzzy logic programs reason with degrees of truth rather than plain true and false, which suits uncertain data. Over the years, several rival meanings, called semantics, have grown up for such programs.

The authors rebuild the stable model and well-founded semantics inside approximation fixpoint theory, a general theory of how meanings can be approached step by step. This widens that theory from two truth values to many. It also lets a stock of known results transfer to fuzzy programs at once. As first uses, they compare existing semantics, extend the idea of layered programs, and define sharper variants.
arxiv-2507-12661:
Pardha Sai Krishna Ala and co-workers learned the noise stats of vehicle state estimators from data in a 2025 paper. Kalman-style filters that track a ground vehicle's state are only as good as their process and reading covariance matrices. Usually hand-picked by an experienced designer, and a bad pick degrades accuracy or even diverges the filter. Tuning over innovation sequences is the classic remedy, but learning methods promise to read the noise character straight from recorded actions.

The authors present a learning methodology with several loss functions for identifying those stochastic characteristics, aimed at Army ground vehicle models. Approaches are tested for real-time state estimation. Automating the tuning removes a craft narrow point in deploying estimators to new platforms.
arxiv-2507-13761:
Palash Nandi, Maithili Joshi, and Tanmoy Chakraborty examine the role of skip connections when visual language models are jailbroken in a 2025 security study. Small prompt changes can flip a model from refusing harmful content to producing it. The authors ask which prompt ingredients drive successful attacks on models that read images and text together.

Three factors are tested: detailed visual information, adversarial examples, and a third prompt component. Their analysis connects attack success to the model's internal skip connections, pathways that carry early information forward. Knowing which parts of the network enable jailbreaks helps defenders harden the right places instead of patching prompts one by one.
arxiv-2507-15761:
Zheng and a team including Peng and Liu built a team of smart agents in twenty twenty-five to cut waste in smart contracts. Such contracts run on their own on a chain once set, and each step costs a fee called gas. Waste forms in code are oft found by hand, which is slow and hard to scale.

Four agents split the work: seek, dream up, run, and lead the loop. On one hundred real contracts the team fixed most, with near ten parts in a hundred saved on set-up fees. On five hundred made-up contracts from chat models it fixed most too. Each part of the loop was checked on its own.
arxiv-2507-17761:
Kalo and co-authors sketch an assistant that builds AI explanations together with its user in this 2025 vision paper. Modern AI systems chain many components and data sources, so their outputs are hard to explain. Provenance records, which trace where data came from, could ground explanations.

Raw provenance is usually far too detailed for a person to use. The authors propose an interactive agent that questions the records with the user and shapes an explanation both useful and grounded. They present an early prototype of the agent. They also present a scalable test framework that simulates users and uses a language model as judge. The work sets an agenda rather than reporting a finished system.
arxiv-2507-18061:
Zehan Li and eleven co-authors built TELEVAL in twenty twenty-five. It is a test set for spoken language models in Chinese conversation. Voice models must chat in a natural way. They must do more than finish tasks. Yet most tests grade semantic correctness in tidy settings. TELEVAL runs free, audio-led scenarios with no instructions.

It grades two things. One is how well a model gives the right content. That is tested when sound and speech vary a lot. The other is fit: do replies suit the sounds heard and the social moment? Models did well on content. They fell off when sound varied and in live chat. The authors name a flaw that kept coming back, the Caption Trap. The model describes the audio. It does not reply to it. The test set aims at the gap between skill at transcription and skill at real talk.
arxiv-2507-18661:
Ruixing Zhang, Yang Zhang, Tongyu Zhu, Leilei Sun, and Weifeng Lv predict the next GPS location from visual maps in two thousand twenty-five. People guess a next stop by picturing the path on a map. They read road links and motion trends by eye. Most past models never reason over a map at all.

Their first test checks if a stock vision language model can reason from a drawn map. A two stage model then learns road and path structure by fine tuning. Reinforcement from map feedback lets it self improve from there. Tests in four cities gave top scores. Cross city skill beat rival language model methods.
arxiv-2507-19061:
Alice Tarzariol, Marco Maratea, and Mauro Vallati attacked traffic light timing in 2025 with logic programming. Cities must choose how long each signal stays green across a network. And the best prior answers used machine-run planning in a language called PDDL+, which struggles to state optimization goals and to compute truly optimal plans.

The authors instead encode the problem in Constraint Answer Set Programming, a logic formalism extended with constraints, and solve it with an established solver built on that method. They benchmarked on real historical traffic data from Huddersfield in the United Kingdom, weighing against the strongest PDDL+ model for the task. Their method boosted on the quality of the planning answers, showing that the logic-based encoding is a credible other route to better signal timing.
arxiv-2508-00061:
Ciavarella, Hariprakash, Halimeh, and Bauer present a paper from twenty twenty-five on truncation errors in quantum simulations of gauge theories. Putting gauge fields on quantum computers forces cutting each link's state space. Those cuts cause errors versus the exact theory. In the electric basis, large fields turn out to be rarely excited. The team build a method to size the resulting errors. The error falls factorially as the cut grows, they show. Tests cover a classic model and a pure gauge theory.

Their error bounds beat earlier estimates by an enormous factor. Reasonable settings make the cuts safe for accurate runs. The work helps plan trustworthy quantum simulations of particle physics. It turns a feared error source into a bounded one.
arxiv-2508-01461:
Soumyabrata Paul and four co-authors train a machine to draw and read picture-like maps of quantum states of light. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. These maps, called optical tomograms, can be treated as patterns. A generative network learns to copy the patterns for several basic states of light.

Training ran until the gap between real and drawn patterns shrank to a low, steady level. From the drawn maps the team pulled out photon counts and spread measures directly. Those values told apart states that look much alike, with no extra sorting network. Checks with two error models and varied color schemes held up. The method also matched trends seen in a recent lab study of boosted light states. It points to faster state checks for quantum optics labs.
arxiv-2508-02761:
Eunsu Hur wrote a solo mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on the slopes of modular forms. Modular forms are highly symmetric functions central to number theory. Their slopes form sequences that show puzzling patterns, and a conjecture known as the ghost conjecture aims to explain the structure behind them.

Hur gives an algorithm that computes the whole slope sequence for forms with fixed Galois components from just its first few entries. The method builds on recent results about the ghost conjecture and sharpens an older conjecture on these sequences. The patterns may also explain hidden symmetries seen in certain curves that organize modular forms.
arxiv-2508-02961:
Boshi Huang and Fabio Nonato de Paula wrote a computer security paper in two thousand twenty-five on defending chatbots from prompt injection. In such attacks, hostile text hidden in the input tricks the model into ignoring its rules. Most defenses bolt on an outside classifier to screen the traffic.

Their defense instead uses the model's own reasoning as a kind of self-consciousness. Added modules let the model judge and regulate its own outputs. They tested the method on seven leading models and two attack data sets. Defense success rose sharply across the board, and an enhanced mode reached near-perfect blocking on some models.
arxiv-2508-03561:
Richard Fitzpatrick models how fast the current in a tokamak can be raised or lowered with safety. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A tokamak holds hot plasma in a ring with a strong toroidal current. Faraday's law of induction caps how fast that current can change.

His simple model gives least safe ramp times for three known machines, JET, SPARC, and ITER. The JET value matches what operators see in practice. The SPARC and ITER least times sit below the ramp times in their designs, so the designs look workable, against a recent claim. Field ratios in the new machines also sit below JET's, which hints they can dodge runaway electrons as JET did.
arxiv-2508-04661:
Marco Bertola extends a classic approximation problem to curved surfaces of higher genus in two thousand twenty-five. The Chebotarev problem asks for the smallest shape, in a capacity sense, that ties a set of points on the plane. Moving it to a doughnut-like Riemann surface, with holes, bends the rules.

A fit notion of capacity must first be built, following earlier work by Chirka and by Bertola with partners. The surface's loops force an extra choice: which homotopy class, which winding family, the tying shape should follow. Ties to Jenkins-Strebel quadratic differentials, a tool from surface geometry, are also drawn. The aim is groundwork for Padé approximation on algebraic curves.
arxiv-2508-05561:
Jean Alexandre and Emilio Meryn wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It derives the phase a neutral scalar particle picks up as it travels near a charged black hole, a Reissner-Nordström object, when two flavors take split paths that cross.

Gravity lenses the paths, and the two flavors interfere where they meet. The hole's charge barely bends the metric, yet it shifts the phase pattern by a clear step next to the plain Schwarzschild case. The pattern holds two oscillation lengths. If both were read, each flavor's eigen mass could be found on its own. The work links flavor physics to curved space in a testable way.
arxiv-2508-08161:
A large international collaboration reports a precision test of quantum electrodynamics using exotic atoms of neon, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In these atoms, a heavy kaon replaces an electron and orbits the neon nucleus, letting physicists probe bound-state theory at middling nuclear charge.

The team calculated the energies of the light these atoms emit using the Dirac-Fock method. For the strongest line, their value lands almost exactly on a recent measurement made by the SIDDHART(H)A-2 experiment. The match holds to within a fraction of an electron volt out of about nine thousand four hundred fifty. A shift from bound-state quantum electrodynamics forms a clear part of that energy, far larger than the measurement's error bars. Because theory and experiment agree so closely, the result firmly tests this corner of quantum theory.
arxiv-2508-08261:
Elvin Rada extends fixed point theory for set-valued maps into cone metric spaces, carrying a weaker notion of contraction along. A multivalued map sends each point to a set of candidates; a fixed point is one that its own image contains. Berinde's weak contractions relax the usual shrinking demand while keeping fixed points reachable. Cone metrics replace real distances with vectors ordered by a cone in a Banach space.

Rada proves existence and uniqueness results for such maps under weak contractive conditions, using the geometry of normal cones. Iterative schemes approximate the fixed points with explicit convergence rates. Stability of the fixed point sets is analyzed as well. Applications to differential inclusions and variational inequalities close the paper. The contribution is a toolkit: analysts facing set-valued weak contractions in generalized spaces now have theorems with rates, not just existence.
arxiv-2508-08361:
Banik and Bhattacharjee build a theory for how hot plasmas settle when waves and fields act together, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Plasmas near the sun hold many fast particles that do not fit a simple bell curve. The authors seek a shared rule for how electron and ion speeds spread out. Their theory tracks slow relaxation driven by large fields.

Both electrons and ions settle toward the same tail shape. Speed counts fall as the fifth power of speed in that tail. Large fields speed up fast, unscreened particles but leave slow ones alone. In the sun's outer layer, that tail lets fast particles escape gravity. Escaped particles leave hotter gas behind, which may explain why that layer is so hot.
arxiv-2508-09861:
Muhammed Shafeeque, Arun Mathew, and Malay Nandy model ultra-heavy neutron stars in a modified gravity theory in a 2025 study. Starobinsky gravity adds a squared curvature term to Einstein's equations, changing how matter and gravity balance inside a star. The stellar matter is hybrid: a quark core described by a simple bag model, wrapped in hadronic layers from established equations of state.

The construction keeps signals at or below light speed throughout the star, preserving causality. Modified field equations then give the star's structure and maximum mass. Such supermassive models test whether modified gravity can support the heaviest neutron stars astronomers observe.
arxiv-2508-14961:
Yuto Nakajima, Umang Mehta, and Hart Goldman develop a theory of exotic particle gases in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Anyons are particles in two-dimensional systems whose statistics fall between bosons and fermions. Recent experiments on two-dimensional materials moving between fractional quantum anomalous Hall phases and other correlated states have made anyon dynamics newly urgent. The authors treat the dilute, weakly interacting regime at finite temperature.

Their central result is economical. From a minimal set of universal braiding and fusion data, plus the hierarchy of anyon energy gaps, one can build the gas's distribution function. Its thermodynamic observables then follow. The engine is an exclusion principle expressed as a constraint on fusion outcomes of physical states. The framework unifies and streamlines earlier results across itinerant anyon models, from solvable lattice Hamiltonians to large-N field theories.
arxiv-2508-18561:
Janisiow, Kochanczyk, Zielinski, and Danel propose counterfactual masking to explain chemical models in twenty twenty-five. Models that predict the traits of molecules guide the search for new drugs and new materials. Tools that explain such models point to the parts of a molecule that drive a prediction. Many of those tools mask atoms, and that step creates molecules that could not exist.

Their method swaps a masked part for a fragment that could occur. A generative model picks the fragment so the molecule stays chemically sound. The team then judges the result against real molecules of that kind, not against a blanked out baseline. That keeps the account in line with the data the model was trained on. The swapped versions also show how a change in structure may shift the trait in question. Tests across data sets gave insights that chemists can act on in design work.
arxiv-2508-20161:
Christoph Bartsch and co-authors unveiled a new shape-based object in 2025 that encodes string theory scattering heights. Positive shapes are shapes whose edges compute particle contact heights. Their associahedral grid does this for the inverse KLT kernel of string theory, catching the full dependence on the string tension setting for a scalar theory. For pions in a nonlinear sigma model. And for mixed heights of the two.

As the tension setting shrinks to zero, the geometry returns the normal field theory heights, as it must. Along the way it displays the endless tower of resonances that distinguishes stringy heights from rational field theory ones. A recently offered kinematic shift relating the scalar and pion theories emerges naturally as the geometry's leading contribution, showing the grid geometrizes a link before seen only algebraically.
arxiv-2508-21261:
Hossein KhademSohi, Hadi Hemmati, Jiayu Zhou, and Steve Drew score each client in shared learning at low cost. Shared training pools data from lots of clients and keeps raw data home. Fair pay and smart client picks both need scores of what each client adds. The Shapley value is the fair yard-stick. But its true cost grows at a wild rate with client count.

Their frame, FedOwen, uses Owen sampling to near the Shapley scores. It spends the same test funds as past plans and keeps the miss small. A pick rule that adapts blends two pulls: use clients known to help, and probe clients tried too little. Bias falls a lot. Rare but rich data comes to light. On tests where clients' data did not match in kind, end scores ran up to 23% high. That lead came in the same count of rounds as past best plans.
arxiv-2509-00061:
Ekansh Singh, working alone, designs and tests a low-cost thrust vector control gimbal for model rockets in 2025. Thrust vector control steers a rocket by tilting its motor, a key means to keep flight stable. Standard builds are pricey and hard for students and hobbyists to make. The gimbal here is 3D-printed and driven by small servo motors on two axes.

More than sixty design rounds shaped the part, with servo choice guided by torque, response speed, and stability. A high-speed camera and design sims probed tilt range, response, and strength. Tilt stays stable within five degrees, with response near forty-five thousandths of a second. Servo wear and pin stress limit long runs. The work shows students can build real steering gear cheaply.
arxiv-2509-00161:
Jon Nelson and Daniel Gottesman settle the complexity of the rotation-invariant Hamiltonian problem in 2025. The local Hamiltonian problem asks for the lowest energy state of a system built from local terms, a core question in quantum computing theory. Here the terms sit on a lattice and stay the same under shifts and rotations of that lattice.

The one-dimensional case was known to be complete for a class called QMA_EXP, which captures very hard quantum checks. Nelson and Gottesman prove the same completeness when lattice dimension is fixed but length scales. Their result answers an open question from 2013 by Gottesman and Irani. It maps a broad range where such symmetric systems stay computationally hard.
arxiv-2509-00561:
Yuwen Pu leads seven authors in total, with Zhou Feng, Chunyi Zhou, Jiahao Chen, Chunqiang Hu, Haibo Hu, and Shouling Ji, in defending voices against synthesis attacks. Attackers can copy a short clip of a victim's speech and fake new statements in that voice, a risk made cheaper by zero-shot voice conversion, methods that need no retraining.

Pu and his co-authors propose FreeTalk, a lightweight plug-and-play defense that adds a frequency-domain perturbation, a small change spread across sound frequencies, to speech in a black-box setting. Data augmentation, varied training examples, noise smoothing, and a universal perturbation per speaker improve robustness and lower user cost. Tests across many synthesis, verification, and recognition models show strong protection with good sound quality.
arxiv-2509-00661:
Jose Manuel Alcalde-Llergo leads six authors in total, with Aurora Ruiz-Mezcua, Rocio Avila-Ramirez, Andrea Zingoni, Juri Taborri, and Enrique Yeguas-Bolivar, in automatically identifying and describing jewelry. Precise jewelry descriptions usually require industry experts, yet translators and interpreters often need accurate detail about unfamiliar pieces.

Alcalde-Llergo and his co-authors use computer vision and neural networks to detect jewels in images and generate natural language descriptions at three levels of detail, imitating expert analysis. They assembled a broad database of accessory images and compared image captioning architectures, focusing on an encoder-decoder model. Their final model exceeds ninety percent captioning accuracy, giving language professionals a quick way to resolve queries about diverse jewelry styles.
arxiv-2509-00761:
Boqin Yuan and one co-author, Ziqi Wang, present L-MARS, a multi-agent system for legal question answering with a focus on citation faithfulness. Accuracy on multiple-choice tests misses a common failure: a cited source may not exist or may not support the rule claimed.

L-MARS combines agentic search with judge-driven evidence checks, auditing each atomic claim against its cited source using a six-class taxonomy and strict scoring, with answerer and verifier from different model families. On a one hundred question bar exam audit, a multi-turn judge loop lifts strict citation scores and cuts the no-citation rate sharply against naive retrieval. A repair step drops unreachable citations below one percent, though without further faithfulness gains.
arxiv-2509-00961:
Lun Ai, with three co-authors, tests whether language models can teach humans active learning strategy. Ultra Strong Machine Learning is a system whose explanations improve human performance. Prior work relied on hand-crafted explanation templates. Those templates need expert effort for each new domain. They do not scale to new problems well.

The team built a pipeline combining inductive logic programming with large language models. It automates explanation generation and scoring. A human trial taught active learning across three related domains. Concise expert-written explanations helped learners with higher initial performance. Pipeline-generated explanations gave no advantage over self-learning. Yet a language model judge rated those explanations as higher quality. The gap shows such metrics do not predict human learning outcomes.
arxiv-2509-01161:
Brain tumors can return soon after surgery, and spotting high-risk patients early shapes how closely they are followed. Cheng Cheng, with four co-authors, builds a prediction framework that joins MRI scan features with clinical biomarkers, measurable signs from the body. Four learning methods are used, including gradient boosting and random survival forests.

The models are checked with several tools: a concordance index for ranking risk, time-based accuracy curves, calibration plots, and decision curves that weigh real clinical benefit. Cheng and the team report promising results across these checks. They present the framework as a possible aid for sorting patients by risk and planning personal follow-up care, though it is offered as a tool to support, not replace, clinical judgment.
arxiv-2509-01261:
Finding the largest clique in a graph, a set of points all linked to each other, is a famously hard problem with uses from biology to social networks. Wenmin Han, Shiqi Zheng, Peian Chen, and Yukun Wang propose an improved quantum method based on Grover's search algorithm. Their design tracks the best clique size as the search runs.

Prior knowledge from Turan's theorem and complete graph traits is encoded into global variables through a pre-check in the quantum circuit. An auxiliary qubit scheme updates the tracked size during the search, removing repeated measurements. The authors report far fewer search rounds and a constant number of measurements, an n-fold gain over prior Grover-based methods. Tests confirm the method finds the right answers, offering a faster quantum route to a hard task.
arxiv-2509-02161:
Pablo Ayuso-Albizu, Juan C SanMiguel, and Pablo Carballeira test image to image tools that grow training sets for trait reads on street shots. Tagged data sets for this task are small, which hurts skill with blocked views, odd poses, and mixed scenes. Tools that make images from noise can make rich fake shots, but the best knobs for this task were not known. The team sweeps text prompts, image traits, and new tweak tricks.

Prompt fit and image traits prove key to good fake shots in their sweeps. The best growth recipe makes fake shots that enrich zero shot training sets. Trait read scores rise by a clear share with the tuned setup in place. The study gives hands on guidance for fake data growth in watch systems. Looks alone do not make fake shots worth training on.
arxiv-2509-02661:
Andrew Ferguson is the lead author of a 2025 community paper with well over a hundred co-authors. It came from an NSF workshop. The workshop asked how AI and the mathematical and physical sciences should grow together. The fields span astronomy, chemistry, materials, mathematics, and physics.

The authors call the link between AI and basic science increasingly inseparable. Their strategy works both ways. AI can speed discovery. Science concepts can improve AI itself. Priorities include joint research, an interdisciplinary community, and training across the boundary. The paper is a snapshot of community views from spring and summer 2025. It closes with advice for funders, universities, and researchers. The field moves fast, so the snapshot matters.
arxiv-2509-02761:
Ananth Hariharan, Vardhan Dongre, Dilek Hakkani-Tür, and Gokhan Tur present a 2025 embodied AI paper on cleaning up task plans written by language models and human demonstrators. Such plans often include needless actions, redundant wandering, and logical slips that poison training data for robot policies.

Their iterative loop pairs a Judge model, which critiques action sequences in plain language, with a Planner model that applies fixes. No hand-written rules are needed, so varied error types are covered. On annotated actions from the TEACh dataset, four leading models reached high recall and perfect precision in spotting problems. Most sequences settled within three rounds, gaining temporal efficiency and spatial order. Human error-recovery habits were preserved rather than erased, which the authors value for robust behaviour.
arxiv-2509-02961:
Kushantha P. K. Withanage and 4 co-authors offered a 2025 method for computing how molecules vibrate when simple spring-like motion is not enough. Real molecular vibrations are anharmonic, meaning their swings stray from a perfect repeating pattern. Ignoring that straying throws off predicted vibration frequencies.

Their approach builds on density functional theory, a workhorse method for electron structure, and uses a basis of Gaussian-shaped functions with polynomial factors. Many needed quantities can then be worked out exactly on paper, while the rest are handled on a numerical grid. The team computed corrected frequencies and bond lengths for two-atom molecules. They also handled linked vibrations, including nitrogen tunneling in ammonia and a resonance effect in carbon dioxide.
arxiv-2509-03061:
Abdul Karim and 3 co-authors used transfer learning in 2025 to classify handwritten Bangla characters. Bangla has fifty basic characters and many compound ones, so a recognizer must handle a large set of shapes. Transfer learning reuses knowledge from a network already trained on other images instead of starting from nothing.

The team combined three deep designs, including a residual network and a mobile-friendly one, into an end-to-end classifier. They trained on a public dataset with well over a hundred thousand samples across eighty-four classes. Reported accuracy passed ninety-nine percent on both training and test data. Comparisons with earlier benchmarks favored their model. Such tools can help digitize handwritten Bangla documents and forms.
arxiv-2509-03361:
Yiyang Guo and 5 co-authors traced the past path of 3I/ATLAS in 2025, the third known interstellar object visiting our solar system. The object moves fast, at a stated heliocentric speed, and shows cometary activity. Knowing which star might have ejected it would pin down its origin.

The team ran the orbits of the object and of thirty million nearby stars backward in the galaxy's gravity, carrying measurement uncertainties along. Twenty-five past encounters came within about a light-year's fraction, but every one was too fast for common ejection mechanisms to explain. One wide binary of small red stars was the strongest gravitational perturber among them. Overall the encounters barely nudged the object's speed or direction. Its motion strongly favors an origin in the galaxy's thin disk.
arxiv-2509-03461:
M. A. Agüeros and ten co-authors study Coma Berenices, a sparse open star cluster only about 85 parsecs away, in a 2025 research paper. Its members had been hard to pin down because the cluster is spread out and moves slowly across the sky. The team uses Gaia data to settle membership and basic properties.

From roughly 400 earlier candidates, about 300 stars are confirmed as members. Iron measurements point to a composition much like the Sun's, and fitting stellar models gives an age near 675 million years. Rotation periods are measured for 137 low-mass stars, expanding the known sample sixfold. Magnetic activity, traced through hydrogen emission and X-rays, follows a rotation pattern much like that of similar clusters.
arxiv-2509-03561:
Antonio Macaluso and four co-authors introduce a 2025 hybrid quantum-classical method for correlation clustering. Clustering groups items by similarity, and here items are nodes in a signed graph. Edges can signal agreement or disagreement, and no cluster count is fixed in advance.

Their method adapts a quantum-assisted solver first built for splitting coalitions. The graph is divided step by step, always aiming to keep agreement inside each group. Every split is written as a binary optimisation problem and solved with quantum annealing, a quantum method for finding low-energy configurations. Tests use synthetic signed graphs and real hyperspectral imaging data, which records scenes across many light wavelengths. Against classical algorithms, the adapted solver proved more robust and gave better clusters on real data, especially when cluster sizes were uneven.
arxiv-2509-03661:
ACT, a framework for keeping recommender systems inside their guardrails on their own, is examined in a 2025 research paper by Daryl Chang and four co-authors. A recommender must usually maximise one main goal, like engagement, while holding secondary goals above minimum thresholds. Unrelated system changes keep knocking those secondary measures off target, forcing manual retuning.

Automated Constraint Targeting searches for the smallest set of hyperparameter changes that restores every guardrail. Hyperparameters are the dials that control how the system ranks and mixes content. The search uses offline pairwise tests on unbiased data, avoiding risky live experiments. The framework retrains continuously, adapting as the system and user behaviour drift. The authors show it works in practice. They also describe running ACT inside a large-scale production environment.
arxiv-2509-04361:
The NOvA Collaboration reports its most precise neutrino oscillation measurements yet after ten years of data taking, in a 2025 research paper. Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, and NOvA watches a beam between two detectors in the NuMI beamline. Muon neutrinos vanishing and electron neutrinos appearing, plus their antimatter counterparts, reveal the oscillation settings. The new analysis doubles earlier beam exposure and adds improved simulations.

A joint fit within the three-flavor picture gives the sharpest single-experiment limit on the atmospheric mass splitting, a key gap between neutrino masses. Mixing sits near maximal, and the data mildly favor the normal mass ordering over the inverted one. Adding Daya Bay reactor data strengthens that preference considerably.
arxiv-2509-04761:
Quantum circuits cost less when gates that do nothing useful for a known starting state are removed. Toshiaki Kaji, lead author with two co-authors, improve a state-dependent circuit optimiser called AQCEL in a 2025 paper. The optimiser measures control qubit states to find and eliminate unnecessary control operations.

Two additions drive the gains: a state label manager that cuts needless measurements, and a process that removes redundant gate pairs. Applied to circuits for a quantum parton shower algorithm, the method reduces two-qubit gate counts. Experiments on an IBM quantum computer show better fidelity than conventional optimisation and the original optimiser.
arxiv-2509-05061:
Estimating a tiny failure chance for a structure with hundreds of uncertain inputs defeats many standard methods. Aryan Tyagi and one co-author investigate a deep transport framework for that reliability problem in a 2025 paper. The method combines a tensor train decomposition with an inverse Rosenblatt transformation. Together they approximate the target distribution at low rank.

That form scales linearly with input dimension while staying compact and reusable. Tests cover three analytic problems and one numerical solid mechanics example. Dimensions run up to the hundreds. Compared with a leading method, the framework appears to lower estimator variance while capturing rare failure regions with care.
arxiv-2509-05161:
Sharing radio network analytics helps optimise a network, but a malicious consumer of that data could aim jamming precisely. Abiodun Ganiyu, lead author with three co-authors, demonstrate that risk for the O-RAN Y1 interface in a 2025 wireless security paper. The interface shares analytics between the radio controller and authorised consumers, internal or external.

The authors build two analytics-aided jammers, one clustering-based and one threshold-based, and test them on an over-the-air testbed against always-on and random baselines. Smart jammers nearly match always-on disruption while transmitting less, and under tight budgets the clustering jammer cuts bitrate most while staying hidden longer.
arxiv-2509-05261:
Fake heart ultrasound movies can help train software, but only if they age like real scans, Thierry Judge and four co-authors note in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Speckle, the grainy pattern in ultrasound, slowly loses its match to itself over time, an effect earlier simulators ignored.

Their method starts from real patient scans and heart wall outlines, then builds meshes that shape the simulated images. A coherence map, drawn from correlations measured in the real data, lets speckle vary locally over time instead of staying fixed. Tested on scans from ninety-eight patients, the new sequences matched real decorrelation curves better than the baseline pipeline.
arxiv-2509-05461:
Nuclear reactions inside exploding stars depend on a model whose uncertainty blurs predictions, and Caleb Marshall with five co-authors tighten it in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. The alpha optical model describes how helium nuclei scatter when many reaction channels are open.

The team measured elastic scattering of helium nuclei from strontium-86 at several energies. A fully Bayesian analysis then built a local version of the optical potential from those data. With the potential pinned down, the uncertainty on low-energy cross sections relevant to astrophysics comes out at roughly fifty percent. Better values feed the reaction rate linking this scattering to neutron-producing reactions in stellar environments.
arxiv-2509-05761:
Counting identities for Bell numbers are extended to their degenerate polynomial cousins by Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Spivey's method produced a famous recurrence for Bell numbers, which count set partitions, using Stirling numbers of the second kind.

The authors derive Spivey-type recurrences for fully degenerate Bell polynomials and for their Fubini cousins. These versions deform the classical objects with a parameter, recovering the originals in a limit. The proof runs through degenerate Stirling numbers and two-variable Fubini polynomials of a given order. Recurrences of this kind turn hard direct counts into stepwise counts.
arxiv-2509-05861:
The cold glow around massive, unstable stars called luminous blue variables is mapped in a 2025 study by J. R. Rizzo and two co-authors. At millimeter wavelengths, starlight, dust, stellar winds, and ionized gas all shine together, and their shares were poorly known. Untangling them shows how much mass and energy these stars dump into the galaxy.

Observations with the NIKA2 camera on the IRAM thirty-meter telescope covered five targets at two wavelengths, joined by archival data spanning six decades of the spectrum. Four stars were detected at both wavelengths, showing compact cores, shells, and extended nebular emission. Spectral patterns fit thermal wind emission, and full energy-distribution models separated photosphere, hot dust near the star, winds, and surrounding ionized gas, also giving first parameter estimates for one poorly studied target.
arxiv-2509-05961:
A single number that tracks a runner's aerobic fitness over years is formalized in a 2025 paper by Evgeny V. Votyakov and two co-authors. Amateur runners already collect heart rate and pace from wearables, but each metric alone is hard to interpret. Their Heart Rate Efficiency metric multiplies pace by heart rate, giving an explainable score a runner can follow personally.

The team first built Fitplotter, a browser tool for viewing fitness device data. Then they tested the metric on more than a decade of one athlete's training plus public logs from twelve other runners. Heart Rate Efficiency proved steadier and more meaningful than either input alone, tracking training volume and seasonal progress. The authors discuss how such transparent metrics can challenge the black-box scores of commercial platforms.
arxiv-2509-06461:
Why do vision-language models stumble on cluttered scenes? Yuyao Ge and eight co-authors investigate that question in a 2025 computer science paper. These models answer questions about images, yet busy pictures hurt their reasoning. Earlier fixes needed extra training, outside tools for cutting out objects, or worked only at a coarse level.

Studying attention maps, the patterns showing where a model looks, the team finds that clutter raises attention entropy and lowers accuracy. Attention also sharpens from early to deep layers. They prove that comparing attention for a general query with attention for a task query can separate useful signal from visual noise. Their method, CARVE, uses that contrast without any retraining and improves results sharply, by up to three quarters on some open models.
arxiv-2509-06661:
Moving a sharp boundary between fluids across a computer grid, in one unsplit step, is the contribution of Jieyun Pan and three co-authors in a 2025 computational physics paper. Their setting is the edge-based interface tracking method, where markers sit on grid edges and connections are stored in a color field at vertices. Earlier versions advanced the interface direction by direction.

Splitting made three-dimensional extension easy but blocked high-order time stepping and broke the tracking of quantities along the interface, which boundary-layer models need. The unsplit scheme refits circles to reposition markers and updates the color field so connections stay consistent, even in ambiguous cases. Implemented in the free Basilisk platform, it passed four standard tests, including rotation and a single vortex, with results compared against the split version.
arxiv-2509-06961: All ways to measure size on a quaternionic Heisenberg group turn out to be equivalent, show A. O. Ariyo and one co-author in a 2025 geometry paper. The group is a higher-dimensional cousin of the Heisenberg group, built from quaternions, with a layered structure mixing four- and three-dimensional directions. Homogeneous quasi-norms are size functions fit to that scaling. The authors identify homogeneous norms on the group and prove any two quasi-norms are equivalent for finite dimension, so each bounds the other up to a constant factor.
arxiv-2509-07261:
Nischal Kafle and 1 co-author introduce nsEVDx in 2025, an open-source Python library for modeling extreme events. Extreme value distributions describe rare, severe outcomes such as floods, heat waves, and market crashes. Many existing tools are hard to use or lack Bayesian options, which let users fold prior knowledge into the fit.

The library fits both stationary models, where risk stays fixed, and non-stationary ones, where risk shifts with other factors. Rainfall extremes can be tied to temperature, or stock losses to a volatility index, through user-defined formulas for the model's parameters. Both classic and Bayesian fitting are supported, with advanced samplers for the Bayesian side. The design uses only standard Python science libraries at its core and aims to stay friendly for working analysts.
arxiv-2509-07561:
Simple robots with weak sensors make frequent sensing errors, yet a swarm of them can still agree on the best option. Raina Zakir and 3 co-authors compare two bio-inspired decision rules in a 2025 research paper. One rule, direct-switch, lets robots copy better options directly. The other, cross-inhibition, lets support for one option actively suppress rivals, as in insect colonies.

The authors extend existing mean-field models by adding asocial biases, private leanings that pull robots away from the group. Without bias, direct-switch reliably picks the best option. Once bias enters, it often deadlocks. Cross-inhibition stays faster, more accurate, and more robust across many biased conditions. The findings guide designers of cheap robot swarms for tasks like disaster response and environmental monitoring, where individual errors are guaranteed.
arxiv-2509-07661:
Jonathan Keeling and 3 co-authors review process tensor methods for non-Markovian quantum dynamics in a 2025 article. Open quantum systems appear across many fields. In them, only part of the world is tracked, and the rest acts as an environment. Examples run from quantum optics and cold atoms to superconducting qubits and impurities in solids. The common Born and Markov approximations assume weak coupling and a forgetful environment.

Those assumptions are often made for ease, not for accuracy. They fail when coupling is strong. They fail when the environment is structured, with resonances. They fail when low-frequency modes dominate, or when information flows through the environment itself. Process tensors give a complete account of such dynamics, with memory carried across time. The review presents that framework as the rigorous path past Markovian shortcuts. As quantum devices grow more complex, faithful modeling of memory effects becomes a practical need.
arxiv-2509-07761:
Alix Barraud, writing alone in 2025, computes the dual of a family of algebraic geometry codes built on Hirzebruch surfaces. Algebraic geometry codes turn curves and surfaces into error-correcting codes with strong parameters. The dual code is made of all vectors at right angles to the code. It matters for decoding, and for building quantum codes. Hirzebruch surfaces are a classic family of ruled surfaces, indexed by an integer e.

Barraud first gives a new explicit form of the code itself. The code is parameterized by a divisor with two coefficients. From that form, the dual is written in explicit terms. A lower bound for the dual's minimum distance is computed. Puncturing the codes recovers other known codes from toric surfaces. A sufficient condition is given for orthogonal inclusions between family members. CSS quantum codes are constructed from them. The work links classical geometry codes to quantum error correction.
arxiv-2509-07961:
Can a language model's welfare be measured at all? Valen Tagliabue and 1 co-author build experiments to try, in a 2025 paper on artificial intelligence welfare. They compare what models say about their own preferences with what the models actually choose when moving through a virtual environment and picking conversation topics.

Costs and rewards are varied to see whether behaviour shifts sensibly, and a eudaimonic welfare scale, covering states like autonomy and purpose, is checked for stability across reworded prompts. The measures largely supported each other, and stated preferences matched behaviour reliably. The authors suggest preference satisfaction could serve as a measurable welfare proxy in some current systems, opening careful empirical study of a contested question.
arxiv-2509-08161:
April Niu and 2 co-authors compute game equilibria with gradients alone in a 2025 paper. The games have a leader and many followers. Followers first settle their own best replies to the leader. The leader's best move depends on that reply. Past methods need second-order data, which is costly or missing.

The new method uses only first-order steps. The whole game is recast as one constrained problem. A Lagrangian then tracks how the leader's goal shifts as the followers settle. The steps swap between the two sides and settle near a valid equilibrium, with proof. Markets, security games, and platform rules all have this shape. Cheap equilibrium maths serves them all.
arxiv-2509-08261:
Nuclei that rotate around three unequal axes get an algebraic treatment from Yu Zhang and 4 co-authors in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Their approach maps a triaxial rotor Hamiltonian onto the interacting boson model with a finite number of bosons, exposing dynamics that conventional rotor modes hide. The famous B(E2) anomaly, an unusually weak gamma transition, serves as a showcase.

Specific examples show the framework explaining puzzling low-lying states in osmium nuclei on both the neutron-rich and neutron-deficient sides. Rigid and soft triaxial rotation are incorporated in one Hamiltonian. Finite boson number matters because real nuclei are finite; an algebraic map that respects that finiteness can connect elegant rotor pictures to measured spectra without hand-waving.
arxiv-2509-08361:
A low-frequency radio telescope in Western Australia has spent over a decade listening to the early universe's neighborhood. Steven J. Tingay reviews the Murchison Widefield Array from the inside in a 2025 research paper written alone. Tingay managed and directed the array across much of its life. The instrument operates at the Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory, the future site of the low-frequency Square Kilometre Array.

Science operations began in 2013 after a long development period. The array has since been upgraded several times and pursued a wide range of science goals. It also served as a working precursor that taught the Square Kilometre Array project hard lessons. Tingay reflects on the array's successes and the approaches behind them. His personal account preserves institutional knowledge that formal project reports rarely capture.
arxiv-2509-08461:
Neutrino events in pixelated detectors are classified by a fine-tuned vision-language model in a 2025 paper by Dikshant Sagar and 4 co-authors. Language models have shown surprising reach over structured and unstructured data far beyond text. The team adapts a LLaMA 3.2 vision variant to recognise interaction types in high-energy physics detector images.

The model is benchmarked against a state-of-the-art convolutional network of the kind major neutrino experiments use, which classify electron-neutrino events with high efficiency and purity. Whether a general vision-language model can stand beside a purpose-built network is the practical question. A positive answer would let experiments reuse foundation models instead of engineering a classifier for every new detector.
arxiv-2509-09061:
Elena Bratkovskaya and 1 co-author review the equation of state with light clusters and hypernuclei in a 2025 paper. Heavy ion collisions recreate matter at extreme temperature and density, like the early universe. The equation of state links pressure, temperature, and density for that matter.

Flow harmonics, patterns in how particles stream out, are among the most sensitive probes of the equation. Microscopic transport models are compared with experimental data in the few GeV energy range. Light clusters and hypernuclei add extra degrees of freedom that affect the flow. The review sums up current understanding from both theory and experiment.
arxiv-2509-09161:
Chayan Chatterjee and 3 co-authors use machine learning to confirm GW231123 as a lite intermediate mass black hole merger in a 2025 paper. The gravitational wave event has a total mass well above ordinary stellar black holes. Waveform systematics and noise glitches made analysis hard.

Three tools handle signal detection, glitch characterization, and waveform reconstruction. The merger segment is identified with high confidence in both detectors, verifying its astrophysical origin. Scattered light glitch parameters are given in physically interpretable form for the first time. Reconstructed waves agree slightly better with model agnostic forms than circular models. Tests on simulated massive mergers show the method probes this mass regime well.
arxiv-2509-09261:
A. Egorov and 1 co-author identify the minimal covolume right-angled Coxeter group in hyperbolic three-space in a 2025 paper. Coxeter groups are generated by reflections in the faces of a polyhedron. Right-angled means all dihedral angles are right angles.

Among all such groups in hyperbolic three-space, one group is proved to have the smallest covolume, a measure of the group's fundamental domain size. It comes from a triangular bipyramid with three ideal and two finite vertices. The group is arithmetic, a number theoretic property that aids computation. Its covolume equals Catalan's constant, a known mathematical constant. The result settles an extremal problem in hyperbolic geometry.
arxiv-2509-09361:
Galina Weinstein examines convergences and divergences between Einstein, Poincaré, and special relativity in a 2025 paper. A 2024 book by Jean-Marc Ginoux claims to end the controversy over their respective roles. Weinstein argues similar equations can conceal divergent conceptions.

The 1905 derivations of Poincaré and Einstein are reconstructed side by side in a novel way. Similarities are traced, but differences receive stronger emphasis. Einstein's ether free, principle based kinematics is presented as the path that became canonical special relativity. The aim is not a priority dispute rehearsal. It is a careful analysis of how two routes to similar formulas diverged in meaning.
arxiv-2509-09461:
Doctors exploring patient pathways through hospital data usually drag sliders and tick boxes, memorizing cryptic field codes as they go. Ambre Assor and 3 co-authors propose replacing that chore in a 2025 research paper. Their system lets clinicians state an analytical intent in natural language. A large language model translates the request into an editable, executable database query.

The generated query stays visible and correctable, keeping the human in charge. Dynamic query controls return on demand when users want direct manipulation. The demonstration system visualizes care pathways using France's national health data system, among the world's largest health repositories. The authors argue clinicians already know what filtering options medicine needs; the burden is remembering attribute names and code values. Removing that burden makes exploration fluid again, at the price of not showing every filter at once.
arxiv-2509-09561:
Argyrios Deligkas and 4 co-authors open a new topic in mechanism design in 2025: what changes when a designer may simply discard a few outliers? Some agents report extreme wishes, and excluding the worst-served handful from the social cost can look like an easy win. Their test case places a facility on a line for strategic agents who state preferred spots.

Surprisingly, dropping outliers can hurt rather than help. The authors derive tight bounds for honest, deterministic rules under both total and worst-case cost measures. Once half or more agents may be discarded, no honest rule keeps a bounded guarantee at all. For worst-case cost, a simple order statistic rule reaches the best possible factor, even when a prediction is available.
arxiv-2509-09761:
William M. Baker and 8 co-authors announce two unusually light galaxies that had already stopped forming stars when the universe was young in a 2025 discovery paper. Both were confirmed with James Webb spectroscopy, backed by camera imaging in the near and mid infrared. Seen at redshifts above five, each holds only about a tenth the mass of previously confirmed quiescent systems at such distances.

Modelling their starlight tells two different life stories. One shut down in a single burst roughly 150 million years before it was seen, near the heart of a crowded region. The other had finished forming far earlier and sat near the edge of a dense area. Neighbourhood, the authors suggest, may speed a small galaxy's whole life along.
arxiv-2509-10261:
Nicholas Abell, Elizabeth McDermott, and Christian Millichap classify a family of graph products in this 2025 paper. A Cartesian product combines two graphs in a grid-like way. The question is which such products can be drawn on a projective plane. That surface has a twist, and it resists ordinary flat drawing.

The authors work out the smallest products that fail to fit. They gather the traits of those failures as constraints. Then they build explicit embeddings for every product that meets the constraints. One neat outcome follows. Of the thirty-five known forbidden minors for the projective plane, only six are ever needed here. The result gives a complete yes-or-no test for a broad family of graphs.
arxiv-2509-10361:
Deliveries by a fleet of vehicles, each starting and ending at a depot, form the vehicle routing problem. Michelle Döring and eight co-authors study its parameterized complexity in this 2025 theoretical computer science paper, asking which structural features of the road network make the problem tractable.

For plain vehicle routing, they give an efficient fixed-parameter algorithm when the network's treewidth, a measure of how tree-like it is, is small. Adding capacity limits changes the picture sharply: the capacitated versions prove hard for many parameter choices, treewidth included, making similar algorithms unlikely. One mixed result survives, an algorithm that is practical when both treewidth and vehicle capacity are bounded together. The paper maps the border between feasible and hopeless for a classic logistics problem.
arxiv-2509-10461:
Hao Wang and six co-authors build a stock recommendation system that learns two jobs at once in this 2025 financial technology paper. Investors need both trend forecasts and rankings of which stocks look best, yet models trained as plain forecasters often miss one or the other. Their framework, MiM-StocR, trains forecasting and ranking together as a multi-task problem.

A momentum indicator feeds the model a sense of short-term trend. A custom listwise ranking loss, Adaptive-k ApproxNDCG, concentrates effort on the top of the list where money actually goes. Because stock data invite overfitting, a converge-based balancing method keeps the tasks from fighting. On three benchmarks, SEE50, CSI 100, and CSI 300, the system beats established multi-task baselines on both ranking quality and profitability measures.
arxiv-2509-10561:
