Keeping a local language model's queries private is Madhava Gaikwad's goal in this solo 2025 position paper. His framework is AVEC, short for Adaptive Verifiable Edge Control. It enforces privacy on the user's own device. It adds clear checks when a query is sent elsewhere for help.

An adaptive budgeting algorithm hands out privacy allowances per query. The amounts turn on sensitivity, local confidence, and past usage. Verifiable changes to the query police the traffic that leaves. Integrity checks on the device back them up. Gaikwad states the guarantees with Rényi differential privacy and odometer-style accounting. He derives utility ceilings and leakage bounds. He also proves that simpler gating designs cannot work. The limits are stated plainly. The tests are simulations, by design. No deployment readiness is claimed. The paper offers theory and a design as a path for later work.
arxiv-2509-10661:
Tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions could store data at the single-layer limit. Megha Arya and six co-authors find a new way they can transform, in this 2025 paper. Their material is single-layer Janus MnSeTe, a two-dimensional magnet. Higher-order exchange interactions are usually ignored next to the interaction that twists spins. Here they drive a topological transition, which the authors name the ferric transition.

Their evidence combines first-principles calculations with atomistic spin simulations. Skyrmion stability barely notices the extra interactions, and collapse barely notices them either. The usual twisting force dominates at the critical saddle point. The Bloch point changes strongly, though, and that opens the new transition. The route differs from known radial and chimera routes. The material also promises very high skyrmion energy barriers, among the highest reported for natural two-dimensional magnets.
arxiv-2509-10861: Sara Al Hajjar studies 2-distance coloring of planar graphs in this solo-authored 2025 graph theory paper. In a distance coloring, vertices within a set distance of each other must receive different colors; here the distance is two, so neighbors and next-nearest neighbors all need distinct colors. The graphs are planar, drawable with no crossing edges, and the paper focuses on the case where the maximum degree of the graph is at least six.
arxiv-2509-11161:
Zhen-Na Zhang and six co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on how groups competing for limited resources can end up cooperating without any central planner. Their test bed is the minority game, a model where players win by choosing the option fewer others pick, populated by two kinds of reinforcement learners.

One sub-population learns with Q-learning and the other follows a classical policy, and the authors find a synergy between them that switches on sharply as the mix changes. Inside the Q-learning group, clusters form that synchronize or oppose each other, and one cluster linking the two groups rediscovers the momentum strategy known from financial markets. The work maps when this cooperation appears and what it costs the players who carry it.
arxiv-2509-11361:
Yichen Han and nine co-authors treat prompt design as teamwork in this 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Optimizing the instructions given to a language model usually follows one search path at a time, which adapts poorly, wastes compute, and lets different improvements fight each other.

Their framework, MAPGD, splits the job among specialized agents, each refining one dimension such as instruction clarity, example choice, format, or style. The agents' edits are embedded as semantic gradients, checked for conflicts, and fused, while two added mechanisms keep the clusters of edits tidy and reweight agents by how well their changes validate. On classification and reasoning benchmarks the collaborative setup beat single-agent and random baselines in accuracy and efficiency, and the authors supply convergence guarantees for the method.
arxiv-2509-11561:
Guang-Peng Zhang, writing on his own, computes a one-loop correction in quantum chromodynamics. This 2025 particle physics paper treats the single transverse spin asymmetry in the Drell-Yan process. A lepton pair emerges from quark-antiquark annihilation. The asymmetry reveals how partons move inside a spinning proton.

The work uses collinear twist-three factorization. The Feynman gauge is the working choice. The virtual photon's mass is measured. The final lepton's angles are read in the Collins-Soper frame. The photon's transverse momentum is integrated out. The quark equation of motion removes dependent distribution functions. Results respect QED and QCD gauge invariance. All divergences cancel under collinear subtraction. Finite hard coefficients are presented.
arxiv-2509-11661:
Lifei Hao and four co-authors generate extra practice data for a niche inspection task. This 2025 computer vision paper treats dirty tableware recognition. Smart dishwashers and food-safety systems must judge how dirty a plate is. That is a fine-grained call. Real examples are few and hard to collect.

Their scheme is DTGen. A generative diffusion model is specialized with low-rank adaptation. Structured prompts produce varied dirty tableware images. A vision-language model filters the output for quality. From a tiny set of real photos, supply can grow without bound. Classifier accuracy on fine grades rose sharply. Deployment into embedded dishwashers is sketched. The recognizer could tune water, energy, and detergent to the load's true state.
arxiv-2509-11861:
Designing chips that process light at the single-photon level calls for optimization tools that respect quantum behavior, and Mathias Van Regemortel with one co-author supply one in 2025. Their setting is the quantum photonic integrated circuit, built from nonlinear coupling gates plus lossy parts that must be sampled rather than modeled exactly.

The method leans on differentiable tensor networks, which stay accurate when photon numbers are low and entanglement between modes is modest, and it adjusts circuit parameters by following gradients. Field simulations of gallium arsenide samples first characterize the gate hardware. Two demonstrations follow: circuits shaped to prepare chosen quantum states of light, and readout layouts tuned for sensing a phase as precisely as possible.
arxiv-2509-11961:
Slow step-by-step generation is the bottleneck Spec-LLaVA attacks, in a 2025 paper by Mingxiao Huo and six co-authors on speeding up vision-language models. These systems reason over images and text together, but producing one token at a time keeps them from real-time use.

The design pairs a small draft model with the large target model. The draft guesses several upcoming tokens, arranged in a tree of branches that grows or shrinks with the draft's confidence, and the target checks them all in parallel, accepting many per step. On out-of-domain photos from MS COCO, decoding ran up to about 3.3 times faster on two LLaVA-1.5 sizes with no drop in output quality. The lightweight draft also suits deployment on modest hardware.
arxiv-2509-12161:
A short 2025 proof by Alex Bishop and one co-author settles a question in group theory about branch groups, a family of groups that act on rooted trees. The authors show that any finitely generated group with a certain finiteness property can sit inside a finitely generated branch group without changing which of its elements count as conjugate.

That embedding does the real work. From it they build a finitely generated branch group whose word problem can be solved but whose conjugacy problem cannot. The result answers a question posed by Bartholdi, Grigorchuk, and Sunik, and it separates two decision problems that might have seemed equally hard.
arxiv-2509-12261:
Matching a degraded song clip to its source is one face of a hard pattern problem called the longest filled common subsequence problem. Marko Djukanovic and four co-authors attack it in 2025 with an adaptive method that builds candidate solutions, merges the best parts, solves the merged piece exactly, and adapts.

Older test sets were too small to separate good algorithms from lucky ones, so the team built larger benchmarks. Their method matched the proven optimum on nearly all of the more than fifteen hundred instances where the optimum is known. A case study then applies the machinery to identifying songs from damaged audio energy profiles.
arxiv-2509-12361:
Karl Higley and 3 co-authors reflect on building a real news recommender in a 2025 paper. Their platform, POPROX, is a live system for news recommendation research with a persistent user base. The goal was to apply published research to personalization features like those in news aggregators and publisher products.

The authors found unexpected challenges that trace back to surprising gaps in the literature. Many common product features were poorly supported by existing studies, they report. Building and running the live system exposed questions that offline experiments had not answered. The paper ends with lessons learned and opportunities to make future news recommendation research more applicable in practice. It is a builder's account rather than a new algorithm.
arxiv-2509-12461:
Alex Hinkle and 3 co-authors use photon links to reveal hidden states in single quantum dots in a 2025 paper. Their dots are lead-halide perovskite crystals, well-known quantum emitters that could generate entangled photon pairs through multiexciton cascades, series where several excitations decay in steps. The energy levels and changes of those many-body states were poorly known.

At low temperatures, the team done time- and frequency-resolved photon-link spectroscopy using a single-photon sensor array. They measured biexciton binding energy levels and assigned charged states that switch quickly. Most notably, they found a spectral feature shifted from the main exciton line as the bound triexciton, a state of three excitations, and well-known the order of its cascade emission. The work shows the power of multidimensional link methods.
arxiv-2509-13061:
Josef Kadlec, Artur Barasinski and Karel Lemr detect high-size entanglement via two-qubit tests in 2025. Full tests grow fast with size and strain labs. Their map shrinks the state space onto a two-qubit space.

Known two-qubit witnesses can then be used as-is. The map fits no one class alone. It flags the vast share of pure linked states. Test counts stay flat as size grows, a key gain. Two hard classes check out well: near-symmetric states and noisy random states. Current lab tools can run the method today.
arxiv-2509-14061:
Chiara De Luca and Elisa Donati detect queen bees without opening the hive in a 2025 paper. A queen's presence keeps a colony stable, but checking for her means manual inspections that disturb the bees and do not scale to large apiaries. Audio listening systems exist, yet they draw power, need heavy processing, and suffer in ambient noise.

The pair fuse cheap environmental signals instead: temperature, humidity, and pressure differences between inside and outside the hive. A quantized decision tree runs on a commercial microcontroller, giving real-time answers at very low power. Detection accuracy topped ninety-nine percent on environmental inputs alone, and adding audio features brought no meaningful gain. The result is a scalable, non-invasive monitor built from off-the-shelf parts.
arxiv-2509-14261:
Hamady Gackou, writing alone in 2025, works on a small grammar puzzle in English: the word that after a noun. Sometimes that starts a relative clause describing the noun, and sometimes it starts a complement clause giving the noun content. Automatic taggers often mix the two uses up.

Gackou first tested the TreeTagger English model built by Helmut Schmid on the task, then relabelled a corpus first parsed under the Universal Dependencies scheme. Retraining TreeTagger on the corrected data gave a model that separated the two uses more cleanly. The study also varied how much training data the model saw and checked how well the treebank files used stand in for English more broadly. Gains were modest but consistent for the harder distinction.
arxiv-2509-14761:
Daniela Saraiva and three co-authors subjectively evaluate in 2025 how view synthesis interacts with compression of light fields, images that record both light intensity and direction. Light fields enable new viewpoints after capture, but their data volume demands strong compression. Dropping views is one way to shrink them.

A sparsely sampled light field is built by dropping views from an original capture, then coding it at low distortion and synthesising missing views. Human viewers rate the results in a subjective study, the ground truth for perceived quality. The study shows how synthesis quality and coding artefacts trade off in viewer judgement. Immersive media pipelines need such viewer evidence, since pixel metrics alone misrate synthesised views.
arxiv-2509-15161:
Felipe Flores and James Harbour study symmetry algebras of measured groupoids through a Gaussian deformation in a 2025 operator algebras paper. A discrete measured groupoid blends group-like symmetry with a measure space, and its von Neumann algebra packages that symmetry for analysis. Popa's deformation and rigidity theory supplies the tools.

The authors build the Gaussian deformation attached to any one-cocycle of the groupoid, a standard way to flex the algebra along a chosen direction. Under suitable assumptions they prove the algebra is prime, meaning it cannot split as a product, and full, a strong indecomposability property. They also characterize the largest rigid subalgebras and prove unique prime factorization for algebras built from products of groupoids. Such factorization results anchor the classification program for these algebras.
arxiv-2509-15361:
Zichen Wu, Hsiu-Yuan Huang, and Yunfang Wu tackle a flaw in models that read both images and text. Such models often lean on false links in the data instead of the true meaning. A photo and caption may share a side detail, and the model learns that detail as if it were the point. This makes the models weak on hard tasks.

Their fix uses what-if tests to split core meaning from side details in both words and images. A routing system then calls on expert parts of the model, each tuned to clean one kind of input. Tests on sarcasm and mood tasks show the method beats older fixes. The result is a model that reasons from the right cues.
arxiv-2509-15561:
Om Naphade, Saksham Bansal, and Parikshit Pareek tune learning models with small language models instead of huge ones. Tuning the settings of a model is a must, but it costs much compute and can be opaque. Recent work used language models with over a hundred billion parts for this task. The team ask whether small models can do the job.

Their frame rests on a block that sums up a training run into a clean, structured brief. With that brief, small local models can judge how tuning is going. In ten tries per task, their pipeline lands within about a point of a top large model across six tasks. The block, not raw size, does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2509-15861:
Van-Tuan Tran, Hong-Hanh Nguyen-Le, and Quoc-Viet Pham help federated learning systems forget a user's data. In federated learning, many devices train one model without pooling data. Networks still memorize training items, which opens privacy attacks. Rules may also require a user's trace to be removed. Past removal methods act after training and struggle with deep memory.

Their frame, ToFU, argues systems should be built ready to forget. Changes applied during training bound how much any single item can lodge in the model. Theory shows those changes cap item specific information, which makes later removal simpler. The frame plugs into past removal methods and lifts them. Tests on image sets show it beats past baselines.
arxiv-2509-16061:
Humanoid and four-legged robots often learn one skill at a time, which wastes effort when jobs grow complex. Maciej Stępień and three co-authors train a single broad motion policy by copying example moves, with a hidden control space that steers how each skill is done. Safety limits are built in, and a diffusion-based judge helps sharpen the copying.

The policy drives both walking and object handling in tests. It runs in simulation on a humanoid and a four-legged robot, and on real hardware for the four-legged one. Moves come from simple made-up clips or from dog motion reshaped for robots.
arxiv-2509-16261:
Radar images are noisy and full of ghost echoes, which makes spotting objects from radar alone a hard task for self-driving cars. Shuocheng Yang and five co-authors add motion to the mix with RaFD, a detector that estimates how the scene flows between frames from a bird's-eye view. That flow guides features from the past frame into the current one, sharpening the detection.

The flow task is trained alongside the detector, so both improve together. On a standard radar data set, the radar-only system set a new best mark. The result shows that shape and motion cues matter as much as raw meaning for radar.
arxiv-2509-16861:
Rui Yang and co-authors build a guardrail that adapts for language model software in a 2025 paper. Fixed rules cannot cover the open range of chats these systems allow. Attackers craft prompts to jailbreak the model into unsafe replies. A guard must evolve as attacks change after launch.

Their system, AdaptiveGuard, updates its defenses in response to new attack styles. Results show it keeps pace with fresh jailbreak tactics. Code and datasets are shared in public. Adaptive guards could help firms keep chat tools safe without freezing them in place. The work treats safety as a moving target, not a one-time check.
arxiv-2509-16961:
Hamd Alsobhi and co-authors use neural networks as test functions in a finite element method in a 2025 paper. Minimal-residual methods solve partial differential equations by shrinking an error measure. That measure lives in a dual space, which is hard to handle directly. Their method keeps a standard finite element solution space but lets networks evaluate the residual norm.

They prove an error bound that rests on a compatibility condition. Tests on advection-reaction problems with sharp or broken data gave robust, accurate answers. Blending learned test functions with classic elements could widen the range of hard flow problems that solvers handle reliably.
arxiv-2509-17061:
Shiladittya Mondal, Christopher H. K. Chen, and Davide Manzini probe solar wind turbulence at tiny scales in a 2025 physics paper. Below the electron scale, how turbulence dies out has stayed an open question. That death heats electrons in the wind. Spacecraft data long covered magnetic wiggles alone, which left the picture half drawn.

New results fit predictions of an electron entropy cascade. In that picture, turbulent energy dissipates in a one-way, irreversible flow. The magnetic spectrum is less steep than expected, though. Weak signal and lingering wave modes may explain the gap. The findings sharpen models of heating in the solar wind and other space plasmas.
arxiv-2509-17561:
Edwine Nabahirwa, Wei Song, Minghua Zhang, and Shufan Chen test whether YOLO detectors stay robust underwater. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that underwater scenes warp images badly: color fades, edges blur, and texture washes out. YOLO models lead real-time detection on land, yet their strength under the sea's chaotic conditions has rarely been checked in a systematic way.

The team graded recent YOLO variants across six simulated underwater settings. Their data set joins ten thousand labeled images from two public sources under one protocol. YOLOv12 came out strongest overall but proved highly vulnerable to noise. The authors trace the damage: noise breaks the edge and texture features the detectors lean on, which explains the poor scores in noisy water. Class imbalance adds its own drag. The study gives divers and marine engineers a clear-eyed map of where these detectors can be trusted.
arxiv-2509-17661:
Jacob J Webber and seven co-authors score disease severity from speech recordings. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves neurodegenerative disease care, where tracking progression guides treatment and drug trials. Most past systems sort patients from healthy controls or predict one clinical metric. The team instead wants a single severity score that orders patients by how far the disease has run.

Their model trains on a comparator loss, which forces the scores to respect a stated order, from diagnosis, clinical scales, or the recording date. That design can fuse facts from several mismatched metrics, a boon for the small data sets health research lives with. Trained on lightly labeled data, the system separates patients from controls. Its score also tracks measures it never trained on, including a standard ALS rating scale and therapist judgments. The authors offer it as a cheap, repeatable monitor.
arxiv-2509-17861:
Eduard P Kontar and 3 co-authors probe small-scale plasma churn near the Sun. Their 2025 paper links that churn to how the corona gets hot and how the solar wind speeds up. Direct probes cannot fly close to the Sun, so the fine detail there is poorly known.

Radio bursts from the Sun give a way to read density wiggles at ion scale. The team checks those wiggles against magnet wiggles caught by probes farther out. Both fit waves of a known plasma type. From that fit they map heat flow from the low corona out to Earth's orbit, and it matches the push the wind needs.
arxiv-2509-17961:
Li Siyan and 5 co-authors judge virtual teaching aides by how well they teach, not just how right they sound. Their 2025 paper deals with online courses where students post in forums and wait for help. A virtual aide can cut staff load, but past checks lean on shallow scores.

Their frame rests on learning science and fits forum-based courses. Expert tags on aide replies train classifiers that grade new replies. Some methods raised score, while others failed to travel to new posts. The work sets a base for checks that are tied to real teaching goals.
arxiv-2509-18261:
Chong-Chong He and 4 co-authors speed up how particles and grids swap mass and heat in galaxy sims. Their 2025 paper is built into QUOKKA, a GPU-native code for radiation and magnet flow. Past ways to find particle neighbours or sort them scale poorly across many GPU nodes.

Their scheme runs in two stages through a buffer grid with ghost zones. Shares are summed with atomic adds, then sent across memory ranks. Cell-wise caps keep the real grid physical, such as holding density above zero. Tests span gas inflow and blast waves, and scaling held near half strength on thousands of GPUs.
arxiv-2509-18361:
How happy are developers with AI coding helpers? Surveys are rich but small, and star ratings are sparse. Daye Nam, Malgorzata Salawa, and Satish Chandra propose reading the mood hidden in developers' own prompts. Their 2025 paper tests whether prompt sentiment can act as a feedback signal at scale. They studied usage logs from a real work setting.

The logs covered 372 professional developers. The team found a usable mood signal in about eight percent of chats. That rate is more than thirteen times higher than direct feedback given in the product. Even a ready-made sentiment tool read the signal with fair accuracy. The authors present prompt mood as a cheap extra channel, not a swap for user studies. It could help teams spot pain points across thousands of users.
arxiv-2509-18461:
Deepfakes threaten trust in media, and detectors usually need examples of each new fake type. Ayan Sar, Sampurna Roy, Tanupriya Choudhury, and Ajith Abraham survey zero-shot detection in this 2025 paper. Zero-shot methods aim to spot fakes they were never trained on. The paper also covers prevention: stopping fakes before they are made.

The survey weighs four detection routes: self-supervised learning, transformer classifiers, generator fingerprints, and meta-learning. Prevention ideas include jamming generator inputs, watermarking real content, live monitoring of creation tools, and blockchain records of origin. The authors list hard open problems: attacks on the detectors, scale limits, ethics, and missing standard benchmarks. They point to future work on explainable detection and mixed media analysis. A joined defense, they argue, needs researchers, security experts, and policymakers together.
arxiv-2509-18661:
Keeping up with fast-growing research fields is hard, and survey papers are slow to write by hand. Yixin Liu, Yonghui Wu, Denghui Zhang, and Lichao Sun present Agentic AutoSurvey in this 2025 paper. Their system lets a team of language model agents write the survey. Four specialist agents split the work: search, topic mining, writing, and quality checks.

The team tested the system on six topics in language model research. It handled from 75 to over 400 papers per topic, 847 in total. Scores on a twelve-point quality rubric reached 8.18 out of 10, well above the prior AutoSurvey baseline. Citation coverage was often high on mid-size sets and lower on the largest ones. The authors argue that splitting the job among specialists beats a single writer model. The design targets fields where the literature grows too fast for manual synthesis.
arxiv-2509-18861:
Dark matter might reveal itself when two of its particles annihilate into gamma rays. Stefan Fröse, Dominik Martin Elässer, Hendrik Hildebrandt, and Elisa Pueschel search for that glow from a small galaxy in this 2025 paper. The target is the Coma Berenices dwarf, watched for about 25 hours by the MAGIC telescopes in La Palma. Earlier searches used energy alone.

Their search adds the spatial pattern expected from the dwarf's dark matter halo, making it three-dimensional. A new background method stacks the data, cuts the source zone, and rotates the model to fix telescope acceptance. A public software package speeds the statistics with synthetic data sets. No signal appeared for any of four annihilation channels across a wide mass range. The team sets the first upper limits of this three-dimensional kind. Sensitivity improved over the earlier MAGIC result.
arxiv-2509-18961:
Maria Koller and two co-authors ask what sets the metal content of the gas inside a galaxy. Heavier galaxies tend to hold more metals, an effect called the mass-metallicity relation. It was not clear whether that link tracks how many metals a galaxy has made, or how well it keeps them. The team attacked the question with data on about 4,500 galaxies from the MaNGA survey.

Using a random forest method and checks for linked factors, they found two drivers matter most: the mass in stars, and the strength of gravity from that mass. Near a galaxy's center, stellar mass rules, since metals there stay bound and reflect past star making. Farther out, gravity takes over, because keeping metals at the edge depends on how deep the gravity well is. Star formation rate ranks third.
arxiv-2509-19061:
Marcel Ferrari and three co-authors speed up a core computation inside simulations of slow, sticky fluid flow. The Stokes equations govern such flows, which matter for modeling Earth's mantle. Solvers work on a grid in passes called smoothers, and the team writes these passes to avoid building the full system matrix. That matrix-free style saves memory but demands careful tuning for modern chips.

They test five smoother variants, including blocked versions and a new one that reuses cached data by reworking small overlapping tiles. A sinker test with sharp viscosity contrast checks correctness through an energy-based error measure. On a Grace Hopper supercomputer node, the new smoother kept over ninety percent efficiency up to 64 cores. It ran up to three times faster than the standard baseline.
arxiv-2509-19161:
Textbook computer theory counts circuits as if wires were free and space unlimited, but real chips obey physics. Benjamin Prada and Ankur Mali introduce circuit classes that live in physical space of a given dimension. In their classes, a circuit's volume grows only so fast, the information crossing its boundary per second is capped, and the circuit can grow only through local, buildable edits. These laws bind any causal system, classical or quantum.

Within that frame they prove hard limits. Algorithms whose running time grows too fast cannot handle the hardest inputs, and a parallel machine in fixed dimension gains only a bounded polynomial speed-up over the best serial one. As the dimension rises without bound, their classes recover the classic model of parallelism. Parallelism thus appears as an idealization that physics never quite grants.
arxiv-2509-19361:
Liudmyla Morozova, writing alone, reframes classic ruler-and-compass construction problems as walks through an ordered set. In this view, the figure being built is one element of a set generated step by step by the construction itself. Each new element follows logically from those before it, forming a chain. The required solution is not hunted in isolation; it emerges inside that ordered structure when the chain reaches it.

Three classical problems illustrate the method, involving proportional segments, a Gothic architectural detail, and proportional angles. In the third, discrete links meet a continuously varying radius, giving a two-parameter structure that is part discrete, part continuous. The examples also motivate a limited reading of information conservation inside an ordered construction. The work offers geometers a unifying lens on problems usually treated as separate puzzles.
arxiv-2509-19561:
Optimization with momentum can race downhill fast, but real gradients arrive with errors. Harsh Choudhary, Jalal Fadili, and Vyacheslav Kungurtsev study a gradient method that carries both friction-like damping and curvature-driven damping. Gradient errors may be fixed biases or random noise. The setting is a general Hilbert space, so the results cover functions and signals, not just finite vectors.

Under stated budget rules on the errors, function values and gradients converge fast. Random noise with zero mean allows weaker assumptions and still gives fast rates, both on average and with near certainty. The authors also sharpen several rates from big-O bounds to strictly faster little-o ones. Such methods run inside machine learning and imaging pipelines. Knowing which errors they tolerate keeps those pipelines honest.
arxiv-2509-19861:
Catching depression early in online conversation can route help sooner, but the signals are faint and tangled. The SINAI team, Alba Maria Marmol-Romero and three co-authors, report their eRisk 2025 entries. One task flags depression in long multi-user threads. Their pipeline cleans text heavily, then applies transformer models tuned for mental health language.

A second, pilot task probes chatbots powered by large language models. Their conversational strategies aim to gain the most information within few turns. The thread system placed mid-pack on the headline score, yet issued its warnings among the fastest. Speed matters in early detection: a late perfect call may arrive after harm. The report documents design choices for teams entering future shared tasks.
arxiv-2509-20161:
Heine Havneraas Rostum and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on greener bridge design. Construction is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, and better structural design can cut them. Optimizing a bridge girder normally means running many costly finite element simulations. Bayesian optimization can search such problems with far fewer runs.

Their method aims at one specified trade-off between goals rather than a full menu of options. It compresses simulation output with proper orthogonal decomposition and speeds the model with a Kriging variant. A constrained expected improvement rule picks each next design to test. The case study covers a three-span concrete bridge girder with fifteen design variables and nine constraints. Against conventional design, the method saved roughly ten to fifteen percent in cost and about twenty percent in environmental cost.
arxiv-2509-20661:
Huimin Chang proves a clean algebraic result in a 2025 mathematics paper on cluster categories. The paper studies the Grothendieck groups of n-cluster categories of infinite type A, a family built by Holm and Jorgensen. These groups collect formal differences of objects in the category.

Chang shows that for every n of one or more, the group in question is just the integers. The proof settles the structure for the whole infinite family at once. As an application, the result extends an earlier finding by Murphy, who covered the case where n equals one. The paper is short and focused, aimed at readers in representation theory and homological algebra.
arxiv-2509-20961:
Financial advice now spreads through long podcast videos, and few viewers watch forty minutes to find one key point. Sarmistha Das and three co-authors present FASTER, a 2025 framework that summarizes financial advisory videos with multimodal output. The summary pairs text with the relevant images from the video.

FASTER extracts features from each channel separately. A vision model describes keyframes, optical character recognition catches on-screen text, and speech transcription with speaker separation handles the audio. A modified preference optimization loss then shapes concise summaries. Finally the system aligns visual keyframes with the textual points they support. The authors aim to make advisory content searchable and digestible without losing the charts and slides that carry much of the advice.
arxiv-2509-21061:
Telling apart two nearly identical bird species or car models takes attention to fine detail. Riccardo La Grassa, Ignazio Gallo, and Nicola Landro present EnGraf-Net in a 2025 paper on fine-grained classification. Their network branches across multiple levels of granularity at once.

Most fine-grained models lean on part annotations, such as bounding boxes or text attributes, or on attention maps that crop to parts. The authors argue part-based views lose local features that matter. Humans recognize objects both by details and by where they sit in a hierarchy. EnGraf-Net grafts fine and coarse branches together, so leaf-level decisions benefit from coarser context. The design aims at classes where within-class variation is high and between-class differences are small.
arxiv-2509-21161:
A model that keeps learning new classes must also stay honest about its own uncertainty. Giuseppe Serra and Florian Buettner present DATS in a 2025 paper on calibrated class-incremental learning. In safety-critical uses, a confident wrong answer is worse than an admitted guess.

Most calibration fixes in continual learning share one temperature across all tasks, a data-centric choice. The authors argue that this overlooks how distances between classes shift as new ones arrive. Their distance-aware temperature scaling adjusts confidence using the geometry of the learned classes. The aim is to prevent catastrophic forgetting while keeping confidence scores aligned with true accuracy. Calibrated uncertainty lets hospitals, vehicles, and other high-stakes systems know when to defer to a human.
arxiv-2509-21461:
Cosmic ray nuclei break apart when they strike photons during their long journeys. Leonel Morejon and Karl-Heinz Kampert give an analytic probabilistic account of those interactions in a 2025 paper. An iron nucleus can fully disintegrate over distances from a few to hundreds of megaparsecs. The outcome depends on the cosmic ray energy. Each single interaction is stochastic, not deterministic.

Monte Carlo simulations and differential equations dominate current practice. Equations neglect stochasticity, and simulations capture the process only in part. No exact formulation of the probability distributions was available. The authors present an analytic description of ultra high energy cosmic ray interactions. It aims to connect compositions observed at Earth with those emitted at sources.
arxiv-2509-21661:
Characterizing a new detector can eat a year of expert time, slowing instrument building. J. Cuevas-Zepeda and 8 co-authors automate that stage with Bayesian optimization in a 2025 paper. Design and prototyping have sped up through model run and nanofabrication. Testing remains the bottleneck. Their technique runs a closed loop: real time readings guide setting choice toward optimal operating states.

Bayesian optimization balances exploring uncertain settings against exploiting known good ones. Optimal operating settings are identified with far less manual effort. The method aims at devices that must be described under many operating settings. Sensor building cycles shorten when the testing stage accelerates. The authors demonstrate the approach on detector characterization tasks, presenting it as a general technique for novel instrumentation.
arxiv-2509-21861:
Chemists read molecules through spectra, the patterns a sample gives off when probed, but language models have barely been used on that data. Shuaike Shen and eight co-authors present SpecMol in this 2025 paper, a foundation model grounded in spectroscopy. Two gaps held the field back: no standard way to write spectra for models, and no shared way to judge them.

SpecMol joins three jobs in one interface: reading spectra, learning molecular representations, and building three-dimensional structures. Alongside it, the team set up SpecMol-Bench, a test protocol with tasks that cross between forms. The tasks run from spectra to structure, from structure back to spectra, and from a text formula of a molecule to its 3D shape. SpecMol read structures from spectra accurately and matched real nuclear magnetic resonance traits closely. It also built valid 3D shapes and beat general molecular language models on the shared measures.
arxiv-2509-21961:
Driving data is lopsided: easy, common maneuvers fill the records, while rare and risky scenes are scarce. Lingguang Wang, Ömer Şahin Taş, Marlon Steiner, and Christoph Stiller tackle that imbalance in this 2025 paper on trajectory planning for self-driving cars. A planner trained on lopsided data leans toward the common cases and weakens exactly where safety matters most.

The team first compared ways to rebalance the training data, and found that reweighting samples by trajectory pattern worked well. Their planner, FlowDrive, then learns a flow that turns noise into trajectory distributions in a few steps. A moderated guidance trick adds small nudges between steps, widening the variety of paths while keeping them consistent with the scene. On two benchmarks, FlowDrive led learning-based planners and neared rule-refined methods. With guidance and light post-processing added, it reached top overall results on nearly every split.
arxiv-2509-22361:
Ricard Ravell Rodríguez, Martí Perarnau-Llobet, and Pavel Sekatski ask how well an atom can gauge a quantum light field. In the classic setup, the field is treated as fixed, and the atom's precision grows fast with time. Here the field itself is quantum, made of coherent states of light. The team tracks the quantum Fisher information, a measure of how much the atom's state reveals about the field strength.

With one light mode, that measure stays capped at a low value. Long trains of modes do better, but back-action from the atom slows the gain. In a steady stream of weak light, the best rate stays finite and depends on source strength.
arxiv-2509-22561:
Ethan Marx and 9 co-authors validate a machine learning system that locates gravitational-wave sources fast. Quick sky maps let telescopes chase light from the same event, so speed and reliability matter for public alerts. Their system, AMPLFI, uses likelihood-free inference to estimate source parameters for binary black holes at low latency. They tested it on simulated signals injected into data from the third LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run.

Its sky maps matched the production tool BAYESTAR on searched area and volume. It also recovered source traits, like chirp mass, with sound uncertainty estimates. On real candidate events from the third catalog, its results agreed with the collaboration's analysis. The system looks ready to support public alerts.
arxiv-2509-22661:
Lingyu Zhang and 6 co-authors predict a rider's next pickup point by separating habit from momentary intent. Raw trajectories show where someone went, but not what the trips meant. The team first turns trajectories into semantically enriched activity sequences that encode stay behavior and movement meaning. Two parallel streams then model the user. One stream captures long-term habitual patterns, the other short-term dynamic intentions, each with attention over space and time.

A fusion module weighs the two streams by context. An attention-based matcher then scores candidate pickup locations. On real ride-hailing data sets, the model consistently beat state-of-the-art methods. The authors credit semantic trajectory abstraction and the dual-stream design.
arxiv-2509-22861:
Rayhan Rashed and Farnaz Jahanbakhsh propose transforming sensitive content for each user instead of suppressing it for everyone. Centralized moderation both under-protects and over-reaches: harm is subjective, yet flagged content is simply removed. Formative interviews showed how benign content can wound through personal life experience. Their browser extension, DIY-MOD, works from the user's own definition of harm.

The tool rewrites sensitive elements in real time, choosing from a palette that runs from obfuscation to artistic stylizing. The content's informational value survives the change. Two user studies found the approach raised users' sense of agency and safety. People could engage with content and communities they once had to avoid.
arxiv-2509-22961:
Ports can run above their safe pace for a while, but not forever. Debojjal Bagchi and 5 co-authors build a framework that splits port capacity into two kinds. Operating capacity is the rate a port can sustain under stable conditions. Ultimate capacity is the top rate it can hit at all. Long-term plans need both numbers, yet older models blur them.

The team used the Port of Houston as their case study. A queueing model gave the operating rate, and a fitted equation model gave the ultimate rate. Liquid-bulk terminals were the main bottleneck in calm times. After disruptions, pilot supply became the binding limit instead.
arxiv-2509-23161:
Giant gravitons meet half-BPS operators in a two-loop computation of correlation functions. Yu Wu, Yunfeng Jiang, Chang Liu, and Yang Zhang compute all such two-point functions. The theory is maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills. Two tools do the heavy lifting. A partially contracted giant graviton method simplifies the combinatorics. Harmonic superspace methods from a smaller supersymmetry handle the rest.

The results encode rich conformal field theory data. From them, the team derive sum rules for OPE coefficients. Those rules agree fully with integrability predictions. At the integrand level, a hidden higher-dimensional symmetry shows up. It appears at both one-loop and two-loop order.
arxiv-2509-23261:
AI coding help favors popular languages, and that edge may compound over time like interest. Fei Gu and 3 co-authors measure that asymmetry at scale. Thousands of algorithmic tasks and hundreds of framework choice tasks frame the tests. Mainstream languages and frameworks scored far higher success rates. Niche tools lagged by a substantial margin.

The pattern fits the Matthew effect, where rich ecosystems get richer support. Better AI help draws more use, which yields more training data. The authors call the gap a hidden bias in software evolution. It is not the sole driver of adoption, they note. Still, the friction for niche tech is real.
arxiv-2509-23461:
Training on every data point costs time that smarter sampling can save. Ziheng Cheng and 2 co-authors propose Evolved Sampling, a method that picks data batch by batch while training runs. The picks rest on loss values and on how losses change when data are altered. How often the picks refresh can be tuned, which cuts backward-pass time while keeping model quality.

A second version adds set-level pruning for still more speed. Across pre-training and post-training tasks, the framework sped training with no loss in results, saving up to nearly half the wall-clock time. The authors present it as a plug-in that fits many training setups.
arxiv-2509-23561:
Robot joints need strong, thin motors, and shrinking them below twenty millimeters across has been hard. Jianren Wang and 7 co-authors built a micro axial-flux motor whose windings are printed on circuit boards. Standard wound stators waste space at this scale, which raises resistance and caps torque. The team's stator stacks four high-density boards into forty-eight layers, reaching a record copper fill in a disc five millimeters thick.

The design serves quasi-direct-drive robots, which skip high-ratio gearboxes and demand high torque at low speed. The authors ran detailed electric and thermal analyses to shape the motor. A built prototype then confirmed the predicted performance in lab tests.
arxiv-2509-23661:
Training a top vision-language model from scratch is usually a rich lab's game. Xiang An and 22 co-authors release LLaVA-OneVision-1.5, a fully open framework meant to change that. It bundles three parts: a large concept-balanced pre-training set, a curated instruction set, and an end-to-end training pipeline with offline data packing. The whole training run fits a modest stated budget.

The eight-billion-parameter model beat Qwen2.5-VL-7B on most of twenty-seven benchmarks, and the four-billion version beat its rival on all of them. A light reinforcement learning stage then drew out chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors frame the release as a reproducible path for smaller teams.
arxiv-2509-23761:
A bump near the very start of a two-pion mass spectrum had never been seen before in these decays. The BESIII Collaboration reports it from a huge sample of psi(3686) events recorded with the BESIII detector, studying decays to two charged pions plus a J/psi. A resonance-like structure sits right near the pion pair threshold. A Breit-Wigner fit gives its mass and width, with statistical significance above ten standard deviations.

Two theory frames are tried against the data. Chiral perturbation theory fits the spectrum above a point but misses the threshold rise. A QCD multipole expansion model, treating the psi(3686) as a mix of S and D wave charmonium, matches well.
arxiv-2509-23861:
Search engines that embed each document as one vector usually take that vector from the encoder's last layer. Zhongbin Xie and Thomas Lukasiewicz argue that earlier layers hold different linguistic knowledge worth using. Their multi-layer representations combine vectors from several layers of the document encoder. The team first tests the idea in a multi-vector retrieval setting, checking how each layer's contribution shifts performance.

Pooling strategies then compress the multi-vector form back to a single vector for efficiency. In single-vector tests, the method beat dual encoders, ME-BERT, and ColBERT. It also combined well with advanced training tricks such as retrieval-oriented pre-training and hard negative mining.
arxiv-2509-23961:
Testing a neural network with adversarial inputs works better when the most fault-revealing cases run first. Sheikh Md Mushfiqur Rahman and Nasir Eisty fuse Learning-Based Testing with hypothesis and mutation testing to order those cases. Their method picks adversarial inputs likely to expose faults without leaning on architecture details or formal verification, so it adapts across network designs. Coverage and confidence heuristics, by contrast, often miss the sharpest tests.

Across data sets, architectures, and attack methods, the approach beat baselines at surfacing faults and found all faults much faster. It also preserves input diversity and guides retraining, which the authors cite as practical wins.
arxiv-2509-24061:
Special curves earn their names from how they sit with respect to their own frames. Fatma Almaz and Handan Oztekin sort these curves inside four-dimensional pseudo-Galilean space, a setting with its own distance rules. They describe a general admissible curve through its curvature functions, the values that say how it bends and twists.

The pair then give tests for named types: position, osculating, normal, and rectifying curves, plus slant helices and spherical curves. Each type gets a condition that is both needed and enough to certify it. Such tests pin down each named type in this space.
arxiv-2509-24161:
DNA can store data for a long time at high density, but stray inserted symbols corrupt the message. Hengfeng Liu and 2 co-authors study a noisy insertion channel tuned to how DNA errors behave. Insertions may repeat or mirror the true symbol many times, and noise can add at most one random insertion on top.

The team determines the coding capacity of this channel, the highest rate at which data can still be recovered in full. They also construct error-correcting codes that come close to that limit as they grow. The pair of results pins down both the best possible rate and a concrete way to near it.
arxiv-2510-00361:
Hita Kambhamettu and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on helping people verify AI answers that cite sources. Systems now attach attributions to their claims, yet checking each citation by hand is impractical. The authors propose attribution gradients, an interface that unfolds evidence step by step. A reader first splits an answer sentence into its separate claims.

For each claim, the interface shows supporting and contradictory excerpts mined from the sources. Color coding marks direct support, direct contradiction, and secondhand references at a glance. Clicking an excerpt leads into the source paper, and nested citations unfold further still. In a usability study, participants revised AI answers with the tool and a plain baseline. Revisions made with attribution gradients scored higher in quality by expert judges. Engagement with the underlying sources also ran deeper across nearly all gradient levels.
arxiv-2510-00561:
Henrik Pichler, Janis Keuper, and Matthew Copping published this 2025 paper on counting mold colonies with far less hand labeling. Technicians tally colonies on Petri dishes to judge indoor air quality and ventilation. Automating the count traditionally demands thousands of annotated images and long training. The team assembled five thousand annotated dish images, then carved out small curated subsets.

Three vision foundation models faced traditional detectors under few-shot and low-shot conditions. One model, MaskDINO, nearly matched a heavily trained YOLO detector after fine-tuning on just one hundred fifty images. With only twenty-five images, it still performed reliably on roughly seventy percent of samples. The authors argue exhaustive annotation is no longer a prerequisite for new vision tasks. Their suggested workflow annotates a little, deploys early, then grows the dataset through use. Colony species differentiation is the planned next frontier.
arxiv-2510-00661:
Yang and five co-authors report magneto-absorption measurements on cuprous oxide in pulsed fields up to five hundred tesla, in this 2025 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. Excitons in Cu2O form a hydrogen-like yellow series, and crushing their wavefunctions with magnetic fields tests where the effective mass approximation breaks down. That breakdown should appear once the magnetic length shrinks to the crystal's own lattice scale, a regime earlier experiments could not reach.

The team assigned the strong low-energy features to Zeeman-split 2p and 3p exciton states and extracted a reduced effective mass from the high-field data. Above roughly three hundred tesla, the ground-state transition suddenly broadened far more than expected. The authors read that jump as possible evidence of Harper broadening. It would mark the first sighting of the effective mass picture failing at the natural lattice scale.
arxiv-2510-00761:
Lang and five co-authors study how the choice of optimizer affects machine unlearning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Unlearning aims to remove the influence of unwanted data from a trained language model while keeping its other skills. Recent work showed that this forgetting is fragile, since quantization or light fine-tuning can undo it. Most fixes change the unlearning objective itself.

The authors instead vary the optimizer, from gradient-free zeroth-order methods up to second-order ones. Surprisingly, simpler optimizers often produced forgetting that resisted later tampering far better. Their noisier updates settle into flatter regions that are harder to disturb. Building on that insight, they propose a hybrid optimizer mixing first-order and zeroth-order updates. Experiments show the hybrid keeps unlearning strength while adding clear robustness against post-training changes.
arxiv-2510-01261:
Palit defends federated learning systems against poisoned participants by teaching a controller to manage trust over time. Hospitals and phones train shared models without sharing raw data, but malicious clients can sabotage the result. Partial observability makes spotting them a sequential guessing game.

A trust-aware deep Q-network fuses multiple weak signals into running trust scores for each client. Experiments on a standard image dataset showed accuracy rising while attack success fell as client overlap grew. Shrinking the signal budget hurt detection, yet sequential belief updates cushioned the loss. Against simpler controllers, the learning approach achieved the best robustness-accuracy balance. CIFAR images supplied the shared training task for the federation. Backdoor and poisoning attacks are the threats under study. Long-horizon objectives keep the defender from overreacting to noise. Trust bands separated suspected clients visibly in the traces over rounds.
arxiv-2510-01861:
Casarin, Craiu, and Wang compress tensor regressions before running Bayesian inference in this 2025 statistics paper. Tensor-valued predictors carry so many entries that standard Bayesian fits become slow and unstable. Their answer is a generalized random projection that embeds the tensors into far smaller subspaces. The projection can act on the whole tensor, on single modes, or on a mix of both.

A hierarchical prior and a low-rank parameter form keep the Bayesian model structured after compression. The authors prove the projection concentrates information well and that the posterior stays consistent. A Gibbs sampler performs inference on the compressed data at much lower cost. Bayesian model averaging, with constants estimated by reverse logistic regression, softens the randomness of any single projection. Simulations and a real-data application both favored the compressed method. It predicted better out of sample than the full Bayesian tensor regression while costing far less.
arxiv-2510-01961:
Mangal and four co-authors package scientific document styling into a modular LaTeX framework in this 2025 paper. Manuscripts usually gain their visual emphasis from ad-hoc formatting choices. Those choices clash across papers and break when documents move between templates. The ktbox framework replaces them with semantic, reusable components.

Separate modules handle semantic color palettes, structured highlight boxes, taxonomy trees, and ORCID-linked author metadata. Each part works alone, yet all interoperate under one naming scheme. Features include auto-numbered takeaway boxes, wide-format highlights, and flexible tree diagrams. Multi-column layouts can embed tables, lists, and code blocks inside the boxes. The system fits major templates such as IEEEtran, acmart, ICLR, and beamer slides. By treating styling as a building block rather than decoration, the framework improves consistency and portability. Authors can restyle a paper, poster, or talk without rewriting its markup.
arxiv-2510-02161:
Zeng compares the two workhorse losses of deep metric learning in this 2025 paper. Contrastive loss and triplet loss both teach embeddings to cluster by meaning. Practitioners choose between them largely by habit, since their effects on representation quality are poorly understood. Zeng studies them through class variance and optimization behavior.

Triplet loss preserved more variance both within and across classes in the experiments. That extra spread supports finer distinctions between similar items. Contrastive loss compacted same-class embeddings tightly, which can hide subtle semantic differences. Optimization traces told a matching story: contrastive loss makes many small early updates. Triplet loss makes fewer, stronger updates and keeps learning from hard examples. Across classification and retrieval on four datasets, triplet loss won consistently. The author recommends triplet loss where fine detail and hard examples matter most. Contrastive loss still suits tasks where compact clusters matter most.
arxiv-2510-02461:
Lie, Simonsen, and Dommersnes find turbulence-like behavior inside active elastic solids. Their 2025 physics paper simulates a model of self-driven solid matter. Active solids include bacterial colonies and sheets of migrating cells. The team tracked how polar order develops in the material. Energy spectra followed classic power law scaling. Velocity jump statistics turned out non-Gaussian. Both traits are hallmarks of turbulent dynamics. Yet the system showed no energy cascade between scales. That absence matches earlier findings in active fluids.

The results extend active turbulence ideas from fluids to solids. Living tissues are solids that crawl, heal, and reshape themselves. Turbulent style analysis may help describe their motion. The authors note that nonlinear elasticity could change the picture. Real cell sheets carry such elasticity in abundance. Experiments on motile cell layers can test the predictions. Synthetic active matter offers another test bed.
arxiv-2510-02561:
Shi and co-authors fine-tune video-language models with rankings from an AI oracle instead of costly scores. Their 2025 machine learning paper rebuilds a common training pipeline. Human preference data gets expensive as video models grow. Earlier AI feedback systems trained a separate reward model. That reward model needed costly calibration on video narratives. Oracle-RLAIF swaps the scorer for a ranker. The oracle simply orders candidate answers from best to worst. A new algorithm, GRPO-rank, learns directly from those orderings. It adapts a group based policy method to ranked feedback.

Benchmarks for video and text understanding tested the framework. The method outperformed leading fine-tuning approaches directly. A drop-in ranker also travels across tasks more easily. Audio and other modalities are next on their list. Preference training without human panels gets cheaper. Ranking is a weaker demand than scoring, yet it suffices.
arxiv-2510-03261:
Coelho and co-authors predict a machine tool's full temperature field so any thermal error can be corrected downstream. Heat warps precision machines and ruins machining accuracy. Thermal effects cause up to three quarters of positioning errors. Older neural methods predict one error type at one spot. Such models shatter when the machine setup changes. This framework predicts temperature and heat flux everywhere instead. Error computation then becomes a swappable downstream module.

Finite element simulations generated the training data under varied starts. A correlation strategy picks the most informative sensor points. Few physical sensors are then needed at run time. Six time-series architectures entered the benchmark. Recurrent, gated, attention, and convolutional designs all competed. Specialized and general models were trained side by side. General models had to extrapolate to unseen conditions. Predictions proved accurate and cheap across the board. Flexible correction for many error types becomes possible.
arxiv-2510-03361:
Kayyam, Gopal, and Lewis present a 2025 arXiv paper on neural networks that can point to the training examples behind each answer. Most networks compress data into smooth inner codes and lose track of single examples. Their provenance networks keep those links by design. Each output is justified by concrete past examples, weighted by how relevant they are. The model behaves much like a learned nearest neighbor system with deep features.

Training optimizes the main task and the explanation goal at the same time. Users can check whether a given input sat inside the training set. The links also expose mislabeled or odd training points that may poison results. Tests in the paper probe how memorization trades against broad generalization. Extra computing cost and modest data scale remain limits for now. Still, built in evidence trails could help users trust models in medicine, law, and other high stakes fields.
arxiv-2510-03461:
Malakar and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper automatically repairing resource leaks in Java programs, including leaks hidden inside wrapper classes. Programs leak sockets, file handles, and database connections when code forgets to release them, and the damage surfaces only after long runs. Detectors find leaks, but repair tools only handled a list of library resource types. Real code wraps resources in classes that store them in fields. The team's tool, Arodnap, infers resource management rules for those wrappers, transforms programs to expose root causes, and reasons about how long fields hold resources.

On the NJR benchmark, Arodnap fixed sixty eight percent of leak warnings. The prior managed forty one percent. A repair pattern for resources stored in non final fields accounted for part of the jump.
arxiv-2510-03761:
Dubniczky and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper auditing one hundred thousand arXiv submissions for secrets hiding in their source files. Preprint servers distribute not just PDFs but the LaTeX sources, files, and author comments, with no sanitization. Their four stage framework, LaTeXpOsEd, mixes pattern matching, logical filtering, harvesting, and language models to find disclosures. They built a benchmark to grade twenty five models at spotting secrets. The audit combed through more than a terabyte of source data.

The haul included thousands of personal data leaks and location tagged photo files. Editable SharePoint links, shared Drive and Dropbox folders, and exposed GitHub, Google, and cloud credentials all surfaced. Confidential reviewer material and internal author arguments were public. Hundreds of exposed credentials granted access to private accounts and documents. The authors released their tools but withheld the findings. Any researcher who has uploaded a source bundle should treat this as a warning.
arxiv-2510-03861:
Ma and Ye present this 2025 arXiv paper developing optimality theory for minimax problems whose inner feasible set depends on the outer decision. Such coupled constraints appear in adversarial training and generative adversarial networks, and they break classical theory: even nice problems can violate the max-min inequality or become NP-hard. A recently introduced notion, the calm local minimax point, weakens local optimality in a way suited to these difficulties. The authors extend that notion to nonsmooth, nonconvex-nonconcave problems with coupled constraints.

They derive comprehensive first-order and second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for calm local minimax points. Because the framework unifies earlier formulations, several known results reappear under weaker assumptions than they originally required. The second-order conditions come in matched necessary and sufficient forms with no gap. For practitioners, sharper optimality conditions are what algorithms for robust training can actually target and verify.
arxiv-2510-04361:
Iszály and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper comparing two theories of magnetic nanoparticle heating for focused cancer therapy. Injected metallic nanoparticles collect in tumors and convert an alternating magnetic field into local heat. Combining alternating and static fields can superlocalize the heating where the static field vanishes, sparing healthy tissue. Heating arises either from the particle physically rotating or from its magnetic moment rotating internally.

The first mechanism follows the Martsenyuk-Raikher-Shliomis equation and the second the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation. Using magnetic and ordinary viscosity concepts, the authors place both frameworks on common ground for direct comparison. At low frequencies and large field amplitudes, perpendicular alternating and static fields gave better spatial focusing in the Brownian regime. The authors propose that perpendicular geometry for image-guided thermal therapy combined with magnetic particle imaging. Better focusing is the difference between a tumor treatment and collateral tissue damage.
arxiv-2510-04461:
Yuntian Wang, Lizhu Sun, and Changjiang Bu wrote this 2025 paper in graph theory on limits for networks with no long cycles. Classic results from 1959 cap the number of edges in a graph that avoids long cycles or long paths. Many later versions replaced edge counts with spectral measures of the graph. A newer measure, introduced in 2023, reads the spectral radius of a tensor built from cliques. The team used that measure to remake the classic results.

They found the exact graphs that reach the highest value of the new measure under each ban. One family of graphs avoids cycles of a set length or more. The other family avoids paths on a set number of vertices. Naming the extremal graphs matters because they show where the true boundary lies. The proofs employ the clique based tensor that defines the measure.
arxiv-2510-04661:
Kirill Boguslavski wrote this 2025 overview paper on the first instants of heavy ion collisions. When two nuclei crash, quarks and gluons form a soup that later becomes quark gluon plasma. The stage before that plasma settles is hard to describe and rich in physics. These proceedings gather the talks and posters of the Quark Matter 2025 meeting on that stage. Boguslavski surveys the theory of the early matter and ways to probe it.

Work has built a weak coupling picture of how the plasma reaches flow behavior. Teams now push that picture toward three dimensional dynamics and into models that face data. Hard probes, energetic particles that cross the fireball, may reveal the early stage as they pass. Small collision systems offer a test bed for the same questions. The overview weighs what is settled and what remains open about the state. It maps where simulations, kinetic theory, and experiment meet.
arxiv-2510-04961:
Théophane Vallaeys, Jakob Verbeek, and Matthieu Cord present a faster building block for image generators in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generators first compress an image into a compact code, then decode that code back into pixels. The standard decoder design is slow to train and can blur fine detail. Their replacement decodes in a single step.

Their system, SSDD, trains a diffusion decoder without any adversarial losses. A distillation step then squeezes the multi-step decoder into one fast pass. On ImageNet, SSDD cut the reconstruction error score from 0.87 for the standard design to a value of 0.50 in their tests. It also sampled faster while keeping image quality. The decoder can drop into existing generators in place of the old one.
arxiv-2510-05061:
Anastasios Manganaris, Vittorio Giammarino, and Ahmed H. Qureshi teach robots to follow ordered instructions safely in this 2025 arXiv paper. A warehouse robot must visit stations in sequence while avoiding hazards. Safety rules can also change over time. Standard reinforcement learning struggles to honor both demands at once.

Their algorithm, ACQL, pairs goal-conditioned value learning with guidance from an automaton. The automaton encodes each task written in linear temporal logic. It tracks stage-by-stage progress and both fixed and shifting safety constraints. Across continuous control tasks, ACQL beat existing methods, including cases where rivals failed outright. The team also deployed it on a real six-axis robot arm working inside a cluttered cabinet.
arxiv-2510-05261:
Yuezhu Xu and S. Sivaranjani make neural network safety certificates fast enough to use in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Lipschitz constant bounds how much a network's output can change when inputs wiggle. That number certifies robustness against perturbations. Computing it exactly is NP-hard, and standard estimates need huge semidefinite programs.

Their framework breaks the big estimation problem into small sequential sub-problems. Cost then scales linearly with network depth instead of exploding. A closed-form variant answers almost instantly while keeping strict guarantees. Local versions use information about the specific input region for tighter bounds. In small regions the estimates approach the exact Jacobian values. Experiments showed large speedups and bounds that track real network robustness closely.
arxiv-2510-05961:
Buchner and four coauthors present a software package for charged particle simulations in 2025. The package, called msmJAX, computes electric forces between many particles at once. Direct sums grow too costly as particle counts rise, so fast methods are vital. Their method splits the force by scale and grows only in a straight line. It builds on JAX, a framework made for fast array math and learning.

The code runs on graphics chips and stays easy to deploy for users. Forces and stresses come from automatic tracing of the energy value. Users can reshape its modular parts to fit new tasks or new physics. Tests confirm the promised straight line growth and accurate energies in test systems. Runs with charged argon stay stable, with no drift in total energy. The tool suits machine learned potentials that need long range forces in chemistry.
arxiv-2510-06161:
Bober, Klurman, and Shala prove distributional results for mixed character sums in a 2025 number theory paper. A mixed character sum blends a Dirichlet character with an oscillating exponential term. They study its statistics two ways: twist angle fixed with random character, and character fixed with random angle.

The results feed several extremal problems about polynomials. They construct Littlewood polynomials, with coefficients only plus or minus one, having unusually large Mahler measure and average size. Those constructions set records in the Mahler and Newman problems. They also show that even norms of the classic Turyn polynomials are minimized at a quarter shift. That settles a Günther and Schmidt conjecture. A general log-integrability method powers much of the argument. The work links random character sums to record-holding polynomials, bridging analytic number theory and extremal combinatorics.
arxiv-2510-06461:
Daul, Tosolini, and Bowern show language-aware tokenization makes speech recognition work for a dormant language in a 2025 language science paper. Modern speech recognition uses data-hungry transformers, leaving small languages without tools. The team fine-tuned wav2vec2 on Yan-nhangu, a dormant Indigenous Australian language.

Two tokenization schemes faced off. Orthographic tokens follow the practical spelling system. Phonemic tokens encode the language's actual sound units. The phonemic system sharply improved word and letter error rates. The gain held against the orthographic baseline throughout. A second test timed the documentation workflow. Fixing model output by hand proved much faster than writing transcripts from scratch. Together, the results argue speech recognition belongs in documentation work today. The study treats recognition as one stage in saving dying languages, alongside transcription and archiving. Careful token choices, not just more data, unlock performance where data barely exists.
arxiv-2510-06661:
Hamidreza Montazeri and Milad Siami work on proving that AI-controlled machines stay safe. Their 2025 paper certifies stability for systems run by neural network controllers. Two realistic risks complicate that proof. Signals arrive with time delays, and the system's parameters are known only within ranges.

Their method bounds the controller's local behavior and exploits a positivity structure in the system. That yields simple linear certificates that guarantee stability near the operating point. The certificates do not depend on the delay size, which is a strong feature. The authors benchmarked their tests against a leading verification pipeline based on semidefinite programming. Their tests ran orders of magnitude faster in the cases studied. They also certified cases that the benchmark method could not handle at all. Faster, delay-proof checks could help clear autonomous vehicles, aircraft, and medical devices for real use.
arxiv-2510-06761:
Zhi Zhang and five co-authors automate scientific research with two cooperating loops of AI agents. Their 2025 paper presents the DLMA framework. Automating research end to end is hard for two reasons. Plans must be fresh and sound, and then someone must carry them out under messy, changing conditions.

The first loop plays the role of professors who evolve research plans. Through structured meetings, candidate proposals are generated, improved, and merged over generations. The second loop plays doctoral students who execute the best plan. They adjust steps during the work, with meetings before and after each task. Steps like drafting and coding stay supported by fresh observations. On benchmarks named ACLAward and Laboratory, the system wrote papers with top automated scores. It beat strong baseline systems by a clear margin. The split mirrors how human labs separate planning from bench work.
arxiv-2510-07061:
Amir Yari, Kalmit Kulkarni, Ahmad Khan, and Fajri Koto check whether the yardsticks for translation work in Indian languages. Their 2025 paper presents ITEM, a benchmark that tests the metrics. Scoring metrics steer translation and summarization. Most of them were built and checked on English or other rich-resource languages.

ITEM tests twenty-six metrics against human judgments in six Indian languages. Fine-grained labels mark quality aspects like faithfulness and coverage. The tests probe agreement with humans, outlier effects, and strength under noise. Four findings emerged from the study. Language-model judges aligned with human ratings most strongly. One compact model topped summarization across all languages. A purpose-built translation system led on translation for most languages. Metrics split by task, favoring fidelity for summaries and fluency for translation. Noise exposed weakness in many metrics. ITEM gives metric builders a testbed for a fifth of the world.
arxiv-2510-07161:
Norouzifar, Kourani, Dees, and Van der Aalst bring expert knowledge into process mining with help from language models. Their 2025 paper addresses a gap in how firms map their own workflows. Software logs show what happened, step by step. Yet logs can be noisy or incomplete. Experts know rules the logs never state. Models built from logs alone may show paths that real rules forbid.

Their framework asks experts to state knowledge in plain words. A language model turns those statements into formal rules. A discovery algorithm then builds the workflow model under those rules. The team built a working tool around this loop. They tested several models and prompt styles in an extensive study. A case study checked the approach on a real process. Adding expert rules should yield workflow maps that managers can trust for checks and redesign.
arxiv-2510-07261:
Leon, Cardoso, and Berland compute how collective electron waves behave inside twenty-five pure metals. Their 2025 paper studies bulk plasmons, the ripples of charge that run through a metal's electron sea. The team used first-principles calculations at a standard level of many-body theory. From the results they built spectral band maps showing plasmon energies across momenta. A compact analytic model, extended from their earlier work, captures the main excitations across both frequency and momentum.

The maps reveal rich structure: non-parabolic dispersions, direction-dependent breaks, and bands that cross or avoid each other. Computed spectra matched laboratory data well in the optical limit. The dispersions run much flatter than a free-electron picture would predict. The catalog gives spectroscopists a reference for interpreting measurements. It also guides plasmonic device design, where exact loss shapes decide what is buildable.
arxiv-2510-07361:
Geeraerts, Herbreteau, Raskin, and Reynouard revisit timed games, where two players race moves against clocks. Their 2025 paper builds on a well-known semantics for such games. Parity objectives decide the winner by the pattern of priorities seen over an infinite play. Controller synthesis needs algorithms that handle both time and parity. The authors first adjust the semantics, arguing that some original rulings clash with synthesis intuition. They then build a zone-based algorithm, zones being the standard compact way to bundle clock values.

The algorithm is implemented with a mature zone library from the UppAal tool family. The prototype shows the approach is feasible on test games. In their benchmarks, calculation time grew linearly with the number of edges. A naive cap on zone size would have caused exponential blow-up instead. Two timing variants kept that linear behavior at different speeds.
arxiv-2510-07461:
Hale and De Silva calculate how graphene sheets could sort hydrogen isotopes by quantum tunneling. Their 2025 paper targets a separation problem with medical and fusion-energy stakes. Heavy hydrogen, deuterium, is valuable but mixed with ordinary hydrogen in nature. Passing the gas through two-dimensional graphene exploits the isotopes' different masses: their tunneling and sticking probabilities through the carbon sheet differ. The authors use a recent analytic potential between hydrogen and graphene carbon atoms. They compute classical trajectories near the sheet, then apply several quantum methods to get tunneling and sticking rates for each isotope.

The calculations indicate an effective enrichment route for deuterium with a high separation factor. The method also looks economically feasible compared with incumbent industrial processes. The authors are candid about approximations: estimated interaction parameters and a simplified potential very close to the surface.
arxiv-2510-07561:
Pathirana and Werner prove that randomness in a quantum chain's construction does not destroy its correlation structure. Their 2025 paper studies stochastically generated matrix product states, the workhorse ansatz for one-dimensional quantum systems. Here the local tensors are drawn from a common distribution as a stationary sequence, with no assumption that neighboring tensors are independent. Under natural conditions on the associated transfer operators, the authors prove thermodynamic limits exist for expectations of local observables. Two-point correlations decay almost surely and exponentially with distance.

The independent case sharpens the guarantee: the probability of seeing slow decay itself vanishes exponentially in distance.
