Their method builds upper and lower bounds step by step. Bounds certify accuracy, unlike point guesses. Sequential bounds can stop once tight enough. Certified moments serve signal processing and Bayesian learning, where downstream choices rest on those values. Sequential bounds adapt to hardness, spending steps where the integral resists and stopping early where the shape is tame and clear.
arxiv-2512-01861:
How much can the simplest neural network remember? A 2025 paper by Yingying Xu, Masayuki Ohzeki, and Yoshiyuki Kabashima studies the perceptron. The perceptron is a basic model of how neurons compute. The paper asks how many patterns it can store when it may choose which inputs to use.

The question matters because real data have many dimensions. They are full of chance links that look like real structure. By adding variable selection to the classic storage problem, the authors test how picking the right inputs changes what the model can hold. The work speaks to anyone trying to sort real signal from noise in large data sets.
arxiv-2512-02161:
Text-to-image models produce striking pictures that often quietly disobey the prompt: wrong counts, wrong colors, wrong attributes. Kevin David Hayes and five co-authors introduce FineGRAIN in 2025, a framework for grading those failures in fine detail using vision-language models as judges.

The sheer variety of prompt-following errors calls for a hierarchy of checks rather than a single score. FineGRAIN compares models on how faithfully they render specified attributes in user prompts. Dependable grading matters because these generators now serve designers and advertisers whose instructions are exact, and small disobediences are real defects.
arxiv-2512-02361:
Vision-language models learn from mountains of real data, yet can still flub basic perception that ordinary vision models handle easily. Zhengzhuo Xu and five co-authors revisit in 2025 an underused remedy, visual data augmentation, and rethink it for these multimodal models under the name VACoT.

Augmentation, deliberately varying training images, is a cornerstone of robust vision training but has drawn little attention for vision-language models. The authors argue that targeted augmentation can repair weak perception without endless data collection. Stronger basic perception is a foundation skill: every higher-level visual reasoning task inherits its errors.
arxiv-2512-02461:
Peng Zhang and seven co-authors work on keeping wireless signals private at the physical level. Future systems may use fluid antennas, whose parts can shift position, inside near field links with many antennas at once. Working close to the antennas gives new ways to shape and protect a signal.

Their 2025 study adds planned noise that harms eavesdroppers more than the true receiver. Beam shaping and the added noise are designed together, for both compact and large antenna arrays. The goal is strong privacy built into the radio link itself, not just into software above it. Strong links that stay private are a key need for the next wave of phones.
arxiv-2512-02661:
Alexander Van Werde and Jaron Sanders study how fast a wandering particle mixes when walls partly block it. Brownian motion models random wandering, here inside a smooth flat region. Semipermeable barriers, drawn as closed curves, slow the crossing between zones.

The pair bounds the mixing time above and the steady distribution below, using geometric features of the domain. Barriers that are hard to cross keep the particle unevenly spread for longer. Such estimates inform models of diffusion in cells, porous media, and other spaces where membranes shape random motion. The bounds hold for a wide class of walls, so labs can use them with shapes they meet in real cells.
arxiv-2512-02861:
Oscar G. Lira, Oscar M. Caicedo, and Nelson L. S. Da Fonseca automate network setup with small, locally run language models. Modern networks keep growing in scale and complexity, so manual configuration turns slow and error prone. Large models can configure from stated intent, but they cost heavy compute and raise privacy worries in the cloud.

Fine tuned small models offer a leaner route that can stay on site. The team builds network self configuration around such models. Local automation could cut configuration errors while keeping sensitive network details inside the owner's walls. Small tools that run on site keep keys and maps at home, a trait big cloud tools can not match with ease.
arxiv-2512-03061:
Paulina Kaczyńska, Julian Sienkiewicz, and Dominik Ślęzak bring a classic explanation method to graph neural networks that predict links. Accumulated Local Effects show how one feature's value shifts a model's output, averaging over the data. Link prediction asks which missing connections a network will form next.

The authors adapt the method to visualize how node features influence link predictions. Both graph convolutional and graph attention networks serve as test models. Clearer explanations help analysts trust link forecasts used in fraud detection, biology, and recommendation systems. Plots that show which trait did the work let a team fix the trait, not just curse the tool. That counts when a call goes wrong in the field late at night.
arxiv-2512-03161:
A matrix model of physics may hold new shapes of space. Henry Liao and Reishi Maeta study the Euclidean IKKT matrix model in this 2025 work. They look at its equation of motion and seek new steady solutions, called saddles.

They find a new type of saddle that exists only as the matrix size grows without bound. Assuming the matrices match a known symmetry algebra, they identify a unique solution. From it, a geometry emerges. Such work probes how space itself might arise from matrices in quantum gravity research. Emergent geometry from matrices remains a bold idea, and each exact solution tests its reach.
arxiv-2512-03661:
Steering a generative model away from toxic output usually means nudging its internal activations in a fixed direction. Alex Ferrando and colleagues point out a weakness in that habit in a 2025 machine learning preprint. A fixed nudge is applied to every input, even harmless ones, and the unnecessary push can damage the quality of ordinary answers.

Their framework, Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering, separates whether to steer from the steering method itself. It computes scaling factors from context, adjusting strength across layers and inputs. It pushes hard only when unwanted behaviour shows up. The scaling can also be trained jointly with the steering function. In tests, adding this control improved the balance between reducing toxicity and keeping the model useful. The team also applied it to an image diffusion model, adjusting specific visual concepts with little extra computing cost.
arxiv-2512-04161:
GJ 436 b is a warm Neptune whose atmosphere has dodged characterisation for years. A. Peláez-Torres and a large team combine five CARMENES transits and one CRIRES+ transit to squeeze the tightest limits yet, in a 2025 preprint. Stellar and telluric contamination is scrubbed from the data before the hunt for molecular signals begins.

No molecules were detected, consistent with earlier attempts. Injection tests and Bayesian retrievals then map what the silence means. Either high-altitude clouds near the one-millibar level mute the spectrum at modest metallicities. Or the atmosphere is enormously metal-rich, hundreds of times the solar value, suppressing features on its own. The joint dataset gives the most stringent constraints to date on this planet. Simulations of the coming ELT's ANDES instrument suggest the boost needed to settle the question, possibly within a single transit.
arxiv-2512-04561:
Yuksel Arslantas, Ahmed Said Donmez, Ege Yuceel, and Felix Grezes study a defender that learns, facing an attacker who knows everything. Reinforcement learning now guards power grids and other vital systems, adapting its defense from experience. That learning itself opens a hole: a savvy attacker can steer what the defender learns. Prior work showed the risk in simple repeated games. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends the study to stochastic games with linked nodes.

The team uses a tractable linear influence network, where pressure spreads between tied sites. They solve the attacker's side with neuro-dynamic programming, a blend of neural nets and classic planning. In experiments, the all-knowing attacker beat a naive learning defender by wide margins. The attacker bent the defender's lessons toward weak spots. The results warn that adaptive defense must be tested against foes who study the learning itself, not just the system.
arxiv-2512-04761:
Yizi Chen, Sidi Wu, Tianyi Xiao, and co-authors present VRSketch2Shape, the first system that builds three-dimensional shapes from virtual reality sketches while honoring stroke order. Drawing in VR lets designers think in space, faster than classic CAD. Older sketch-to-shape tools flatten a sketch into one picture, throwing away the sequence that reveals structure and intent. Their 2025 arXiv paper keeps the sequence and learns from it.

The team built a pipeline that turns any shape into a plausible stroke order, then assembled tens of thousands of synthetic pairs plus hundreds of hand-drawn ones across four categories. An order-aware encoder reads the stroke stream, and a diffusion generator grows the shape. Results beat prior tools in geometric fidelity. The system also transfers from synthetic practice to real hand sketches with little supervision, a step toward design tools that think in strokes.
arxiv-2512-04961:
Gabrielle Nornberg and Ricardo Ziegele study a class of partial differential equations built to resemble harmonic maps, the energy-minimizing layouts that appear across geometry and physics. The equations are fully nonlinear and evenly elliptic, which makes them hard. Their behavior is governed by the extreme curvatures of the unknown function. That runs through operators named after Pucci, together with terms for slope, growth, and forcing. The authors ask when solutions exist and how large they can grow.

Working on smooth bounded domains, they prove existence when the coefficients stay small. They also rebuild the standard toolkit for this class. It includes a ceiling estimate of Aleksandrov, Bakelman, and Pucci type, a comparison principle, and growth bounds for the boundary-value problem, even when the equation lacks a helpful damping term. They also show that multiple solutions can occur, with some results new even for the classic Laplacian case.
arxiv-2512-05061:
Thomas Sangy, Nicolò Burzillà, Breno Giacchini, and Tibério de Paula Netto examine the weak-field limit of nonlocal gravity. These theories smear gravity's response over a small distance rather than letting it act point by point. Each model in the family is set by an exponential form factor with its own sharpness and scale. The authors ask how the models differ where gravity is weak — the regime of the Newtonian potential around a mass.

Using an effective-source method, they compare the smeared stand-ins for a point mass, the resulting mass profiles, and the potentials, through series, integrals, and special functions, plus simple approximations for practical use. Only the sharper models make the potential oscillate, yet the effective masses stay positive, and none of the solutions hides a singularity. They also compute the leading quantum correction here, mapping what weak-field tests could distinguish.
arxiv-2512-05261:
Roberto Mazzoleni and Hamza Virk model how a lone antibiotic maker defends its market when a rival looms. The setting matters beyond profit: every course of antibiotics sold today breeds resistance that erodes the drug's value, so an incumbent's output decision is a conservation decision. The authors build a two-period model in which a differentiated rival may enter, after which they compete head-to-head on price.

Price competition of that kind produces a winner-take-all outcome. Against that threat, the incumbent's best move is strategic deterrence — and the authors find deterrence is optimal regardless of how much cross-resistance the bacteria develop to the rival drug. Compared with quantity-based competition, a looming price war gives the incumbent a stronger incentive to conserve the drug. The analysis links strategy to stewardship: how competition unfolds after entry changes how much of a drug's usefulness is spent today.
arxiv-2512-06261:
Taekyung Kim and five co authors present a planner that charts safe paths for robots while honoring how they can actually move. Diffusion based planners can dream up smooth routes, but a route that looks fine may break a safety rule or ask for a turn the machine cannot make. Fixing the route after the fact can be slow, or can break it again.

Their planner, Safe MPD, builds the checks into every step of the path making process. Each draft path is screened for safety and for fit with the machine's motion limits as it is refined, so the final path is sound by design. Tests used hard cases with sharp bends, even a truck pulling a trailer. The method beat rival safety schemes on success and safety, and it ran in under a second. It suits robots that must plan fast in tight, risky spaces.
arxiv-2512-07361:
Giuseppe Leo and co-authors build a silicon neuron that hums before it fires. Most artificial neurons simply accumulate input and spike; resonate-and-fire neurons, modeled on cells that pace oscillations in the brain. Prefer inputs arriving at their favorite frequency, making them natural filters for time-varying signals. The team fabricates one in standard CMOS technology as a mixed-signal circuit, aiming at analog computing at the edge, where processing locally saves the energy of storing and shipping data.

The chip communicates asynchronously, shaking hands with its neighbors only when events occur, in the spirit of real neural tissue. The authors characterize how reliably it detects frequencies and how much its behavior varies across fabricated copies, the unglamorous tests that decide whether a design can scale. Their results support large-scale integration into neuromorphic systems.
arxiv-2512-07461:
Tong Wu, Yang Liu, and Jun Bai wrote this 2025 machine learning paper with Zixia Jia and four co-authors. Language models usually reason step by step in a single chain. The authors want models that can truly reason along several branches at once.

Their framework, Native Parallel Reasoner, needs no teacher model to learn from. A self-distilled training plan moves the model from finding the right format to obeying strict branching rules. A new optimization method, PAPO, trains the branching policy inside the execution graph itself. The model then learns by trial and error when to split a problem apart. A rebuilt engine handles memory and flow control for large-scale parallel training. Tests cover eight reasoning benchmarks using a mid-size open model. Scores rise clearly, and answers come several times faster than before. Unlike earlier attempts, the model runs in a fully parallel way every time.
arxiv-2512-07661:
Shihao Li and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on generating driving scenes for testing self-driving cars. Real logs of traffic rarely contain the dangerous moments that matter most. Synthetic scenes are cheaper, but they must obey physics and social sense.

Their framework, OMEGA, guides a diffusion model while it samples new scenes. It needs no extra training of the base model. After each reverse diffusion step, a constrained optimization re-anchors the scene. That steering pushes trajectories toward plausible, coherent behavior. The team also frames an ego-and-attacker contest as a game. Both sides are optimized toward a Nash equilibrium. The result is realistic yet safety-critical adversarial traffic on demand. Experiments use the nuPlan and Waymo datasets for evaluation. Valid scenes, physical and behavioral, rise sharply under OMEGA's guidance.  Near-collision frames multiply while overall scene realism holds steady.
arxiv-2512-07961:
Guilherme Seidyo Imai Aldeia, Joseph D. Romano, and three co-authors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Doctors lean on clinical scores that blend risk formulas with plain rules. Such scores stay trusted because clinicians can read and audit them.

Symbolic regression normally searches only smooth formulas and their constants. Rule-based branching, the grammar of real decision scores, escapes that search. Their new algorithm, Brush, fuses tree-like splitting into the regression itself. Nonlinear constant optimization runs alongside the split search in one method. Rule logic and smooth math thus live inside a single model. On the SRBench benchmark, Brush reaches Pareto-optimal performance overall. The authors then ask it to rebuild two famous clinical scoring systems. It recovers both with high accuracy and readable structure. Against decision trees, random forests, and rival methods, it holds its own. Simpler models at equal accuracy are exactly what medicine wants.
arxiv-2512-08061:
Ashkan Shahbazi, Ping He, Ali Abbasi, and colleagues, machine learning researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, LUNA, attacks a core cost problem in transformers: standard attention grows quadratically with sequence length, which blocks very long inputs. Linear attention methods cut that cost, but they rely on fixed random feature maps and usually lose accuracy.

LUNA makes the feature map itself learnable, so the kernel adapts to the data and the task at hand. The design keeps a valid positive definite kernel and a streaming form, giving linear time and memory in sequence length. On the Long Range Arena benchmark, LUNA reached the best average accuracy among efficient transformers under equal computing budgets. It also converted already trained BERT and vision transformer models, recovering most of their performance after brief fine tuning. That combination of theory, speed, and drop in use is the paper main appeal.
arxiv-2512-08261:
Yibowen Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Zhixiang Su, Lizhen Cui, and Chunyan Miao, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system predicts diseases from patient side information alone, meaning demographics and symptoms people report themselves. Such tools could raise patient awareness and prompt earlier care, but skewed disease frequencies and opaque reasoning often make predictions biased or hard to trust.

Their framework, called KPI, builds trusted medical knowledge into one disease knowledge graph. From it, the system constructs meaningful disease prototypes and uses contrastive learning to sharpen accuracy, especially for rare, long tail diseases. A large language model then writes patient specific explanations in medical terms the person can follow. In experiments on real world data, KPI beat leading methods on accuracy, and its explanations matched patient stories closely. The authors present it as a step toward healthcare tools patients can both use and understand.
arxiv-2512-08361:
Maxim Dvornikov, a theoretical physicist in Russia, posted a short proceedings paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is neutrino flavor oscillation, the change of one neutrino type into another, treated inside quantum field theory. In that framework neutrinos are virtual particles, and the math runs through propagators of the neutrino mass states.

In earlier work on oscillations in external fields, Dvornikov and his group split those propagators and kept only the particle part, dropping the antiparticle part. Here he carefully justifies that step, using the simpler case of oscillations in vacuum. The argument shows the transformation is valid, so the earlier shortcut rests on firm ground. He notes the reasoning should extend to the field theory treatment of oscillations in external fields. The paper appeared as a contribution to a long running seminar on high energy physics problems, held in Dubna.
arxiv-2512-08561:
John Anthony Dixon, a theoretical physicist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025, the eighth in his series on an Exotic Model of particle physics. The model modifies the supersymmetric standard model by adding an exotic invariant, which changes the supersymmetry algebra itself. That change gives the model a way to split particle masses without spontaneous supersymmetry breaking, the standard mechanism he regards as deeply unsatisfactory.

For the model to be viable, its basic action must not produce tachyons, which signal a broken theory. An earlier paper posed that question for the quadratic action. Here Dixon answers it for the fermionic sector, which contains four fermion fields. The tachyons disappear at tree level provided all four fields share the same mass. The result is demonstrated with a Mathematica notebook issued with the paper. One crucial viability check is passed.
arxiv-2512-08861:
Louis Boucherie and coauthors assemble a large data set to track how human beauty standards in media and fashion have changed over twenty five years. Through social comparison, beauty ideals shape health and self perception, yet long term quantitative and intersectional studies have been scarce. Their records cover advertising, magazine covers, runway shows, and editorials.

The team finds a paradox. Representation diversity has grown, yet the median model physique has stayed stable over the period. Growth is driven by selective plus size inclusion at the upper tail, while the typical physique keeps diverging from the general population in the United States. Non white models are far more likely to be plus size, so size inclusion falls unevenly across identities. A data driven prestige ranking shows thinness is overrepresented at the top tier. Comparing two policy interventions, numeric thresholds work better than other rules at reducing underweight appearances.
arxiv-2512-09061:
Dusan Begus, Chenyu Zhang, and J B Marston present Hamiltonian and Lagrangian forms for two dimensional quasi geostrophic fluid flow, linearized around a zonal basic state. The quasi geostrophic equations are a standard model for large scale air and ocean motion. Working with the linear form removes wave interactions that would otherwise cloud the structure.

Because of that absence, the forms show an endless symmetry of a simple phase type. By the theorem of Noether, that symmetry yields an endless set of conservation laws. The conserved quantities are the well known pseudomomenta of the flow. The authors stress that pseudomomentum is conserved on its own at each zonal wavenumber. Past treatments have sometimes hidden that separation. Clearing it up matters for how wave activity budgets are read in earth flows. The work gives a clean Lagrangian base for a conserved quantity widely used but not always derived with care.
arxiv-2512-09161:
Kizito Salako works on a classic problem in probability: bounding the chance of combined events when only the chances of the individual events are known. Results of this kind grow out of the Boole-Frechet inequalities, which give the sharpest possible bounds from such limited information. Salako presents a constructive way to compute the generalized version of these bounds.

His method uses dynamic programming, a technique that solves a large problem by storing and reusing the answers to smaller pieces of it. Rather than only proving that sharp bounds exist, the approach builds them step by step. That matters for anyone who must reason about compound events, such as several failures or several conditions holding together, while knowing only the separate event probabilities. The paper adds a practical computing route to a corner of probability theory that is often handled only in the abstract.
arxiv-2512-09861:
Michael L. Palumbo examines a standard shortcut in modeling the light of stars, and shows where it fails. Astronomers usually build a spectrum by computing thermal line shapes from a model atmosphere, then smearing them with a broadening kernel for rotation and turbulence. Palumbo shows the assumptions behind that smearing can break down at high spectral resolution, causing real errors in the modeled light. He then studies how rotation and turbulence affect contribution functions, which assign each spectral segment a formation height.

Handling two points carefully changes the answers a lot: the difference between intensity and total flux, and including rotation and turbulence inside the contribution functions. Modeled formation temperatures can shift dramatically. Palumbo supplies a software package computing these functions quickly from basic stellar properties. He closes by warning where the convolution shortcut should be avoided, and how a single formation temperature can oversimplify radiative transfer.
arxiv-2512-10061:
João Lucas Luz Lima Sarcinelli and Ricardo Marcondes Marcacini present Text2Graph, a cheaper way to classify text when labels are scarce. Big language models classify well with no training examples, but running them over huge collections costs computation, money, and carbon, a concern in high performance computing centers. Text2Graph is an open source Python package implementing text to graph classification. A language model labels only part of the data. A graph neural network then propagates those labels across a graph of similar texts, finishing the job at a fraction of the cost.

The package is modular, with swappable components. The authors benchmark it in a zero shot setting on five datasets covering topic classification and sentiment analysis, against zero shot methods. They also report energy use and carbon emissions. Graph propagation proved competitive with full language model annotation while spending only a fraction of the energy.
arxiv-2512-10161:
Emilio J. Estrada, Alejandro Miranda, and Pablo Roig review how Resonance Chiral Theory finds the hadronic contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. That quantity, how much the muon's magnetism deviates from the simplest prediction, is a precision battleground between theory and lab data. The stubborn part is hadronic: quarks bound inside particles, where the math is hard. The review covers the hadronic vacuum polarization, computed using data on electrons or tau decays into hadrons, and the hadronic light by light contribution, long the most uncertain piece.

Within light by light, the authors report settled results for the lightest pseudoscalar and tensor pole contributions. New here is the first costing of the pseudoscalar box contribution in this formalism. Scalar, axial pole, and other subleading pieces are also covered. The results agree with the community's White Paper values at similar precision.
arxiv-2512-10361:
Wei Shao and co-authors study how attackers can end up sharing the same physical machine as a victim in serverless cloud computing. Their paper, set for the NDSS Symposium in 2026, notes that renting space side by side is the first step toward side-channel attacks. Yet the schedulers that place each job had not been mapped for weakness in a full, practical way.

The team lays out a method to find features in scheduling software that an attacker can exploit through normal user accounts alone. They achieved co-location on widely used open-source systems and on Microsoft Azure Functions. They also propose a defense, the Double-Dip scheduler, and draw lessons for making serverless platforms harder to attack this way.
arxiv-2512-10461:
Haoyu Zhu and co-authors build neural networks that must respect hard linear constraints, a need in safety-critical work such as power grid optimisation, robot path planning, and self-driving. Earlier methods either cost too much computing or only handle narrow kinds of constraints. The team reaches instead for a randomised solver called the Sampling Kaczmarz-Motzkin method.

Their framework, T-SKM-Net, turns mixed problems into pure inequality problems through a null space change, solves them with the randomised method, then maps the answer back. The solver's key step is not differentiable, which normally blocks training, but the authors prove training still works using unbiased gradient estimates. On a standard power flow benchmark it ran far faster than a conventional solver, with a tiny optimality gap and no constraint violations within tolerance.
arxiv-2512-10561:
Amartya Roy and co-authors compare neural architectures on causal reasoning, the multi-step kind of thinking where several conditions must all hold at once. In-context learning drives modern language models, but the authors doubt it suffices here, since a model can lean on word associations instead of the causal chain. Their guess: models with encoders, which project input into a latent space, should reason more soundly.

They fine-tuned encoder, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only models and also tested plain in-context learning, in both ordinary language and artificial non-language tasks. Prompting alone proved unreliable and easily distracted by irrelevant features. Fine-tuned encoder models generalised robustly and resisted distribution shift, while decoder-only models were brittle and only caught up at large scale. For cheap, dependable causal reasoning, the authors recommend encoders with targeted fine-tuning.
arxiv-2512-10861:
Cade Lueker, Andrew Fox, and Bor-Yuh Evan Chang modularise abstract interpretation, the technique that reasons about all possible runs of a program at once. A truly flexible framework should let the analyst choose direction, forward or backward, sensitivity to paths and flow, and whether to over- or under-approximate. In practice, interpreters tangle syntax and semantics together, and existing modular designs lean on heavy machinery such as monad transformers that users find unwieldy.

Their answer is cumulative abstract semantics, built on scoped effects. Effects are sorted into two handler families: handlers that eliminate syntax, and handlers that introduce domain semantics. Against one fixed syntax, semantic fragments accumulate through these handlers, so a single interpreter can spawn many dynamic evaluators and static analyses. The authors present the design as a cleaner, more elegant route to modular program analysis, with effects doing the organisational work.
arxiv-2512-11061:
Felix O'Mahony, Roberto Cipolla, and Ayush Tewari propose a varied route to world models, the systems AI uses to predict how a scene will change. Video generators often break physical or logical rules and cannot be questioned or controlled. Their setup, VDAWorld, instead turns an image and its caption into a clean abstract scene description.

A vision language model acts as an organiser, choosing vision tools to build a two or 3D scene, then picking a matching physics simulator, such as one for rigid bodies or fluids. From that static scene it infers hidden motion and predicts plausible futures. Tests show strong simulations across many scenarios, with uses in interactive control, what-if generation, and physical and logical reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2512-11361:
Rasmus Møgelberg extends a logical setup for programming with endless and productive data forms to higher levels of infinity. Guarded recursion uses clocks to ensure that definitions unfolding over time stay productive, and multiple clocks add flexibility for coinductive types. Earlier meaning based models for this idea lived in extensional type theory and in cubical settings, each verifying certain encodings of data types.

The open task was to push the set based presheaf model beyond the first endless ordinal. That would let encodings involving finite sets of options, finite probability spreads, and such predicates be verified there too. Møgelberg carries out that extension, handling general sized functors rather than only finitary ones. Results proved in clocked cubical type theory can then be interpreted in an ordinary set theoretic model, confirming their correctness in the standard math sense.
arxiv-2512-11661:
Brenda Nogueira and co-authors ask how researchers really use large language models to write literature reviews. Many studies cover AI help with writing in general, but the review task has its own pains. The team ran a user study with scholars from many fields.

Three gaps kept coming up: users do not trust the output, checking it eats the time saved, and work is split across too many tools. The authors answer with six design goals and a draft system. It would show related papers in clear views, support checks at each step, and explain its choices using user feedback. The aim is help that scholars can verify, not just accept.
arxiv-2512-11761:
Trisha Dawn and Jesús Arroyo improve graph matching, the task of lining up two networks node by node when no shared IDs exist. Most methods use only network shape. Yet real data often carry rich node and edge traits, like ages or tie types, that shape alone wastes.

The pair study seeded matching, where some pairs are already known. They give two trait aware methods: a global one based on quadratic assignment, and a fast local one that grows from the seeds. Both rest on a flexible model that accepts anything from plain regressions to machine learning. Error rates and exact recovery rules are proven, and a test case matches academic family trees with collaboration networks.
arxiv-2512-11961:
Vivek Kumar Jha and co-authors sort jet driven from disk driven flicker in a class of active galaxies. Radio loud narrow line Seyfert 1 galaxies host black holes with jets in some cases and bare disks in others. Light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility span many timescales for each type.

Gamma ray detected systems and a quasar comparison set show steeply rising structure functions, a sign of long term coherence from boosted jet light, despite modest total flicker. Non jetted systems flicker most yet plateau, the mark of random disk noise. Gamma quiet jetted systems barely flicker at all. Color trends split the same way: jet sources redden as they brighten, disk sources turn bluer.
arxiv-2512-12061:
Junling Fan and co-authors present a scalable way to disguise chip designs against reverse engineering. Chip intellectual property theft costs hundreds of billions yearly. A recent trick, IP camouflage, makes one module masquerade as a wholly different design. It works, but needs a costly fix up step and does not scale.

Two end to end models replace it. A graph matching algorithm fixes the representation clash with standard analysis flows. A search based NAND array model supplies scale, helped by a mimicry aware partitioning that splits big designs into safe chunks. Tests show resilience against SAT solver and graph neural network attacks. The result is deceptive design that fits real chip workflows.
arxiv-2512-12161:
G Flores-Hidalgo studies how a false vacuum decays in quantum field theory in a 2025 paper. The decay rate per unit volume depends mostly on a factor built from the bounce, a field shape that solves a hard nonlinear equation. Finding that shape is the main task.

Most work uses the thin wall shortcut, which only holds when two energy levels are close in size. Flores-Hidalgo extends the method to cases where that shortcut fails. He uses a simple trial method to estimate both the bounce and the decay rate. His results agree well with full numerical calculations, giving a faster route for such cases.
arxiv-2512-12461:
Eray Erturk, Saba Hashemi, and Maryam M Shanechi transfer knowledge from spike models to field potential models of brain activity in a 2025 paper. Local field potentials, or LFPs, are broad electrical signals recorded alongside spikes in brain experiments. They last longer and use less power than spike data, but their pooled nature makes them harder to model well.

The team first trains a teacher model on spikes from many sessions, using masked autoencoding and session specific tokenization. A student LFP model then learns to match the teacher's inner representations. The distilled LFP models beat single and multi-session baselines in both unsupervised and supervised tests. They also carried over to new sessions with no extra distillation.
arxiv-2512-12561:
Kedarnath Buda, B V Rathish Kumar, and Anil Rathi analyze a Nash equilibrium control problem for fluid flow in a 2025 paper. Two objectives compete in steering flow governed by the Stokes equations, which describe slow viscous motion. Each player in the Nash setup pursues its own goal, and an equilibrium is a state where neither gains by shifting alone. State constraints in the L2 norm bound the flow.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and characterize it analytically. A finite element framework then approximates the coupled control system, with optimality conditions derived for both continuous and discrete forms. Error estimates ensure convergence and stability. Numerical experiments confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the approach.
arxiv-2512-12861:
Shyam Popat and Zhengyan Wu prove a long-run property for a class of equations that model a fluctuating density, called Dean-Kawasaki equations. They work with fixed boundary conditions of Dirichlet type and with noise that can be rough. The rough case involves a square-root type term.

The authors show that solutions settle toward a steady statistical state, a property called ergodicity. For the classic form, the approach to that state is fast, at an exponential rate. For a porous medium form, it is slower, at a polynomial rate. When the noise is smoother, that slow rate improves to exponential as well.
arxiv-2512-13461:
Luna Bloin-Wibe and co-authors assess how climate change affects net load, the demand left for dispatchable power after wind and solar output, in European power systems. Net load spikes are moments of system stress. Past studies treated climate shifts and system design choices in isolation, missing their interactions.

Using hourly historical and future climate data across eight system designs, they find the sign of climate impact depends on the design itself. Wind-heavy systems with today's heating saw 30 percent more high net load events, mostly in summer and fall. Fully electrified net-zero systems instead saw winter and spring events drop by about 50 percent under climate change.
arxiv-2512-13661:
Robert Pinkston and co-authors use matrix product states to simulate reacting shear flows with far less memory. Direct simulation of turbulent reactive flow is costly because turbulence and chemistry act across many time and space scales. Matrix product states come from quantum many-body physics, where they compress large states well.

The team applies that ansatz to shear flow under non-reacting and nonpremixed reacting conditions. They show memory cuts of 30% for all transport variables, with results in excellent agreement with direct simulation. The method captures reduced mixing from heat release and the shocklets that form at high Mach numbers. Analysis at higher Reynolds numbers found compression as large as 99.99% for some variables.
arxiv-2512-13961:
Team Olmo introduces Olmo 3, a family of fully open language models at 7B and 32B parameter scales. Fully open means the release includes the entire model flow: every stage, checkpoint, data point, and dependency used to build the family. That level of openness is rare among strong language models.

Model construction targets long-context reasoning, function calling, coding, instruction following, general chat, and knowledge recall. The flagship model, Olmo 3 Think 32B, is described as the strongest fully open thinking model released to date. The report documents the full lifecycle of the family, so other groups can study, reproduce, and build on each step of its creation.
arxiv-2512-14261:
Melih Solmaz and five coauthors describe ALMOND, a mobile neutron detector for the Gran Sasso National Laboratory, in a 2025 paper. Deep underground labs host rare event searches, and neutrons from the cavern walls form a background that can mask those signals.

The neutron flux and spectrum change a lot with place and time, so one fixed measurement is not enough. ALMOND is a low flux mobile spectrometer built to map the whole facility. The paper covers its design, construction, and calibration. It also reports the first underground neutron measurement and looks ahead to future runs. Better maps help labs design shielding and veto systems and raise sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-14361:
Nicholas Tagliapietra, Katharina Ensinger, Christoph Zimmer, and Osman Mian present CaDyT in a 2025 paper on causal structure learning for dynamical systems. Real systems evolve in continuous time under unknown causal links, and most methods either chop time into steps or ignore causality.

CaDyT is grounded in difference based causal models, which allow milder assumptions about continuous dynamics. It uses exact Gaussian process inference to model the motion, and finds the causal structure with a greedy search guided by the Algorithmic Markov Condition and the Minimum Description Length principle. In experiments, CaDyT beat state of the art methods on both regularly and irregularly sampled data. The networks it found sat closer to the true underlying dynamics.
arxiv-2512-14661:
Vision-language models can caption videos and answer questions about them, but their size and video-length inputs make them heavy to run. The cost in computation and memory is a real barrier to real-time use on hardware accelerators.

Focus is proposed as a streaming concentration architecture that trims that overhead while the model processes video as it arrives. Concentrating on what matters in the stream is meant to keep accuracy while cutting waste. Efficient designs like this one decide whether vision-language models can leave the data center and run live in cameras, vehicles, and other everyday devices.
arxiv-2512-14761:
David Ball of Superficial Labs argues that modern AI systems have no good way to state a requirement and make a model obey it. Training builds skill and preference tuning shapes taste, but neither promises that a clear rule will hold in a new setting. His 2025 paper names the fix Capability Engineering, put into practice through a protocol called CAPE.

CAPE runs a loop of specify, verify, correct, and train, turning requirements into executable checks. Two findings support it: once context is fixed, raters agree on seemingly subjective labels far more, and checking accuracy grows with model size. Across 109,500 examples in six domains, CAPE cut rule violations by 81% compared with DPO. Ball also released the tools openly, plus a public registry that grades models against shared policies.
arxiv-2512-14861:
Ronnie de Souza Santos, Maria Teresa Baldassarre, and César França study what employers want from people who test quantum software. Testing quantum programs is not like testing normal software, since the hardware itself is part of the test. The team read 110 job postings from groups that build quantum software and hardware.

They catalogued the tasks, skills, and traits named in the postings. Testing in this field mixes classic quality checks with hands on validation of real devices. Calibration, control of the hardware, and checks that span quantum and classical parts all matter. Employers want staff who can code and automate, know quantum basics, and work across fields. The authors call the field young but fast changing, and urge schools to match their teaching to it.
arxiv-2512-14961:
Aref Farhadipour and four coauthors build a person recognition system that keeps working when some of its senses go missing. Identification tools may use voice, face, or body cues, but real settings often lose one or more of them. Their framework combines upper body motion, face, and voice from the start.

Body motion alone beat face and voice in same session tests, and it strengthened the mix in multi session tests. The system fuses features and scores together, trains each sense on its own task, then blends them with cross attention and gated fusion. A confidence weighted step corrects mistakes when data is missing. On the CANDOR interview dataset it reached 99.51 percent top one accuracy, and 99.92 percent on VoxCeleb1 in two sense mode. Accuracy stayed high even with one or two senses gone.
arxiv-2512-15161:
U. Bekbaev classifies a family of small algebras where every product of two elements with itself vanishes. The algebras are three dimensional and anti-commutative, meaning swapping the order in a product flips its sign. The base field is general, with two conditions: its characteristic is not 2, and every element of the algebra admits a square root.

The study is devoted to the classification problem for these algebras. Classification here means listing the algebras up to isomorphism, so that any such algebra matches exactly one entry on the list. The abstract states the scope in a single sentence, marking a focused algebra paper for specialists.
arxiv-2512-15461:
Janos Barat, Andrea Freschi, and Geza Toth study matchings that avoid ordered patterns in a 2025 combinatorics paper. In an ordered graph the vertices come in a fixed line, and two disjoint edges can sit separated, nested, or crossing. For each pattern type, the question is how many edges a graph can have without containing a matching where every pair shows that pattern.

Exact answers were known for four of six cases. The authors settle the non separated case, with a maximum near three halves of (k minus 1) times n. For the non nested case they pin the maximum between two close bounds. They also solve a related question about alternating paths of a given length.
arxiv-2512-15661:
Sergi Masot-Llima and co authors map prospects for quantum advantage in machine learning through function representability in a 2025 paper. Many quantum learning models have been proposed, and classical methods keep simulating more of them. A clear map of which models can still win is missing.

Their framework links the structure of parametrized quantum circuits to the functions those circuits can actually learn. Circuit depth and non Clifford gate counts decide whether outputs admit efficient classical simulation or replacement by a classical surrogate. The analysis sorts models into fully simulatable ones, ones with classically tractable function spaces, and ones that stay robustly quantum. It also uncovers shared pathways behind many dequantization results.
arxiv-2512-15961:
A Semenaite leads a very large DESI collaboration team in this cosmology paper, posted on arXiv in 2025. The team combines galaxy clustering data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's first data release with weak gravitational lensing surveys. Lensing measures how galaxy shapes are bent by the gravity of unseen matter along the line of sight.

Fitting clustering and lensing together sharpened measures of the cosmic power spectrum by 15 to 36 percent. Their lensing strength values, called S8, range from 0.771 to 0.787 across the three surveys used. Those values sit below the value favored by the Planck satellite by about two to three standard deviations. The results agree well across all three lensing surveys, which strengthens the finding.
arxiv-2512-16061:
Fernando Baltazar-Larios and Alejandra Quintos tackle a statistics problem in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Phase-type distributions model how long a process takes to reach an absorbing end state, like a disease reaching a final stage. Their time-scaled versions let the pace change over time, which fits heavy-tailed data better.

The catch is that real studies often record the process only at scattered check-up times, so exact transition times are missing. The authors build an inference method that fills in the hidden paths by simulation, then updates the parameters in a stochastic expectation-maximization loop. Some updates have closed-form answers, while the time-scaling parameter is tuned by gradient steps. Tests on simulated data and on heart transplant blood vessel disease records showed accurate, practical fits.
arxiv-2512-16161:
V Venkatraman Krishnan leads a large SKA team in reviewing gravity tests in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Binary pulsars, spinning neutron stars in tight orbits, are natural laboratories for strong gravity. Timing their pulses has produced the sharpest tests yet of the strong equivalence principle and of how gravity radiates.

The Square Kilometre Array's sensitivity in the southern sky will time known recycled pulsars far more precisely. A galactic census should also find dozens of new relativistic systems, perhaps including a pulsar orbiting a black hole, which could test cosmic censorship and the no-hair theorem. The chapter surveys tests of dipole radiation, extra gravity fields, frame dragging, and spacetime symmetries. It closes by spelling out which SKA capabilities matter most for this science.
arxiv-2512-16661:
Shikshya Shiwakoti, Samuel Goldsmith, and Ujjwal Pandit build a search tool for science papers based on the Microsoft Academic Graph. With so much work online, finding the right papers is hard, and graph networks paired with language models offer a way through.

Their system, an attention-based subgraph retriever, prunes a huge citation graph down to a small, focused subgraph around a query. That subgraph then goes to a large language model, which can reason over the linked papers, authors, and topics. The design aims to give research help that uses links between works, not just word matches, to suggest what to read next.
arxiv-2512-17061:
Madjid Eshaghi Gordji and Mohamadali Berahman offer a Trust-Building Game, a model of how trust grows between two players over repeated rounds. Classic trust models center on the first player choice to trust, leaving the second player response in shadow.

Their model flips the stress to the second player, whose replies decide whether trust pays. Through a repetitive structure, the first player cultivates the second player trust by steady, strategic acts. The frame is pitched for public policy, marketing, and diplomacy, anywhere one side must earn cooperation over time. The authors claim it deepens the account of how trust forms and gives levers for lasting cooperation.
arxiv-2512-17361:
Alexander Zhuravlev and three co-authors show how a smart surface can make a radio field die away faster with distance. Above plain ground, a distant antenna's field near the surface mixes three parts, the weakest and slowest fading being the Norton wave. Old theory treated its fade rate as a hard floor for how fast fields can fall.

Lay a nonlocal metasurface, a patterned sheet with a special surface response, over the ground, and the Norton wave can be choked off. The fields then fade far more steeply than the old floor. In computer tests, a shield just one wavelength wide cut edge spillover by 10 decibels. Faster fade means antennas can sit closer together with less crosstalk, aiding compact designs.
arxiv-2512-18161:
Taewon Yang and coauthors at the University of Michigan bring full 3D diffusion models to CT reconstruction. Diffusion models make strong image priors for rebuilding scans from limited data, but training one on whole 3D volumes needs more computing power and data than most labs have.

Their model learns from 3D patches instead of whole volumes, which keeps training light enough for limited data. Each patch is learned together with a downsampled copy of the full volume, so local detail stays tied to global anatomy, and position codes tell the model where each patch sits. Across several datasets the method beats prior state of the art systems in both quality and speed. It rebuilds a 512 by 512 by 256 volume in about 20 minutes.
arxiv-2512-18261:
M. Mehdi Kholoosi, Triet Huynh Minh Le, and M. Ali Babar survey how working teams use AI to hunt and fix software flaws. AI coding help is now common, yet its role in the full flaw cycle, from spotting to patching, had not been mapped in real firms. The team asked 60 practitioners across 27 countries how the tools fit their work.

AI help showed up at every stage of the cycle, and 69 percent of users were satisfied with it. Speed, coverage, and ease of access won praise, while false alarms, thin context, and trust gaps drew complaints. In practice, human review and firm rules filter every AI call, and the authors urge clearer reasoning and smoother fit into team workflows.
arxiv-2512-18361:
Michael V. Klibanov and three co-authors address a practical imaging problem: how to picture a target that moves. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, recasts the task as a coefficient inverse problem for a wave equation, where the unknown coefficient depends on position and time. The setup uses a point source that travels in a straight line while measurements are taken.

The authors first prove a Lipschitz stability estimate, which bounds how errors in the data affect the image. They then build a convexification method, a numerical scheme designed to converge to the right answer from any starting guess, based on a Carleman estimate. Computer experiments close the paper, showing the method at work. Such schemes matter for radar and medical imaging of moving objects.
arxiv-2512-18461:
Rémi Tailleux, Thomas Dubos, and Benedict J. Hatton revisit the Boussinesq approximation. This workhorse model for ocean and atmosphere flows treats density changes as small. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, notes a weakness in the standard version. It hides its links to the full compressible equations, leaves internal energy implicit, and handles diffusion in an ad hoc way.

The team derives a new Boussinesq model step by step from the two-component compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The derivation keeps exact energy conservation and consistent thermodynamics. The model separates in-situ and potential temperature and produces entropy at a properly non-negative rate. A companion soundproof model highlights how compressibility shapes stratified turbulence. Together they offer cleaner tools for studying ocean mixing and energy budgets.
arxiv-2512-18561:
Saad Alqithami builds a watchdog for swarms of AI agents. Networked multi-agent systems run pieces of critical infrastructure, but their collective behavior can drift into bad habits like collusion, resource hoarding, and quiet unfairness. His Adaptive Accountability Framework, posted to arXiv in December 2025, is a runtime layer that records, detects, blames, and corrects.

The framework logs interactions with cryptographic provenance, watches streaming traces for distributional shifts, and traces responsibility through a causal influence graph. It then intervenes with reward shaping or targeted policy patches, under a bounded budget. In 87,480 simulation runs, it lowered the compromise ratio against a PPO baseline in 96 percent of regimes, with a median relative reduction of 11.9 percent and social welfare nearly unchanged. Violations were flagged with a median delay of 71 steps.
arxiv-2512-18661:
Hafiz Saif Ur Rehman, Ling Liu, and Kaleem Ullah Qasim present a forecasting system for crypto prices in this 2025 paper. Their system, ASTIF, treats prediction as a fusion problem: price history alone misses forces like policy news and market stories. A small language model with a dual-channel MirrorPrompt setup reads market cues, while a hybrid LSTM and random forest model tracks time patterns. A confidence-aware meta-learner then weighs each part in real time.

Tested on AI-focused cryptocurrencies and major tech stocks from 2020 to 2024, ASTIF beats leading deep learning and Transformer baselines such as Informer and TFT. Ablation tests show the meta-learner matters most in turbulence, shifting trust between the text and price channels as conditions change.
arxiv-2512-18761:
Dimitrios Tyrovolas and seven co-authors ask how many pinching antennas a programmable wireless system really needs. Pinching antennas radiate from points pinched onto a dielectric waveguide, letting a network move its effective antennas. Most studies assume the pinch point slides continuously, but real hardware offers only fixed spots. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, analyzes the two-state version, where each antenna is simply on or off.

They derive closed-form formulas for outage probability and average data rate that respect the discrete positions. A new measure, pinching discretization efficiency, quantifies the gap to the ideal sliding case. Simulations confirm that near-continuous performance arrives with only a limited number of antennas. For engineers designing programmable wireless environments, that is a direct shopping list: this many pinch points buy nearly all the benefit.
arxiv-2512-19061:
Chi Liu tackles fraud rings in online payment systems, where many accounts act together. Linking accounts only by strong identity matches misses much of the ring. Using every weak link instead shatters the network into fragments that cluster poorly.

Liu separates hard links, such as phone numbers, cards, and national IDs, from soft links like device fingerprints, cookies, and IP addresses. Hard links first merge accounts into super-nodes. A weighted soft-link graph is then built, embedded, and clustered with standard tools. The design aims to give fraud teams full coverage of a ring without losing the structure that makes clusters meaningful.
arxiv-2512-19161:
Alessandro Lucca, Francesco Corso, and Francesco Pierri test whether speech recognition is ready to subtitle Italian television on its own. Subtitles drive access and engagement, yet most recognition research leans on English and short clips. The authors worked with an Italian media company on a real production system.

Four leading systems, including two Whisper variants, were scored on fifty hours of Italian programs against professional human subtitlers. None met the accuracy the industry needs for full autonomy. All four, though, proved strong as assistants that speed up human work. The study argues for a human-in-the-loop design for long-form, non-English subtitling.
arxiv-2512-19261:
René Pollmann, Franz Roeder, Christine Silberhorn, and Benjamin Brecht set a hard limit test for a delicate light-matter effect. Entangled two-photon absorption promises imaging and sensing gains, yet claimed sightings are hard to judge across setups. Their method scores any experiment's sensitivity in one shared unit.

Every signal and noise source in the measurement enters the model. The result is a single number, in Göppert-Mayer units, that says whether the effect can be seen at all under stated conditions. Different designs become directly comparable. Builders can also test each change to an apparatus on paper first, and follow the clearest path to a detectable signal.
arxiv-2512-19461:
Mark Grant uses secondary cohomology operations to bound the sectional category of a fibration, a number that measures how hard a space is to cover with well-behaved pieces. Primary invariants often fall short of the true value. His stage is the total space of the fibred join, where the secondary operations live.

The bounds motivate a refined invariant, the secondary module weight, meant to sharpen the older module weight of Iwase and Kono. Worked examples show the new weight, at the prime two, detecting sectional category in cases where the older one stays silent. The paper is a tool-building contribution to algebraic topology.
arxiv-2512-19561:
Johannes Michl and five co-authors link a semiconductor hole spin to telecom light, and show the spin stays coherent for a long while. Quantum networks need matter qubits that talk to photons in the fiber-friendly C-band, near fifteen hundred fifty nanometers. Dot spins had shone at shorter wavelengths, while telecom versions lagged.

Their indium arsenide dots sit inside a precisely placed circular Bragg grating that boosts emission at the target wavelength. Polarization-resolved measurements in a magnetic field give electron and hole g-factors. A pulsed correlation test then heralds the ground-state hole spin, whose dephasing time lands near sixteen nanoseconds, a strong mark for telecom dots.
arxiv-2512-19761:
Muhammad Atif Zaheer works in analytic number theory. His topic is a set of series tied to a great open question. The series use an analogue of the Riemann xi function. This one is built for Dedekind zeta functions. The series also involve the zeros of those functions. All of the work rests on a clear premise. He assumes the Extended Riemann Hypothesis is true. That premise says all such zeros lie on the critical line.

Under that premise, he finds closed forms for the series. He then proves the reverse. If a closed form holds, all zeros past a set height must lie on the critical line. The two ways together give many equal forms of the hypothesis. They are restatements of it, not a proof.
arxiv-2512-19961:
Futoshi Minato asks how atomic nuclei answer when hit by two forces at once. One-body fields excite single particle-hole pairs. Their giant resonances are well studied. Two-body fields drive double-phonon modes instead. He models them with the subtracted second random-phase approximation. The test nuclei are oxygen-16 and calcium-40. Both are light enough to dissect with care.

With only diagonal residual terms, the strength patterns barely move from a Hartree-Fock base. The one-particle-one-hole sector counts for little here. That is unlike one-body cases, where such coupling builds collectivity. Switch on the full mixing of two-particle-two-hole setups, and all changes. Double isoscalar modes shift down, with new strength up high. The double isovector dipole mode moves up. Amplitude checks show low modes built in step from all nucleon pairings.
arxiv-2512-20261:
Edith Elkind, Michele Flammini, and Giovanna Varricchio study coalition formation when every agent labels the others as friends or enemies. These hedonic games ask for a partition of agents into groups. Egalitarian welfare judges a partition by its worst-off member, so fairness is built into the goal from the start.

Two preference styles are analyzed. Under enemies aversion, avoiding enemies matters most; under friends appreciation, gathering friends matters most. The authors prove hardness results for both and design polynomial-time approximation methods with stated guarantees. Randomization and symmetric friendship recover stronger guarantees for the friends-first case. They also find special cases where the best partition can be computed exactly and quickly.
arxiv-2512-20361:
Rémy Mahfouf identifies the large-scale limit of fermions in the planar Ising model on very general lattices. The lattices are s-embeddings, which need not look like regular grids. In the scaling limit, the Kadanoff-Ceva fermions are described by solutions of conjugate Beltrami equations with prescribed singularities.

For the Ising model itself, energy correlations converge to objects built from Green kernels of uniformly elliptic operators and quasiconformal mappings. On grids approximating bounded domains, the energy density shows conformal covariance even on doubly periodic graphs. All scaling factors are local and read off the embedding geometry, even where it varies wildly. The results confirm Chelkak's predictions and reveal a richer conformal structure than the classic Euclidean picture.
arxiv-2512-20561:
Kaitong Cai and co-authors slim down the visual input of large multimodal models without dulling them. Such models chew through hundreds or thousands of image tokens per picture, paying quadratic attention costs for mostly redundant content. Earlier pruning methods ignored the user's question or leaned on unstable attention maps.

FlashVLM instead scores each visual token against the text query directly, computing cross-modal similarity in the language model's own space. That relevance score is fused with intrinsic visual saliency, and a diversity-preserving partition keeps a small set of background tokens for global context. The results border on free compression: pruning over three quarters of tokens slightly beats the unpruned benchmark on LLaVA, and accuracy holds up even past ninety percent pruning.
arxiv-2512-20761:
Marcel Meyer and co-authors built a forecast arena where cheating cannot happen. Large time series models are usually graded on past data that may already sit inside their training sets, through direct overlap or linked series. TS-Arena instead evaluates on the future: models must register predictions before the true data exists.

A strict pre-registration protocol makes contamination impossible by design. A modular micro-service platform tidies streams from many sources and runs packaged model submissions. One year of operation on energy time series shows established models building robust scores over time while newcomers can prove themselves immediately. Compared with static competitions repeated rarely, the live arena grades true skill on new data continuously. The platform and its code are public.
arxiv-2512-20861:
Pierre Abillama and five co-authors make compressed foundation models run fast on modest graphics cards. Block low-rank methods such as Monarch and BLAST shrink weight matrices while keeping accuracy, promising big savings. In practice, generating several tokens at once becomes limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic, so the promised speed often vanishes.

The team wrote custom Triton kernels that fuse steps and rearrange memory layouts for both methods. On constrained NVIDIA hardware, including Jetson Orin Nano boards, they report speedups approaching fourfold and models compressed to a third of dense size. The kernels handled several well-known models, from Llama and GPT-2 to image models, broadening their reach.
arxiv-2512-21061:
Ohad Vilk and Baruch Meerson ask what a crowd of particles looks like when every member diffuses strangely and occasionally teleports home. Each particle follows scaled Brownian motion, whose spreading rate itself grows or shrinks as a power of time. Each also resets to the origin at random moments, restarting its own clock. Building on the known steady state of a single such particle, they compute the statistics of the whole ensemble's radius and center of mass.

Typical radius fluctuations belong to the Gumbel universality class of extreme-value statistics for every value of the time exponent. The center of mass is stranger: for exponents above one half its rare large deviations scale anomalously. The rate function develops a singularity traced to a big-jump effect: one particle wandering far enough to drag the average. Statistical physicists gain a solved example where resetting and anomalous diffusion interact.
arxiv-2512-21161:
Qi Wu, Gang Li, and three co-authors calculate how the enigmatic particle X(3872) sheds energy by emitting two pions and settling into the chi_cJ charmonium states. They treat X(3872) as a loosely bound molecule of D mesons, an assumption heavy-hadron chiral perturbation theory can exploit, and sift the loop diagrams for the decay. Power counting shows the box diagrams dominate the triangle ones, simplifying the prediction.

Branching fractions come out as functions of a mixing angle encoding the molecule's neutral-versus-charged makeup. They land near one part in a thousand for the chi_c1 channel. The chi_c0 channel gets one in ten thousand, and chi_c2 one in a hundred thousand. Ratios between charged and neutral pion modes break isospin symmetry to varying degrees, and two mass spectra develop testable double-bump shapes. Future measurements can interrogate both the decay and the molecular hypothesis.
arxiv-2512-21261:
Schrödinger bridges bend a reference diffusion so its endpoints match chosen distributions, and Camilo Hernández and Ludovic Tangpi generalize the setup in two directions at once. They replace the usual relative entropy penalty with any convex divergence, and they impose the terminal condition only weakly. Their formulation lives on path space, the arena of whole trajectories.

Well-posedness and a convex dual problem follow, with explicit formulas for the best primal and dual solutions. The winning path measure has a clean density against the reference diffusion, extending the classical Schrödinger system. When transport cost vanishes, they trace how the bridge's snapshot distributions evolve in time, recovering known entropy-based results and adding new ones, including the chi-squared divergence.
arxiv-2512-21461:
Kyosuke Maeda, Tomohiro Okuma, Kei-ichi Watanabe, and Ken-ichi Yoshida study rational surface singularities, isolated rough points on surfaces. A central object is the canonical trace ideal, which measures how far a singularity is from being Gorenstein, a well-behaved class. They work through the minimal resolution, the standard smoothing used to inspect such points.

They show the canonical trace ideal is integrally closed for every rational surface singularity. It is given by the minimal anti-nef cycle on the resolution. When the singularity is not Gorenstein, that cycle is at least the fundamental cycle, another key divisor. From this they derive a practical criterion for a singularity to be nearly Gorenstein, a relaxed form of the property. They classify all nearly Gorenstein rational singularities when the fundamental cycle is almost reduced, and for quotient ones.
arxiv-2512-21861:
Md Rafid Islam, Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Khan, and their co-authors test whether combining convolutional neural networks improves screening for diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that remains a leading cause of preventable blindness. Screening is limited by specialist availability and by image quality that varies across clinics and cameras.

The team pooled over eleven thousand fundus images from five public datasets and framed detection as a yes-no classification. They compared three pretrained backbones, ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, and DenseNet121, against pairwise and triple fusions of their features. Across five independent runs, fusion consistently beat single models. The pairing of EfficientNet-B0 with DenseNet121 performed best overall, at about eighty-three percent accuracy with balanced scores for healthy and diseased eyes. The triple fusion was competitive but cost far more computation. The fastest single model processed an image in just over a millisecond.
arxiv-2512-22061:
A. V. Kopyev, A. S. Il'yn, V. A. Sirota, and K. P. Zybin study how magnetic fields grow in moving fluids. Their subject is the small-scale turbulent dynamo, where tangled fluid motion stretches field lines and makes weak fields stronger. They focus on fluids with a low magnetic Prandtl number, a case where theory and computer simulations have rarely been compared in detail.

The authors argue that the Kazantsev equation, a standard theory tool, should use a quasi-Lagrangian measure of fluid motion rather than the usual Eulerian one. With that change, the theory's threshold and growth rates match simulation results well. They also link the falling critical magnetic Reynolds number to intermittency, the uneven burstiness of turbulence, which changes as flow speed rises.
arxiv-2512-22161:
Romain Dalidet and four co-authors present a device for measuring chromatic dispersion, the spreading of light pulses because different colors travel at different speeds in fiber. That spread limits telecom links and ultrafast optics, yet measuring it fast and precisely is hard, mainly for short fibers. Their tool is an all-fiber nonlinear Sagnac interferometer working at telecom wavelengths.

Cascaded second-order processes inside the loop create idler light whose colors mirror each other and cancel odd-order spread without active stabilization. Because the reading compares two counter-propagating processes in the same loop, it needs no outside reference arm or prior calibration. The team shows readings on fibers from 25 cm to 4 km, read out on a standard spectrum analyzer.
arxiv-2512-22361:
Alberto Guilabert, Ernesto Fuenmayor, Pedro Bargueño, and Ernesto Contreras connect two exotic objects: ghost stars and traversable wormholes. Ghost stars are compact configurations with total mass as tiny as one likes, which forces regions of negative energy density, normally dismissed as not physical. Wormholes, though, need exactly that condition violation to hold their throats open, hinting ghost-like matter may live naturally in wormhole physics.

The authors analyze ghost configurations through their Hawking mass. Extending the ghost condition beyond spherical symmetry runs into topological blocks, they show, which hinder a direct realization. As a concrete case, they construct a Casimir-like traversable wormhole inside the system. A Penrose-Carter diagram illustrates the resulting geometry's global structure for readers.
arxiv-2512-22561:
N. Dinh, M. A. Goberna, D. H. Long, and M. Volle introduce a robust generalized S-procedure, a decision tool for optimization problems whose data are uncertain. The classic S-procedure certifies when one quadratic constraint implies another. The robust version must keep that guarantee valid across a whole set of possible problem instances. That matches how robust optimization is posed.

The authors give two characterizations of when the procedure is valid. The first is a primal characterization that works directly with the problem's own objects. The second is a dual characterization, proved under the assumption that the decision space is locally convex. They also analyze an extension of the procedure that incorporates a right-hand side function, widening the class of robust problems the machinery covers.
arxiv-2512-22761:
Qianqian Liu, Ajit Diwan, and Heping Zhang work in pure graph theory on the forcing number of perfect matchings. A forcing set is a small part of a perfect matching whose presence pins down the whole matching uniquely. A graph's maximum forcing number is the largest such minimum over all its perfect matchings. A conjecture linked the number of edges in a graph to this maximum, predicting a lower bound on edges.

The authors confirm that conjecture and turn it into an upper bound on the maximum forcing number in terms of the edge count. For extreme graphs, and bipartite graphs close to that value, they show any two perfect matchings can be transformed into each other by switches along short even cycles. They also settle the possible minimum forcing numbers for the near-extreme bipartite case and answer a follow-up question for small values.
arxiv-2512-23461:
Reward models score the answers of large language models so the models can be trained to match human taste. Zhuo Li and nine co-authors warn that the training data for these scorers carries hidden biases. Longer answers, flattering answers, or certain formats get preferred for the wrong reasons, and models learn to exploit that. Simple fixes that assume straight-line correlations miss much of the problem.

Their method, DIR, uses information theory to attack bias directly. It pushes the reward score to share as much information as possible with true human preference, while sharing as little as possible with biased attributes of the input. Tested on length, sycophancy, and format bias, DIR reduced all three and improved downstream training results across several benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-23661:
Ariel Silva, Claudia González, and Rodrigo Laje study how we tap a finger in time with a beat. Labs have used this task for a long time to probe how we fix timing slips. Two ways to shift the beat give a puzzle. A step change in pace and a shift in phase look the same up to the shock beat. Yet run apart, the two give clashing next taps.

The two sets of taps clash if each test stands alone. Each test builds its own sense of time, so one rule can't fit both. But mix the two shifts at random in one test, and the taps fit one rule well. The claim is that we do not keep two fix-up tools, one for phase and one for pace. We keep one, tuned by the feel of the session.
arxiv-2512-23861:
Sayeh Rezaee, Cesar Nieto, and Abhyudai Singh generalize a well-tested rule of cell size control. Measurements show many cells obey the adder principle: each cycle adds a nearly constant amount of size, regardless of birth size, which keeps sizes from drifting. Theory explains the adder when cell-cycle progress is tied to size. The authors ask what changes when growth itself saturates.

Their stochastic model lets the growth rate follow a Hill-type function of size, so very large cells grow roughly linearly instead of exponentially. It splits the path to division into internal regulatory stages. Exact formulas for the moments of the size distribution follow. Stronger saturation raised the average steady-state size yet slightly reduced fluctuations, and the adder property survived intact, evidence that the variability drop comes from the growth law, not from rescaling. Clonal proliferation analysis rounds out the picture.
arxiv-2512-23961:
Junjie Xu compares recommendation systems that lean on KYC, the Know Your Customer profiles of the financial world, with an eye toward agentic recommenders. The study evaluates an agentic AI recommender across five content verticals: advertising, news, gossip, user-generated sharing, and technology. Four experimental groups, split by how intensely they use KYC information, are benchmarked against each other.

Performance is measured by normalized discounted cumulative gain, the standard ranking-quality score, at cutoffs of one, three, and five results. Experimental data are read alongside theory and industry benchmarks from platforms such as Baidu and Xiaohongshu. Xu presents the comparison as engineering evidence for building a large-scale agentic recommender that uses customer knowledge as an input, in a short five-page report. It is a short, practical report, not a theory paper.
arxiv-2512-24061:
Bogdan Dumitru writes short notes on a stubborn geometry problem. The Erdős–Szekeres problem asks how many points guarantee a convex polygon of a given size. The first open case concerns convex heptagons. The general conjecture predicts that thirty-three points always force one.

Dumitru encodes the thirty-three-point case as a satisfiability problem. Each triple of points is described by its orientation. A four-point convexity test rules out convex heptagons. Extra constraints fix the outer layers of the point set. The setup produces formal unsatisfiability certificates. These cover a collection of anchored subfamilies. So a counterexample cannot hide in those families. Running times varied wildly across configurations, though. A heavy-tailed pattern now dominates the computing effort. Dumitru argues that better encodings are the next step.
arxiv-2512-24261:
Manish Das and a large team report first positronium lifetime imaging with two unusual isotopes. The imaging extends standard PET scanning. Positronium atoms form in tissue before annihilating. Their lifetime probes the tissue's molecular architecture. The scanner used is the plastic-based modular J-PET. The isotopes are manganese-52 and cobalt-55.

Four samples were studied in each run. Two were certified reference materials, polycarbonate and fused silica. Two were human tissues, cardiac myxoma and fat. Events were selected by triple coincidence of two annihilation photons and one prompt gamma. Lifetimes in polycarbonate matched certified values for both isotopes. Cobalt-55 gave cleaner spectra with better peak-to-background ratios. Manganese-52 offers a longer half-life but more background. The study shows complex decay schemes still allow lifetime imaging.
arxiv-2512-24361:
