Joshua Arroyo and Adam Gregory solve a pattern problem about bumpless pipe dreams. These are combinatorial diagrams used to study Schubert and Grothendieck polynomials. Weigandt recently attached a companion object, the co-BPD, to each diagram. Co-BPDs yielded new change-of-basis formulas between the two polynomial families. She asked which permutations have only reduced co-BPDs.

The answer is a pattern-avoidance characterization. Seven forbidden patterns decide membership exactly. A permutation qualifies precisely when it avoids all seven. The result converts a structural question about diagrams into a concrete test on permutations. Pattern avoidance is a mature language in combinatorics. Schubert calculus gains a sharper description of a special permutation class. Later work can count or generate these permutations using the seven patterns.
arxiv-2512-24461:
Seohui Bae, Jeonghye Kim, Youngchul Sung, and Woohyung Lim build an exploring agent for partly hidden worlds. Their agent is a language model system that adapts at test time. No gradient updates or extra training are allowed. The world is only partly observable. The agent must still act well inside it.

An external structured belief tracks the environment's state. Each action brings an observation that refines the belief. Actions are chosen to maximize predicted information gain over that belief. A light language-model surrogate estimates the gain. A new reward measures world alignment. It scores how well the posterior belief matches the true configuration. Experiments beat inference-time scaling baselines. Prompt-augmented and retrieval-enhanced language models both lost. The winning method also carried lower integration overhead.
arxiv-2512-25061:
Rishi Rao and Li Zhu compare ways to warm-start charge-self-consistent DFT plus DMFT calculations, a costly fixed-point loop for correlated electron materials. Reliable starting points decide whether group sampling is feasible at all. One option fetches the most similar converged structure; the other uses a symmetry-aware learned model predicting a physics-ordered self-energy and Fermi level.

Across metallic iron, correlated iron oxide, and Mott-insulating nickel oxide, learning reduced typical loops to sustained convergence, while every final result remains a fully converged answer. Computational materials readers get faster correlated-electron workflows without sacrificing rigor, since the full loop still refines each start.
arxiv-2601-00061:
W H Elsanhoury works with five co-authors to analyze four young open star clusters sitting near the Milky Way's mid-plane, using precise Gaia DR3 positions and brightness data. Their 2026 study covers NGC 663, NGC 2301, NGC 2384, and NGC 7510. A membership algorithm sorts true members from field stars, finding hundreds to well over a thousand probable members per cluster.

Bayesian fitting of stellar isochrones gives ages and dust reddening for each cluster, with reddening varying greatly across the four. Their mass distributions closely match the classic Salpeter form, while total masses span nearly a factor of ten. Only two clusters count as dynamically relaxed. Orbit calculations show nearly circular paths hugging the thin disk. A closer look also splits one supposed cluster into two groups separated in space, an optical pair rather than one system.
arxiv-2601-00561:
Jintao Lin and colleagues benchmark how well unified multimodal models, systems that understand and generate both images and text, can apply world knowledge across tasks. Existing tests usually probe one task at a time, which limits what they reveal. Their benchmark, AEGIS, covers visual understanding, generation, editing, and interleaved generation in a single suite.

AEGIS contains one thousand fifty hand-annotated questions across twenty-one topics, from science and humanities to daily life, and six reasoning types. To avoid fuzzy scoring, the team also proposes a checklist protocol that replaces open-ended judging with atomic yes-or-no checks. The combination is meant to show concretely where a model's world knowledge holds up across different kinds of multimodal work.
arxiv-2601-00761:
Zhenyu Xiao and Shinsei Ryu make it much cheaper to measure quantum magic, the resource that lets quantum computers outperform stabilizer circuits. Nonstabilizerness is quantified by quantities such as stabilizer Rényi entropies and stabilizer nullity, but computing them for a general many-qubit wavefunction was exponentially expensive per sample.

Their framework pairs the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform with an exact partitioning of Pauli operators, cutting the average cost per sampled Pauli string from exponential in the number of qubits down to linear. A Monte Carlo estimator with Clifford preconditioning needs a number of samples that shows no visible growth with system size in their tests. Applied to random Clifford circuits doped with T gates, the method identifies the gate ratio governing magic growth.
arxiv-2601-01061:
Yajing Liu, Erkao Bao, and Linqi Song tackle a clash between two tools. Bandit methods choose among options step by step, balancing trial of new options against use of the best known one. Machine learning models can predict each option's payoff well, but bandit theory needs firm error bounds that most models cannot supply.

Their algorithm, ML-UCB, works around the gap by using how a model's error shrinks as it sees more data. When error falls off as a power law, they derive a new bound and prove the method's total loss grows slowly over time. Any model whose learning curve can be measured can plug in. Tests on a recommendation task with matrix methods show clear gains over a standard linear bandit method. The result opens sequential choice to modern machine learning without giving up guarantees.
arxiv-2601-01561:
Qiu and 3 co-authors help four-legged robots find their place inside narrow tunnels and corridors. In such long, plain spaces, laser scans look much the same from spot to spot, so position errors build up over time. Older methods that merge sensor data struggle for the same reason.

Their system, AIMS, blends laser data, motion sensors in the body, and leg movement estimates in a Kalman filter frame. It also watches for weak data and adjusts how much each source is trusted on the fly. Tests in narrow corridors showed better accuracy and steadiness than leading methods. Reliable indoor position matters for inspection robots that cannot use satellite signals.
arxiv-2601-01961:
Phase transitions on the Bethe lattice are a classic topic in statistical physics. The lattice is an infinite tree graph. Simple mean-field behavior is usually expected there. Rudrajit Banerjee and three co-authors study a family of scalar field theories on it. A parameter in the kinetic term sets the interaction range.

The team uses two tools. One is the functional renormalization group. The other is lattice perturbation theory. First, a spectral gap in the graph Laplacian is closed. The theories then develop non-trivial fixed points. Their exponents are set by the range parameter and a spectral dimension of three. Strikingly, a Wilson-Fisher fixed point appears for the short-range theory, hinting that this field theory and the nearest-neighbor Ising model on the same lattice may belong to different universality classes.
arxiv-2601-02061:
Reinforcement learning controllers often jitter, issuing rapid-fire action changes that waste energy and wear out equipment. Faizan Ahmed, Aniket Dixit, and James Brusey investigate smoothing those actions by penalizing their higher-order derivatives, from simple changes up through jerk, the third derivative.

Across four continuous control benchmarks, jerk penalties gave the best smoothness while keeping task performance competitive. The team then carried the idea to building heating and cooling control, where smooth policies cut equipment switching by sixty percent, a direct operational saving. The work argues higher-order action regularization is a practical bridge between reinforcement learning's optimization goals and the physical constraints of energy-critical deployments.
arxiv-2601-02161:
Grand unification usually hides its new particles far above collider reach. Asymptotic grand unification is different. Its couplings flow to a safe high-energy fixed point. New particles can sit near the tera-electronvolt scale in five-dimensional versions. Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Aldo Deandrea, and Christian Verollet test a minimal SU(5) version. Electroweak precision measurements are the testbed.

Current precision measurements turn out to be blind to this model class. The negative result is itself useful. Recasting LHC analyses does yield bounds, though. They sit in the tera-electronvolt range on the Kaluza-Klein mass scale. Future electron-positron colliders such as CEPC and FCC-ee could push further. The indirect limit could pass the LHC's direct reach. The scenario stays answerable to tests.
arxiv-2601-02361:
Ziheng Ni and a large team rethink the ranking step in a food delivery advertising system, the step that decides which ads and listings a user sees and in what order. Older rankers stitch together separate modules and hand made features, which limits how well they read a user's intent, especially when place, time, and personal taste all shift at once.

Their model, GCRank, treats ranking as understanding context in a generative way. A contextual encoder holds three enhancers, one for personal patterns, one for group patterns, and one for the live situation, and a fusion part joins their signals in one architecture. The aim is ranking that adapts to dynamic local context instead of scoring each item in isolation.
arxiv-2601-02761:
Kim Yesol, Koo Bon-Chul, and Lee Jae-Joon present near infrared evidence for a new supernova remnant candidate in the inner Milky Way, catalogued as G25.8+0.2. The source was first noticed in a United Kingdom infrared survey that maps ionized iron emission. With a high resolution infrared spectrograph on the Harlan J. Smith Telescope, the team resolved the iron line emission into several velocity components.

The fast components carry the elevated iron to hydrogen line ratios expected from shock excitation. The signature of a supernova blast, while the slow components match photoionized gas from a neighboring star forming region. The candidate sits inside a large star forming complex tens of parsecs across. Its shock excited iron filaments trace the shape of a bright radio shell that partly encloses softer X ray emission, strengthening the case that a stellar explosion hides in the crowded field.
arxiv-2601-02861:
Yechi Zhang and twenty-five co-authors report the physical properties of 161 candidate galaxies seen when the universe was very young, at redshifts from seven to fourteen. The galaxies come from the second data release of BEACON, a James Webb Space Telescope imaging program that uses spare telescope time. Because the survey covers thirty-six separate pointings, it samples many environments with less bias from chance clustering.

The team measures each galaxy's ultraviolet slope, stellar mass, star formation rate, and size. Their most distant candidate, if confirmed, would be the brightest known galaxy beyond redshift twelve, with a very blue color and compact shape. Three fields show strong galaxy overdensities, yet galaxy properties look similar across environments, suggesting crowded regions had not yet sped up galaxy growth.
arxiv-2601-03061:
Felipe M. Affonso identifies a new market failure created by AI shopping agents, which are being rolled out to hundreds of millions of consumers. He calls it vertical tacit collusion: platforms that control product rankings and sellers that control product descriptions can each learn, independently, to exploit documented cognitive biases of the AI agents. No agreement or coordination between them is needed.

Using multi-agent simulations calibrated to measured biases of large language models, Affonso shows the joint exploitation more than doubles the consumer harm compared with independent strategies. Platform ranking decides which products sit in bias-triggering positions, while seller wording sets conversion rates, so the harms multiply. Because the damage grows from aligned incentives rather than agreement, current antitrust tools would struggle to detect it.
arxiv-2601-03261:
Shuo Lu and five co-authors name and fix a failure of deep research agents: the retrieval-utilization gap. These agents are tuned to find evidence, yet they often fail to use the right passage even after retrieving it, blinded by the noise around it. The team's framework, DeepResearch-Slice, inserts an explicit grounding step between retrieval and reasoning.

Instead of trusting soft attention, the method predicts exact span boundaries and applies a deterministic hard filter, slicing the retrieved text down to the evidence before the model reasons over it. Applied to frozen model backbones across six benchmarks, it lifted performance from about nineteen percent to thirty-three percent, a large relative gain with no retraining of the reasoning model. The results argue for explicit grounding in open-ended research agents.
arxiv-2601-03361:
Shamik Banerjee, Raju Mandal, and Biswajit Sahoo study the symmetries hidden in soft photon theorems. These theorems give the rules for very low-energy photons in scattering processes. The authors include loop corrections at every order. Soft theorems can be read as Ward identities for asymptotic symmetries, the base of celestial holography. At loop level, though, the soft factors contain sums over many particles. That complicates the reading.

The authors restrict attention to highly energetic charged particles. They show the celestial operator product expansion needs extra fields. These fields live on the celestial sphere but never appear as real particles in any experiment. Even the one-loop logarithmic soft theorem needs a pair of special currents to work as a Ward identity. The paper maps what structure the all-loop theorems force onto the celestial sphere.
arxiv-2601-03561:
Hao Tang and three co-authors design neural operators for biomedical data that lives on spheres, such as brain or heart surfaces mapped onto a ball. Spherical models often force a choice: respect the sphere's symmetry, or adapt to the messy variation of real tissue. Their answer starts with designable Green functions, math tools that build solutions respecting rotation symmetry.

Their model, GSNO, fuses three kinds of solutions. One keeps symmetry, one removes steady background effects like a uniform field, and one handles direction-dependent tissue such as aligned fibers. Together they aim to model real heterogeneity without abandoning spherical geometry. Better spherical models could sharpen analysis of organs whose shape and internal variation both carry medical information.
arxiv-2601-03661:
Amir Hossein Yari and Fajri Koto improve GRPO, a reinforcement learning method widely used to train language models on hard reasoning tasks. GRPO has structural flaws: its group scoring favors certain answer lengths, weak answers escape strong penalties, and it wastes the ranking information inside each group of sampled answers. Their version, AMIR-GRPO, squeezes more teaching signal from the same expensive rollouts.

The fix adds a contrastive regularizer built directly from the reward rankings within each group, in the style of preference optimization. No extra human labels are needed. The change suppresses low-reward answers more strongly and softens length bias, turning each rollout group into denser supervision. Across mathematics reasoning benchmarks, the method consistently improved results, showing that better use of existing samples can rival collecting more data.
arxiv-2601-03861:
Matteo Pracchia and Om Sharan Salafia measure how long short gamma-ray bursts wait between the birth of their parent stars and the final explosion. These bursts are thought to come mainly from merging neutron star pairs, so their cosmic history encodes the delay between a massive binary's formation and its merger. If delays are long, the burst rate should drift away from the history of star formation.

Using a large burst sample inside a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the pair modeled the delay time distribution two ways, as a power law with a minimum delay and as a log-normal curve. They also tried two models of burst luminosity, an empirical one and one based on structured jets. Every combination pointed the same way: average delays are short. Progenitor systems evidently merge quickly on cosmic timescales.
arxiv-2601-03961:
E. A. M. Jensen and fifteen co-authors settle a debated question about the exotic nucleus aluminum-22, a prime candidate for a proton halo, where one proton would orbit far outside the core. The answer required fixing the nucleus's ground state spin and parity. Their experiment, at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, was the first of its kind in its gas stopping area. It used pristine low-energy beams and thin silicon detectors to suppress a dominant proton background.

They observed a weak beta-delayed alpha transition never seen before, which uniquely fixes the ground state as spin four with positive parity. The last proton is then held in by a strong centrifugal barrier plus electric repulsion, hindering the tunneling a halo needs despite the proton being barely bound. The title states the verdict plainly: a ground state halo is unlikely.
arxiv-2601-04161:
Ayan Ghosh, writing alone, proves ergodic results for a walker moving through a random medium that itself stays statistically steady. Uniform ellipticity, a uniform lower bound on step chances, is not assumed. Only a minimal condition is kept, which makes limit results harder to secure.

The work has two parts. First, Ghosh adapts arguments of Lawler to prove a uniqueness principle, using a general notion of environment functions. For balanced media the principle yields an invariance principle, and any balanced elliptic walk shares the transience behaviour of the simple symmetric walk. Second, a control technique moves the results to general ergodic media by building a measure under which the local process stays steady. A law of large numbers and an invariance principle follow.
arxiv-2601-04461:
Vivian Lai and seven co-authors catch people misreading their own minds in a 2026 arXiv paper about AI writing help. A proactive assistant must guess when a user wants drafting help, and designers naturally ask users what drives that wish. In a factorial vignette study, fifty participants made seven hundred fifty pairwise choices between writing scenarios that varied in effort, urgency, and other factors.

Behaviour and introspection pointed opposite ways. How much compositional effort a task demanded dominated actual choices, while urgency — which participants ranked first when asked — predicted nothing at all. The inversion is costly: a system designed from stated preferences scored worse than a naive baseline, while one fitted to behaviour did significantly better. The lesson for proactive language tools is blunt: watch what users choose, not what they say.
arxiv-2601-04661:
Armen Sargsyan, Anahit Gogyan, and David Sarkisyan watch atoms feel a wall they never touch, in a 2026 paper. When cesium vapour is confined in a cell only tens of nanometres thick. The atoms sit close enough to the sapphire windows for van der Waals attraction to the surface to shift their spectral lines. The team built a wedge-shaped nanocell — its gap varying from fifty to two hundred fifty nanometres — and recorded transmission spectra for a blue cesium transition never studied this way before.

Below about three hundred nanometres the line shifts clearly red from the surface interaction. At high pressures a second red shift from cesium-cesium collisions must be subtracted before the surface effect can be isolated. Doing so yields the first determination of the van der Waals coefficient for this transition. Results feed both atom-surface physics and miniature frequency reference design.
arxiv-2601-04961:
Gilson A. Ferreira and 5 co-authors ask how the Fermi boost changes when the base rules of space and time bend in a 2026 paper. Fermi boost is the pick-up of speed by charged grains as they bounce off clouds of magnet force in space. It is a stock way to explain how cosmic rays reach such high speeds. The team build models for both the first- and second-order forms of the boost.

Their models let the frame rules, the speed laws, and the bookkeeping of what stays fixed all take a freer form than the norm. They then study a bent form of the Lorentz rules, in two schools, plus a straight break of those rules. Each road gives the rays' speed spread its own shape. Those shapes could let ray data test if the base rules of space and time are exact.
arxiv-2601-05161:
Ioannis Kolotouros and 5 co-authors bring a quantum edge to a plain model of how stuff shakes in a 2026 paper. The plain model, the elastic network model, treats the shakes of a stuff as a web of linked springs. Such models link the make-up of a stuff to how stiff or soft it is. Yet a full, atom-by-atom run on a big chunk is past the reach of the best plain machines. That holds even for this most plain of models.

Their quantum form runs on a quantum rule that can beat the plain kind by a vast edge for linked springs. They put it to work on graphene, the famed one-atom-thick sheet of carbon. In time, such runs could tie make-up to traits for chunks far too big for plain runs, and speed the hunt for strong, light stuff.
arxiv-2601-05361:
Daniel Ahlberg, Malo Hillairet, and Ekaterina Toropova prove noise sensitivity for a spatial growth process in a 2026 paper. Noise sensitivity, introduced for Boolean functions in a celebrated 1999 paper, asks whether tiny random perturbations completely change a system's output. The phenomenon is well understood for Bernoulli percolation, but few results exist for other random spatial processes, leaving a gap in probability theory.

The authors show travel times in geometric last-passage percolation are noise sensitive. The perturbations they use act on a Bernoulli encoding of the environment. Last-passage percolation belongs to the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class, a major family of growth models. A first noise sensitivity result there opens a line of questions about how fragile optimal routes through random landscapes really are.
arxiv-2601-05561:
Neha Kukreti and Amol R Holkundkar investigate, in a 2026 physics paper, interference patterns in electrons knocked out of neon by two delayed ultraviolet pulses. The setup mirrors Ramsey interference, where two separated interactions create fringes that reveal accumulated phase. The team solved the full time-dependent Schroedinger equation for a single active electron.

Wave packets released by each pulse overlap and produce clear fringes in energy and angle distributions. Fringe positions followed a phase built up during the delay, shifting linearly with the pulses' relative phase. Varying intensity ruled out a competing explanation. Bound-state analysis showed temporary population transfer to another level controls fringe contrast, and a two-level model reproduced the effect quantitatively. In short, the fringes act as a clock that reads out the phase built up between the two pulses.
arxiv-2601-05661:
Matija Markulin and 7 co-authors develop, in a 2026 paper, a robotic system that keeps ultrasound scans steady during prostate examination despite patient movement. Prostate biopsy diagnosis depends heavily on operator skill. A robot-assisted pre-biopsy scan could make the procedure faster, more accurate, and more widely available.

A collaborative arm scans a prostate phantom while a second medical arm moves that phantom to mimic a patient. Software holds the probe's relative position constant, then segments each slice into contours and builds a 3D point cloud for biopsy planning. Scans took about thirty seconds, with reconstruction in about three seconds. Registration tests across horizontal, vertical, and combined motion showed small errors and sub-second compensation delay.
arxiv-2601-06061:
Running AI applications in real organizations takes more than building a model. Daniel Jönsson and 5 co-authors lay out a framework for that work in a 2026 paper, drawn from experience across diverse organizations. Data-driven projects depend on data at every stage, which creates extra challenges.

Their AI Application Operations framework maps the main steps and roles from idea to production. Monitoring is built in as a feedback loop, not just a safeguard, because problems can emerge at any step. Statistical and formal checks support continuous improvement, compliance, and lasting value. The framework covers core technical processes and supporting services, guiding both new initiatives and programs that are maturing.
arxiv-2601-06261:
Paula Heim and 2 co-authors show every countable group can arise as the full symmetry group of some metric space in a 2026 geometry paper. The symmetries considered are quasi-isometries, maps that preserve large-scale shape while allowing bounded distortion. A space's quasi-isometry group captures all its coarse self-symmetries.

Given any countable group, the authors construct uncountably many distinct classes of proper geodesic spaces whose quasi-isometry group equals that group. When the group is hyperbolic, the spaces can also be taken hyperbolic. The method exploits strong quasi-isometric rigidity, a phenomenon where certain symmetric spaces admit no unexpected coarse symmetries. New rigid examples are built as graphs combining rigid rank-one symmetric spaces.
arxiv-2601-06461:
Visual reasoning CAPTCHAs ask users to find objects matching a spoken-style query in a scene, and they are a frontline defense against bots. Minfeng Qi and 3 co-authors present ViPer in a 2026 paper, an attack framework that solves such challenges by pairing structured visual perception with language model reasoning.

ViPer parses the visual layout, grounds object attributes to the question's meaning, and infers target coordinates in a modular pipeline. Against six major CAPTCHA providers, it reached success rates approaching human performance, beating prior solvers that relied on template detectors or reasoning alone. Accuracy stayed high across different model backbones. The authors also propose a defense, Template-Space Randomization, which perturbs question wording without changing the task and measurably weakens solvers.
arxiv-2601-07361:
Tian-Nuo Li and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with strong evidence for dark sector interactions. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data reveal deviations from Λ CDM cosmology, conventionally attributed to dynamical dark energy (DE).

We show that these deviations are equally. If not better, explained by interactions between dark matter and dark energy (IDE), without requiring a time-varying DE equation of state. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07461:
Matteo Milani and six co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a new way to test tiny drops. The way is called Rheofluidics. It tests rheology, the study of how a thing flows and bends, one drop at a time. Each drop is at the micron scale, far too small to see by eye.

Most tests of flow work on a bulk sample. A bulk test reads the traits of the whole batch at once. It can miss how one drop acts on its own. Rheofluidics sends drops through thin channels. The channels have necks that widen and narrow in a set rhythm. That rhythm puts a back-and-forth stress on each drop. The team watches how each drop bends under the stress. From the bend, they read the flow traits of that one drop. Such reads had not been in reach before this tool.
arxiv-2601-07561:
Elisabetta Mangino and Álvaro Vargas-Moreno analyze how a translation process behaves on a tree-shaped network. Their 2026 preprint studies the left translation semigroup on weighted function spaces over a directed metric tree. A metric tree is a branching network where distances are measured along edges. Translation moves functions along that structure over time.

The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions on the weight family for strong continuity of the semigroup. Strong continuity is the basic property that lets such a process be treated as a well-behaved evolution. Weighted spaces let some branches count more than others. Results of this kind support models of flow and transport on networks. The paper is aimed at functional analysts working on semigroup theory.
arxiv-2601-07961:
Benjamin Brindle and colleagues find that how feelings move in therapy talk predicts whether treatment works. Predicting non-response in anxiety and depression care is hard, partly because symptom checks are sparse. The team analyzed twelve weeks of de-identified teletherapy transcripts. The patients numbered 12,043 in the United States, with moderate to severe symptoms. Their 2026 preprint studies fine-grained emotions captured passively from language.

Emotion flexibility means feelings shift and adapt rather than staying stuck. Language markers of that flexibility may forecast outcomes earlier than questionnaires. Passively captured markers need no extra work from patients or therapists. Early warning of non-response lets clinicians change course sooner. The study serves mental health scholars and digital care providers. It links a psychological concept to measurable traces in everyday therapy speech.
arxiv-2601-08061: Alex Lewandowski, Marlos Machado, and Dale Schuurmans ask how much computing language models can do. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that models now phrase and often solve broad problems in plain language. Yet experts still debate their true computational limits. A language model is trained to predict the next piece of human text, step by step. The paper studies whether universal computation sits inside that decoding process itself, rather than in tools added around the model.
arxiv-2601-08461: Chao Wang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that proves a claim about pi first made by a machine. The claim came from the Ramanujan Machine, a program that hunts for new math forms on its own. It dealt with a class of polynomial continued fractions that give minus pi over four. The fractions are of a non-standard kind. Wang proves them in a strict analytic way. He links the fractions to ratios of contiguous Gaussian hypergeometric functions. He then derives the results by a chain of equal-form steps.
arxiv-2601-09061:
Francisco Santiago Nieto-de la Rosa, Osvaldo Guzman, and Ulises Ramos-Garcia study a class of forcing tools in set theory. Forcing is a way to build new set worlds with set traits. Laver forcing is a classic tool of that kind. Their form builds it from a co-ideal, a set of sets that codes what counts as large.

They read the traits of these tools through a rank called the Katetov order. They tell when such a tool adds a Cohen real, a type of new real line point. They also show such tools never add a random real. A reader in set theory gets a crisp split. One type of new point can come, the next can not.
arxiv-2601-09361:
Jiaying Zhang and six co-authors work on training large reasoning models at low cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper, GeoRA, adapts low-rank fine-tuning to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. In that setup, a model earns rewards only when its answers can be checked as right.

Older low-rank methods were built for supervised fine-tuning, not for this reward-based training. Used directly, they suffer spectral collapse and unstable optimization, which cap the model's skill. GeoRA is shaped to respect the geometry of the reward-based process instead. The aim is stable training that keeps the gains of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2601-09461:
Reemt Hinrichs and three co-authors measure the ceiling on short-term prediction of sustained speech. Their 2026 arXiv paper centers on prediction gain, a classic score in signal coding. Predictive coding stores or sends speech by guessing the next sample and keeping only the error.

A better guess means a lower bit rate for the same quality. Prediction gain links the mean-squared prediction error to the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of a coder. The authors analyze how much gain is even possible on sustained speech sounds. Knowing the ceiling tells codec designers when better predictors stop paying off.
arxiv-2601-09561:
Hector Galindo-Silva and Paula Herrera-Idárraga ask whether civic schooling can shift a country's faith. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies religious change in Colombia after its 1991 Constitution. The new charter ended the confessional regime and ordered constitutional instruction in high schools.

The authors exploit the fact that cohorts differed in how much reform-era schooling they received. With nationally representative survey data, they run a difference-in-differences design across those cohorts. The setup lets them tie shifts in religious identification to the reform itself. The study speaks to a wider question: how much can state education reshape belief?
arxiv-2601-09861:
Roland R. Netz follows particles over energy barriers when the medium remembers. His 2026 arXiv paper studies barrier crossing and energy relaxation in non-Markovian inertial systems. Simulations show a memory-turnover: at mid-range memory times, crossing is faster than in the memory-free limit.

For long memory times, the crossing time grows with the square of the memory time, at fixed total friction. The authors reach these results with an analytical Green-Fokker-Planck approach. Barrier crossing sits at the core of chemical reaction rates. A theory that tracks memory effects sharpens rate predictions for real, sticky environments.
arxiv-2601-10361:
S. Vanderwoude and co authors test if bent radio galaxies twist their light in new ways. A radio galaxy spews jets of charged grains. In a galaxy cluster, those jets can bend. The bend is thought to come from the gas and fields in the cluster. The cause is still not firm.

A bent jet may also twist its light waves in a set way. The team ask if bent forms part from straight forms in that trait. They match bend size to twist traits in known cases. A match would tie bend cause to jet traits. It would guide how clusters shape the jets in them.
arxiv-2601-10461:
Adam Siegel and Simon Benjamin turn lost qubit states into a known kind of error. Their qubits are singlet triplet pairs in small dots. Such qubits can be shuttled fast and well in a chip. Shuttling lets a chip move states to where they are needed. That aids a shuttling based form of error fix.

Some errors hide from fix tools. Erasure conversion turns a hidden error into a flagged loss. A flagged loss is far more easy to fix. The team show how to add that step for these qubits. It lifts the grade of the whole fix chain.
arxiv-2601-11061:
Lecheng Yan and co-authors investigate a paradox in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The method, RLVR, boosts language model reasoning by rewarding correct answers. Yet models like Qwen 2.5 gain even when rewards are spurious or wrong. The authors dig into the mechanism behind that puzzle. They name what they find the Perplexity Paradox.

Under spurious rewards, answer-token perplexity drops while the prompt side's coherence degrades. That split suggests the model bypasses reasoning in favor of memorization shortcuts. If gains can come from shortcuts, benchmark jumps may overstate true reasoning growth. The work warns trainers to audit what RLVR actually teaches, not just what scores say.
arxiv-2601-11461:
Radhika Kulkarni, Aluisio Pinheiro, Brani Vidakovic, and Abdourrahmane Atto smooth a denoising rule. Their 2026 preprint is named Smooth SCAD, for wavelet denoising. Wavelets split a signal into pieces at many scales. Thresholding kills small pieces as noise and keeps big ones.

SCAD is a known threshold rule with prized traits. It gives sparsity for small coefficients, zeroing them out. It stays near unbiased for large coefficients, a rare pair. Its flaw is a piecewise linear kink in the middle. The team swaps that kink for a raised cosine curve. The new rule is odd, continuous, and smooth off the threshold. It keeps the SCAD traits while easing numeric work.
arxiv-2601-12161:
Tomoki Koike, Prakash Mohan, Mark T. Henry de Frahan, Julie Bessac, and Elizabeth Qian stream operator inference for smaller models of large dynamic systems. Projection methods shrink big systems to low-dim models that run fast. Operator Inference learns such models from data in two steps.

First, SVD compresses the data to a low-dim basis. Then a least squares fit learns the small operators, with no need for the source code. A streaming form can handle data too large to hold at once. That helps climate and fluid models at scale.
arxiv-2601-12361:
Bernd Finkbeiner, Hadar Frenkel, and Tim Rohde study model checking for a rich logic of hyperproperties. The logic is called Hyper 2 LTL. It grows out of HyperLTL, a known logic for facts about sets of traces. The new logic adds quantification over sets of traces, a second order step.

That extra power lets one state complex facts that older logics cannot. The authors name facts about knowledge and facts about systems that do not move in lock step. The core question is cost: how hard is it to check such facts on finite structures? Work of this kind maps the price of expressive power in formal verification. It shows where checks stay feasible and where they blow up.
arxiv-2601-12461:
Jingche Chen and Han Hong prove a systolic inequality for manifolds with a curvature condition. The systole is the length of the shortest loop that cannot be shrunk to a point. A homological version of it is their focus here. Their manifolds have positive triRic curvature, a condition in higher codimension terms.

They show their inequality is optimal, meaning the bound cannot be improved. They also characterize the case of equality, when a manifold hits the bound exactly. The work extends prior results by Bray, Brendle, and Neves, and by Chu, Lee, and Zhu. Systolic results tie local curvature to global size in a sharp way. Equality cases often reveal rigid, model shapes worth study on their own.
arxiv-2601-12561:
Catriona A. Thomson and four co authors work on photonic crystal nanolasers with a tiny footprint. Photonic crystals give unmatched control over how light is confined and guided. They also shape how light interacts with matter at small scales. That control has reshaped optics and spawned many practical devices over past decades.

A nanolaser built in such a crystal can be extremely small. Small size matters for the goal named here: biointegration. A laser that can sit inside or on biological tissue opens new sensing routes. The team stress a minimal footprint design for that end. Work of this kind links photonics with medicine and life science tools.
arxiv-2601-12861:
Zhangliang Chen and six co authors launch Project FOSSO, a study of brown dwarfs in binary systems. Brown dwarfs are substellar companions, too light to burn hydrogen like stars. Their hosts here are main sequence stars that will one day become white dwarfs. What happens to the companion as the host swells and dies is the central question.

Recent discoveries found many substellar companions around white dwarfs. Those survivors constrain how the post main sequence phase treats close companions. The team investigate long term evolution and final outcomes of these systems. Some companions may be engulfed, others may drift to wider orbits. The project maps those fates across the known population.
arxiv-2601-13461:
Megan M. Kerr and Tracy L. Payne study submanifolds that hang off special subgroups in bent spaces with symmetry. Their spaces are solvmanifolds, group based spaces that solve by steps. The sub forms at stake have an odd trait next to Ricci curvature, the mean bend of space.

The work grows a study by H. Tamaru. He built such forms in symmetric spaces of non compact type from parabolic subgroups of the isometry group. He called them attached submanifolds. Kerr and Payne carry that build past symmetric spaces. For shape staff, each new host class tests if the odd Ricci trait is rare or wide.
arxiv-2601-13761:
Shengda Fan, Xuyan Ye, and Yankai Lin work on AI systems that improve themselves through self-play in 2026. In self-play, one model poses questions and an other solves them. Past setups face two flaws. The questioner's goals shift as the solver's feedback changes. And the solver learns from its own pseudo-labels, which can bake in errors.

Their method, DARC, splits the training into a decoupled, asymmetric curriculum. Separate paths for questioner and solver aim to calm the training. Stable self-play could let models grow with less human data. That path draws much hope, and much need for care.
arxiv-2601-13861: M. J. Dunwoody studies patterns in triangulated 2-spheres and 3-spheres in 2026. A triangulation splits a sphere into triangles that fit edge to edge. Patterns in such splits can encode deep facts on shape. Dunwoody gives a new proof of a lemma in Abigail Thompson's work. That lemma feeds her Recognition Algorithm for 3-spheres. The algorithm tests if a given space is in fact a 3-sphere.
arxiv-2601-14461:
Lukas Netterdon, Veronica Montanaro, Manuel Torrilhon, and Hossein Gorji improve gas simulations in this 2026 paper. The Fokker-Planck particle method speeds up rarefied-gas simulations. It replaces the binary collisions of Direct Simulation Monte Carlo with a drift-diffusion process. Like all particle methods, it is stochastic by nature.

That randomness causes statistical fluctuations in macroscopic quantities. Accurate results then need large particle numbers, which cost time. The team applies quasi-random numbers for variance reduction in the method. Quasi-random points fill space more evenly than pure random ones. The gain is clear. Runs take less time, and the noise in the end maps drops a lot. Less noise means fewer runs. That saves both time and funds on each test case. Readers get a way to calm the noise in rarefied-gas runs without simply adding more particles.
arxiv-2601-14661:
C. de León searches for dark matter signs in gamma rays in this 2026 paper. Axion-like particles are hypothetical particles and compelling candidates for cold dark matter. Their existence could be probed through conversions into photons in magnetic fields. If axion-like particles mix with light, some gamma rays from distant sources would vanish along the way.

The author searches for attenuation in the observed gamma ray spectra of galactic sources that emit at energies of hundreds of TeV. The data come from the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory, HAWC. The source is 3HWC J1908+063. Readers get constraints on axion-like particles from one of the most energetic light sources in the galaxy.
arxiv-2601-15261:
Sophie Vo, Konstantin Y. Bliokh, and Miguel A. Alonso weigh the spin of a pulse of light with a toy model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with spatiotemporal vortex pulses. These wavepackets carry transverse orbital angular momentum, a twist across the pulse.

How to quantify that twist has been debated in recent work. The authors build a simple mechanical model of the pulse. It is a loop of free point particles, all moving at one speed but at slightly different angles. That ray-like picture gives a clean way to compute the momentum.
arxiv-2601-15461:
Amalendu Krishna and Subhadip Majumder work in algebraic geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is the Brauer group of schemes over local fields of positive characteristic. They study Kato's ramification filtration on that group. The filtration sorts elements by how wildly they ramify. A second sorting, the evaluation filtration, comes from a different route.

The authors show the two sorts agree in this setting. More precisely, the non-log version of Kato's filtration matches the evaluation filtration. The schemes in view are regular, separated, and of finite type. The result extends recent work by Bright and Newton. Their earlier result is now carried into positive characteristic. Readers in arithmetic geometry will follow the proof details.
arxiv-2601-15861:
Daniel Lokshtanov, Michał Pilipczuk, and Paweł Rzążewski hunt for large sparse patterns in graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their measure is the tree-independence number. Start with a tree decomposition of a graph. Its independence number is the largest independent set inside one bag. The graph's tree-independence number is the minimum of that value over decompositions. Recent work by Lima and others set up this frame.

The authors look for large sparse induced subgraphs. They target graphs whose tree-independence number is small, but not very small. That middle zone is where the theory gets hard. Induced subgraphs keep only chosen vertices and their links. Finding big sparse ones inside structured graphs feeds algorithm design. Such results often unlock faster methods for hard graph problems.
arxiv-2601-15961:
Fengwu Sun and a large team trace dust around massive young galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. They use JWST NIRCam imaging and grism spectroscopy from the JADES Origins Fields. The team reports redshifts for 1,445 emission-line galaxies between redshift zero and nine. Within that sample, two galaxy protoclusters stand out. They sit at redshifts 3.47 and 3.69. Each is anchored by massive, dusty star-forming galaxies.

The title names the discovery: large reservoirs of small dust grains in the circumgalactic medium. Dust far outside galaxies, at redshift near 3.5, is hard to detect. Its presence says galaxies expel or shed material early and widely. That outflow shapes how galaxies and their surroundings evolve together.
arxiv-2601-16261:
Magoon and a large team show first tests of a new THz probe build. Their 2026 preprint sets out the SQUAT probe type. SQUAT stands for a transmon that boosts charge sense from split pairs. The probe ties straight to a wave line, with no ring in the path. A hit breaks pairs in the chip caps and makes loose charge grains.

Those grains cross a join and shift the chip state. The shift is the sign of the hit for read out. First tests weigh if the build sees hits as planned. A work probe of this type could sense faint far light. The work is a first proof of the build.
arxiv-2601-16361:
Philani Majozi sets out local link ideas for spaces that lack full same form. His 2026 preprint deals with spaces built on one way rules. Such spaces span quasi metrics, quasi uniform sets and modular sets. Old link and whole ideas rest on two way rules. Those rules fail to fit one way spaces with care.

Majozi gives a one way form of local link for such spaces. The form tracks links that hold in a set dir sense. New forms let teams sort such spaces by their link traits. They also aid sums of whole ends for one way spaces. The work is a base step in one way maths.
arxiv-2601-16461:
Anuj Yadav and coauthors set a loss for squeeze that keeps sense, not bits. Their 2026 preprint deals with loss based squeeze of a source. Loss is set by a log score from a fixed joint law. That law ties the source to a sense code for it. Squeeze then keeps the sense the law cares for most.

Bits that do not shift sense can be cut with low loss. Such cuts serve pics, speech and text sent at low rate. The team sums the best rates for this loss form. Firm rates guide build of sense first squeeze tools. The work joins squeeze maths to sense laws.
arxiv-2601-16661:
Monika Gupta, Ajay Meena, Anamitra Roy Choudhury, Vijay Arya, and Srikanta Bedathur study code moved across languages. Large language models now turn code from one tongue to the next. Most such models learned from code full of notes. Those notes, called comments, sit in plain words by the code. The team's 2026 preprint asks if the notes help.

The authors test the hunch that comments aid the move. Good notes can tell what a block of code should do. That clue may guide the model when syntax shifts. The study checks when notes help and when they do not. Its lessons can shape how teams write code for smooth moves.
arxiv-2601-16761:
A large team of UK astronomers sets out a plan for a new space scope. The scope, named SIRMOS, would ride on a satellite. It would split infra-red light from many space objects at once. Such split light tells what far galaxies are made of. Their 2026 preprint links that tool to big cosmic themes.

Those themes span the birth and growth of the cosmos. Star birth, galaxy growth, and dark stuff all leave marks in such light. A fleet of spectra beats one-by-one work by far. The plan shows what a mid-size craft could reap. It makes the case for funds in the years ahead.
arxiv-2601-16961:
Francesco Cesa and a team of six co-authors fake local acts in shared-drive atom grids. Atom grids trap atoms in light for quantum work. Two kinds of atoms share one grid here. All atoms feel the same drive pulse at once. Yet the team fakes acts that strike each site in turn. Their 2026 preprint shows the trick with Floquet steps.

Steps in time swap which kind feels the drive. Wide block rules for near and far pairs aid the fake. Faked local acts let plain grids run rich sims. Such sims probe new stuff states at low cost. Dual-kind grids gain a broad new use.
arxiv-2601-17061:
Dan Adler argues that facts can evolve with no genes at play. His frame is called Stability-Driven Assembly. Chance builds join bits in new forms all the time. Forms that last long pile up by that fact. No copy step or score rule is set in advance. His 2026 preprint says that bias acts like a born genetic rule set.

Lasting forms seed more joins as time runs. Fresh forms thus skew to the long-lived kinds. The frame speaks to how life first rose from raw stuff. It may also speak to how codes and tongues grow. Plain physics, in this view, can breed fit forms.
arxiv-2601-17861: Ioana Ciuclea and Cornelia Vizman study vortex loops through the lens of group geometry. Their 2026 preprint treats manifolds of such loops as coadjoint orbits of the group of area-preserving maps of the plane. A vortex loop is a closed curve carrying a vorticity density that may drop to zero at points. The result ties fluid shapes to the algebra of the group that moves them.
arxiv-2601-18061:
Kiana Jafari and co-authors test a core belief behind AI safety work in mental health. Their 2026 preprint is a preprint under review, as its note states. Learning from human feedback assumes that expert judgments, when pooled, give a valid ground truth. Mental health is a field where that truth matters most, since safety stakes are high. Three certified psychiatrists rated language model replies on their own, using a calibrated rubric.

The study checks how far the experts agree with each other. If experts diverge, then pooled feedback hides real doubt. That would shake how models are trained and tested for clinic use. The work gives safety teams hard data on the limits of expert consensus.
arxiv-2601-18161:
T. Worrakitpoonpon simulates how bars form in disk galaxies under halos of different density. His 2026 preprint uses N-body simulations. A bar is a long, straight band of stars across a galaxy's center. How a bar starts depends on the dark halo around the disk. In a highly concentrated halo, the bar's growth is limited early on. Dominant multi-arm modes, boosted by swing amplification, crowd the young disk and hold the bar back.

Other halo densities let bars grow by other routes. Comparing the routes shows how much the halo steers the disk's fate. Bars reshape galaxies and drive gas inward, so their origins matter. The work maps one control knob of galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2601-18261:
Chao-Hong Tan and co-authors present FGGM, a method that helps models learn new tasks without erasing old ones. Their 2026 preprint addresses catastrophic forgetting in large language models. The method masks gradients, blocking updates to some parameters while others learn. The mask is guided by diagonal Fisher information, a score of how much each parameter matters for past tasks. Thresholds adapt as training goes on, so critical parameters stay protected while the rest stay free to move.

The aim is balance: stability for old skills, plasticity for new ones. The method needs no replay of old data, by its design. Continual learning without old data suits privacy-bound deployments.
arxiv-2601-18361:
Jean Michel de Souza Sant'Ana and three colleagues weigh new ways to link small devices that send data over the net. Ground towers serve towns well but leave gaps at sea, in fields, and in far off zones. The team looks at high platforms that float in the thin upper air. It also looks at small craft in low Earth orbit.

The study counts how often a sent signal is lost for each setup. It tests craft on their own and platforms on their own. It also tests mixed plans that join space, air, and ground links in one system. Cost counts as much as strength here, since a link that costs too much will not be built. The aim is a clear view of which mix gives firm links for the least spend.
arxiv-2601-18761:
Wout Slabbinck and three colleagues argue that web data needs a shift from who may see it to how it may be used. New laws in Europe press for data groups that can be shared across firms with trust. A right to see a file is not the same as a right to use it for each aim. Laws set terms on use that shift with the aim and with the time.

Web stores now tie their rules to files, in a tight knot. That knot makes use terms hard to state and hard to change. The team set out a path built on a shared way for users to hold and state their own terms. Such a path could let a user grant use for one aim and bar it for the next. It would bring web data rules close to the law that now binds them.
arxiv-2601-18961:
Uma Girish and five co-authors study proofs that pin down when and where a claim was made. Position proofs let a party show it stands at a set place, which backs claims of the form: I am at this spot. Such proofs cannot be made safe with classical tools alone, even with strong computing bounds.

Quantum tools, though, can make them work. The team gives private versions of these proofs, so a party can prove its place without giving away more than the claim needs. Private place proofs could serve location based services that must not leak a user's exact track.
arxiv-2601-19061:
Harsh Chaudhari and six co-authors show a stealthy way to poison the reasoning of language models. Models that think in chains of thought now draw on shared public data sets of reasoning traces. Some sets are downloaded tens of thousands of times a month. That sharing opens a door for quiet attacks.

Their attack, Thought-Transfer, aims poison at a chosen target in a roundabout way. Tainted traces can bend a model's chain of thought without blunt signs. The work warns data curators that popular reasoning sets need checks, since a few bad traces can steer many models at once.
arxiv-2601-19461:
Yida Lin and four co-authors grade depth sensing methods on tree branches, a hard test for drone forestry. Self flying drones in forests need sound depth estimates that travel well to new woods. Past grades focus on city and indoor scenes, leaving vegetation, the hardest case, largely unchecked.

The team runs the first systematic zero shot test of several stereo depth methods on branches. Zero shot means the methods get no practice on forest data first. Knowing which method sees twigs and gaps best guides the design of drones that must not snag or fall among trees.
arxiv-2601-19761:
Jin Huang, Fethiye Irmak Doğan, and Hatice Gunes propose a new way to think about social robots. A social robot should personalise its behaviour to each user. Current systems lean on language models that adapt replies from user data. Others learn from the user's immediate reactions in real time.

The authors argue these robots should be framed as recommender systems. A recommender picks items for a user from their tastes; a robot could pick actions and topics the same way. The paper lays foundations and a framework for that view. It also surveys applications where the framing helps. Treating robots as recommenders imports decades of research on personalisation, evaluation, and user modeling.
arxiv-2601-19961:
Huanlin Gao and colleagues speed up flow matching, a generative modeling method. Flow matching learns a velocity field that carries noise into data. Inference follows that field step by step, which costs many evaluations. Caching reuses earlier computations to skip steps, but most caches use instantaneous velocity snapshots.

That shortcut bends the trajectory, and errors pile up at high acceleration. Their framework, MeanCache, caches average velocity instead of instantaneous values. Averages track the true path more faithfully over long jumps. The method needs no retraining of the underlying model. Faster generation matters for image and video tools used interactively. The work improves the speed-quality trade-off at aggressive settings.
arxiv-2601-20061:
Dhruv Parikh, Jebacyril Arockiaraj, and Viktor Prasanna accelerate an unusual computing paradigm. Hyperdimensional computing represents data as very long, low-precision vectors called hypervectors. Learning and inference use light, noise-tolerant operations on those vectors. The catch is the dimensionality itself: huge, sparse vectors mean heavy data movement that conventional processors handle badly.

The authors build acceleration from primitive operations tailored to the paradigm. Their target is real-time image classification. If hyperdimensional methods run fast enough, they suit edge devices that need robust, low-power learning. The work treats hardware and algorithm as one design problem. It is part of a broader search for post-neural computing models. The chips are small and cheap to run. Speed is the test that counts most. A fast score here opens real use. The aim is not raw size but smart use of size. Less heat and less cost come with it.
arxiv-2601-20161:
Isadora Krsek and five colleagues study how to warn people about the privacy risk of what they share online. People often discuss sensitive topics under a sense of anonymity, yet that safety can be misjudged, which leads to over-disclosure. New language tools make it possible to estimate the risk that a post could identify its author.

The authors give design recommendations for showing users these population risk estimates. Their focus is informed self-disclosure: people should see a clear estimate before they post, not after harm is done. Good design here must be honest about risk without scaring users away from support communities.
arxiv-2601-20261:
Damian Guenzing, Dayne Y. Sasaki, and a large team demonstrate soft X-ray ptychography in reflection rather than transmission. Ptychography is a scanning method that builds high-resolution, element-specific images of nanoscale structures. Transmission setups, though, demand very thin samples, which excludes many extended or bulk specimens, above all in the soft X-ray range.

By imaging in reflection geometry, the team opens the method to samples that cannot be thinned. The work was published as a research article in an optics journal. Reflection imaging could widen soft X-ray studies to real devices and materials as they are, not only as thin slices.
arxiv-2601-20361:
Chen-Yang Dai and four colleagues present TINNs, time-induced neural networks for solving time-dependent partial differential equations. Physics-informed networks learn a smooth solution that can be read at any point in space and time. Standard versions feed time in as one input but share a single set of weights across all times.

That sharing forces the same features to represent very different dynamics at early and late times. TINNs are designed to relieve that strain. Better solvers of this kind would speed up work on heat flow, waves, and fluids, where the time evolution is the whole point.
arxiv-2601-20961:
Steve Hanneke provides a complete theory of optimal learning rates without hopeful assumptions. His 2026 paper concerns universal agnostic learning for binary classification. Agnostic learning makes no promise that the data follow a simple rule. The learner must still perform nearly as well as the best rule in a class. Universal rates describe the best possible speed of learning across settings. Hanneke pins down those rates in full.

The work extends an earlier realizable-case theory. That theory, by Bousquet, Hanneke, Moran, van Handel, and Yehudayoff, assumed a perfect rule exists in the class. Removing the realizability assumption is a major step. Real data are noisy, and perfect rules rarely exist. A complete agnostic theory tells practitioners what accuracy is even possible. It closes a foundational question in statistical learning theory.
arxiv-2601-21261:
Abrar Hamed Al Barwani, Abdelaziz Amara Korba, and Raja Waseem Anwar work on catching phishing emails without flagging too many honest ones. Fake emails keep getting harder to spot, and simple rule-based filters no longer keep up. Language models read text well, but used alone they mark too many real emails as fake.

The authors pair a language model with a search step that pulls in helpful context first. The design is built around the user, not just the message. Fewer false alarms mean less wasted work for staff who must check each warning. The aim is a filter people can trust day to day.
arxiv-2601-21361:
A model-independent search looks for a new particle that decays into pairs of muons, using data from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The search covers a low mass range where a light new particle might hide. It uses proton collisions recorded over several years of running.

Rather than assume one specific theory, the team scans for any bump in the muon-pair mass. A bump would hint at a particle no model has catalogued yet. Null results still matter, since they rule out wide classes of theories. The dataset is among the largest ever used for such a low-mass scan.
arxiv-2601-21461:
Albert Tseng and Christopher De Sa replace a popular sparsity trick in language models with simple lookup layers. Sparse models usually route each token to a few expert networks. Dynamic hard routing can waste hardware and needs extra losses to train stably.

Their large lookup layers work more like a table the model reads from. Reading a table is cheap and predictable for hardware. The design keeps the capacity gains of sparsity without the routing headaches. If it scales, future models could grow in knowledge while each token still costs little to process.
arxiv-2601-21761:
Esteban Parra, Sonia Haiduc, Preetha Chatterjee, Ramtin Ehsani, and Polina Iaremchuk chart a sustainable future for peer review in software engineering. Review is how the field vets its results. Submissions keep growing fast, while the pool of qualified reviewers does not.

The imbalance threatens the long-term growth of the whole research community. The authors examine the strain and look for paths that keep review rigorous without burning out the reviewers. Options touch incentives, tooling, and how venues match papers to expertise. The stakes are field-wide: when review fails, weak work slips through and strong work stalls.
arxiv-2601-21961:
Kuai Yu and co-authors ask how the look of a web page steers the agents that browse it. Web agents now perform tasks across many sites with strong results. Research on their weak points has focused on attacks, on whether hostile pages can fool them.

Far less is known about how ordinary design choices sway agents in benign settings. The team's 2026 preprint evaluates how visual attributes of user interfaces influence agent behavior. Colors, layouts, and emphasis may push an agent toward one element over another, much as they do with people. Designers and testers need that map, since agent-friendly design could soon matter as much as human-friendly design.
arxiv-2601-22061:
Li Zhang and Pengtao Xie make a strong image tool work on its own. The Segment Anything Model can split an image into clean parts for things it has never been taught. But it needs a prompt, a hint from a human hand, for each new image. That need blocks full use in the field.

A fast finder tool called YOLO can spot things and give those hints on its own. But when the two tools are just chained, their goals do not match. The team trains them as one team, with a two-level scheme that keeps both goals in line. Their tool is called BLO-Inst. Fast, prompt-free splitting helps in scans, farm work, and plant checks, where no hand can mark each new frame.
arxiv-2601-22161:
Anmol Guragain tests a trend in how machines read feelings from face and voice. His test uses the EAV set of clips. He asks if the new, large attention tools beat plain ones when the data set is small. He runs three groups of tools: plain Transformers, new split-attention tools, and strong CNN tools with tweaks.

The fancy tools did not win. Plain traits drawn from the clips, built with care by hand, beat the Transformers. His point is that small sets reward craft more than scale. A tool that knows the task can beat a big tool that does not. This is a warn for fields where data will stay scarce, such as care work and mood care.
arxiv-2601-22861:
Refael Sheffer and co-authors map the ground hidden under thick forest canopy. The terrain below the trees matters for search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest checks. Today's tools lean on costly airborne laser scans, or on thermal imaging tuned to find people.

Their method uses plain color images plus neural three-dimensional rebuilding to recover the ground shape. Cheaper mapping from normal cameras could put forest surveys within reach of small teams. It also opens a path to robots that can plan safe routes under trees. The team frames the work around applications like search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest inventory in dense woodland.
arxiv-2602-00061: Zhou Ziheng and colleagues argue that simple role assignment beats principle lists for safety alignment. Roles such as mother or judge pack in values plus the habits of mind to apply them. Their training free pipeline pairs a role conditioned generator with iterative role based critics that refine its output. Across five model families it beats principle based, chain of thought, and other baselines. On WildJailbreak it cuts unsafe replies sharply for DeepSeek-V3, and the method also holds on agentic safety tasks.
arxiv-2602-00261: Ketevan Danelia and team argue that future biochemical concentrations can be predicted well. Sensing chemical levels matters for many life processes, but small molecule counts limit accuracy through shot noise. Limits for static and at random fluctuating concentrations are well studied, yet developing systems show predictable patterns in space and time. Using prior knowledge of structured profiles, the authors frame sensing as Bayesian inference over allowed profile classes, deriving new limits. Information from current binding events thus predicts future levels, and the best guess from that frame beats older limits.
arxiv-2602-00561: Tianhao Huang and colleagues ask how large-scale cognitive patterns arise from fine-scale neuronal wiring, using structural and functional connectivity. Current methods fuse the two at regional level but miss the latent links between regions that explain why structural and functional patterns couple and vary together. Their Adaptive Flow Routing Network models how structural limits give rise to functional communication patterns, enabling interpretable discovery of key neural pathways. Tests show it beats state-of-the-art baselines by a clear margin.
arxiv-2602-00661: Ahsan Raza Siyal and colleagues propose a physics-guided neural design for forecast of 3D change over time. The task spans medical imaging, fluids, materials, and geophysics. The model learns amplitude, phase, and potential fields from volume sequences. These form a complex wavefunction. A differentiable Schrödinger stepper advances it in time. The structured evolution curbs drift over long horizons. The learned potential shapes how parts affect each other. On synthetic benchmarks mimicking realistic shape changes, it predicts future volumes and deformation fields well and stably.
arxiv-2602-00761: Andre Hora and colleagues argue tests should check one behaviour each, and propose a new smell for tests that check too much. The older Eager Test smell counts production method calls, but research suggests call counts poorly proxy functionality. The authors hypothesise that multi-behaviour tests tend to cover several paths of one production method. They name this Test Obsessed by Method: a test method covering multiple paths of a single production method. In 2,054 tests from 12 Python Standard Library suites, they detect 44 such tests across 11 suites.
arxiv-2602-00861: Kushal Chakrabarti and colleagues show cutting Gamma tightens the Price of Anarchy, and GAME-LoRA cuts hallucination up to 18% with no knowledge loss. They treat attention heads as players, where cross-entropy training creates a potential game among heads. Gradient descent then reaches Nash equilibria that can be arbitrarily inefficient. Their key result bounds the Price of Anarchy by Gamma, the off-diagonal mass of a head matrix. Excess hallucination probability and excess head redundancy both scale with the Price of Anarchy, unifying two failure modes.
arxiv-2602-01561: Yejin Son and co-authors introduce Multimodal UNcommonsense, a benchmark for cases defying typical norms. It pairs visual scenes with odd or strange results in natural language. Models must explain odd images with plain logic or uncover unexpected interpretations in normal scenes. Their search-based in-context learning system transfers reasoning from larger to smaller models without extra training. A multimodal ensemble retriever finds relevant cases even when image-text pairs are planned to clash. Standard in-context learning methods improve by an average of 8.3% in rare, odd settings.
arxiv-2602-02261: Daniil Shlenskii and colleagues unlock a duality between conditional flow matching and interaction field matching in generative modeling. The two start from different objects: flow matching specifies a conditional probability path through data space, whereas field matching specifies an interaction field inspired by physics in an augmented space. They show coincidence for a natural subclass called forward-only field matching, constructing a bijection between it and flow matching. General field matching proves strictly more expressive, including fields unrealizable in standard flow matching, and the duality benefits both sides.
arxiv-2602-02561:
Xinyu Liu and 7 co-authors mine the missing folklore lemmas that formal mathematics libraries need, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Lean's Mathlib library powers formal reasoning, yet many intermediate facts mathematicians take for granted were never formalized. That absence limits Lean as an everyday tool.

Their modular pipeline uses language models to discover, formalize, and prove reusable folklore lemmas automatically. It produced a verified library including over fifteen hundred Lean-checked proofs that pass a proof-bypass screen. A small curated subset has already been merged into Mathlib itself, evidence that outputs can meet expert standards. The team also built a benchmark of over four thousand non-trivial, type-checked Lean statements spanning many domains. The work recasts language models from passive consumers of formal libraries into active contributors that expand them.
arxiv-2602-02861:
Chiara Caprini's solo 2026 review explains how gravitational waves could reveal physics beyond the Standard Model. The review grew from a seminar at a 2025 workshop on Higgs pairs. Its focus is first-order phase transitions, sudden changes in the early universe that can produce a background of waves.

Caprini summarizes recent work by the LISA Cosmology Working Group. LISA is a planned space detector for such waves. The summary covers whether LISA could detect these signals. Strong overlaps between model settings make reconstruction hard. Once a scenario is assumed, though, LISA limits could complement results from particle colliders, present and future.
arxiv-2602-02961:
Pinterest content must now be found by generative search engines, and Faye Zhang and 5 co-authors describe a production system for that shift in a 2026 paper. Systems like ChatGPT answer questions directly, synthesizing evidence instead of listing links. Single images lack the depth such systems favor, risking lost traffic for visual platforms.

Their framework fine-tunes vision-language models to predict what users would search for, rather than merely describing images. Agents mine live internet trends for emerging demand. Predicted queries drive collection pages built with multimodal embeddings. Linking structures then spread authority signals across billions of assets. Deployed at scale, the system delivered strong organic traffic growth and millions of added monthly users.
arxiv-2602-03161:
Jet precession around the black hole in M87 constrains its magnetic surroundings in research by Chao-Hui Wang with 2 co-authors. The jet's roughly eleven-year precession period probes strong gravity and the electromagnetic environment near the supermassive black hole. Their setting is a rotating black hole immersed in a uniform electromagnetic field, described by Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson geometry, where ordinary geodesic methods fail because motion is not separable.

A Hamiltonian method handles the spherical orbits instead. For strong magnetic fields, such orbits exist only within a finite radial range at a given inclination. Requiring orbit existence bounds the field from above, with tighter limits for retrograde motion. Imposing the observed precession period tightens the bound further, giving a constraint stand-alone of the black hole's shadow.
arxiv-2602-03461:
Safety-critical learning systems must respect hard constraints, not just prefer them. Philipp J. Schneider and Daniel Kuhn address a hidden flaw in the usual fix, projecting predictions back onto the allowed set, in their 2026 paper. Standard projection flattens outside points onto a boundary surface, which kills the gradients that training depends on.

Their Soft-Radial Projection layer instead maps points radially inward, landing well inside the feasible set. Every output stays strictly feasible, while the Jacobian keeps full rank almost everywhere, so optimization no longer stalls. The authors prove the architecture keeps universal approximation power. Experiments show better convergence and solution quality than optimization-based and projection-based baselines.
arxiv-2602-03661:
Zhu-Ding Duan and 5 co-authors predict how matter-antimatter asymmetry should appear in a rare baryon decay. Their 2026 paper studies bottom lambda baryons decaying into pentaquark states plus a pion or kaon. A recent LHCb measurement of related decays into charmonium final states supplies the experimental motivation.

Working within a final-state rescattering framework, the authors compute branching ratios plus the direct CP asymmetry for each of the three known pentaquark states. The pion channel's branching fractions land near one part in a million, with CP asymmetries around one percent. The kaon channel shows almost no CP violation, but its rates depend strongly on the pentaquarks' spin assignments. The predictions guide future precision measurements in the pentaquark region.
arxiv-2602-03761:
A laser pulse can melt the ordered pattern of a charge-density wave, and watching the pattern heal reveals how electrons and lattice talk. Sankha Subhra Bakshi and 2 co-authors model that recovery in a 2026 paper, using a two-dimensional spinless Holstein model in a semiclassical framework. Fully nonadiabatic dynamics are too expensive to run for long times on large lattices.

The authors split the lattice force into a smooth quasi-adiabatic part and a noisy bath-like remainder from fast electronic fluctuations. The smooth part depends only on the local lattice configuration, so machine learning can fit it efficiently. A minimal Langevin description handles the bath. Combined, the pieces simulate long recovery dynamics at scales direct methods cannot reach.
arxiv-2602-04861:
Ryan Liu and 4 co-authors argue that machine-learned atomistic models should be judged by physical smoothness, not just accuracy on energies and forces, in a 2026 paper. A model's energy surface can be jagged in ways standard tests miss, causing later simulations to misbehave.

Their Bond Smoothness Characterization Test probes the surface through controlled bond stretches. It detects breaks, fake minima, and spurious forces near and far from balance, at a fraction of the cost of full dynamics runs. The test matched simulation stability closely. Using it as a design guide, the team refined a transformer model with a new neighbor method and temperature-controlled attention. The result combined low error, stable runs, and robust trait predictions.
arxiv-2602-04961:
Yu-Hsueh Chen and Tarun Grover wrote this 2026 theory paper on matter driven out of equilibrium. When a system is pushed by noise or decay, physicists still want rules that limit how its phases can change. The authors derive such rules from quantum information, using a quantity that measures correlations between distant regions that are not explained by the space between them.

Two results stand out. First, under mild assumptions, a scaling exponent built from this correlation measure cannot increase as the system is viewed at larger scales. Second, mixing states cannot raise the measure beyond what its ingredients allow, which implies that certain symmetry-broken phases survive small symmetry-breaking noise. Examples cover decoherence-driven transitions, conserved dynamics, and shifts in pure quantum states. The paper also notes what the results mean for classical steady states.
arxiv-2602-05161:
A sterile neutrino with a mass in the kilo-electronvolt range would leave a kink in the spectrum of tritium beta decay. A large Korean-led team, with Y C Lee as first author, covers the LiFE-SNS experiment in this 2026 instrumentation paper. Tritium is created inside lithium fluoride crystals by neutron capture, and sensitive magnetic microcalorimeters at millikelvin temperatures record each decay's heat.

Phase one of the experiment is complete, and the paper focuses on calibration and detector testing rather than the neutrino result itself. The team models how the response varies with position inside the crystal, measures the detector's nonlinearity, and lists the systematic uncertainties that will matter for the search. The achieved performance supports precise spectrum readings, and the projected reach is competitive in the target mass region.
arxiv-2602-05261:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards makes models reason longer. Fanfan Liu and 5 co-authors show in this 2026 paper that response length is partly an artifact of the algorithm, not purely a sign of deeper thought. Varied training methods inflate or collapse lengths in characteristic ways during training.

The authors dissect the parts of mainstream algorithms and derive which factors push length around, confirming the theory with extensive tests.
