Building on that study, they propose LUSPO, a length-unbiased sequence policy optimization method. It repairs a bias inside a recent group sequence method, making the loss truly neutral about response length and fixing a collapse failure. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and multimodal reasoning tasks, LUSPO consistently beat established methods such as GRPO and GSPO. The paper reframes length from a mysterious emergent trait into a knob the algorithm designer controls.
arxiv-2602-05361:
Huanqing Dong and Jingtao Shi examine how two pillars of stochastic control theory fit together in this 2026 mathematics paper. The maximum principle gives necessary conditions for optimality through adjoint processes, while dynamic programming characterizes the value function. For risk-sensitive problems, where the cost punishes bad luck, their link is delicate, especially when the control set is not convex.

The first task is recast as a recursive optimal control task for a forward-backward system with quadratic generators. Working in the viscosity solution framework, which handles value functions that are not smooth, the authors prove the precise links. Those links join the adjoint processes, the generalized Hamiltonian, and the value function. Worked examples illustrate the theorems. The contribution is a rigorous bridge. Results proved from the dynamic programming side can now be read in maximum-principle language and the reverse, for a class of problems used in finance and engineering.
arxiv-2602-05561:
A constant magnetic-like field inside hot quark matter, called a chromomagnetic condensate, is unstable in classic theory, and rotation may change that picture. Hao-Lei Chen and Xu-Guang Huang study the finite-temperature SU(2) Savvidy model under imaginary rotation, a mathematical stand-in used to probe rotating systems. Using the background-field method, they derive the one-loop effective potential and study both its real and imaginary parts.

They show that imaginary rotation modifies the condensate and the Polyakov loop, a key marker of confinement. It can also partly suppress the Nielsen-Olesen instability that afflicts the chromomagnetic background. A high-temperature expansion adds two more findings: the effective coupling grows stronger under imaginary rotation, and the field contributes negatively to the moment of inertia. The paper is a theory study of how rotation and background fields interact in Yang-Mills theory.
arxiv-2602-05961:
Drawing samples from a spread known only up to a scale factor is a hard task in statistics. Diffusion samplers are a newer family of fast methods, but most work on them has dealt with smooth, continuous spaces. Arran Carter and four co-authors bring those ideas to discrete spaces, where values come in separate steps. Their ICML 2026 paper adds off-policy training to discrete diffusion samplers.

The team shows the new training lifts results on old and new test tasks. They also extend discrete samplers to bridge work, linking any two spreads with a first discrete form of data-to-energy bridge training. Finally, they use the samplers for data-free posterior sampling in discrete latent spaces of image models. The work widens a fast sampling toolkit to discrete settings, such as codes and categories.
arxiv-2602-06161:
Diffusion language models can reveal many words at once, which speeds up writing, but haste hurts quality. Yanzheng Xiang and 10 co-authors tackle a wasteful pattern in the checking step. Tokens get hidden again for review, then restored unchanged, flip-flopping without progress.

Their method, COVER, checks selected tokens while keeping their stored context active for all other positions. A correction term stops a token from leaking its own answer into its check. Tokens are picked by a score mixing doubt, influence on later words, and drift from stored context. The number checked adapts each step. Benchmarks showed far fewer wasted revisions and faster decoding at the same quality.
arxiv-2602-06261:
Differential equations with delays appear wherever a system's change depends on its past, and Ábel Garab and Gergő Tóth study when every solution must oscillate. Their equations are neutral, meaning the rate of change itself involves delayed values, and they carry several positive and negative coefficient terms with time-varying delays.

The pair give sufficient conditions that guarantee oscillation of all solutions. Their tests improve and generalize earlier criteria that handled only simpler cases, like constant delays or no negative terms. Under extra assumptions about slowly changing parameters, they derive sharper conditions. Worked examples show the tests in action. Such results matter for control and biology, where delayed feedback can destabilize a steady state.
arxiv-2602-06461:
Equations that blend diffusion with wave behavior, driven by fraction time derivatives, model materials with memory. Masterson Costa and 2 co-authors study a semilinear version of these diffusion-wave equations with critical nonlinear terms, set in Lebesgue spaces. Critical strength is the borderline where standard estimates just barely apply.

The first half of the study settles local questions: answers exist for short times, depend steadily on their starting data, and gain smoothness in space. The second half proves that mild answers can exist for all time. It also examines how those global answers behave as time grows large. The results extend the toolbox for odd transport models used in physics and engineering.
arxiv-2602-06661:
Masanori Tanaka, Jun-Chen Wang, and Jing-Jun Zhang ask whether primordial black holes, formed in the early universe, could change how matter passed through the chiral phase transition. Working with a three-flavor model of quarks, they compute the transition inside the curved spacetime around a black hole rather than in flat space.

Near the event horizon, black holes push matter toward restored chiral symmetry. They also create a mixed local phase pattern that flat space never shows, with both gentle and abrupt transitions side by side. The holes act as catalysts, speeding the transition while keeping its strength about the same. Even a small population of them could shift the peak of the resulting gravitational-wave signal by an amount future detectors might notice.
arxiv-2602-06761:
Yingyu Yang and six co-authors build a tool that finds two key moments in an unborn baby's heartbeat cycle from ultrasound video, without hand-labeled training frames. Fetal echocardiography can reveal congenital heart disease, and doctors read the four-chamber view by inspecting the end-diastolic and end-systolic frames. Labeling those frames by hand is slow, and earlier automated methods assumed the heart always sat in one orientation.

Their system, ORBIT, learns the heart's motion trajectory from unlabeled video by treating image registration as its own supervision task. Turning points in that trajectory mark the switch between relaxation and contraction, which locates both phases even when the fetal position varies. Trained only on healthy videos, it missed the target frames by about two frames on average, for healthy and affected cases alike, beating earlier annotation-free methods.
arxiv-2602-06961:
Felix M. Heinze and two co-authors give the N-body energy function at second post-Newtonian precision. That level of precision goes beyond Newton and is needed for exact gravity work. Before this paper, a closed analytic form was known only for three point masses at most.

The new form works for any count of bodies in the ADM gauge. One integral term has no known closed form, so it stays as an integral. The team shows those integrals can be worked out by number to machine precision. That allows checks against analytic results and full numeric use of the whole energy function. They also show the motion equations for N bodies can be integrated by number in practice, and they discuss ways to speed the computation up.
arxiv-2602-07061:
Daniel Nobrega offers TACIT, a diffusion-based transformer that reasons wholly in pixel space. Because it never leaves pixel space, its reasoning can be watched directly at each inference step. It uses rectified flow, and the demo task is maze solving. The model learns to turn pictures of unsolved mazes into solved ones. Tests used one million synthetic maze pairs.

The numbers are stark. Training loss fell 192-fold over 100 epochs. Distance to ground truth improved about 23-fold. Only 10 Euler steps were needed, versus hundreds for typical diffusion models. Most striking is a phase flip. The solution stays hidden for 68 percent of the transform, with zero recall. Then it bursts out within just 2 percent of the process, at t equals 0.70. All samples burst at once across all regions. That rules out step-by-step path building and points to holistic rather than algorithmic reasoning.
arxiv-2602-07161:
Seeing a faint two-photon signal at very low light levels would open new kinds of sensitive spectroscopy.  Alan McLean and seven co-authors report two-photon-excited fluorescence measurements on rubidium atoms cooled in a magneto-optical trap, for both common isotopes.

They detect fluorescence at excitation powers as low as one microwatt, an extremely low photon flux.  That result marks laser-cooled rubidium as a promising platform for spotting delicate two-photon signatures without blasting the sample with light.  The paper is short, experimental, and useful to atomic experts chasing weak signals.  Such low-flux sensitivity matters for tests where stronger light would disturb the atoms under study.
arxiv-2602-07361:
Answering questions about Vietnamese healthcare regulations means thinking across several legally linked documents, a multihop task with almost no benchmark for a low-resource language.  Long S.  T.  Nguyen and five co-authors present ViHERMES, a benchmark and system for graph-grounded multihop question answering over those regulations.

The dataset holds high-quality question-answer pairs that require chaining across regulations, capturing amendment and cross-reference structure that single-document tests miss.  The accompanying system grounds retrieval in a graph of regulatory relations.  Teams working on legal question answering, and on Vietnamese language technology, get an testing that reflects how regulation works.
arxiv-2602-07661:
Cold fronts in galaxy clusters, sharp discontinuities from mergers, should ripple with Kelvin-Helmholtz instability unless viscosity or magnetic tension holds them back, making them probes of how sticky the medium is. Ming-Hsueh Hsieh and two co-authors model cluster mergers under four viscosity models.

Isotropic Spitzer viscosity strongly smooths fronts, while inviscid and microinstability-limited models show clear ripples. Plain Braginskii sits in between, with plasma beta varied to test field strength. Space experts get a side-by-side map linking front smoothness to the small-scale physics of the medium. Front shape thus becomes a readable test for models that are otherwise hard to pin down.
arxiv-2602-08061:
AI models for biology learn from pathogen data, and the choice of training data shapes capabilities that could enable bioweapon development. Doni Bloomfield and eight co-authors, writing after more than a hundred researchers endorsed data controls at the Asilomar Conference's fiftieth anniversary, propose a governance framework for dual-use pathogen data.

Their five-tier Biosecurity Data Level system categorizes pathogen data by how much it could contribute to capabilities of concern when used for training, with technical restrictions matched to each tier's risk. They also outline governance for newly created dual-use data. Biosecurity policymakers and AI labs gain a concrete, tiered proposal for drawing lines around training data before harmful capabilities are built.
arxiv-2602-08161:
Robust design must account for factory spread, but gauging results data for curved systems is costly and stand-in models often fail. Hyunho Jang and Dongjin Lee combine Bayesian neural networks with poly sized split for robust design tuning.

Doubt-based active learning sharpens the stand-in where it matters, while a multi-point single-step plan splits the design space into dynamically tuned zones where the split gauges stats moments analytically. Check on a ten-sized benchmark and an power-motor shape problem shows settling to robust optima with far fewer tests, including a 99.97 percent mean cut in the benchmark. Builders gain a method that buys toughness without paying full model costs.
arxiv-2602-08361:
Some magnetic materials host an exotic quantum state labeled Jeff equals one half, prized for the strange magnetism it may support. M. M. Ferreira-Carvalho and nine co-authors test whether the triangular-lattice compound Na2BaCo(PO4)2 comes close to that ideal. Their arXiv paper uses X-ray tests that vary the light direction, paired with detailed quantum models of the cobalt sites.

A careful fluorescence method yields clean spectra from this strong insulator. The analysis finds only a tiny 11 milli-electronvolt twist in the cobalt-oxygen octahedra, close enough to ideal for the desired ground state. The same model also matches the magnetic response along different crystal directions. Readers get a promising platform for exploring exotic magnetism on triangular lattices.
arxiv-2602-08461:
Causal inference usually reports average effects, but two patients can respond very differently to the same treatment. Liyuan Xu and Bijan Mazaheri introduce two new measures for that spread: the variance of the treatment effect, and its group-wise version. Their arXiv paper shows these measures can be pinned down from observed data under mild assumptions, even with hidden confounders.

Flexible kernel methods are proposed to estimate both measures, with theory showing that the estimates converge. Extensive tests on fake and semi-real data show performance better than or on par with naive baselines. Readers get a principled way to quantify how much treatment response varies, not just where its average sits.
arxiv-2602-08561:
Reproducing a published analysis should be as simple as rerunning code and data, yet missing packages, fragile paths, and version clashes often break it. Syed Mehtab Hussain Shah and two co-authors test whether language models and agents can diagnose and repair such failures automatically. The testbed drew on five social-science studies in R that already reproduced cleanly.

The team then planted realistic failures, from simple glitches to missing logic, and both repair workflows ran in fresh Docker sandboxes. Prompt-based repair succeeded in 31 to 79 percent of runs, depending on context and complexity. Agent-based repair, which inspects files and reruns analyses itself, reached 69 to 96 percent. Readers get evidence that agents can shoulder much of the reproduction burden.
arxiv-2602-08861:
Video models waste effort when they chew through every frame of a long clip. Xiangtian Zheng and two co-authors propose TiFRe, a scheme that cuts frames while keeping what matters. First, the user's request is turned into a prompt, and a CLIP-style encoder scores each frame against it, keeping only the most relevant ones.

Dropping frames outright would still lose detail, so a matching-and-merging step folds information from skipped frames into the kept ones. The result is a leaner input that preserves the video's meaning. Experiments show TiFRe lowers compute cost while improving scores on video-language tasks, a rare combination for frame-cutting methods.
arxiv-2602-09061:
What spread should replace a Bayesian posterior when some data must be forgotten? Hans Montcho and two co-authors revisit Zellner's information-processing view of Bayes' rule, in which it processes prior and data information without loss. For ordinary Bayesian inference, they show the information-dropping goal is met by the leave-data-out spread, the answer retraining would give.

The work extends to generalized Bayesian updating based on loss functions, where coherent sequential dropping yields exactly the spread from retained information alone. An axiomatic theory for possibilistic dropping yields a principled rule for exact unlearning of that kind. Restricting the exact rules to tractable families yields variational and maxitive methods as natural approximations.
arxiv-2602-09161:
Neural belief estimators trained on simulations break when real sightings drift from training data, a mismatch problem that usually forces retraining or linked error models. Sherman Khoo and three co-authors propose minimum-distance summaries, a plug-in fix that adapts test-time summaries on their own, apart from the prebuilt guesser. The fix uses maximum mean gap to measure how far seen data sit from a summary-based forecast spread.

Random Fourier features make the steps fast and light, with proof-based toughness promises. Tests on fake and real tasks show big toughness gains at tiny extra cost, while keeping reuse and split design: one trained guesser can serve many shifted sightings. The method offers simulation-based guessing a handy shield against model mismatch.
arxiv-2602-09261:
Marina Palaisti studies broad Koszulity under math gluing and field composita. For square fibre products, square-split pullbacks collapse into direct sums, while Stanley-Reisner pullbacks come from graph gluing that keeps broad Koszulity under a ruling-clique guess. For composita, the norm-residue theorem and Kummer theory give a graph test from limit images and degree-two cup-product links, checked for repeated Laurent-series fields with nonzero mixed marks.

In a nonabelian right-angled Artin group family, every finite p-extension has plainly set broadly Koszul cohomology, with a stated product split of the extension's group. The work links gluing builds, Galois cohomology, and Koszul duality in a single setup.
arxiv-2602-09461:
Power grids with many inverters, flexible loads, and fast-changing conditions need assessment of high-order outages, where several components fail at once. Fully testing every combination with full power-flow runs is infeasible in daily operation, forcing reliance on heuristic screens with no guarantee of catching every critical case. Lihao Mai and two co-authors propose a scalable, state-aware method in their 2026 paper that generates high-impact outage scenarios directly.

A guided diffusion model drafts candidates tailored to the current operating state. A grid-aware graph neural network, trained only on base and single-outage cases, builds high-risk training samples offline. The method offers adjustable safety promises for severe outages, letting operators bound the risk of missing critical events under limited run budgets. On standard benchmark grids, it evaluates more severe outages than uniform sampling for the same budget.
arxiv-2602-09561:
Archana Dixit and three co-authors compare two two-parameter dark energy models, Barboza-Alcaniz and log forms, against a broad observed set in their 2026 paper. Star blasts, baryon sound waves, and cosmic clocks jointly constrain each model's free settings through Monte Carlo sampling. Best-fit values and confidence bands follow for single and combined datasets.

Both models prove in line with current data, with the log form constraining model change slightly better. A statefinder test, which probes shape trends of cosmic expansion, effectively tells apart the two cases. The study thus sharpens understanding of dark energy change and shows which model the present data can and cannot separate.
arxiv-2602-09761:
Matteo Pannacci and three co-authors address how a reinforcement learning agent in sub-symbolic environments can be taught to carry out several temporally extended instructions written in linear temporal logic. Their 2026 paper drops a common unrealistic assumption: previous multi-task work mostly relied on knowing the mapping between raw observations and symbols in the formulae. Instead, a multi-task policy and a symbol grounder are trained jointly on the same experience.

Training of the symbol grounder draws solely on raw observations plus sparse rewards, using neural reward machines under a semi-supervised approach. Experiments on vision-based environments show performance comparable to using the true symbol grounding, significantly outperforming the only other previous multi-task method that avoids assuming true grounding knowledge. Agents can thus follow temporal logic instructions without a hand-supplied observation-to-symbol map.
arxiv-2602-09861:
N. Jafari and A. Boumali study the one-plus-one Dirac spring within doubly special rel models made by linear-fraction push shifts in their 2026 paper. These shifts keep the fixed speed of light and a high watcher-free scale. Starting from bent Casimir fixed points, place-space Dirac rules are built for three unlike bending choices: time-like, space-like, and light-like.

For time-like and light-like forms, bending induces push-tied mass ops, making the place-space form touchy to op order. A flipped-product order rule keeps form and yields solvable second-order rules. Closed-form rel energy spectra and waves are found in all three shapes, with Dirac-spring results regained as the scale tends to endless. Finally, the slow spread of the plus-energy branch is derived, showing bending shape ruling the rest-energy shift and the retune of the spring level spacing.
arxiv-2602-10161:
Omni-modal language models gain broad powers but also open cross-modal safety holes that single-modality testing misses. A 2026 paper led by Kun Wang, with ten co-authors, establishes a modality-semantics decoupling principle and builds the AdvBench-Omni data set, revealing a significant weak spot in omni-modal models. Mechanistic analysis finds a mid-layer fading effect tied to shrinking refusal-vector size, plus a mode-proof pure refusal direction.

Inspired by those findings, the team extracts a golden refusal vector by singular value decomposition and proposes OmniSteer, which uses lightweight adapters to tune intervention strength on the fly. Experiments lift refusal success against harmful inputs from about seventy percent to over ninety percent while keeping general powers across all modalities.
arxiv-2602-11061:
Two groups that look other can share the same counting pattern. Peter Kagey and Kai Mawhinney build a statistic-swapping involution on the product of a generalized symmetric group and a plain symmetric group. The map swaps fixed points on one side with cycles of a given length on the other.

That swap gives a combinatorial proof of a chance-based match. Fixed-point counts on the generalized group follow the same spread as cycle counts on the plain group. The paper is short and self-contained, turning an observed coincidence of spreads into an explicit, reversible construction.
arxiv-2602-11361:
Thinking models err in steps, and a few key tokens steer the rest. Weili Shi and five co-authors propose PPCV, a frame that finds and fixes those tokens through paraphrastic probing and consistency checks. First, an initial thinking path is rolled out, then paraphrased questions are joined to it.

Mismatches between predicted and expected tokens flag key tokens, confirmed by a final criterion. In stage two, candidate substitutes spawn new thinking paths for first and paraphrased questions, and the final answer follows from cross-path consistency. Tests on mainstream models across benchmarks show large gains over rivals. The work turns thinking fragility into a diagnosable, repairable property.
arxiv-2602-11761:
Long-context language models strain under the compute and memory costs of full attention, and existing sparse or linear attention schemes trade memory savings against performance. The MiniCPM team introduces MiniCPM-SALA, a nine-billion-parameter hybrid that combines high-fidelity sparse attention for long contexts with the global efficiency of linear attention. A layer selection algorithm blends the two mechanisms in a one-to-three ratio. A hybrid positional encoding keeps positions straight across long contexts.

A cost-effective continual training framework converts pretrained Transformer models into hybrids, cutting training costs by about 75 percent versus training from scratch. Tests show general capability comparable to full-attention models with better efficiency. On a single graphics processor the model runs up to three and a half times faster at 256 thousand tokens. It supports contexts up to one million tokens, where full-attention models of similar size fail on memory.
arxiv-2602-12261:
Percolation on a grid asks whether infinite clusters of open edges can coexist in a half-plane and its dual. Frederik Ravn Klausen led this work with one co-author, Noah Kravitz, proving they cannot, under translation invariance, ergodicity, and finitely many infinite clusters. Either the half-plane process has no infinite cluster, or its dual has none, almost surely.

The classical Burton-Keane argument shows those conditions hold for finite-energy measures, so the result covers many natural cases. Crucially, no positive-correlation assumption is imposed, unlike earlier non-coexistence theorems. The proof also reaches the random-cluster model even where that assumption fails, plus the uniform spanning tree and the uniform odd subgraph.
arxiv-2602-12461:
CLIP's zero-shot robustness can be improved by adversarial fine-tuning, but the usual attack examples may be weaker than they look. Jiacheng Zhang led this work with five co-authors. He shows that examples made by minimising cosine similarity to a hand-crafted template, such as a photo of a label, may fail to fool CLIP. That failure appears when similarity is measured with semantically richer alternatives. A fine-tuned encoder trained on those examples is then less robust than hoped.

The fix starts with a semantic-ensemble attack, generating semantic-aware examples by minimising average similarity to an ensemble of refined textual descriptions. Those descriptions come from a foundation model capturing core semantic features beyond templates, then refined to cut hallucinations. Fine-tuning CLIP's image encoder on those examples, as SAFT, beats current methods, with substantial gains in zero-shot adversarial robustness across 16 data sets.
arxiv-2602-12561:
Recovering CAD programs from 3D shapes is widely studied, yet recent language-model methods need paired shape-program data that often does not exist. Yuanbo Li led this work with four co-authors, presenting PLLM, a self-training framework for CAD program synthesis from unlabelled 3D shapes. Given a pretrained CAD-capable language model and a shape data set, PLLM iteratively samples candidate programs, selects high-fidelity executions, and augments programs to build synthetic program-shape pairs for fine-tuning.

Experiments adapting CAD-Recode from DeepCAD to the unlabelled ABC data set show consistent improvements in geometric fidelity and program diversity. By learning from shapes alone, PLLM sidesteps the paired-data bottleneck that limits existing methods. Readers get a practical route to CAD program synthesis where labelled pairs are scarce, using self-training to turn unlabelled shapes into training signal.
arxiv-2602-12661:
Infall and outflows, coupled with magnetic fields, rapidly shape the gas around newborn protostars, and shocks encode heat and density spread. Kazuki Tokuda led this work with eleven co-authors, giving ALMA Band 9 views of the Taurus dense core MC 27/L1521F, which hosts a Class 0 protostar. The CO line J equal to 6-5 was targeted at about 2 arcseconds detail, about 300 astronomical units.

An off-centred ring-like shape with a width of about 1000 astronomical units is found, not seen in previous low-J CO data. The ring is read as warm gas shaped by outflow contact with the dense envelope, tracing shocks around the embedded protostar. Results show high-excitation CO lines can reveal warm envelope shapes missed by lower transitions in the earliest protostellar phase.
arxiv-2602-13261:
Brains solve hard tasks with sparse spikes, looped wiring, and local learning rules, and brain-like chips try to copy that thrift to cut energy use. The snag is training: most mixed-signal brain-like devices rely on weak learning rules that fail at supervised tasks, which blocks learning directly on the chip. This paper offers a feedback control optimizer for spiking networks that pairs spike-based weight updates with control signals from a spiking controller.

Single-layer networks trained this way matched standard artificial networks on classification tests, and the method held up in live online learning on mixed-signal hardware despite mismatched settings. That resilience matters for edge devices, where learning must run on the device itself rather than in a data center. Matteo Saponati leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13361:
Separating two images mixed into one observation is hard when the mixing is unknown and the scenes are complex. Old methods lean on independence assumptions or GAN-style nets and leave bias, texture damage, and residue under strong noise. The Diffusion Duet brings diffusion models into dual-channel blind separation, learning source feature distributions and rebuilding structure through a dual-branch reverse denoising process.

A wavelet suppression module exploits the coupled noise between sources to sharpen detail separation. On synthetic rain and snow tasks, the model beat Histoformer and LDRCNet on restoration scores, and on complex mixtures it surpassed rivals by over 4 decibels in PSNR. Jingwei Li leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13861:
Hans Raj Tiwary and one co-author introduce a 2026 arXiv paper on a new graph cut problem. Given a graph and a set of terminals, the task splits vertices into connected parts, one terminal each, and shrinks the largest boundary of any part. That worst-part cost, plus the connectedness demand, sets it apart from the classic multiway cut.

The motive is a link to the spanning tree congestion problem, where little progress has been made. The authors prove hardness results, including weak NP-hardness on treewidth-two graphs and parameterized hardness by treewidth. To balance those bounds, they give a pseudopolynomial algorithm and an approximation scheme for bounded-treewidth graphs, and show the plain min-max cut is NP-hard even with three terminals.
arxiv-2602-14161:
Max Fomin, writing alone, warns in a 2026 arXiv paper that benchmarks flatter malicious-prompt detectors. Spotting prompt injection, jailbreaks, and harmful requests is vital for safe agents, yet standard tests overstate how well detectors generalize. The author trains activation-based classifiers, or linear probes, on 18 datasets of attacks and benign prompts.

A stricter Leave-One-Dataset-Out test, where the held-out set never appears in training, tells a harsher story. Pooled AUC from standard cross-validation ran 8.0 to 16.5 points above the strict test, with per-dataset gaps up to 25 points. The author traces the gap to dataset-dependent shortcuts: 28 to 44% of top features were shortcuts, and a dataset-identity classifier hit 96.6%.
arxiv-2602-14261:
Yongbo Deng and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv topology optimization method for low-temperature type-II superconductors. Geometric design matters greatly for these materials, since well-placed defects in the current path pin magnetic flux, cut dissipation, and raise achievable current density. Finding good geometries by hand is hard.

The paper offers topology optimization as an inverse design route, targeting structures with superconductor-dielectric and vacuum interfaces. The approach rests on Ginzburg-Landau theory under Weyl gauge, a framework suited to superconducting order. By searching geometry space directly, it aims to deliver layouts that pin flux effectively and carry more current.
arxiv-2602-14461:
Tai Hyun Yoon, writing alone, builds a 2026 arXiv hardware-native time-frequency GKP logical qubit for light fault tolerance. The qubit is coded in the smooth phase space of single photons, giving a moving light form of bosonic grid coding. Finite-energy grid states are made on rails from coherently driven linked non-linear biphoton sources making single-photon rate-comb supermodes.

A light-rate-comb guide anchors the time-rate phase space and forces commuting shift stabilizers straight in hardware, steadily marking the logic subspace. Timing jitter, spectral drift, and phase noise map neatly onto Gaussian shift errors inside the lattice, giving built-in fixability inside a stabilizer cell. Logic acts use on-hand phase and delay controls, enabling on-rails state making and steering, with a path toward live syndrome pull and shift recovery.
arxiv-2602-14561:
Arik Laemmle and six co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv simulation-driven method for automating electrical cabinet assembly. Force-tuned building of terminals on DIN-rails is slowed by high coding effort and product spread. Deep reward learning joins tunable robot skills in a physics-based run world, with two joining models for snap-fit building: analytic beam-theory models and rigid-body models in MuJoCo.

Those models mimic touch forces truly, key for training reward-learning agents. Robot skills follow the pitasc setup for modular, reusable control plans, with Soft Actor-Critic and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient training and domain randomization for toughness. Plans moved to a real UR10e robot with no extra tuning, showing high win rates in tests and a path to flexible cabinet auto work.
arxiv-2602-14761:
Stefano Woerner, Seong Joon Oh, and Christian F. Baumgartner argue that meta-learning lacks precise terms for universality, with key words used inconsistently across the literature. They offer a theoretical framework that formally defines practical universality and distinguishes algorithm-explicit from algorithm-implicit learning, giving the field a principled vocabulary.

Guided by that framework, they present TAIL, a transformer-based algorithm-implicit meta-learner that works across tasks with varied domains, modalities, and label spaces. Current meta-learners, the authors note, stay narrow, bound to fixed feature and label spaces. TAIL aims to widen meta-learning toward genuinely general purpose.
arxiv-2602-14861:
Roberto Vila and Helton Saulo study the slant of a rank-based gap index. That line joins the old Gini gauge, the m-th Gini gauge, its wide form, and some S-Gini cases, with a link to spectral gap gauges through an integral form.

Their gauge means weighted rank gaps over all same-size sub-groups and scales by the group mean. A broad slant split follows, with each rank's share of the slant from chance scaling laid bare. Under gamma crowds, the gauge proves slant-free. Gap gauges thus gain a plain tale of their own slant.
arxiv-2602-14961:
Filos-Ratsikas and Kalantzis open the study of distortion in stable matching. They ask how good a stable outcome can be when an algorithm sees only limited information about what agents truly value. Their first blow is negative. Classic deferred acceptance, and indeed any deterministic method using ordinal rankings alone, has unbounded distortion.

Two escapes work. A simple randomized deferred acceptance scheme reaches a distortion bound that is optimal among randomized stable methods. The same bound follows from just one cardinal value query per agent, with better bounds demanding more queries. The paper adds improved query bounds under structural restrictions and average-case results for preferences drawn at random.
arxiv-2602-15261:
Proudkii and colleagues retrieve Io's heat profiles from ALMA sulfur dioxide spectra. Io's air is shaped by venting, thawing, cooling, and heating, yet no heat profile had pinned it. The team used ALMA Band 7 and Band 8 epochs of spectra to retrieve profiles. They combined multi-line study with Doppler speed maps and a forward model, splitting thermal and motion parts.

On the front side, they retrieved a cold lower air layer to about half a nanobar. It rises to hundreds of kelvins by one hundredth of a nanobar. On the back side, fits yielded similar profiles but lower sulfur dioxide amounts, limiting line making to a few km. Back spectra fit a steady air layer. Across datasets, gas cover ran 35 to 50 percent and sub-beam speed spreads 25 to 85 meters per second. The retrievals deliver by-height heat profiles of its air and reveal vertical shape on the dayside.
arxiv-2602-15461:
Ivanovska and Štruc offer a zero-shot review of open-source multi-mode models for single-image finding, using open files and a plan. Face morphing menaces checks, yet finding nets need specific teaching and stretch badly to attacks. Open-source multi-mode models have shown visual thinking, but their body-ID sleuthing promise stays untried.

Across varied tricks, many models show telling skill without any fine-tuning or field tuning. LLaVA Mistral 7B hits state-of-the-art scores, beating rival finding rivals by at least 23 points in miss score. The findings show multi-mode pre-teaching can hide fine-grained face flaws of marks. Their results cast open-source multi-mode models as open foundations for body-ID safety and study. This rising power spots chances to build finding nets through aimed fine-tuning or tuning, lifting scores. All code and protocols will be shared.
arxiv-2602-15561:
Vila Crespo and colleagues recover a missing piece of solar motion: sideways plasma flow at each height in the solar atmosphere. Spectra reveal only line-of-sight speed through the Doppler effect, while many solar processes hinge on strong horizontal motions. Older methods give horizontal speeds on one plane only, with no height detail, yet modern inversions now yield height profiles for line-of-sight speed and magnetic field.

As a first step, the team works in two dimensions, discretising the magnetic induction equation by finite differences into an overdetermined system that yields the horizontal component. Tests on analytic cases and on two-dimensional solar surface simulations recover the flow with a mean error near one percent. The method lays groundwork for full three-dimensional reconstructions of horizontal solar flows.
arxiv-2602-15761:
Dristi and Dwyer test whether code refactorings produced by large language models truly preserve behaviour. Prior checks usually rely on preset test cases. This paper uses differential fuzzing instead. Thousands of auto-generated inputs are run through old and new code and compared, with no preset tests needed. That wider input sweep can catch changes that fixed tests miss.

In a large test of six models, CodeLlama, Codestral, StarChat2, Qwen-2.5, Olmo-3, and GPT-4o, across three data sets and two refactoring types, models alter program meaning in 19 to 35 percent of refactorings. About 21 percent of those non-equivalent cases slip past existing test suites. The lesson is blunt: existing tests alone overstate how faithful model refactorings are.
arxiv-2602-15861:
Xie and colleagues introduce CAST, or Consistency via Algorithmic Prompting and Stable Thinking, a framework enhancing output stability by constraining the model latent reasoning path. Text analysis of tabular data relies on two operations: digests for corpus theme pulling and tagging for row-level tagging. A key flaw of using large language models for those tasks is meeting high bars of output calm wanted by data work. CAST combines algorithmic prompting to impose a stepwise frame over valid reasoning steps, plus think-first to enforce middle pledges before final output.

To measure progress, the team introduces CAST-S and CAST-T, calm metrics for bulleted digests and tagging, checked against human calls. Tests across public tests on several language model bases show CAST always hitting the best calm among all rivals. Stability Score lifts by up to 16 point 2 percent, while output grade holds or improves.
arxiv-2602-15961:
Sheng and colleagues build a large benchmark for forecasting wind and solar power when weather turns extreme. Average accuracy has improved with deep learning, but storms and heat waves still threaten grid stability, and models that look strong on average can fail exactly when operators need them most.

Their benchmark gathers more than ten million hourly records from over nine hundred wind and solar stations across four Chinese provinces. All models share the same weather prediction signals under a fair, leakage free protocol. Expert labels for extreme weather let the authors score models regime by regime, revealing a robustness gap hidden by overall averages. Under extremes, success tracks how a model uses weather inputs rather than how complex its architecture is, a lesson aimed squarely at safety critical grid work.
arxiv-2602-16061:
Hongyu Chen leads a team of three researchers tackling missing data that depends on the missing values themselves. This trap is common in business and social work. A customer rating, for instance, may go unreported precisely because of what the rating would have been. That makes population figures hard to pin down without strong claims about how data goes missing. The authors build new measures from raw records such as service chats, using large language models to turn them into neat proxies.

These proxies serve as weak shadow variables. They track the outcome, yet they do not link to missingness once the true outcome and known traits are fixed. Sharp bounds on population figures come from a pair of linear programs. A penalized estimator and subsampling give intervals. In semi-synthetic tests on real chats, the intervals shrink sharply versus using no extra data, with lower error than classic methods.
arxiv-2602-16161:
Rong Fu leads a team of six authors modeling feeling across channels with curved geometry. Their framework, Emotion Collider, represents channel hierarchies with Poincare-ball embeddings. It fuses information through a hypergraph web that passes messages both ways between nodes and hyperedges. Contrastive learning in curved space, with decoupled radial and angular objectives, sharpens separation between classes.

High-order meaning relations across time steps and channels survive through adaptive hyperedge building. Tests on standard emotion benchmarks show robust, coherent codes and steady accuracy gains. Gains are largest when channels are partly missing or spoiled by noise. The findings suggest that explicit layered geometry combined with hypergraph mixing makes feeling understanding tougher. That trait matters for real systems where sensors drop out or signals degrade.
arxiv-2602-16261:
Weiyi Yun and coauthors identify stripe antiferromagnetism in the van der Waals metal HoTe3, decoupled from charge density wave order. The rare-earth tritelluride family of layered van der Waals compounds hosts coexisting magnetic and charge density wave orders. Combining polarized and unpolarized neutron diffraction on single-crystal HoTe3, the team identifies two distinct antiferromagnetic phases. Both show a collinear up-up-down-down motif within individual layers.

The two phases differ in how magnetic layers stack. Ferromagnetic stacking marks the higher-temperature phase, termed vertical-stripe. Antiferromagnetic stacking marks the ground state, termed tilted-stripe. Their propagation vectors differ accordingly. Relative alignment between magnetic and charge density wave propagation vectors, plus single-ion anisotropy, likely prove essential for coupled spin and charge orders.
arxiv-2602-16361:
Riccardo Biagioli, Christophe Hohlweg, and Elisa Sasso study two combinatorial problems about reflections in a Coxeter system. The first asks whether the language of palindromic reduced words for reflections is regular. The second seeks formulas for the Poincaré series of reflections, the generating function of reflection lengths. Both problems trace to Stembridge's conjecture that the Poincaré series is rational, and to the solution given by de Man.

For the first problem, the authors introduce reflection-prefixes, arising naturally from palindromic reduced words. They study links between reflection-prefixes and the root poset, the dominance order on roots, and dihedral reflection subgroups. Using m-canonical automata tied to m-Shi arrangements, they prove the language of reduced words for reflection-prefixes is regular. For the second problem, they focus on affine Coxeter groups and derive a simple formula for the Poincaré series from Hasse diagram symmetries of the root poset.
arxiv-2602-16761:
Luc Ramsès Talla Waffo gives explicit closed formulae for two families of even polynomials arising from integral forms tied to zeta and beta ratios. A prior paper introduced the polynomials from integral representations of beta ratios and zeta ratios. Here, their formulae are written in terms of Eulerian numbers, and their structural traits are studied.

Those traits may aid study of the arithmetic nature of the ratios themselves, a classic question about whether such constants are rational, algebraic, or transcendental. Number theorists get concrete formulae and structure results for polynomials that encode deep constants in a tractable algebraic form.
arxiv-2602-16861:
EunJeong Cheon and Do Yeon Shin propose Walk-Along with Robots. It is a method for studying autonomous robots in crowded public streets. Delivery robots now use campus walkways and neighborhood sidewalks beyond researcher control. They follow dynamic routes through unpredictable settings. Field studies often rely on controlled tests with prototypes. They also use structured observation such as Wizard of Oz. Those fits poorly here.

Drawing on public realm ethnography from urban studies, geography, and sociology, the paper outlines the Walk-Along method. It states its key features and the steps used in the study. It states the unique insights it offers and ways to evaluate it. Researchers get a deliberate approach for following real robots through real streets. The aim is to spur further discussion on methods for studying autonomous robots in public spaces.
arxiv-2602-16961:
Rahul Thomas, David Hidary, and Arka Pal present greedy multi-path block verification for faster decoding in speculative sampling. Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive output by using a cheaper draft model to generate a candidate path of tokens. A checking method involving target and draft model odds accepts a prefix of the draft sequence. An additional correction token is sampled from a residual distribution to ensure the final output adheres to the target distribution.

Standard speculative decoding verifies each token independently along the path. Block verification uses a joint condition involving all sampled on-path odds, shown optimal among checking methods using only on-path odds. The paper first shows block checking is optimal even over methods using off-path odds, via an information-agnostic linear program. That program extends to draft models sampling multiple draft paths, yielding a natural class of multi-path block checking generalizations.
arxiv-2602-17361:
Yuan-Hao Wang led a two-author paper on estimating quantum Fisher information with Krylov shadow tomography. Estimating that information is crucial yet challenging across quantum science and technology. The recently proposed Krylov shadow tomography, or KST, opens a new avenue by introducing a series of Krylov bounds on the Fisher information. The paper addresses whether KST works in practice.

Low-order Krylov bounds already enable efficient, accurate estimation, the authors show. The bounds converge to the Fisher information exponentially fast with increasing order and can surpass the best-known polynomial lower bounds. Certain low-order bounds can even match the Fisher information exactly for low-rank states common in practice, a feat beyond prior polynomial bounds. Extensive numerical simulations confirm practical advantages over existing polynomial approaches, promising to unlock Fisher-information-based applications.
arxiv-2602-17561:
Jaswanth Gurudev and a coauthor wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on tuning density-graded BCC lattices for crash safety and heat removal. Such lattices promise impact absorption and heat removal, yet past tuning used raw shape numbers blind to gradient tilt. The study tunes lattices for crash safety and heat removal together, using surrogate-based goal programming with raw truss diameter first.

The lattice is split into three zones, and Pareto-optimal designs beat a non-graded lattice on specific energy absorption, peak stress, Nusselt number, and pressure drop. The authors then introduce Physics-Informed Geometric Operators, drawn from the diameter profile and the triangulated surface mesh. Correlation checks find raw diameter variables still strong, with the porosity gradient most telling. Heat transfer resists all tested variables, needing many factors at once. The framework extends beyond three zones to finer steps and other shapes.
arxiv-2602-17761:
Greta Heine and team design a hardware-aware hit filtering method for the Belle II Level-1 trigger. The Belle II experiment runs at high luminosity, where beam-induced background strains the hardware trigger system under tight latency and bandwidth limits. Online data reduction within that trigger needs a lightweight approach, and the team builds on the Interaction Network design.

Their workflow adapts the net to detector and trigger conditions. It uses model-size and graph-size reduction. It uses four-bit fixed-point arithmetic. It uses unstructured pruning. A hardware-aware complexity metric, the total number of bit operations, guides the design. The chosen setup cuts that cost by more than a hundredfold against the full-precision reference. Performance stays close to the reference in hit efficiency and background rejection, with only a modest drop in AUC score on Belle II collision data.
arxiv-2602-17861:
Ryan McKenna and team present JAX-Privacy, a library for differentially private learning. The library eases use of robust, fast tools for DP learning, guided by ease, flex and speed. It serves experts needing deep tuning and users wanting an out-of-the-box use.

JAX-Privacy gives checked, plug-in parts for all aspects of tool design, including batch picking, gradient clipping, noise adding, tracking and checks. It brings together a large body of recent research on DP learning in one place. Readers gain a handy toolkit: plug-in, checked building blocks for private learning, usable both for custom research tools and for plain user deployment.
arxiv-2602-17961:
Kaori Ikematsu and Kunihiro Kato present DuoTouch, a passive attachment for capacitive touch panels that adds tangible input while limiting content blocking and input area loss. It uses two contact footprints and two traces to encode motion as binary sequences and runs on unmodified devices through standard touch APIs.

The team offers two setups with paired readers: an aligned setup mapping fixed-length codes to discrete commands, and a phase-shifted setup estimating direction and distance from relative timing. To characterize reliability, they derive a sampling-limited bound linking press speed, internal trace width and device touch sampling rate. Technical evaluations on a smartphone and a touchpad report metrics tying those parameters to decoding accuracy. Finally, they show the range of DuoTouch by embedding the mechanism into varied forms, including a hand strap, a phone ring holder and touchpad add-ons.
arxiv-2602-18561:
Fakher Assaad and five co-authors rebuild spectral densities with a neural network. Their 2026 paper tackles a central many-body physics problem: recovering the spectral density from the imaginary-time Green's function, typically generated by Monte Carlo methods. Because the one-point fermionic kernel diverges exponentially at large frequencies, numerical noise causes instabilities.

The team trains a convolutional network on data generated from random Gaussians, improving the training set by including collision centers rather than uniform Gaussians. The network's output fulfills positive semidefiniteness by construction. Compared with the standard Maximum Entropy method across Gaussian test data, the one-dimensional Hubbard case with spin-charge separation, plus the two-dimensional SSH case, the network wins on data near the training set. MaxEnt recognizes physical features more precisely on physical models.
arxiv-2602-18761:
How fast is the universe expanding, how much matter does it hold, and is dark energy really constant? D. Forero-Sánchez, leading a large DESI team, combines two DESI releases in 2026 to answer those questions from galaxy clustering alone, without leaning on outside datasets.

Full-shape clustering from DESI DR1 is joined to baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from DESI DR2, with their correlation handled through ShapeFit compression and a joint covariance from EZmocks. That compression tames prior-volume effects that had dominated earlier Bayesian results. The outcome is a first reliable DESI-only Bayesian look at extensions to the standard model, with tighter dynamical dark energy limits and competitive bounds on neutrino mass and spatial curvature.
arxiv-2602-18861:
Shrinking vision transformers to a few bits usually costs accuracy, especially without labelled data. Shile Li, with two co-authors, presents a joint post-training quantisation framework in 2026 for vision transformers trained on ImageNet. Unlike block-wise methods, it optimises all layers and inter-block dependencies together, with no labelled data at all.

The method scales with sample count and finishes in about an hour on one GPU for a small vision transformer. It reaches leading accuracy at four-bit and three-bit settings. It also gives, to the authors' knowledge, the first strong post-training results at extremely low-bit settings on several transformer families. A data-free calibration strategy synthesises diverse samples with Stable Diffusion Turbo, guided by learned multi-mode prompts. Its performance matches real-data calibration.
arxiv-2602-19061:
Bounding gains for superelliptic equations needs a new frame. Karsten Müller, writing alone in 2026, builds one for coprime solutions of a generalised diagonal superelliptic equation. Two gains matter. Power gain and approximation gain multiply into an ABC-quality.

A structural lower bound for approximation gain comes first. It shows these equations lean toward high ABC-quality. Combined with the Strong ABC conjecture, it caps power gain uniformly. For one special case, structural density forces quality above half the exponent. That rules out solutions at exponent four or higher under a modest quality cap. Tests on classic high-quality triples, from Reyssat, de Weger, and Nitaj, confirm the bound is sharp. Theory thus explains a numerical pattern long observed at low exponents.
arxiv-2602-19461:
Flow matching builds images by learning flows between distributions, but handling multiple scales usually means cascaded steps with renoising between them. Zelin Zhao and three co-authors present LapFlow, Laplacian multiscale flow matching, which splits images into Laplacian pyramid residuals and handles scales in parallel. A mixture-of-transformers architecture with causal attention handles the scales together.

Generating multi-scale representations in parallel removes the need for bridging processes between scales. The design improves generation quality, speeds up sampling, and helps flow matching methods scale. On CelebA-HQ and ImageNet, LapFlow reaches superior sample quality with fewer computational operations and faster inference than single-scale and multi-scale baselines, a win on both quality and cost.
arxiv-2602-19561:
Sensor networks need several equally informative node subsets activated in sequence, so no single subset bears all battery drain or failure risk. Ryouke Ikura and three co-authors propose a dynamic sensor scheduling method based on graph node partitioning from sampling theory for graph signals. Subset quality changes over time, so schedules must adapt.

The partitioning problem is framed as difference-of-convex optimization using a subspace prior for graph signals. It is solved by the proximal difference-of-convex algorithm, which guarantees convergence to a critical point. Unlike conventional single-subset selection, the method minimizes average reconstruction error across all node subsets. An online extension adapts as the signal subspace and optimal subsets evolve.
arxiv-2602-19761:
Doctors treating primary biliary cholangitis track serial biomarkers to judge the risk of liver failure, and dynamic prediction models turn those histories into updated survival estimates. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nina van Gerwen and eleven co-authors extends an ensemble method, Super Learner, to combine such dynamic predictions.

Joint modelling and landmarking are two standard routes to dynamic prediction, and machine learning offers others, but no single method wins everywhere. Super Learner weights a library of candidate methods by cross-validated performance, and this paper pays special attention to choosing objective functions suited to dynamic prediction. Applied to primary biliary cholangitis, the ensemble matches or beats every method fitted alone, giving clinicians a flexible way to pool models with different assumptions.
arxiv-2602-20061:
AI voice clones now sound human enough to run phone scams at scale. Can listeners tell the difference? A 2026 arXiv paper by Zoha Hayat Bhatti and five co-authors ran a study where twenty-two participants judged sixteen clips, half AI and half human, and rated confidence.

Listeners performed poorly, with mean accuracy below chance in a binary task. Errors ran both ways. Three quarters of AI clips were majority-labelled as human, while nearly two thirds of human clips were majority-labelled as AI. Discriminability was near zero. Listeners could not separate synthetic from human voices, not merely favouring one answer. Participants leaned on pauses, filler words, vocal variety, cadence, and emotion. Yet AI samples often reproduced those cues, and wrong answers came with moderate to high confidence. The authors conclude vocal heuristics are unreliable guides to authenticity in voice scams, with lessons for security and user education.
arxiv-2602-20361:
Mohanad Obeed and Ming Jian propose a learning method that lets neural receivers for orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing, or OFDM, adapt while they detect signals. Deep neural receivers handle complex settings without explicit channel models, but channels shift over time, so periodic retraining is often needed. Their method adds no overhead: it reuses existing demodulation reference signals, known as DMRS, to demodulate signals and adapt the model at the same time.

Three pilot designs support the joint task: fully randomized, hybrid, and additional pilots. Two receiver designs fit those pilots: a parallel design that keeps inference and fine-tuning apart for uninterrupted operation, and a forward-pass reusing design that cuts compute cost. Simulations show the method tracks both slow and fast channel shifts with no extra overhead, no service breaks, and no catastrophic loss under distribution shift. Receivers can thus stay accurate as channels change.
arxiv-2602-20661:
Quantum error correction and lattice gauge theories connect deeply, and Luca Spagnoli and two co-authors extend that connection to gauge theories with matter. They show that a prime-dimension gauge theory coupled to moving matter can be expressed as a qudit stabilizer code. Using the stabilizer formalism, they map the encoded gauge theory exactly onto two different bosonic models, uncovering a logical duality generated by error correction itself.

From this view, quantum error correction offers a unifying language that exposes dual descriptions of lattice gauge theories. The paper also extends earlier two-level constructions on qubits to prime-dimension systems on multi-level qudits. State injection across qudit codes that work together provides the route by which the authors realize gates that stay universal and tolerate faults.
arxiv-2602-21061:
Humans recombine learned ideas to solve new problems, a skill called out-of-distribution reasoning, and language models are often credited with it. David Koplow, Tomer Galanti, and Tomaso Poggio argue the skill is hard to measure in this 2026 arXiv paper, because most tasks admit many decompositions, some shallow or memorized. Their benchmark sidesteps the confounds: a model progressively solves a Boolean circuit from data, a minimal yet general task.

Standalone models collapse in next-step accuracy as circuit depth grows. Tool use through synthesizing and executing code prevents that collapse in both small and frontier models. The authors conclude that tool synthesis plays a crucial role in supporting out-of-distribution reasoning. Readers get a cleaner yardstick and evidence that tools, not scale alone, sustain deep reasoning.
arxiv-2602-21361:
A 2026 arXiv paper by Oliver Hoidn and five co-authors offers one self-taught network for two kinds of X-ray imaging: single-frame Fresnel coherent diffraction imaging and overlapped ptychography. Ptychography at synchrotrons and X-ray free-electron lasers now needs dense, overlapping scans, which slow work down and raise the dose on samples.

The network rebuilds each patch of a sample from one diffraction frame or from several overlapping frames. In single-frame mode, a curved-wavefront probe gives enough phase variety to drop the overlap rule, so scans can be sparser and doses lower. Tests show image quality above 0.90 on synthetic patterns, tenfold better dose efficiency at low photon counts, and a 10,304-frame job run about 36 times faster than a fast iterative solver.
arxiv-2602-21961:
Bendegúz Sulyok, Gergely Palla, Filippo Radicchi, and Santo Fortunato test how tough sparse neural networks stay when their wiring keeps changing during training. Their design uses three sparse layers with nearly all weights removed, followed by one dense layer, applied to handwritten digit and fashion image tasks. Rewiring between epochs keeps accuracy competitive despite the tiny weight count.

The main contribution is a robustness study: the team stresses the networks by deleting links at random, launching adversarial attacks, and shuffling link weights. Adaptive rewiring, they find, preserves robustness as well as efficiency. The paper presents sparse adaptive networks as a promising path to deep learning models that are both light and dependable.
arxiv-2602-22061:
Generative models that learn distributions of quantum data could aid chemistry and physics, but existing quantum diffusion models lean on costly random circuits. Quoc Hoan Tran and three co-authors propose a chaotic quantum diffusion model instead, which builds its ensembles through chaotic Hamiltonian evolution over time. The design needs only global, time-independent control, a much simpler demand on hardware.

That simplicity makes the method fit analog quantum platforms, where circuit-based random operations are hard to run and sensitive to control flaws. The authors report accuracy comparable to circuit-based quantum diffusion models, with better trainability and robustness. The work broadens where quantum generative modeling can run, moving it closer to real analog devices.
arxiv-2602-22461:
Human first-person videos offer scalable handling demos, but robots copying human viewpoints often lose sight of task-critical details. Daesol Cho and three co-authors propose EgoAVFlow, which learns handling and active vision from egocentric videos through a shared three-dimensional flow picture. That picture supports geometric sight reasoning and transfers without any robot demos.

Diffusion models predict robot actions, future 3D flow, and camera paths, while test-time tuning maximizes a sight-aware reward figured from predicted motion and scene geometry. Real-world trials under changing viewpoints show EgoAVFlow consistently beats human-demo baselines, keeping sight and robust handling. Robots gain eyes that move with purpose, not just mimicry.
arxiv-2602-22861:
Jimmy Kornelije Gunnarsson and one co-author build structure-keeping discontinuous Galerkin methods for the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes systems with weak mobility. Their SWIPD-L and SIPGD-L methods use tuned flow fluxes with edge-wise flow treatments for stronger steadiness control.

The team proves coercivity for the broad three-way form and shows optimal approach rates while keeping mass conserved, energy loss in check, and the discrete maximum principle intact. Checks with past SIPG-L and SWIP-L methods confirm similar steadiness. Careful tests on hp-tuning meshes for solo Cahn-Hilliard and for coupled systems show large compute savings with no score loss at all.
arxiv-2602-23561:
Somjit Roy and two co-authors present VaSST, a chance-based method for symbolic regression (SR) using variational inference and soft symbol trees. SR learns closed-form physics laws and aids AI-driven finding, yet current methods lean on rule-of-thumb search or data-hungry methods, assume low-noise regimes, and lack sound doubt scores.

VaSST replaces discrete sign and feature picks in formula trees with spreads over allowable parts. That turns combo search through a vast formula space into efficient gradient-based tuning, keeping a coherent chance-based reading. Learned soft forms induce post-fit spreads over symbol forms, enabling doubt scores across plausible symbol forms through post-fit-aware symbol model choice. On mock tests and the Feynman SR data set, VaSST gets strong form finding and forecast scores versus state-of-the-art rivals.
arxiv-2603-00161: Kalaycioglu and colleagues present SKINOPATHY AI, a smartphone-first web app with five explainable eye-screening modules running entirely on ordinary phones. It scores redness, counts blinks, tracks pupil light reflex, grades scleral colour for jaundice and anaemia signs, and measures lesion spread with millimetre estimates and trend tracking. All algorithms are deterministic and privacy-preserving, built as a React/FastAPI stack with OpenCV, MediaPipe, MongoDB sessions and PDF reports. The system needs no cloud AI inference and is framed strictly as non-diagnostic consumer triage.
arxiv-2603-00761: Peng, Liu, and Kowalski present COMPOSER, a compile once oracle for similarity encoded Hamiltonians in electronic structure. Low rank factorisations compress Hamiltonians and generators into bilinear and projected quadratic ladders at near linear scaling. Each ladder gets deterministic preparation and block encoding on few signal qubits. A PREP-SELECT-PREP template combines the ladders while one QSP step performs the spectral shift. With the orbital pool and qubit register fixed, the two qubit fabric compiles once, and geometry, mask, and cut updates are handled by re dialled qubit gates.
arxiv-2603-00861: Kjos-Hanssen and Lakshmanan extend a construction of quantum channels with synchronizing words of length 3 for qutrits. They build qutrit channels whose minimal synchronizing words are arbitrarily long, pushing the length without bound. The result contrasts with Černý's conjecture for finite automata, which bounds synchronizing word length, showing quantum channels behave differently from classical automata.
arxiv-2603-01361: Zhao and four colleagues present MixerCSeg, a mixer for pixel-level crack cutting, built like a team of experts. CNN-like pathways focus on local grains, Transformer-style paths capture global links, and Mamba-like flows model stepwise context in one encoder. Its TransMixer probes Mamba's latent focus while building pathways showing both nearness and global reach. A spatial plan plus Direction-guided Edge Gated Conv sharpens edge sense for odd crack shapes with minimal cost.
arxiv-2603-01761:
Vaggelis Dorovatas, Malte Schwerin, Andrew Bagdanov, and colleagues argue that modular memory is the missing piece for agents that keep learning. Their 2026 position work grows from a seminar on continual learning in the foundation model era. Big pre-trained models excel at set tasks, yet they struggle to run nonstop, gather experience, and personalize.

Classic continual learning updates one set of weights, which makes old skills fade as new ones land. The group proposes splitting memory into modules that pair two learning modes. In-context learning, which adapts from prompt examples, handles fast uptake and storage of new facts. In-weight updates handle slow, stable growth of core skills. Their roadmap charts how that split could scale to agents that adapt for life, not just for one benchmark.
arxiv-2603-02061:
Lorenzo Maggi, Boris Bonev, Reinhard Wiesmayr, and colleagues estimate wireless link quality from very sparse feedback. Their 2026 work targets the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio that schedulers need for radio resource choices. Devices report only acknowledgments, quality indicators, and past coding choices, a thin evidence trail.

Their framework casts estimation as online convex optimization that learns as feedback arrives. A regularized cross-entropy loss is minimized by mirror descent boosted with Nesterov momentum for fast tracking. An expert-advice algorithm tunes the estimator parameters online, which endows it with continual learning. Ray-traced numerical experiments show better accuracy than top existing schemes across scenarios. The estimator also adapts robustly when the true ratio drifts over time, a must for live networks.
arxiv-2603-02661:
Andrei Lebedev and Vincent Gramoli compare how five live blockchains handle attacks on their peer-to-peer messaging. Their 2026 paper notes that past security work usually targets one chain at a time. No one had tested several chains under the same hostile conditions.

They attacked Algorand, Aptos, Avalanche, Redbelly, and Solana in five different ways and measured the damage. Each chain failed somewhere different: Algorand under packet loss, Aptos under targeted load and leader isolation, Avalanche under brief failures. Redbelly slowed under packet loss, while Solana faced stopping and leader isolation attacks. The shared test setup, released as open source, gives builders a fair way to compare network defenses.
arxiv-2603-02761:
Jens Wagner, Zeno Romero, Kerstin Münnemann, and colleagues predict how fast molecules spread through liquids. Their 2026 paper targets diffusion coefficients, key values for modeling mass transport, where lab data are scarce. Pure formulas miss real mixtures, while pure machine learning can break basic physics.

Their hybrid model, called ESE, joins the classic Stokes-Einstein equation with machine learning corrections. The result stays physically consistent across temperatures for a wide range of two-part liquid mixes. Trained on a large gathered dataset, it beat the prior best model by a clear margin. It needs only standard molecule codes as extra input, and a public web tool makes it easy to use in process design.
arxiv-2603-02961:
Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, and Nisheeth Vishnoi model what happens when workers choose how much to trust AI help. Their 2026 paper treats delegation and checking as one rational decision: hand the task to the AI, then decide how hard to verify the output. Institutions, meanwhile, grade workers by outcomes that may not reflect private checking costs.

The analysis shows sharp phase transitions, where tiny gaps in checking skill flip behavior from careful oversight to near-total delegation. AI then amplifies strong checkers while quietly degrading measured quality for workers who rationally over-delegate and under-check. This happens even when raw task success improves and nobody acts irrationally. The mechanism is structural, offering managers a new lens on uneven AI gains.
arxiv-2603-03261:
Yvain Bruned and Aurélien Minguella unite the proofs behind a core tool of modern chance analysis. Regularity structures tame rough random equations by building a renormalized model, a fixed-up local sketch of the noise. Proofs that the model settles lean on spectral gap claims, and one map, the recentering map, sits at their heart.

Their 2026 paper gives an algebraic union of those convergence proofs. The key map, most often defined through analytic bounds, gains several equal characterizations in purely algebraic terms. Equal definitions let scholars move between views and check the same object in the tongue that suits the task. The result streamlines a forbidding corner of the field that supports many results on singular equations.
arxiv-2603-03461:
Marco Salathe and five colleagues keep radiation detectors honest without heaters or reference sources. Detectors in urban security networks must hold energy calibration through wild swings in temperature and background radiation. Classic fixes burn power on temperature stabilization or lock onto single peaks that weather can shift. Their 2026 method instead calibrates from the whole spectrum, continuously, in software.

Each spectrum is fitted with a model combining natural background components, potassium, uranium and thorium series, radon progeny, and cosmic rays, with a physics-based detector simulation. That simulation accounts for non-proportional light yield and photomultiplier saturation. Validation spans simulated data, an environmental chamber run from deep cold to serious heat, and a multi-day outdoor deployment. Calibration stayed stable through temperature swings and rain, cleanly separating instrument drift from real background change.
arxiv-2603-03561:
Brian C Crow and six colleagues sharpen how detectors tell which direction an antineutrino came from. Reactors emit antineutrinos that escape freely, so reading their direction could monitor reactors from outside. Segmented detectors using inverse beta decay can estimate direction, but the standard method's quantification can be ambiguous. Their 2026 paper supplies a cleaner algorithm with a full error analysis.

Detector segment data becomes a matrix, and the algorithm scores direction by a distance between matrices, an efficient two-dimensional pattern match. Validation compares a simulated empirical dataset, generated for one beam orientation, against simulated alternatives. The study also identifies the best segment size when counts are scarce. Though built for reactor monitoring, the authors stress the matcher suits any pattern-matching task, and they discuss hybrids and detector designs beyond their own.
arxiv-2603-04161: Kouwenhoven and colleagues trace social competence in large language models through False Belief Tests. Testing 17 open-weight models on 192 balanced variants, they find scaling helps performance but not strictly. Explicating propositional attitudes alters response patterns; instruction tuning partly mitigates this effect, reasoning-oriented fine-tuning amplifies it. An OLMo 2 case study shows the effect emerges during pre-training, with vector steering isolating a think vector as its causal driver.
arxiv-2603-05361: Zirong Chen and team offer PACE, a personalized 9-1-1 curriculum co-pilot with Metro Nashville. Call-taking training needs over a thousand skills amid a labor shortage. PACE augments trainer choices by tracking skill-state beliefs and recommending retention-balanced cases. Skill-graph evidence accelerates diagnostics, and contextual bandits select cases for gaps trainees can handle. PACE reaches competence 19.50% faster with higher terminal mastery. Training-officer studies show strong PACE-expert alignment. PACE cuts estimation turnaround from minutes to seconds.
arxiv-2603-05761: Bansal and Scott propose Score-Guided near casting for straight flow editing. Straight flow models achieve state-of-the-art quality, yet editing control stays hard. Current methods split into flipping guidance, hit by shape locking, and shaky sampling. Seeing getting back as near tuning weighs input trueness with score truth. They prove normal shrinking, snapping out-of-spread inputs onto the surface and reaching the limited best guess. The framework covers editing methods, with flow flipping as edge case. Loosening spread enables soft guidance between self keeping and freedom.
arxiv-2603-05961: Bernstein and team employ Bayes methods to spread measured doubt for shock squeeze. Shock tests produce shock speeds linked in line with particle speed. For downstream model work, many Hugoniot curves matching data prove more useful. This guide samples many Hugoniot curves matching shock-particle speed readings via Bayes methods. First, a math after-look for linear settings via Bayes fitting; second, spreading samples through Rankine-Hugoniot rules to yield Hugoniot curves. Shown with argon, copper, and nickel data, the Bayes method proves clear, cheap, and less touchy than redoing.
arxiv-2603-06261: Michielan and his team look at large deviations in subgraph counts for inhomogeneous random graphs, where set degrees act as soft constraints and degree distributions often follow a power law. Rare events for these counts come down to the chance that very large hubs show up. An optimization problem catches the most likely way to make many more subgraphs. When expected subgraph counts grow sublinearly with graph size, polynomially large deviations can occur, and the team derive sharp results on clique counts.
arxiv-2603-06361: Ghahramani and Zhou set out CLAIRE, a hybrid learning method combining unsupervised deep representation learning and supervised sorting for smart factory quality control. An optimized autoencoder packs raw input into a compact latent space, capturing inner structure while cutting noisy features, and a downstream sorter performs binary fault prediction. Tests on a high dimensional dataset show CLAIRE beating usual sorters trained straight on raw features. A post hoc phase with a game theory based method reads the latent space to identify the most telling input features for fault guesses.
arxiv-2603-06761: Salloum and colleagues rethink collocation choice for physics-informed neural networks as coreset construction. Uniform sampling and residual-based refinement can oversample smooth regions and waste training time. From a large candidate pool they select a fixed-size subset that is both informative for PDE error and diverse under a space-time similarity notion. They frame this as a sparse graph-based QUBO with a repair step enforcing the budget. Hybrid coverage anchors guarantee enforcement, and tests on viscous Burgers flow match or beat variants with less overhead.
arxiv-2603-06861: Kang and colleagues introduce IGLU, an activation function for networks, where activations control gradient flow and stability. Modern transformers favor smoother choices over ReLU, like GELU, yet the math linking them is unclear. IGLU comes from mixing GELU gates with a half-normal distribution, giving a closed-form Cauchy gate. That yields a one-parameter family sliding between identity-like and ReLU-like shape via sharpness. Its Cauchy gate falls as a power law for negative side, so gradients never hit zero for finite inputs, unlike GELU's Gaussian gate.
arxiv-2603-06961: Zhang and colleagues show quadruped walking can be learned from seconds of demonstration. Quadruped locomotion tests when model-free learning beats model-based control, exploiting data patterns to bypass optimization over contacts and mode changes. They analyze why imitation learning works well with little data, based on limit cycles, Poincaré return maps, and numerical traits of neural networks.
