With Qualcomm AI Runtime, regular vision models go from PyTorch to runnable inference within 7 to 20 minutes. API costs run around USD 0.7 to 10, while complex models still need further advances.
arxiv-2604-14761: Russeil and 12 others built NOMAI, a classifier that spots superluminous supernova candidates from photometric alerts alone, live inside the Fink broker. It works from ZTF light curves spanning at least 30 days, using features fitted with SALT2 and the blackbody-based Rainbow framework, and needs no spectroscopic redshift. Trained on 5,280 labeled sources including 225 confirmed superluminous supernovae, it reached 66 percent completeness and 58 percent purity. Running nightly since December 18, 2025, it recovered 22 of 24 active superluminous supernovae in its first two months, and adaptation to the Rubin Observatory survey is planned.
arxiv-2604-14861: Du, Han, Notarnicola, Johansson, and Rikos tackle resource sharing over one-way graphs with limited bandwidth. Their method merges central proximal Jacobian ADMM with a finite-level quantized consensus scheme, letting nodes solve it jointly. For convex goals, it converges sublinearly near the optimum, with accuracy bounded by quantization. Tests show it has strong performance against existing methods with low communication cost.
arxiv-2604-14961: Pershin, Golovanov, Baltabaev, and Trankova tackle cold-start regret in contextual bandits with LLM pseudo-observations. After each round, a large language model predicts counterfactual rewards for unplayed arms, injected into Disjoint LinUCB as pseudo-observations. A calibration-gated decay schedule tracks LLM accuracy on played arms, suppressing influence when calibration error is high. With a task-specific prompt, pseudo-observations cut cumulative regret 19 percent on MIND-small versus pure LinUCB. Generic counterfactual prompts instead raise regret on both environments, showing prompt design matters most.
arxiv-2604-15261: Bernardi and ten colleagues design and run RNG, the first flat datacenter network built from quasi-random graphs, now the default for most workloads at Amazon. A new distributed routing protocol finds many disjoint paths between endpoints, while a passive optical device shuffles cables internally, keeping wiring as simple as fat trees. RNG matches or beats fat-tree performance across traffic patterns at up to 45 percent lower cost.
arxiv-2604-15561: Ivchenko exposes evaluation leakage in chest CT segmentation, where mixing slices from one study across train and test inflates reported scores. His CTSCAN benchmark enforces patient-disjoint splits across 89 cases from three sources. Slice-mixed scoring reaches 0.6665 foreground Dice against 0.2066 under case-disjoint scoring, a 69 percent relative drop that shows how much published performance rests on patient reuse.
arxiv-2604-15661: Gao, Jiang, and Lu study tweaks to debt pact books when pacts are patchy, since set rules can sound false alarms or paint too rosy a view. Bosses pay a price to spot flaws in private and pitch fixes. Flaws left in place hand control to the wrong side and force dear re-talks. Tweaks always fix false alarms but fix rosy views only when small, and bosses may burn cash hunting flaws, giving claims that can be tested.
arxiv-2604-15861: Pradhan and three colleagues study how rich content-based access rules affect database query planning. Such rules grant access based on data values in a query, and complex policies can slow or destabilize optimization in poorly understood ways. The paper builds a structural framework and policy grammar for modeling these compliance policies, then adds policy workloads to an analytical benchmark. Tests show policy structure decisively shapes optimizer behavior and end-to-end speed, arguing for policy-aware database design.
arxiv-2604-16061: Funk and three colleagues study discrete k-clustering in metric spaces under two fairness rules: even traits within clusters, and even center members from each attribute. Prior work stays within 8 times the best, with small gap. For k-center, they improve this to 4 times the best, with small additive gap. For k-median and k-means, they give the first constant-factor methods. They convert a diverse pick into a fair grouping via linear methods, extending to matroid and knapsack constraints.
arxiv-2604-16561: Li and Hannuksela investigate how combining repeated lensed images improves sky localization for gravitational waves. Localization matters for multimessenger follow-up and finding host galaxies. Areas near ten square degrees are needed to link signals to lensing structures and find faint images. Using simulated lensed mergers and BAYESTAR localization, they find gains from combining images. The largest gain comes from one to two images, shrinking the 90 percent credible region tenfold. Four-image systems reached ten to one hundred square degrees, and subthreshold images added modest, non-harmful gains.
arxiv-2604-16961: Adhikari and Nötzel ask how well an eavesdropper tapping an optical fiber can be detected and located. They use stimulated Brillouin scattering, a light-sound interaction that reveals fiber changes. They model that scattering and compare three detectors: the current state of the art, a photon-counting method expected soon, and the ultimate quantum limit. Two lenses, asymmetric hypothesis testing and quantum metrology, show what modern quantum technology can add to intrusion detection for quantum key distribution.
arxiv-2604-17061: Majumdar studies the complexity of singularity for multilinear maps, where the determinant's higher cousin exists only in boundary format and grows messy fast. He proves tensor degeneracy is complete for ∃R, via an exact algebraic chain with no added tricks. In boundary format, the two coincide, while deterministic hardness transfer reduces to a polynomial identity test.
arxiv-2604-17161: Baltazar, Silva, and Martini study the automorphism group of a differential Ore extension acting on its derivations, describing isotropy groups. They first describe that group when the degree of h is at least one. Then they pin down isotropy groups for derivations built from an inner part and a Delta part, covering the square-free case fully. They also give a general test for the singular case via localization.
arxiv-2604-17261: Chen, Coughlin, and Bond present &inator, a correct, precise C-to-Rust tool making Rust decls for top-level C decls for modular work. &inator uses constraints for meaning match and type soundness, including borrow rules. It yields a correct version — with a meaning-keeping safe Rust build — that is precise, using the simplest types. Tests show &inator yields correct, precise versions for real C programs, though certain C parts and large-program scaling remain issues. It is the first correct, precise C-to-Rust approach.
arxiv-2604-17761: Tan and five colleagues study contrastive, LRP-based attribution for analyzing LLM failures on realistic benchmarks, where prior work uses short prompts. Failure analysis becomes contrastive attribution: the gap between a wrong output token's logit and the right alternative's is traced to input tokens and internal states. An efficient extension builds cross-layer graphs for long-context inputs. Comparing patterns across datasets, model sizes, and checkpoints, token-level contrastive attribution yields informative signals in some failure cases. It is not universally applicable, showing its utility and limits.
arxiv-2604-17861: Yiwei Yang and five colleagues present GPUOS, a graphics processor runtime that cuts launch overhead for workloads made of many small tensor operations. Instead of launching a fresh kernel for each task, one long-lived kernel drains a host-managed work queue, while operators are compiled just in time and injected through function pointer tables without restarting. The design supports varied shapes, strides, types, and broadcasting, and reaches up to 15.3 times the speed of standard PyTorch on small-operation workloads.
arxiv-2604-18061: Yuan Wang and three colleagues strengthen the case for the X(7200) state and improve measurements of X(6900) parameters from a combined LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS analysis of the di-J/psi mass spectrum. Simultaneous fits observe X(6900) with overwhelming significance above twelve standard deviations and sharpen its mass and width. For X(7200), consistent signals across interference models range from 3.7 to 6.6 standard deviations, with the best-fit CMS three-resonance scheme at the top of that range. The results highlight interference effects in fully charmed tetraquark spectroscopy.
arxiv-2604-18161: Onoda, Parmas, Yaguchi, and Matsuo ask whether differentiable simulators truly improve policy gradients in reinforcement learning. First-order gradients from a differentiable model should speed learning, but discontinuous dynamics bias them. Earlier work detected discontinuities with noisy REINFORCE bounds, needing task-specific tuning and many samples. The authors offer DDCG, a one-knob test that switches estimators in rough regions, plus IVW-H, a per-step variance control for robotics tasks that stabilizes learning without explicit detection.
arxiv-2604-18261: Huang, Gagnon, Založnik, and Appolaire propose DeepRitzSplit, a neural operator that speeds up phase-field models of solidification. Such models need fine space and time grids, making runs slow. The method trains a Deep Ritz operator on an energy-splitting variational form, enforcing energy dissipation, with a custom reaction-diffusion architecture matched to the equations. Tests on the Allen-Cahn equation and dendritic growth show better out-of-distribution generalization than pure data training, plus faster inference than Fourier spectral methods.
arxiv-2604-18361: Walsh introduces the Quandary Den, an artificial-life model that explores how protein machines grow more interlocked without adaptive benefit. Adaptation explains some interlocking, but neutral stories may suffice elsewhere. Two neutral routes emerge: subfunctionalization, where function spreads thin across the complex, and masking, where internal interference builds up in genes until expression must block it. The model shows interlocking rising with no greater need for information.
arxiv-2604-18661: Alpay and Sarioglu study list-limited modular equation deletion over powers of two. Each variable sits in a dyadic coset, each pair rule sets, flips, or doubles variables, and the aim is fewest deletions. Their key result is a coordinatewise balanced covering claim for gain graphs tagged by binary vectors. From any balanced subgraph costing at most k, a random routine returns vertex and edge sets leaving a balanced graph. This yields a random one-sided-error method with time exponential in k and rank but polynomial in n.
arxiv-2604-18761: Kuskova and Zaytsev study Web3 ecosystems as social spaces, not just markets for digital assets, using fused on-chain trades and off-chain social media data from more than 100 NFT collections. Network analysis finds distinct roles: long-term holders, active traders, and short-term speculators, each shaping network shape, cohesion, and influence in different ways. Talk and visibility persist even as trading falls. Holder-led groups grow into dense social ecosystems, while trader- and speculator-led networks stay fragmented and transactional.
arxiv-2604-18961: Sepahvand, Janabi-Sharifi, and Aghili present an AI enabled hybrid vision force controller for tendon driven aerial continuum manipulators. The controller supports autonomous contact with a static environment while steadying image feature error. It pairs fixed time sliding mode control with a radial basis function network, learning vision and force uncertainties online without offline training. Line features come from a graph neural network servoing system rather than hand built geometric extractors. Tests against rigid arm aerial methods show robust performance across varied scenarios.
arxiv-2604-19061: Wadayama and Takahashi propose three module score based VAMP for nonlinear channels. A latent variable for the mixing output splits inference into three modules. The likelihood part handles channel observations by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, the coupling part enforces linear constraints by LMMSE, and the denoiser applies code constraints by belief propagation. Modules swap Gaussian notes with Onsager corrections from posterior variances. BPSK LDPC codewords through a tanh channel show a clear bit error rate waterfall, with the capacity gap shrinking as block length grows from 128 to 2304.
arxiv-2604-19461: Polyakov and Kuznetsov introduce Involuntary In-Context Learning, an attack using abstract operator framing with few-shot examples to force pattern completion past safety training. Safety alignment rests on behavioral training that strong in-context patterns can override. Across 3,479 probes on 10 OpenAI models, semantic operator naming reaches a 100 percent bypass rate, while identical examples in direct question-and-answer form yield 0 percent. Example order also matters: interleaved examples reach 76 percent, against 6 percent for harmful-first order.
arxiv-2604-19561: Janicki and colleagues study membership inference attacks for detecting data contamination in large language models. Language models train on vast data, some possibly from copyrighted sources. Membership inference attacks aim to detect whether specific documents entered training corpora. Black-box attacks need significant data manipulation, making comparison hard. The authors compare state-of-the-art black-box attacks on unified datasets and develop Familiarity Ranking, a new method giving models more freedom of expression. Whether any current method works well remains open.
arxiv-2604-19961: Samsonau and Pearce argue that guiding others through real research deserves recognition as its own profession, the Research Guide. Such guides work between the classroom teacher and the PhD advisor, serving school students, undergraduates, and citizen scientists. Current programs mostly copy a simplified PhD apprenticeship, one mentor with a few students, and frame research as a single hypothesis-testing cycle. The authors call for a named role with training, a career ladder, hiring standards, and institutional backing, built on cognitive apprenticeship.
arxiv-2604-20061: Duraisamy argues that neural surrogates for multiscale partial differential equations are strong but bounded, not all-purpose rivals for classical solvers. Many benchmarks sit on low-dimensional manifolds where any decent reduced model fills in well. Spectral bias leaves fine detail blurry, and coarse-graining destroys information for good, so no training can recover what coarse data discard. Weather outlooks on reanalysis data are a sweet spot, but chaotic multiscale cases will not carry over, and hybrids plus better reports are urged.
arxiv-2604-20161: Zhao, Kolar, and Lv propose SMART, a spectral transfer scheme for multi-task regression with small target samples. It assumes spectral likeness, not bounded gaps between source and target models: target singular subspaces sit inside source ones and align sparsely with source bases. SMART builds the target coefficient matrix with structured regularization from source clues, needing only a fitted source model. Though the optimization is nonconvex, an ADMM routine delivers error bounds and a minimax lower bound, with near-minimax rates when the source is noiseless.
arxiv-2604-20461: Islam and Zacchiroli redo a 2023 study that found security-related commit messages too uninformative for patch triage, using only the paper itself and none of the original artifacts. Pulling 50,673 security-related commits from GitHub over the same period, June 1999 to August 2022, their fresh implementation confirms the original finding with statistical significance. Extending to October 2025, they find informativeness is worsening over time and varies sharply by ecosystem. Surprisingly, commits following the Conventional Commits Specification prove less informative than ones that do not follow it.
arxiv-2604-20561: Grizzi, Aligia, and Roura-Bas derive exact analytical edge states for the extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, which adds hopping between distant atoms beyond nearest neighbors. Edge wavefunctions decay exponentially from the boundary with a unit-cell decay factor. From the winding number of the bulk Hamiltonian under periodic boundary conditions, they map the topological phase diagram and establish bulk-boundary correspondence. Winding changes coincide with bulk gap closings and with the decay factor reaching unity. For finite chains they obtain analytical, approximate low-energy edge states of high accuracy.
arxiv-2604-20961: Tripathi, Mathur, and Tripathi test the variational quantum eigensolver on the transverse-field Ising model in one, two, and three dimensions, for systems of up to 27 spins. They benchmark three trial circuits, a hardware-efficient design, a physics-inspired Hamiltonian variational form, and that form with symmetry breaking, against exact answers. Energy spread, entanglement, spin correlations, and magnetization gauge how faithfully each circuit captures the ground state.
arxiv-2604-21261: Victor Duarte Melo presents ECCFROG522PP, a 522-bit prime-field elliptic curve in short Weierstrass form built for deterministic generation and public reproducibility. Every critical parameter derives from a fixed public seed through a transparent, checkable procedure, unlike curves whose constants invite trust questions. The curve has prime order, cofactor one, and a fully ordered base point, with a twist carrying a large proven prime factor. Full generation and validation scripts allow independent reproduction end to end.
arxiv-2604-21361: Ankur Sharma and three colleagues show that tiny clock skews can corrupt observability in distributed AI inference even when the system itself runs fine. In controlled multi-node experiments, no causality violations appear under synchronized clocks or skews up to 3 milliseconds, but clear violations emerge by 5 milliseconds, while throughput and output correctness barely move. Violation rates also drift over long runs as relative clock drift evolves. The lesson: timing alignment is a first-class concern for distributed AI, not a mere operational detail.
arxiv-2604-21461: Chentao Li and five colleagues ask whether multimodal models truly grasp pointing in first-person vision, where smart glasses must resolve what a gesture refers to. Current systems often lean on visual nearness or saliency instead of pointing geometry, a flaw the authors call referential hallucination. Their EgoPoint-Bench spans over 11,000 simulated and real samples across five dimensions and three complexity levels. Models tuned on the synthetic data gain a lot and carry over from simulation to reality, pointing to spatially aware supervision as the fix.
arxiv-2604-21561: Danylo Radevych and three others explain superconductivity in nonmagnetic MnB4, which tests find with a critical temperature reaching 14 K at 158 GPa, above the below-1-K value from electron-phonon coupling. Density-functional results place MnB4 close to an altermagnetic instability, so the authors propose altermagnetic spin fluctuations as the driver. A two-orbital tight-binding model, with boron states at the Fermi level removed, finds extended-s symmetry as the leading pairing instability. If confirmed, this would be the first known case driven by altermagnetic spin fluctuations.
arxiv-2604-21761: Wong and five colleagues make physics-informed neural networks transfer to new equations with little or no training data. Their Pi-PINN framework learns a shared physics-informed representation, then solves known and unknown partial differential equation instances through closed-form head adaptation with a least-squares-optimal pseudoinverse. Tests cover Poisson, Helmholtz, and Burgers equations. Predictions run 100 to 1000 times faster than a typical PINN, with far lower error than a typical data-driven model.
arxiv-2604-21861: Kumar and Ganesan show reservoir computing with oscillators driven by a varying pump, in a two-mode system at 2:1 parametric resonance. Prediction tasks use Mackey-Glass, Rössler, and Lorenz chaotic time series. The lowest prediction errors fall always within that regime, where nonlinear effects switch on while timing stays in step. Comb states, by contrast, do worse in the chaotic comb regime as phase timing is lost. Pump depth, detuning, damping, and input rate change which regimes are open and shape system performance.
arxiv-2604-21961: Zhao, Huang, and Hao propose a reduction method, OP-to-MaxSAT reduction, and a general optimization solver based on it, called GORED. GORED unifies solving multiple problem types by reducing them to MaxSAT instances and solving them with a state-of-the-art MaxSAT solver. The authors validate generality and quality on 136 instances across 11 problem types. Results show GORED solves a wide range of problems with solutions comparable in quality to existing methods. Automated reduction shifts solvers from specialized algorithms per problem type to a single algorithm for diverse problems.
arxiv-2604-22261: Alam, Surdeanu and Riloff tackle relation completion, filling in missing links between entities, where language models struggle when evidence is rare. Their RC-RAG framework weaves paraphrases of the target relation through retrieval, summarisation and generation, widening the wording under which relevant passages can be found, without any model fine-tuning. Across five language models and two benchmarks it beat retrieval baselines, and in long-tail settings the best model gained 40.6 exact-match points over its standalone score.
arxiv-2604-22361: Fujiwara and three colleagues extend a type system for checking programs using arrays and pointer arithmetic to handle nested arrays. Tanaka and colleagues proposed a system extending ConSORT, which combines shared ownership and refinement types for imperative checks, with pointer arithmetic support, letting control depend on an array index. That version does not handle nested arrays, essential for common data structures such as matrices. The authors extend control to outer array indices, prove soundness, and build a checker showing it checks programs handling nested arrays, beyond Tanaka's reach.
arxiv-2604-22561: Pathok and three colleagues prepare nickel-doped cadmium manganese sulfide films by a low-cost chemical bath method to test their optoelectronic fit. Adding nickel should shift lattice strain, defect density, and electronic structure, giving another tuning knob. X-ray diffraction confirms a cubic zinc blende crystal structure, backed by high-resolution electron microscopy. Crystallinity rises while microstrain and dislocation density fall as nickel content grows. Microscopy shows uniform, dense, crack-free films with grain size growing with nickel content and nearly constant thickness.
arxiv-2604-22861: Ma and seven colleagues define a new task, IntraView, in which answers to research queries must be retrieved faithfully from given literature rather than recalled loosely. Their agent, IntrAgent, mimics human reading: it ranks relevant sections, then reads iteratively to extract details and refine answers. To test the idea, they build IntraBench, with 315 expert-written questions across five science and technology fields. Across seven backbone models, IntrAgent beats strong retrieval and research-agent baselines on cross-domain accuracy by 13.2 percent on average.
arxiv-2604-22961: Rahvar treats planetary systems as dark matter detectors, studying primordial black hole scattering of Oort cloud objects. Energy transfer in these encounters gives ejection and Earth-crossing injection rates for stellar-mass black holes, scaling linearly with mass. Comparison with Oort cloud survival, comet fluxes, and Earth and Moon impact records yields strict upper limits on their share of dark matter. The limits exclude them as the dominant dark matter in the intermediate-to-high mass window. Solar motion predicts a testable dipole pattern in injected comets.
arxiv-2604-23261: Murayama and Nitta study Mabuchi solitons on admissible manifolds of Apostolov-Calderbank-Gauduchon-Tønnesen-Friedman type. They prove a Fano admissible one admits a Mabuchi soliton exactly when its own Mabuchi constant is below 1. An explicit formula for the Mabuchi constant on Fano admissible manifolds extends the formula of Mabuchi himself. With this formula in hand, they fully settle which Fano admissible manifolds over complex projective space admit Mabuchi solitons.
arxiv-2604-23761: Zhao and six colleagues teach wheeled-legged robots to dodge obstacles with fast reflexes, exploiting their hybrid rolling and stepping build. Their AWARE framework splits avoidance into navigation and reflexive regimes under a threat-aware high-level policy, with specialised low-level experts. It discovers rolling, stepping, and hybrid dodges, including lunges and sidesteps, and tests in simulation and on a real robot show smooth switching between gaits.
arxiv-2604-23861: Dizabadi studies convolutional network optimisation for CIFAR-10 image classification through systematic ablation. He tests 17 progressive changes spanning training length, learning-rate schedules, dropout, pooling, depth, filters, and dense layers. Longer training helps steadily, while several structural redesigns hurt despite added variety. A weighted ensemble of the best configs reaches about 86 percent on reduced data and about 89 percent on the full set, up from under 80 percent at baseline.
arxiv-2604-24161: Govaers proposes a gate-based quantum method for predicting how densities move on a grid of positions and speeds. The density lives in the amplitudes of a quantum state, and a repeating operator pattern lets the motion run in the spectral domain with quantum Fourier transforms and phase shifts. Drift maps exactly into amplitude space, while diffusion enters through a Wick-rotation stand-in that turns it into dispersive phase motion. Tests match the exact Fokker-Planck answer closely, and the grid doubles with each added qubit.
arxiv-2604-24261: Lachaud and colleagues present the coded mask of the ECLAIRs telescope aboard SVOM, built to detect and localize high-energy transients, especially gamma-ray bursts. Working from 4 to 150 keV, ECLAIRs extends coded-mask imaging to an unusually low threshold. Reaching 4 keV while holding performance to 150 keV required a novel self-supporting mask, solving scientific and mechanical challenges through dedicated pattern algorithms and a stiffened sandwich structure. The paper gives the rationale, development, and final implementation of the mask.
arxiv-2604-24461: Attig and five colleagues present two scales for human-AI teaming. They are the Perceived Cooperativity Scale from joint activity theory and the Teaming Perception Scale from evolutionary cooperation theory. Cooperativity captures skill and practice in one exchange; teaming sense comes from mutual help and support. Both scales were adapted for human-human teaming. Across three studies with 409 participants, with a card game, LLM use, and a support system, both scales told partners apart by quality and showed construct strength as hoped.
arxiv-2604-24661: Fang and seven colleagues study reinforcement learning under changing faults such as weather, sensor noise and background distractions. Real cameras face weather and noise. They introduce the Visual Degraded Control Suite, a test set that injects Markov-switching degradations into rendered scenes. They show that faithfully rebuilding corrupted views forces latent states to encode corruption-specific nuisance info. Their frozen, plug-and-play ACO-MoE adapter instead anchors its view to the clean foreground, avoiding that contamination, and recovers 95.3 percent of clean-input performance under hard corruptions.
arxiv-2604-24961: Zhang and Thompson model a warm scattering corona near an accreting Kerr black hole. Accretion runs slow, at about 0.01 times the Eddington rate. Monte Carlo runs cover Compton scattering, pair creation, relativistic lensing and frame dragging. Soft photons seed from the inner disk, with electron spread tuned for fixed amplification. Pair creation by photon collisions greatly raises scattering charge density near the innermost ion disk. The pair cloud sits closer to the black hole, with escaping spectra and polarization recorded by observer angle.
arxiv-2604-25061: Bai presents the Spark Policy Toolkit, a toolkit for policy learning in Spark. Custom pipelines fail: rowwise Python execution makes inference impractical. Driver-side candidate materialization leaves split search fragile at feature scale. The toolkit provides two primitives: vectorized inference, and collect-less split search scoring on executors. Both follow one fixed-input contract: same rows and split boundaries must preserve scores, decisions and outputs. On a 40-worker cluster, one backend reaches 4.72 million rows per second. Across 24 settings, one backend wins 18 and the other 6, so backend choice is workload-based.
arxiv-2604-25161: Chen and six colleagues propose capability-based testing for vision-and-language navigation agents. Such agents rely on perception, memory, planning and decision, so failures are hard to localize. Existing system-level tests say little about which capability caused a failure. Their approach combines test generation that adapts by changing seed cases, oracles that flag errors by capability and a feedback loop that attributes failures and guides further tests. Experiments show the method finds more failure cases and pinpoints weak capabilities more accurately than current baselines.
arxiv-2604-25461: Kudo and Nogata study cyclotomic numbers of order q minus 1 over the finite field with q to the r elements. Here r is at least 2, and k is q to the r minus 1 over q minus 1. They prove the cyclotomic number is at most the ceiling of k over 2 for all a and b between 0 and q minus 2. The exception is q equal to 2 with r at least 3. They also give sharper bounds for prime r, especially 2 and 3.
arxiv-2604-25661: Bai and four colleagues present SlicerRoboTMS, an open-source 3D Slicer add-on for robotic transcranial magnetic stimulation. Robo-TMS is an image-guided robotic method that improves accuracy and reproducibility over conventional TMS. Building Robo-TMS systems is hard because it spans medical imaging, vision, and robotics. The extension supports MRI-based neuronavigation and robot links through standard protocols. An example integration shows how SlicerRoboTMS fits a typical Robo-TMS workflow.
arxiv-2604-25761: Greinecker and Podczeck show that core analysis in economics needs no explicit list of agents, only the distribution of their characteristics. When single agents are negligible, most relevant properties of an economy follow from the distribution alone. Many have claimed this description is too sparse for core analysis, since coalitions and blocking seem to need single agents. The authors locate blocking coalitions directly in distributional terms. They prove the classical core-equivalence theorem purely distributionally, with the version for single agents as a corollary.
arxiv-2604-25961: Fathi and Ahmed study strong-field signatures of a regular black hole in an Einasto dark matter halo. The black hole is static and spherically symmetric. One dimensionless halo parameter controls the geometry below a critical value. Timelike observables stay close to Schwarzschild values along most of the branch. Photon sphere scale, shadow diameter, and optical structures respond most sensitively near criticality. Event Horizon Telescope shadow data fit the full branch for Sagittarius A* within one standard deviation, while M87* mildly disfavors near-critical values.
arxiv-2604-26161: Arntzenius and Willsey unite functional and logic programming by recasting predicates as functions carrying their support. Support means the inputs that yield a nonzero result. With only finitely many such inputs, each function becomes an input-output table. Datalog then reads as a language of boolean functions with finite support. Moving beyond booleans to other pointed sets enables aggregation and weighted logic programming. A simple type system checks finiteness through graded effects for grounding and relevance types for pointed sets.
arxiv-2604-26461: Zeng and three colleagues proposed PKS4, parallel kinematic scanners for efficient video understanding. Dense attention costs balloon with length, adapter fine-tuning bloats activation memory, and plain state-space models break 2D spatial structure. Their design keeps a standard 2D backbone, adds one plug-and-play time module with linear cost, and steers it with motion priors from frame links and gaps. Parallel scanners per spot kept structure intact, reached top accuracy, and converged in just 20 epochs.
arxiv-2604-26561: Sela tested whether multi-agent policy talks can keep disagreement alive instead of collapsing into fake consensus. Her AI Council ran 120 talks across two policy scenarios with two fixes. Giving each value view a different mid-size model cut first-choice clustering sharply. On child welfare it fell from about 71 percent to about 46 percent, and on housing from about 46 percent to about 23 percent. Coherence checks then showed a fidelity-diversity trade-off, helping where one option ruled but hurting where options truly competed.
arxiv-2604-26761: Chambers and three colleagues build a theory linking three common measures of how hard a choice feels: grasp beforehand, random picks, and trust afterward. With two options in a Bayesian expected-utility setting, they show the three measures are generally unrelated, a warning against treating them as the same thing. They give cases where the rankings line up, including tasks paying only for correct answers, where trust matches grasp. Willingness to accept a switch, measured in utility units, equals grasp.
arxiv-2604-26861: Gomez and thirteen colleagues report the largest trapped-ion demonstration of lattice protein folding to date, on a 64-qubit barium system. Six short peptide chains of 14 to 16 residues are encoded on a tetrahedral lattice, producing dense Hamiltonians with interactions among up to five bodies. A bias-field counterdiabatic method steers sampling toward low-energy shapes, and a consensus pipeline merges quantum contact data with feasible backbone geometry. The hybrid workflow reaches classical reference energies in several cases and beats random-seeded pipelines.
arxiv-2604-27161: Heinrich and seven colleagues present XRISM observations of the merging galaxy cluster Abell 2034. It shows the broadest emission lines yet seen in a cluster. They measure a velocity spread near 470 kilometers per second. That gives a kinetic pressure share near 15 percent. The value sits at or above the high end of predictions for similar-mass clusters. A gas bulk velocity gradient near 380 kilometers per second runs opposite to the galaxy gradient. That shows galaxies and dark matter decoupling from the hot gas.
arxiv-2604-27261: Habibollah and Rafiei introduce SynSQL, a framework that synthesizes relational test databases for robust evaluation of text-to-SQL systems. Judging correctness by running predicted and gold queries on one static database is fragile, since the same queries may behave differently on other instances. SynSQL instead generates schema-consistent data from the natural language question itself, without relying on gold SQL. Its three stages, schema selection, question-guided data synthesis, and a further checking stage, stress-test systems beyond fixed benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-27661: Milano and three colleagues test whether large language models can detect language ideologies in Luxembourgish news comments. They hand-annotate a corpus of user comments with set ideological categories, then judge models on replicating those human labels under varied prompts. Because Luxembourgish is small and thinly represented in training data, they also test machine-translating the data into high-resource languages. Models are not yet fully reliable for multi-class ideological annotation, but they work as practical tools for spotting ideological content.
arxiv-2604-27861: Sun and four colleagues present TwinGate, a two-encoder guard against split-up jailbreaks. Such jailbreaks split a harmful goal into harmless asks that, side by side, rebuild banned text. TwinGate groups intent-matched bits in one hidden space with Asymmetric Contrastive Learning, while a frozen encoder cuts false alarms. Each ask needs one light pass, so the guard runs beside the host model. On more than 3,620,000 prompts across 8,600 intents, it spots most harmful intents at a low false-alarm rate and beats watchful and watch-free baselines.
arxiv-2604-27961: Zimper and colleagues model how clusters form when views and social ties change together. Their cut-down random equations track only social ties, treating views as a flow-like term, which runs far cheaper than full models while still matching cluster patterns. The method also fits large poll data, including decades of United States General Social Survey answers.
arxiv-2605-00161:
Hasan Amin and 6 co-authors work on diffusion language models, which draft text by refining noisy drafts in parallel. In practice these models still need hundreds of refinement steps for good text, which erases their speed edge. A trick that speeds up image diffusion does not carry over, since text has no smooth path between noise levels.

The team finds the right substitute: an exact formula linking any two noise levels for a draft. Their training method makes a denoising model agree with itself across these links, with no trained teacher needed. The resulting model set new best scores on guided and unguided text generation. Gains were largest when only a few refinement steps were allowed.
arxiv-2605-00461:
Ge Luo and 8 co-authors design a lighter network for fusing images from several sources, such as infrared with visible light or multiple exposures into one. Deep unfolding networks, which turn an iterative optimization algorithm into network layers, fuse well but usually update each modality separately, costing memory and compute. That overhead blocks use on small edge devices.

Their network, CDNet, instead unfolds a coupled dictionary model whose prior splits image content into a shared part and modality-specific parts. The resulting block updates both together in one joint step, under a block-sparse interaction pattern. A compact loss on high- and low-frequency fidelity lets it train without ground-truth fused images. Across four fusion tasks, including medical imaging and fusion for road-scene segmentation, CDNet matched or beat heavier rivals while running lean, with clear margins on standard infrared benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-00961:
Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay develop a unified math formulation for post-quantum secure telemetry and actuation in aircraft engine control systems. The setting couples a FADEC controller with a dual-spool turbofan, a safety-critical cyber-physical system. Their model joins lattice-based key set-up, attestation entropy from physical unclonable functions, authenticated encryption, radar-altimeter integrity, bus timing, and Kalman residual checks in one stochastic hybrid model.

Within that model, plant behavior, latency, leakage, hostile channel quality, and cryptographic state evolve together. Channel doubt tightens how often keys can be renewed, ciphertext growth affects bus scheduling, and sensing limits shape alarm thresholds. The analysis, framed defensively, shows how post-quantum security, real-time timing, and closed-loop stability interact.
arxiv-2605-01161:
Hemanta Ban and two co-authors analyze distributed formation control for multiple agents driven by the gradient of the Lennard-Jones potential, a classic attraction-repulsion law. Each agent follows local rules, yet the group must form a stable pattern without collisions. For collision-free initial data, the authors prove global well-posedness together with a uniform lower bound on all distances between agents, excluding hard crashes.

Using total energy as a Lyapunov function, an invariance argument shows every positive limit point is an equilibrium. Because paths stay uniformly away from collisions, the energy is analytic along the flow. A further step yields convergence to a single resting state up to translation. Illustrative numerical examples accompany the proofs.
arxiv-2605-01261:
Kiyoharu Kawana and Kyosuke Adachi improve a standard tool for predicting liquid-liquid phase separation, the process behind protein droplets in cells and the splitting of polymer mixtures. The tool, the random phase approximation, is widely used, but how accurate it is for polymer solutions away from high density was not well mapped. The authors build a loop expansion around it, treating inverse polymer density in the role that Planck's constant plays in quantum field theory.

They compute the first two corrections to the free energy of the standard method. Tested against molecular dynamics simulations of bead-spring chains, the first correction gives a better estimate of the dilute-phase density where the two liquids coexist. The error at the critical point stays about the same as the uncorrected method. The authors present the expansion as a step-by-step route to sharper predictions for polymer phase separation.
arxiv-2605-01361:
Junhyeong Lee, Sangjin Jin, and Yongjae Lee work on decision-focused learning, where a forecast model is trained to make the final decision good, not just the forecast close. Finding the training signal for that goal usually means grinding through a solver or using stand-in losses, both costly or off target.

The three authors show that, when the active limits of a problem stay stable, the regret signal has a clean geometric form. It is the forecast error cast onto the flat space set by the active limits, scaled by local curvature. In plain terms, parts of the error that cannot change the decision are filtered out. Their method, PEAR, solves one small linear system over the active limits instead of tracing solver steps. On linear benchmarks and a real quadratic task, it gives the best decisions at the lowest cost.
arxiv-2605-01561:
Diego Vallarino models economic crises as avalanches on the real web of world production. Borrowing from the physics of the Hall effect, where a field pushes current sideways, he treats shocks as fields. Those fields strike flow-heavy nodes with little backup and thin capacity, turning stress sideways through a conversion rule.

Built on World Input-Output Database networks from 2000 to 2014, with over two thousand country-sector nodes, the model lets stress pile up until nodes topple in sandpile fashion. Monte Carlo runs over shock strength and redundancy stress yield four ordered regimes, from stable absorption to a full avalanche regime. Big-event odds and mean avalanche size rise together as stress grows. The tails thicken by regime, yet not enough to claim universal power-law criticality: the author stresses a finite, real-network account of fragility, not self-organized criticality for the world economy.
arxiv-2605-01661:
F S Gama extends supersymmetric versions of Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory, a three-dimensional gauge theory with a topological twist, by adding higher-derivative terms. The extension is defined in both the one- and two-supercharge superspaces, with the new operator a polynomial in the wave operator of any chosen degree, placed only in the gauge sector.

The goal is the one-loop quantum correction to the superfield effective potential, the quantity that tells whether the quantum vacuum keeps the classical shape. Gama computes it with background field methods in a higher-derivative gauge choice built for such terms. The result comes out in closed form, written through the roots of the polynomial functions that define the extension. Closed forms at one loop are the checkpoints of supersymmetric model building: they let later work test stability and symmetry breaking without redoing the loop machinery.
arxiv-2605-01761:
Quanchen Zou and six co-authors defend text-to-video models against prompts engineered to make them produce violence or explicit footage. Guards inherited from image safety read the prompt's wording, so rephrased attacks slip through. Video adds a second hole: a mild prompt can drift into unsafe scenes as the generator stretches it into a story.

TrajShield works at inference time with no retraining. It simulates the trajectory a prompt implies and finds the causal origin of the risk inside that unfolding path. It then rewrites the prompt just enough to cut the risk while keeping harmless meaning intact. Blatant prompts, disguised jailbreaks, and this slow temporal drift are handled by one mechanism. On a safety benchmark spanning fourteen categories and several video backends, it posts the best defense scores with high fidelity to the original request, cutting attack success by over half on average.
arxiv-2605-01961:
Maheed Ahmed and Mahsa Ghasemi bring fairness into dueling bandits, a setting where a learner picks between options based on human preferences. Most systems train on average preference, which can leave minority groups poorly served when tastes differ widely. The authors assume each user has a personal Condorcet winner, an option that beats every other option for that user.

Arms are scored by how they perform relative to each user's own winner. To balance users, the method uses Nash Social Welfare, which multiplies user gains and so punishes inequality. The framework aims to learn good choices for all users, rather than letting a majority preference marginalise any single group.
arxiv-2605-02161:
Z Papp extends the Feshbach-Villars form of relativistic quantum mechanics to two particles, both with spin zero. That form rewrites a relativistic wave equation as a pair of coupled equations, which can clarify its structure. For two bodies, the challenge is to separate the motion of the whole system from the motion of the parts relative to each other.

Papp shows the extension can be done so that centre-of-mass motion splits off cleanly. What remains is an equation of Feshbach-Villars type written only in the relative coordinate. The short paper gives the construction and its resulting form. Such a separation is a standard first step before solving or approximating two-body relativistic problems.
arxiv-2605-02261:
Dennis Bromley, Diana Wang, and Vidya Setlur explore how people express data queries through proximity, by sketching near, pointing near, and writing near. Data tools often miss analytical intent that is hard to state in a formal query or in words alone. Their multimodal probe lets users query time-series and geographic data by free-form sketching, natural language, and visual annotation in one shared space.

Users sketch trends or paths and add notes and directives tied to shared spatial and temporal context. A hybrid system joins geometric sketch matching with vision-language models to handle queries that mix pattern and meaning. In a study with twenty participants, people repeatedly used spatial, temporal, and visual proximity to link sketches, notes, and language.
arxiv-2605-02361:
Liqian Ma, Zishun Liu, Glen Chou, and Yongxin Chen plan feedback motion for stochastic nonlinear systems that must satisfy signal temporal logic specifications, formal statements about how signals should behave over time. Their goal is a closed-loop system that meets a given formula with very high probability, such as 99.99 percent, despite random disturbances.

The method erodes predicates to turn the hard stochastic problem into a deterministic trajectory optimisation with tightened constraints. The erosion amount comes from a probabilistic reachable tube, which bounds how far the stochastic path can stray from a nominal one. Contraction theory and feedback design compute those bounds, and several tracking controllers are developed. The result is a full planning pipeline that runs through numerical optimisation.
arxiv-2605-02561:
Zhongwei Shen, Yao Xu, and Jinping Zhuge develop homogenization theory for elliptic equations whose coefficients oscillate at infinitely many scales at once. Homogenization replaces rapid wiggles with an effective smooth equation. Problems with endless scales arise in fractal materials and in diffusion in fluids, where structure repeats at finer and finer levels without end.

Under assumptions that the scales stay separated, the authors prove a qualitative homogenization theorem with optimal convergence rates in the mean-square sense. They also establish interior and boundary Lipschitz estimates that hold uniformly across all scale choices. Those uniform bounds are the technical core: they keep control of solutions no matter how many scales are active. The work gives a general frame for multi-scale media with no smallest scale.
arxiv-2605-02661:
Junjie Yu and seventy-seven co-authors introduce AcademiClaw, a benchmark of tasks that university students set for AI agents. Prior benchmarks in this agent ecosystem covered assistant-level work only. AcademiClaw instead draws eighty complex, long-horizon tasks from real student workflows: homework, research projects, competitions, and personal projects that current agents failed to solve well.

The tasks were picked from hundreds of student submissions by expert review and span more than twenty-five fields, from olympiad-level math and linguistics to heavy reinforcement learning and full system debugging. Each runs in an isolated sandbox and is scored by multi-part rubrics, with a separate safety audit. Six frontier models were tested, and even the best passed only a little over half the tasks. Sharp gaps by field and differing model strategies round out the findings.
arxiv-2605-02761:
Justice Owusu Agyemang and six co-authors present a mathematical framework for adaptive video streaming that draws on several providers at once. Current systems probe providers in a line, fail over only after trouble, and keep cold standbys that start slowly. Together those traits cause stalls and visible quality drops when a provider falters.

Their theorem treats acquisition as filling a reservoir from all providers in parallel, while keeping a set of pre-checked, pre-fetched standby streams ready for sub-second failover. Four results are proved. They give a lower bound on uptime from independent streams, and a speedup over batched probing. They show steady quality gains under lazy refill. They also give a switching rule, drawn from prospect theory, that provably stops thrashing between similar streams. The work is theoretical, with practical gains stated as analysis.
arxiv-2605-02861:
Yanis Le Fur and five co-authors benchmark quantum error detection on real hardware, weighing its promise against its costs. Error detection can give unbiased values that converge to the noiseless answer as the code grows. Two costs hold it back: sample counts rise steeply with circuit depth and noise, and classical processing generally grows steeply with code size.

Embedding a code on hardware also adds overhead that can hurt accuracy at first. The team runs memory and logic tests with two codes, a repetition code and a triangular color code, on real and simulated noisy machines, using up to dozens of physical qubits. Pseudothreshold estimates map where detection starts to pay. Despite the challenges, results show strong promise for scaling the technique on current and future machines.
arxiv-2605-03061:
Houman Safaai and Alessandro Marin Vargas introduce Dynamic Vine Copulas, a tool for tracking how dependence among many variables changes over time. Correlations can look steady while tails, asymmetry, or conditional links shift, and simple models miss those moves.

Their method holds a vine factorization fixed and lets pair-copula states drift smoothly or switch families in a controlled way. A held-out test splits plain pairwise links from higher-order conditional effects. In benchmarks it caught changes Gaussian tools missed, and in brain recording data it found a repeatable higher-order signal across areas.
arxiv-2605-03361:
Honglei Zhang, Yuting Chen, Chenpeng Hu, Pengfei Zhou, Siyue Zhang, and Yilei Shi introduce ReasonAudio, a benchmark for reasoning in text-to-audio retrieval beyond simple sound matching. Existing sets mostly test whether a clip matches its caption, not whether a system can handle negation, order, co-occurrence, or duration in a query.

The benchmark pairs synthetic tasks over composite clips with a natural task on real recordings. Eleven leading systems scored poorly overall, and a controlled test still left the best model far behind its own generative backbone and far behind humans. Reasoning-rich audio search remains an open challenge.
arxiv-2605-03461:
Qi Chen, Hao-Xuan Luo, Jin-Kang Guo, Qian-Qian Hong, Li-Bao Fan, and Chuan-Cun Shu give an analytic two-pulse recipe for universal single-qubit gates in ultracold sodium-cesium molecules. Molecular qubits promise rich control, but complex protocols and sensitivity to flaws have slowed practical gate work.

Encoding qubits in the lowest rotational levels, they use a first-order Magnus expansion to derive closed-form evolution and exact amplitude and phase conditions for any rotation. Simulations show fidelities above the four-nines level with little leakage, and molecular orientation tracks the gate action for practical readout. The method extends to other molecules and platforms.
arxiv-2605-03661:
Yuxuan Yang studies optimal embeddings of orders into maximal orders of central simple algebras of degree three over number fields. An embedding is optimal when the order being placed is exactly the intersection of the larger order with the embedded field. Yang considers degree-three extensions and asks when such optimal placement fails.

He determines exactly when an order cannot be optimally embedded into all maximal orders of the algebra. In the remaining cases, he further pins down exactly when the order embeds optimally into one third of the isomorphism classes of maximal orders, and when it manages two thirds. The result gives a complete arithmetic picture for this degree-three setting.
arxiv-2605-03861:
Ankit Satpute and six co-authors tackle content-based recommendation of mathematical research papers. In this setting, relatedness is conceptual rather than textual. Two mathematics papers may share proof techniques, logical links, or generalizations. Yet they may have minimal textual or citation overlap, so recommenders built for computer science or biomedicine fail. An expert-driven study first describes what mathematicians actually want from a recommendation.

Relevance turns out to be aspect-driven at its core, so the team built GoldRiM, a small expert-annotated dataset, and SilverRiM, a large automatically derived one, the first for aspect-aware recommendation in mathematics. Their AchGNN model is an aspect-conditioned heterogeneous graph network. It jointly models text semantics, citation structure, and author lineage. It beat prior aspect-based methods throughout, on both datasets.
arxiv-2605-03961:
Jessica Braudo and Noam Soker compare the shapes of core-collapse supernova remnants and jet-shaped planetary nebulae. Both can share an unusual feature: a narrow, faint zone, called a pipe, extending from side to side. They present two jet-shaped planetary nebulae with a pipe. They present three more with two opposite narrow jet-shaped lobes. The lobes, they argue, can later merge into a single pipe.

A three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation reproduces two opposite narrow lobes similar to those observed. The simulation explodes a massive star with three pairs of jets, within the jittering jets explosion mechanism framework. The simulated and observed morphologies look alike in both object classes. From that similarity, the authors argue jets shaped the pipes in the supernova remnants as well. That strengthens the case for the jittering jets mechanism.
arxiv-2605-04061:
Bryan Cheng and Jasper Zhang report a striking dissociation in how large language models encode task identity from few-shot demonstrations. Linear probes can classify the task from specific layer activations with perfect accuracy, which earlier work took as evidence that task representations live at those positions. The authors test whether those positions are causally important, and find they are not.

Intervening at a single position achieved zero percent task transfer across all twenty-eight layers of one model, despite perfect probing accuracy there. Replacing activations at all demonstration output tokens simultaneously, by contrast, reached up to ninety-six percent transfer at an early-middle layer. The pattern generalized across four models from three architecture families, with a universal intervention window near thirty percent of network depth, and tracing showed an asymmetric architecture of positions.
arxiv-2605-04161:
Lucas C. Céleri, Krissia Zawadzki, Ivan Medina, and Diogo O. Soares-Pinto connect dynamical quantum phase transitions to rugosity, a recently introduced measure of quantum state texture. Dynamical transitions describe critical behavior in systems driven out of equilibrium by a quench. They come in two standard formulations. One is based on a dynamical order parameter. The other is based on nonanalyticities in a return-rate function.

For the first type, the authors show the time-averaged rugosity, evaluated in the pre-quench energy basis, behaves like an order parameter across the transition. In the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model they trace that behavior to the semiclassical structure. Crossing an excited-state transition separatrix redistributes the state over the basis. The response function's critical peak grows algebraically with system size, giving finite-size evidence of sensitivity to the dynamical critical point.
arxiv-2605-04261:
Jie Zhang and three co-authors show a risk in trusting vision-language models as judges of images, for tasks like fact-checking, product comparison, and content moderation. A tiny crafted change to an image, invisible in normal viewing, can make the model speak with confidence about the wrong content.

The attacks do not break the model's safety training. They work at the level of perception. Methods built on open vision models also transfer to leading commercial systems. Across tests on identity, unsafe content, and product advice, success rates ran from about a fifth to total, raising concerns for platforms that rely on these models.
arxiv-2605-04361:
Saranyan Vigraham tests a common assumption in systems of cooperating software agents: that giving agents more shared context always improves their design work. He runs multi-agent software design across ten tasks and seven ways of injecting context, totalling thousands of runs.

The same kind of added document helped greatly on some tasks and hurt badly on others, and on several tasks an irrelevant document did as well as relevant ones. One simple measure, how widely agents explore with no context at all, predicted the direction of the effect strongly. Vigraham argues context should be added only after a cheap no-context trial.
arxiv-2605-04461:
Tu and six colleagues bring test-time scaling to streaming video generation. Test-time scaling improves video quality without retraining, but diffusion-based versions burn compute exploring many candidate clips and offer little temporal guidance. Streaming generation, built chunk by chunk with few denoising steps, suits the approach better: it is cheaper and allows fine-grained control over time. Stream-T1 exploits this with three units. One refines chunk noise from proven earlier chunks, one prunes candidates by balancing short-term looks against long-term coherence, and one routes evicted memory through reward-guided paths.

On five-second and thirty-second benchmarks, Stream-T1 markedly improved consistency over time, smoothness of motion, and visual quality frame by frame. The design shows that scaling effort at generation time can lift streaming video. History-aware noise and memory handling matter as much as raw candidate count.
arxiv-2605-04761:
Wu-Yuin Hwang and three co-authors present the Personalized Thinking Model, a way to build a cognitive twin of a learner for AI-supported education. Their model sorts evidence from learner journals into five layers, from single actions up to core values. It is grounded in Marzano's New Taxonomy of Educational Objectives.

The team built the model with a large language model, sentence embeddings, and clustering, then tested it on forty learners over seven weeks. Checking against human judgment, scores rose slightly after people reviewed and refined the output. Learners also rated the twins as matching their thinking, and deeper layers showed clearer themes and less direct copying of journal words.
arxiv-2605-04861:
Rakshit Gharat and three co-authors build a quantum algorithm for solving differential equations on a lattice using SLAC derivatives. A lattice derivative that matches smooth behaviour correctly must be non-local, acting across many sites at once. That makes it hard to encode efficiently on a quantum computer.

The team constructs efficient encodings for the first derivative and Laplacian in this representation, using state preparation suited to smoothly decaying functions. Wavelet transforms then give multiscale versions, and a preconditioner keeps the system well conditioned. The result is a quantum linear-system method for partial differential equations with stated gate costs, opening a route to large lattice problems.
arxiv-2605-04961:
Byunghoon Kang develops a more efficient version of the generalised method of moments, a workhorse estimation technique in econometrics, for cases where the model's conditions do not hold exactly. Under such misspecification, the standard estimator's behaviour depends on both those conditions and their slopes. Kang builds estimators from widened, shifted conditions that include that extra information.

Weighting the widened system optimally gives an estimator with the smallest large-sample spread for the same target quantity, with the standard method as a special case. Kang also proposes a feasible bootstrap version and proves uniform lower bounds over weighting choices. Simulations and two real-data examples show the gains.
arxiv-2605-05061:
Johan Gaume and three co-authors derive exact solutions for how failure spreads in the weak layer under a snow slab, the process that releases slab avalanches. Many earlier models treat the weak layer as perfectly brittle or ignore its elasticity before the peak load. Both softening after the peak and compliance before it shape stress redistribution and the critical crack length.

Their solution divides the failing zone into a softened core, a fracture process zone, and intact elastic material, recovering the classic brittle length when softening vanishes. Particle simulations confirm the predicted stress profiles and lengths. The same framework is then extended to collapse-driven anticrack propagation, linking two avalanche release pictures.
arxiv-2605-05161:
Bernhard Kainz and three co-authors reframe spotting anomalies in medical scans with vision-language models as a comparison problem rather than a lone-image judgement. Zero-shot localisation is limited because the model lacks healthy anatomical context. Their training-free framework, WALDO, compares a scan against reference distributions of normal anatomy using optimal transport measures.

Reference choice matters in a non-obvious way: moderately similar references work best, a Goldilocks effect the authors analyse theoretically. Similarity-weighted distance measures pick references, and self-consistency steps merge the results. On a brain MRI benchmark the method improved localisation substantially over zero-shot baselines, with consistent gains also seen across other large vision-language models.
arxiv-2605-05461:
Robots usually must grab an object before they can judge whether the grip will hold. Kyle DuFrene and Cindy Grimm remove that step with sensors built into the gripper's fingertips. Their time-of-flight sensors measure distances across several zones without any contact at all.

The team gathered more than twenty-five hundred real grasps over fifteen objects to train a classifier. It then judged grasps on six unseen objects, kept for validation and testing. Accuracy reached about eighty-six percent on the test objects, and the check cycles fifteen times per second, far faster than touch-based methods that must grasp first.
arxiv-2605-05561:
Shrinking a reasoning model to four bits saves memory but can break its sense of when to stop thinking. Sai Babu Patarlapalli and Surya Teja Avvaru present BitCal-TTS, a runtime controller for that problem. Under a fixed token budget, poor confidence signals can end a trace too early or let it ramble.

The controller blends cheap uncertainty proxies with a confidence rescaling tuned to the bit width. On small GSM8K test shards with Qwen2.5 models, it raised exact-match accuracy at two sizes. Premature stops fell at both sizes as well, while most token savings survived.
arxiv-2605-05661:
When a Type Ia supernova's shock wave runs into surrounding gas, the gas glows in Balmer lines. Priyam Das and six co-authors report the first helium lines from such shocks, found with the MUSE integral-field spectrograph. They studied filaments in three remnants in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Both broad and narrow helium emission appeared, including ionized helium lines that current shock models struggle to explain. Because helium traces the gas the progenitor system shed before exploding, the detections constrain what those progenitor environments contained. The narrow ionized helium, in particular, challenges existing pictures of these collisionless shocks.
arxiv-2605-06061:
Elena Wang and Bastian Rieck extend a classic expressivity test for graph learning to cover geometry. The Weisfeiler-Lehman test and its simplicial version judge what message passing networks can tell apart, but they ignore shape. Two meshes with the same connections and different embeddings look identical to those tests.

Their Geometric Simplicial Weisfeiler-Lehman test folds vertex coordinates into the color refinement process. They prove that geometry aware simplicial message passing is bounded above by this test. They also show matching schemes exist whose power equals the test on any fixed finite family of complexes. Paired with a known complete invariant, the result gives a full geometric expressivity picture, and experiments on synthetic and mesh data confirm the predicted hierarchy.
arxiv-2605-06161:
Shihao Weng, Yang Feng, and Xiaofei Xie argue that language model safety judges must pass a reliability test beyond accuracy. Such judges now grade agent safety by default, yet their verdicts may hinge on how the evaluation policy is worded rather than on what the agent did. The authors name the needed property policy invariance and split it into three testable principles.

Their stress test applies certified equivalent rewrites and deliberate strict to lenient shifts to the judging rubric. Today's judges reacted about as strongly to meaningless rewrites as to real normative shifts, and could not tell them apart. Meaning preserving rewrites flipped up to 9.1 percent of verdicts. A new Policy Invariance Score and Judge Card protocol expose wide reliability gaps that accuracy leaderboards hide.
arxiv-2605-06261:
Eugenio Lomurno and four co-authors close the gap between synthetic and real tabular data at inference time rather than in training. Diffusion generators make the best synthetic tables, yet their output rarely beats real data in downstream use. Past attempts to close that gap retrained or rescaled monolithic generators, leaving the outputs of a frozen model untouched and unrefined, the authors note.

Their framework, TARDIS, refines a frozen backbone's samples with per data set configuration search. One mathematical pattern, bidirectional Chamfer refinement, drives both a continuous score level push and a discrete batch ranking step. Across fifteen benchmarks the method improved downstream results over real data training by a median of 8.6 percent. It beat its backbone on every data set while matching it on fidelity, diversity, and privacy measures.
arxiv-2605-06761:
Oğuzhan Fatih Kar and four co-authors present Weblica, a framework for building reproducible training environments for visual web agents. The live web is complex and ever-changing, so training data has stayed limited to offline demonstrations or a few simulated sites. Weblica instead replays real websites through HTTP-level caching that preserves interactive behavior while freezing visual states.

It also synthesizes new environments with a language model, grounded in real sites and core navigation skills. That scales reinforcement learning training to thousands of environments and tasks. Their Weblica-8B model beats similar-size open baselines on web navigation benchmarks while taking fewer steps, scales well with extra test-time compute, and rivals commercial API models.
arxiv-2605-06861:
James Rowbottom, Nick Huang, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Ben Adcock place sensors to estimate state without assuming Gaussian data. How well states are rebuilt depends on where sensors sit. Measurements are often sparse and costly. Classical tools assume Gaussian distributions. Newer diffusion-based rebuilding handles complex distributions those tools cannot match. That leaves placement methods mismatched to the recovery models they serve.

Their method uses the Christoffel function from sampling theory to derive a placement strategy. It gives explicit bounds on how many sensors recovery needs, for any distribution. Offline and online variants beat Gaussian and other generative placement methods, most when sensor budgets are low, across several generative models.
arxiv-2605-07161:
Jackson Clark and seven co-authors present SREGym, a live benchmark for AI agents that fix failures in production computer systems. Existing tests for site reliability work are often too simple and hard to extend. SREGym instead runs on real cloud-native software stacks, with faults injected at different layers.

The setup adds background noise and tricky failure modes, including failures that feed on themselves or strike together. Its ninety problems are modular, so new scenarios can be added. Frontier agents varied widely by failure type, with large gaps in end-to-end results, showing current reliability agents remain uneven in realistic conditions.
arxiv-2605-07461:
Jiachen Yu and three co-authors move grading rubrics inside a language model's reasoning instead of leaving them as an outside scorecard. Rubrics usually judge open-ended answers after the fact, or feed reinforcement rewards, without guiding generation itself. In Think-with-Rubrics, the model first writes its own rubric, then answers under its guidance.

A trained verifier supervises training by checking consistency between the answer and both self-written and gold rubrics. Across benchmarks, the method beat a rubric-as-reward baseline by several points on average. Analysis credits better self-rubrics for quality and consistency checks for steadier responses, giving instruction-following models a new internal compass.
arxiv-2605-07661:
George Rapakoulias and three co-authors speed up diffusion model sampling while keeping it genuinely random. Most fast samplers collapse the process into something more deterministic, which hurts downstream tasks like posterior sampling and inverse problems that need true stochastic draws. Their method instead distills the full transition map of the sampling equation.

Called Stochastic Transition-Map Distillation, the approach parameterizes those transitions with a conditional mean-flow model, giving a one-step or few-step stochastic sampler. It needs no pretrained teacher, no two-level optimization, and no stored trajectories, which keeps training efficient. The authors prove convergence bounds in the Wasserstein distance and validate the sampler on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA image generation.
arxiv-2605-07761:
Kentaro Nomura and two co-authors simulate how a shared social reality of emotion could emerge between agents. The theory of constructed emotion says emotion concepts are a community-level consensus applied to bodily sensations arising from allostasis, the body's predictive regulation, and social interaction. Testing that emergence story needs a working computational model.

Their model joins symbol emergence, where interpretation of signs is flexible, with active inference. Two agents receive interoceptive signals, exchange inferred symbols, and adapt both their bodily control goals and their symbol interpretations toward each other. In experiments the agents' prior preferences over bodily states and their symbol probability distributions converged, which the authors read as social reality emerging from social consensus in miniature.
arxiv-2605-08161:
Hussain Alasmawi studies training strategy for automatic tumor segmentation in whole-body PET/CT scans, built for the AutoPET III challenge. Outlining tumors by hand is slow and varies between readers, while lesions differ widely in size, contrast, and location. Challenge models must also generalize across tracers and hospitals.

Using nnU-Net with a ResNet encoder as the baseline, Alasmawi varies intensity normalization, batch dice optimization, and augmentation with CraveMix, and measures the effect of each choice. The experiments show training strategy strongly shapes performance, especially in cutting false positives and staying robust when lesions look unusual. The best configuration is reported for the challenge setting.
arxiv-2605-08261:
Pierluca D'Oro, Sneha Silwal, William Wong, Yuxuan Sun, and coauthors show that top computer-use benchmarks can be gamed. A one-megabyte replay script repeats recorded actions blindly. It never looks at the screen. Yet it beats frontier models on prominent static benchmarks. Its expected score equals the source agent's pass-at-k rate in deterministic settings.

The authors trace the failure to weak environment design. The settings are static, unsandboxed, or poorly verified. Naive aggregation and misuse of pass-at-k add to the problem. They propose PRISM, five design principles for agent environments. The principles cover privileged checks, realistic settings, integrity-checked setups, sandboxed runs, and varied conditions.
arxiv-2605-08461:
Arnob Saha, Bibhas Manna, Nikhil Kotikalapudi, Md Zesun Ahmed Mia, and coauthors tune compute-in-memory chips with Bayesian optimization. Crossbar accelerators promise dense, energy-efficient neural inference, but their design space mixes hardware and algorithm choices in a highly non-convex way, and every candidate costs an expensive simulation.

Their multi-objective framework co-optimizes both sides while querying the simulator sparingly. Even for deep models the spaces are large, reaching dozens of dimensions and astronomical candidate counts for a VGG network on Tiny-ImageNet. Bayesian search focuses trials on promising regions, and the authors show the method attains strong designs for efficient deep network inference on crossbar hardware.
arxiv-2605-08661:
Hadi Kharaghani, Ali Mohammadian, and Behruz Tayfeh-Rezaie search for Hadamard matrices of Williamson type, arrays of plus and minus ones built from four structured blocks. Their focus narrows to near Williamson matrices, where one block circulates freely and the other three are symmetric circulant. A computer search classifies all inequivalent examples at odd orders up to thirty five.

Existence is also shown for every odd order up to sixty three. As a payoff, the search yields the first known quaternary Hadamard matrix of order one hundred eighteen. Combinatorics gains both a complete small order census and a new record object in a design family with roots in signal processing and coding.
arxiv-2605-09061:
Runyao Yu and eight co-authors forecast imbalance prices in electricity markets, the charges that settle gaps between planned and actual power use. Fast, accurate forecasts matter for battery owners and automated trading systems, yet prices form through market rules and arrive through messy, delayed data feeds.

Their neural network builds the market's own price rules into its inner structure, so it learns around a clear prior instead of from raw signals alone. Tests show accuracy on par with generic deep learning models while using far fewer trainable parts and much less training time. The team also checks how the forecast holds up when some price data is missing and how it changes with horizon length.
arxiv-2605-09161:
Tom Benhamou, Sebastiano Thei, and Ben-Zion Weltsch study the models that sit between a starting universe of set theory and a larger one built by a method called strongly compact Prikry forcing. Forcing adds new sets in a controlled way, and the models in between are often hard to pin down. Their 2026 paper finds a simple property that sorts these in-between cases.

For a fixed large cardinal, the property characterizes which smaller forcing methods arise as views of the big one. Working level by level, the authors extend several known results and give criteria for when such a view exists. They also show that, at a fixed size, the relevant views are exactly those whose rule depends only on the stem of a condition.
arxiv-2605-09461:
Tang and thirteen colleagues build VulTriage, a three-path context booster for LLM-based vulnerability detection. It targets a fundamental software security task where learning-based methods still struggle with structural dependencies, vulnerability knowledge, and program semantics. Prompting LLMs with source code often misses vulnerabilities or raises false alarms, above all when flawed and clean functions differ only in fine semantic details.

VulTriage enriches LLM input through three paths. A Control Path turns AST, CFG, and DFG structure into words to reveal control and data links. A Knowledge Path pulls CWE-derived vulnerability patterns and examples with mixed dense-sparse search, and a Semantic Path sums up what the code does before the final judgment. These contexts join in one instruction guiding the LLM toward sounder vulnerability reasoning. On the PrimeVul pair test set, VulTriage reaches state-of-the-art performance, beating deep learning and LLM baselines.
arxiv-2605-09661:
Ha and two colleagues introduce MedMeta, the first benchmark for judging conclusion building from medical meta analyses. Language models have topped standard medical benchmarks. Yet building conclusions from many sources remains underexplored. MedMeta covers 81 meta analyses and tests models with retrieval help and with no outside text. Retrieval grounding proves critical: models with retrieval beat models using only built in chain of thought reasoning across the board.

Domain specific fine tuning, by contrast, helps only slightly, and its edge largely vanishes once outside text is supplied. A universal flaw also emerges: every tested model fails to reject factually wrong evidence, folding it into coherent but false conclusions.
