Even with oracle retrieval, the best model scores just over 3 out of 5. The benchmark's model judge protocol is checked against human experts, showing strong accord and tiny systematic bias.
arxiv-2605-10161:
Fernández-Hernández and five co-authors replace fixed weight decay for convolutional networks with a scheduler that adapts per layer over time. Weight decay is a standard control, yet usually one fixed number shared by all layers in training. That misses layers following different built-in ways and may need varied strengths. Their OUIDecay timer is driven by the Overfitting-Underfitting Indicator, an activation-based metric giving signals about regularisation.

A light batch-based gauge watches each layer's built-in ways online, retuning its decay next to other layers at intervals. Unlike gradient-based adaptive decay, the method uses working information from signal patterns and needs no validation data. Tests on EfficientNet-B0/Stanford Cars, ResNet50/Food101, DenseNet121/CIFAR100 and MobileNetV2/CIFAR10 show OUIDecay achieving the best mean validation loss in seven of eight settings. That makes it a handy, lightweight option to fixed and gradient decay.
arxiv-2605-10361:
David Beck-Tiefenbach, Robin Kaiser, and Julia Überbacher study the final shape of a random sandpile on a line. In their model, n particles start at the origin and stabilize under p-topplings: an unstable vertex sends one particle left with probability p and one right with probability p, independently. Their 2026 paper asks what the settled configuration looks like as n grows large.

The authors prove that the macroscopic limit shape is a symmetric interval around the origin. By analyzing the center-of-mass martingale, a fair-game process tracking the pile's balance point, they also establish a central limit theorem for boundary fluctuations. After proper rescaling, those fluctuations converge to a Gaussian distribution. Readers get a rigorous picture of how randomness at each toppling still yields a clean, symmetric large-scale shape with normally distributed edge wobble.
arxiv-2605-10461:
Hongyuan Qu, Chengliang Tian, and Guangwu Xu sharpen a classic tool of lattice-based crypto. Banaszczyk's result, introduced in 1993, gives a tail estimate for the discrete Gaussian measure on a lattice. In essence, once short vectors' contributions are set aside, the leftover Gaussian mass is exponentially small next to the total. It underpins the transfer theorem relating ordered minima of a lattice and its dual. Their 2026 note improves the result further.

Tian, Liu, and Xu had previously improved it with a transparent proof. Qu and colleagues improve it again by imposing an appropriate condition, obtaining a much better bound. The refined result gives a tool for probing dual attacks against the Learning With Errors problem, a foundation of post-quantum crypto. Readers get a tighter estimate with a clear proof, strengthening a widely used result in lattice cryptography.
arxiv-2605-10561:
Alessandro Taloni and two colleagues derive the diffusion equation for non-Markovian Gaussian processes. They derive the evolution equation for the chance density of particle shifts from any Gaussian velocity processes, without Markov property or stationarity. Their 2026 paper builds the result from the key function of the position density.

The approach builds a ladder of equations from Wick's theorem, where motion follows sums of shape-linked Wick contractions. That yields a closed diffusion equation for such processes beyond the Fokker-Planck description, keeping Gaussian shape only in the endless-order limit. In the long-time limit or under thermal initial conditions, velocity reduces to the stationary Gaussian Markov process with exponential self-link, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Position shows lasting effects due to finite time correlations of velocity. Readers get a diffusion equation holding without the Markov or steady-state needs behind Brownian motion theory.
arxiv-2605-11161:
Hadas Orgad and eleven others argue that interpretability research should be judged by actionability: whether its insights enable concrete decisions and acts beyond the field itself. Despite fast growth, work in this field has had weak real-world impact, raising doubts about its relevance.

This position paper defines actionable work through concreteness and validation, maps barriers blocking real-world impact, and names five domains where the field offers unique leverage. A framework with evaluation criteria tied to practical outcomes follows, aiming to make actionability a core goal without downplaying exploratory research. Researchers get a checklist for work that changes decisions, not just understanding.
arxiv-2605-11661: Lebsir and seven others study how probes and bases change Mie resonance view in silicon spheres. Silicon spheres are quality Mie-tronic blocks, but real devices need bases shifting the seen response. The team tests a thin silicon nitride membrane acting as a free particle, bulk silicon, and gold with mirror-charge hybrid modes. Cathodoluminescence and dark-field spectra plus models show signals depend on setting and drive method. Base effects and probe rules can suppress, enhance or invert charge and spin marks, guiding device design.
arxiv-2605-11761: Faten Hendaoui and four colleagues measure how hydrogen gas widens carbon dioxide absorption lines. Such data are needed to model the skies of hydrogen-rich planets far from Earth. They measured spread and shift values at room temperature across the full nu3 band near 4.3 microns with a high-detail device. They then ran molecule motion models spanning 200 to 1000 kelvin. Theory matched lab results within 3 percent, yielding the first precise, wide-ranging dataset of its kind.
arxiv-2605-12561: Haroon and three colleagues teach one policy to decide what to do and when to act, cutting talk in safe learning. A run-time safety layer steps in with a one-step Lyapunov prediction and a precomputed LQR backup. That beats methods that enforce safety only on average. The policy learns control and timing together under a pointwise Lyapunov shield around a known equilibrium. On pendulum, cart-pole and quadrotor tests, it stretches mean sample gaps by roughly two to three and a half times over a Lyapunov-triggered baseline.
arxiv-2605-12961: Li and five colleagues propose GSEC, a framework for clustering unlabelled images that cuts both bias and variance. Multimodal language models generate semantic descriptions and image embeddings, while a two-layer ensemble merges cross-modal information inside and aligns outputs outside. Across six benchmarks it beats 18 state-of-the-art methods, and further analysis confirms it reduces bias and variance together rather than trading one for the other.
arxiv-2605-13161: Zhou and six co-authors address Branch Bias in few-shot vision-language image classification: tuning the image encoder does not always help when data shifts. Their adapter, A3B2, damps image-branch tuning when prediction uncertainty is high, with no manual intervention. The design is light and asymmetric, inspired by mixture-of-experts with load balancing. Across three few-shot tasks on 11 datasets it consistently beats 11 prompt- and adapter-based baselines.
arxiv-2605-13261: Zhou, Karaturhan, Weilenmann and Zhu study how cycle tracking apps shape users' sense of their own bodies. From fourteen interviews and a group self study, they find users read their lived experience through app predictions, even when faulty logging skews those predictions. App screens and explanations rarely help users notice or question this entanglement. Users outside typical patterns also report isolation, prompting design advice for predictive features and explanations.
arxiv-2605-13461: S. Rendon Restrepo resolves a long-standing convergence problem for gravitational instability in thin discs, using a new Bessel-kernel prescription for gravity in two dimensions. Gravitational instability is a leading theory for early planet formation, yet early 2010s simulations failed to converge. The new prescription sets a length below which gravity shifts smoothly from three-dimensional to two-dimensional scaling, beyond standard smoothing. Built into FargoCPT, it resolves convergence in two dimensions. The author also finds small softening overstates fragment masses by a factor of two to three.
arxiv-2605-13661: Ikenna Chinazaekpere Ijeh, Mohammad Ali Khalighi and Wasiu O. Popoola study air-sea surface roughness effects on AUV-to-UAV optical wireless links. They use two tested models, the classical Cox-Munk model and the Elfouhaily-Chapron-Katsaros-Vandemark model. A tractable analytical form of the second model is derived and checked against measured sea-state data. Link ergodic capacity is evaluated by analytical and Monte Carlo methods, covering operating range, pointing errors, receiver field-of-view and solar noise.
arxiv-2605-13761: Phillip Si and six colleagues present the Conditional Latent Flows Network, a latent neural ODE driven by rainfall with a decoder tuned on static terrain. Point reading frees memory from grid size and handles odd basins well. CLDNet roughly halves the scaled root-mean-squared error of a plain rival. A full 96-hour basin-wide outlook takes about 29 seconds, a 115-times speedup over a 55-minute model run.
arxiv-2605-13961: Antinucci, Copetti, Galati and Rizi tie odd scattering at defects to local anomalies. Where wide defects sit, incoming bits can scatter into odd outgoing states made by twist operators. The paper shows local 't Hooft anomalies on the defect's worldvolume can drive this twist scattering. Anomalies trap odd charges where symmetry lines meet the interface, opening paths that seem to break selection rules. Massless chiral fermion models and new massive integrable theories test the idea.
arxiv-2605-14061: Patel and nine co-authors present MathAtlas, the first large-scale autoformalization benchmark drawn from real graduate-level mathematics. Past benchmarks center on olympiad or undergraduate problems, leaving graduate and research math largely untested. MathAtlas holds about 52,000 theorems, definitions, exercises, examples and proofs pulled from 103 graduate textbooks. A math dependency graph with about 178,000 relations makes it the first benchmark of its kind to support dependency-aware systems, yet strong baselines top out near ten percent on theorem statements.
arxiv-2605-14261: Kim and Sandholm expose heuristic flaws in AIVAT variance reduction and spread heuristic uncertainty. AIVAT rates agent results in multiagent settings with few samples or costly trials, using unbiased low-variance estimates. A heuristic value function splits low- and high-value counterfactuals, yet little guidance exists on choosing it. Sample variance can be gamed low by gradient descent, and desired results can be p-hacked via gradient moves. Fix the function before seeing the evaluation data. That uncertainty quantifies AIVAT estimates, and averaging cuts variance at the cost of unbiasedness.
arxiv-2605-14361: Moharana argues altermagnetic spin splitting by itself is not what makes Chern matter; what counts is how exchange mass projects onto Hall-active sectors. He states this projected-mass rule for compensated topology. The resulting two-channel test separates hidden compensated signals from additive phases within a global insulating gap. It also informs interface and thickness design.
arxiv-2605-14461: Ledun Zhang and colleagues present ClickRemoval, an open-source interactive tool for object removal in diffusion models, driven solely by user clicks. Existing tools often need manual masks or text prompts, making precise removal hard for non-experts and leaving incomplete removal or unnatural backgrounds. ClickRemoval needs no extra training, hand-drawn masks or text descriptions. It locates targets and restores backgrounds through self-attention modulation during denoising. Experiments show competitive results across quantitative metrics and user studies, and the full package is released under the Apache-2.0 licence.
arxiv-2605-14561: Prasad, Gerschwitz, Li, Xiao, Liu, Wu, Leontjeva and Pizzato optimise prompts by splitting them into segments. Each segment gets a plain importance tag, such as not important or very important. These tags steer a language model to allocate attention and resolve confusion. The original prompt stays in the candidate pool to prevent regression. The authors present this segment-level approach as a proof of concept improving reasoning accuracy and self-consistency.
arxiv-2605-14661: Zheng, Liu and Zhang use large language models to design optimisation algorithms for fluid antenna systems, where radiating elements shift position or port. Port selection for many users is a hard large-scale combinatorial problem, and hand-built heuristics are labour-intensive and weak. The authors tune genetic algorithm crossover and mutation with language models, and also design a new heuristic, AutoPort, from scratch. Simulations claim near-optimal results beating standard genetic and deep learning methods.
arxiv-2605-14761: Abe, Daikoku and Kuniyoshi build a system that predicts one person's aesthetic ratings for images. Taste is subjective, so the system first interviews the target person. A language model runs semi-structured interviews for this step. Low-level image features and high-level semantic features are then combined for prediction. In tests against conventional systems, human predictors, and the person's own later re-ratings, the system wins overall. Its prediction error is smaller than within-person variability.
arxiv-2605-15061: Tao Gui derives a graded character formula for any finite group's action on the Artinian reduction of the Stanley-Reisner ring of a complete fan. It is given by an equivariant h-polynomial. For rational fans this gives the group's action on the cohomology of the linked toric variety. A hybrid fan tool then finds the Poincaré polynomial of invariants under finite reflection groups. The quotient of a compact toric orbifold by such a group shares the hybrid fan's own count.
arxiv-2605-15361: Ilia V. Chugunov and Alexander A. Marchuk disentangle two spatial modes of star formation in 159 spiral galaxies at redshifts 0.1 to 3.3, observed by Hubble and JWST. Identifying clumps in residual images after modeling spiral arms separately, a step prior work skipped, they catalog 3,003 clumps. Clump luminosities, masses, and sizes run smaller than commonly reported, and clumps concentrate toward spiral arms with correlated arm and clump parameters. Arm clumps tend to be smaller yet brighter than inter-arm clumps, with differing colors.
arxiv-2605-15461: Yikun Zhang, Xiwei Cheng, Tianyu Liu, Yuanqi Du, and Wengong Jin present DrugSAGE, an agent setup that recalls drug-discovery work. Old agents search from scratch on each new task and pay search cost each time. DrugSAGE stores tried skills, proof about what works, and past slips with their fixes. At times it reuses a working answer with no test-time search. On 33 molecule trait tasks it ranked first of nine top agents. With recall from small tasks, it beat rivals on held-out tasks with no test-time search.
arxiv-2605-15561: Jiayan Yang, Zhuoyu Wu, and Wenqi Fang present RoiMAM, a compact vision-language model for medical visual question answering. A training-free module finds lesion-relevant regions and suppresses other semantics, while a prompt enhancer adds modality-specific context without new trained parameters. Compared with a widely used medical model, it reaches accurate diagnosis at under a fifth of the size, improving accuracy by about two percent on one benchmark and 4.6 percent on another.
arxiv-2605-15761: Hosna Oyarhoseini, Jimmy Lin and Amir-Hossein Karimi probe how easily model leaderboards built from pairwise human votes can be shifted. Their test set drops, adds or flips single matches and removes players. They track top-rank spots, global rank order and error bars. Across Chatbot Arena and six other sets, targeted shifts under one percent moved the top model, hurt rank order and moved error bars. The same influence scores also let attackers push chosen models up or down with few moves.
arxiv-2605-15961: Fabian Morelli and three colleagues propose SAE-FT, a robust fine-tuning method for CLIP using Sparse Autoencoders. Fine-tuning large vision-language models often harms robustness against distribution shifts, and recent fixes rely on costly text-guidance. SAE-FT works only on visual representations, penalizing addition and removal of meaningful features found by a Sparse Autoencoder. This constraint prevents catastrophic forgetting and makes fine-tuning clear, enabling analysis of semantic changes. SAE-FT matches or beats top performance on ImageNet and its shift benchmarks, while staying transparent and efficient.
arxiv-2605-16161: Dhakad and Vishvakarma present an SRAM-based digital compute engine for AI hardware, built around a 10T SRAM cell for XNOR-based in-memory computing. Placing a full adder between in-memory multiplication cells cuts routing complexity by half. The design performs multiply-accumulate operations for binary neural networks, with a 14T adder building an N-bit ripple carry adder. Overall area efficiency improves 2.67-fold over the state of the art, with lower latency and area overhead.
arxiv-2605-16261: Milovanov constructs a universal decompressor for plain Kolmogorov complexity such that the Halting Problem cannot be decided by any polynomial-time oracle machine given the set of random strings. The result resolves a problem posed by Eric Allender about the computational power of Kolmogorov-complexity-based oracles. The proof builds the decompressor so its random set defeats every polynomial-time oracle machine on the Halting Problem. It thus limits what random-string oracles can compute, even with full polynomial-time machinery.
arxiv-2605-16361: Chen and three others present TailedTS, a large benchmark dataset from Wikipedia hourly page views through 2024, built to test forecasting under heavy-tailed, zero-inflated, non-Gaussian conditions. It holds about 24.69 billion points across roughly 3 million pages per month, with about 5 percent of pages drawing over 70 percent of views. A periodicity framework based on sparse autoregression finds popular pages show weaker periodic structure than less-viewed pages. Standard Gaussian-based estimators degrade on high-volume pages, while robust alternatives gain across all traffic scales.
arxiv-2605-16461: Ahmed, Al-Badawi, and Sakallı study paths around a black hole with a Kalb-Ramond field coupled to nonlinear fields. The paper derives the effective potential and the energy and angular momentum of particles on orbits. They analyze the photon sphere, shadow, and Lyapunov exponent for null paths, which sets eikonal quasinormal-mode frequencies. Shadow radius is compared with EHT observations of M87* and Sgr A*, identifying the parameter region. They compute Hawking temperature, horizon area, and sparsity, showing Kalb-Ramond and magnetic charge raise it from Schwarzschild value 496 to 1.7×10^3.
arxiv-2605-16861: Chai and colleagues propose the Prefix-Adaptive Block Diffusion Model for document recognition. Block diffusion models support generation and KV caching, but fixed block boundaries shrink parallelism in intra-block denoising and delay caching until a block completes. PA-BDM replaces bidirectional denoising with causal prefix-to-suffix denoising and treats block size as a max range. A confidence-gated loss builds low-entropy prefixes, and prefix commitment caches the longest reliable prefix at inference. The 3B model tops benchmarks and lifts throughput 71.6% over a 2.5B MinerU model.
arxiv-2605-16961: Zhai's team proposes Latent Action Control, a way to make reasoning actionable inside unified image generation. Unified models can infer objects, relations, and knowledge cues yet fail to place them in the generated image. Given a prompt, LAC rolls out a role-structured trajectory for planning, visual drafting, diagnosis, and refinement. It feeds those actions into the stream that drives flow-based generation, with no reasoning tokens or drafts. Built on BAGEL-7B-MoT, it improves compositional and knowledge-grounded generation, most on spatial relations, attribute binding, and world knowledge.
arxiv-2605-17061: Shaw presents quantum-safe, a hybrid-by-default Python library closing the production gap, plus a nine-library audit. Hybrid combiners exist in three of six, and none offers discovery or inventory tools; quantum-safe adds a CBOM. Only Bouncy Castle holds a FIPS 140-3 certificate, while quantum-safe passes all 225 ACVP known-answer cases, conformance evidence, not validation. Bouncy Castle supports LMS and XMSS where quantum-safe has LMS only, with defaults below CNSA parameter sets. A full X25519 plus ML-KEM-768 handshake takes 231 microseconds, 5.3 times an X25519-only handshake.
arxiv-2605-17161: De Domenico and colleagues prove the Lyndon interpolation trait for basic lattice expansion logics in any signature, using display calculi. Their proof builds the needed middle claims straight from derivations. The method is modular: new axioms need only a local check on their added rules. The work covers all signatures, not just a few. As a test case, the tense form of Holliday's core modal logic gains the same trait.
arxiv-2605-17361: Xuefei Wang and colleagues tackle topology forgetting in multi-agent systems, where new tasks erase team patterns earlier tasks needed. Their MasFACT frame transfers past team knowledge as priors across agent spaces via fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport, with careful posterior adaptation balancing plasticity against stability. Tests across continual settings lift average accuracy and cut that loss against generation and replay baselines.
arxiv-2605-17561: Gon and colleagues standardize root-cause subclassification for invalid bug reports, which need no code changes and resolve with no-code fixes. On a manually curated gold-standard benchmark they test vanilla language models, retrieval-augmented generation and agentic web search. Retrieval-augmented generation leads subclassification at 0.66 weighted F1, while agentic web search leads no-code fix generation at about 69 percent judge success. Wrong Version remains hardest, scoring near zero.
arxiv-2605-17761: Kaichuan Kong, Dongjie Liu, Xiaobo Jin, and Guanggang Geng target insider threats that creep in slowly. Such threats show up first as shifts in behavioral statistics rather than suspicious event meanings. Their MV-Gate framework builds three aligned views of user activity: tokens, recurrence patterns, and short-versus-long-term frequency shifts. It then gates attention toward statistically odd events. On CERT and ADFA-LD benchmarks it beats classical, deep, and domain baselines, especially on gradual, faint threats that sequence-only models miss.
arxiv-2605-17961: Orr Fischer and Ran Gelles study Task Completion, where n crash-prone nodes must finish M tasks despite crashes. Their deterministic congested-clique algorithm finishes all tasks in rounds proportional to the ceiling of M over n times log n. Its key ingredient is a load balancing covering family, assigning each task responsible nodes. Its properties guarantee no node overloads and no task lacks assignees. Applied to simulation, any T-round congested-clique algorithm runs under crash faults in T squared log n plus T log squared n rounds.
arxiv-2605-18061: Florin Felix Nichita builds the core of this paper around racks, setting out trigonometry inside racks and the Euler formulas that belong to that framework. The opening discussion grows from a high-school problem, and the whole piece carries on his series recalling meetings with Solomon Marcus, whose spirit it tries to recapture. It closes as a tribute to Marcus.
arxiv-2605-18161: Paloma Guetzoyan's 2026 paper presents a large new X-ray sample of 380 red quasars from the eROSITA and SDSS-V surveys. Red quasars prove intrinsically X-ray weak beside blue quasars, with over half the sample at low X-ray luminosity, yet they are not optically faint. Spectra point to heavy gas columns beside modest dust reddening, suggesting X-ray absorption by dust-free gas near the black hole rather than a classic dusty torus. The pattern marks a phase where black hole growth lags behind host galaxy growth.
arxiv-2605-18361: Siddique Abubakr Muntaka and eleven colleagues present iHAC, a hybrid cluster design blending active-active and active-passive setups to remove single points of failure and balance workload. Simulations with Riverbed Modeler in the 2026 study show it cutting average HTTP page response time by over forty percent, from five seconds to under three, while lowering latency and raising throughput. The authors present it as a practical route to stronger operational continuity.
arxiv-2605-18461: Marcelo Vilas Boas and four co-authors report a 2026 case study of a one-person squad in a regulated enterprise. A single staff engineer, aided by four AI agents under Spec-Driven Development, delivered a brownfield initiative scoped for four people in half the planned time. First-review acceptance of AI-generated code hit 90 percent, integration tests fully passed, and direct staffing cost fell over 85 percent. The authors conclude AI multiplies an experienced engineer's throughput rather than replacing teammates.
arxiv-2605-18561: Santosh Kumar Radha and Oktay Goktas fix, in a 2026 paper, BM25 code retrieval under frozen generic tokenization. They replace the outer logarithm of RSJ odds with a q-logarithm. At q equal to 1 it recovers BM25 exactly, and below 1 it gives a Box-Cox transform. On CodeSearchNet Go, oracle-tuned NDCG at 10 rises from 0.2575 to 0.4874, an 89.3 percent relative gain with zero sign reversals in 10,000 bootstrap resamples. A closed form estimates corpus-level q from hapax density, and query latency stays unchanged.
arxiv-2605-18661: Lingdong Kong and nineteen co-authors survey, through April 2026, AI across the research lifecycle. Fully automated systems now generate papers for as little as fifteen dollars, yet frontier models still fabricate results and judge novelty poorly. AI excels at structured, retrieval-grounded, tool-mediated tasks but stays fragile for novel ideas and scientific judgment. Greater automation can hide failure modes rather than remove them, so human-governed collaboration is the credible deployment model. The survey adds a taxonomy, benchmark suite, tool inventory, and playbook.
arxiv-2605-18861: The ICARUS and SBND collaborations build a neural network that spots useful signal regions in liquid argon neutrino detectors. Instead of thresholding each wire alone, their method reads the full two-dimensional readout and matches signals across detector planes. Training on varied simulated samples helps it cope with changing detector behavior. Tests show it beating the older wire-by-wire method on signal finding and reconstruction for cosmic rays and accelerator neutrinos.
arxiv-2605-19061: Sara E. Duval and 26 colleagues use JWST infrared spectra to study warm molecular hydrogen in the starburst core of M82. Extending temperature models to allow for dust extinction and spin ratios out of equilibrium, they map heating across a region about 500 parsecs wide at roughly 15-parsec resolution. The temperature slope matches work and runs opposite to shock-tracing iron emission, pointing to shock heating. On average the spin ratio sits near half its equilibrium value, which the authors attribute to gas mixing faster than spins can convert.
arxiv-2605-19461: Li and team attack mode collapse in reinforcement learning, where methods like GRPO lock onto the first high-reward path and stop exploring. They trace the fault to reverse KL minimization, which rewards the first good trajectory rather than covering many solutions. Their DMPO method builds a target distribution over sampled trajectories weighted by reward, then aligns the policy to it, approximating forward KL minimization. On NP-hard tests it beats GRPO by about nine percent on text tasks and twelve percent on vision tasks, with smaller gains elsewhere.
arxiv-2605-19561: Xu, Hu and Yang propose TORQ, a training-free quantization method that rescues MXFP4 activation accuracy. Direct MXFP4 activation quantization degrades accuracy badly through two imbalances: uneven variance across blocks and uneven codebook use within blocks. TORQ rotates activations at two levels: energy spreads across blocks by the Schur-Horn theorem, and codebook use spreads within blocks. On Qwen3-32B it brings WikiText perplexity to 8.43, near the 7.61 full-precision figure, and lifts average accuracy to 73.63 percent from 38.40 percent, near the 74.82 percent mark.
arxiv-2605-19661: Eales and team stack COSMOS-Web sources to trace star formation along the early Hubble sequence and dust to redshift 12. Mean star-formation rates rise with redshift, reaching over 80 solar masses per year for massive galaxies at redshifts 2 to 4. In that range rates fall along the Hubble sequence from about 280 solar masses per year for irregulars to 80 for spheroids. Spheroid decline matches a starvation model with depletion near 10 to the power 8.2 years, and dust-to-stellar ratios rise out to redshift 8.
arxiv-2605-19761: Chatterjee, Guttmann, Novak, Oertel and Steil compare two ways of modelling strongly magnetised neutron stars, called magnetars, whose fields warp their shape and gravitational-wave output. One method treats the field as a small perturbation from dipole currents; the other solves the full equations numerically with the LORENE library, both restricted to poloidal fields. The perturbative route fails only at extreme polar fields, yet stays accurate at observed magnetar strengths, while the numerical code loses precision at low fields. The comparison clarifies where each tool can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-19961: Khattabi and three colleagues show in a 2026 paper how to certify safe regions for unknown nonlinear systems using only measured data. From point samples of the dynamics plus known Lipschitz bounds, they build a polyhedral set of possible behaviours and solve a linear program for a piecewise-affine Lyapunov function. The resulting function guarantees a region of attraction that fits all the data, and examples show the method works even from sparse samples.
arxiv-2605-20461: Xiong and five co-workers audit monocular polyp sizing, where size over 5 millimeters drives closer follow-up. With no metric reference in single-camera colonoscopy, they test binary size classification across public multi-center sets, model families and patient-stratified splits. Results stay fairly steady across looks, depth and photometry, hinting models lean on exam-behavior cues. Depth estimation and global calibration add little, and mask errors under shift erase most remaining potential, leaving scale and mask robustness as twin bottlenecks.
arxiv-2605-20761: Rajarshi Roy and eighteen colleagues report findings of the Counter Turing Test for AI-generated text detection. Fluent machine text now strains systems that guard the authenticity of digital content, raising risks of misinformation and biased narratives. Their paper reviews state-of-the-art detection techniques and tests them through shared tasks. Task A asks systems to separate human-written from AI-generated text, while Task B asks them to name the specific model behind a text.
arxiv-2605-20961: Zhangchi Hu and seven colleagues present PREX, a region-aware design for faithful 4D video editing with preserve, reveal, and expand roles. While 4D-driven video diffusion models generate plausible videos, faithful 4D editing is stricter: source-observed content should be kept, while disoccluded and out-of-view areas must be synthesized naturally. Existing methods suffer evidence-role mismatch, entangling source-backed observations, uncertain rendered cues, and unsupported regions in one conditioning signal. PREX splits the target spatiotemporal volume into three clear roles based on observation support and scene reach.
arxiv-2605-21461: Pin-Hsun Lee and Harry Leib present a machine learning method for weighted least squares GNSS fix based on trigger functions. In urban canyons, high-rise buildings and narrow streets cause signal blocking, non-line-of-sight receipt, and echo effects introducing errors in range readings. Although multi-constellation GNSS increases satellites in view, weak signals can cause severe errors. Their method uses signal quality signs as training features for ensemble learning methods to identify poor-quality signals.
arxiv-2605-21561: Mathieu Cherpitel and co-authors study objective-induced bias in multi-goal unsupervised feature selection. Feature selection is framed as a multi-goal problem tuning subset quality and size. Yet behavior hinges on scoring objective choice, penalty direction, and start strategy. They test these factors on a synthetic dataset with known useful, extra, and useless feature types. Six versions combine three scoring objectives with subset-size shrinking or growing, showing version choice strongly affects search dynamics.
arxiv-2605-22461: Howey and colleagues study perceived safety of workers near large automated guided vehicles. Physical safety is regulated, but perceived safety is less settled. Prior work understudied large-payload vehicles and used students, not professionals. The team tests real workers in person and in virtual reality, varying passing distance and avoidance shape. Threat is rated with a pressure trigger and a questionnaire. Workers also set their own avoidance parameters from experience. Passing distance of 1.5 to 2 metres is preferred, though threat reads higher in VR.
arxiv-2605-22861: Nennouche, Ijeh, and Khalighi model a vertical optical link from an underwater node to a drone. Wind bends the beam at the moving sea surface and shakes the drone itself. They fit wind-driven pointing errors with a Beta mixture. Then they derive closed-form formulas for the channel distribution and outage chance. Their account covers breaks from total internal reflection and a limited receiver field of view. It finds a reflection-driven outage floor that caps link reliability.
arxiv-2605-23861: Aneesh Komanduri and Xintao Wu build FM-CGM, a modular route to visual causal reasoning from pretrained foundation models. It needs no retraining for causality. Three tools form the pipeline: one pulls out concepts, one changes them, one draws the imagined result. A large reasoning model handles causal inference, while a diffusion model renders the alternatives. Their Causal Semantic Guidance steers edits through cross attention, so changes reach later concepts while untouched regions stay fixed, enabling faithful counterfactual images.
arxiv-2605-23961: Klypa, Bietti, and Grudinin frame RNA design for protein targets as a multi-stage alignment task. Their suite, Moirain, starts with large-scale pretraining on varied RNA corpora to learn what plausible sequences look like, then conditions synthesis on protein structure and sequence through multimodal fine-tuning. A final preference-optimization step, using synthetic interaction data, sharpens functional fitness without collapsing the natural sequence distribution. Tests show the Moirain models yield novel, diverse, plausible RNA with stronger binding than current baselines.
arxiv-2605-24461: Ardestani and twenty co-authors describe end-to-end power management for a hyperscale AI datacenter. Power supply now bottlenecks the race toward artificial general intelligence more than accelerator availability. The paper claims to be the first to describe the full process. It spans planning power 6 to 12 months before new accelerators arrive, tuning settings after deployment, and dynamic runtime management for evolving workloads. Detailed measurements cover a 150-megawatt datacenter hosting 83,000 GB200 GPUs. The authors share insights from building the cluster and hope practitioners share their own experiences.
arxiv-2605-24661: Ali Şenol and others argue that grading language models on final answers alone hides how they reason. Their scheme scores six distinct traits rooted in cognitive science: correctness, consistency, robustness, local logical coherence, efficiency, and stability. Scores combine with deployment-aware weights, so rankings can shift with context. Tests across models and benchmarks show coherence and correctness can pull apart. Small locally run models show distinct profiles, and the six traits carry largely non-overlapping signals. The result is a diagnostic tool for choosing models by behavior, not just accuracy.
arxiv-2605-24761: Po-Chien Luan and others propose a drift-resistant world model. Existing methods feed generated frames back, accumulating noise, while predictions drift from motion. Prediction becomes an anchor-guided rollout: sparse future anchors are predicted first as stable targets. Intermediate frames generate within each chunk from past and future anchors. The anchors also supply geometric constraints through epipolar geometry, localizing where content should appear. Tests on four benchmarks improve looks, geometric consistency, and multi-view coherence, with gains carrying into downstream planning.
arxiv-2605-24961: Da Zhang leads MedMamba, an architecture for classifying medical time series that joins state space models with domain biases. Medical time series drive monitoring and timely clinical calls, yet existing methods struggle with local-global dynamics and drift like baseline wander. They also miss latent links between channels. MedMamba uses multi-scale convolutional embeddings to catch local morphology. A tri-branch differential encoder processes raw, difference, and frequency views, fusing them to stress informative patterns and suppress drift. A spatial graph module then learns directed links between channels.
arxiv-2605-25261: Sebin Oh, Marta González, and Ziqi Wang model the S&P 500 with physics tools, tracking daily up-or-down moves from 1996 to 2026. A static pairwise model uncovers a sector-organized web in which links inside a sector run about 2.8 times stronger than links between sectors. A kinetic version adds shifting outside influences, memory, and lagged links, capturing slow shifts around the dot-com bust, the financial crisis, and the pandemic. Together the models describe lasting market structure and short-run cross-stock motion.
arxiv-2605-25461: Zhuoqun Li and 15 colleagues build the first systematic benchmark for metaphorical video understanding. The benchmark tests a high-order skill where current multimodal models lag far behind humans. Their MetaphorVU-Bench tests whether models can map ideas across domains in video, and experiments blame defective cross-domain mapping for the gap. To help, the team builds a metaphor knowledge graph used as mapping support at inference time, in a method called MetaphorBoost. The benchmark, analysis, and method together give future research a foundation for advancing multimodal models.
arxiv-2605-26161: Li and nine colleagues audit pretraining contamination in time series foundation models, a first. Such models train on vast corpora, raising the worry that test sets were seen in pretraining, inflating scores. Auditing is hard because time series signals vary smoothly, differ widely, and often lack corpus records. TSFMAudit formalises the problem and probes adaptation after fine-tuning: contaminated sets show fast loss reduction with smaller backbone movement. Tested on six foundation models and 187 sets with known training sources, the method beats ten adapted baselines.
arxiv-2605-26461: Rixin Liu and six colleagues harden NVIDIA Multi-Process Service, which shares one graphics processor across processes, against faults that kill every co-running process. A survey of graphics-processor faults guides the design. Memory faults get full isolation through software work in the open driver kernel module, keeping fail-stop behavior. Other faults fall back on a recovery base sharing state via virtual memory and pre-started standbys. Tests show no outage for isolation and full throughput back in 355 milliseconds after recovery.
arxiv-2605-26661: Yuanwei Hu and five others challenge text prototypes for spotting out-of-distribution images with vision-language models. Standard zero-shot detectors treat class-name text vectors as prototypes. Yet theory shows these sit askew from the best visual prototypes, a gap prompts alone cannot close. Their online method instead learns visual prototypes from unlabeled test streams with soft model predictions, with convergence guarantees. Tests across varied setups reach new best scores, respecting the gap between sight and language rather than papering over it.
arxiv-2605-26761: Dong and seven colleagues ask whether a data-selection signal for multimodal instruction tuning can be learned once and reused across datasets and models. Their OnceSelect selector encodes image-instruction pairs in a fixed joint space, groups them into coarse semantic clusters, and picks low-confidence samples as the most informative. Using just 15 percent of LLaVA-625K, it keeps 99.2 percent of full-data performance, and it transfers to unseen datasets and models without retraining.
arxiv-2605-26861: Li and six colleagues build REVERSE, a framework that trains image geo-localization agents to search for evidence and check it, rather than guessing from landmarks alone. The system learns three choices: where to look, what to query, and which evidence to trust, with rewards for grounding, query value, and evidence quality. With a 4B model, it beats strong retrieval baselines and rivals far larger models on Im2GPS3k and YFCC4k.
arxiv-2605-27061: In their 2026 paper, Chen and Pohoata study above-below Ramsey functions for point sequences in d-dimensional space whose projections have cyclic order type. For three dimensions, they prove the sharp estimate that the function equals two raised to two raised to a linear function of k. More generally, the higher-dimensional functions relate closely to the higher-order cup-cap function and the monotone Ramsey numbers of Balko.
arxiv-2605-27261: Jarma and co-authors run a pilot study that gathers synchronized multimodal data on player experience. Nineteen players took part across three Atari 2600 games, yielding game telemetry, self-report surveys, biometric traces, and cued retrospective think-aloud records. The team uses the set to study difficulty in player experience and to showcase a protocol for future multimodal work. The dataset, now public, could support research on dynamic difficulty tuning, game balance, and wider games user research, and the authors see strong potential for generalizing the approach.
arxiv-2605-27361: Melissa Pan and colleagues let each query pick its own full retrieval pipeline configuration. Their BRANE system turns a query into workload traits, then predicts per-configuration success to maximize correctness net of cost at inference time. Across three benchmarks it matches the best fixed setup's accuracy at up to 89 percent lower cost.
arxiv-2605-27861: Juergen Dietrich compares three graph neural networks at predicting not just whether two drugs interact but what kind of interaction occurs. A dual network with cross-attention between molecules beat simple concatenation on mechanism-type accuracy by a wide margin, while barely improving simple yes-or-no detection. On ten held-out aspirin drug pairs it named every interaction type correctly, unlike the ternary rival, which named none.
arxiv-2605-28561: Saurabh Dash and six colleagues introduce Soft-RLVR, learning from decomposed verification signals for partially verifiable tasks. Many prompts carry several requirements, and responses may meet only some. Soft-RLVR turns each prompt into a checklist, scores responses item by item, and trains on the soft reward. Checklist rewards densify sparse pass-fail signals but can reward incomplete responses. Self-verification needs stabilization against reward inflation, and controlled tests show IFEval gains up to about eleven points.
arxiv-2605-28661: Ryuto Fujitani, Masahiro Hino, and Takashi Higuchi present spin phase continuous modulation, a way to size up neutron beams. Two magnetic fields that swing back and forth wobble neutron spins, letting the method pin down beam speed and monochromaticity. They work out the signal math and test it on a beam with one color. Test and math agree well, letting users gauge beam speed and color purity in numbers.
arxiv-2605-29061: Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarioglu study predecessor and rank search in a routed, atom-budgeted learned index with certified repair. A directory routes queries to ranges, a predictor returns a certified rank window, and repair closes the rest by comparison. Their core measure is conditional residual answer entropy, the uncertainty left once leaf, predictor, certificate, and prior data are known. They prove a two-sided accounting theorem tying that measure to query time scale for that design. Benchmarks against PGM-index, RadixSpline, and binary search expose overheads, not speed gains.
arxiv-2605-29461: Zekang Zhang and colleagues propose FlowSeg, which adds dynamic meaning guidance to language-tuned masking. Current pipelines make strong mask options, yet the result may fail to match the prompt. Language meaning serves as static prompts or post-hoc matching signals rather than in stepwise mask making. FlowSeg adds a two-way meaning flow between decode states and language-model-derived prompt vectors. Language prompts guide mask tuning, while prompt vectors are updated by visual evidence. Tests show it improves language-mask match and gives best results.
arxiv-2605-29561: Zekai Yu and five colleagues present ParaTool, a framework that moves tool knowledge from context into parameters for language-model tool calling. Stuffing tool documents into context inflates inference cost and hallucination risk as contexts grow, while tuning alone often fails to internalize specific tools. ParaTool pre-trains each tool into its own loadable parameter module, combines relevant modules through a gating network, and fine-tunes tool parameters jointly with the model. Tests on Stable ToolBench and BFCL show it beating strong context-based baselines with lower computational complexity.
arxiv-2605-29761: Deniz Sayin Mercadier and four colleagues stop objects in scene models from sinking into each other. Compositional surface models give each object its own signed distance field, but separate fields can overlap, breaking physical sense. Soft penalties shrink overlaps without ending them and demand fussy loss weights. Their plug-and-play layer, S2MDF, imposes a hard constraint on vector-valued distance fields for any compositional model, with no architecture change and negligible extra cost. Tests show intersections fall to numerical precision while rebuild quality holds, beating rivals.
arxiv-2605-29861: Chenghao Zhang and five colleagues build Ptah, a harness for verifiable deep research. Deep research must weave scattered evidence into reports, yet open-ended synthesis lacks ground truth and must interleave text and visual evidence. Ptah runs from question to finished web report through planning, research, and writing. Its agents plan visually, gather grounded evidence, hold source-aligned images in working memory, and compose through declarative tools. A verifier enforces grounding in facts, faithful citations, and cross-mode consistency. Tests show Ptah beats baselines on reliability and usability.
arxiv-2605-29961: Russell Steele, Naftali Weinberger, Tess Baker, and Ian Shrier ask how to sort short-lived from lasting effects over time. They show standard potential-outcome and graph tools miss interventions holding or shifting a steady state. A system-and-state view replaces a measure-based view, letting steady-state assumptions sharpen what effects mean. The team ties identifiability to measured time points, and offers a new null-effect form splitting transient from lasting impact. The result gives time-varying studies a cleaner way to state what an intervention changes.
arxiv-2605-30061: Vanuildo S. de Carvalho, Hermann Freire and Rodrigo G. Pereira study how repulsion between electrons drives a Lieb-lattice altermagnet from metal to insulator. Using the slave-rotor method at half filling, they find a cascade from normal metal to altermagnetic metal, to altermagnetic insulator, and to a Mott insulator where quasiparticle weight vanishes. Spin-split bands mark the spectra in the metallic and insulating stages but fade sharply in the Mott stage. Spin splitting in such d-wave altermagnets may show up only under weak to moderate correlations.
arxiv-2605-30261: Chandan Sarma and Paul Stevenson compare three qubit-mapping strategies for shell model ground states using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver, each from a Hamiltonian matrix in many-body or Slater determinant basis. Mappings were tested on boron-10, with the qubit-efficient mapping extended to carbon-12. 26-qubit circuits ran on simulator and hardware. The best boron-10 hardware result came from Slater determinant mapping, within a fraction of a percent; others erred by several percent, and carbon-12 landed several percent from exact. Hardware fidelity supports qubit-efficient scaling across mass regions.
arxiv-2605-30361: Dhruv Patankar and Sachit Ramesha Gowda train spiking networks with EGGROLL, a low-rank form of evolution strategy noise. Spiking networks save power, but training is hard because spike cutoffs do not give smooth gradients. Evolution strategies need no gradients, but their cost grows with the number of weights. EGGROLL cuts memory from scaling with the product of sizes to scaling with their sum times rank. On a benchmark, gradient-free training hits 79 percent test accuracy and cuts run time by more than half.
arxiv-2605-30461: Santiago Amaya-Corredor, Miguel Calvo-Fullana and Anders Jonsson present a shared approach for limited multi-agent reward learning, joining state-boosted learning with shared dual values. They target systems with split agent setups but must meet global resource constraints, where solo learning fails to give feasible plans. Unlike CTDE, their method scales well in training and running. Tests on smart grid demand response show shared values are key: with shared values, agents converge to a shared dual value and satisfy grid constraints and demand delivery.
arxiv-2605-30661: Loubet and Appignanesi give wetting a molecular basis, recasting Young's equation for water with a molecular wetting coefficient. The coefficient tracks how a surface offsets the energy cost of hydrogen-bond defects against bulk water. Across diverse lab and model surfaces, contact angles collapse onto one master curve when expressed through the coefficient. The recast closes the Young and Young-Dupré relations on energetic grounds, linking wetting, adhesion, cavitation, and nanoconfined filling. Wetting thus comes from water itself rather than from the surface.
arxiv-2605-30761: Marshman and colleagues characterize radio interference in the 2.4 gigahertz band around Murriyang, CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals dominate, varying with time of day. It is confined in time and frequency and can be cut. Using ten seconds of Vela Pulsar voltage data, most channel data remain unaffected. Three detection and mitigation methods all perform well and could run in real time, raising usable band from thirty percent to over ninety percent. A basic power-threshold approach offers a simple fix.
arxiv-2605-30961: Li and colleagues turn idea generation into a search over a pool of ideas. Language models can help make ideas, but old methods converge in meaning, limiting variety and novelty. EvoGens applies rank-based changes with outside search planning, and mixing to fuse matching concepts. A scoring signal guides picks, keeping search alive while curbing early stall. Tests show EvoGens lifts search over strong baselines, raising novelty and variety while holding idea quality steady.
arxiv-2605-31161: Panraksa and Ruengrot give a test for when averages of roots of unity are whole algebraic numbers. They then use it to settle a conjecture on functions over cyclic groups. They prove that if all such averages of a function are algebraic integers, the function must be linear modulo n. For prime powers they add a local-global argument. As a payoff, they fully describe the perfect isometries of cyclic prime-power groups as affine permutations.
arxiv-2605-31261: Zhao and colleagues explain why linear recurrent memory works in partly seen reinforcement learning. They build and study two linear filters. The first filter reproduces the belief vector's pre-softmax logits in a hidden Markov model under a deterministic matrix, covering optimal policy learning. The second cuts state-decoding error to almost nothing under a nearly fixed matrix. Action-led hidden Markov models extend the results, with filters varying over time under action rules. Test runs and a small reward game confirm the filter as a strong extractor.
arxiv-2605-31361: Leroy-Stone treats teammates as learnable parts of a world model for multi-agent reinforcement learning. Agents must work with partners whose policies and intents they cannot see directly. World models like Dreamer do well alone, but struggle with teammate-induced uncertainty in multi-agent settings. The architecture splits a Dreamer-style model into environment and teammate parts, with an extra Theory-of-Mind head inferring partner character, intent and actions from partial paths. Teammate latents steer actor and critic, letting agents imagine diverse collaborators, with tests proposed.
arxiv-2606-00061:
Park asks whether teaching language models about market reflexivity makes them better forecasters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reflexivity, George Soros's theory, holds that prices shape the fundamentals they are said to reflect, creating self-reinforcing booms and busts. Standard forecasting treats markets as external systems to observe, and ignores that they are part of the loop. Park tested three models, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Pro, under four increasingly reflexivity-aware prompts.

The episodes were the dot-com bubble and the global financial crisis, with inputs anonymized to prevent memorized answers. Performance was scored by accuracy and by the risk-adjusted return of a trading strategy. Awareness improved accuracy, but differently for each model and context window length. The same theoretical briefing produced different behavior in each model. Park presents this divergence as the finding: awareness is not an upgrade, and how a model metabolizes it depends on the model.
arxiv-2606-00261:
La Grotteria and co-authors map harsh driving acts street by street in Milan. Crash logs, the norm for road risk work, miss much and lag in time. Sharp speed-ups and hard brakes can stand in as risk signs. Past work used small city samples for such signs.

Their set joins car data from more than four million rigs. Street traits come from maps, flow data, and street views parsed by a vision model. Wide roads, cross points, and bus stops link to more harsh acts. Open views of sky and road do too. Dense fronts of built forms link to fewer such acts. Marked bike lanes show more harsh acts than split bike paths. Tailored fixes beat one-size rules, they argue.
arxiv-2606-00361:
Escobar, Linares, and Martín-Ruiz study the Casimir push near a field form that breaks space rules on its own. Their field is a bent light law in the Plebański form. Some states of that field break Lorentz ties through their own rest state. The break point is set by a mark built from the field's core curve.

Twin plates set the stage for the push test. Past the break zone, light splits in a plain branch and a bent branch. Bend strength is set by the mark at the base state. Plate-wise sums give the push for both plate leans. Near the break, the bent branch turns wild and the sum blows up. That blow-up marks a fail of the two-branch view, not a real vast push.
arxiv-2606-01361:
Horovicz, Hel-Or, and Moses teach machines to see animals in clouds. People often spot animal shapes in clouds by pareidolia. Top recognition tools usually fail on such faint shapes. Their method predicts which animals people are likely to see. It also helps people perceive a chosen animal they missed. A diffusion model reshapes cloud segments toward an animal form. The trick works only when the animal fits the cloud shape.

A generated image then serves as the prediction. Subtle visual hints often suffice to guide the eye. A short morphing video runs from the image back to the cloud. That video further boosts human perception of the shape. The work blends machine vision with human perception cues.
arxiv-2606-01461:
Nogueira and co-authors design drug candidates tuned to cancer genotypes. Tumors differ a lot from patient to patient. Many cancer subtypes lack clear molecular targets. Models that generate molecules given a genotype offer a path. Past tools do not jointly tune key traits. Sensitivity, ease of synthesis, and binding plausibility all matter at once.

Their method shifts the latent space of a diffusion model. Gradient ascent pushes it toward a composite reward. The reward joins sensitivity, drug-likeness, and synthetic access scores. Real cell line data ground the reward and the tests. A multi-agent pipeline checks that candidates make biological sense. Gains appear across 15 cancer cell lines in held-out sets.
arxiv-2606-01661:
Safaai and Sabatini ask what simple neural models really prove about computation. Neurons receive thousands of inputs on branching dendrites. Population activity is often modeled with direct input-output rules. Each input adds independently to a scalar drive in such rules. Good prediction by those models may not reveal the mechanism. For maximum-entropy models matched to rates and coactivities, explained entropy is a prediction measure. It is not a mechanism-identification test, they argue. Omitted terms can be absorbed into first-order parameters when correlated.

They introduce diagnostics that separate prediction from rule recovery. State reweighting holds the response rule fixed while input spreads change. Log-odds contrasts and temporal leakage controls join the toolkit. In simulations, higher-order responses pass naive tests but get caught after reweighting. CA1 recordings show many tables turn distribution-sensitive under reweighting.
arxiv-2606-01761:
Gao, Ma, and Pikhurko write a short graph theory note from 2026. Their topic is how to bound a graph power's free set. A graph power joins points that lie close in the graph. A free set holds no joined pair of points. Three past authors gave ratio and inertia bounds for this case.

The note weighs those bounds against two known tools. One tool is the theta function of Lovasz. The other is a weighted inertia bound. The authors show both tools do at least as well. The theta bound can be computed fast in graph size. That makes it a strong choice for this task.
arxiv-2606-02061:
Brzozowski and Chung challenge a claimed fix for sparse autoencoder instability. Sparse autoencoders learn bases from neural network activations. Their features often read as clear concepts. But features vary a lot across random seeds. That instability limits trust in the extracted concepts.

Archetypal variants claimed more stable dictionaries after training. The pair show the claim rests on a setup artifact. All runs shared identical initialization in those tests. That shared start, not the method, drove agreement. They clarify two notions that are often conflated. Stability means agreement between independent trained models. Stabilization means independent runs converge to one solution. Metric design also shapes the reported effect.
arxiv-2606-02261:
Feskov and co-authors break down the light absorption spectra of molecular dimers into their parts. In systems with more than one chromophore, the excited state structure is complex. It is driven by excitonic and charge-transfer links between the chromophores. Broadening from vibrations and from the solvent hides the transitions underneath, so they are hard to name directly.

The team build a framework that can split a dimer spectrum into the parts that make it up. Frenkel exciton states and charge-transfer states are treated in one unified formalism. The solvent's effect on zwitterionic states is also part of that formalism. Mixing of exciton and charge-transfer states reshapes the absorption profile a lot and makes it much broader. Yet the first spectral moment stays almost the same. A BPEA dimer is the test case for the method.
arxiv-2606-02361:
Martins-Filho offers a teaching-focused study of spin links in a two-particle quantum system. Each particle carries spin one-half. Such links sit at the heart of entanglement and Bell-type tests. The goal is not new physics. The goal is to show clear ways to compute the key averages.

Three methods are set side by side. The first uses plain algebra in the product basis. The second writes the joint state with two-by-two matrices. That form keeps Pauli-matrix algebra close at hand. It also shows how each operator acts on its own particle. The third method leans on symmetry. It works for the singlet state, which stays the same under rotation. A naive stretch of the method fails for triplet states. The contrast teaches how symmetry, tensor structure, and entanglement interact.
arxiv-2606-02661:
Zhou and co-authors refine rain forecasts by splitting them across frequency bands. Short-term rain forecasts guide flood and storm response. Regression models blur fine storm detail and break known turbulence power laws. Diffusion models invent sharp detail that lacks a physical anchor. The team's framework, SDIR, casts the task as step-wise refinement. A stable low-frequency skeleton comes first. Fine textures are then refined under physical constraints.

Two paths share the work. The Synoptic Frequency-Guided Former handles global structure with scale-adaptive transformers. The Fourier Residual Refiner handles fine residuals with Fourier neural operators. A loss on the power spectrum enforces spectra that match turbulence. A dynamic mask shapes that loss. Tests on three benchmarks beat top methods in spatial accuracy. Spectral fidelity rivals diffusion-based methods. Both blur and invented detail are cut. The aim is nowcasting that field users can trust.
arxiv-2606-02961:
Gao and co-authors present AtlasGS, a framework for harmonizing brain MRI resolution across contrasts. Scans of the same brain often differ in resolution and slice spacing by modality. AtlasGS learns one explicit Gaussian scaffold for a subject's anatomy from the isotropic structural scan. That scaffold is then reused to fit other modalities acquired with sparse slices.

Training runs in two stages: scaffold learning, then appearance fitting per target modality. Tests cover the UK Biobank, GBM, and ABCD datasets. Tasks span through-plane super-resolution for T2-weighted, FLAIR, DWI, and ASL scans, with degradation factors of three, five, and seven times. Pathological cases include glioblastoma. The authors report state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity. The shared geometry also supports arbitrary-view generation with strong structural consistency. The team frames the method as a flexible, interpretable path to retrospective multi-contrast MRI harmonization.
arxiv-2606-03061:
Lapkovskis and co-authors give one formal model for distributed computing systems. New forms, such as the computing continuum, mix many machine kinds and act at random. To use all resources well, the whole system needs one model. Their frame casts the system as a generative Markov model.

The state splits into factors over structured variables. Each variable splits again over its parts. That shape mirrors the sparse links of such systems. It makes simulation, inference, and policy learning workable on states that would else be out of reach. A case study covers joint AI inference. A server pools its resources with ones users volunteer. Central scheduling choked at scale. Spreading the work across user devices cut wait times and server load. The frame thus ties system design to Markov chain tools that control theory can use.
arxiv-2606-03261:
Taylor and co-authors report a nine-member baby star system found by chance in ALMA images. The system sits in the high-mass protocluster NGC 6334. Its members are protostellar and candidate prestellar sources. A stability check says the system is bound. Mean pair spacing is about 7,930 astronomical units.

The system seems to have formed by the breaking of one large filament. The filament shows in dust continuum and in a tracer emission line. Inside the nine, a triple and a binary match formation by core fragmentation at smaller scales. One hot core splits into two parts about 618 units apart, driving a bipolar outflow. One other source clearly drives an outflow too. Virial masses come from a molecular line fit. The other six sources look young, with sparse line emission and no radio detection. The find adds to the small sample of young high-mass multiple systems.
arxiv-2606-03561:
Liu and Chen study when a famous quantum inequality reaches equality. The distillability conjecture concerns two copies of four-by-four Werner states. It has stood open in quantum information for years. The team examines the saturated cases, where the conjectured bound becomes exact. For every verified case known, they characterize the saturation conditions.

Equality forces the two matrices involved into two-by-two block-diagonal form. Several prior partial results reduce to that same structure. Those cases include one normal matrix, unitary similarity links, and anti-diagonal blocks. A manifold optimization method adds numeric evidence. It suggests the block-diagonal form is essential for saturation. The identified saturation points are also proven to be critical points on the constraint manifold. Quantum information readers get a unified account of when the bound is tight.
arxiv-2606-04161:
Tyler Crosse and co-authors diagnose in 2026 why model selectors so often fail. A selector picks the best model for each input. It should beat any single model, yet trained only on logged data it often does not.

The snag is ambiguity: many inputs look the same in the logs but need different models. The team proves that no method trained on logged choices alone can beat this limit without new information. Then they redesign the data itself. Logging richer features about each input breaks the ties that cause the failure. This turns a hidden flaw into a clear design rule. The rule: log more about inputs, or accept selector limits.
arxiv-2606-04261:
Feiyang Kang and colleagues ask in 2026 whether generalist coding agents can automate data curation, the slow loop of proposing, testing, and revising rules for selecting training data. They built Curation-Bench, a benchmark that fixes the model and training recipe and hands agents the loop itself.

Given command-line access to inspect data and submit policies to a fixed pipeline, off-the-shelf agents matched strong published data-selection baselines within ten iterations. But trajectory analysis exposed an execution-research gap: agents mostly tweaked local variants instead of exploring new policy families. Forcing each iteration to cite and adapt a prior published method changed that. The scaffolded agent then composed, unaided, a policy beating the baselines on a tenth of their data budget.
arxiv-2606-04661:
Kumar and colleagues optimize prompts for both accuracy and cost at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on prompt engineering. They raise inference cost on every call. The best trade-off depends on the task and budget. The usual shortcut collapses both goals into one weighted sum. This fixes the trade-off before the search. It often recovers only a narrow slice of the Pareto front. The authors call this failure scalarization collapse.

Their optimizer, CRAFT, treats calls to the target model for validation as the scarce resource. It spends them on candidates near the optimistic front. Each round, accuracy-oriented and cost-oriented generators propose edits. A Pareto-gap acquisition rule allocates the validation budget. NSGA-II retention keeps a spread-out population of prompts. Accuracy-only, cost-only, and weighted-sum baselines each concentrated in narrower regions. The trade-off stays a post-search choice.
arxiv-2606-04861:
Nazari and colleagues study how rotation helps objects sink through fluids that refuse to flow until pushed hard enough, in a 2026 arXiv fluid mechanics paper. Yield-stress fluids, like the Carbopol gel used here, behave as solids until a stress threshold is crossed. The team rotated cylinders and spheres of varying surface roughness inside a Helmholtz coil within such a fluid.

Measured drag depends strongly on both roughness and rotation: the plastic drag falls as rotation rises at fixed Bingham number, so spinning reduces resistance. Flow shows rotation generating a plastic deformation zone in the orthogonal plane and promoting wall slip. Simulations reproduce the scaling but underpredict drag, likely missing wall slip. The yield limit for sinking rises with rotation and roughness.
arxiv-2606-04961:
Koshelev calculates how much magnetic flux stays trapped in a superconducting strip after it cools through its transition, in a 2026 arXiv superconductivity theory paper. Trapped flux plagues superconducting electronic devices, and the residual vortices in a long narrow strip cooled in a small perpendicular field are his subject. The low-temperature vortex configuration forms very near the critical temperature. Flux density is set by a balance between entries and exits over the geometrical barrier.

As cooling proceeds, the escape rate drops exponentially, and the vortex density falls out of equilibrium at a field-dependent freezing temperature. The freezing point sits above the transition's fluctuation width by a large logarithmic factor. The frozen flux depends very strongly on field, which lets him define an effective flux-expulsion field.
arxiv-2606-05561:
Xueyang Wu and co-authors confront a privacy risk in speech-based health checks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Voice recordings can flag depression, which makes screening cheap and wide-reaching. The same recordings can also leak a speaker's age and gender. Older fixes fail against new attacks or blur every feature with noise. The team instead trims the shared information between the speech code and private traits.

Their system, InfoShield, keeps depression scoring while cutting what the code reveals about the speaker. A new estimator aligns sound frames with trait codes over time, a step older tools handled poorly. On a public speech corpus, guesses at gender fell from about ninety-three percent to about fifty-six percent. Age guessing fell from about fifty-six percent to about thirty percent. The depression score stayed strong and beat the prior best mark, with only a small loss from the privacy step.
arxiv-2606-05661:
Asawa and colleagues built a benchmark for whether AI systems truly learn on the job in a 2026 arXiv paper. Continual learning means improving through a stream of related tasks. No hard, trusted test for it existed. CL-Bench spans six domains, from software work to outbreak forecasting and games. Domain experts validated every task stream. Each stream hides a shared pattern that a stateful system can pick up over time.

Frontier models ran under several agent designs, from plain in-context learning to dedicated memory systems. A gain metric separates real learning from starting skill. The results leave wide headroom: agents often overfit to the latest case or failed to reuse past lessons. Dedicated memory systems did not rescue them. Plain in-context learning beat the memory managers outright. The authors release the benchmark as a yardstick for the next wave of learning systems.
arxiv-2606-05761:
Wenxuan Wang and colleagues test whether AI assistants track how their memories relate in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-running assistants pile up memories that support, shade, or contradict each other. Correct help often depends on those relations, not on single facts. Existing memory benchmarks seldom probe relation handling. SubtleMemory plants controlled memory variants with known relations inside realistic chat histories.

The benchmark holds over fifteen hundred test cases across ten long histories. Its memory sets come in three flavors: complementary, nuanced, and contradictory. Eleven systems were graded, from standalone memory stores to agent frameworks with plug-in memory. All current systems proved weak at telling fine relations apart. Diagnostic stages separated failures of storage, retrieval, and reasoning. Profiles differed sharply by stage, which shows where each design breaks. The authors release the benchmark to push memory research past simple recall.
arxiv-2606-06061:
Kakroudi and Pieters let people boss a robot arm around in plain words, with a human checkpoint before anything moves in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework splits the work across distributed ROS 2 nodes. Language understanding, visual grounding, motion execution, and orchestration each run separately, deployable on different machines. Free-form commands become structured requests for picking, placing, and handovers.

A vision-language model returns targets in image space. Depth and calibration convert those pixels into metric goals in the robot's frame. A web dashboard shows the interpreted intent and grounding overlays at every stage. No motion executes until an operator explicitly confirms. Experiments on a Franka FR3 arm measured reliability and latency as table scenes grew more ambiguous. Different language and vision model pairings were compared inside the same pipeline. The design lesson is architectural: distribute the intelligence, centralize the accountability. Collaborative robots in real workplaces need both.
arxiv-2606-06461:
Luzhe Sun and co-authors offer a gentle way to fix a robot's imperfect helper in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robots often start from a pretrained policy or a human operator whose actions are noisy or off. Retraining is expensive, and full autonomy throws away the helper's intent. Their GLOVES framework instead edits actions on the fly, transporting each proposed action toward what an expert would do, using flow matching learned from a few demonstrations.

The clever part is restraint. The learned flow also scores how expert like an action looks, and that score gates intervention: normal actions pass through untouched, while odd ones get corrected. Assistance therefore appears only when needed. Across simulated and real robot experiments, the method steadily improved noisy imitation agents and large vision language action models, learning from only a few expert demonstrations or reusable skill segments.
arxiv-2606-06561:
C Dedes rewrites the quantum wavefunction with a twist that changes how quantum fluids flow in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Madelung transformation recasts the Schrödinger equation as fluid equations, splitting the wave into amplitude and phase. Dedes replaces that split with a new ansatz. Phase is tied to amplitude through a hyperbolic cotangent, a singular coupling. The flow velocity then picks up a term driven by density gradients.

Effects follow for both continuity and the quantum force. Read as the order parameter of a superconductor, the ansatz changes the London equations, which govern how superconductors expel magnetic fields. The Meissner response becomes sensitive to density gradients, not just phase winding. Dedes concludes that superconductor rigidity need not be purely phase driven. The condensate behaves like a medium whose screening and currents are shaped by its own amplitude landscape.
arxiv-2606-06661:
The nonlinear Fourier transform extends the classic Fourier idea to signals where waves interact as they pass. Denisov studies when this transform settles down to a well defined limit in this 2026 arXiv paper. His data are sparse, meaning most entries are zero, and square summable, meaning the total energy stays finite even over an endless line of entries.

The note covers two versions of the transform, linked to two symmetry groups used in physics and signal work. Denisov proves convergence for this sparse class and draws a direct payoff for a related family of polynomials defined on the unit circle, whose long run behavior follows from the main result. The paper is a companion to his earlier study of the general square summable case, borrowing its setup and notation while sharpening what can be said when the data thin out.
arxiv-2606-06761:
A robot can recognize every object in a room and still fumble picking one up when it sits in a new spot. Jang and co-authors trace that failure to a missing link in this 2026 arXiv paper: the robot policy understands the scene, but not how its own movement directions look from the camera. Its action coordinates, the axes of its base frame, remain invisible in the image it sees.

Their fix, AxisGuide, paints those axes directly onto each camera view. Using the camera settings and the gripper's pose, it renders small cue channels showing which way each base direction moves in the picture, with no depth sensor or extra labeling needed. Trials in the LIBERO simulator and on real robots showed solid gains in task success and much better handling of objects placed at unseen locations, a common way these policies break.
arxiv-2606-07061:
Proving identities between endless sums is a craft that computers have steadily mechanized. Wang advances one core technique in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is q-holonomic sequences, families indexed by an integer with a deformation parameter q. A reduction method splits any test polynomial into two parts.

One part is summable, meaning its sum telescopes away neatly. The other is a remainder of lower degree. Wang pins down exactly which multiplier polynomials make a product summable. He then adds a power partible refinement for mirror cases. It removes the highest and lowest degree terms together while keeping the mirror symmetry. The machinery is applied to q-central-Delannoy numbers, a deformed counting sequence. New q-identities and q-congruences fall out as demonstrations. The work sits in the Wilf-Zeilberger tradition of machine assisted identity proof.
arxiv-2606-07161:
Reading text in surveillance video fails frame by frame: blur, occlusion, and scale shifts corrupt each glimpse. Tran and co-authors aggregate whole trajectories instead in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, TraRA, is a plug in layer for video text spotting. A sign or plate visible across thirty frames should be read once, jointly, not thirty times separately.

Two modules do the work. Temporal Clustering groups detections that stay coherent across time and appearance, cleaning fragmented tracks. Vision-Language Aggregation then fuses the frames using a vision language model tuned with low rank adapters. Language context helps disambiguate smudged characters. Four public benchmarks covered road scenes and urban footage. TraRA consistently improved tracking stability and recognition accuracy over leading methods. The design needs no changes to the underlying spotter. Future work targets lighter models and real time speed for live surveillance feeds.
arxiv-2606-07361:
