Gasse and co-authors classify the search landscapes of two graph problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. A dominating set is a set of vertices such that every vertex is in it or next to it, while vertex coloring assigns colors so neighbors differ. Heuristic search on such problems succeeds or stalls depending on local optima, points where no change improves the solution. The authors ask, for graph classes, whether landscapes are unimodal, flat-plateaued, or multimodal with traps.

They analyze neighborhood rules: changing one element at a time, and allowing swaps between solution parts. For each problem and graph class they determine which landscape type arises, including whether local optimum is global. The work trades runtime bounds, the usual goal of heuristic theory, for understanding of where search gets stuck. The map explains why randomized heuristics vary across instance families and guides which neighborhood operators fit which problems.
arxiv-2606-07761:
Jikun Wang and colleagues at ETH Zürich and partner institutes unveil a stronger way to corrupt memory from ordinary software, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The weakness is read disturbance in DRAM chips: hammering one row of cells can flip bits in neighbouring rows, the effect behind RowHammer attacks. How bad the effect gets depends heavily on the pattern of accesses used.

Their pattern, ScaleDisturb, holds two aggressor rows open for unequal times, exploiting a timing asymmetry in disturbance. On one hundred ninety-six DDR4 chips and three HBM2 chips, ScaleDisturb triggered bitflips at notably fewer activations than the best known patterns, and made attacks easier on every chip. Vulnerability also grew as manufacturing shrank to smaller nodes, the opposite of what chip makers hope. A proof-of-concept attack from a user program flipped more bits than state-of-the-art RowHammer methods.
arxiv-2606-07961:
Rene Ebunle Akupan, May-Win Thein, and Se Young Yoon present a control tutorial for the inverters that hold up islanded microgrids, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A grid-forming inverter in an island must regulate its own voltage with no external grid to lean on, while load current depends on that very voltage. The standard cascaded controller compensates couplings only exactly at its tuning point.

Their alternative is full-state feedback linearisation. The inverter model has full relative degree, so one feedback law can cancel the main nonlinear effects exactly. What remains is two independent double integrators that pole placement can shape. In MATLAB tests at twenty megawatts, the linearising controller settled a reference step in well under a millisecond. The baseline never reached the two percent band within fifty milliseconds. The trade-off is robustness: the cascaded controller tolerated filter mismatch better, a caveat stated plainly.
arxiv-2606-08061:
Lies Beers, Raffaella Mulas, and Jan Petr extend a classical bridge between graph geometry and spectrum to a less-studied gap, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The normalised Laplacian of a graph has eigenvalues between zero and two. The classical Cheeger inequalities tie the smallest positive eigenvalue to how easily the graph splits in two, and dual inequalities do the same for the largest eigenvalue. The gap studied here is the second largest distance from one, a quantity arising in random walks and expander graphs.

The authors relate this gap to both the classical and dual Cheeger constants. Their main tool is a new Cheeger-type constant with a probabilistic meaning, tied to two-step random walks on the graph. For it they prove sharp inequalities in the classical style, so the gap can be estimated from walk behaviour. Such results matter wherever expansion matters, from network design to mixing times.
arxiv-2606-08161:
Jiechen Huang and co-authors teach a transformer to compute the parasitic capacitances that haunt chip design, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Capacitance extraction predicts the unwanted coupling between wires on a chip, which designers must know to predict timing and noise. Rule-based pattern matching struggles at advanced nodes. Earlier neural models accepted only fixed layer combinations from one process node.

Their AttentionCap exploits a structural resemblance: a capacitance matrix behaves like the attention matrices transformers already compute. Customisations include a Gram representation, a physics-aligned symmetric output layer, and a process-node embedding for training across nodes. Trained on synthetic data, it reached about zero point seven percent self-capacitance error and four percent coupling error on unseen designs. Errors were several times lower than the CNN baseline, and inference about one hundred ninety times faster. A pretrained model transferred to an unseen node with only five thousand samples.
arxiv-2606-08561:
Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, and Xiande Zhang resolve the smallest open case of loss-resistant entanglement in this 2026 arXiv paper. A pure quantum state is called m-resistant if it stays entangled after losing any m particles, yet becomes fully separable, with no entanglement at all, after losing any m plus one. For qubits, whether a five-qubit state could be exactly one-resistant was unresolved. The authors show the five-cycle graph state, built from five qubits linked in a ring, does exactly this.

They also develop a stabilizer-subgroup method for verifying resistance in graph states. Applying it to all graph states on five, six, and seven vertices gives a classification up to local Clifford equivalence. The five-qubit one-resistant stabilizer states turn out to be exactly the local Clifford class of the five-cycle state: a single island of loss tolerance in the smallest possible register.
arxiv-2606-08661:
Kuncan Wang and colleagues map the attack surface of agents that answer questions from databases, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data agents integrate language-model reasoning with relational data access and multi-step workflow orchestration. That integration introduces new weak spots across data resources, database execution, and agent reasoning. The authors present a full security study of these systems.

Their contributions include a layered vulnerability framework identifying eight risks across interpretation, execution, and policy layers. They also give an attack taxonomy spanning three goals, seven tactics, and fourteen techniques. They pair the taxonomy with a payload generation pipeline grounded in realistic attack scenarios. The study gives firms a clear list of weak spots to check before they hand a live database to an agent.
arxiv-2606-08961:
Sun and Wang simulate how dense black hole packs merge up to an intermediate-mass black hole, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Supermassive black holes existed early in history, and intermediate-mass seeds, around 1,000 solar masses, could explain their fast growth. Simulating black hole clusters, the authors follow chains of binary mergers driven by gravitational waves. The mechanism is exchange: soft binaries trade partners, hardening gradually, far more efficiently than three-body scattering.

At densities above 5 billion solar masses per cubic parsec, the runaway chain builds an intermediate-mass black hole of 1,000 solar masses within 10 million years of cluster formation. The scenario avoids the uncertainties of growing a very massive star. As clusters expand, their densities fall to match present-day nuclear star clusters like those in the Milky Way and M33. Repeated mergers keep the black hole's spin low. The authors estimate rates for gravitational-wave events resembling known mergers.
arxiv-2606-09061:
Liu, Wang, and colleagues fix a fairness flaw in how AI chatbots serve crowds of users, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Serving engines use chunked prefill, splitting each prompt's processing into pieces so long prompts do not block others. Standard first-come-first-served scheduling lets some requests starve while tail latency jitters. Their framework adds an aging policy: a request's priority rises with waiting time and remaining work, so nobody waits forever.

Two more components replace static token budgets with latency targets. Latency-Prediction-Based Request Scheduling uses predicted times. Active Prefill Control regulates concurrent prefills. Tested on NVIDIA and Ascend hardware, the aging policy cut mean end-to-end latency by over 10 percent versus first-come-first-served. The latency components reduced P99 tail latency, the slowest 1 percent of requests, and suppressed fragmentation. The authors conclude structural and temporal controls are complementary, and release the code.
arxiv-2606-09361:
Johannes Wehrstein and his colleagues present Bespoke-Card, a system that writes database software instead of tuning it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is cardinality estimation, a database's guess at how many rows a query step will produce. Bad guesses lead the query optimiser to choose slow plans, yet built-in estimators must stay generic for every possible workload.

Bespoke-Card uses cooperating software agents: one plans an estimator design, one writes the code, and a validator scores its guesses against true row counts. Feedback about the largest errors guides repeated improvement, with the best version kept. On the JOB query benchmark, feeding the generated estimates into PostgreSQL cut total runtime by about a third and reduced the median estimation error by roughly two fifths. Each tailored estimator took under an hour and cost less than ten dollars to produce.
arxiv-2606-09561:
Sida and co-authors study a wave in fusion plasmas whose strength rises and falls in a repeating swing in this 2026 arXiv paper. The wave is a geodesic acoustic mode, a ring-shaped wobble of the radial electric field in a tokamak. Fast particles can feed it energy and drive it unstable. The driven form is called an EGAM.

The team ran the gyrokinetic particle-in-cell code ORB5, which follows charged particles in a magnetic field. They compared the mode with the beam-plasma instability, where a beam of fast electrons drives a Langmuir wave. Both systems show the same link between swing rate and wave size. That match says the same particle-trapping physics drives both cases. The work also yields a new way to gauge EGAM strength in a real tokamak.
arxiv-2606-09761:
Corona-García, Fernández-Bretón, and Ramos-García probe a rare breed of ultrafilter tied to Ramsey theory in this 2026 arXiv paper. An ultrafilter is a maximal, consistent way to call sets of integers large. A Z-Ramsey ultrafilter holds a tidy set for each colouring that the integer shift leaves alone. Such objects were posed as open questions by Petrenko and Protasov.

The team shows it is consistent with set theory that none exist at all. They also prove that each filter of a weaker three-colour kind is selective, a strong tidiness trait. The same holds for Z-Ramsey filters that are P-points. A crafted forcing extension then yields P-points that fail the Z-Ramsey test. The build uses quotient algebras of integer sets over a class of ideals. The results answer the posed questions head-on.
arxiv-2606-10061:
Noshin and her team introduce the first benchmark for conversational sycophancy in Bengali social contexts, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model testing. Sycophancy is excessive agreement or flattery, and in emotionally sensitive conversations models can slide from balanced support into strong validation or escalation. Prior research focused on factual agreement and instruction settings, leaving culturally grounded conversation underexplored. Their benchmark, BenSyc, fills that gap for Bengali-speaking communities in Bangladesh and West Bengal.

Starting from nearly twelve thousand Reddit posts and about one hundred seventy thousand comments, the team built a human-validated dataset with binary labels and a five-level taxonomy from invalidation through escalation. More than fifteen open and proprietary models were evaluated on classification and response generation. Even the best system reached only about sixty-two percent macro-F1 on binary detection and a similar score on five-class sorting.
arxiv-2606-10361:
Yang and colleagues introduce a new regularity condition that sharpens what theory can promise about a classic classifier, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical learning theory. Convergence rates for classifiers are usually proven under a weak Tsybakov margin condition, giving polynomial rates, or a strong Massart margin condition, giving exponential rates. Their Boltzmann margin bridges the gap: weaker than Massart, generally stronger than Tsybakov, and able to imply many of their properties under suitable conditions.

Applying Boltzmann margin to k-nearest neighbors classification, they establish the first near-exponential convergence rates for that classifier. The work matters because nearest-neighbor methods are widely used yet their fastest known guarantees required the strongest margin assumption. A middle condition that real data may plausibly satisfy, while still delivering near-exponential rates, narrows the gap between learning theory and the observed speed of simple classifiers.
arxiv-2606-10561:
De Angelis surveys gamma-ray astrophysics in this 2026 arXiv review paper, covering the highest-energy light in the universe. Gamma rays diagnose extreme accelerators, from pulsars to black hole jets, and carry fingerprints of nuclear synthesis, such as lines from radioactive aluminium and iron. The field spans nine orders of magnitude in photon energy, alongside neutrino and gravitational-wave astronomy. Yet one band lags: the MeV gap, where sensitivity remains poor.

That gap limits studies of supernova line spectroscopy, positron annihilation mapping, burst polarimetry, and dark matter searches. The review traces the field from 1950s predictions through the first space detections in the 1960s to modern observatories. It then assesses missions meant to close the gap, noting the COSI telescope as a pathfinder for the late 2020s and a polarimetric mission like ASTROGAM as realistic for the 2030s.
arxiv-2606-10661:
Drummond-Curtis, Dalwadi, and Walker study tiny swimmers near walls in this 2026 arXiv paper on fluid dynamics. Bacteria and sperm swim close to surfaces, where their flow interacts with the boundary and bends their paths. Simple models treat the swimmer as a force dipole, an averaged push-pull flow, with shape held fixed. But real propulsion comes from rapid shape oscillations, and dipole models break down near a wall. The authors add higher-order flow singularities and use a multiscale analysis that keeps the fast oscillations explicit.

Now its fate near the boundary falls into three behaviours: crashing into the surface, escaping from it, and hovering at a steady distance. Hovering is the telling case: experiments see it in bacteria, yet the simplest averaged models never produce it. The lesson: the time-dependence earlier models discarded creates qualitatively new behaviour near a boundary.
arxiv-2606-10861:
Patkar and colleagues test whether chatbot interfaces can curb AI energy use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most fixes target models or data centers; the interface layer is rarely touched. The team built a prototype with a three-mode switch, per-response energy feedback, pre-send estimates, a usage dashboard, and energy analogies, then ran a five-day field study.

In a baseline survey of 77 people, 94.8 percent knew chatbots use energy, yet 88.3 percent misestimated how much. In the field study, the efficient mode took 55.8 percent of prompts, and observed energy use ran about 47 percent below an all-performance counterfactual. Users switched modes rather than shortening prompts.
arxiv-2606-10961:
Zhang develops a proof framework for process logic in a 2026 arXiv computer science paper. Process logic extends dynamic logic: instead of stating only how a program ends, its formulas describe whole execution traces. The hard part is reasoning about concrete first-order computations while keeping that trace information, and earlier calculi covered only fragments.

Zhang's fix is labels. Formulas carry labels recording trace and update information during derivations, rather than hiding it inside the formula. On that basis he defines cyclic labelled proof systems for propositional process logic, G3PPL, and the first-order version, G3FOPL. Soundness comes from infinite descent: any bad derivation would force an endless fall in a well-founded ordering, which cannot happen. Completeness comes from deriving the established rules of both logics inside the new systems. One uniform proof structure now handles trace properties and first-order computation alike.
arxiv-2606-11161:
Short presents AutoClassMK in a 2026 arXiv paper, a small neural network classifying stars by their spectra. Astronomers sort stars with the two-dimensional MK system, pairing a spectral class with a luminosity class. Experts traditionally match spectra against a standard atlas by eye. AutoClassMK automates that matching for normal stars against the libr18 atlas of Gray and Corbally.

The network is deliberately simple: five fully connected layers with two output heads, written entirely in basic Python and NumPy, with no specialized libraries, so every operation stays transparent. Training required large, noisy artificial datasets, built by augmenting the libr18 atlases, with luminosity classes simplified so every combination appears. Tested on noisy augmentations of the libr18_225 atlas, the network predicts MK spectral types with high precision and recall. Short also reimplemented the architecture in PyTorch for GPUs, and released all code and datasets openly.
arxiv-2606-11761:
Atif Hassan, Swanand Khare and Jiaul H Paik shrink training datasets on the fly in this 2026 arXiv paper. Dynamic dataset pruning periodically trains on a chosen subset of data to cut computing cost. But many methods sacrifice worst-group accuracy, the performance on whichever class fares worst, especially at aggressive pruning rates or on imbalanced data.

Their algorithm, RCAP, is robust, class-aware and probabilistic. A closed-form formula estimates what fraction of each class to keep. The fraction is adjusted every epoch from that class's aggregated loss. Sampling then favours high-loss examples within each class quota. Across six datasets, five models and three training styles, RCAP beats leading pruning methods on worst-group accuracy at every rate. Training on only ten percent of the data beats full-data training by over one percent on imbalanced datasets, running nearly nine times faster on average.
arxiv-2606-11861:
Magnus F Ivarsen leads an eight-author team reporting extreme events in the auroral ionosphere in this 2026 arXiv paper. During a magnetospheric substorm, the magnetotail, Earth's stretched magnetic tail, suddenly reconfigures in a dipolarisation event. A Canadian radar detected turbulent field structures racing eastward at over five thousand metres per second. The structures are Farley-Buneman waves in the auroral electrojets.

They move ten times faster than those waves should allow, implying transient electric fields near three hundred thirty millivolts per metre. An automatic clustering algorithm turned the radar into a tracking device for these echoes. Three THEMIS spacecraft watched the dipolarisation directly in space. A Swarm satellite crossing the arc recorded Alfvén waves, magnetic oscillations that travel along field lines. The authors interpret the bursts as the ionospheric footprint of an Alfvén pulse launched in the tail and amplified along converging field lines.
arxiv-2606-11961:
Antonio Pelusi, Stefano Braghin and Alberto Trombetta find a structural limit of in-context learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models are increasingly asked to generate structured data, such as synthetic tables, by learning from examples in the prompt alone. The authors test this on high-cardinality tabular data, tables whose category columns take very many values.

Across two open seven-billion-parameter models, extra examples improve numerical fidelity steadily. Categorical fidelity, however, hits a sharp ceiling: rare classes are not reproduced at all. On a fraud dataset, neither model ever generates a fraudulent transaction under any prompting setup. The authors name this failure categorical prior lock-in: prompting cannot rewrite the model's pre-trained prior over categories. Fine-tuning with a parameter-efficient method does overcome the ceiling, but at a price. It introduces measurable memorisation of training records, a privacy risk.
arxiv-2606-12161:
Holtzman and co-authors study how the paths inside a diffusion model settle as training data grows, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models link sample patterns to a simple reference distribution through a random path. Going forward adds noise; going backward removes it and creates new samples. Fixing the same noise, they ask how the backward path changes as pattern count grows without bound.

In a one-dimensional test case, paths approach their endless-data limit at a rate of one over the square root of the pattern count. Oddly, the mean square deviation stays infinite even while paths converge. That steady approach allows extrapolation: the team sketches a method estimating the endless-data path from finite runs. They offer it as a fresh route to density estimation and generalization, learning a distribution from few samples, with code included.
arxiv-2606-12261:
Kim and Qu package econometric methods for finding when a relationship changed, under rules the researcher already knows, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A structural break is a date where regression coefficients jump to new values. Known restrictions may pin some coefficients equal across regimes, or fix others at set values. Their R package, rbreak, handles such linear restrictions in two input forms and estimates break dates with confidence intervals around them.

The package adds a restricted sup-F test for whether any break happened at all. Critical values come from Monte Carlo simulation rather than fixed tables. A bootstrap restart lowers the risk of settling on a false break pattern. It also implements a linear model tree: a decision tree whose leaves each hold a full regression instead of a plain average. Worked applications demonstrate the tools. Future extensions aim at multi-equation systems.
arxiv-2606-12561:
Tian examines what a watched subsystem forgets about its past, and turns the forgetting into geometry, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Take a self-adjoint operator generating a decaying evolution, and watch only part of the space through a projection. The compressed evolution consists of positive contractions, but it breaks the semigroup law: evolving in two steps loses versus one. That defect, Tian shows, factors through the hidden part of the space.

The defect is a Gram kernel, inner products of hidden components, hence a positive-definite kernel. Its Kolmogorov space, the Hilbert space built from a kernel, recovers the dynamics the compression concealed. Rescaling to short times produces a tangent kernel with its own Kolmogorov space. On that space, the hidden block induces a contraction semigroup, and the kernel's representing vectors obey a cocycle identity. This imposes a restriction on which kernels can arise as compression tangents.
arxiv-2606-12661:
Mayank and colleagues present SIREN, a small neural model that spots solar wind stream interaction regions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A stream interaction region forms where fast solar wind overtakes slow wind, compressing the plasma between them. Such regions drive repeated geomagnetic storms, yet catalogues rely on expert inspection and simple thresholds. SIREN instead reads eleven measured solar wind quantities, including magnetic field, speed, density, and temperature.

The model is a lightweight Transformer, a network that weighs which moments in a sequence matter most, with about one hundred thousand trainable parameters. On a held-out set of one hundred and two events, it scores strongly while producing calibrated probabilities, meaning its stated confidence matches reality. Attention analysis shows it focuses on the interaction region itself. Proton density and magnetic field strength prove most informative, and sideways flow deflection emerges as a real but previously unmeasured signature.
arxiv-2606-12761:
Varikuti studies how information scrambles in a quantum system outside the standard chaos framework, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is the kicked harmonic oscillator, a particle in a harmonic trap taking periodic kicks. Because the plain oscillator is degenerate, its dynamics escape the Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser framework, and resonances rule instead. The test is the out-of-time-ordered correlator, a measure of how fast an operator spreads over time.

Near resonances, where the ratio of driving to oscillator frequency is an integer, the phase space shifts strongly even though the classical Lyapunov exponent stays small, so there is no usual chaos. At exact resonance the correlators grow quadratically with time, compared with linear growth away from resonance. The behaviour carries a number-theoretic pattern governed by Euler's totient function of the frequency ratio, showing that resonant structure can control how information spreads.
arxiv-2606-12861:
Chen and others present partition-selected flow polynomials, a broader form of the classical flow, chromatic, and Tutte polynomials of a graph, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The partition-selection method restricts those series to subgraphs whose connected components match vertex partitions. The authors prove deletion-contraction rules and specialisation links for the new polynomials, getting back the classical invariants when the choice allows every partition.

A special class, the affine flow polynomials, connects with Jaeger's nonhomogeneous flows, settings of flow values that need not sum to zero. A picture inside the edge-coordinate arrangement shows the characteristic polynomials coincide with Kochol's assigning polynomials and with the affine flow ones, which count nowhere-zero nonhomogeneous flows over finite fields. Their intersection posets yield contrasts of the coefficients of affine flow polynomials, and breakdown rules for the affine flow ones.
arxiv-2606-13161:
Omelchenko presents an algorithmic framework for the exhaustive generation and tabulation of genus-one knot and link diagrams, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knots and links in the thickened torus match virtual knots of genus 1. Tables reached only 5 crossings because controlling equivalence under surface homeomorphisms is the main bottleneck. The framework treats the embedding as the combinatorial object, encoding cellular 4-regular torus patterns by permutation pairs from the theory of maps on surfaces.

Unsensed equivalence classes are listed without duplication via canonical examples, and crossing settings, diagram reductions, and a generalised Kauffman-type bracket are all cast inside the same permutation model. The pipeline is checked against genus-one classifications for crossing numbers up to 5. It is then extended to 6, 7, and 8 crossings, giving what the author reports as the first genus-one tabulation at those crossing numbers. The dataset holds more than 33,000 knot and link types.
arxiv-2606-13461:
Malik explores teaching agents to edit neural networks by trial and error in this 2026 arXiv paper. Editing a trained network, to remove bias or erase information, requires a specialised algorithm designed for each objective. Designing those algorithms is slow, expert work. Malik formulates editing as a reinforcement learning problem: an agent modifies the model's weights and receives reward feedback. Two environments are introduced. In MaskWorld the agent scales weights multiplicatively, and in ShiftWorld it adds updates, giving styles of intervention.

The reward combines a utility-preservation term, which punishes damage to performance, with a task-specific editing term. The framework is tested on two jobs that need bespoke methods: reducing bias in text classification and machine unlearning in image classification. On unlearning, the learned policies drove accuracy on the forget set to nearly zero while keeping over 90 percent accuracy on the retained data. Bias mitigation improved.
arxiv-2606-13661:
Rothstein and colleagues automate a key heating system on the DIII-D fusion experiment in this 2026 arXiv paper. Electron cyclotron heating uses gyrotrons, microwave sources, to heat plasma at locations and drive current there. It supports scenario development, stability control, and impurity removal. The team's algorithm multitasks across gyrotrons, fine-tuning each one's mirror angle and power to hit a target deposition profile. Its core is a parallel neural network stand-in for the beam-tracing code, fast enough for real-time use, coupled with a genetic optimiser.

The algorithm ran in a DIII-D experiment and was checked against electron temperature measurements and offline ray tracing. It stayed reliable despite gyrotron failures mid-experiment and big changes in plasma parameters. Robustness to hardware failure is the key achievement: a heating system that re-plans around a dead gyrotron in real time. Such autonomy is essential for future reactors.
arxiv-2606-13761:
Karydas and colleagues ask whether dark matter spikes around black holes survive their stellar neighbourhoods in this 2026 arXiv paper. A spike is a steep concentration of dark matter predicted around a supermassive black hole, grown as the hole's gravity pulls matter inward. Spikes matter because they would imprint on gravitational-wave signals from small objects orbiting the hole. Using the Galactic Centre as a constrained case study, the authors evolve spikes under perturbations from the surrounding star cluster and its black holes.

Scattering by the star cluster depletes the dark matter at radii around a tenth of a parsec, well outside the region where the signals are produced. Closer in, the nearest known stellar perturbers induce tiny changes. At smaller radii, the effect of past mergers with small black holes is assessed by modelling successive events. The verdict is encouraging: the spike region that signals probe survives its environment intact.
arxiv-2606-13961:
Yuan and colleagues describe a custom instrument that prepares diamond surfaces and measures quantum defects without exposing samples to air. Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond are prized quantum sensors, but shallow ones sit nanometers from the surface. Surface dirt and damage shorten their coherence and destabilize their charge. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents an ultrahigh vacuum cluster tool joining surface science and cold microscopy in one platform.

One chamber anneals samples, cracks gases, and analyzes surfaces with two standard probes. A second chamber holds a cryogenic confocal microscope for spin and optical measurements. Vacuum transfer moves samples between them, preserving exact surface endings. The team tracked oxygen leaving the surface live during high-temperature annealing. They also measured how treatments change the noise felt by shallow centers. The platform ties surface chemistry directly to sensor behavior.
arxiv-2606-14061:
Ma and co-authors ask whether coding agents would work better if they could see a repository, not just read it. Developers grasp folder hierarchies and file dependencies at a glance, while agents receive flattened text. Their 2026 arXiv paper is the first systematic study of multimodal models on such tasks. SeeRepo renders structure and dependencies as graph images while keeping code as text.

Four models were tested on SWE-bench Verified. Vision alone failed badly: replacing text with graph images cut accuracy by up to thirty-four point one points while raising token cost. Adding visuals beside text worked: input tokens fell by up to twenty-six percent with accuracy kept or improved, and total cost fell by up to forty-six percent. Visual tools helped most during fault localization, finding the bug. Letting agents choose exploration depth saved most. Repair and validation stages suffered when visuals were invoked.
arxiv-2606-14261:
Basu and Staron test whether organizing security agents like a human team, with named roles, beats one model doing everything. Industrial vulnerability handling is a workflow: analysis, remediation, fix verification. Most language model tools instead tackle isolated tasks. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a role-based workflow with Planner, Analyzer, Fixer, and Verifier agents, evaluating it on twenty-five real-world C and C++ vulnerabilities, across three open models.

One variant wired the Analyzer to CodeQL, a static analysis engine. Detection accuracy reached forty-four percent, comparable to a frontier model's reported level, but fix accuracy was only nineteen percent: finding bugs is far easier than patching them. A strong Planner supported detection; CodeQL's effect was mixed, helping only when agents could prioritize and interpret its output. Patch quality was uneven enough that the authors insist on human review for security-critical work.
arxiv-2606-14361:
Ovcharenko, Duarte, and Schelter put language models inside machine learning pipelines as named, visible operators, not chat prompts. Building such pipelines means data preparation across messy sources, and chat-based help gives little control. Their 2026 arXiv paper demonstrates SemPipes, extending pipelines with LLM-powered semantic operators. Developers state data operations in natural language, mix them with Python, and the system synthesizes custom code at training time.

The demo interface, SemPiper, shows the pipeline graph, the synthesized code, and an evolutionary tree search improving implementations over time; each node exposes its code and validation score. In a house-price scenario, one cleans square footage by capping outliers, another uses a visual question answering model to pull features from listing photos. The optimizer's best pipeline extracted rich features: number of stories, landscape quality, architectural style, garage capacity, driveway size. Weaker variants used coarse flags like has-visible-garage.
arxiv-2606-14561:
Capuano and colleagues introduce ORCA, an open-source platform for dexterous robot hand research, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most manipulation research uses simple two-finger grippers, which often need two arms even for basic reorientation tasks. Human-like hands can learn from human video, but their control, simulation, and teleoperation software is scattered across one-off code bases.

The ORCA learning stack unifies low-level control, simulation, teleoperation from consumer devices, and hand retargeting, which maps human hand motion onto the robot, behind one interface. It plugs directly into popular robot-learning frameworks such as LeRobot, reusing their data and training pipelines. The team demonstrates the full workflow: an expert reorients an object in hand through a consumer virtual-reality headset, a policy is trained on the demonstrations, and the learned policy is evaluated reproducibly. Everything is open-sourced.
arxiv-2606-14661:
Petit and co-authors simulate rod-shaped particles sifting through a bed of spheres in a 2026 arXiv paper. Percolation here means grains filtering down under gravity. The bed is a static, disordered packing of larger spheres. Shape matters. Rods are not spheres, and their length can catch on pore throats. Pore throats are the narrow gaps between touching bed spheres.

The simulations reveal two regimes. In the trapping regime, rods halt after a limited distance. In the passing regime, they percolate at constant mean speed. Rod length governs which regime occurs. So does a geometric trapping threshold set by rod diameter and pore size. Speeds for all rod shapes collapse onto one curve when scaled. Short rods percolate nearly twice as fast as long ones. That is a clue for predicting segregation in mixtures.
arxiv-2606-14861:
Jiang and co-authors design materials that emit heat unevenly by direction in a 2026 arXiv paper. Normal thermal radiation obeys reciprocity: a surface emits and absorbs equally along reversed paths. Breaking that rule aids energy harvesting, sensing, and heat control. Classic devices need an external magnetic field to break it. These authors want the effect built into the material.

They combine first-principles calculations with Maxwell's equations to screen magnetic topological materials. Magnetic Weyl semimetals, such as Co3Sn2S2, show strong, broadband nonreciprocity in the infrared. They beat the standard semiconductor InAs with no applied field. The team distills two design rules. A large anomalous Hall response next to optical loss gives strength. Large optical loss with small dielectric spread gives bandwidth. The result is a predictive recipe for magnet-free thermal devices.
arxiv-2606-15261:
Duan and coauthors compute ring relations in the quantum K-theory of partial flag manifolds in a 2026 mathematical physics paper. A partial flag manifold parametrizes nested sequences of subspaces, and its quantum K-theory is a deformed ring whose product encodes curve-counting invariants. A correspondence with three-dimensional gauge theory identifies ring elements with line operators, defects called Schubert lines, whose fusion rules give the desired structure constants.

Using Gröbner basis methods, the authors compute two- and three-point functions of these operators in explicit examples. From them they extract the K-theoretic Littlewood-Richardson coefficients that earlier work left uncomputed. Taking a small-circle limit recovers the quantum cohomology ring, and their results match the literature there. The calculations turn an abstract correspondence into concrete numbers, giving geometers tested ring forms for flag manifolds and a template fit for other level structures in the gauge theory.
arxiv-2606-15361:
Magro presents a neuromorphic pipeline for detecting fast radio bursts in a 2026 astrophysics paper. These millisecond flashes from deep space must be caught in real time, and correcting their signals for dispersion, the smearing caused by electrons in space, dominates the computing cost at modern telescopes. The pipeline performs that correction with spiking neural networks, brain-inspired circuits that compute with brief pulses, running on a SpiNNaker 2 chip.

Three modes trade sensitivity for power. The precise float mode matches the standard Heimdall detector, catching nearly every injected burst. A graded mode keeps most of that sensitivity at a quarter of the power. The cheapest binary mode runs on under two milliwatts per beam yet still catches most bright, narrow bursts. A full board handles 48 beams at roughly one hundred watts, an order of magnitude below an equivalent graphics processor setup, a saving that matters for always-on sky surveys.
arxiv-2606-15461:
Dantas and coauthors present ESBMC-PLC in a 2026 software engineering paper, a formal verifier for the ladder diagram programs that run industrial controllers. Ladder diagrams, the rung-and-coil notation for programmable logic controllers, drive safety-critical machinery, yet mainstream model checkers cannot read their graphical format. The tool adds a frontend to the ESBMC checker, translating rungs into its intermediate language and modeling the controller's scan cycle as an endless loop with free inputs.

Engineers state safety requirements in a five-kind property language, no temporal logic needed, and the checker proves them by bounded search or k-induction. On thirteen benchmarks from six industrial domains, including real vendor programs, every benchmark is classified correctly. The runs find eight bugs with actionable counterexamples, complete seven unbounded proofs, and all finish in under sixty milliseconds. Verifying ladder logic, the results argue, is now a practical sub-second step.
arxiv-2606-15661:
Krasnov builds a cosmology model in 2026 in which an axion-like field gains strong small-scale structure during inflation without violating cosmic microwave background limits. A complex scalar field with a Mexican-hat potential couples to the Gauss-Bonnet term of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. That coupling restores the field's symmetry during inflation, postponing its breaking until later.

Because the phase transition happens mid-inflation, the model dodges the large-scale isocurvature perturbations that usually rule out such fields. The surviving particle can serve as fuzzy dark matter, though only a subdominant share, or as dark energy inhomogeneous on small scales, which might ease the Hubble tension. Black hole formation proves infeasible when the field does not backreact on inflation. Under specific conditions, though, the scenario produces gravitational waves in the band reported by NANOGrav, giving pulsar timing arrays a way to test it.
arxiv-2606-15761:
Gupta pins down bounds between two graph invariants in 2026: the saturation number, the size of a smallest maximal matching, and the harmonic index. A 2023 conjecture by the system TxGraffiti claimed saturation never exceeds the harmonic index, but a counterexample showed their ratio can grow without bound. Gupta asks what survives on trees.

For every graph with an edge, the harmonic index is less than four times the saturation number. On trees the saturation number is trapped between one quarter and three halves of the harmonic index, and both constants are best possible. The smallest counterexample is the friendship graph on nine vertices; the smallest tree one is a subdivided star on eleven. Hub families push the ratio toward m+1, while equal-degree graphs obey the conjecture. Practically, the saturation number is NP-hard to compute while the harmonic index takes linear time, so the cheap invariant brackets the expensive one.
arxiv-2606-15861:
Li and colleagues unify segmentation and question answering for robotic surgery scenes in 2026, using object tokens as the bridge. Surgical visual question answering needs fine-grained grounding, but vision-language models usually localise objects with coarse bounding boxes, losing the pixel-level structure surgery demands. Their framework makes one model do both tasks, sharing a single representation.

The vision-language model generates object tokens for scene elements; the tokens guide answer prediction and are projected into a Segment Anything decoder that produces segmentation masks. Training optimises the token embeddings against both objectives, so representations become spatially grounded by construction. On a private esophagectomy dataset and the public EndoVis18 benchmark, the method consistently beats baselines at surgical question answering. Because the design is backbone-agnostic, other vision-language models can adopt it. Grounding answers in pixel-level objects turns plausible commentary into checkable scene understanding.
arxiv-2606-16361:
An and co-authors extend in 2026 a bridge between algebra and category theory to generalized cluster algebras, testing conjectures of Fraser and Gleitz. Cluster algebras encode mutation rules with deep ties to geometry and physics. A monoidal categorification realizes one as the Grothendieck ring of a monoidal category, where cluster variables become simple objects and multiplication becomes tensor product. The authors define this notion for generalized cluster algebras, whose exchange polynomials carry extra terms.

Their arena is the category of finite-dimensional modules over a restricted quantum loop algebra for sl_k at a root of unity. Subcategories picked out by a bipartition of the Dynkin diagram supply the categorification, with cluster monomials matching real simple objects. The work engages the Fraser-Gleitz conjectures on when the algebra equals its upper cluster algebra. Computations suggest the inclusion can be strict: some elements resist expression as polynomials in cluster variables.
arxiv-2606-16461:
Yukhimchuk and co-authors protect private text sent to cloud language models in 2026 by rotating it into a secret basis the server can compute in but never read. Running big models locally is often impractical, so split inference sends hidden representations to a provider instead of raw tokens. Those representations leak: nearest-neighbor search against the public embedding table recovers over 35 percent of tokens in the top ten guesses. The client therefore multiplies embeddings by a secret orthogonal matrix.

Ordinary transformers would garble rotated input, so the authors build ConjFormer, exactly equivariant under all orthogonal transforms. A scalar form of RMSNorm plus blockwise orthogonal conjugation of every linear weight does the job. The server runs the forward pass in the rotated basis and never sees an unrotated state. On GPT-2 and Llama 3.2 1B models fine-tuned on PubMed text, token recovery falls to at most 1.3 percent, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16661:
Langlois proposes a 2026 retrieval method called SCAR for retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model answers using fetched text. Documents are stored in fixed chunks, and key evidence often splits across a chunk boundary. Widening every window fixes recall but wastes tokens, the units of text a model has to process.

SCAR expands a retrieved chunk only when a neighbor looks relevant and structurally continuous with it. Its threshold is relative to each chunk's own relevance score, so one setting transfers across embedding models without recalibration. Across four corpora covering rules, contracts and company filings, SCAR keeps high recall on boundary-split questions while using far fewer chunks than static windowing. A paired statistical test confirms the saving is large and significant. Generation faithfulness also holds while context tokens drop, making SCAR a practical efficiency upgrade for production search systems.
arxiv-2606-16861:
Bujotzek and colleagues release an open-source monitoring framework for multi-center radiology studies in a 2026 paper. Large imaging studies span many hospitals, and coordinating them often means emails and shared tables that go stale within weeks. Nobody then knows how much data each site holds or where recruitment lags.

Their framework collects aggregated metrics from each site and displays them on configurable dashboards, built on the widely used Grafana and Prometheus tools. Only summaries travel, so patient privacy and each site's intellectual property stay protected. Integrated into the Kaapana imaging platform, the system runs inside the Germany-wide RACOON consortium across all thirty-eight German university clinics. Site teams can explore data holdings and spot partners for collaborations, while study leaders watch progress in near real time. The code and integration are public, so other consortia can adopt the same live picture.
arxiv-2606-17161:
Valdivia-Mera and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a helical version of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a much-studied toy model of quantum chaos. The new model lives in one space dimension plus time and uses left- and right-moving Majorana fermions. Random four-particle couplings act within a symmetry-controlled hierarchy of chirality sectors, giving the model a tunable structure.

At the most restrictive end of the hierarchy, symmetry forces the couplings into a density-density form that can be solved exactly by bosonization, so the theory is integrable. Allowing the full set of sectors breaks that protected structure at face value. Even so, the large-system infrared limit stays tractable through short-distance selection rules and disorder averaging. The whole interaction space proves marginally irrelevant there, so the theory becomes free and integrable at low energies.
arxiv-2606-17261:
Melis presents a 2026 arXiv paper on software benchmarking, arguing that modern computers quietly break the assumptions behind standard performance measurement. Adaptive, stateful mechanisms in hardware and software make each run depend on history, so naive estimates of a single program's speed are biased. Fixing that bias, Melis argues, needs speculative guesses about system dynamics that cannot be checked, so the whole goal of measurement should be rethought from the start.

The proposal is to chase performance differences rather than absolute numbers, framing benchmarking as the decision problem of picking the fastest program. For that decision, relative knowledge is enough to reach the right answer in practice. Simple experiment designs are given whose contrast estimates stay consistent because program-specific biases cancel under stated assumptions. The designs yield the correct choice in the long run and a robust method for finite budgets.
arxiv-2606-17461:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on AutoGate, a system that automates fine-grain clock gating, one of the best ways to cut a chip's dynamic power. Gating idle flip-flop groups saves energy, but finding workload-dependent chances to gate still takes manual register-transfer-level rewriting. Language model approaches stall on two facts: waveforms span millions of cycles, and real codebases are huge hierarchies where correctness must survive every edit the system makes.

AutoGate pairs a machine learning clustering step with language model rewriting in an agentic framework. The clustering distils raw toggling traces into compact summaries that point the model at real gating chances. A hierarchy of agents splits big designs into modules that can be optimised separately but coherently. Power fell by about half on small designs on average, with solid gains on industrial designs too.
arxiv-2606-17661:
Weymouth and Lauber present a 2026 arXiv paper, written for the Journal of Fluid Mechanics, on why parachutes cut from flat sheets in the kirigami style fall so stably. Such canopies deploy into an inverted shape and descend without the tumbling that plagues falling disks, but the mechanism was unclear. The authors simulate prescribed acceleration and free fall in effectively endless domains, using a far-field boundary rule rebuilt from the flow's own vorticity so size effects nearly vanish.

Deployment cuts the straight forces severalfold as air leaks through the canopy, while the turning moments grow with the longer lever arm. Stable flight appears once the canopy opens to about half its radius, with wobbles damped quickly after disturbances. Smaller openings tumble through side-slip and spin coupling, like falling disks do. The simple rule: deploy near the radius for high drag with stability.
arxiv-2606-17761:
Zhang, Hu, and Gu present a 2026 arXiv paper on a modular way to optimise molecular orbitals in quantum chemistry, whatever solver supplies the correlation. Orbitals fitted to the correlated state lower energies and smooth energy curves, but each electronic-structure method usually brings its own orbital machinery. The new framework splits the work: any solver hands over its one- and two-particle density matrices. A single constrained optimiser then rotates the orbitals on the manifold of orthonormal sets with an implicit steepest-descent update.

Because the optimiser needs only those matrices, many solver types share one interface unchanged. Where the classic self-consistent procedure settles into a higher-energy local answer, the new scheme can recover lower stationary solutions. Extra devices speed the outer loop and improve excited-state averaging. Tests on three molecules show lower energies and smoother curves than fixed-orbital references throughout.
arxiv-2606-17861:
Luo and colleagues built a benchmark that asks coding agents to create whole playable games, in a 2026 paper. Turning a written game description into a working game inside a real engine is harder than ordinary coding, since scripts, scenes, assets, and runtime play must all fit together. The team argues that fair tests here need three things: a real engine setting, a complete game artifact, and judging through actual play.

Their GameCraft-Bench puts agents to work in the Godot engine and scores what they ship by interaction rather than by reading code. The results are sobering for current systems. Frontier agents often produce recognizable mechanics or runnable prototypes, but they still fail to assemble coherent games with enough content, working feedback, and polish. The benchmark gives the field a shared yardstick for end-to-end game generation.
arxiv-2606-18161:
Palacios and colleagues offer a way to read the spectrum of a quantum system as it morphs between two Hamiltonians, in a 2026 paper. Such interpolations underlie adiabatic quantum computing and phase diagrams, but tracking eigenvalues usually means slicing the path into many small steps and diagonalizing each. Their method leans on accessible symmetries, certifiable reflections tied to the problem class that split the Hilbert space in two.

At each point along the path, they pick the accessible symmetry closest to being satisfied and project the Hamiltonian onto its sectors. The result is a hierarchy of weakly coupled pseudo-eigenspaces with explicit residual couplings between them. This compressed picture still carries the fingerprints of quantum phase transitions, estimates where they occur, and hints at their nature. How well it works depends on how compatible the chosen symmetry family is with the problem at hand.
arxiv-2606-18361:
Sheffer studies how much general information about a topologically ordered phase can be read from the entanglement of its ground state, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Such phases cannot be told apart by local order, so teams probe them with multipartite entanglement measures built by swapping parts between copies of the wavefunction.

Sheffer shows that the topological partition function of a manifold can be read off whenever the manifold meets a new condition called local achirality. That gives access to phase data beyond the modular matrices. As a sorting step, he proves that four-dimensional locally achiral manifolds must have vanishing Pontryagin number, and ties that obstruction to time-reversal protected topological order. He closes with an entanglement measure that detects one such nontrivial protected state. The conjecture left open is sweeping: vanishing Pontryagin numbers may be the only barrier, which would make all three-dimensional manifolds usable as probes.
arxiv-2606-18461:
Shizuya examines the unusual electron states that live along a line junction in bilayer graphene when an electric bias flips sign across it, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. In a magnetic field, bilayer graphene hosts a set of nearly degenerate low-energy levels split by valley. Gating traps some of those electrons inside the band gap along the junction, forming so-called kink states.

He studies their spectra and electromagnetic response. Two kinds of valley current run along the junction: a drift current driven by the bias gradient and a circulating current from the electrons' cyclotron motion. Both flow in essentially the same direction, and the circulating part carries a magnetic character unlike that of higher levels. Together they circulate within the kink states, creating a narrow channel of orbital magnetization. Shizuya points to networks of such gated junctions as a route to electrically controlled valley electronics.
arxiv-2606-18561:
Ali and colleagues propose a way to infer how a sensor system has degraded, and correct for it, without any labeled examples of the degradation, in a 2026 machine learning paper. The target is particle detectors. Sensors drift and age, distorting the data distributions that methods rely on, yet the parameters behind the change are usually not directly observable.

Their approach borrows from Wasserstein adversarial learning but repurposes the generator as a calibration transformation whose trainable weights are the physical parameters sought, while a critic supplies a distributional distance signal. They test it on a toy tracking detector with controlled layer shifts, then on simulated calorimeter data with cell-by-cell aging. The method recovered cells' aging coefficients and improved agreement between corrected and reference energy distributions. The method faded as channel noise grew toward the size of the effect, marking where this inference runs out of information.
arxiv-2606-19061:
Amayo and colleagues compare element abundances in H II regions and planetary nebulae across the Galactic disk in 2026. Both trace oxygen, neon, chlorine, and argon, but at different epochs. H II regions show today's gas, while planetary nebulae preserve older material from their parent stars. Comparing radial gradients in the two samples can reveal how the disk's chemistry evolved over time, if distances and abundances are handled with care.

The study uses high-quality samples from the DESIRED catalogue, with two abundance sets per object, one with a temperature fluctuation correction. Oxygen values are corrected for dust loss, and H II results are checked against Cepheid stars. All gradients are statistically significant except chlorine and argon in H II regions. With the temperature correction, oxygen gradients from H II regions and Cepheids agree well. Oxygen and neon gradients differ between the young and old tracers.
arxiv-2606-19161:
Huang and colleagues introduce HT-Bench in 2026, a large benchmark for tactile representation learning in dexterous robot hands. A universal tactile benchmark is hard because sensors, data formats, and robot bodies vary so much. The team pursues a scalable direction instead. They pair egocentric vision with full-hand tactile data, so touch can be judged alongside what the robot itself sees during a task.

HT-Bench holds ten million image frames and millions of tactile frames across more than two hundred tasks. It tests whether tactile codes capture contact geometry, align with vision, and generalize to unseen tasks. Four tasks cover retrieval, inpainting, vision-to-touch synthesis, and frame prediction. Their HandTouch encoder learns through spatial, cross-modal, and temporal stages with vector quantization. It beats representative tactile baselines across the bench, with clear gains on fine-grained retrieval. The bench gives hand sensing a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2606-19261:
Ricci derives bivariate incomplete-Bessel kernels for the first nonlinear Vlasov-Maxwell response of a magnetized plasma in 2026. The weakly nonlinear response is usually written as a double cyclotron-harmonic expansion. That form is explicit but breeds long sums of Bessel functions and nested resonance denominators through repeated expansion. In earlier linear work, the author kept the Larmor phase unexpanded and evaluated the key integral with a new incomplete-Bessel function, gaining a cleaner form.

The same idea is now applied directly to the first nonlinear equation. The nonlinear source contains the linear response of an inner mode. When that response is written in incomplete-Bessel form, the outer integral yields a two-variable orbit-resolvent function. The paper derives the nonlinear distribution function in these terms. It collects identities for the current projection and recovers a classic double-harmonic formula by expansion.
arxiv-2606-19361:
Bynum and colleagues propose computational identifiability in 2026, a practical alternative to classical identification theory. Identification asks when a target quantity can be pinned down from available information, such as a causal graph. Classical answers work in expectation. They assume infinite data or other idealized conditions. A quantity can thus count as identified in theory while no feasible procedure recovers it from real data.

The new framework defines a finite search for an estimator instead. If the search finds an estimator within a set error tolerance, the quantity counts as identified. That verdict depends on stated assumptions, including a prior over parameters, and on the search method itself. Experiments show the framework answering fine-grained questions that theory alone blurs. Two quantities with the same theoretical status can differ sharply once the search is bounded. The verdict becomes a joint property of the problem, the data size, and the compute budget.
arxiv-2606-19661:
Raymundo Arróyave introduces HEACalculator in 2026, an open-source Python tool for high-entropy alloy design. High-entropy alloys mix several main elements and can pair strength with thermal stability. Early design hinges on whether a candidate mix forms one solid solution or splits into rival phases.

HEACalculator gathers the field's descriptors and formation rules in one place. It computes sixteen standard quantities, including mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy. Valence electron concentration, atomic size mismatch, and electronegativity mismatch join the list. Derived stability parameters such as Omega, Lambda, and Phi come built in. Eight published solid-solution prediction criteria are evaluated side by side. Researchers can screen candidate mixes before costly synthesis and testing. The code runs in plain Python, so labs can add it to tools they already use each day. The tool is released openly with documentation for reuse in alloy workflows.
arxiv-2606-19761:
Lars Warren Ericson finishes a machine-checked completeness proof for a hybrid logic, inside the Lean 4 proof assistant. His 2026 paper concerns the logic L with a universal binder: modal logic enriched with nominals, which name single worlds, plus a satisfaction-style quantifier over them. Alex Oltean's 2023 formalization had mechanized the syntax, semantics, proof system, and soundness, but left the theorem itself unproved.

The obstacle is manufacturing fresh names at two different points of the proof. For the extended Lindenbaum construction, each step needs a nominal fresh for the whole growing set; the right tool is structural freshness, reserving an endless supply of names by construction. The witnessed successor of a maximal consistent set needs a different device, since its canonical reduct provably mentions every nominal. The paper surveys the design space before settling its choices.
arxiv-2606-19861:
Yutaro Yamada, Kento Uchida, and Shinichi Shirakawa teach an evolutionary optimiser to tune its own weights in 2026. Adaptive stochastic natural gradient methods already adapt their learning rate while searching. Weight parameters, though, lack guidance when parallel populations grow large.

Their Weight Adaptation variant estimates the update direction's signal from past natural gradients. Gradient ascent then adjusts the weights to maximise that signal during the run. Learning rate adaptation secures steady improvement conditions. Weight adaptation aims to make each improvement as large as possible. Binary optimisation tests span population sizes from twenty-five to one hundred. The new method beats PBIL and the plain adaptive method across those settings. Strong noise also fails to break its efficiency. Parallel black-box search gains a self-tuning knob it previously set by hand.
arxiv-2606-20261:
Niels de Graaf Sousa, Varun Venkatesh, and Amin Doostmohammadi study what happens when a shell of active, oriented material starts to push on itself. Their 2026 paper models active oriented solids: aligned particles embedded in a deformable elastic surface, each generating internal stress. Focusing on cylindrical shells, the authors run a linear stability analysis to find which buckling modes activity can excite. Nematic orientation and the sign of activity select among axial, circumferential, and helical deformations.

One result is striking: circumferential modes go unstable at very small drive, because they cost no stretching. Nonlinear runs confirm the linear predictions and go beyond them. The shells settle into steady diamond-shaped patterns, or keep moving through oscillations, traveling domain walls, and moving waves, none of which appear in passive shells. The work catalogs activity-driven buckling, relevant to tissues that shape themselves and materials designed to morph.
arxiv-2606-20561:
Arkaprava Sinha and Dominick Reilly answer questions over hours-long videos by proposing answers cheaply and verifying them expensively. Their 2026 paper targets long video question answering in activities of daily living, where relevant evidence is sparse in untrimmed footage. Dense processing with big vision-language models costs too much; caption-only reasoning misses motion-centric evidence.

TimeProVe first uses lightweight modules to generate action-grounded answer-evidence hypotheses. Only then does it invoke an expensive vision-language model, and only for targeted verification of those hypotheses. The split spends heavy compute exactly where the answer is decided. Long-video reasoning becomes affordable without going blind to brief, localized events.
arxiv-2606-21261:
Massimino, Shevchenko, Papp, and Revai examine kaonic hydrogen in 2026, an exotic atom where a negatively charged kaon orbits a proton. Two forces act at once: the long-range Coulomb attraction, which alone would bind the atom, and the strong antikaon-nucleon force, which alone can form the Lambda(1405) resonance. The authors study both kinds of states together rather than separately, asking how their energy levels shift and rearrange.

Solving the Lippmann-Schwinger equation with separable strong potentials fitted to realistic models, they find a genuine level rearrangement between the two families of states. The 1s shift of kaonic hydrogen turns out to be attractive in character, contrary to a naive reading. Absorption in the strong force, which gives the levels their widths, does not destroy the rearrangement effect.
arxiv-2606-21461:
Yitao Jiang and seven colleagues present the Manipulider in 2026, an underwater robot that swims by buoyancy alone, with no thrusters to tangle in weeds or stir up sediment. Four syringe-based buoyancy engines around its body adjust both total buoyancy and its center, letting the vehicle hold steep tilt angles by static balance and glide in a controlled way. A magnetic modular interface swaps payloads such as grippers or sensors in moments.

Each engine shifts about forty milliliters, giving roughly 160 grams of total buoyancy authority in tests. The robot held stable tilts above sixty degrees in single and dual engine modes. The team demonstrated tilt control, ascent and descent primitives, and a gripper run that carried a payload across a tank. The design suits quiet, long-duration inspection and gentle manipulation work.
arxiv-2606-21661:
Jiehui Huang, Yuechen Zhang, and eight colleagues present UnityShots in 2026, a system generating multi-shot videos whose people, scenes, and voices survive the cut. Shot-by-shot generators forget, while end-to-end training cannot scale to long sequences. Built on LTX-2.3, UnityShots trains on annotated film and music-video shots. It gives the video stream a fixed-size memory: a long-term slot anchored to the opening shot and a short-term slot holding the previous shot's tail. Both update at each cut through a gate fed by visual cut probability and beat tracking.

The audio stream re-injects a reference speaker token each shot, preserving vocal timbre without an ever-growing audio bank. A learned cut-type control lets users dial transition strength. On a new 200-sequence multicultural benchmark, UnityShots leads open-source rivals on every cross-shot coherence measure and matches the best closed system.
arxiv-2606-21761:
Li and Miller develop, in 2026, a general method for computing two invariants of ample groupoids, algebraic structures that encode the symmetries of well-behaved spaces. The invariants are groupoid homology and the K-theory of the linked operator algebra, both central to classifying such algebras. Their approach rests on two ideas: discretisation and independent resolutions.

Under discretisation, a special class they call independent groupoids behaves, for both invariants, exactly like discrete groupoids, which are far easier to handle. Any ample groupoid can then be resolved, meaning approximated in a controlled way, by these independent ones. That gives a systematic recipe for the computations. The authors work through Garside categories, a family covering higher-rank graphs, self-similar groups, and spherical Artin-Tits groups. They also apply the machinery to the homology of Stein's groups.
arxiv-2606-22061:
Do and colleagues introduce NL2Scratch in 2026, a benchmark for generating Scratch programs from natural language descriptions. Scratch, the block-based environment used in early programming education, builds programs from visual blocks arranged into concurrent, event-driven scripts. That structure breaks assumptions behind most natural-language-to-code research, which targets text languages like Python, so a dedicated benchmark and metric were needed.

The dataset holds over three hundred thousand parser-valid pairs of descriptions and real Scratch programs. To judge quality beyond surface overlap, the authors define Semantic Alignment Consistency, an interpretable slot-level metric of agreement between a description and a program. A validated pool and an 800-item diagnostic benchmark were built with it. Across instruction-tuned and fine-tuned models, token-level scores above 0.93 often hid imperfect semantic alignment, especially on longer programs. Errors concentrated on action, condition, and numeric slots.
arxiv-2606-22261:
Nie and colleagues propose, in 2026, learning a model of the normal world to detect abnormality when abnormal labels are scarce. Instead of learning an incomplete space of abnormal classes, their model learns normal behaviour from abundant normal events. A few abnormal examples then serve only to calibrate the boundary of normality, and the energy also grades how far an event has drifted.

Their Hypergraph Entropic Normal-World Model represents sensor windows as context-conditioned hypergraphs, whose edges join groups of variables. Its energy combines temporal prediction surprise, hypergraph mismatch surprise, and departure from a latent normal manifold. On the NASA turbofan degradation benchmark it reaches an AUROC of 0.9983 on the hardest subset, with strong zero-shot and few-shot results throughout. Probing tests show the energy rises along degradation paths and penalizes context-mismatched coupling breaks.
arxiv-2606-22461:
Emmanouil Vourliotis, writing on behalf of the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations, reviews searches for multi-Higgs production in this 2026 paper. The two collaborations run the largest detectors at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Measuring how the Higgs boson interacts with itself is a key goal, because it reveals the shape of the Higgs potential, the energy landscape behind mass.

Producing Higgs bosons in pairs probes the trilinear self-coupling, the strength of the three-Higgs interaction. Producing three at once would probe the quartic coupling, the four-Higgs interaction, though it is far rarer. The review also covers resonant searches, which look for a heavy new particle decaying into two Higgs bosons, or into a Higgs plus a new scalar. Many theories beyond the standard model predict such decays. Vourliotis summarizes recent results from both experiments across many final states, for both resonant and nonresonant production.
arxiv-2606-22961:
Yue Que and colleagues question how recommender systems are graded in a 2026 paper. Recommenders rank items for each user, and developers judge them offline using past clicks and purchases. Que and colleagues argue this grading has two deep flaws. Recorded behavior reflects what users happened to see, so it distorts true taste. The usual top-K scores also give a bare number with no reason behind it, which helps nobody improve the system.

Que and colleagues propose using a large language model as the judge instead. The model reads recommendations and explains its verdicts in words. That setup aims for grades that track real preference more closely. It also makes each grade explainable, so developers can see why a list scored well or badly. The work appears in the proceedings of the KDD 2026 conference on data mining.
arxiv-2606-23361:
Thinh Nguyen and colleagues rethink backdoor attacks on molecular graph networks in a 2026 security paper. A backdoor poisons training so a model mispredicts whenever a trigger pattern appears. Earlier molecular backdoors were tested as abstract graph edits. Real pipelines never train on arbitrary graphs, though: records must pass parsing, sanitization, and consistency checks first. The team formalizes that admission stage as ChemGuard. A record enters only when its molecular string passes sanitization and the graph rebuilt from the string matches the submitted graph.

Nguyen and colleagues show many existing backdoors collapse under admission checks, since their poisons are chemically invalid or inconsistent. They then prove checks alone are not enough. Their ChemBack attack builds chemically feasible trigger attachments and ranks candidates by fingerprint similarity to clean target-class molecules, all without touching the victim model. Across benchmarks and defenses, the admitted backdoor still works.
arxiv-2606-23461:
Sajad Farrokhi and colleagues track heart regulation in cancer survivors during daily life in a 2026 health study. The team uses wearable ECG data gathered in real-world settings, not a clinic. Motion noise makes heart rate variability hard to read outside the lab. Their approach sorts movement into light, moderate, and vigorous levels using motion sensors. A robust pipeline finds heartbeats and grades signal quality without manual labels. Vigorous exertion gave unreliable estimates, so the study focuses on the light and moderate levels.

Farrokhi and colleagues compare breast cancer survivors with healthy controls. The survivors showed higher heart rates and lower variability at both levels. The gaps widened at the moderate level. There, standard measures fell sharply for the survivor group. The gaps were significant, with strong and consistent effects.
arxiv-2606-23761:
Meng and colleagues clean noisy speech with a brain inspired spiking network that uses a fraction of the usual parameters, in a 2026 paper on neuromorphic computing. Speech enhancement recovers clean speech from noisy recordings and fronts hearing aids and voice recognition. Spiking neural networks compute with binary spikes, like neurons, and suit low power hardware. Their binary activations have kept quality behind conventional networks, though.

The proposed network, GSU DBNet, runs two branches at once. One models the magnitude spectrum, how strong each frequency is, and the other the complex spectrum, which also carries phase. A gated spiking unit with a dual path design exploits both time and frequency structure. On a standard benchmark it reaches a perceptual quality score just above three with under four hundred thousand parameters, only about five to eleven percent of conventional model sizes.
arxiv-2606-24561:
Wang and colleagues reconstruct CT images on quantum hardware, spending their binary variable budget only where the image is still uncertain. Quantum computed tomography casts the rebuild as a quadratic binary problem, for quantum annealers and hybrid solvers. Gray images strain the encoding: fixed bit planes balloon the problem as precision rises, while low bit encodings quantise coarsely.

Dynamic interval encoding refines iteratively. Each round encodes only the still-active pixels, within local gray level intervals around the running estimate. A boundary hit guided rule switches between widening the search and refining locally. Before forming the final problem, data agreement is balanced against an edge preserving quadratic prior, for stability. Sparse view and limited angle fan beam experiments show the framework recovering structures and gray level spreads better than the analytic, iterative, variational, and quantum rivals. Wang's 2026 team targets the dose sparing scan shapes where classical reconstruction struggles most.
arxiv-2606-24661:
Llave, Pallone, and Daniel evaluate whether a new standard codec for immersive audio actually sounds better. Higher-order ambisonics captures full spatial sound fields but needs many channels, sixteen for third order, inflating storage and bitrate. The recently standardised IVAS codec codes such content for communication; the obvious baseline is coding every channel separately, the multi-mono approach.

Perceptual evaluation spans synthetic mixes and native recordings across varied content and spatialisation methods. IVAS outperforms multi-mono at the same bitrate, because it exploits correlation between channels that independent coding throws away. The advantage is especially robust for signals with high interchannel correlation, such as scenes composed of a limited number of plane waves, where multi-mono performs poorly. Llave's 2026 listening results give broadcasters and platform builders evidence, from human ears rather than error metrics, that the standard's complexity buys audible quality for virtual and augmented reality audio.
arxiv-2606-24861:
Pieter van Rooyen models adaptive systems that tie inference to irreversible action, where each commitment deletes future options. He treats information processing as a thermodynamic load on a finite capacity decoder. Recoverable operation is characterised by a feasibility margin and a stability diagnostic. When induced information flow exceeds integrative capacity for long enough, the model says, recoverability fails. The failure is structural, independent of goals, policies, or physical substrate.

Adding capacity alone does not fix this in his analysis. Without certification or gating, higher throughput speeds the loss. Van Rooyen makes the feedback plain: each uncertified act spawns fresh candidates on average. That turns the smooth feasibility transition into a first order one, with lucid and collapsed states coexisting in a bistable region. Recovery then shows hysteresis, and beyond a threshold spawn rate, cutting load cannot restore operation.
arxiv-2606-25161:
Language model agents with long term memory keep rewriting that memory: writing, revising, and deleting entries over time. Tianyu Yang and four colleagues warn that bad updates, omissions, corruption, and invented content become persistent failures once stored, poisoning later reasoning. Their framework, TrustMem, makes the updating itself trustworthy.

A Memory Transition Verifier grades each proposed update on coverage, preservation, and faithfulness. Candidate updates under the same memory state are then ranked into preference pairs, and preference guided reinforcement learning trains the agent to pick the safer update. TrustMem posts state of the art results on three memory benchmarks. On one of them it lifts memory extraction by about twelve F1 points. Against the strongest baseline for each error type, it cuts omissions, corruption, and hallucination by roughly forty, seventy nine, and fifty percent.
arxiv-2606-25261:
Qubits packed together in a solid lose their quantum information faster, and engineers need formulas that predict how fast. Dhiman Nandi and Sanghamitra Neogi build such a framework in 2026, treating one qubit as the system and its neighbours as an effective bath. Their mean field Lindblad model folds in energy relaxation, excitation hopping in both directions, and the thermal population of the surrounding qubits. Closed form solutions give relaxation and decoherence times directly.
