Simulations show that crowding qubits closer shortens both lifetimes, while flicker noise erodes only the coherence time. Applied to erbium doped cerium oxide, long range energy transfer of the Förster type reproduced the measured drop in relaxation time as doping rose. Short range exchange could not match the data, identifying the long range route as dominant.
arxiv-2606-25561:
Proving a cryptographic scheme secure with formal tools takes experts who can translate the scheme into a verifier's private language. Zhaoxuan Li and colleagues benchmark whether language models can do that translation in 2026. Their test set holds seven hundred instances drawn from over six hundred schemes, seven formal verifier languages, and one hundred sixty security properties. Five skills are probed separately: interpreting, generating, completing, transforming, and correcting formal descriptions.

Nine leading models were evaluated, and a split pattern emerged. Interpretation and completion went well, helped by the models' general code fluency. Generation, transformation, and correction lagged badly, with the best model scoring under half marks overall. The authors add practical remedies, from few shot prompting to light fine tuning, aimed at the executability bottleneck where outputs look plausible but no verifier will accept them.
arxiv-2606-25761:
When no gradient exists, optimiser families wander the landscape by sampling. Evolution strategies keep a parametric search cloud. Consensus methods herd loose particles. Integration based methods tilt a distribution by fitness. Johannes Ackermann and Stefano Peluchetti unify these spherical black box optimisers in 2026 within one theoretical frame. The families differ mainly in two choices. One is how fitness is aggregated, setting a taste for sharp or flat minima. The other is how widely consensus is gathered, setting whether one peak or many are kept.

Knowing the dials, the pair build hybrids that interpolate between the classics. One hybrid steers the flatness preference explicitly, trading raw performance for robustness in continuous control. Others fuse parametric efficiency in high dimensions with particle based multimodality, and proved competitive at merging language models on tight evaluation budgets. On standard benchmarks and locomotion tasks, the hybrids sometimes beat both of their parents.
arxiv-2606-25861:
A coplanar waveguide both delivers microwaves to a sample and reads its magnetic response, yet designers have lacked a rule for the geometry that hears faintest best. Scott Dietrich and Artur Solodovnyk supply one in 2026 by an analogy. Coupling to the sample and loss in the conductor scale together, and that shared scaling maps the design problem onto the Beer Lambert optimisation of optical spectrophotometry. The whole question collapses to one parameter. Its answer depends on the sample's shape and the dominant noise source, not on the material, the frequency, or the system's losses.

The prediction is a near universal optimum at one neper of attenuation. Seven published resonance instruments, benchmarked against the rule, split into two fabrication classes. Board milled designs hit a ceiling set by their narrowest slot. Photolithographic ones approach the theoretical optimum. A meander layout offers big board samples a direct route to near optimal sensitivity.
arxiv-2606-25961:
Oleksiy Shcherbina, a mathematician at Karazin Kharkiv National University, proves well-posedness for the magnetic Zakharov system on two-dimensional bounded domains. The system comes from plasma physics and couples three fields: a high-frequency electric field, the ion density fluctuation, and a self-generated magnetic field. Well-posedness means solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on their starting data, the basic licence for trusting any simulation of the model.

Initial and boundary value problems are treated together, with the fields pinned to zero at the domain edge in the stated pattern. Shcherbina proves the problems are globally well-posed in Sobolev-type function classes, which measure both size and smoothness of the fields. Dropping the magnetic field reduces the system to the classical Zakharov equations of plasma physics, so the result extends a well-studied theory to the magnetic case on realistic bounded regions.
arxiv-2606-26161:
Viola Zhong and Qirui Li show that a chat model's persona can switch its refusals off. Refusal and persona each correspond to directions in the model's activation space. The two were studied apart until now. Working with Qwen and Llama instruction-tuned models, the pair extract a compliant-persona direction and a refusal direction. Interventions on both reveal the interaction directly.

Steering toward a compliant persona crushes refusal. In the Llama model, refusal falls from near total to almost none. Adding the refusal direction back restores refusal only at late layers. Early layers stay suppressed. Removing the persona direction in a late window brings refusal back to baseline. A random direction does nothing. Refusal, then, is expressed late, downstream of the persona gate. Safety work that treats refusal as one isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.
arxiv-2606-26361:
Emma Kasteleyn and Ana Lucic peer inside Aurora, a machine learning weather model, to see what it knows. Foundation models now emulate the atmosphere cheaply and well, but their reasoning is opaque. Layer-wise relevance propagation and pooled principal component analysis are the probes. Seasonality organizes the model's inner space above all: its latent geometry is ruled by the annual cycle. Extreme storms, strikingly, do not cluster apart in that space.

Attribution tells a warmer story. For the Great Storm of nineteen eighty-seven, the model attends to features matching the storm's true three-dimensional structure. Masking the regions it relies on hurts its forecasts far more than random masking does, by a factor above three. Nobody taught Aurora vertical structure directly. Coherence about the atmosphere's shape emerged from forecast training alone. Interpretability results like these are how black-box weather models earn operational trust.
arxiv-2606-26661:
Sangjin Han, Hoseong Jung, Jeongtae Her, Changhyun Choi, and H. Jin Kim present LAMP, a motion forecasting framework for self-driving cars. Forecasting where nearby road users will go is essential for safe planning. Standard predictors minimise distance errors but ignore lane structure. Their less likely guesses often cut across lanes impossibly. Planners cannot trust such prediction sets.

LAMP anchors its guesses to motion primitives aligned with lanes. Primitives are reusable movement shapes learned from data by a compression model. A selector then filters the intentions behind each guess. It keeps only intentions reachable under the lane layout, guided by a lane-topology prior. Diversity among the surviving guesses is preserved. On the Argoverse 2 driving data set, LAMP matched leading rivals on accuracy. It beat them on feasibility and diversity measures.
arxiv-2606-26761:
Daniel Iľkovič determines the maximum forest number for general bipartite graphs under degree conditions. A bipartite graph splits its vertices into two camps with edges only between them. An induced forest is a set of vertices containing no cycles. The maximum forest number is the largest such set, tied to the classic problem of deleting few vertices to break all cycles.

Recent work solved the balanced case, where both camps are equal. Iľkovič extends the exact formula to general bipartite graphs under Ore-type conditions, which bound the combined degrees of non-adjacent vertices. The maximum is governed by an optimisation over at most six critical structural points. He also proves a hardness result: deciding whether a balanced graph's forest number reaches a modest threshold is NP-complete. Exact values for individual graphs therefore remain computationally out of reach.
arxiv-2606-27161:
Wang and colleagues prune the flood of visual tokens that slows multimodal language models. Such models split images into many tokens, and attention cost grows steeply with token count. Earlier pruning rules keep redundant tokens or ignore the user's question. Their TOPS module instead builds Token Optimal Preservation Sets, chosen from first principles. During 2026, an information-theoretic analysis yields three rules for keeping tokens: task relevance, information coverage, and semantic diversity.

TOPS needs no training and plugs into many model backbones. Tests span seven backbones and fourteen benchmarks under varied pruning settings. Prior methods are beaten across those settings. On one leading model family, over three quarters of visual tokens are removed while benchmark scores hold at or above full-token levels. Cutting redundant tokens can even reduce hallucination slightly. Lightweight multimodal design gets a principled, ready-to-use pruning tool.
arxiv-2606-27261:
Assiotis and Nyamundanda study Markov chains that evolve in space and time without ever colliding, in an environment that itself varies from place to place and moment to moment. Such varying chains model interacting particle systems with push-block interactions, where particles shove neighbours aside. The team establishes explicit leading-order asymptotics, with an error bound, for the tail probabilities of collision times, in discrete and continuous time alike. The irregular setting rules out the usual coupling-with-Brownian-motion techniques, in a probability paper appearing in 2026.

The proof pairs a steepest-descent analysis with a Karlin-McGregor semigroup expansion. The process conditioned never to intersect is built and identified with a stated change of measure of the original chains. A prediction from particle-system work is thereby confirmed. Non-colliding systems in lumpy environments gain exact asymptotics.
arxiv-2606-27461:
In 2026, Zhang and Akan decide which sensors of a large wave receiver to switch on, when hardware limits force a choice. Future receivers offer many candidate ports, but only a subset can be active. Their framework demands modal recoverability at finite signal-to-noise ratio: every direction of a chosen modal subspace must be reliably recoverable. Three nested criteria formalise the demand, from single modes up to target modes amid interfering ones. A Schur-complement information floor gives the strictest criterion an exact worst-direction error meaning.

Stricter criteria provably need at least as many active accesses, and tests flag reliability targets that stay unattainable even with every access on. For spherical-wave sampling, greedy selection rules are compared head to head. Global log-determinant selection is more access-efficient at moderate reliability floors in the reported results. Schur-based selection wins at stringent floors.
arxiv-2606-27561:
Waller leads a team building the first quantum generative diffusion model aimed at time series, and running it on real quantum hardware. Their design swaps the feed-forward parts of the denoising transformer for quantum neural networks, which yields a hybrid quantum transformer. Each replaced component carries roughly a thousand times fewer trainable parameters. In the 2026 quantum machine learning paper, financial series from two technology giants supply the test data, and the model trains and samples on a commercial quantum processor.

The synthetic data reproduce the real distributions more faithfully than the classical counterpart, cutting the Wasserstein distance by about forty-four percent across both datasets in the reported comparison. Augmenting a forecasting model with the generated data improves its error by up to seventy-one percent over training on real data alone in the same study. Quantum components match or beat classical ones with far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2606-27861:
Reinforcement learning can control robots through hard tasks. Safety limits are often ignored in that work, though. Jiatao Ding and three colleagues propose PPO-EAL in 2026 for safe robotic control. It folds an exact augmented Lagrangian method into proximal policy optimisation. Clipped updates combine with exact quadratic penalty terms. Constraint enforcement gains a firm theoretical basis without huge penalty factors.

A momentum-regulated update steadies the multiplier variables. Constraint swings and unsafe behaviour fall. Task performance is preserved at the same time. Exactness is analysed under standard assumptions. Benchmarks span cart-pole balancing, a double-pendulum task, a Franka arm reaching task, and quadrupedal locomotion. Safety precision and reward beat leading first-order safe baselines. A real-world test follows the simulations. Zero-shot transfer to a contact-rich gear assembly task improves success and cuts peak contact force.
arxiv-2606-27961:
A transversal picks one element from each coset of a subgroup. Its size is fixed, but the size of its difference set can vary. Mugurel Barcau, Vicenţiu Paşol, and George Ţurcaş define the transversal difference number in 2026 as the smallest possible difference-set size. The invariant connects to factorisation, tiling, and sumset questions. It is motivated by Galois labels in homomorphic encryption transforms.

A general lower bound is proved, involving twice the quotient size minus a term from the largest disjoint subgroup. The bound is sharp for cyclic quotients. Kneser's theorem yields exact product families when one cyclic coordinate does not split. The hard core is one residual case, a square plane over a prime field, where transversals become graphs of functions. The authors conjecture the exact value for all odd primes. They also prove a weaker unconditional bound, plus evidence from small primes, probability, and fixed polynomials.
arxiv-2606-28361:
Kuan Yan, Zhiqing Tang, Tian Wang, and Weijia Jia cut the cost of multi-step retrieval services, where a language model answers hard questions through repeated rounds of searching and reasoning. Each round appends documents and reasoning traces, so the context bill grows roughly with the square of the round count, along with the noise.

Yan's team proposes ConCise, a training-free protocol that replaces the raw transcript with a chain of structured conclusions that only grows by appending. Growth drops from quadratic to roughly linear in the number of rounds. A fused generation step emits reasoning and conclusions in one call, avoiding double billing. Across twelve paired setups spanning three models, two datasets, and two frameworks, the method saved nearly two thirds of tokens on average while keeping accuracy acceptable.
arxiv-2606-28561:
Manisha Shrestha and a large team of collaborators turned the James Webb Space Telescope on SN 2024abup. It is a nearby broad-lined Type Ic supernova, an especially energetic explosion of a massive star stripped of its outer layers. Such explosions are candidate sites for forging the heaviest elements by rapid neutron capture, and possible dust factories for the early universe.

Theirs are the first mid-infrared Webb observations of this supernova type, taken about six weeks after peak brightness, backed by radio and optical data. Spectral modeling finds carbon, oxygen, magnesium, and carbon monoxide, the earliest detection of molecules in any core-collapse supernova. A continuum glow hints at heated dust, preexisting or newly formed. Despite a careful search, no convincing fingerprints of rapid-capture elements appear, though broad blended lines could be hiding them.
arxiv-2606-28661: This paper studies when more sampling hurts: the modal ceiling and correlation ceiling of test-time scaling. The studying studies. Their studying is when more sampling hurts. The ceilings are modal correlation test-time. It is AI. The studying is scaling.
arxiv-2606-28961:
Debata, Mukherjee and Lal use a tiny quantum system to mimic ideas from black hole physics, tracking how entanglement moves between parts. Their model couples two qubits, the basic units of quantum information, through an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange, a magnetic interaction favouring opposite alignment. One qubit also couples to a fermionic environment, a bath of electron-like particles, through a second exchange.

Tuning the ratio of the two couplings drives a quantum phase transition at zero temperature. Entanglement then shifts from the qubit pair toward the environment. Carefully chosen information measures behave like the entropy curves expected during black hole evaporation, including a Page curve, the expected rise and fall of radiation entropy. An effective temperature, from how ground-state energy changes with mutual information, grows with the coupling ratio. It resembles Hawking temperature as a black hole shrinks. Strange-metal-like behaviour appears near the critical point too.
arxiv-2606-29361:
Cipollini settles a problem posed by Erdős about sums inside large sets of whole numbers. Take a set of integers drawn from one up to N. How large must the set be before it must contain three distinct elements whose three pairwise sums also lie in the set? The threshold function for this question was known only within a range.

He proves the threshold is at most five eighths of N, up to a bounded error. A standard construction shows that five eighths is also necessary, so the value is pinned down exactly apart from the small error term. That resolves Erdős Problem 865. His proof is self-contained. A conditional version of the reduction, developed earlier, was also formalised in the Lean proof assistant, with no gaps and no added axioms. The manuscript's note credits the proof's development jointly to Cipollini and an AI system.
arxiv-2606-29661:
Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, and Day study how to ensemble AI forecasts, combining several models' predictions about future world events. Top forecasting systems now approach superforecaster-level accuracy, pairing off-the-shelf large language models with special scaffolding. The authors ask which model forecasts should be combined when the sample budget is fixed.

On binary questions from the Metaculus AI Benchmark, individual accuracy is not enough. Many frontier models make highly correlated forecasts, so extra forecasts from similar models add little. The strongest ensembles mix forecasters that are both accurate and diverse. Some models contribute most because their forecasts are less correlated with the rest of the field. The authors conclude that the AI crowd draws its strength from errors that differ, not from sampling more forecasts indiscriminately. Forecasting systems should optimize for both quality and diversity.
arxiv-2606-29761:
Zhang, Liu, Yu, and Wu propose a cleaner way to use fast radio bursts as cosmological probes. Fast radio bursts are brief, intense flashes from distant galaxies. Their dispersion measure, the delay between high and low frequencies, records the electrons along the path. That signal includes an uncertain Milky Way contribution.

Their method eliminates that Milky Way part by taking dispersion differences between localized bursts in the same sky region. Nearby sightlines share nearly the same Galactic contribution, so it cancels. Mock samples validate the method: it recovers the fiducial cosmological parameter used to generate them. Applied to current localized burst data, it yields a constraint on a key parameter combination that differs from the standard treatment.
arxiv-2606-29961:
Hosseini and eight colleagues present DuoMem, a way to give small on-device language models the memory skills of a large teacher. Capable memory agents usually need big models, long contexts, and many inference calls, which resource-limited devices cannot afford.

DuoMem distils the teacher in two spaces at once. In context space, the student's self-written memories are replaced by higher-quality teacher-written procedural memories placed in its input. In parameter space, small LoRA adapters, low-rank add-on weights, are finetuned on successful teacher trajectories. On the ALFWorld household-task benchmark, a 4-billion-parameter model jumps from 4.3 to 77.9 percent success, near the 72-billion teacher's 87.1 percent, runs over three times faster, and adds under ten million trainable parameters.
arxiv-2606-30161:
Dario Fenoglio, Daniil Kirilenko, Martin Gjoreski, and Marc Langheinrich refine how federated learning servers combine client updates. Federated learning trains one model across many data owners. Servers usually average client models with fixed or heuristic weights. When client data differ wildly, those rules underperform badly. The authors let a conditional random field set the weights.

The field assigns unary potentials to single clients. Pairwise terms capture links between every pair of clients. Client reliability and client interplay are modeled together this way. Inference in the field produces the aggregation weights. Those weights aim at better convergence of the global objective. Experiments focus on non-IID data, where client datasets differ most. The method consistently beats well-established standard baselines there. Structured inference, they argue, suits server side combining well.
arxiv-2606-30261:
Vinko Zlatić, writing alone, studies where to hide the pieces of a secret across a network so it survives both failures and attacks. Splitting information among agents is an old security strategy. Reconstruction needs only a prescribed subset of the shares. Placement on the network shapes both recoverability and exposure. Zlatić frames placement as optimizing a single robustness functional.

It balances survivability under network degradation against resistance to compromise. An exact formula expresses survivability through minimal information-carrying subgraphs. Those subgraphs capture the reconstruction events that actually matter. Semi-local optimization methods are built from that representation. They need no global knowledge of the network structure. In a limiting case, it maps to an effective spin Hamiltonian. Physics tools for spin systems then apply to secret storage. Applications span technological and social network systems.
arxiv-2606-30461:
Nguyen and four colleagues stabilize state space models for long sequences by fixing the geometry of their memory updates. State space models rival attention with linear-time sequence handling. Over long horizons they often suffer wobble and fading memory. Poorly conditioned updates and unbalanced update shapes are the culprits. MuonSSM shapes the updates directly rather than the transition matrix.

A momentum-based pathway augments the standard model. A lightweight Newton–Schulz transform acts on low-rank input injections. Updates become bounded and spectrally well behaved as a result. Parallel scan efficiency is preserved throughout. Theory shows better gradient propagation across long spans. Spectral amplification is mitigated and memory representations enriched. Experiments span language, vision, and time-series benchmarks. Gains in accuracy and robustness appear across diverse backbones. Long-context performance improves consistently as well. Geometric conditioning emerges as a principled route to stable models.
arxiv-2606-30561:
Aspen Hopkins and four colleagues argue that disagreement among expert judges of creative work is not always measurement error. Their Human Creativity Benchmark collects judgments on AI-generated creative output while keeping two signals apart: convergence, where professionals share standards, and divergence, where personal taste legitimately differs. Collapsing both into one quality score, they say, throws away the most useful information.

The benchmark gathers pairwise preferences, ratings on prompt adherence, usability and visual appeal, plus written reasons from working professionals. Its fifteen thousand judgments span five creative domains and three workflow phases: ideation, mockup and refinement. Agreement clustered on checkable qualities such as technical correctness and visual hierarchy. Disagreement clustered on taste-driven choices such as aesthetic direction and conceptual risk. No model led across all phases, so the results separate where models must be correct from where they should stay steerable.
arxiv-2606-30761:
Gerard Machado and eleven colleagues show that counting every photon, not just clicks, widens the window where quantum sensors beat classical ones. Quantum sensors promise phase measurements finer than the shot-noise limit, but photon loss usually erases the advantage. The team use a nonlinear interferometer, where two parametric processes couple light to the sensor and then mix the beams. Standard detectors register only whether photons arrived; theirs resolve exactly how many arrived in each output.

Using transition-edge sensors, they reconstructed the photon-number statistics at the output. With roughly a quarter of photons lost inside the device and nearly half outside, the sensor still beat the shot-noise limit by about two point four decibels. No post-selection or loss correction was used. That is a forty-four percent gain in estimation precision over click detection. Checks against an analytic model and the raw statistics confirmed the performance.
arxiv-2606-30861:
Yohan Poirier-Ginter, Jeffrey Hu, Jean-François Lalonde and George Drettakis make reflections in captured 3D scenes editable. Radiance fields such as 3D Gaussian Splatting render scenes from photos in real time and show shiny reflections well, but they fake them with phantom geometry hidden behind the mirror. That trick blocks editing: you cannot move the reflected object or roughen the surface. The team's proof of concept reconstructs the reflector and the reflected objects in one representation, so reflections become physical.

Learning-based tools first split each photo into diffuse and specular layers plus geometry and material buffers. A diffuse scene is optimised, and path tracing then generates true specular reflections, aided by a fast ray tracer for Gaussian primitives that handles multiple bounces. Results use ground-truth buffers on synthetic scenes, with early tests on real ones.
arxiv-2606-31061:
Takeda, Miyatake, and Furihata present Online TT-ALS, an algorithm for keeping a tensor train decomposition current as data streams in. Tensor trains compress high-dimensional data, such as video, into a chain of small core tensors. Batch methods rebuild the decomposition accurately but can exhaust memory, while earlier online methods are efficient yet lose accuracy.

The new algorithm updates the decomposition with alternating least squares while sequentially enforcing orthogonality constraints on the cores. The authors prove these constraints guarantee the local objective decreases monotonically and the decomposition changes smoothly over time. A deterministic single-sweep update cuts the rank dependence from quadratic to linear. In experiments the method beat existing online techniques on approximation accuracy and on video quality scores, and ran orders of magnitude faster than deep learning approaches.
arxiv-2606-31161:
Vincenzo models how the Milky Way's disc built up its chemistry when gas drifts slowly inward. A star's chemical pattern records gas accretion, star formation, and mixing across the disc. Untangling those threads is the only way to reconstruct how the Galaxy formed. Most models treat each ring of the disc on its own. Vincenzo instead follows the gas along its inward journey, a Lagrangian approach solved with the method of characteristics.

The model gives fast, semi-analytic formulas for gas density and for oxygen and iron abundances. Enrichment from both kinds of supernova is included, under a two-infall history for the Galaxy. With a mild inflow of about 1.5 kilometers per second, the model matches the observed abundance patterns, the stellar density profile, and the radial gradients at once. The lesson is sharp: gas carries the memory of every radius it crossed, so local models misread the enrichment history.
arxiv-2606-31461:
Shi and three colleagues present CSTrader, a multi-agent testbed for trading game items with language models. Counter-Strike 2 weapon skins form a small, jumpy market driven by community talk and platform rules. Formula-based trading models fit it badly, which makes it a sharp test of turning text into trading action.

Specialist agents handle technical analysis, liquidity, events, and reversed sentiment, while risk, friction, and portfolio agents turn their calls into buy, sell, or hold orders. On real data from a volatile stretch, the system beats a falling market index and single-prompt baselines, earning up to about 7.6 percent with controlled risk. Ablations credit the liquidity, reversed sentiment, and friction agents for turning noisy talk into steady gains.
arxiv-2606-31661:
Arya, Soale and Rekabdarkolaee design a procedure for recommending nitrogen fertilizer rates across many farm sites. The best rate varies by location. Many choices near the optimum are statistically hard to tell apart. Chasing one estimated best rate per site wastes fertilizer and money. Their procedure instead screens first and refines second.

Sequential screening at a broad level removes clearly inferior choices, then hierarchical refinement picks locally among the survivors, with theory guaranteeing the screening stays safe. In a multi-state, multi-year corn nitrogen trial, no single regime wins uniformly within a state, and the most common recommendation covers only about a third to a half of decision units. The method often recommends less total nitrogen than state-level or hindsight benchmarks while keeping yields competitive.
arxiv-2606-31861:
Belardinelli and Zhang give dynamic epistemic logic a way to model belief contraction, the giving up of a belief. Standard DEL only eliminates possibilities, so it handles expansion but not an agent reconsidering what was ruled out. The usual fix adds plausibility orderings and promotes possibilities instead.

That fix has expressive limits, the authors show. It forces positive introspection, so agents cannot be wrong about their own beliefs. It also cannot handle contraction after a hedged announcement that a claim might be false. Their alternative works directly on ordinary Kripke models, adding possibilities back when a hedged announcement lands. Sound and complete axiomatizations are given, and a general logic extends the idea to private announcements.
arxiv-2608-00161:
Folsom and co-authors study corotation of dark matter halos in TNG50 galaxies. Nearly one hundred Milky Way-like galaxies form their sample. The standard halo model assumes isotropy near the Sun. That view skips how halo phase-space facts vary by galaxy. They ask which variance aspects drive direct detection forecasts.

The median azimuthal velocity of dark matter is nonzero, they find. It preferentially follows the baryonic disk's rotation. Values range from 6 to 70 km per second across the sample spread. Corotation suppresses scattering rates for dark matter below 50 GeV. It also shifts expected daily modulation for directional detectors. The effect adds a 21 percent uncertainty to cross-section limits. That uncertainty falls to 7 percent if the rotation speed is pinned down.
arxiv-2608-00461:
Sun and co-authors speed up JUNO's OMILREC reconstruction eightfold without changing its physics output. OMILREC fits each event's vertex and energy by maximum likelihood. Every Minuit evaluation scans all 17,612 large photomultiplier tubes. About 470 evaluations run per event, so the inner loop dominates CPU cost. Profiling shows the production code is latency-bound at under ten percent of peak.

Staged optimizations keep equivalence with a frozen reference at each step. Flattened layouts, vectorizable geometry, and hoisted invariant work lead the list. Per-event precomputation and reduced-precision fast paths follow. Single-thread time fell from 1,524.8 to 189.2 ms per event on an Intel Xeon. The likelihood stays bit-identical through seven releases. Vertex and energy match the baseline within 4 mm and 7 keV for typical events.
bonaventure-itinerarium-mentis-latin-186:
Bonaventure wrote the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, the Journey of the Mind to God, in 1259. He was on retreat at La Verna, where Francis had borne the stigmata. Karl Joseph von Hefele edited the Latin text in 1861. No English version in the public domain exists, so the Latin stands here as the record of the central Franciscan ascent text.

Six steps, like the six wings of the seraph, lift the soul. They climb through the world, through the senses, and through the mind's powers, to the vision of Being and of the Good. A seventh step is rest, the peace past thought. The little book is dense and burning at once. Generations of mystics climbed by its ladder.
boyle-sceptical-chymist-1661:
Robert Boyle's Sceptical Chymist, published in 1661, is a dialogue that demolishes the old theories of matter. Speaker after speaker defends the four elements or the three principles of the alchemists, and each defense fails. The book is counted the founding text of modern chemistry.

Boyle argues that elements must be found by experiment, not assumed from ancient systems or furnace habits. His careful trials with air, acids, and colors model a new way of asking nature questions. Later chemists looked back to Boyle's dialogue as the moment their science learned to doubt in an orderly way.
brasseur-popol-vuh-1861:
The sacred book of the K'iche' Maya reached Europe in print through Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1861. Popol Vuh: Le livre sacré gives the creation epic in French, its first European edition. Brasseur had found the old manuscript in Guatemala and knew its worth at once.

His French version carried the gods, the making of man, and the Hero Twins to Western readers. The edition tied the Popol Vuh to the wide debate on American antiquity and lost lands. Every later Maya-Atlantis claim leans on the text he brought out. The book is a landmark of American studies in its own right.
camerarius-history-strange-wonders-1561:
Joachim Camerarius was a German scholar of the Reformation age, and his writings on omens circulated widely. This English History of Strange Wonders appeared in 1561. It carried German prodigy lore across the Channel to English readers early in Elizabeth's reign.

Strange births, signs in the sky, and monsters crowd its pages. Each wonder is read as a warning from God about wars, deaths of princes, or sins of the age. Lutheran Germany scanned the book of nature for such omens with great care. The English version shows how fast this habit crossed borders. Fear and faith, more than curiosity, drive the whole collection.
catcott-treatise-on-the-deluge-1761:
Alexander Catcott defended the Deluge as Earth's great agent in his Treatise of 1761. Catcott was a Bristol clergyman of the Hutchinsonian school. That school set Moses's philosophy, drawn from Hebrew scripture, against Newton's system. His treatise reads the Flood as the force that shaped the crust.

Strata, fossils, and mountains all become the Deluge's work in his hands. Remarks on the Bishop of Clogher's account of the same subject join the argument. Catcott writes as a divine who trusts scripture above the new philosophy. His book shows diluvial thought fighting on into the age of geology. It preserves a losing side argued with learning. The controversy itself is the lesson.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporation-a:
Bernard Ward's entry treats the Corporation Act of 1661, a test act keeping public offices for Church of England members. Though counted among the Penal Laws, it aimed not directly at Catholics but at Presbyterians. Parliament passed it in December 1661, the year after the Restoration. Cavaliers aimed at bringing back old England, and only Clarendon restrained them.

Anyone voted to city or corporation office must first have taken the Lord's Supper within twelve months past, according to Church of England rites. He must also take the Oaths of Allegiance and Supremacy, swear Passive Obedience, and renounce the Covenant, or his vote stood void. The act bore heavily on Catholics, barring them from public life. It stayed in force in name through the eighteenth century, repealed in 1828, the year before Catholic Emancipation.
cia-0000014661: Samuel Novick is the subject of an untitled CIA file dated April 3, 1957. The file draws on an article by Victor Riesel in his newspaper column. Columnists fed the files with names and claims the agency then checked. Novick was a businessman whose left wing ties drew watch in the anti Communist years.
cia-0000014761: Spies in the United States told Russia all is the bold headline of a CIA file dated March 5, 1951. The file describes in detail how agents stole secret data. Headline style files like this summed up the spy scare for busy readers. They also show the alarm that ran through official Washington in the trial spring of 1951.
cia-0000015461: Near Baku, an unconventional flying object was sighted, and a CIA record dated in 1956 lays the report out as a tabulation. A memo came with the table. Baku was a Soviet oil city on the Caspian Sea, deep inside closed land. Turning a strange sighting there into rows and columns was how analysts made distant claims easier to compare and judge.
cia-0000022361: Text on the indictment, noting the Soviet government ordered the U-2 shot down, fills a CIA record dated in 1960. The shoot down order came from the top, by the heading's account. That point mattered, since Moscow wanted the flight framed as a crime met by lawful defense. The legal text and the order together form the Soviet case in brief.
cia-0000037161:
A CIA record dated May 4, 1983 concerns the 1967 crash site of an American Air Force F-4 aircraft. The site lay in My Hao district, in the Haiphong area of North Vietnam. F-4 Phantoms flew many of the bombing missions over the north during the war years. The two-man Phantom was the workhorse of the air war, and many were lost.

The record fixes where one lost aircraft came down, sixteen years after the crash. Crash sites mattered because they often held the answer to a crew's fate. Marking this one kept open the chance that searchers could one day visit the ground and learn what happened to the men aboard.
cia-0000043361:
Cuban government reactions to current crises fill a CIA record dated December 23, 1958. The date is the story: Fulgencio Batista's regime had days left to live. Rebels under Fidel Castro were closing on power across the island.

Inside, Havana's responses to the crises around it are recorded. A government in its final week speaks in a special tone. Orders, denials, and appeals all carry the sound of an ending. Within days, the government issuing them would be gone from the palace. The file preserves that sound from inside the old order, days before Batista fled and the revolution remade Cuba for the rest of the century.
cia-0000046761: Hanoi's running count of claimed American planes downed reached 4,036 in a CIA item dated October 5, 1972. The same dispatch carried word of an F-111 lost, naming its commander. Such tallies were propaganda, but they were filed and studied all the same. Each figure had to be matched against the real losses the air war was costing.
cia-0000049061: Captain Eduardo Avila's travel to El Salvador in 1983 is logged in a CIA item, kept with the Truth Commission records. Avila was named in this series as an alleged conspirator, which made his movements worth filing. The item is a small piece of the paper watch kept on officers tied to the war's crimes.
cia-0000049161: An FMLN representative worked in 1990 to arrange a visit to Costa Rica's president, and a CIA item preserves the effort. Costa Rica, the region's standing mediator, hosted much of the diplomacy that ended Central America's wars. A guerrilla envoy seeking a president's door showed how far the rebels' campaign had moved toward talks.
cia-0000049261: Update number five on the Jesuit killings is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. The numbered series let readers follow the case's slow public life, one bulletin at a time. The fifth adds its week of movement, or of waiting, to the chronicle the series built.
cia-0000049361: Human rights abuses in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049361, dated February 4, 1983. Carrying a Truth Commission note, the item focuses on abuses rather than on battles or politics. Readers find a brief declassified record whose title states its grim topic directly, kept among the agency's Salvadoran files from the war years.
cia-0000096661: Continued Unrest in Chekiang Province is reported in declassified CIA document 0000096661, dated September 3, 1968. The heading stresses duration, unrest that kept going in one province. The brief file sits one day after the neighboring Wenchou fighting item, and together the two records show the agency returning to Chekiang in consecutive daily filings.
cia-0000102961:
Work Treatment Prophylaxis Camps, Moscow, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102961, dated July 1, 1987. The sample covers the years 1977 to 1979 and names five or six such camps near Moscow. Each camp held several thousand people and was run by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Entry took a judge's order and a medical exam to show a person could perform hard labor. In practice, treatment for alcohol dependence was almost absent, beyond Antabuse or a few vitamin C tablets. A typical day meant ten hours of construction or heavy labor, plain meals, and political lessons before bed. Guards could be bribed for alcohol, and the camps failed at treating alcoholism.
cia-0000105161:
Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism is declassified CIA document 0000105161, dated January 2, 1975 in the catalog. The sample shows the issue dated January 7, 1975. It was presented to the Working Group of the Cabinet Committee to Combat Terrorism, whose members are listed on its cover.

The contents page names the week's articles, opening with an attempted hijack in London by an unknown gunman. That single named article shows the report's mix: short items on attacks and attempts around the world. The issue is one early installment of the weekly series named in its title.
cia-0000109061: Cuban Sugar Production in 1967 and Prospects for 1968 and 1970 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109061, dated October 3, 1967. The heading looks backward and forward: one harvest year, then prospects for two more. Sugar is the single crop named in the title itself. The brief record is a crop production item from the autumn of 1967.
cia-0000119761: A September 1956 CIA chronology issued as a special supplement updates the master timeline of events. During that autumn, keeping the sequence current meant keeping pace with a revolution, and the supplement preserves the order of events as the agency assembled it. Supplement pages show the timeline being corrected in near real time, a working record revised as cables arrived faster than printers could reset it.
cia-0000126861: A February 1953 CIA document filed under the name John P. Hayes. The title offers no role, no charge, no context — just the name. Whatever made Hayes interesting to the agency, the answer is inside the file.
cia-0000126961: An October 1968 CIA report carries the blunt heading Haiti: Duvalier's Primitive Totalitarian State. By then the Tonton Macoute had terrorized the country for more than a decade in Papa Doc's name. The paper lays out one of the hemisphere's most brutal regimes as the agency judged it. The heading's harsh wording is itself evidence: analysts rarely wrote so bluntly about a government Washington still dealt with, which shows how far Haiti stood apart.
cia-0000132661:
The future of the Castro regime is weighed in a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The American election was days away, and the new president would inherit the Cuba problem at once. How long Castro could last was the question running through Washington that fall.

The agency's forecasters were split on the answer, and the paper sets out their views. For readers, it preserves a moment of honest doubt before policy hardened. Within five months the invasion at the Bay of Pigs would test every forecast in the file. The paper shows what the experts said before that test came.
cia-0000132761:
Spring tensions run through this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated May 4, 1960. Castro's government was a year old and pressing ahead with its revolution. The United States, still weighing its options, had not yet settled on a course.

May 1960 sits in the hinge of the story: relations were bad and worsening, but the final break was still months away. Briefings from that month record an agency watching land seizures, sharp speeches, and colder diplomacy pile up. The declassified paper preserves the moment before Washington chose confrontation, and it rewards reading beside the harder papers of 1961.
cia-0000135861: With a date of 3 September 1952, a CIA routing sheet in the open files deals with a memo whose heading spells the country as Guiatemala, typo and all. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136061: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 March 1954, long since declassified, on the K Program, a recurring subject in the station files through the spring of 1954. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136161: A cable dated 4 March 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on criticisms and recommendations from headquarters, the rare cable grading the field from above. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136261: Filed on 6 May 1954, this CIA cable concerns waiting until the twentieth of June for a decision before taking action, a hold order. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136961: Letters from an appropriate man are suggested in this May 1954 cable. Communist-led mass groups are rallying support for Arbenz. Unions sent sympathy messages. So did the peasant federation and student groups. They hold mass meetings against foreign intervention. They rally public sympathy with some success. Headquarters proposes a counter-move. Letters should go to conference delegates. They should also go to non-communist labor groups. The letters would decry the regime's totalitarian acts. Exile stories of arrests and tortures would be replayed.
cia-0000139161: Distribution of particularly sensitive intelligence reports is restricted in this 1985 memorandum signed for the Director of Central Intelligence. In July 1985 a sensitive source reporting format was established for highly sensitive CIA reporting concerning the well-being and possible locations of American hostages in Lebanon. The format limits distribution within the CIA and restricts dissemination to named addressees in other agencies, including the national security advisor and the directors of DIA, NSA, and State's intelligence bureau. Recipients must share it only with those having a clearly evident need to know.
cia-03003761:
Korea opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 December 1953, with a comment on the broken talks. Peiping radio answered Ambassador Dean's walkout of 12 December at once. The Communists, the comment judges, want no political conference except on their own terms. They blame Seoul's prisoner release and American cold-war policy, while insisting they remain ready to negotiate.

Moscow and Peiping appear to have reserved their decision pending other conference proposals. Iran follows: Hoseyn Makki, a former National Front leader, takes over the National Resistance Movement. The coalition wants Mossadeq restored, but Makki is judged likelier to advance himself. French deputies return from Poland fortified against the European Defence Community. Italy would not oppose Yugoslav attendance at informal talks on Trieste.
cia-03191561:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 9 December 1959, marked Top Secret, leads with talks in Peiping during a Japanese political visit. The bulletin reports that Foreign Minister Chen Yi told Matsumura that Communist China accepted the outcome of the Eisenhower-Khrushchev talks only after setting conditions for Khrushchev. Matsumura would not reveal what those conditions were.

Asia-Africa items cover leftist students in Japan planning a 10 December protest at the Diet against the United States-Japanese Security Treaty. The United Arab Republic had asked for an emergency Arab League meeting on Israeli diversion of Jordan water. A long Saudi dispute with Aramco and Tapline is reported to have cost Saudi Arabia second place in Middle East oil output. Chinese anxiety over the revised security treaty is treated at length in the middle pages.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-10-april-ma:
Coronation spring fills Volume 10 of Pepys's Diary, April and May 1661, though the diarist spends much of it on smaller crowns. His Privy Seal waiting comes round again; he is up early among his workmen, dining with Sir William Batten, and drinking Privy Seal talk with Dr. Castle at the Goat. At Whitefriars he catches part of Rule a Wife and Have a Wife and does not like it. His parents quarrel about a maid at home while London prepares to crown Charles II in Westminster Abbey.

When the coronation comes, Pepys records the procession, the Abbey, and his own place in the crowd with a subject's pride and a clerk's eye for cost. The entries after it return to leases, dinners, and his wife's painting lessons. Readers get the Restoration's set-piece month at ground level, glory and grocery bills alternating as they do everywhere else in the Diary.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-11-june-jul:
Summer 1661 in Volume 11 of Pepys's Diary is ruled by a death in the family. His uncle Robert, the Brampton farmer, dies in July. The will leaves property tangled between Pepys's father, his uncle Thomas, and the diarist himself. Pepys rides down to Huntingdonshire to bury his uncle and fight the settlement. The shorthand fills with acres, annuities, and hard words between brothers. Inheritance is turning the Pepyses into litigants, and the diarist minds every shilling of it.

London pulls him back between journeys. The Navy Office, his wife's company, and the summer theatres fill the gaps in the quarrel. He is learning the double life the Diary will always lead: estates by day, music by night. Readers get a season of family law here. It is unglamorous, exact, and completely absorbing, because Pepys writes a disputed will the way other men write a battle.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-12-septembe:
Rain through the roof opens Volume 12 of Pepys's Diary, September and October 1661, spoiling the ceilings of the Seething Lane house on the first of the month. Pepys dines at Sir William Batten's and laughs over a stolen tankard: Batten took Sir William Penn's tankard, Pepys forged the thief's letter, and Penn still does not understand the joke. The Navy Office circle at play is the volume's keynote, colleagues whose pranks and dinners fill the autumn.

Work runs underneath: ships paying off, stores accounted, and Pepys's growing credit at the Office. He is twenty-eight, newly a householder, and learning how patronage actually moves. Church, theatre, and his wife's company fill the Sundays and evenings between sittings. Readers get the Diary in its settled rhythm here. Two ordinary months are made vivid by a writer who noticed everything, from his own ceiling to his rising place at the Office.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-13-november:
Winter closes the Diary's second year in Volume 13, November and December 1661. Pepys is deep in Navy Office routine now: sittings, letters, and the endless arithmetic of ships. His credit stands high enough that great men borrow his diligence. At home the Seething Lane house is warm, his wife is learning to paint, and the dinners improve with his salary. Frost, church, and theatre fill the short days between office hours.

Christmas ends the volume in feasting and reckoning. Pepys audits his year the way he audits a stores account, item by item, and finds himself richer in every column. The shorthand has become a mirror he trusts more than memory. Readers get two quiet months here, and quiet is the point. Between the coronation spring and the coming wars, this is the Diary's baseline: an ambitious man at peace, writing down exactly how good it felt.
dickens-great-expectations-1861:
Charles Dickens published Great Expectations in 1861, a late novel many call his most perfect. Pip, Miss Havisham, and the convict Magwitch anchor its tight, ironic plot of ambition. Dickens shaped the tale with care and gave it a revised, softer end in print.

Pip, an orphan smith's boy, helps a convict and dreams of a finer life. A secret fortune lets him train as a gentleman in London town and lodgings. He snubs Joe, the kind smith who raised him, and chases cold Estella in vain. The fortune's true source shocks him and teaches him where worth truly lies in men. Few novels trace shame, love, and growth with such clean, hard force.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-1861:
Henry Dircks, an English engineer, spent years on the hunt for self motive power, and this survey came out in 1861. Men had tried for three hundred years to build a wheel that would turn for ever with no fuel. Dircks set out to list them all.

The book walks through scheme after scheme, with drawings of wheels, weights, and fluids. Dircks shows where each one fails, in plain terms a lay reader can grasp. His survey is still the main guide to the long hunt for a machine that cannot work.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-first-series-186:
Henry Dircks was an English engineer with a rage for one theme. His Perpetuum Mobile, First Series, came out in 1861. The book lists scheme on scheme for a wheel that runs for all time. Dircks dug through rolls, tracts, and tales of three hundred years.

Wheels with weights, mills with pumps, and craft with magnets all get their due. Most tales end in fraud, flaw, or a hid spring of force. Dircks meant the book as a warn to men who waste life on the dream. The pair of series is the full tale of the vain hunt.
du-chaillu-explorations-equatorial-afric:
Paul Du Chaillu came out of the Gabon forests in 1861 with skins, skulls, and a sensation. Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa made the gorilla a household word in Europe and America. No living gorilla had yet been seen by the crowds who read him.

Du Chaillu tells of hunts, river trips, and tribes of the deep forest, with the great ape as his star. His monster ape, charging and roaring, fixed the gorilla in the public mind for good. Later travelers faulted parts of his tale, but the fame held. The book turned a rumor of the woods into a beast of science.
eisenhower-farewell-1961:
Dwight D. Eisenhower gave his Farewell Address in January 1961. The old general warned against the military-industrial complex by name. No presidential warning since Washington's has been quoted so often.

Eisenhower had led the crusade in Europe and built much of the arms world. Yet he cautions that its vast sway could harm free government itself. He urges balance, thrift, and care for the nation's schools and farms. A soldier's farewell doubles as a prophecy Americans still debate. The speech gains force from the speaker's own unmatched war record in Europe. Only the supreme commander could warn so credibly against arms buildup.
eliot-george-silas-marner-1861:
George Eliot published Silas Marner in 1861, her flawless fable of a betrayed weaver and a foundling child. A betrayed weaver hoards gold until a foundling child redeems him,. Eliot said the tale came to her as a legend meant to show the fruits of a recovered faith.

Silas, falsely cast out by his chapel, lives alone at Raveloe weaving and counting his guineas in isolation. His gold is stolen by Dunstan Cass, and a golden-haired child crawls to his hearth from the snow. Eppie, the child of an opium-dead mother, becomes his treasure and his bridge back to church, neighbors, and human trust in Raveloe. Sixteen years later her choice of the weaver who raised her seals the fable's moral. Its symmetry and warmth make it the Eliot novel most often given to the young.
europmc-pmc10017761:
Zhang and colleagues review engineered exosomes as a tool for targeted cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Exosomes are tiny parcels that cells release to send signals to other cells. Researchers can load them with drugs and add surface features that steer them toward tumors.

The review covers exosomes from different cell sources and how each source affects their use. It explains how loading and steering are done in the lab. It also weighs safety and the steps left before clinic use. The paper maps a lively field in drug delivery.
europmc-pmc10192861:
Dave, Athaluri, and Singh give an overview of ChatGPT in medicine in a 2023 paper. They cover its applications, advantages, limits, future prospects, and the ethical questions it raises. ChatGPT is a language model trained on vast amounts of text that can hold a fluent conversation on medical topics.

The authors survey uses in study, writing, diagnosis support, and patient communication. They weigh gains in speed against risks such as confident errors and bias. They close with advice on consent, privacy, and oversight. The paper is a balanced early guide to AI in care.
europmc-pmc10495961:
Abril-Pla and a team of co-authors presented PyMC in 2023, a Python library for chance-based models. Such models, called Bayesian, state a guess as a spread of odds, not one fixed number. PyMC lets users write a model in code that reads close to plain math. A math engine then compiles it for fast chips.

The library fits a wide range of models. Abril-Pla lists layered line fits, time series, smooth curve models, and equation-based models. Work can run on plain processors or on graphics and tensor chips. Sample uses walk through common stats tasks step by step. The authors also credit PyMC for growing the open-source scene in this niche.
europmc-pmc10589261:
Hou and co-authors reviewed macrophages in atherosclerosis in 2023, the fatty build-up inside artery walls. Such plaques narrow vessels and can trigger heart attack or stroke. Macrophages sit at the core of each stage, from first growth to rupture and healing. Their states shift with the plaque's local cues.

These cells vary widely and can reshape their fuel use on the fly. Hou shows how low oxygen in a plaque flips a switch, HIF-1alpha, that alters cell acts. Some states stuff the plaque with fat and stir swelling. Others clear dead cells and calm the zone. A ring-shaped sugar, beta-cyclodextrin, helped plaques shrink in past work by aiding fat exit. Drugs that steer these states may yield precise care.
europmc-pmc1088961:
Schug and co-authors hunted for DNA traits that mark genes used in just one tissue in this 2005 paper. Turning a fertilised egg into an adult needs genes switched on at the right place and time. Some genes run in all cells, while others run in one tissue only. The stretch of DNA before a gene, called its promoter, helps set that pattern.

Using human gene activity data from tissue surveys, the team measured how varied each gene's use was. Most genes did vary by tissue in a clear way, they found. They then flagged promoter traits that split tissue-specific genes from those used everywhere. Tissue breadth was scored with Shannon entropy, a maths measure of how spread out a pattern is. Genes used in one tissue scored low on spread, while genes used everywhere scored high.
europmc-pmc11382761:
Su and colleagues review how cells talk to each other and what that means for medicine in this 2024 paper. Multicellular life requires diverse cell types to coordinate their behaviour. Cells communicate by direct contact or at a distance through ligand-receptor pairs, where a signal molecule docks onto a receiver protein. Two processes define the exchange: conduction sends the signal, and transduction lets the receiver process it.

The review first traces the historical milestones of the field. It then details how signal molecules travel and the main pathways they mediate. Diseases caused by faulty communication are surveyed systematically. Clinical applications that target these networks follow. The authors argue that decoding communication networks is critical for grasping cell differentiation, development, and metabolism. They close with the field's open challenges.
europmc-pmc11445061:
Liu, Prentice, and Webber explain how bacterial biofilms resist antimicrobial drugs in this 2024 review. Most bacteria in nature live in aggregated communities called biofilms, glued in a self-made matrix. Cells inside differ deeply from free-floating cells of the same species. Biofilm infections are often chronic and stubbornly hard to treat with antibiotics.

Intrinsic factors drive the tolerance: the matrix barrier, slow growth rates, altered drug targets, and fast swapping of resistance genes. A special cell type, persisters, survives drug exposure by lying dormant. The review describes the biofilm lifecycle and how resistance evolves and spreads within the film. Mixed-species biofilms add cooperation and competition that further shift drug tolerance. The authors argue these features, not single mutations, explain most treatment failures.
europmc-pmc1253661:
Lubin and co-authors tackled detection limits in environmental studies in 2004. Lab tools cannot read values below set limits. Studies often fill gaps with half the limit or random picks. The team tested those habits with simulations.

Half-limit filling biased results unless few values fell below limits. Bias stayed small only when under 5 to 10 percent were censored. Random fill-ins gave unbiased estimates but shaky error ranges. Distortion grew when 30 percent or more were censored. Lubin points to Tobit regression and multiple imputation as sound fixes. Tobit methods fit truncated data of this kind.
europmc-pmc1475661:
Malaria germs must cross the mosquito gut, where most of them die. Dong and co-authors mapped how the mosquito Anopheles gambiae reacts to two malaria species in 2006. One infects humans, the other infects rodents and serves as a lab model. They tracked which mosquito genes switch on during invasion.

The rodent germ stirred a wider change in gene activity. The human germ drew a broader immune reply. Silencing tests on 12 genes found seven that guard against both germs. A few guards were specific to one germ each. Dong shows the mosquito's defense blends shared and tailored weapons.
europmc-pmc1526461:
Proteins that juggle many partners tend to be floppy, not rigid. Haynes and co-authors tested that link in 2006 across four species: worm, yeast, fly, and human. Hub proteins, those with ten or more partners, were compared with proteins holding just one partner.

In all four species, hubs carried more disordered stretches, regions with no fixed shape. Wholly disordered proteins were enriched among hubs, wholly ordered ones scarce. In yeast, hubs tied to regulation and development leaned disordered, while enzyme and transport hubs leaned ordered. Haynes argues disorder gives hubs the flex to bind many unlike partners.
europmc-pmc1550961:
A shared scale for sudden kidney injury needed a real-world test. Hoste and co-authors gave it one in 2006, tracking 5,383 intensive care patients over a year. The RIFLE scale grades injury as risk, injury, or failure, based on kidney function.

Two thirds of patients had some injury. Death rates climbed with grade: 8.8 percent at risk, 11.4 at injury, and 26.3 at failure, against 5.5 with no injury. Over half of those at the risk grade slid to worse grades. Hoste confirms the scale forecasts death and heavy care use, and flags patients likely to worsen.
europmc-pmc161361:
Oxidative stress may start Alzheimer's long before plaques appear. Perry, Cash, and Smith reviewed that case in 2002. Cell changes tied to oxidation, damage by reactive oxygen, precede the disease's hallmark tangles and plaques.

The initial source of the stress stays unclear. Redox-active metals, iron and copper, likely feed the process, since they can spawn damaging oxygen species. Perry argues that pinning down this early chemistry could open new treatments. Most Alzheimer therapies of the time chased late damage; this line points upstream, to the spark itself.  Their focus on metals points to iron and copper handling as a testable lead.
europmc-pmc1764161:
Tiny engineered particles promise much in medicine and industry, but their health effects are largely unknown. Gwinn and Vallyathan reviewed the pros and cons in 2006. Particles under 100 nanometers, billionths of a meter, gain surface traits that plain dust lacks.

Proof from ultrafine particles of human activity suggests harm to heart and lungs. Engineered ones may behave alike, traveling to distant body sites. Beneficial uses, like drug delivery and gene therapy, can themselves cause exposure. Gwinn argues for a precautionary duty: pin down toxic effects now to keep workplace and environmental exposure low.
europmc-pmc1829161:
Bennett and colleagues surveyed people with fibromyalgia online in 2007 to test whether internet surveys can capture this chronic pain condition. The National Fibromyalgia Association built a 121-item questionnaire with expert help and refined it through several rounds of testing. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, fatigue, and poor sleep.

A total of 2,569 people completed the survey, and every one of the 50 states sent at least one respondent. Most were middle-aged white women with symptoms for four years or more. The top complaints were morning stiffness, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, pain, and trouble with focus and memory. Emotional distress, weather changes, insomnia, and hard exertion made things worse. Respondents rated rest, heat, pain medicines, antidepressants, and sleep medicines as the most helpful measures.
europmc-pmc1971061:
Levitt and Peña reviewed anorectal malformations in 2007, birth defects where the anus and rectum form abnormally, often with the urinary and genital tracts involved. They occur in about one in 5,000 live births, in boys and girls alike. Severity spans a wide spectrum.

Minor defects are easily repaired with excellent function, while complex forms are hard to manage, often come with other anomalies, and carry poor functional outlooks. Surgery changed radically in 1980 with the posterior sagittal approach, which let surgeons see the anatomy directly and repair under vision. Better imaging and knowledge of pelvic anatomy at birth further refined early care. The surgeon's core concerns are sexual function, plus control of the bowel and the bladder. With early diagnosis and meticulous repair, patients gain their best chance of good function.
europmc-pmc1994261:
Levine and colleagues used maths and experiments in 2007 to describe how small RNAs control genes in bacteria. These short RNA pieces, called sRNAs, help coordinate stress responses in Escherichia coli. They bind target messages and can block protein making or speed message breakdown. The team studied two distinct classes of bacterial sRNA in detail.

Their results show sRNA control differs from protein-based control in clear ways. It gives a threshold-linear response, where output stays low then rises in a straight line. The threshold can be tuned. The system also resists noise well and allows built-in cross-talk between pathways. These traits may help bacteria coordinate stress relief. They may also guide design of synthetic genetic circuits.
europmc-pmc2117961:
W. G. MacCallum of Johns Hopkins wrote in 1898 on the blood parasites of birds, infections then loosely called avian malaria. Work he and Opie began in the summer of 1896 covered birds in Maryland; in 1897 he continued at Dunnville, Ontario, focusing on crows, which carried the organisms most reliably. Sparrows, blackbirds, and owls also proved infected.

 In fresh blood MacCallum found two adult forms, a granular form rich in coloring matter and a clearer form, and he reads them as female and male. The clear form, he argues, gives up its life to produce four or more sperm-like flagella. That reading links the strange whipping forms seen in bird blood to a sexual stage like the one suspected in the malaria organism. It is a careful field-and-microscope study from years when malaria's own life cycle was still being pieced together.
europmc-pmc2124861:
Hideyo Noguchi and J. Bronfenbrenner measured in 1911 what shaking and heat do to complement, the fragile serum factor behind many immune tests. Guinea pig serum was their material. Shaking hurts complement most when kept up at body temperature; at ten degrees the harm is extremely small.

Within the first hour, shaking at body temperature does almost nothing. After the first few hours, destruction runs much faster, and by six hours it is nearly complete. That timing reassures test practice: the brief shakings used in fixation work should not skew results. Heat tells a similar story with a twist. Destruction quickens from forty-five to fifty-five degrees. The fall also comes in an irregular rhythm. Readers get practical numbers for handling a reagent that spoils invisibly.
europmc-pmc2125961:
Wilson G. Smillie tried to grow the globoid bodies linked to poliomyelitis and to judge what they really are, publishing alone in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. He took tissues from monkeys sick with experimental poliomyelitis and cultured them by the methods Flexner and Noguchi had described, then tested whether his grown strains could cause the disease.

Smillie obtained the globoid bodies in twenty-two cultures from seven monkeys. Twenty strains came from the central nervous organs, nearly all from the brain, and two from the spleen. Yet none of the cultured strains produced typical poliomyelitis when injected into fresh monkeys. Regrowing the bodies from an injected monkey proved as hard as the first culture. Nothing in his work tied the common streptococcus to the disease itself, though it often appeared as a stray invader in animals that had died before examination.
europmc-pmc2128361:
Philip D. McMaster, G. O. Broun, and Peyton Rous opened their total bile series with a method for collecting a dog's entire bile output. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. A permanent tube drew off all the bile in sterile condition over long periods, so the flow could be measured exactly, day by day.

The first days after the operation the flow ran scanty and thick, rich in pigment. Injury to the liver and ducts explains the scant flow, and blood escaped at surgery explains part of the pigment. One animal poisoned by accident with mercuric chloride stopped secreting almost entirely before death. An infected bile tract in another dog slowly replaced bile with a colorless, glairy fluid. Only after a week to ten days did the bile settle into its lasting character. That later output runs far smaller than earlier workers had recorded.
europmc-pmc2128561:
Franklin A. Stevens and A. R. Dochez sorted scarlet fever streptococci from other hemolytic streptococci by clumping tests, in the third paper of a streptococcus biology series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from Columbia's medical school. Strains came from scarlet fever cases in five cities, New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Baltimore, and Copenhagen.

All the scarlet fever strains clumped with one another's immune sera, freely and in both directions. Sera made from them did not clump pus-forming streptococci or strains from septic sore throat. Strains from one epidemic's patients, and the strain from the milk that caused that epidemic, both fell into the scarlet fever group by the same tests. Absorption tests, properly run, worked with these strains and sera too. A biologically distinct family of streptococci, the authors conclude, goes constantly with scarlet fever and can be named by its clumping pattern.
europmc-pmc2131261:
Louise Pearce and Thomas Rivers, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, asked in 1927 whether a filterable agent called Virus III changes a transplantable tumor of the rabbit. Their stock tumor was found to carry the virus. They compared the disease caused by virus-bearing tumor tissue with that caused by tumor tissue free of it.

The virus-bearing tumor gave a more severe disease on the whole, though the gap was not large and not steady in every feature. The authors weigh two routes: a direct effect on the tumor cells, or a change in the host. They favor the second, holding that the host's fight against the virus leaves it less able to resist the tumor itself.
europmc-pmc2131461:
Alexis Carrel and Albert Ebeling wrote part three of their fibroblast and macrophage series in 1928, turning to a malignant fibroblast. They had isolated a pure strain of fibroblasts from Sarcoma 10 of the Crocker Foundation and kept it alive in culture. The question was how a cancer strain of this cell compares with a normal rat fibroblast strain.

After about sixteen months in vitro, the strain kept the full malignancy of the original tumor. Its cells were larger and coarser than normal ones, yet sound in form, moving the same way and never dying off. Growth rates and life span in nutrient medium were nearly the same as normal. Two marks set them apart: the cancer cells dissolved a rat plasma clot, and they turned phenol red a deeper yellow.
europmc-pmc2140661:
John Klopp, at the University of Pennsylvania and Woods Hole, studied heat injury in frog skin in a 1924 paper. The voltage between the two surfaces of frog skin, measured under standard conditions, falls when the skin is injured. Klopp used that voltage as a gauge of injury, recovery, and death after brief exposures to high temperature.

Judged by the gauge, heat-injured skin follows one of three courses set by the severity of the burn. Mild injury allows complete recovery of the voltage. Middling injury allows only partial recovery. Severe injury starts a progressive change that leads to death of the tissue. The method turns injury into a quantity that can be followed over time.
europmc-pmc2169261:
Clarke argued in 2007 that clinical trials and systematic reviews need standardised outcomes. Fifteen years earlier, the group that became OMERACT first met to tackle the many outcomes used in rheumatoid arthritis trials. Studies answering the same question often report findings in different ways. That makes evidence hard to combine for healthcare decisions. Even a systematic review can fail when primary studies measure results inconsistently.

Selective reporting makes the problem worse, Clarke warns. Researchers who measure an outcome several ways may publish only the most positive or significant result. Readers then get an overly optimistic estimate of a treatment's effect. That bias can push decisions in the wrong direction. Standard outcome sets, agreed in advance, are offered as the remedy.
europmc-pmc2229861:
Yang and co-workers uncovered new roles in 2007 for the formin protein mDia2 in moving cells. Formins and the Arp2/3 complex build actin filaments, the cell's internal scaffolding, and were thought to split jobs neatly. Arp2/3 was credited with sheet-like lamellipodia, while formins made spiky filopodia. The team depleted mDia2 with interfering RNA and also expressed an always-active version, examining the actin network by light and electron microscopy.

Unexpectedly, depleting mDia2 severely blocked lamellipodia, not just filopodia. The few remaining sheets held abnormally short filaments. Active mDia2 built long filaments, prolonged sheet protrusion, and promoted filopodia. Those spikes formed by lamellipodial filaments gradually converging into bundles. A partner protein, Abi1, targeted mDia2 to the membrane. The authors propose mDia2 creates and protects the long filaments that both structures share.
europmc-pmc2291561:
Zybailov and co-workers catalogued the chloroplast protein set in 2008 for the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Chloroplasts power plant growth, yet most of their proteins are made from nuclear genes and imported. The team ran ten independent chloroplast preparations through high-end mass spectrometry, requiring multiple matching peptide pieces for each identification. They also measured protein abundance from spectral counts and examined targeting signals and chemical modifications at protein starts.

They unambiguously identified 1,325 proteins, including new kinases and nucleotide-binding proteins. Nine hundred and sixteen were confidently assigned to the plastid, and 86 percent carried a predicted import signal. Abundances of soluble stromal proteins spanned four orders of magnitude. Forty-eight abundant proteins manage protein upkeep, from proteases to chaperones. A new start-modification motif emerged, and targeting signals differed between Arabidopsis and rice. No evidence supported import through the secretory pathway.
europmc-pmc2292261:
Rodriguez, Ehlenberger, Dickstein, Hof and Wearne built an automated three-dimensional system in 2008 for finding and classifying dendritic spines in microscope images. Spines are tiny protrusions where excitatory synapses form, and their shapes relate to learning, memory and brain disease. Measuring them precisely in 3D was slow and low-throughput. Their software module, part of NeuronStudio, processes laser scanning microscopy volumes automatically, using adaptive thresholding, voxel clustering and a sampling technique to estimate spine diameters.

The system proved more accurate than existing tools and at least ten times faster. Working fully in three dimensions, it resolves spines that two-dimensional tools miss entirely. Diameter profiles classify spines into shape types while limiting optical blur and measurement artefacts. The technique enables objective studies of spine change during learning, development, ageing and neurodegenerative disease. Large volumetric datasets can finally support robust statistics on spine morphology.
europmc-pmc2386861:
Copetti, Soldati, and Copetti tested chest ultrasound for telling two lung emergencies apart in 2008. Both fill the lungs with fluid and cause severe breathlessness: heart-driven fluid build-up, called cardiogenic edema, and lung injury syndrome, called ARDS. Treatment differs, yet telling them apart at the bedside is often hard.

They scanned 58 intensive care patients on admission and checked seven ultrasound signs. Some signs appeared in every ARDS patient and no edema patient at all: loss of the normal sliding motion of the lung surface, and spared healthy patches amid diseased areas. Thickened, uneven lung lining appeared in all ARDS cases but only 25% of edema cases. Solid lung patches showed in 83.3% of ARDS cases and none of the edema group.
