Fluid around the lung, by contrast, favoured edema, at 95% of cases. The authors called the pattern strongly predictive.
europmc-pmc2394461:
Robey and colleagues pinned down how one building block changes a drug pump protein in 2003. The protein, ABCG2, sits in cell membranes and pumps many cancer drugs out of cells, causing drug resistance. A single change at position 482, where the normal letter is arginine, had been reported to alter what the pump carries.

The team put normal and two mutant versions into human kidney cells. All three pumped out mitoxantrone and two other test drugs. Only the mutants also carried rhodamine 123, daunorubicin, and one more dye. Mutant cells resisted several classic cancer drugs 13 to 71 times more strongly than normal-pump cells. One blocker drug, novobiocin, fully reversed the normal pump but only partly reversed the mutants. The authors warned that such mutations in patients could blunt pump-blocking drugs.
europmc-pmc2475661:
Andersson and colleagues demonstrated a high-throughput way to profile human gut microbes in 2008. Knowing which microbes live in patients versus healthy people could reveal new treatment targets. Their method reads a variable stretch of the bacterial 16S gene, a standard identity marker, using a fast sequencing technique called pyrosequencing.

Each sample got its own short barcode tag, so hundreds of samples could be pooled and read in one run, then separated by computer. Computer modelling showed the method reconstructs communities correctly down to types below genus level. They applied it to throat, stomach, and stool samples from human volunteers. The profiles matched expectations for each body site. The authors offered barcoded pyrosequencing as a cheap, deep way to compare microbial communities across many people at once.
europmc-pmc2621261:
Curtin and colleagues uncovered in 2009 how a gene therapy for glioblastoma, the deadliest primary brain tumour, recruits the immune system to destroy the cancer. The therapy injects viruses carrying two genes into the tumour: one summons immune cells, the other makes tumour cells killable by a drug. It worked in animals, but the activation pathway was unknown.

Tumour regression required both CD4 and CD8 T cells and depended on a sensor called TLR2 on dendritic cells entering the tumour. The trigger proved to be HMGB1, an alarm protein spilled by dying tumour cells, which accumulated in treated mice's blood. Blocking HMGB1 with a drug or antibodies abolished the therapy's benefit entirely. Radiation and chemotherapy also released HMGB1 from several tumour types. The authors argue the pathway supports clinical trials of the approach.
europmc-pmc2631461:
Hirdes and colleagues tested in 2008 whether the interRAI assessment instruments, used across home care, mental health, long-term care, palliative care, and post-acute care, give consistent results between assessors. These instruments share common items plus specialised ones, forming an integrated information system. Reliability had to be proven in real settings before data could be pooled across countries and care types.

In twelve countries, trained assessors independently assessed the same 783 people within 72 hours, blind to each other's answers. For the 161 items shared between instruments, the average agreement statistic, kappa, was 0.75, comfortably above standard acceptability cut-offs. Specialised items averaged from 0.63 to 0.73 depending on the instrument, and over 60 percent of all items scored above 0.70 on this scale. The authors conclude the suite is substantially reliable across settings.
europmc-pmc2736161:
Damschroder and co-authors built in 2009 the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, a unified structure for judging why proven health interventions succeed or fail in real settings. Many theories existed, but they overlapped, used inconsistent terms, and each missed constructs found in others. That fragmentation slowed efforts to learn what works where and why.

Their framework merges constructs from published theories into five domains: the intervention itself, outer setting, inner setting, the individuals involved, and the implementation process. Thirty-seven constructs are defined explicitly, from evidence strength to leadership engagement and reflection. It is meant to guide evaluations before, during, and after roll-out and to build a shared knowledge base across studies.
europmc-pmc2745661:
Moody and Laimins showed in 2009 that human papillomaviruses switch on the ATM DNA damage pathway to copy their genomes when host skin cells mature. That pathway is a cell alarm for broken DNA. The viral life cycle is tied to epithelial differentiation, with genome amplification and late gene production only in upper layers. What triggers that productive amplification step was poorly understood.

In HPV-31-positive skin cells that began to differentiate, markers of ATM pathway activation rose, including tagged forms of CHK2, BRCA1, and NBS1. Blocking ATM kinase stopped viral genome amplification and replication focus formation, but did not affect genome maintenance in undifferentiated cells. A related kinase, CHK2, also drove caspase cutting needed for amplification.
europmc-pmc2758861:
Cook, Dickinson, and Eccles tracked in 2009 response rates in postal surveys of healthcare professionals published between 1996 and 2005. Postal surveys are a workhorse of health services research, but low response can bias results and threaten validity. They sampled three hundred fifty studies from major databases and modeled which factors raised response.

Doctors responded at an average rate below sixty percent, significantly lower than in the prior decade. Response rose when reminders were sent, yet only half of studies used them. Smaller surveys and countries outside the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand also did better. Only seventeen percent of studies checked for non-response bias at all, which leaves the size of that bias largely unknown.
europmc-pmc2764861:
Schram, Baan, and Pouwer systematically reviewed in 2009 how depressive symptoms relate to quality of life in people with diabetes. Diabetes already worsens quality of life, and patients face a raised risk of depression, which may lower it further. Searching five databases for studies from 1990 to 2007, they compared patients with and without depressive symptoms.

Twenty studies qualified, eighteen cross-sectional and two following patients over time. Every study found a negative link between depressive symptoms and at least one aspect of quality of life. Diabetes-specific quality of life was severely lower in depressed patients. Generic and domain-specific quality of life ran mildly to moderately lower. They urge greater awareness and routine monitoring for depression across diabetes care settings.
europmc-pmc2769161:
Tokiwa, Calabia, Ugwu, and Aiba reviewed in 2009 the biodegradability of plastics, how microbes and enzymes break these high-molecular-weight polymers down. Common plastics such as polyethylene and polystyrene barely degrade, and their buildup in the environment threatens the planet. Microbial attack looks like the most effective route, given how abundant microbes are and how specifically some attack plastics.

They argue that judging a plastic's degradability takes more than its chemical structure. Physical traits matter too: melting point, glass transition temperature, crystallinity, and stiffness all shape how fast microbes can work. The review sorts plastics into biodegradable and bio-based kinds, which do not always overlap. It then discusses microbial and enzymatic breakdown and the factors that speed or slow it, as a guide for greener materials.
europmc-pmc2799461:
Frisbee and colleagues described the design and reach in 2009 of the C8 Health Project, a study born from a court settlement over tainted drinking water. A DuPont plant near Parkersburg, West Virginia had released a chemical called PFOA, or C8, into water serving six districts across two states.

Over thirteen months the project enrolled just over sixty-nine thousand people, the largest study of its kind. Each person gave background facts, health history, lab tests, and blood levels for ten related chemicals. Average blood PFOA ran about five times higher than in a typical American sample. The dataset now supports health studies and gave each person their own exposure results.
europmc-pmc2815961:
Mooi and colleagues reported in 2009 that whooping cough bacteria making extra toxin have spread as the disease resurges. Whooping cough, or pertussis, fell sharply after childhood vaccination began in the nineteen fifties, yet it has climbed back in well-vaccinated countries since the nineteen nineties. The team read a control region for the main toxin gene in over fifteen hundred bacterial samples collected worldwide from 1935 to 2004.

A newer control variant, called ptxP3, appeared in strains that produce more pertussis toxin than older strains. Those high-toxin strains expanded in the Netherlands during the resurgence years. The authors argue the bacteria have adapted under vaccine pressure, and that this evolution helped drive cases upward, mostly among older people whose vaccine protection has faded.
europmc-pmc2851561:
Salathé and Jones explored in 2010 how the clumpy structure of human contact networks changes the course of epidemics. People cluster into communities with dense ties inside and sparse ties between, and most epidemic models ignore that shape. Using real and simulated networks, the authors tracked how infections move within and between such groups.

Community structure strongly shaped spread, slowing travel between groups. When vaccine was scarce, shots aimed at people bridging communities beat shots aimed simply at the most connected people. Because full network maps are rarely known, the authors built a vaccination algorithm using only local information, and it outperformed rival methods especially where community structure ran strong.
europmc-pmc2861661:
Flanagan and co-authors reviewed in 2010 the role of carnitine, a nutrient the body uses to move fats into cells for burning as fuel. People make some carnitine and get more from meat, and strict vegetarians absorb it more efficiently. Shortages arise from faulty transporter genes or alongside diseases of the liver and kidney.

The review ties low carnitine to diabetes, sepsis, heart muscle disease, poor nutrition, and aging itself. Supplements prove life-saving when the shortage is the primary genetic defect, and they help dialysis patients and ease nerve pain and weak immunity in diabetes. Early evidence also supports uses in some brain disorders, in obesity and blood sugar control, and even as a protective eye drop for dry eye.
europmc-pmc2876761:
Klein, Smith, and Laxminarayan counted in 2007 the American toll of MRSA, the antibiotic-resistant staph germ, across 1999 to 2005. Staphylococcus aureus already led hospital infections of lungs, surgical wounds, and blood. Its resistant form had become entrenched in hospitals, nursing homes, and increasingly the wider community, and national burden numbers were badly needed.

Drawing on national hospital and death data, the authors tracked steady growth in admissions and deaths tied to the resistant germ over the period. The rises outpaced what improved coding or awareness could explain, pointing to a real expanding epidemic. Their totals made the case that resistant staph deserved standing as a national control priority, on par with better-known infectious threats, rather than a problem left to each hospital alone.
europmc-pmc2965761:
Snider and colleagues traced a muscle disease called facioscapulohumeral dystrophy to incomplete silencing of an ancient copied gene in a 2010 study. The disease follows loss of some repeats near a chromosome end, each repeat holding a gene for a switch protein named DUX4.

Healthy muscle made only a shortened message from that gene, while patient muscle made small amounts of the full message and protein, concentrated in few nuclei. Testis normally produced the full form, as did reprogrammed stem cells until they began maturing. The results recast the disease as a failure to keep a germline gene off in muscle.
europmc-pmc2984261:
Reuter and Mathews described RNAstructure, a software package for predicting how RNA molecules fold, in a 2010 update. Knowing an RNA's shape is key to knowing how it works, and shape also guides design of gene-silencing tools.

The package uses energy rules from the freshest measured parameters to forecast folding, base pairing odds, two-molecule structures, and shapes shared by two sequences. New additions include a programming library for embedding in other tools, a friendly graphical interface, and plain text interfaces for Unix-style systems. The older Windows interface remains maintained alongside.
europmc-pmc3035261:
Auch, Klenk, and Göker wrote in 2010 a standard procedure for computing genome to genome distances, meant to support computer based naming of new microbe species. The older lab method behind species decisions is slow and cannot feed a growing database. Digital methods can replace it, but results shift with software choices and settings, so shared rules are needed.

The paper lists every choice that must be recorded when distances come from matching DNA stretches found by search tools. It gives practical advice on finding those matches with common programs and on handling repeated regions. As a shared reference, the authors present their web server that runs the calculation the same way for everyone. Clear reporting, they argue, is what makes digital taxonomy trustworthy enough to replace bench work.
europmc-pmc3045361:
Redzic reviewed in 2011 the two main gates that protect the brain's fluid environment from the blood. One gate sits in brain capillary walls and the other in the tissue that makes cerebrospinal fluid. Both seal their cells tightly so stray molecules cannot slip between them, yet both must also ferry food in and waste out.

The review compares the seal proteins at each gate, then the carrier proteins that move sugars, amino acids, salts, and waste in each direction. A third set of pumps throws foreign chemicals back out, guarding the brain from drugs and toxins. The two gates share much, but their carrier lineups differ in telling ways. Those differences shape how medicines reach the brain and how fluid balance is kept. The paper maps both gates side by side for researchers designing brain targeted drugs.
europmc-pmc3093361:
Allen and Wynn argued in 2011 about the allergy like arm of immunity, called Th2 in short. They held it first evolved not to fight germs but to repair tissue torn by worms and biting creatures. Big invaders cannot be swallowed by single cells, and blasting them with the oxidative weapons used against microbes would wreck host tissues. Tolerating the invader while patching damage fast may have been the cheaper survival strategy.

Th2 responses wall off large bodies with scar like tissue, recruit repair cells, and drive mucus and muscle responses that can expel gut worms. In blood fluke infection, mice lacking the Th2 signal receiver die of sepsis when parasite eggs breach the gut wall, showing repair saves lives. The authors reframe allergy and asthma as a repair system firing at the wrong targets. That lens, they suggest, explains both its power and its collateral damage.
europmc-pmc3131561:
Sinéad Lordan, Paul Ross, and Catherine Stanton reviewed sea-derived ingredients for health foods in a 2011 paper in Marine Drugs. The oceans hold many compounds barely used in food, several of which act on processes behind long-term diseases. The review gathers evidence on fish, seaweed, shellfish, and marine microbe products.

Fish protein fragments and seaweed fibres showed blood-thinning, cholesterol-lowering, and anti-cancer activity in studies. Fish oils supply the well-known healthy fats, while shellfish and seaweeds carry strong antioxidants. The authors argue these ingredients could fortify everyday foods to help prevent chronic disease. They note that most evidence still comes from lab and animal work rather than large human trials.
europmc-pmc3149661:
Sovan Sarkar and colleagues showed that nitric oxide, a cell messenger, brakes the cell's recycling system in a 2011 paper in Molecular Cell. That recycling system clears long-lived and clump-prone proteins and matters in development, immunity, cancer, and brain degeneration. The team traced how the messenger interferes with the machinery that builds the recycling sacs.

The gas chemically tags and disables two control enzymes, which loosens a key partnership needed to start sac building and switches on a growth pathway that further suppresses recycling. Cells making extra gas-producing enzymes formed fewer sacs. Blocking gas production, in contrast, sped clearance of clumping proteins and reduced nerve damage in models of Huntington disease. The work links chemical stress to failed cleanup in degenerative disease.
europmc-pmc3313861:
Yang, Hanna, and Sun reviewed what to do with the flood of crude glycerol left over from biodiesel making, in a 2012 article. For every batch of biodiesel, roughly a tenth of the output is this thick liquid byproduct. The glut crashed glycerol prices and now threatens the economics of biodiesel itself, a renewable fuel meant to cut reliance on oil.

The review explains what crude glycerol contains and why its quality varies with the catalyst and feedstock used. Most of it now goes into making other useful chemicals, with animal feed the next largest outlet. The authors survey further options, from burning and fermentation to new chemical processes, arguing that profitable uses for the byproduct are key to making biodiesel pay.
europmc-pmc3326161:
Desai reviewed the hurdles facing medicines built from nanoparticles, in a 2012 article. Particles this small can cross body barriers, carry water hating drugs, and aim at diseased tissue, all prized abilities in drug design. Yet very few nanoparticle medicines have won approval, and the author asks why the pipeline stays thin.

A nanoparticle is a multi part, three dimensional construct, so tiny variations in making it can change how the body handles it and how safe it is. Production must be consistent at scale, and tests must capture size, shape, and behavior from several angles at once. Regulators also lack settled standards for this class, including for copycat versions. Using one approved cancer nanomedicine as a running example, the author suggests strategies for developers and agencies to speed the field along.
europmc-pmc3348161:
Jia, Melville, Utzinger, King, and Zhou combined studies on how fast intestinal worms return after deworming treatment, in a 2012 analysis. The three main soil transmitted worms infect more than a billion people, and mass drug giving is the main control tool. The catch is that treatment does not stop new worms from arriving, so the team asked how quickly infection rebounds.

Pooling fifty one studies, they found roundworm prevalence climbed back to about a quarter of its starting level within three months and nearly all of it within a year. Whipworm rebounded almost as fast, while hookworm returned more slowly, reaching a little over half by one year. Heavier starting infection meant faster, heavier return. The authors say drugs must be given often, and that sanitation and health education are needed to break transmission for good.
europmc-pmc3375761:
Scallan and co-authors estimated in 2011 how much sickness known germs in food cause inside the United States each year. Only a small share of foodborne illness is ever lab-confirmed and reported, so raw counts mislead. Their study is one of two companion reports updating older national estimates.

Thirty-one known pathogens, they calculate, cause millions of episodes of foodborne illness yearly. Those episodes lead to tens of thousands of hospital stays and more than a thousand deaths. The authors explain how they bridged gaps in reporting and testing to reach the totals. Health agencies use such estimates to set priorities and aim inspections where they matter most.
europmc-pmc3420961:
de Haan and colleagues used a computer model in 2012 to test why the brain's most connected hubs fall first in Alzheimer's disease. Hub regions collect heavy amyloid deposits early, and excess nerve activity is known to raise amyloid. The model wired seventy-eight brain regions together following human scan data, each region a mass of excitatory and inhibitory cells.

In the model, the busiest regions were indeed the hubs, matching the high resting activity of real hub networks. Letting overactivity erode connections reproduced signature features of the disease: slowed rhythms, weaker signals, lost long-range synchrony, and hub failure. Brief rises in activity seen in early memory trouble appeared too, and looked harmful rather than helpful. Activity itself, they suggest, may drive the damage.
europmc-pmc3473361:
Festuccia and colleagues showed that one gene can stand in for a master stem cell factor, in a 2012 Cell Stem Cell paper. Nanog is a protein that helps embryonic stem cells keep renewing instead of changing into body cell types. How Nanog works, and which genes it directly controls, stayed unclear. The team compared cells with high, low, and no Nanog to find its real targets.

Among the few genes that truly answered to Nanog, one stood out: Esrrb. Nanog binds that gene directly and boosts its activity. Adding Esrrb alone kept stem cells renewing without outside support signals, even in cells lacking Nanog entirely. Removing Esrrb erased Nanog's defining effect. Festuccia's work places Esrrb squarely downstream of Nanog in the renewal circuit.
europmc-pmc3482661:
Suraweera and co-authors found why blocking the cell's protein shredder kills cells, in a 2012 Molecular Cell paper. The shredder, called the proteasome, chops up worn and unneeded proteins, and drugs that jam it treat a blood cancer. Everyone assumed jammed shredders kill by letting waste pile up. The team tested that idea in yeast, mammal cells, and flies.

In all three systems, blocking the shredder starved cells of amino acids, the building blocks recycled from chopped proteins. Adding amino acids rescued the cells, even though waste proteins stayed high. Starved cells switched on stress and self-eating programs in a failed bid to refill the pool. Suraweera's group concludes cells can bear waste, but not the shortage that follows a jammed shredder.
europmc-pmc3508861:
Splitting a muscle sample into its compartments lets researchers see where a protein lives, and Ivan Dimauro, Timothy Pearson, Daniela Caporossi, and Malcolm J. Jackson publish a simple protocol in 2012. Their method works on mouse skeletal muscle tissue and on cultured myoblasts and myotubes, the immature and mature muscle cell forms.

One low-cost procedure isolates nucleus, cytosol, and mitochondria from the same starting sample, quickly and at the same time. Purity is checked by western blotting for marker proteins unique to each compartment. Against a commercial kit, the protocol gives better yield and a cleaner nuclear fraction. The authors aim it at studies of aging and treatment effects on protein distribution.
europmc-pmc3524761:
A spurge-family plant from Pakistan may hold protective chemistry, and Naima Saeed, Muhammad R. Khan, and Maria Shabbir test whole-plant extracts of Torilis leptophylla in 2012. They make a methanol extract and five fractions with solvents of rising polarity, then screen them in test tubes and in rats.

The methanol extract holds the most phenolics, about 122 milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per gram. The ethyl acetate fraction leads in flavonoids, near 61 milligrams per gram. In rats the extracts blunt carbon tetrachloride liver injury, curbing fat damage and keeping glutathione up. A first screen maps the plant's main compounds. The team pitches the species as a candidate source for future protective products.
europmc-pmc3547661:
Some statistical models are too complex for their likelihood to be computed, and Mikael Sunnaker and six colleagues explain approximate Bayesian computation in this 2013 primer. ABC sidesteps the likelihood altogether: simulate data from the model, keep the parameter values whose simulations land close to the real data, and treat those as the answer's distribution.

The trick widens Bayesian inference to models in genetics, ecology, and beyond that were previously out of reach. Approximations are unavoidable, and their cost must be checked; summary statistics that compress the data help efficiency when chosen well. The article lays out the logic, the algorithms, and the open problems in estimation and model choice, for a method spreading quickly.
europmc-pmc3707861:
Soorya and colleagues carefully assessed thirty-two people with SHANK3 deficiency, the gene at the heart of 22q13 deletion syndrome. They mapped how the condition relates to autism. Most participants carried deletions of varying size; two had new mutations in SHANK3 itself. A specialist team ran standard autism tests alongside medical and thinking tests.

Autism was the rule. Eighty-four percent met criteria for an autism spectrum disorder. Three quarters met criteria for autistic disorder specifically. Severe to profound learning disability affected most patients. Only a fifth used any words on their own. Low muscle tone, gait problems, reflux, seizures, and repeated chest infections were also common. The authors supply a fuller clinical picture for families and clinicians.
europmc-pmc3905661:
Rachel L. Pullan, Jennifer L. Smith, Rashmi Jasrasaria, and Simon J. Brooker count worm infections worldwide in Parasites & Vectors, with the record dated 2014. Soil-transmitted worms, roundworm, whipworm, and hookworms, infect huge numbers of people, mostly in poor regions. Sound global counts are needed to weigh their burden against other diseases.

The team drew on a world atlas with prevalence data from thousands of sites in over a hundred countries. Map-based statistics filled gaps for Africa, while simpler methods served elsewhere. Counts were split by age and by infection intensity, then fed into the Global Burden of Disease frame to yield healthy years lost. The estimates update the world picture for 2010 and guide deworming programs.
europmc-pmc3923761:
Rik van Dinteren, Martijn Arns, Marijtje L. A. Jongsma, and Roy P. C. Kessels chart how a brain signal of attention and memory changes across life, in PLoS ONE in 2014. The signal, called P300, is a positive wave in the brain's electrical activity, drawn out by asking people to spot a rare tone among common ones. It is widely used as a window on thinking.

Their review and meta-analysis combined 75 studies with 2,811 healthy people, then checked the pattern in a second dataset of 1,572 people aged 6 to 87. Both the speed and the size of the wave improve from childhood into the teens, level off in a plateau, then worsen with age. Curve fitting pinned down the ages where the wave peaks, giving clinics a lifespan yardstick.
europmc-pmc3930561:
Ece A. Mutlu and a large team compare gut microbes in people with and without HIV in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. HIV progression involves constant immune activation and gut microbes leaking into the body, and a disturbed gut community is one suspect driver. The team collected 121 specimens from 21 HIV-positive patients on treatment and 22 controls during colonoscopy, sampling both the gut wall and its contents.

The HIV patients' lower-gut communities differed clearly from controls. Diversity was lower in the right colon and the end of the small intestine, friendly resident bacteria were lost, and some disease-linked bacteria gained ground. Microbe patterns lined up with immune activation measures and with bacterial products in the blood. The authors present this as the first map of these gut sites in HIV.
europmc-pmc3944461:
Florian A. Siebzehnrubl and a large team link one gene regulator to glioblastoma's worst traits. Their paper appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2013. Glioblastoma is the most common adult brain tumor. It is also among the most lethal. It almost always returns after surgery, radiation, and drugs. The regulator is ZEB1. Healthy cells use it to change identity as they develop. Cancers can hijack that same program.

ZEB1 was strongest in the invasive cells at the tumor's edge. Through a feedback loop with a small RNA, it fed three dangers at once. The dangers were invasion, drug resistance, and new tumor seeding. Its downstream targets include ROBO1, c-MYB, and MGMT. MGMT is a known shield against the standard drug for this cancer. In patient data, high ZEB1 meant shorter survival. It also meant a poorer drug response. The team presents ZEB1 as both a warning sign and a target.
europmc-pmc4013461:
Dharmalingam Subramaniam, Ravi Thombre, Animesh Dhar, and Shrikant Anant review enzymes that mark DNA as drug targets in cancer, in Frontiers in Oncology in 2014. The enzymes, called DNA methyltransferases, place chemical tags on DNA that can switch genes off. Tag levels often run high in cancer tissue.

Extra tags can silence the guard genes that hold tumours back, helping cancers grow. One enzyme keeps tag patterns as cells divide, while others lay new tags down. Raised levels of the newer-tag enzymes show up in many cancer types and cell lines. Blocking these enzymes in tests cut tumour growth, in part by waking silenced guard genes. The enzymes also help sustain colon cancer stem cells, the seed cells that regrow tumours. Plant compounds in food can block them too. The review frames the family as a target for both prevention and treatment.
europmc-pmc4018261:
Yoan Fourcade, Jan O. Engler, Dennis Rödder, Jean Secondi, and John F. Valentine test ways to fix biased species records in range maps, in PLoS ONE in 2014. A common tool, MAXENT, predicts where a species lives from sighting records and climate data. Sightings cluster where sampling is easy, and that bias can warp the map.

The team took three data sets, one made up and two real ones for a turtle and a salamander. They imposed four kinds of sampling bias, then tried five fixes and scored each map against the unbiased truth. No fix won everywhere: results swung with the bias kind, its strength, and the species. One simple fix, thinning records on a regular grid, ranked near the top in nearly all runs. Other fixes lagged in most cases. Grid thinning is the safest default for now.
europmc-pmc4036061:
Nai Ding and Jonathan Z. Simon review how brain activity locks to the rhythm of speech, in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. The loudness envelope of speech rises and falls at the pace of syllables. Cortex activity follows that beat, and the lock can be read while a person simply listens.

What the lock is for is still debated. Three candidate jobs are weighed: coding sound traits, marking syllable borders, and picking one voice out of a noisy mix. The signal is likely not one thing: parts from unlike brain sources may do unlike jobs. Slow waves in one band seem to carry traits vital for clarity, while a slower band tracks the felt rhythm. Finer work must split the signal by source and band before firm roles can be set.
europmc-pmc4036761:
Ziad A. Memish and eleven co-authors trace a human case of MERS to infected camels, in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2014. MERS is a severe lung illness caused by a coronavirus first found in Saudi Arabia in 2012. Camels across the region carry antibodies to it, hinting they host the virus.

A man in his forties fell ill after weeks of caring for sick camels in his small herd, some with runny noses. The team read the full virus genome from the man and part of the virus from a camel. Shared rare variants in the two pointed to a jump from camel to man. A third source for both cannot be ruled out. Still, the match makes camels a direct source in at least this case.
europmc-pmc4081561:
Michael A. Pfaller and a team of peers charted grave yeast infections caused by Candida types other than the best known one. Their study came out in PLoS ONE in 2014. It drew on a North America-wide list of cases kept from 2004 to 2008, with close to two thousand five hundred sick people in all.

One type, Candida glabrata, caused the most cases. Two more types came next, and a long tail of rare types made up the rest. Some sick people had two or more types at once. At most sites, the less known types as a group beat the well known one. Which type ruled changed with the type of case: glabrata led in organ swap cases and in those with solid growths. Of the drugs in use, one newer class was given most.
europmc-pmc4178461:
Frédéric Mahé, Micah Dunthorn, and four co-authors offered a new clustering method called Swarm in PeerJ in 2014. Environmental DNA studies read millions of short gene fragments and must group near-identical ones into units that stand for species. Common grouping tools rest on one fixed similarity cut-off, and their results can change with the order the data go in.

Swarm instead links fragments step by step with a small local threshold, letting each group grow to its natural edge. It then uses the group's inner structure and fragment counts to clean up the result. The method runs fast, scales to huge data sets, and gives the same answer whatever the input order. That steadiness makes diversity counts from amplicon studies more trustworthy.
europmc-pmc4190561:
Theerawut Chanmee, Naoki Itano, and two co-authors reviewed macrophages inside tumours in Cancers in 2014. Blood monocytes are drawn into growing tumours and settle there as macrophages. Once inside, tumour signals bend them toward the M2 type, which calms inflammation and heals wounds rather than fighting.

These tumour-associated macrophages help the cancer instead of attacking it. They feed new blood vessel growth, help cells invade nearby tissue and spread, and blunt the immune attack. Patient studies link heavy macrophage counts in a tumour with worse outcomes, and animal work backs the pattern. The review covers how the cells are recruited and reprogrammed, and it weighs ideas for blocking them or turning them back into tumour fighters.
europmc-pmc4204661:
Alfonso J. Cruz-Jentoft and a large international panel summarized sarcopenia evidence in Age and Ageing in 2014. Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age and raises the risk of falls and frailty. The report comes from the International Sarcopenia Initiative, joining two major study groups.

Searching studies from 2000 to 2013 that used a shared European definition, the panel found the condition in 1 to 29 percent of older people living at home. In long-term care the share ran from 14 to 33 percent. Exercise programs reliably improved strength and physical performance. Food-based evidence was murkier: protein supplements alone gave inconsistent gains, while certain amino acid products showed some benefit. The panel calls for standard, well-designed trials before firm treatment guidelines can be written.
europmc-pmc4322961:
Wenfeng Fang and eleven co-authors showed that a virus driven protein helps a throat cancer hide from the immune system. Their study appeared in Oncotarget in 2014. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is often linked to Epstein-Barr virus, and such tumors commonly display PD-L1, a protein that switches attacking immune cells off.

The viral protein LMP1 raised PD-L1 through three signaling routes, and interferon gamma, an immune signal, added its own push in synergy. Cutting LMP1 lowered PD-L1 again. Patients whose tumors carried more PD-L1 had worse disease free survival. The findings argue for pairing drugs that block the PD-1 pathway with treatments aimed at the viral driver.
europmc-pmc4352761:
Timothy Nott and a team of co-authors described in Molecular Cell in 2015 how a disordered protein can build droplets inside cells. Cells hold some structures without a membrane skin, such as germ granules. The team studied Ddx4, a main part of germ granules also called nuage, and asked what lets its loose tails gather into such bodies and what controls them.

Tails of Ddx4 formed phase-separated droplets both in living cells and in test tubes, with no membrane around them. Weak charge-based contacts held the droplets together, and they responded to heat, salt levels, and chemical changes to the protein. The droplets took in single-stranded DNA but largely kept out double-stranded DNA. The team proposes this droplet forming by disordered proteins as a general way cells build such bodies.
europmc-pmc4490361:
David Kleijn and a very large international team questioned a popular argument for saving wild bees in Nature Communications in 2015. Diverse ecosystems deliver benefits to people, and pollination of crops by wild bees is a flagship example used to justify conservation spending. The team asked how much of that service the full range of bee species actually provides, across crops, years, and regions.

Crop-visiting bee communities, they found, are dominated by a small number of common species, and threatened species are rarely seen on crops at all. The dominant pollinators persist even as farming expands and are easy to help with simple measures. So the cheapest way to protect pollination targets a different set of species than saving threatened bees. Conserving bee diversity, the authors conclude, needs arguments beyond crop pollination alone.
europmc-pmc4490561:
Georgia Atkin-Smith and nine co-authors discovered a new way dying cells break into pieces, in Nature Communications in 2015. When a cell dies by apoptosis, it disassembles into membrane-wrapped fragments called apoptotic bodies, which help clear debris and carry messages to other cells. The mechanics of that breakup were unclear when the team set out filming dying white blood cells.

Time-lapse microscopy revealed protrusions like beads on a string growing from the dying monocytes. The beads often sheared off the string to become apoptotic bodies, and this route sorted contents, keeping nuclear material out of the fragments. Formation depended on the cell's contractile machinery and on earlier foot-like protrusions. A screening of drugs found that the antidepressant sertraline blocks the beaded protrusions and body formation, giving researchers a tool to modulate the process.
europmc-pmc4507461:
Mohit Kumar Jolly and seven co-authors review a half-way state of cancer cells in a 2015 Frontiers in Oncology paper. Cancer spreads when cells shift from an epithelial state, where they stick in sheets, toward a mesenchymal state, where they move freely. The review focuses on cells caught between the two, holding both sticking and moving traits at once.

Such hybrid cells can travel as clusters rather than alone. If a cluster reaches the blood intact, it can seed groups of tumor cells at new sites. The authors lay out the core switch network that yields three states: epithelial, mesenchymal, and hybrid. They also link the hybrid state to drug resistance and to cells that can start new tumors, and to cluster traits that help cells survive the trip.
europmc-pmc4520061:
Julian R. Marchesi and Jacques Ravel wrote an editorial in Microbiome in 2015 asking their field to use its words with care. Gene sequencing and computing have remade the study of microbe communities in the human body, and papers have multiplied. Growth outran the vocabulary: terms like microbiome, microbiota, metagenome, and metabolomic get swapped and misused, muddying results for scientists and the public alike.

Earlier reviews had defined the terms only in passing sidebars. Marchesi and Ravel set out plain definitions with cases for each key word. Microbiota, for one, names the microbes living in a defined setting; microbiome has a broader sense. The pair urge colleagues to adopt the shared definitions and refine them, so studies can be read and compared without confusion.
europmc-pmc4682161:
Jean Albrengues, Thomas Bertero, Eloise Grasset, and nine colleagues studied how fibroblasts near tumors turn into helpers of cancer spread, publishing in Nature Communications. Fibroblasts are support cells that build the tissue around tumors. A signal called LIF can reprogram them into a state that remodels nearby tissue and helps cancer cells invade. The puzzle was how this harmful state stays switched on.

The team traced a chain of chemical marks on DNA and proteins that locks the state in place. One enzyme adds a mark to the STAT3 protein, which then raises a second enzyme that silences a brake gene called SHP-1. With the brake gone, a growth signal stays active on its own. Blocking both the marking enzymes and the signal, in lab tests and in animals, restored the normal fibroblast state. The findings name targets that might slow tumor invasion.
europmc-pmc4709861:
M. P. Francino wrote a solo review of antibiotics and the human gut microbiome in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. Antibiotics reach our microbes not only through prescriptions but through farm animals and crops as well. A course can swiftly thin the gut community, letting resistant opportunists bloom and sometimes cause acute illness. The deeper concern of the review is slower: what disturbed gut communities do to health over years, and what they store.

Gut microbes help run immunity and metabolism, so lasting shifts can tilt both. Recovery after antibiotics is often partial, with changes lasting months or years. Meanwhile the gut becomes a reservoir of resistance genes, ready to share with pathogens. Francino sorts the evidence under three heads: effects on the community, effects on the body, and the resistance store. Antibiotic use, the review argues, must be weighed as an ecological act, not only a medical one.
europmc-pmc4713061:
Elise Landais, Xiayu Huang, Colin Havenar-Daughton, and a large team followed antibody development in a sub-Saharan HIV cohort, in PLoS Pathogens in 2016. A protective HIV vaccine probably needs broadly neutralizing antibodies, which defeat many virus strains at once, yet no vaccine has coaxed the body into making them. The study tracked 439 people from early infection in eastern and southern Africa, testing their blood against diverse virus strains over years.

About fifteen percent developed broad responses, almost all between the second and fourth years. Breadth tracked with high virus levels, low CD4 counts, subtype C infection, and certain gene variants, but not with sex, age, or country. Nearly half of the broad responders aimed at one sugar-coated patch on the virus, the N332 region. The authors flag that patch as a promising vaccine target, and the cohort as a map of what grows such antibodies.
europmc-pmc4730261:
Gaby Danan and Rolf Teschke updated RUCAM, the standard scoring method for judging whether a drug or herb injured a patient's liver, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. When liver damage follows a medicine, proving the link is hard, yet the verdict drives treatment, regulation, and published case reports. RUCAM scores set items, from timing to competing causes, and sums them into a graded judgment of causality for each suspect product.

The update, built from two decades of worldwide use, sharpens definitions, simplifies handling, and tackles muddy points such as alcohol use and how thoroughly other causes were excluded. The goal is less disagreement between assessors and results that travel across countries. The authors recommend the revised scale for clinics, regulators, journals, and expert reviews alike. A shared ruler, they argue, is what turns scattered case stories into dependable knowledge about liver harm.
europmc-pmc4769261:
Barbara Kremeyer leads a team of many co-authors in Neuron in 2010 tracing a family pain disorder to one gene change. The family suffers attacks of severe upper body pain, set off by fasting or strain, passed down through generations in a dominant pattern. Gene mapping narrowed the search to a stretch of chromosome 8.

Inside that stretch sat TRPA1, a sensor channel that detects irritants like mustard oil. The family's copy carried a single letter change that leaves the channel's drug responses normal but makes it pass far more current once switched on. Skin tests matched: base feeling was normal, yet mustard oil stung with extra after-soreness. Drugs that block the channel also blocked the faulty one, which points to a treatment route.
europmc-pmc4772061:
Michael J. Weiser, Christopher M. Butt, and M. Hasan Mohajeri review a brain fat called DHA in Nutrients in 2016. DHA is the main omega-3 fat in the brain, and it shapes how nerve cells signal, grow, and connect. The brain loads up on it before birth and in early infancy, drawing on the mother's supply.

The review follows DHA across the whole life span. In childhood it bears on learning and memory growth. In adult life it supports sharp thinking, and in old age its lack tracks with decline. Modern diets carry little of it, the authors note, so most people must get it ready-made from food or supplements. They weigh the human trial record and the ways DHA may act inside brain cells.
europmc-pmc4820961:
Jenny van Dongen leads a large author team in Nature Communications in 2016 charting what shapes the human methylome. Methylation marks differ between people under both gene and life influences, and those influences may shift with age and sex. The team measured marks at over four hundred thousand sites in 2,603 people from twin families.

On average about a fifth of a mark's spread between people traced to inheritance, but the share swung widely by site. Thousands of sites showed sex-specific inheritance, and at others the environmental share grew with age. Laying the catalogue beside older data linked sites to metabolism, smoking, and aging. The map, the authors say, tells researchers where a methylation gap between people likely flags a real exposure or a gene effect.
europmc-pmc4912661:
Ke Fan and co-authors built a nickel-vanadium layered catalyst in Nature Communications in 2016 that splits water with high efficiency. Water oxidation is the slow half of making fuel from water, and cheap, strong catalysts are in demand. Their material is a single-layer double hydroxide, one sheet thick, pairing nickel with vanadium.

The sheet reached a current density of 27 milliamps per square centimeter at an overpotential of 350 millivolts, matching the best nickel-iron layered catalysts in alkaline baths. Mechanism studies credit the thin build and the vanadium partner for high inborn activity. Earth-common metals in a single layer can thus rival top catalysts, a hopeful cost path for solar fuels.
europmc-pmc4915361:
Erfan Sayyari and Siavash Mirarab offered a fast way in 2016 to compute local branch support for species trees from quartet frequencies. Rebuilding species trees is tangled by incomplete lineage sorting, where gene trees clash. Trust in each branch needs a support score, and older routes lean on slow repeated sampling. Their algorithm counts how gene trees vote on four-species splits around each branch.

From those counts it derives a local posterior probability that the branch belongs in the species tree, plus branch length in coalescent units. On simulated and real data the score showed very high precision and better recall than multi-locus bootstrapping. Species tree builders gain a swift trust gauge for every branch.
europmc-pmc4927261:
James Davey and nine co-authors test the brain region that helps people pull up the right meaning for a task. Their brain imaging study appeared in NeuroImage in 2016. Making sense of the world needs selective retrieval, picking facts that fit a current goal. The study asks whether that control for meaning uses general effort systems or a system built for semantics. Their candidate site is the left posterior middle temporal gyrus.

Scans showed the site active for semantic tasks but not for matched non semantic ones. During those tasks it worked in step with the inferior frontal gyrus, another key site for semantic control. Connectivity tests linked the spot to a wider meaning network. The authors argue the region joins stored knowledge from the front temporal lobe with executive control. That joining, they say, is what lets people retrieve the meaning a moment calls for.
europmc-pmc4927461:
Pablo Vidal-Ribas and four co-authors ask what irritability is, as a psychiatric symptom, and whether it can be measured well. Their review appeared in the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry in 2016. Irritability had drawn rising research and clinical interest, yet its status was unsettled. Open questions included whether it differs from other symptoms, forms its own disorder, and predicts later outcomes.

The authors mix a narrative review with a systematic review and meta-analysis. They screened 163 articles and included 24 in the pooled analysis. They found irritability forms a distinct dimension that stays fairly stable over time. It links in a specific way to later depression and anxiety, and genetic work shows it is moderately heritable. The authors note a gap on treatment, since few trials target irritability itself as the main outcome.
europmc-pmc4978761:
Mike F. Müller, Ashraf E. K. Ibrahim, and Mark J. Arends review the molecular classification of colorectal cancer. Their review appeared in Virchows Archiv in 2016. Colorectal cancers differ widely in their molecular faults. Two instability routes dominate: chromosomal instability, with large gains and losses, and microsatellite instability, with many small repeat errors. The review sets out the pathways of cancer development and then compares two new classification systems built from large molecular datasets.

One system, from The Cancer Genome Atlas, splits tumors into hypermutated and non-hypermutated groups by mutation load. The other, from a consensus consortium, defines four subtypes by gene expression. Both aim to match patients to the biology of their tumor rather than its look alone. The authors weigh how the systems overlap and where they clash, as guides for pathologists adopting molecular reports.
europmc-pmc5064361:
Valeriy A. Poroyko and a broad team of co-authors link broken sleep to gut microbes in Scientific Reports in 2016. Fragmented sleep, common in sleep apnea, does not shorten sleep or shift its timing, yet it drives overeating, weight gain, and insulin resistance. Since gut microbes shape those same traits, the team fragmented the sleep of mice for four weeks, then let them recover for two.

The mice ate more and their gut communities shifted: fermenting families bloomed while Lactobacillaceae fell, and the gut wall grew leakier. Body-wide and belly-fat inflammation rose, and insulin sensitivity fell. Two weeks of normal sleep reversed the changes. The decisive test used germ-free mice given the microbes of fragmented-sleep mice: they developed the same inflammation and metabolic faults. The authors read this as proof that microbes carry part of broken sleep's harm, and a hint that gut-targeted treatment could help.
europmc-pmc5105161:
Tianyun Wang and a large team of co-authors sequenced autism risk genes in a Chinese cohort, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Most earlier work on new, harmful gene changes in autism drew on European families. The team read 189 risk genes in 1,543 Chinese people with autism, over a thousand of them with both parents sampled.

New gene-breaking changes appeared far more often than chance predicts, and about four percent of patients carried one in just 29 known risk genes. The most common hit was SCN2A, followed by CHD8 and several others, and the team found fresh repeat hits in five more genes. Follow-up on symptoms pointed to distinct subtypes, showing how large cohorts outside Europe sharpen the picture of autism genetics.
europmc-pmc5115861:
Andrew W. Brooks, Kevin D. Kohl, Robert M. Brucker, Edward J. van Opstal, and Seth R. Bordenstein tested phylosymbiosis in PLoS Biology in 2016, with David Relman also named in the text's byline. The idea is that related host species carry related microbe communities, so a host family tree and a microbe tree should match.

Under controlled rearing, they profiled microbes from 24 animal species across deer mice, fruit flies, mosquitoes, and wasps, and rechecked data on wild apes and humans. Microbe mixes identified each host species with high accuracy, and the match between host and microbe trees held across groups of very different ages. Swapping microbes between host species lowered survival and performance, which suggests the matching is not just pattern but function.
europmc-pmc5137861:
Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Xavier Montagutelli defended animal research in Future Science OA in 2015. Barré-Sinoussi leads with her first surname in the hyphenated byline. Animal use in science is long-standing and often debated, most recently through a European citizens' push to end vivisection, and the authors aim to clear up mixed arguments.

They argue that cell cultures, however advanced, can mimic organs only in part, while whole-body questions, such as hormone control, infection spread, or gut microbes shaping the brain, need a living organism. Animal studies also test new therapies before human trials. The piece concedes that animal results do not always transfer to people, a point critics stress, and works through where models remain essential and where replacements already serve.
europmc-pmc5171261:
R. H. Elliot and A. C. Ingram reported an eye parasite case in The Indian Medical Gazette in June 1911. Elliot, superintendent of the Government Ophthalmic Hospital in Madras, and Ingram, acting professor of pathology there, describe a patient seen in November 1910: a 24-year-old French Eurasian man from Pondicherry.

Two years earlier a shard of broken glass had cut the surface of his right eye and healed in ten days with sight intact. Six months before admission he noticed a peppercorn-sized growth under his lower lid, which grew steadily. Examination found an ovoid cyst, 11 millimeters across, under the conjunctiva, somewhat tender and movable. At operation the surgeons freed it from its fibrous strands and removed it whole; it proved to be a cysticercus, the larval stage of a tapeworm.
europmc-pmc5241961:
Milija D. Mijajlović and a large international group reviewed post-stroke dementia in BMC Medicine in 2017. Up to a third of stroke survivors develop dementia or lasting thinking problems afterward. Definitions of the condition vary, and the authors propose using post-stroke dementia for any dementia that follows a stroke in time.

The review compares screening and diagnostic tools, from quick tests such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment to full test batteries. A complete workup, it argues, should also cover thinking before the stroke, mood, and daily function. Many proposed blood and spinal fluid markers, gene variants, and inflammatory signals are surveyed, but none yet reliably picks out at-risk patients or separates this dementia from Alzheimer's disease. Brain imaging, above all magnetic resonance imaging, remains central. Prevention of dementia here means prevention of stroke itself, alongside treatment of vascular risk.
europmc-pmc5297061:
W. E. Foggie, physician at Dundee Royal Infirmary, reported hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurring blood in the urine in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1928. Osler had first outlined the disease in 1901: it runs in families, causes nosebleeds, and shows small dilated vessels on the skin and in the mouth and nose. Hanes in 1909 traced the fault to weak muscle and elastic tissue in those surface vessels and gave the condition its lasting name.

Later reports widened the picture. The faulty vessels were found in the stomach at post-mortem, on the throat, and suspected on the brain's surface. Reviewers counted dozens of affected families, and Williams thought the condition far commoner than supposed. Foggie's contribution is a case where the bleeding came from the urinary tract, showing the fragile vessels can sit, and bleed, in the bladder or kidney as well as the familiar sites.
europmc-pmc5316861:
Niclas E. Bengtsson and co-authors tested gene editing for a muscle disease in mice, in Nature Communications in 2017. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a grave inherited illness of boys. A flaw in the dystrophin gene strips muscle of a key support protein, so fibers tear and waste away. The team used CRISPR editing tools, sent into muscle by harmless virus shells.

The Cas9 cutter was set to run only in muscle cells. With guide RNAs, it fixed the flaw in three ways: direct repair, cutting out bad sections, and full correction using a template. Treated mouse muscles made dystrophin across much of their area and pulled with more force. Shots into the blood spread the fix to limb and heart muscle. The work shows that muscle-only editing can ease the disease in a mouse model of the human illness.
europmc-pmc5483461:
Nagoor Meeran and co-authors present a detailed review in Frontiers in Pharmacology on thymol. Thymol is a natural compound found in thyme and other herbs. People have used it in folk medicine for centuries. Lab studies link it to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and germ-killing effects. The authors assess its promise as a drug or supplement.

The review gathers test tube and animal data across many diseases. Heart, brain, gut, and metabolic disorders all feature, as does cancer. Much of the benefit traces to free radical control and calmer immune signals, they say. The authors also weigh safety and drug development hurdles. Human trial data remain a key gap.
europmc-pmc5503661:
Li and co-authors present a review in Oncotarget on melatonin against cancer. Melatonin is the hormone the pineal gland releases in darkness. It sets the body's daily clock. Population studies hint that it may also slow tumors. Lab work shows growth restraint in several tumor cell types.

The review gathers evidence across breast, prostate, stomach, and bowel cancers. Melatonin may act as an antioxidant and trigger cell death pathways. It can cut blood vessel growth and spread as well. Paired with standard therapy, it may boost gains and ease side effects. The authors call it a strong candidate for prevention work.
europmc-pmc5509761:
Walton, Johnson, and Harrison present a review in Frontiers in Pharmacology on blocking fibrosis signals. Fibrosis is scarring run wild, where tissue lays down too much matrix. It strikes the heart, liver, lungs, and kidneys. Signals from the TGF-beta family drive much of that excess. Those signals collect in the scarred tissue itself.

The signals act through SMAD proteins inside cells, they explain. That chain switches on collagen and other matrix genes. The review weighs drug plans that trap the signals or block their receptors. Related family members, such as activins and myostatin, get covered too. Gentler BMP signals may push the other way.
europmc-pmc5530561:
Wen and co-authors report a gut microbiome study in Genome Biology on ankylosing spondylitis. This autoimmune disease inflames the spine and joints. Diagnosis often lags symptoms by eight to ten years. Gut microbes are suspected partners in the disease. The team sequenced gut DNA deeply from 211 Chinese participants.

Over 23,000 microbial genes differed between patients and controls, they report. Several Prevotella species ran high in patients. Bacteroides species ran low instead. Even the probiotic genus Bifidobacterium piled up in patients. The imbalance looked stronger than in bowel disease cases. Marker sets from the data could classify patients, aiding earlier diagnosis.
europmc-pmc5583361:
Lao and co-authors report a modeling study in Scientific Reports. Their aim is to predict survival in glioblastoma, the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. Median survival is only 12 to 14 months. A noninvasive forecast from scans could help plan care.

The team used MRI scans taken before surgery. One set held 75 patients, and a second held 37 for validation. They drew both handcrafted features and deep features learned by a neural network. Six deep features formed a signature that split patients into distinct risk groups. Adding age and performance score improved the forecast. Readers see how deep image features can act as a biomarker.
europmc-pmc5654761:
Allen and co-authors map global hotspots for emerging zoonotic diseases. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Wildlife diseases that jump to humans threaten health worldwide. The team updated a global event database. They built a new measure of reporting effort. Boosted regression tree models tested possible correlates.

Risk rose in forested tropical regions. Land-use change raised risk further. High mammal species richness also mattered. The team adjusted for uneven reporting between places. They present a new global hotspot map. Partial dependence plots show each link. The authors say the map can guide surveillance. Better monitoring may catch new diseases earlier. Field experiments can test the mechanisms proposed.
europmc-pmc5707461:
Das and co-authors make thin porous sheets that can sense an explosive compound. Their study builds covalent organic nanosheets from layered frameworks called COFs. The target compound is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, or TNP. Bulk frameworks sense such compounds only weakly. Their stacked layers limit contact with the target.

The team peeled the layers apart to form two-dimensional sheets. One sheet type lit up more in solid form when TNP was present. In liquid, its glow instead dimmed. The sheets beat the bulk material by about tenfold on one measure. They picked TNP out from close chemical cousins such as TNT. Detection worked even at very low levels.
europmc-pmc5762761:
Stokholm and co-authors study whether how the gut microbiome matures in infancy affects asthma risk. Gut microbes take shape over the first years of life. Gaps in that growth may unsettle the immune system. The team tracked gut microbes in 690 children through their first year.

One year olds with an immature gut mix faced higher asthma risk at age five. That link showed only in children of asthmatic mothers, they report. For those children, a slow start may trigger an inborn risk. Full growth of the gut mix in that window may guard them instead.
europmc-pmc5805861:
Thomas and co-authors ask how often type 1 diabetes starts in adults. Type 1 diabetes is often seen as a child's disease. Its gene risk is sharp and well mapped. The team uses that risk to spot cases in UK Biobank.

A gene score from 29 variants split 379,511 adults by risk. Extra cases in the high-risk half marked type 1 diabetes. Of those cases, 42 percent began between ages 31 and 60. Their traits matched young-onset cases, not type 2 diabetes. They were leaner and needed insulin fast. Readers learn that adult type 1 diabetes is common and easy to miss.
europmc-pmc5817861:
Jiao and co-authors review tyrosine kinase blockers and the resistance that beats them. Tyrosine kinases pass phosphate tags that steer cell growth. Faulty ones drive tumor growth, invasion, and new blood vessels. Blocking them has reshaped cancer care.

Blockers compete with ATP at the kinase's active pocket. That cuts the faulty signal and slows cancer cells. Yet tumors learn to escape, and acquired resistance is near certain. The review sorts the escape routes tumors use. It also weighs what the patterns mean for next drugs. Readers get both the promise and the built-in limit of this drug family.
europmc-pmc5850561:
Gorrie and co-authors trace intensive care infections back to the patient's own gut. Their study appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases. Klebsiella pneumoniae rides silently in many patients' intestines. The team screened admissions to an Australian intensive care unit.

Carriers fell ill far more often than non-carriers. Infection struck about one in six carriers, against a small fraction of others. Genome matching showed half the infections grew from the patient's own strain. The gut, not just ward transmission, stocks the reservoir. Screening on admission could flag the patients at risk.
europmc-pmc5877361:
Bullard and co-authors estimate diagnosed diabetes by type in US adults. Their report appeared in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. About 23 million US adults had diagnosed diabetes at the time. Type 1 stems from immune destruction of insulin-making cells. Type 2 mixes insulin resistance with low insulin output. National figures split by type had been sparse. New survey questions in 2016 made the split possible.

The team used the National Health Interview Survey from that year. They estimate 0.55 percent of adults had type 1 diabetes. That equals about 1.3 million people. Type 2 covered 8.6 percent, or 21 million adults. Other types made up the rest of diagnosed cases.
europmc-pmc5937161:
Nemes and co-authors test two vaccine plans against new TB infection in teens. Their trial report was published in The New England Journal of Medicine. Fresh infection raises the risk of TB disease. The trial took in teens who got BCG shots as babies. All tested free of infection and had no HIV. Each teen got a dummy shot, a new vaccine, or BCG once more.

In all, 990 teens took part and were tracked for two years. Both vaccines were safe and woke up immune defences, the authors report. Neither blocked the first sign of infection. But BCG given again did block lasting infection. Its effect was about 45 percent.
europmc-pmc5945561:
Kjøbsted and co-authors review AMPK in skeletal muscle function and metabolism. Their review appeared in The FASEB Journal. AMPK senses the energy status inside cells. It keeps energy stores steady by tuning building and breakdown pathways. Muscle faces sharp swings in energy demand between rest and exercise. That makes AMPK control especially vital there.

The review covers the complex regulation of AMPK in muscle. It follows effects on fuel uptake, oxidation, and storage. Mitochondrial function in muscle fibres also features. The authors focus on exercise and on recovery after it. They also cover training adaptations and muscle plasticity. AMPK as a drug target closes the review.
europmc-pmc6033961:
Cimadomo and co-authors review how maternal age affects eggs and embryos. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Reproductive success falls steeply as women age. The egg supply shrinks over time. Egg quality also drops, raising chromosome errors.

Most such errors come from faulty chromosome sorting in meiosis. Energy output from mitochondria may also decline. The review explains the main mechanisms proposed. It then covers options used in IVF care. Freezing eggs early can preserve younger eggs. Better stimulation and embryo selection can limit harm. Donor eggs can bypass the problem entirely. Readers get a guide to managing older patients in fertility clinics.
europmc-pmc6207061:
Gilbert and co-authors present a world data set on where farm animals lived in 2010. Their data paper appeared in Scientific Data. The set is version 3 of the Gridded Livestock of the World database. It covers cattle, buffaloes, horses, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens, and ducks. Counts come from national and local census records that the team matched and cleaned.

Each species is mapped on grid cells of about ten kilometres at the equator. Two versions of each map are given. One spreads animals within census areas using model weights. The other spreads them evenly, with no added assumptions. Full notes on sources and years travel with the data. Such maps support farm economics, food security work, and disease studies.
europmc-pmc6244861:
Ståhl and co-authors review cell vesicles in kidney health and disease. Cells release tiny membrane particles called extracellular vesicles. Types include exosomes and microvesicles. They carry signals between cells. The review appeared in Pediatric Nephrology.

Vesicles are released in health and under cell stress. They can also clear harmful matter from cells. The authors cover how vesicles form and are taken up. They explain how vesicles can be detected. Their roles in clotting and vessel growth are covered. Roles in tissue repair and immune change also feature. In kidney disease, vesicles appear in blood and urine. That makes them candidate markers for diagnosis. They may also serve as drug targets or therapies.
europmc-pmc6245361:
Hosokawa reviews a family of enzymes that switch prodrugs on inside the body. His review appeared in Molecules. The enzymes are carboxylesterases, found in many mammals. A prodrug is an inactive form that must be split to work. These enzymes split ester and amide bonds in drugs and other chemicals. The family falls into five groups, with two groups doing most of the known work.

The two main groups prefer different substrate shapes. One favours a small alcohol part with a large acid part. The other favours the reverse pairing. Shape of the enzyme pocket explains much of that split. Animal tests guide human drug design, so species gaps matter. Hosokawa argues that knowing each enzyme in detail will help design better prodrugs.
europmc-pmc6263261:
Ferreira and co-authors review plant compounds that may boost the malaria drug artemisinin. Their review appeared in Molecules. Both come from the plant Artemisia annua. The plant is the sole trade source of artemisinin. Its leaf flavonoids have long been less studied. Tea made from the plant carries both parts together. That pairing raised the question of teamwork between them.

Flavonoids show antioxidant and immune effects of their own. They may also slow liver enzymes that break artemisinin down. That would keep more of the drug active in the body. Health bodies now back combination malaria therapy over single drugs. The same logic may apply within one plant's chemistry. Cancer uses are also discussed in the review. Few direct tests of the pairing exist, so the authors map what trials should check.
europmc-pmc6270361:
Khoddami, Wilkes, and Roberts review methods for analysing plant phenolic compounds. Their review appeared in Molecules. Phenolics range from simple acids to complex tannins and flavonoids. They are linked to lower rates of heart disease and some cancers. Lab work on them has grown sharply over twenty-five years. Choosing the right method is now a research skill in itself.

Extraction usually starts with organic solvents. Simple colour tests can count total phenolics. Light based and chromatography methods then name and measure single compounds. Newer tools improve speed and sensitivity. The review weighs each method for plant based foods and drinks. It notes where each method can mislead. Readers gain a guide to matching method to question. That match matters for claims about health benefits.
europmc-pmc6337861:
Uchimido and co-authors present the glycocalyx as a target in sepsis care. Their review appeared in Critical Care. The glycocalyx is a gel coat on blood vessel walls. It helps control leaks and blood flow. It also limits clotting and cell sticking. In sepsis, that coat breaks down fast.

Inflammation drives the damage through cutting enzymes. Oxidants and immune signals switch those enzymes on. Losing the coat makes vessels leakier. It also fuels wild vessel widening and clotting. Blood levels of shed coat pieces track organ failure. They also track illness severity and death risk. The authors weigh ways to measure and protect the coat. Fluid care and new drugs both enter the discussion.
europmc-pmc6349461:
Pasolli and co-authors rebuild over 150,000 genomes from human microbiome samples. Their study appeared in Cell. Most catalogued microbes come from the gut and Western nations. Body sites and world regions remain under-sampled. The team drew on 9,428 metagenome datasets. Those spanned ages, countries, and lifestyles.

Their pipeline recovered 154,723 microbial genomes. About 45 percent were of high quality. The genomes grouped into 4,930 species-level bins. Over three quarters had no public genome before. Unknown species appeared in 93 percent of good samples. They were richest in non-Westernized populations. The team annotated 2.85 million genes in the bins. The resource expands what microbiome studies can detect.
europmc-pmc6356461:
Vivarelli and co-authors review gut microbes in cancer, from cause to treatment. Their review appeared in Cancers. Cancer is a complex, multi-cause disease. Gut bacteria help keep the host and gut in balance. They make compounds the body needs daily. Under imbalance, other bacteria can expand instead.

Those populations can release high levels of toxins. Toxins can spark inflammation and tumor formation. Microbes also act through the gut lining and immune system. Friendly probiotic bacteria protect against tumor genesis. Trials now test them against imbalance in patients. The review covers microbe roles in specific cancers. It also covers how microbes affect cancer drugs. The gut emerges as a partner in oncology care.
europmc-pmc6379961:
Yang and co-authors present a review in Molecular Cancer on targeting the PI3K pathway in cancer. This signaling chain controls cell growth, movement, survival, and blood vessel formation. It goes wrong in nearly all human cancers, which makes it a prime drug target.

The review sorts inhibitors into dual PI3K/mTOR blockers, pan-PI3K drugs, and isoform-specific drugs. It tracks each class through clinical trials, noting where tumor growth slowed. Idelalisib, a delta-specific drug, was the first to win FDA approval. The authors also explain how tumors build resistance to these drugs. They close with strategies to restore drug response.
europmc-pmc6383261:
Sarowska and co-authors review a harmful group of E. coli in Gut Pathogens. These strains live quietly in the gut but cause disease outside it. They include types that infect the urinary tract, newborn brains, and blood.

The review covers the tools these germs use to cause harm. Sticky hairs help them attach, and toxins and iron-grabbing systems help them spread. Such tools often sit on mobile DNA that jumps between bacteria. The authors also track how common each type is and how it spreads. That spread is a growing clinical worry.
europmc-pmc6391761:
Cortellini and co-authors report a multicenter study in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer. Recent work hinted that heavier cancer patients respond better to checkpoint drugs. The team tested that claim in patients treated with anti-PD-1 or PD-L1 drugs.

Patients were split by body mass index at treatment start. Those who were overweight or obese fared better than leaner patients. The pattern also held when the team looked at men and women separately. Reasons for the paradox are not settled, they note. Still, weight may help doctors judge who is likely to benefit.
europmc-pmc6403161:
Xie and co-authors review a plant transcription factor family in Frontiers in Plant Science. AP2/ERF factors switch genes on and off in Arabidopsis. They help the plant answer hormones and harsh conditions like drought, cold, and salt.

Stress changes the plant's hormone mix, and these factors pass those signals to genes. Some family members give broad tolerance across many stresses. Others act in one narrow setting. The review maps the networks these factors form with hormone paths. That map may guide breeding of hardier crops. Field studies in crops come next, they suggest.
europmc-pmc6417261:
Sung and Kim review gene delivery systems in Biomaterials Research. Gene therapy can in principle cure inherited disease by fixing faulty genes. It needs a safe vehicle to carry new genes into cells, and that vehicle has been the hard part.

Viral carriers, built from DNA viruses, RNA viruses, and tumor-killing viruses, lead the field. Non-viral carriers use physical or chemical means to slip genes in. The review compares both families and their recent gains. It also covers the barriers each must pass, from the bloodstream to the cell nucleus. Better carriers are the key to wider gene therapy.
europmc-pmc6429061:
Law and co-authors update the picture of how the body makes, recycles, and clears lysophosphatidylcholine, a fat molecule tied to heart and brain disease. LPC levels rise in cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and several other conditions, yet recent clinical studies disagreed about its role. The confusion stems partly from the tangled enzyme chain that controls it.

Phospholipase A2 creates LPC from membrane fats, and the Lands cycle quickly rebuilds it, while autotaxin converts some into a cancer-linked signal. Trouble starts when production outruns recycling, loading modified LDL particles that damage vessel walls. Mapping each enzyme's kinetics, the authors argue, could reveal drug targets for restoring balance.
europmc-pmc6436961:
Rodriguez-Meira and co-authors introduce TARGET-seq, a method that reads mutations and the full transcriptome from the same single cell at high sensitivity. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals how tumor cells differ in activity, but sparse coverage usually misses the mutation hotspots needed to link behavior to genotype. That gap blocked study of how cancer subclones diverge.

Applied to 4,559 cells from myeloproliferative neoplasm stem and progenitor samples, the method separated genetic subclones and gave each its own transcriptional signature. Mutant and non-mutant cells from the same patient showed different disturbed pathways, including genes tied to leukemia development and drug resistance. Tumor heterogeneity can now be tracked cell by cell on both levels at once.
europmc-pmc6484761:
Zhang and co-authors reported that fat tissue ships liver cancer a growth signal inside exosomes, in the form of a circular RNA they called circ-DB. This article has since been retracted, and it is presented here as a retracted record; its findings should not be relied on. As published, circ-DB levels were said to run higher in hepatocellular carcinoma patients with more body fat.

The paper claimed the circle suppressed miR-34a, freeing the deubiquitinase USP7 and its partner Cyclin A2, so tumor cells grew faster and suffered less DNA damage in culture and in mice. Silencing circ-DB reportedly reversed the fat exosomes' effects. Every element of that account is withdrawn and unverified.
europmc-pmc6543461:
Ma, Gao, Gu and Chen review the part played by monocytes and macrophages in autoimmune disease, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. These innate immune cells start, feed and help settle inflammation, and they also repair tissue. Their crowding into diseased tissue is a hallmark of many autoimmune conditions.

Disease by disease — lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, bowel disease and more — the review weighs what is known about cell counts, entry into tissue, and behavior. The neat split into attacking M1 and healing M2 cells proves too simple: both kinds often appear at once, and cells shift state with place and stage. Whether these cells start disease or only drive it on is still unsettled. Sharper answers, the authors argue, could yield better targeted treatments.
europmc-pmc6547561:
Kosugi and co-authors put 69 genome tools through their paces, writing in Genome Biology. The tools hunt structural variants — deletions, duplications, insertions, flips and swaps of DNA at least 50 letters long. Such variants shape disease risk, but no single program finds every kind well.
