Using simulated and real whole-genome data, the team scored each tool by variant type and size, plus how exactly it placed breakpoints and genotypes. A shortlist stood out: GRIDSS, Lumpy, Manta, Wham and two others led on deletions and duplications. Taking only calls shared by two well-matched tools sharpened accuracy, and the win depended on the pair picked, not the family it came from. The advice: choose tools per variant class, not by habit.
europmc-pmc6565761:
Papazian and co-authors issue formal guidelines for managing acute respiratory distress syndrome in adults, writing in Annals of Intensive Care. ARDS floods the lungs with inflammatory fluid, fills a tenth of intensive care beds, and still kills about 40% of its patients. Worse, clinicians miss the diagnosis in a large share of cases, delaying the gentle ventilation that protects injured lungs.

Using the GRADE method, the panel sets out fifteen recommendations plus a treatment algorithm. Four rest on strong proof: low tidal volumes, capped plateau pressure, no oscillatory ventilation, and prone positioning. High PEEP, muscle relaxants, recruitment maneuvers and ECMO carry weaker backing. On driving pressure, early spontaneous breathing and carbon dioxide removal, the experts state plainly that evidence allows no recommendation yet.
europmc-pmc6602461:
Raudvere and co-authors describe the 2019 update of g:Profiler. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The toolset finds biological categories enriched in gene lists. It also converts gene identifiers and maps genes to orthologs. Many labs rely on it to interpret high-throughput studies.

The update brings a full technical rewrite for speed and flexibility. A modern web interface delivers interactive, configurable results. Users can download publication-ready figures or plain text files. Support now spans 467 species and strains. Custom GMT files let users analyze any organism. Data follow the Ensembl quarterly release cycle. Past releases stay archived, so old analyses remain reproducible.
europmc-pmc6612361:
Wińska and co-authors ask whether essential oils truly fight microbes. Their review appears in the journal Molecules. Plant oils have flavored food and scented products for ages. They also hold a long place in folk medicine. Rising drug resistance now drives fresh interest in them.

About 250 essential oils are sold commercially. Roughly a dozen show strong antimicrobial power. The review sums up recent studies on the most active oils. Named oils include lavender, thyme, cinnamon, clove, and tea tree. Strength varies widely by oil and by target strain. Oils look like a real option beside synthetic compounds, the authors argue. They urge studies that match each oil to the microbes it beats best.
europmc-pmc6650661:
Sundler and co-authors explain how to do thematic analysis within descriptive phenomenology. Their discursive article appears in Nursing Open. Nursing and midwifery research often studies lived experience. Phenomenological methods for analysing such data stay hard to follow. Existing thematic analysis guides rarely fit the descriptive tradition. The authors set out the philosophy beneath the approach. They explain its views on knowledge and being. From those roots they derive practical principles.

The principles guide each step of the analysis. They show how to organise data into meaningful themes. Rigour and validity get explicit treatment as well. The paper targets researchers and students alike. Teachers gain a framework for instruction. The authors aim for clarity without losing coherence.
europmc-pmc6711461:
Cordero-Grande and co-authors proposed a new way to clean up diffusion-weighted MRI scans. These scans trace how water moves in tissue, which reveals fine structure. Noise is their main limit, above all in fast scans and in scans of newborns and unborn babies. Most older methods throw away part of the signal data.

Their method works on the full complex data from the scanner. It shrinks noisy parts of small image patches using rules drawn from how noise spreads in the rebuild. Tests on synthetic data, an adult, and newborn and fetal groups showed cleaner images. Fine spatial and diffusion detail stayed intact.
europmc-pmc6719561:
Donnelly and co-authors set out best practices for measuring whole proteins by mass spectrometry. One gene can yield many protein forms, called proteoforms, each with its own mass. Top-down mass spectrometry reads whole proteins at once, so it can tell those forms apart. The authors belong to a consortium for this field.

Their paper gives a decision tree that leads researchers to sturdy protocols. It covers antibodies, membrane proteins, and mixtures of varying complexity. Shared standard samples let labs grade their own skill across instrument types. The benchmarks help new users match expert results. The guide aims to make intact protein analysis more reliable everywhere.
europmc-pmc6754461:
Garikipati and co-authors studied a circular RNA that aids heart repair after a heart attack. Circular RNAs come from protein-coding genes, but their heart roles were unknown. One, called circFndc3b, dropped sharply in mouse hearts after a heart attack. Its human counterpart also fell in tissue from patients with ischemic heart disease.

Raising circFndc3b in heart vessel cells boosted a growth factor, VEGF-A, and new vessel growth. It also cut cell death in heart muscle and vessel cells. A virus-delivered boost in post-attack mouse hearts improved pumping and healing. The RNA works by binding a protein called FUS. Adjusting this RNA could become a repair strategy.
europmc-pmc6769561:
Zuo and co-authors review inflammaging, the chronic low-grade inflammation that comes with age. This state is tied to an excess of reactive oxygen species in cells. Over time, that excess oxidizes cell parts, feeds inflammation, and triggers cell death paths. The review connects inflammaging to the diseases of old age.

Conditions covered include cardiovascular disease, cancer, brain degeneration, chronic lung disease, diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis. Inflammatory signals such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha rise steadily with age. Constant exposure raises mutation risk in cell genomes. The authors then survey new treatments aimed at cooling inflammaging and oxidative stress. Easing both could cut illness across many conditions at once.
europmc-pmc6828761:
Park and co-authors report a protein survey of heart attack damage, in Cell Death and Disease. Ischaemic heart disease is the world's leading cause of death. During a heart attack, heart muscle cells die, but the full chain of causes is unclear. The team set out to watch how the cell's protein mix changes.

Using a mouse model, they measured thousands of proteins with a tagging method. Pathways for glutathione and for handling reactive oxygen fell sharply. One protective enzyme, GPX4, dropped in particular. GPX4 guards cells against ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of death. Its fall, they conclude, lets that death proceed in heart cells after infarction.
europmc-pmc6943061:
Bagaev and co-authors report the 2019 update of VDJdb, a database of T-cell receptor sequences. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Each record links a receptor to the antigen it recognises. Knowing that match is central to immunology, from reading immune repertoires to designing personalised tumour therapies.

Growth in identification methods let the database expand more than five-fold. New infrastructure adds ways to query and analyse the records. One tool annotates whole repertoire samples in batches, online. The team also built a compact set of high-quality receptor motifs, mined from the data. Those motifs can train prediction software and match new receptors of interest. Together, the additions make hunting for T-cell targets much faster.
europmc-pmc6961361:
Grzybowski and co-authors review short-sightedness in school children across the world. Their review appeared in BMC Ophthalmology. Myopia, or near-sightedness, is rising fast. Children who develop it early risk severe eye damage later, as the eye keeps growing more myopic over time. Genes and environment both contribute.

The team reviewed 80 studies on children aged 6 to 19, published between 2013 and 2019. Prevalence stood higher in Asia, at 60 percent, than in Europe, at 40 percent, when measured with dilating drops. Rates under 10 percent appeared in African and South American children. Risk factors included little outdoor time, much near work, dim light, short sleep, and city living. Reading closer than 25 centimetres also mattered. The authors urge public health action, and consistent measurement methods.
europmc-pmc7017961:
Divers and co-authors report diabetes trends in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. They use the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study, a registry covering selected counties and Indian reservations in five states. The report tracks new cases among people under 20 from 2002 to 2015, split by diabetes type and by racial and ethnic group.

Type 1 diabetes incidence rose from 19.5 cases per 100,000 youths in the first period to 22.3 cases per 100,000 in the final period. Among youths aged 10 to 19, type 2 incidence climbed from 9.0 cases per 100,000 at the start to 13.8 cases per 100,000 at the end. Increases were generally steeper in racial and ethnic minority groups than among white youths. The authors note that diabetes starting young brings early risks of kidney, eye, and nerve damage.
europmc-pmc7033561:
Tamburri and co-authors report a chromatin study in Molecular Cell. Polycomb group proteins keep genes switched off so cells hold their identity. Two complexes do the work: PRC1 adds a mark called H2AK119ub1 to histones, and PRC2 adds another, H3K27me3. Whether the first mark is truly required for repression was disputed.

The team used embryonic stem cells carrying a fully inactive RING1B, the enzyme that deposits H2AK119ub1. Without the mark, Polycomb target genes lost their repression quickly. PRC2 activity was displaced and H3K27me3 fell, hitting one PRC2 variant harder than the other. Variant PRC1 complexes could sense the mark and settled where it was dense. The results place H2AK119ub1 at the centre of the machinery that preserves a cell's transcriptional identity.
europmc-pmc7082961:
Long and co-authors studied how astrocyte exosomes calm brain inflammation after traumatic brain injury, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. They measured inflammatory factors and one small RNA, miR-873a-5p, in tissue from 15 injured patients. Mouse and cell models then tested how the exosomes act on microglia, the brain's immune cells.

Exosomes from activated astrocytes pushed microglia toward their calming M2 state. More than 100 small RNAs rode inside these exosomes, and miR-873a-5p stood out as abundant in injured human tissue. It reduced inflammatory signalling in cells and lessened brain injury in mice. The work points to a natural message system that might be turned into treatment.
europmc-pmc7101061:
Torous and co-authors argue that the COVID-19 pandemic should speed up digital mental health care, in JMIR Mental Health. Telehealth use surged as in-person visits became impossible. The authors draw on their own projects and experiences to show what digital tools can already do.

Phone apps and remote visits could widen access to good mental health care if investment follows the crisis, they argue. Workforce training, solid evidence, and fair access to technology are named as conditions for real gains. The piece is a call to bend the curve on access and quality, using the forced experiment of the pandemic rather than letting old habits return unchanged.
europmc-pmc7136161:
Balaban and co-authors issue a consensus statement that defines antibiotic persistence and how to measure it, in Nature Reviews Microbiology. Persister cells are a small share of bacteria that survive heavy antibiotic treatment without being resistant in their genes. Interest in them has surged as treatment failure rises and new single-cell methods appear.

The statement separates persistence from resistance, heteroresistance, and tolerance, terms often mixed up. It also splits persistence sparked by the antibiotic itself from the kind that arises on its own. Standard measures are proposed so labs can compare results. The authors hope shared definitions will show whether persistence truly drives failed treatment in patients.
europmc-pmc7239861:
Dionigi and co-authors watch catalyst materials change shape while they split water to make oxygen. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Nickel-iron and cobalt-iron layered hydroxides rank among the best catalysts for this reaction in alkaline conditions. What the material becomes under voltage was not directly proven. The team combined electrochemistry with live X-ray methods and computer theory.

Under positive voltage, the layers oxidized from their starting form into an activated phase. The lattice spacing shrank by about 8 percent in the process. Atomic-scale evidence identified the true reaction centers. Calculations backed the proposed mechanism step by step. Knowing the active phase helps engineers design cheaper catalysts. Such catalysts underpin green hydrogen production from water.
europmc-pmc7258461:
Tang and co-authors report a child in China who carried the new coronavirus without any symptoms. Their case report appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. The boy, aged 10, had close contact with two confirmed patients in Zhoushan. Throat and nose samples from him tested negative.

Stool samples told a different story. He tested positive in stool 17 days after his last exposure to the virus, and stayed positive for at least 9 more days. The case shows that a child can shed virus in feces while feeling well and testing negative in the airways. Such silent shedding matters for how outbreaks are tracked and for hygiene advice around toilets and shared bathrooms.
europmc-pmc7274761:
Roschewski and co-authors test a cancer drug, acalabrutinib, in patients with severe COVID-19. Their study appeared in Science Immunology. Severe disease often worsens after initial improvement, pointing to an exaggerated immune response that damages the lungs. The drug blocks Bruton tyrosine kinase, a protein active in macrophages, the immune cells that drive much of this inflammation.

Patients given acalabrutinib showed reduced inflammation alongside clinical improvement. The drug targets activated BTK in macrophages, calming the hyperinflammatory state linked to respiratory failure. Because BTK blockers were already developed for blood cancers, they could be tried quickly in the pandemic. The authors present the results as early evidence that targeting innate immunity can help in severe COVID-19.
europmc-pmc7312261:
Shalaby and Agyapong review peer support in mental health care, where people with lived experience of mental illness help one another. Their literature review appeared in JMIR Mental Health. Such services are centuries old informally, but only in recent decades have they become a formal part of health systems.

Supporters say peer services instill hope, improve engagement and quality of life, build self-confidence, and lighten the load on professionals. Skeptics point to studies with neutral effects and possible waste of resources. The authors trace the field's evolution, types, tools, and evaluation methods, including its use in addiction. Their aim is to show both the proposed value and the unresolved challenges of a service that keeps growing despite the debate.
europmc-pmc7317261:
Neumann-Böhme and co-authors survey Europeans on whether they would actually take a COVID-19 vaccine once one exists. Their survey report appeared in the European Journal of Health Economics. Representative samples in seven countries, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom, answered between April 2 and April 15, 2020, while vaccines were still in early development.

Willingness varied widely: from 62% in France to about 80% in Denmark and the United Kingdom. Overall, 18.9% of respondents were unsure and 7.2% said they did not want vaccination. Opposition was largest in Germany and France, at 10% each. Since herd immunity through vaccination needs high uptake, the authors warn that hesitancy, not just supply, will decide whether programs succeed.
europmc-pmc7347961:
Han and co-authors, with the China Antimicrobial Surveillance Network, track drug-proof gut bacteria across China in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Carbapenems are last-line antibiotics, and enzymes called carbapenemases let bacteria destroy them. The team collected 935 resistant strains from 36 hospitals between 2016 and 2018.

Enzymes turned up in 97.4 percent of strains. KPC-2 led overall, especially in Klebsiella and in adults, while NDM dominated in E. coli and in children. A rarer OXA-48-like family also appeared. The adult-child split matters: the dominant threat differs by ward, so control plans must differ too. Readers get a national snapshot of how a feared resistance trait spreads.
europmc-pmc7440861:
Hanley and co-authors report post-mortem findings in United Kingdom patients who died of severe COVID-19. Full tissue studies of this disease were scarce. The team examined organs from patients whose deaths were directly caused by the infection.

Nine patients had full post-mortem exams and one had a limited exam, all between March 1 and April 30, 2020. The median age at death was 73 years. Diffuse alveolar damage appeared in the lungs of all ten patients. Clotting features showed in at least one major organ in every full autopsy, most often the lung. Lymphocyte loss and acute kidney tubule injury were common. Surprise findings included pancreatitis and adrenal micro-infarction. Viral genes and signs of active viral growth appeared outside the airways in some patients.
europmc-pmc7447761:
Latinne and co-authors trace the origins and cross-species spread of bat coronaviruses in China. This article has since been retracted, so its claims should be read with that status in mind. Bats are thought to host many coronaviruses, including kin of the SARS viruses.

The team used a Bayesian framework on a large set of bat virus sequences, including 630 novel ones. They found host switching was more frequent in alpha-coronaviruses than in beta-coronaviruses. Switching was most common in horseshoe bats and their family. The authors mapped regions of high virus diversity in China. They also suggested a likely origin for SARS-CoV-2 in Rhinolophus bats. Because the article is retracted, none of these claims stand as settled findings.
europmc-pmc7464761:
Tavakoli and Klar review advanced hydrogels as wound dressings and skin substitutes. Skin is the body's largest organ and its main shield. Deep skin defects do not heal alone and need cover.

Hydrogels mimic the wet, porous setting of real skin well. They can serve as short-term or lasting dressings for the surface layer, the deep layer, or both. Gels split into natural and synthetic types by their base material. Adding nanoparticles builds hybrid gels with stronger, tailored traits. Sensors can sit inside a dressing and report wound conditions in real time. The review covers how these smart gels are made and used. It tracks the newest steps toward lab-grown skin replacement.
europmc-pmc7468161:
Xie and co-authors review FGF and FGFR signaling in health and disease. This signal family guides embryo growth and adult tissue upkeep. It steers cell fate, growth, division, and death in many cell types.

The review covers the signal's roles in skeleton growth and repair. It adds lung, urinary system, muscle, and heart development and disease. Single factors such as FGF21 and FGF23 get their own focus. When signaling goes wrong, cancers and chronic kidney disease can follow. Drugs that boost or block these signals may help across many systems. The authors gather current knowledge into one map. It serves readers who track development, injury repair, and disease causes together.
europmc-pmc7505461:
Blackmore and co-authors pool studies on mental illness in refugees and asylum seekers worldwide. Refugee numbers hit record highs in recent years. Older studies gave wild swings in illness rates, partly from weak methods.

The review kept only studies with clinical interviews and proven measures. In all, 26 studies covered 5,143 adults across 15 countries in the pooled data set. Posttraumatic stress and depression each affected roughly a third of adults in the pooled results. Anxiety disorders and psychosis were less common in the pools. Rates still varied a lot between studies and settings. The authors say sound methods narrow the swings but gaps remain. Better data can guide mental health care for displaced people.
europmc-pmc7567861:
Huang, Pareek, Seyyedi, Banerjee and Lungren review deep learning that fuses medical images with health records. Image-only models miss the clinical context doctors use. Records hold history and lab data that guide reading.

The team searched PubMed and Scopus for fusion studies. They screened 985 studies from 2012 onward. Data were extracted from 17 papers in total. Fusion methods for joining image and record data are described. Key results from the field are summed up. The authors give steps for building such systems. Their guidelines aim to help new fusion research. Readers see how context can raise diagnostic accuracy in imaging work.
europmc-pmc7759461:
Harris and co-authors review NumPy, the core array library for the Python language. Array programming lets users work on whole vectors and matrices with compact code. NumPy is the main tool for this in Python. It sits at the base of the scientific Python ecosystem and serves fields from physics to finance.

The authors trace NumPy's roots in two older packages from the 1990s. They show how a few core array ideas yield a simple, strong model for data work. NumPy played a part in the software stacks behind gravitational wave finds and the first black hole image. It now acts as a bridge between rival array libraries.
europmc-pmc7779061:
Martens and co-authors describe WikiPathways, a biological pathway database built by its user community. Anyone can view, use, and help curate its pathway models. The database follows open science practice and lowers barriers to access.

Growth centers on communities that focus on pathway subsets. Rare diseases and lipid metabolism are two examples. Published pathway figures help the team choose what to build next. Optical character recognition and named entity tools mine those figures. The authors show three years of growth and name new collaborations. They also describe links to outside resources such as Wikidata. Their stated path is a lasting, community-run database with wide reuse rights.
europmc-pmc7794761:
Malki and co-authors review the molecular steps behind colon cancer growth and spread. Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer type. It is the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Rates keep rising despite better screening.

Many signaling pathways go wrong in this cancer. The authors cover Wnt/β-catenin, p53, and TGF-β/SMAD. They also cover NF-κB, Notch, VEGF, and JAKs/STAT3. Changes in DNA methylation tie into these pathways. Such changes affect cell growth, death, and vessel formation. Known biomarkers for routine care are noted. A better grasp of onset and spread could yield earlier detection and better risk sorting.
europmc-pmc7829061:
Keller and co-authors review drug delivery through the nose and its safety hurdles. Interest in nasal delivery rose over the past 10 years. The nose offers a non-invasive route into the body. Onset is fast and side effects can drop.

Nasal sprays can act locally or body-wide. They hold special promise for brain disorders. Standard routes often fail to supply the brain well. The authors set out nose anatomy and function first. Approved nasal drugs are listed next. Safety testing of nasal products gets deep coverage. Formula design issues close the review. Both gains and toxic risks must guide development.
europmc-pmc7836161:
Barbeira and co-authors use GTEx data to decode how genome-wide association hits work. GTEx maps how gene activity varies across human tissues. Such maps can explain what a DNA variant actually does. The team studied the effects of gene regulation on traits.

Across many traits, gene expression and splicing showed dose-like effects. The authors built a framework to judge gene-finding methods. No single method beat a mix of several. Colocalization tests pointed to likely target genes. They proposed targets for 47% of the loci studied. That is 2,519 out of 5,385 loci. The paper offers a blueprint for turning association hits into biology.
europmc-pmc7850161:
Gotts and co-authors review what e-cigarettes do to the lungs. E-cigarettes heat a liquid into an inhalable spray. The liquid holds nicotine, flavors, and carrier chemicals. Vaping grew into a multibillion dollar trade. It draws smokers, ex-smokers, and teens who never smoked.

These products reached the market with thin safety testing. Their help in quitting smoking is hotly debated. Studies show clear harm signs in people, animals, and lab cells. Some effects mirror smoking, and others differ. Lung diseases from smoking take decades to appear. Full population effects may not show until mid-century. The authors say proof is too thin to call vaping safer for lungs.
europmc-pmc8035061:
Secinaro and co-authors take stock of artificial intelligence in healthcare through a structured literature review. Few earlier studies crossed disciplines, from accounting to health professions. The team extracted 288 peer-reviewed papers from Scopus. They analyzed authors, journals, keywords, and collaboration networks. A bibliometric package for R powered the quantitative side.

The authors find a young, fast-growing literature. Work clusters around health services management, predictive medicine, patient data and diagnostics, and clinical decision-making. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom contributed the most studies. Keywords show AI helping doctors diagnose, forecast disease spread, and tailor treatment. The authors flag a gap: AI projects demand skills in data quality that many teams lack.
europmc-pmc8074061:
Sroka-Tomaszewska and Trzeciak lay out the molecular machinery behind atopic dermatitis. The disease is a chronic, relapsing skin inflammation marked by fierce itching. It touches up to 20% of children in some populations. Half or more of cases begin in the first year of life. The cost falls on whole families, not just patients.

No single fault explains the disease. A leaky skin barrier lets irritants and microbes in. Genes load the dice before birth. The immune response then skews off balance. Skin microbes fall out of their normal mix as well. These layers define distinct phenotypes and endotypes of the disease. New drugs aim at single molecules in the chain. Matching drug to endotype may finally tailor care. The review ties each mechanism to its clinical face.
europmc-pmc8119461:
Nochaiwong and co-authors pool global surveys of mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic's first months. Lockdowns, fear, and loss pressed on whole populations at once. The team gathered studies from 32 countries with validated tools. Their combined sample reached 398,771 people in the general population. Rates ran higher than pre-pandemic reports everywhere they looked. The pooled estimate for depression came to 28.0% of respondents across the surveys included in the analysis.

Anxiety followed at 26.9% of respondents across the included surveys worldwide. Half the pooled respondents, 50.0% in the estimate, reported psychological distress during the study period. Stress, trauma symptoms, and broken sleep each touched a quarter or more. Rates swung widely between countries and regions. Poverty, weak preparedness, and fragile economies tracked the worst loads. The authors call for research on the social bill. Mental health planning belongs inside pandemic plans, they argue. The next crisis should not find it missing.
europmc-pmc8158961:
Mena and co-authors show that social class shaped COVID-19 spread and deaths in Santiago, Chile. The city is sharply split into rich and poor zones. That split let the team trace how social factors drove the pandemic.

Infection fatality rates ran higher in lower-income municipalities. Comorbidities and poor access to care played a part. Testing delays and thin capacity hid cases and added deaths. The authors rebuilt the early spread and matched excess deaths to COVID-19 deaths. The burden fell hardest on younger people in poor areas. Their data cover testing, deaths, and health care quality across municipalities.
europmc-pmc8164261:
Ayouni and co-authors assess public health measures that slowed the spread of COVID-19. The virus emerged in Wuhan in December 2019 and spread fast. Nations rolled out many control measures at once.

The team searched PubMed, Science Direct, and MedRxiv for studies to March 16, 2021. They kept trials, cohort work, case-control work, and time series studies. Each study was judged for how well its measure cut transmission. The synthesis weighs which steps carried the most effect. It gives policy makers an evidence base for future outbreaks. Quasi-experimental work also entered the study pool.
europmc-pmc8223261:
GBD 2019 Tobacco Collaborators estimate smoking patterns and disease burden across the world. Ending the tobacco epidemic is a core global health goal. Sound, current estimates guide control efforts in each country.

The study covered 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2019. It modelled smoking signs drawn from 3,625 national surveys. Bayesian methods linked smoking to 36 health outcomes. Results split by age and sex. The team tracked both use and the illness it causes. Countries can see where their fight stands against the world. Dose-response curves for the linked outcomes were part of the work.
europmc-pmc8273461:
Collins and co-authors set out a protocol for building TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI guidance. Prediction models now often rest on machine learning. Older reporting and bias tools were not built for that.

TRIPOD guides how model studies are reported. PROBAST helps judge their risk of bias. Both will gain AI extensions through this project. Development follows EQUATOR Network guidance in five stages. The paper states the methods before work begins. That openness lets others track each choice. Better reporting should follow for AI prediction studies in diagnosis and prognosis. Machine learning studies are the extension's clear target.
europmc-pmc8307661:
Marconi and co-authors explain type-2 epithelial-mesenchymal transition in healing and fibrosis. In this transition, epithelial cells take on fibroblast-like traits. They loosen their grip on neighbours and move more freely.

Wound healing runs through bleeding control, inflammation, growth, and remodelling. Transition helps at several of these steps. Inflammatory cells and fibroblasts release the guiding factors. Matrix proteins such as collagens and laminins take part. The same process drives organ fibrosis when it overshoots. The review sorts the three transition types. Type-2 gets the full focus here. Tissue regeneration shares the same machinery as repair.
europmc-pmc8382161:
Bosch and co-authors build a method to rank gene weakness in the tuberculosis bacterium. Drug targets come from essential genes, but standard tests say only whether a gene is essential or not. That misses genes where even partial blocking causes large fitness loss.

The team used CRISPR interference to tune gene expression up and down across the genome. They then tracked how each change affected bacterial fitness. The screen found highly vulnerable genes in many processes, some new to drug research. It also found essential genes that were not vulnerable, which may explain past drug failures. Vulnerability differed between two strains, and those gaps predicted drug response.
europmc-pmc8440961:
Liu and co-authors review PD-1 and PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in tumor immunotherapy. PD-1 sits on T cells and helps damp the immune system. Tumors raise PD-L1 to bind it, switch T cells off, and escape attack.

Blocking this pair with antibodies can free T cells to fight the tumor. Such drugs have worked in many cancer types. Yet some patients respond poorly or grow resistant over time. The review sets out how the pathway works in detail. It covers clinical uses across tumors next. Safety questions are treated as well. The authors look to combined regimens that widen who benefits and sharpen long-term outlooks.
europmc-pmc8639161:
Munro and co-authors report the COV-BOOST trial of seven COVID-19 vaccines used as a third booster dose. Participants first had two doses of the Oxford or Pfizer vaccine. Little data compared booster brands head to head. The trial ran at 18 sites in the United Kingdom.

In total, 2,878 people got a booster vaccine or a control shot. The vaccines used included Novavax, Janssen, Moderna, and others. Some arms used half doses. Staff and participants did not know who got what. The main measures were side effects and anti-spike antibody levels. The team also checked virus neutralization and cell responses. The data help guide booster choice.
europmc-pmc8658661:
Arzumanian, Kiseleva, and Poverennaya take stock of the HepG2 liver cell line after forty years of use. Liver cancer is the third leading cause of cancer death in the world. Cell lines serve as lab stand-ins for tumors in basic research. HepG2 is among the most used of these lines.

The review gathers current data on the line's genes and traits. New deep profiling tools show wide gaps even within one line. Infection and mix-ups can change samples over time. These facts limit how well the line can predict drug effects. The authors ask if its variation still allows sound use. They offer guidance for labs that rely on it.
europmc-pmc8718061:
von Haehling, Coats, and Anker set out updated ethical guidelines for authors in a journal on muscle wasting disorders. The 2021 update covers the main journal and its two sister titles. Editors wrote the rules to stop poor submissions and long disputes. Each rule must be met before a manuscript is sent in.

The lead author must certify the work for all co-authors. Every listed author must have approved the submission and made a real contribution. No one who merits authorship may be left off the list. The work must be original and not under review elsewhere. Overlap with past work must stay within set limits.
europmc-pmc8789561:
Sharrow and co-authors present global trends in under-5 mortality from 1990 to 2019, with projections to 2030. The analysis comes from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation. Its database holds about 18,000 country-year data points for 195 countries. Data came from death records, censuses, and household surveys.

A Bayesian model smoothed biases across data source types. Rates were then paired with birth counts to give death totals. The team also built scenario projections for the next decade. Global goals call for under-5 deaths at or below 25 per 1,000 live births by 2030. The report judges how far each country sits from that mark.
europmc-pmc8950561:
Tuon and co-authors review the biofilm built by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and why it defeats treatment. This bacterium haunts hospitals worldwide. It resists many antibiotics on its own. Its biofilm adds a second shield. The slimy community blocks drugs and immune cells alike. Infections turn chronic and hard to eradicate. Device and tissue infections often trace to biofilms. The review covers the molecular side of that fortress.

The authors describe the bacterium's traits first. Biofilm structure and dynamics follow. Regulation systems, including quorum sensing, get full treatment. Virulence mechanisms are cataloged in depth. Movement tools like flagella and pili feature. Sections then turn to attack. Biofilm-specific treatments and general infection therapies both appear. The authors stress combined approaches. Breaking the fortress, they argue, is as vital as killing its residents.
europmc-pmc9063061:
Parker and co-authors swapped gut microbes between young and old mice to test whether the aging gut drives decline elsewhere. Donor mice were 3, 18, or 24 months old, and transplants took hold in the recipients. Old microbes in young mice sped up inflammation in the brain and retina. A key functional protein in the eye was lost, and the gut barrier grew leakier.

Young microbes sent the other way reversed these harms in old mice. Gene and chemical profiles of the gut shifted with the transfers. The authors propose tuning gut microbes to slow inflammation-linked decline in later life.
europmc-pmc9242861:
Steele and co-authors present signatures of copy number alterations in human cancer. Gains and losses of DNA are common in cancer and drive its start, growth, and drug resistance. They arise from processes like replication stress, mitotic errors, and chromosome shattering. A shared framework to read their patterns was missing.

The team applied their framework to 9,873 cancers of 33 types. They found 21 copy number signatures that explain the patterns in 97% of samples. Seventeen signatures were tied to known biology, like whole-genome doubling and chromothripsis. Four remain unexplained. Some signatures track with survival and with gains in cancer genes like MDM2. The work maps the global landscape of these large genome changes.
europmc-pmc9287161:
Teufel and co-authors introduce SignalP 6.0, a tool that predicts all five types of signal peptides. Signal peptides are short sequences that route proteins for secretion or membrane crossing in all life forms. Older tools missed two of the five types for lack of training data. The new model is built on protein language models.

Those models learn from millions of unannotated protein sequences. SignalP 6.0 also marks the subregions inside each peptide. Its training set held thousands of examples per type, plus many negative cases. The tool works on metagenomic data of unknown origin. It sorts proteins that follow the main secretion and twin-arginine paths. Better sorting helps cell biology studies that cannot test each protein by hand.
europmc-pmc9483361:
Rezaie, Feghhi, and Etemadi review the use of exosomes in clinical trials. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that carry active molecules between cells. They shape many normal and disease processes. Trials now test them as treatments and as test markers.

The authors surveyed two decades of work on exosome trials. Main uses include biomarker tests and cell-free therapy. Drug delivery and cancer vaccines are further uses. Blood is the top source for biomarker work. Mesenchymal stem cells and dendritic cells lead as therapy sources. Stem cell exosomes often target inflammation and drug carriage. Dendritic cell exosomes aim to stir anti-cancer responses. Hurdles include open questions on exosome kinetics in the body. Trial products must also meet strict manufacturing rules, the authors note.
europmc-pmc9647861:
Huang and co-authors review anti-inflammatory hydrogel dressings for skin wound healing. Hydrogels are a mainstay material in modern wound care. Chronic wounds, such as diabetic and burn wounds, heal badly. Excess inflammation is a near universal block in such wounds.

Too much inflammation stalls the normal repair steps. The review sorts new dressings by how they calm that excess. One family mops up surplus free radicals at the wound. A second family traps chemokines that draw in immune cells. A third pushes macrophages from the M1 state to the M2 state. That switch turns cells from attack mode to repair mode. The authors also list the traits a good dressing needs. Water balance, safety, and ease of use all feature. Gaps in proof and scale up close the account.
europmc-pmc9997061:
Dauparas and co-authors present ProteinMPNN, a deep learning method for protein sequence design. Design asks which amino acid sequence will fold into a wanted backbone shape. Most tested designs before this work came from physics-based tools such as Rosetta. Deep learning had changed structure prediction but not yet design practice.

ProteinMPNN scored a sequence recovery of 52.4 percent on native backbones. Rosetta scored 32.9 percent on the same test. Training with added noise made sequences encode their shapes more robustly. The method rescued failed Rosetta and AlphaFold designs in lab tests. Successes spanned single proteins, ring-shaped oligomers, nanoparticles, and binding proteins. X-ray, cryoEM, and functional studies backed the results.
faraday-chemical-history-candle-1861:
Michael Faraday gave the lectures printed as The Chemical History of a Candle in 1861. Faraday, the great experimenter at the Royal Institution in London, delivered them as Christmas lectures for young people. A single candle, he showed, could teach the whole of basic chemistry.

Flame by flame, Faraday explained burning, air, water, and the gases a candle makes and takes. He used simple gear and clear words, testing each claim before his audience's eyes. The lectures became a landmark of popular science writing. They still serve as a first book in chemistry, proof that deep science can be taught from the plainest object on a table.
frus-1861-d161:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 November 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The same day crossing ends the Dayton run in this file. Neither man knew of the Trent seizure as he wrote. Their paired pages form a fitting close: a partnership in full working order on the eve of its hardest test. A fitting close to the run: two partners in step, the storm not yet known. The hardest test of their partnership lay just past the edge of this file.
frus-1861-d261:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from James Shepherd Pike, dated 16 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 261 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d61:
Charles Francis Adams received a letter from William H. Seward dated 21 July 1861. The letter is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote on the very day of Bull Run, before its result was known in full. His words to London kept the calm, firm tone of the spring. The clash of dates shows a chief guiding his envoy in one world, while a battle remade that world at home. The battle was fought on a Sunday, and Seward spent it near the telegraph office. A Sunday battle and a weekday letter frame the strange pace of that summer.
frus-1862-d161:
A second Adams report dated 10 October 1862 stands in the file as Document 161 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its pair, it went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Sending two reports in one mail was normal legation practice when business was heavy. One letter might log a meeting while the other passed on newspapers, notes, or private word from officials. For the reader, the pair shows the London post working at full stretch in a week of sharp debate over British policy toward the war.
frus-1862-d261:
William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862, in a report printed as Document 261 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It followed another Dayton report by a single day.

Spring 1862 was the season when France's break with its allies over Mexico became clear: Britain and Spain withdrew, France advanced alone. That split eased one fear in Washington and raised another, since a France alone in Mexico might seek friends in Richmond. Dayton's quick reports in this week belong to the file tracking that turn. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d361:
Edouard Thouvenel wrote from Paris to Henri Mercier in Washington on 13 March 1862. In an instruction printed as Document 361 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Thouvenel was France's foreign minister; Mercier was his minister to the United States.

Mid-March brought the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads and the news that Britain and Spain were quitting the Mexican venture, leaving France alone in it. Paris had reason to rethink its American course. An instruction written that week carried the court's updated mind to Washington, where Mercier would apply it in his talks with Seward. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d461:
On 18 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to John Lothrop Motley at Vienna. It is Document 461 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the last Austrian order in the year's file.

Seward wrote in the weeks when France was sounding out Britain and Russia on joint mediation. The subject was the American war. The Union rejected the plan flatly. His ministers needed one clear line: no foreign hand in an American quarrel. Motley in Vienna, though far from the main courts in that scheme, had to hold the same line. The letter closes the year's Austrian instructions with the war's diplomacy entering its winter test.
frus-1862-d561:
On 10 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 561 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Four days after the paired orders to Brussels, Seward was writing again. That pace tells its own story about the Belgian file that autumn. Sanford reported gossip from half the courts of Europe, and Washington answered with instructions to match. The matters between them included the watch on Confederate activity and the presentation of the Union's case after Antietam. The letter keeps up a correspondence that stands out in the volume for speed on both ends.
frus-1862-d61:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 9 May 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 61 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d661:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 11 March 1862. Pruyn was on his way to head the American legation in Japan, succeeding Townsend Harris. The letter stands as document 661 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Written orders were the spine of a mission in the age of sail and steam. Seward used them to fix what Pruyn should say and do once he faced Japan's rulers. This letter came late in the chain of orders, close to the start of Pruyn's work in Japan. It rounds out the record of how he was briefed for the job.
frus-1863p1-d161:
Late April's run to London opens with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 20 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 161 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening a late-April run of Seward letters.

Seward wrote as the spring's ship gains settled in. His task now was to hold them: keep the claims warm, the tone right, and the envoy stocked. This letter opens a three-day run in the file. It shows Washington tending the brief with the same care in a fair week as in a foul one. That habit won the long game in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d261: An untitled paper dated 8 August 1863 stands as document 261 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It falls within the volume's long Adams and Seward sequence, the London correspondence that carried Anglo-American business during the Civil War. With no title or named author in the record, only its date, number, and setting can be stated with confidence.
frus-1863p1-d361:
A formal note dated 15 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 361 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d461:
The date 15 April 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d561:
Document 561, dated 10 June 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d61:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 January 1863. Two more Adams letters share the date in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London, and the letter is document 61 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three letters in a day mark a desk clearing a pile of London business at once. Adams wrote on the British government's temper and the acts of the South's friends in the city. Each sheet he sent fed Seward's sense of how near Britain stood to a step toward the South. This one opens the day's set of three.
frus-1863p1-d661:
The 13 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d161: Secretary Hull wrote from Moscow on October 23, 1943, addressing both the President and Acting Secretary Stettinius in one letter. It is Document 161 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter to two readers at once kept the traveling secretary's news flowing to the White House and his own department together. The record names the three men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d261:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers an informal Cairo meeting of 23 November 1943 for which no official record has been found. Its content can be partly recovered, because General Marshall described his dinner conversation with Churchill to the Joint Chiefs of Staff the following day.

From Marshall's report, Churchill had ranged over operations in the Dodecanese, the capture of Rhodes, the deployment of landing craft, and the progress of the Italian campaign. He also raised aid to guerrillas in the Balkans, how Mediterranean operations bore on the date of Overlord, and unified command of strategic air operations. Churchill took up the same subjects the next day with Roosevelt present.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d361:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same first plenary session at Tehran, on 28 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in a fuller American staff version. They run parallel to the Bohlen minutes printed beside them, with the speeches set down at greater length.

Roosevelt welcomes Stalin and Churchill to the family table, Churchill speaks of the future of mankind resting in their hands, and Stalin answers, let us get down to business. Roosevelt's survey stresses three points. America bears the major part of the Pacific war and wants its forces home. Japanese shipping losses outrun replacement. And the north Burma operation under Mountbatten, with an amphibious stroke toward Bangkok's supply lines, is meant to open the road to China and keep that country fighting.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d461:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff were still meeting on December 7, 1943, a day after the Second Cairo Conference ended, and their minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The joint American-British command had followed the leaders from Tehran back to Cairo. Its work did not stop when the public sessions closed.

These minutes carry the conference into its aftermath: decisions confirmed, orders framed, and business handed on to the commands that would carry it out. For readers, the record is a reminder that summits end on paper before they end in practice. The chiefs' last Cairo sessions turned three weeks of talks into instructions the war machine could follow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d561:
Prime Minister Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on March 9, 1944. Two days had passed since his last, which counts as a pause in that season's correspondence. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill file for March 1944 runs thick because the decisions did: shipping, bombing, invasion security, and the politics of liberated Europe all demanded the leaders' own words. Churchill's habit of writing everything down is the reason this record exists at all. For readers, the message adds one more piece to a conversation that, read whole, is the nearest thing to a diary of the alliance.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d61: Ambassador W. Averell Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on October 26, 1943, during the foreign ministers' conference. His dispatch is Document 61 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman had just taken up the Moscow embassy, the post from which he would watch Stalin's government for the rest of the war. The record gives the date and the two men. His news is a matter for the printed text.
frus-1944-quebec-d161:
Hopkins answered Winant's letter on September 4, 1944, with reassurance and candor. A number of people in Washington, he wrote, were greatly concerned about British participation against Japan, and he was hopeful the president would land on the right side. The hostile attitude in certain circles, he insisted, did not represent public opinion.

Some British demobilization after Germany's collapse was inevitable, Hopkins conceded, but it should be played down, with no public announcement. Ways must be found for Britain to take her full and proper place against Japan despite transport and supply difficulties. Lasting peace, he argued, required Russia, Britain, and America to see eye to eye, backed by their peoples.
frus-1944-quebec-d261:
"Rankin" planning, preparing for a sudden German collapse, is the subject of C.C.S. 684, the British Chiefs' paper of September 15, 1944. It asks approval of a directive to General Wilson for the Mediterranean. Wilson was to plan to seize immediate control of Austria with four divisions, Greece with about one British division, the Dodecanese with some 2,400 men, and Venezia Giulia with a division.

No forces would be stationed in Yugoslavia or Albania beyond supply guards, and no British troops would go to Bulgaria. British naval help on the Danube, including mine clearance, required prior agreement with the Russians. The force calculations exclude American troops, who would withdraw, and the four Indian divisions, who would not be used for Rankin duties.
frus-1944-quebec-d61:
H. H. Kung, China's minister of finance, addressed this letter to President Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. Kung was China's chief financial official and a brother-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

China's finances were collapsing under inflation that autumn, and Kung's appeals to Washington sought the aid that might hold his government together. A finance minister writing directly to the President shows the depth of China's need and the personal nature of wartime aid. For readers, the letter brings the fourth ally's distress into a volume dominated by the two Western leaders.
frus-1945-50-intel-d161:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 14" heads a text dated 19 July 1946. It survives in print as document 161 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. The shelf of such orders, read in order, is the true org chart of the system as it grew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d261:
A memorandum dated 11 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Special Procedures Group(Cassady). The reader was the Deputy Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Dulin). It is document 261 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d361:
A letter from Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense reached Allen W. Dulles on 7 February 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 361 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d61:
Minutes dated 26 December 1945 record a meeting held in the quiet week between Christmas and the new year. The intelligence question did not rest for the holiday. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Late December meetings in Washington are usually small and pointed: the men who attend are the ones who must finish the work. These minutes belong to the final clearing of ground before the January directive. Readers can use them to date the moment when argument gave way to drafting. The volume's long autumn of rival plans ends in this season. The papers of the new year open with a president's signature instead of another committee's view.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d161:
Roosevelt passed Stalin's New Year answer on Poland to Churchill on 4 January 1945. His telegram quotes the Soviet reply in full for the prime minister's information. The exchange is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stalin writes that he is extremely sorry he failed to convince the President of the Soviet position's correctness. Events, he hopes, will prove that the Polish National Committee has given the allies real help against Hitler's Germany. The London émigré government, by contrast, spreads disorganization and so aids the Germans. As for delay, Stalin pleads one hard fact. On 27 December the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet already told the Poles it intends to recognize their provisional government.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d261:
The Kurile Islands get a full territorial study in this paper of 28 December 1944. Written by the Division of Territorial Studies, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its problem is stated in one line: the future disposition of the Kurile Islands.

The chain runs some 690 miles from Hokkaido to Kamchatka: forty-seven volcanic islands, thinly peopled. About 17,550 permanent residents, all Japanese, swell by tens of thousands of seasonal fishing hands in summer. Fish give the islands nearly all their economic worth. Their history is a see-saw: Russia yielded the whole chain to Japan in 1875, in exchange for Japan's withdrawal from southern Sakhalin. The paper weighs the islands' strategic value to Japan, Russia, and the United States alike.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d361:
Ships for freed Russians are the subject of a memorandum from Admiral Emory Land, the War Shipping Administrator, to Secretary Stettinius on February 5, 1945. Land reported that the American chiefs had agreed to use troopships for repatriation. The lift would match British help: 10,000 men a month across the Atlantic.

The deal held only while overland routes stayed closed. Once Germany fell, redeployment would need every troopship. Land added that Eisenhower had asked for two large troopships to move Russians gathered at Marseille. The memo turns Eden's prisoner diplomacy into tonnage, ports, and sailing dates.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d461:
Churchill edited like a proofreader, and this list of his changes to the draft communiqué, dated February 11, 1945, preserves his pencil at work. In the part on Germany's defeat, one word should become another throughout. Coordination should read as concert, launched should gain the word continuously after it, and joint should give way to combined.

On occupation and control of Germany, jointly becomes together, and coordinated becomes united. The last change is substance, not style. France, the new sentence should say, would be invited by the three powers to take a fourth zone. She would also sit as a fourth member of the Control Commission. The list shows the communiqué's final polish.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d61:
Keeping the Yalta trip secret is the subject of a 20 January 1945 note from Charles Bohlen to Under Secretary of State Joseph Grew. Bohlen, an assistant to the Secretary of State, reports a White House decision on press censorship. The note is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Two days earlier, Hopkins, Admiral Wilson Brown, and Stephen Early had agreed to invoke the censorship code from 19 January. It barred any speculation about the time, place, or general area of the coming meeting. Staff were also told how to answer questions about absent officials. The only allowed reply was, “He is out of town.”
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d161:
President Truman answered Stalin on recognizing the ex-enemy states in a message sent through Harriman on June 18, 1945. The telegram carrying his words is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had proposed restoring diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland.

Truman fully agrees that recognition would be a constructive step, the message says. But the two governments stand differently toward each state: nothing blocks instant American ties with Finland, while the internal situation in Romania, Hungary, and Bulgaria differs country by country. He is studying the matter further. The practical course, he proposes, is to discuss it at their coming meeting and reach a uniform agreement there. The draft was written in the State Department and approved by the President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d261:
Naval aide George Elsey filed a one-sentence research note on the great rivers, submitted July 1, 1945. The note is document 261 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Elsey had combed the Map Room files to see what the two presidents' papers held on questions that might arise at Berlin.

His whole finding is negative. There has been no reference to the free use of the Rhine and Danube rivers in Roosevelt's and Truman's messages and papers in the Map Room. The tiny memo still earned its place. Free navigation of the Danube in particular was a live question at Potsdam, pressed by Eisenhower among others. And the President's staff needed to know one thing. No past presidential word committed the United States either way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d361:
What to do with captured German war material is the problem in a Combined Chiefs of Staff report dated June 28, 1945. The Combined Administrative Committee drafted a reply to a request from the supreme commander in Europe. He had asked authority on two points: filling London Munitions Assignment Board needs from stocks in Germany and Austria, and scrapping surplus enemy gear.

The report notes informal talks at government level. Some nations, it says, wanted enemy war material shared out among the United Nations. Those nations opposed the wide destruction of German equipment. The paper shows that even captured guns became a diplomatic question in the summer of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d461:
Tito's charges against Greece are answered in MacVeagh's cable from Athens of July 10, 1945. Tito had broadcast on July 8 that Greeks were firing across the border to provoke the Yugoslavs. He claimed thousands of Macedonians and Greeks were being fed in Yugoslavia after escaping terror by Greek reactionaries. Premier Voulgaris called on MacVeagh in alarm.

The Premier planned to fly to Salonika the next day, quietly, to learn the facts himself, then make a temperate factual broadcast on his return. American observers in northern Greece, MacVeagh reports, fail to confirm Tito's statements. Conditions on both sides of the border were disturbed, but the refugee figures struck him as unquestionably fantastic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d561:
Marshal Tito and Field Marshal Alexander signed an agreed note at Duino on June 20, 1945. It is document 561 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The note covers civil rule in the part of Venezia Giulia placed under Allied military government.

The Yugoslav side would not accept the Allied plan for running the zone. It reserved the right to raise the matter through normal state channels. A Yugoslav note attached argues that the old Italian system should not come back. The zone's own wartime organs should be kept if they work well. It also states that Slovene and Italian tongues are equal, and that Rome's government should have no say in the zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d61:
President Truman replied to Ambassador Harriman on June 14 or 15, 1945, with early word on his party for the Berlin conference. The telegram is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam, answering Harriman's question about what to tell the Russians. It gives a first picture of the American group being put together.

Eisenhower, Truman says, has orders to arrange rooms and meeting space, but has not yet been told who is coming. The President plans to bring his Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of State with his aides, two or three other high officials, plus servants and Secret Service men. Names and numbers will follow once they are fixed. The message shows the trip still taking shape a month before departure.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d661:
A Soviet demand on Tangier reached Washington on July 2, 1945, and is recorded in document 661 here. The Secretary ad interim, Grew, relayed it to Ambassador Winant in London. Moscow had just learned of the three-power expert talks set for Paris on July 3.

The Soviet ambassador told Grew his government was interested in Tangier. It was surprised its opinion had not been asked and no Soviet expert invited. It asked that the experts' meeting be postponed until a Soviet expert could attend. Grew records the answer he gave in reply. The United States, he pointed out, never signed the 1923 statute and never joined Tangier's administration. Its presence rested on the interest shown by keeping a diplomatic agent there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1061:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote this letter to Molotov at Potsdam on July 19, 1945. It proposes joint Allied supervision of the approaching Greek national elections. Allied duties to Greece, and the pledges made at Yalta, are given as the grounds. Responsibility to the Greek people, Byrnes argues, makes shared supervision wise.

Four governments would share the task: Britain, the Soviet Union, France, and the United States. Greece's own government has agreed to elections under their watch. That consent rests on Article 9 of the Varkiza Agreement, which provides for Allied supervision. Byrnes closes with earnest hope that the Soviet government will agree to join.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1161:
Washington tabled this proposal on 22 July 1945, late in Potsdam's first week. American papers at this stage laid out what the United States wanted from the postwar order. Each one gave the British and Soviet teams a clear stand to answer.

A proposal fixed words that others had to accept, amend, or refuse. That made the drafting itself a form of power. This paper is part of the American opening hand, played once the first speeches were done. Kept word for word in the record, it lets readers judge what Washington sought before the trades began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1261:
A second Sato cable to Togo bears the date 30 July 1945. The Moscow embassy sent its last July reports in pairs as the crisis thickened. Each tested the Soviet mood one more time and found it unchanged.

By then the pattern was fixed. Moscow gained by waiting, and Tokyo's need grew by the day. Sato's twin reports of 30 July hold that pattern at its end. Within a week the atomic bomb and Soviet entry would end the waiting by force. This cable is part of the record of the days just before, when paper was still Japan's only weapon.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1361:
Henry Villard, chief of the Division of African Affairs, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 27 July 1945. Villard's division handled American ties with Africa inside the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Africa rarely tops the Potsdam story, yet the department kept a full division on it, and its chief could write straight to the acting secretary. Questions of colonies, bases, and trade crossed Villard's desk in 1945 as empires began to loosen. This paper brings that corner of the department into the record. It reminds readers that the postwar world was being argued over on every continent, not Europe alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-161:
Thompson's minutes close his conference run with a session of August 1, 1945. He had recorded Potsdam meetings since the first week. His sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form one of its most complete spines. This last set covers the closing day, when the final protocol was adopted.

Readers who followed Thompson across July meet a familiar, steady hand. The style stays plain to the end. That steadiness is the value: one observer's record, kept the same way throughout. The minutes let the conference be rebuilt day by day. They end where the work ended, with the deal in hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-61:
George Allen memoranda'd a foreign ministers' exchange on the Italian colonies, written up on July 24, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The discussion itself took place at the ministers' meeting of July 22.

Molotov recalled that Moscow had declared at San Francisco its intent to apply as a trustee power. He then turned on a Commons statement by Eden that Italy had lost its colonies in Africa and the Mediterranean. By what right, Molotov asked, had Great Britain decided this question? Who, he demanded, had found the colonies? Eden answered in kind, in a few words. Italy had lost her colonies to the British Army, he said. They sat under British military occupation pending their final disposal in the peace treaty with Italy. Molotov said his delegation had presented a paper on the subject for the next meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d761:
Grew wrote to Byrnes on July 17, 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Document 761 is an early letter in the Acting Secretary's channel to the field. Grew held Washington while the leaders met in Germany. His letter joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

An opening-day letter sets the home office's tone. Grew could pass first news and steady the travelers' rear. Readers see the partnership between the two men at its start. The document pairs with Byrnes's reply of the same week. Together they frame the link that let the summit function at a distance from its own capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d861:
Document 861 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 20, 1945. It closes this run of the volume's papers. Staff drafted it at the end of the conference's first week. The paper stayed in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end working paper shows positions after first contact. The drafters had heard the other sides and written again. Readers can use it as a hinge in the run: behind it, preparation; ahead, the hard second week. The document ends this set where the conference itself paused to breathe, with the largest questions still open and the paper still flowing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d961:
Secretary Byrnes handed this American proposal on German reparations to Molotov on July 30, 1945. He gave it just before the foreign ministers met that day. Russian and Polish claims would be met from the Russian zone. Two additions would come from the Ruhr, in the British zone.

The first addition is a quarter of the surplus factory equipment there. It would be traded for equal value in food, coal, potash, zinc, timber, clay goods, and oil goods from the Soviets. The second addition is a further 15 percent of such equipment. That share would pass to the Soviet government free, with no payment or exchange in return.
frus-1950v07-d161:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent this top secret directive to General MacArthur in the Far East on June 29, 1950. It gathers and widens his orders for South Korea and Formosa. Naval and air forces were to hit military targets so South Korean troops could clear the South.

Army combat units were held back at first, save those needed to keep a port and air base near Pusan. MacArthur was also told to shield Formosa from attack. The Seventh Fleet passed to his control. The cable marks the shift from aid to open war.
frus-1969-76v21-d361:
Minutes of a Washington Special Actions Group meeting on September 20, 1973, record U.S. policy toward Chile days after the coup. The record is document 361 in Volume XXI of the 1969-1976 series. Kissinger chaired the meeting. The group agreed to announce recognition of the new government on Monday, September 24. Ambassador Davis was to tell the junta of U.S. goodwill in advance. Emergency food and medical aid were also approved for fast delivery.

The talk turns to how to fund food aid, with talk of some 18,000 tons needed soon. Longer term needs of 200,000 to 250,000 tons are also raised. No economic team would go until the junta asked.
galileo-discourse-floating-bodies-salusb:
Galileo Galilei's Discourse on floating bodies, written in 1612, appears here in Thomas Salusbury's 1661 English translation, A Discourse Concerning Bodies in Water. Galileo wrote the work in a dispute at the Medici court over why ice floats. His opponents held Aristotelian views on shape and density.

Galileo argued that floating rests on the weight of the body compared with the water it pushes aside, not on flat shape. Experiments with wax and water backed his account of hydrostatics. Salusbury's translation, printed in London, first brought Galileo's physics to English readers in their own tongue. The short work shows Galileo's style: court debate turned into careful test and proof.
galileo-mathematical-collections-salusbu:
Thomas Salusbury published Mathematical Collections and Translations in 1661 in London, a landmark set of Italian science in English. Salusbury chose and Englished works that English readers could not otherwise reach. Galileo stands at the center of the volume.

The set gives the first English forms of Galileo's Mechanics and his early work On Motion, called De Motu. Works by Castelli and Torricelli, Galileo's heirs in the study of water and motion, stand beside them. Salusbury meant to import a whole school of science at once. It shaped how English thinkers, in Newton's age, first met the Italian founders of modern study of motion.
gao-gaoreports-b-296861:
EDO Corporation protested an Air Force award for a smart bomb rack in GAO decision B-296861, dated September 28, 2005. The winner was Raytheon Company. The gear was the Smart Triple Ejector Rack. It holds and drops smart bombs. The firm hit the cost check on its own bid. Its hours had been marked as too low.

GAO denied the protest. Cost bumps were based on sound views that hours were far too low. Low hours with thin proof made the bid high risk. Past skill did not cure thin proof. A risk note not used in the pick did not flaw the pick. The award thus stood on the hour facts.
gao-gaoreports-b-296961:
