Fort Mojave and Hummel protested the rejection of their low bid in GAO decision B-296961, dated October 18, 2005. The buyer was the Labor Department. The work was a new Job Corps Center in Cleveland, Ohio. The bid missed a form to note a change to the call. That change was amendment number 1.

GAO sustained the protest. The change just made clear what the call had said. It had near no effect on the work or the price. A missed note for such a small change does not kill a bid. The bid was wrongly cut as not fit. Small slips with no real effect should not bar the low bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-297061:
ADC protested a Defense Intelligence Agency award for applicant screening in GAO decision B-297061, dated October 14, 2005. The winner was MPRI. The work was to screen new hires for staff jobs. It held staff checks and guard checks before start. The firm said its tech bid was marked wrong. It also claimed hidden tests were used.

GAO denied the protest. The bid failed to show how it would meet the goals in the call. Goals were stated as aims, not task lists. A bid must map its plan to those aims in clear terms. Thin maps give the agency ground to mark a bid low. No hidden test was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-298761:
BST Systems, Inc. protested a Navy award to Yardney Technical Products. The Naval Undersea Warfare Center ran the buy. The contract covered silver-zinc battery cells for an anti-submarine warfare target. GAO ruled in B-298761 and B-298761.2 on December 1, 2006.

The fight turned on past performance scores. Reports told of electrolyte leaks from the firm's cells under past deals. Those same cells were the goods on offer here. The winner's record showed no such leak reports. GAO found the lower score fair and tied to the stated tests. A leaky track record on the same goods can count. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310261:
Command Management Services, Inc. lost its protest in GAO decision B-310261, dated December 14, 2007. The Army sought meals and beds for recruits at a Los Angeles intake post. The award went to LAX Hospitality, LP. The loser fought the tech scores. It also flagged a name quirk in the winner's bid. The name in the bid did not quite match the name on the award.

GAO denied the protest. The tech review was fair and fit the stated points. The name quirk was a mere slip of the pen. The firm's ID code and site matched the winner's own. A small slip in a name does not void a sound pick.
gao-gaoreports-b-310661:
Karrar Systems Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-310661, dated January 3, 2008. The Army sought program and office aid for its R2 program. The award went to BANC3, Inc. Karrar said price talks were not frank. It said the agency found no fault with its price yet gave it no word. It also charged the winner with a clash of interests.

GAO denied the protest. The one price qualm the agency held was put to Karrar in talks. No more was owed on that point. The clash claim was weighed with care. The agency found no real or looming clash on the facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-261:
U.S. Postal Service, GAO-05-261 of April 8, 2005, faults the mail giant's plan to reshape its plant web. Mail sums fall while pay costs rise and foes press in. The service says its sort and haul web holds fat it can cut. Plants may close or merge as mail shifts. How it picks them is the crux here.

GAO tells how trade and crowd shifts strain the web. It tells what steps the service has taken so far. It then grades the grand plan for the reshaping work. The plan lacks clear shape, firm tests for each call, and a clear chain of who answers for it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-461:
Federal spending on climate change, and how clearly it is reported, is taken up in GAO report GAO-05-461, issued on August 25, 2005. Congress requires a yearly report on that spending. The Office of Management and Budget reports in four groups: technology, science, aid to other countries, and tax breaks. GAO compared figures for 1993 through 2004 and asked if they could be trusted across years.

Reported funding rose from $2.4 billion in 1993 to $5.1 billion in 2004. After inflation, technology and science funding grew, while aid funding fell. But the reports changed their formats and definitions without clear notes. That makes it hard to tell how much of the rise is real. One office also changed its science groupings without linking old and new ones. Tax break data were too thin to compare. GAO urged clearer and more complete reporting so Congress can follow the money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-661:
Census Bureau computing is audited in GAO report GAO-05-661 of June 16, 2005. Ten big systems will cost about $4 billion through 2009. Three, worth $2.7 billion, support the 2010 head count, led by a $1.8 billion testing and design effort. Control is split between the chief information officer and program directors. Rules exist for buying, building, and guarding systems.

Practice lags the paper, GAO found. Investment boards run without written procedures, so choices vary by who sits in the room. Similar gaps cross security, staffing, and design planning. With the census nearing, weak habits raise the odds of costly system failures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-961:
Spending by two counsel offices is audited in GAO-05-961, a report dated September 30, 2005. Law requires GAO to audit these offices' expenditures on a set cycle. This audit covers one office of independent counsel and one office of special counsel. The period is the 6 months ended March 31, 2005.

The report is the formal audit record for that half year. It places the two offices' spending under the standing check Congress built into their design. Such offices work apart from normal department control, so outside audit is the main public account of their costs. Readers get the audited figures for the period in one place. The piece continues a series of like audits for these offices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-161:
Counting the money spent fighting terrorism is the puzzle in GAO-06-161, a report dated January 17, 2006. The President's budget reports yearly sums for combating terrorism. Much of that money hides inside accounts that also fund other work. Agencies must split out the terrorism share by their own methods. In 2002 GAO reported how hard that task proved. This report updates that study and checks the fate of its advice.

GAO described the methods agencies now use to carve out terrorism funds. It also tracked which of its 2002 recommendations had been acted on. Weak methods leave Congress unsure what the fight truly costs. They also blur any link between spending and results. The report presses for clearer budget data and a sharper view of performance. It is a study of the numbers behind a national priority, and of why those numbers stay soft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-261:
Certifying nuclear weapons without testing them is the hard science in GAO-06-261, a report issued on February 3, 2006. The United States stopped testing in 1992. A stewardship program must now judge the stockpile's safety and strength from labs and computers alone. Since 2001 the weapons labs have built a shared method for that judgment, known as QMU. GAO weighed the method itself. It also judged how the National Nuclear Security Administration manages the rollout.

The approach needs polish and firmer handling, GAO found. The three labs lack one agreed technical path for the method. Weak management may put key rollout deadlines at risk. GAO made five recommendations to the agency's head. They press for a shared technical approach and tighter control, with clear long-term milestones. The agency broadly agreed that both fixes are needed. It also said the method already works in practice, a claim GAO weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-361:
A law passed to restore trust in company books may cost small firms too much. GAO-06-361 (April 13, 2006) studies the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and smaller public companies. Congress passed the act to protect investors and rebuild confidence. Most saw it as needed, yet concern grew over the cost for small business.

GAO measured the act's effect on smaller firms, with a focus on compliance costs. It traced how the Securities and Exchange Commission and the accounting oversight board replied to concerns. It also checked access to audit services. The report urges care for key principles when easing the load. Readers get costs, responses, and market shifts in one study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-661:
Measuring student growth under the No Child Left Behind Act is the subject of GAO-06-661, a GAO report dated July 17, 2006. The law required all students to reach proficiency in reading and math by 2014. States set yearly targets with a status model, which judges test scores one year at a time. Many states wanted to add growth models, which track gains by the same students over time.

GAO found that nearly all states were using growth models, or weighing their use, to supplement other measures. Some models gave useful facts on school progress toward the law's goals. But GAO warned that certain models could overlook low-performing schools if used for accountability ratings. States also faced data system hurdles that new federal pilot and grant efforts might help ease.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-161:
Reading First put federal money behind early reading instruction in poor schools. GAO surveyed the states on the program in GAO-07-161, dated February 28, 2007. The program serves children from kindergarten through third grade. GAO asked what changed in classrooms under the program. It studied how states chose districts for grants. It also reviewed the guidance and oversight the Education Department gave states.

States reported broad gains, GAO found. In its survey, 69 percent of states saw great improvement in reading instruction. All states reported better training for reading teachers. Over 3,400 districts were eligible to apply in the first funding year. Nearly 1,200 of them received grants. But the department had a control gap, GAO said. It built no guardrails to keep its staff from steering local curriculum choices. That steering is barred by law. GAO urged written procedures for staff dealings with states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-361:
The 2010 Census must hire over half a million temporary workers, and its hiring machine needs tuning. GAO reviewed the plan in GAO-07-361, a report dated April 27, 2007. In 2000 the bureau drew 3.7 million qualified applicants. Recruiting then cost about $250 million, near $66 per applicant. GAO observed the 2006 census test in two states. It judged recruiting, hiring, and training against sound practice.

Targeting is the missed chance, GAO found. The bureau does not study which workers succeed and stay. Its tests treat crew leaders like other staff. Rehiring favors past workers, yet their past performance goes unweighed. No performance records exist to check. Training still relies on scripts read aloud for days. Computer-based lessons on handheld devices are a new step. GAO gave seven recommendations. The bureau's approach worked in 2000, officials replied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-461:
Bases and plants the military cannot lose are the focus of GAO-07-461, a GAO report issued May 24, 2007. The Defense Critical Infrastructure Program exists to find such assets and keep them running. They sit in the United States and abroad, and some belong to private owners. GAO met officials from more than 30 defense bodies for the review.

The program lacked one full management plan, GAO found. Key guidance sat in draft more than 3 years after a lead office took charge in September 2003. Each part of the department went its own way as a result. Defense reckoned it had found only about 25 percent of the key assets it owns. Most private ones stayed unmapped. GAO urged a single plan with clear roles and funds, so the hunt for weak points speeds up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-561:
Cargo that crosses the United States without entering its market slips through a loose net in GAO-07-561, dated April 17, 2007. U.S. Customs and Border Protection runs the in-bond system. Goods in bond can travel under seal to their exit port or inland clearance point. The system speeds trade. It also opens paths to dodge duties or hide suspect freight.

GAO visited headquarters and 10 port offices and spoke with trade groups. Old flaws named in past audits still stood. The agency gathers thin detail on in-bond loads. It does little study of the data it does hold. That leaves targeting of inspections to chance. Diverted goods cost revenue; unseen goods risk security. GAO pressed for richer data and real analysis, so the balance between fast trade and firm control can be struck on facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-761:
Buried nuclear waste from the weapons era is examined in GAO-07-761, dated June 22, 2007. Before 1970, workers buried transuranic waste in shallow pits and trenches. Such waste can stay dangerous for thousands of years. Towns near the sites fear for their water. GAO visited five Energy Department sites with such waste. It read the laws and cleanup deals that govern them. It also tested the department's cost estimates.

Cleanup deals now bind the department at the major sites. In 1989, the Environmental Protection Agency put four on its Superfund list. They are Hanford, Idaho National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, and Savannah River. The department once treated the buried waste as gone for good. It must now study the contamination and weigh cleanup options. Plans for most buried waste are not final, GAO found. Early cost estimates will likely rise. GAO made no recommendations at this time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-361:
The US-VISIT border program is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-361, dated February 29, 2008. Run by the Department of Homeland Security, the program uses fingerprints and photos to track foreign visitors at entry and exit. GAO judged the program's strategic plan, its cost case, and its links to other border programs.

The department had partly defined its plan, building a 'Unique Identity' capability that gives each visitor one identity across border systems. But it had not defined or costed a full plan for tracking exits. It also justified the Unique Identity investment only about 14 months after choosing it, having already obligated about $65 million. GAO said fingerprints remain a sound base technology. It recommended that big spending wait on clear, costed plans. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-561:
GAO-08-561: a GAO report issued May 27, 2008 that covers training for veterans claims processors. The Veterans Benefits Administration is hiring many new staff as disability claims climb. GAO visited 4 of its 57 regional offices and compared its training and rating systems with sound practice.

New staff follow a standard curriculum split between central and home office training. All processors owe 80 hours of training a year, but no one is held to it and completion was not tracked person by person. Feedback on regional training is spotty, and staff fault uneven teaching and dull online tools. The rating system mostly follows good practice, though its formula can flatten top ratings. The department agreed with GAO's advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-661:
Building Afghan army and police forces that can stand on their own has been a U.S. task since 2002. GAO-08-661, dated June 18, 2008, asks whether the Defense and State Departments have a detailed joint plan to finish and sustain those forces, as GAO urged in 2005.

A 5-page reply from Defense in 2007 holds broad goals but few long-term marks and no plan to sustain the forces. It also lacks State's input, though State shares police training. A field plan from January 2008 helps, but it is no joint plan. GAO suggested Congress tie some future funds to a finished plan.
heine-poems-bowring-1861:
Edgar Alfred Bowring translated the complete poems of Heinrich Heine into English in 1861. The volume holds the Book of Songs, the young Heine's lyrics of love and loss, and the later cycles that darkened his tone. Schubert and Schumann set many of these lyrics to music that still fills concert halls.

Heine's short poems turn on a dime from tender to ironic. A love song can end with a shrug that undoes its own sweetness. Bowring kept the meters close to the German so English readers could sing along in spirit. German schoolchildren have learned these poems for generations. Bowring's volume long gave English readers their fullest Heine in verse.
herzen-my-past-thoughts-1861:
Alexander Herzen wrote My Past and Thoughts across the 1850s and 1860s. The hosted text is the authorized English translation by Constance Garnett, first published in 1924. Herzen was the rich, exiled son of a Russian noble. He tells his own life as a window on his times. Readers follow his childhood in Moscow, his university days, his arrest and banishment inside Russia, and then his flight to Europe.

Later parts carry him through the failed revolutions of 1848 in Paris and Italy. They end in London, where he ran a free Russian press and a famous journal, The Bell. Herzen writes about friends, family deaths, and famous exiles with warmth and bite. The memoirs stand among the great life stories of the nineteenth century.
holmes-elsie-venner-1861:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published Elsie Venner in 1861, calling it a romance of destiny. Holmes, a professor of anatomy, wanted to test a medical idea in fiction: how far is a person responsible for traits fixed before birth? The novel is the first American work of biological determinism.

Elsie Venner's mother was bitten by a rattlesnake shortly before her birth, and Elsie grows up beautiful, strange, and half serpentine in temper. Her schoolmaster falls in love with her while a doctor watches the case like an experiment. Holmes weaves New England village life around the central question of inherited sin and free will. The idea came from his medical lectures, and readers argued about Elsie for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-the-surgeo:
Abba the Surgeon is held up in the Talmud as a model of true Jewish piety and kindness. He lived by his earnings, yet would not take pay in person from any patient. To spare poor patients shame, he fixed a box to one part of his house. Each man could drop in what he pleased, in private.

Two young disciples once tested him by trying to sell him his own mattresses, slept on at his house the night before. He knew them as his, but paid the price he was asked. He told himself the men must need the cash for a good cause. When the jest came out, he refused the money back, since in his heart he had given it to charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abi-zimra-abrah: Abraham ben Meir Abi Zimra flourished at Malaga, and seems to have left his home in 1492. He went to Oran, and later lived at Tlemçen. He had quite a name as a poet, the entry says, but very few of his writings survive. One piece is singled out for note. It is a poem that speaks to his own soul, asking how long it will stray. It bids the soul quiet its longing for truth and for the life to come. He wrote it in 1493, at Oran.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-apocaly:
The Apocalypse of Abraham is an apocryphal work kept in Old Slavonic writing. Its first third is really a legend of Abraham's turn from idol worship to one God. The rest gives the vision that gives the book its name.

Young Abraham smashes idols and mocks his father Terah's gods. Then the angel Yahoel leads him to Mount Horeb after a forty day journey. Borne up by a dove, Abraham sees the heavens, the throne, and Leviathan below. God shows him man's fall, Israel's future pain, and final rescue. Scholars place the core text late in the first century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-saba-12:
Abraham Saba was a preacher in Castile, born in the middle of the fifteenth century. He studied under Isaac de Leon. When Spain expelled its Jews, he fled to Portugal, where King Emanuel ordered Jews out and Hebrew books burned on Dec. 24, 1496.

His two sons were taken from him by force. He hid his manuscripts under an olive tree, was caught trying to recover them, and spent six months in prison. At Fez, over ten years, he rewrote his lost works from memory. They include commentaries on Ruth, Esther, the Song of Songs, and the Pentateuch. A later tale says he died at sea and was buried with honor at Verona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-samuel-:
Talmudist Abraham Samuel flourished about the middle of the sixteenth century as a preacher and liturgical poet. He studied under Abraham Motal, rabbi of Salonica. Later he taught and preached at Istib in Rumelia, and died childless about 1650.

To keep his name alive, Nissim ben Moses Cohen printed part of his manuscripts at Venice in 1719. The book, Shirat Dodi, versifies the Sabbath laws of Mishnah Shabbat. The entry rates the poetry as worthless, given the dry legal matter. It also shows that a set of rebukes printed under a like name cannot be his, since its author lived after 1712.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adrianus-matthu: Matthæus Adrianus was a Hebrew scholar of the sixteenth century. He was a Jew of Spanish stock who moved young to Germany. There he took the Christian faith. He was a doctor by trade, but his fame rests on Hebrew teaching. In 1513 he took the Hebrew chair at Heidelberg. In 1517 Erasmus helped him to a post at Louvain. In 1519 he said in a talk that Jerome had erred at times. The claim cost him his post. His sharp tongue kept him from long stays in one place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahadboi-b-matna: Ahadboi b. Matnah was a Babylonian amora of the fourth generation. He was a contemporary of Raba b. Joseph. The entry tells one family story about him. His sister fell ill and willed her goods to a brother, Rab Tobi. Custom favored a learned heir over an unlearned one. Ahadboi warned her what people would say of him. She then changed the will in his favor. A lawsuit followed, and Rab Nahman ruled for Ahadboi. A will made in illness, Nahman held, could be changed during that illness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alashkar-1061:
Alashkar is a Spanish-Jewish family whose name likely comes from an Arabic word for "red." The first member on record is Samuel, a physician at Seville in the mid-fourteenth century. His son Judah, also a physician, claimed a dream visit from an angel. The angel foretold ruin for Spain's Jews in 1391, so Judah moved his family to Malaga.

In 1492 two of his line left Spain for Algeria and led schools there. A later member, Moses b. Isaac Alashkar, lived in Egypt and then in Jerusalem. His "Hassagot" pulled apart the dogmatic system of Shem-Tob's "Sefer ha-Emunot." His 121 responsa were printed with it at Sabbionetta in 1553. His son Abraham carried on learned letters with his father and with Joseph Caro.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-the-z: Alexander the Zealot was a chief of the Zealot party, about the year 50. With his colleague Eleazar he led an armed band against Samaria. They massacred Samaritans without pity, old men, women, and children alike, and burned their villages. The deed was revenge for a murder in the village of Gema. Galilean Jews on pilgrimage to Jerusalem had been killed there. The Roman governor Cumanus chased the Zealots at once. Alexander got away unharmed. Many of his followers were killed, and others were carried to Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allenstein-1261: Allenstein is a town in the district of Königsberg in eastern Prussia. Its small Jewish group took formal shape on Feb. 25, 1862. Before that date a few families rented a room for prayer. The group held a burial ground of its own. A synagogue rose in 1877. A rabbi took post in 1892. In 1880 the town held forty Jewish families. By 1900 the count had grown to one hundred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amarillo-samuel: Samuel Amarillo gathered royal taxes at Tudela in Navarre. He held that post from 1380 to 1391. His chief charge was one set of dues. Jews and Moors paid them on land sold to Christians. He also served the court of Navarre in other ways. He oversaw the buying of clothes for the court. Spices and horses fell under his care as well. The entry rests on one source in a list of sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anan-ben-marinu: Anan ben Marinus ha-Kohen was a legal voice in Siponte. He was born most likely about the year 1040. He signed a joint ruling with a peer of his. That peer was Kalonymus ben Shabbethai. The ruling came before Kalonymus left for Worms in 1070. Two more peers of his town are named. Anan is known from two brief notes by others. Two rulings of law are tied to his name. A poem on Elijah is tied to him as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ansbach-sometim:
Ansbach is an old town of Bavaria, capital of Middle Franconia, on the Rezat, twenty-five miles southwest of Nuremberg. A Jewish settlement stood there in 1328. The Flagellants wiped it out in 1349.

Nuremberg's town records mention Ansbach Jews often in the mid-fourteenth century. A Jews' Street named in 1470-72 points to a large community then, though only seven Jewish taxpayers are recorded in 1470. A synagogue sexton in the records proves a synagogue stood there too. The entry follows the town's Jews through a banishment in 1564, readmission for fairs only, and family counts in the 1600s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-bezal:
Bezalel Ashkenazi ranks among the leading eastern Talmudists of his day. Born toward the end of the sixteenth century, probably in Palestine, he came from a family of German scholars. Most of his life passed in Egypt, where David ibn Abi Zimra and Israel de Curial taught him. While his teachers still lived, he was already held one of the highest authorities in the Orient, and Isaac Luria sat among his pupils.

His standing in Egypt let him abolish the office of nagid, an old dignity decayed into family privilege. In 1587 he ruled that scholars who came to Palestine from love, barely able to feed themselves, should be free of the taxes paid to the pasha. That same year he settled in Jerusalem, where Sephardim and Ashkenazim alike owned him as chief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avenel-paul-216:
Paul Avenel was a French author. He was born at Chaumont-en-Vexin on Oct. 9, 1823. After a brief course in medicine at Paris, he gave up study in 1850 to write full time. He began as a journalist. He went on to work as poet, novelist, and playwright in turn.

His plays number more than fifty. They range from farce-comedies at the Folies Dramatiques to dramas in five acts. His novels include tales of the Latin Quarter and three historical novels of the League's time. "Les Calicots," first a novel in 1866, was later made into a play. His political songs, printed in 1869-72, covered the great events from 1848 to 1860. One book of his verses, "Alcôve et Boudoir" of 1855, was banned by the French courts at once. Thirty years later it was reprinted in a fine edition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baalbek-2261:
Baalbek is a city at the base of the western slope of the Anti-Lebanon, in a fertile region. Greek and Roman writers called it Heliopolis. It is famed for the huge ruins of its temples. A vast court, a great temple, and two smaller ones still stand there. The two smaller temples were probably built in the second century.

The city was the chief center of Syrian sun worship. Its name is found among Syrians and Arabians, and its first half points to the old Semitic Baal. Whether the Bible names the place is in doubt. Some match it with Baal-gad, but the entry objects that Baal-gad lay farther south. Others match it with Aven in Amos, through the Greek rendering On. That too is rejected, since On is an Egyptian name. Baalbek does appear several times in Talmud and Midrash.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bartolocci-giul:
Giulio Bartolocci, an Italian student of Jewish literature, was born at Celleno on April 1, 1613 and died on October 19, 1687. A baptized Jew, Giovanni Battista, taught him Hebrew. Bartolocci became a Cistercian priest, and in 1651 professor of Hebrew and Rabbinics at the Collegium Neophytorum in Rome. He was also "Scriptor Hebraicus" at the Vatican Library. There, with Battista's help, he prepared his great work.

His "Bibliotheca Magna Rabbinica," in Latin and Hebrew, appeared in four folio volumes at Rome from 1675 to 1693. His disciple Imbonati added a fifth volume in 1694. It was the first large-scale account of the literature of the Jews. Richard Simon faulted its judgment and its Talmud translations, yet Wolf credits it as the motive for his own bibliography. It also holds dissertations on Jewish customs and reprints treatises such as the "Alphabet of Ben Sira" in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baths-bathing-2:
Baths and bathing are treated here as signs of a clean soul and a step toward holiness. The entry opens with Bible scenes where washing stands for purity, from Jacob's household to David's prayer for cleansing. It notes how striking free use of water was in a dry land.

Later parts set out the laws for washing after defilement, the priests' laver, and daily washing of hands and feet. Public bath houses and streams get their own section. The closing pages turn to the ritual bath and give plans of old examples in Germany. Streams and ponds were the usual bathing places in early times, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-begging-and-beg:
Begging and beggars, the entry argues, had no place in the design of Mosaic law. Hebrew has no true word for a professional beggar, only phrases like seeking bread. Land shared out by family, debt release, and the jubilee year were meant to keep any Israelite from sinking that low.

City growth later made begging a known sight. The entry then gathers rules: do not send a beggar away empty, give to non-Jewish beggars as well, and keep order among those who ask. Tales and codes from many ages fill the long second half.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-batiah-2861:
Ben Batiah covers two men in this entry, and the entry keeps them apart. The first lived in the days of the Mishnah teachers. His fist, about the size of a grown man's head, served as a standard measure in law. Rules on vessels and on first-born animals cite that measure by his name.

The second was a nephew of Johanan ben Zakkai and a leader of the Zealots. He burned the grain stores of Jerusalem so its Jews would have to fight with desperation. Many hold him to be the same man as Abba Sakkara of another passage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-gidd: Benjamin ben Giddel was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation, in the fourth century. He was a peer of Aḥa the Third. His name, the entry notes, is rarely met in the Talmud. When it does appear, it is in the Halakah alone. The entry suggests he was most likely the son of Giddel ben Benjamin, called Minyomi, and so of Babylonian descent by birth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bergel-joseph-3: Joseph Bergel was a Neo-Hebraic writer of the first part of the nineteenth century. He worked as a private teacher at Prossnitz, in Moravia. In 1826 and 1827 he placed articles and poems in a Hebrew annual. The entry picks out his piece on the immortality of the soul as the best of his articles. It also names a poem written on the grave of his father. He rendered a few sayings of Confucius into Hebrew, working from the French.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bershad-3161:
Bershad was a town in the Russian province of Podolia. It lay in the district of Olgopol. In 1900 it held 7,000 people. Of these, 4,500 were Jews. The community had one synagogue. It also had six houses of prayer. About 500 Jews worked as artisans.

The entry recalls a massacre in June 1648. Cossack leader Maksim Krivonos took the town. His men killed the Jews and Catholics there. This happened during Chmielnicky's uprising. Bershad later won fame for Jewish weaving. Its weavers made the ṭallit, or prayer scarf. Demand fell by 1900. Many weavers then left for America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bible-editions-:
Bible Editions surveys printed editions of the Hebrew Bible. Jews quickly grasped the printing-press's value. Scrolls stayed in use for synagogue service. Print served private reading instead. Every edition before the Complutensian Polyglot was Jewish-edited. After that, Christian scholars took up the work. Reformation interest in Hebrew drove that shift.

The account centers on the earliest printed books. The first Hebrew book appeared in 1474. A Psalms text with Ḳimḥi's commentary followed in 1477. Only 300 copies were printed. The entry then traces the great polyglots. It ends with a modern critical edition in colors. Those colors mark the supposed sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-bianca-ps: Bianca Bloch was a German authoress. She wrote under the name B. Waldow. She was born at Lauban on January 19, 1848. Her family was poor, and her schooling was slight. Wide reading later filled that gap. Dr. Bernhard Stavenow of Görlitz encouraged her talent. With C. von Breckheyde she wrote two plays. One was the farce "Ein Heisser Tag" in 1881. The other was the comedy "Vor dem Fest" in 1889. Her solo works add more farces and a drama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brazen-sea-1336:
Brazen Sea was the great bronze laver Solomon made for the Temple. Kings gives its size: 5 cubits high and 30 cubits around. It was a handbreadth thick and held 2,000 baths of water.

The vessel stood on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each main direction. Ahaz later took it down from the oxen and set it on stone. At Jerusalem's fall the Chaldeans broke it up and carried the metal to Babylon. Rabbinic lore read the sea as an image of the world. Its ten-cubit width matched the ten Sefirot in that reading. The twelve oxen stood for the zodiac signs in the same tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buxtorf-johanne:
Johannes Buxtorf the second was a Christian Hebraist born at Basel on Aug. 13, 1599. He entered the university before age thirteen and took his master's degree in 1615. Study at Heidelberg and the Dordrecht synod followed. On his father's death he took the Basel Hebrew chair himself. People said father and son matched like two eggs.

He kept his father's path, turning down chairs at Groningen and Leyden to stay at Basel. He bought Hebrew books through Jewish contacts from Constantinople to Amsterdam. He finished his father's concordance and Talmudic lexicon for print. His own work includes Latin versions of Maimonides and of Judah ha-Levi's Cuzari. He also fought Louis Cappellus over the age of the Hebrew vowel signs. He died at Basel in 1664.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-capital-punishm:
Capital punishment in the Pentateuch attaches to a fixed list of crimes, from murder and adultery to blasphemy, idolatry, and breaking the Sabbath. Few texts name the manner of death. Stoning covers most named cases, burning a few, and the sword a town's apostasy. Hanging, the rabbis held, meant showing the body after death, not a way of killing.

Rabbinic law then hemmed the penalty in. A court of twenty three members had to try the case. Two eyewitnesses were required, and they had to have warned the offender first. The four deaths of the court were ranked by weight, stoning the heaviest and strangling the lightest. Mixed convicts took the lightest death among them. The long article traces these rules through Mishnah and Talmud in close detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caro-ezekiel-40:
Ezekiel Caro, a German rabbi and historian, was born on Nov. 26, 1844, at Pinne, near Posen. His father, Joseph Ḥayyim Caro, was a rabbi and writer at Wloclawek. Ezekiel studied at Breslau and took his doctorate at Heidelberg. He preached first at Lodz, then held rabbinates at Dirschau, Erfurt, and Pilsen.

From 1891 Caro served as chief rabbi of Lemberg. His books include selected sermons from Danzig in 1874 and a history of the Jews of Lemberg up to the partition of Poland, printed at Cracow in 1894. He also wrote many sermons and essays for scholarly journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caves-in-palest:
Caves in Palestine are called me'arah in Hebrew. The mountains there are mostly soft limestone, and they abound in natural caves and grottoes. Many began as a crack in the rock. A stream widened the crack, then changed its course, leaving a dry hollow passage. Human skill enlarged many caves, above all east of the Jordan and in the Hauran.

Such caves hold high historic interest. They housed prehistoric man, and flint knives, arrowheads, and pottery have been found in them. Animal remains point to a colder climate than the present one. In historic times caves served as dwellings and burial places. In war they became refuges and natural forts. Robbers hid in them, shepherds folded flocks in them, and travelers rested in them at night. The best known burial cave is Machpelah at Hebron, bought by Abraham.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-christian-4361:
Christian denotes a follower of Jesus as the Messiah or Christ, and the entry asks where that label first arose. Acts xi. 26 places it in Antioch, where Barnabas and Paul built the first major church among non-Jews about the year 44. Some scholars doubted that early date, while others defended it, and the entry names voices on both sides.

The name itself, the entry argues, likely came from Latin-speaking outsiders. Pagans heard believers call themselves those of Christ and coined Christiani as a nickname, much like Caesarians or Pompeians. Use inside the New Testament stays rare. By the second century Christians had taken the name as their own, even under persecution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coal-3661:
Coal in the Bible is named by two Hebrew words, one perhaps meaning the glowing and one black coal. Charcoal is always meant, the entry makes clear. It was made from tamarisk and broom, and broom-root charcoal gave a strong, lasting heat still prized in the East. A bellows worked by feet and hands fanned the flame.

Most coal fires cooked food or baked bread, meat, and fish. In winter, live coals sat in a brazier mid-room, or in a floor hole in poor homes, with smoke escaping by door or high window. The word also works as an image: quenching a man's coal means ending his line. Heaping coals on an enemy's head means kindness that wakes his conscience.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coat-of-arms-33:
Coat of arms covers the armorial bearings granted to families by heraldic authorities, a right born of feudal custom late in the twelfth century. Jews held no place in that system once it formed, so heralds recognized no Jewish arms in the Middle Ages. Rich Jewish families still used devices on their seals, the entry notes.

The first recorded grant came on Jan. 18, 1622, when Emperor Ferdinand II gave arms to Bassevi von Treuenfeld. Use spread in the age of the Maranos and after. What follows is a vast catalog of family arms, blazon by blazon, from Sephardic houses to English and Austrian lines. Mottos, crests, and sources are given for each, making this one of the encyclopedia's longest lists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-anne-jean:
Anne Jean Philippe Louis Cohen, who added de Vinkenhoef to his name, was a French man of letters born at Amersfort in the Netherlands on Oct. 17, 1781. He died in Paris on April 6, 1848. Starting as a journalist, he moved to Paris in 1809. He became censor for foreign languages in 1811 and librarian of the Bibliotheque Ste. Genevieve in 1824.

Catalogues and translations fill much of his record. He rendered works from five languages, including Washington Irving's history of the conquest of Granada in 1829. His own books run from a history of the knight Bayard to a four-volume Jacqueline de Baviere in 1821. A late work on the French nobility appeared in 1845, and one on revolutions in 1846.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-columbus-christ:
Christopher Columbus, by his own account, dealt constantly with Jews and Moors, priests and laymen, and this entry gathers his Jewish ties. At Lisbon he knew Joseph Vecinho, doctor to King Joao II of Portugal. Vecinho gave him a Latin rendering of Abraham Zacuto's star tables, which Columbus carried on his voyages and found most useful.

At Salamanca he met Zacuto himself and praised his science. At Malaga he met Abraham Senior and Isaac Abravanel, the first man to aid him with money for his ventures. His will left half a silver mark to a Jew living by the gate of the Jews' street in Lisbon, or to one a priest might name. Whether Lisbon Jews lent him money stays unknown, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-constance-distr:
Constance, District of the Lake of, covers the Jewish communities around Lake Constance in northeast Switzerland. Ueberlingen, Constance, Schaffhausen, and Diessenhofen earn the closest notice among many towns. Ueberlingen's Jewish cemetery is named as early as 1226. Constance's settlement starts at the opening of the thirteenth century, and Schaffhausen's Jews appear in records of 1299.

Persecution marks every town. More than 300 Jews were killed at Ueberlingen in 1332. The Flagellants wiped out its Jews on Feb. 11, 1349, and grave stones went into the cathedral walls. At Constance many Jews burned in 1312 on a host charge, and all were jailed in 1429 and 1443. Schaffhausen saw killings in 1349 and burnings in 1401. Small returns after 1865 close the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corinth-4661:
Corinth, a city in ancient Argos, Greece, had Jewish residents like other Greek cities, though little of their history is known. The apostle Paul preached in its synagogue for eighteen months. He baptized the synagogue ruler Crispus, but other Jews reviled him and accused him before Governor Gallio in 53 C.E. Gallio refused to judge religious quarrels, and the crowd beat Sosthenes before his eyes.

The entry also notes Aquila and Priscilla, who reached Corinth after Jews were driven from Rome. Strife in the young Christian community, blamed on Pharisaic Judæo-Christians, fills the rest. A closing note links Corinthian art to the Temple in Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cresques-lo-juh: Cresques lo Juheu was a chart maker who flourished at Majorca and Barcelona. He worked at the end of the fourteenth century. In 1381 Prince Juan of Aragon sent his mappa mundi to Charles VI. of France, then a boy of thirteen. The map may be the famed Catalan map now in the Louvre. In 1390 King Juan paid him 60 livres and 8 sous for another map. Forcibly converted in 1391, he became Jaffuda Cresques, the map Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crete-or-candia:
Crete, or Candia, is an island in the Mediterranean, about 55 miles south of the Morea. Jews had settled there long before the Christian era. First Maccabees names Jews in Gortynia, and Philo speaks of Cretan Jews. About 4 B.C. a false Alexander drew large sums from them, posing as a Hasmonean heir. Rome took the island in 67 C.E. Under Christian rule the Jews faced persecution, and Theodosius II. expelled them in 408.

The ban proved short. In 440 a pseudo-Messiah led Cretan Jews to abandon their property and await a dry path through the sea. Later sections cover Saracen, Byzantine, and Venetian rule. At Retimo in 1386 Jews paid 800 hyperperes to reopen a closed synagogue. Town by town, the article tracks privileges bought, revoked, and bought again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-damascus-4861:
Damascus is an ancient city at the foot of the Anti-Lebanon, now capital of the vilayet of Syria. Its name appears in Egyptian lists, in cuneiform records, and in the El-Amarna tablets, in forms close to the present one. The modern city stands on the old site, in the rich plain of Al-Ghuṭa. The river Barada splits into seven branches there, two of them passing through the city itself.

The long article traces the city from Bible times onward. Its Jewish history fills the later sections. Refugees from Spain settled among the Damascus Jews in 1492 and built a synagogue. Manuscripts copied and checked in the city show a living learned community. Portions on position, names, and early history rest on Egyptian and Assyrian evidence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-levi-: Levi's son David was rabbi of Narbonne, France, flourishing at the end of the thirteenth century and probably living into the fourteenth. He wrote an important book called "Miktam." It sets out the legal decisions of the Talmud in the order in which they occur in the Talmud itself. Later legal writers quoted it often, including Aaron ha-Kohen, Joseph Caro, and Solomon ben Adret, who signed decisions with David's name and title. Part of the "Miktam" still survives in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deliatitz-nissa: Nissan Deliatitz was a Russian rabbi and mathematician, and this entry is only a few lines long. He wrote "Keneh Ḥokmah," a title taken from Proverbs chapter 4, verse 5, meaning both buy wisdom and the scientific measure. The book is a manual of algebra in five parts, printed at Wilna in 1829. Even his parentage is unsettled in the sources. Benjacob makes him a son of Abraham Deliatitz, while Fürst makes him a son of Elijah ben Abraham Deliatitz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diabetes-mellit:
Diabetes mellitus is a disorder of nutrition marked by the lasting presence of grape sugar in the urine. This medical entry calls it a disease of the wealthier classes, more common in cities than in the country. Death rates run higher in rich districts. People of nervous temperament are often hit, and shock, grief, or worry can bring an attack on.

The article reports that diabetes is far more common among Jews than among other European peoples. Its table for Frankfort-on-the-Main, covering 1876 to 1890, gives 1.9 per cent of Jewish deaths from diabetes against 0.4 per cent among Gentiles. Similar tables for other places follow, with discussion of causes and of the disease among other races.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dictionaries-bi:
Dictionaries, Bible are collections of articles in alphabetical order on the people, places, and things of the Bible. This survey says Jews took very little part in such work until recent times. The earliest attempt of the kind was by Eusebius, bishop of Cæsarea, who died in 340. His book covered the place names of the Old and New Testaments.

Jerome built on Eusebius with Latin works on Hebrew names and places. Learning from the Reformation added much material on Israelite life, but stayed mostly word study. The first successful Bible dictionary, the entry says, came from Johann Heinrich Alsted, a Protestant theologian who lived from 1588 to 1638. The article then follows later Bible dictionaries, Jewish and Christian, in order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-domain-public-l:
Public domain, in rabbinic law, is space that belongs to the many, not to one owner. The term matters most in Sabbath law. On the Sabbath, carrying goods between private and public domain is barred. Carrying more than four cubits inside public domain is barred too.

The entry pictures Palestinian towns as small houses grouped around a shared court. It gives close rules from the treatise Erubin for courts and large houses. Streets, town squares, and country roads count as public domain. So does the wilderness, though a caravan can fence off a private space there. Navigable water is public, while a ship counts as private.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dunayevtzy-5361: Dunayevtzy was a village in the government of Podolia, Russia. In 1898 it counted 13,000 people, of whom 7,000 were Jews. Trade and industry give its Jews their living. Timber, grain, and cloth are the chief goods, and a few merchants do a fairly large trade. Charity funds there keep a wood-yard. At that yard the poor can buy wood at a reduced price, as the entry records in its closing lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ehrlich-adolph-:
Adolph Ehrlich, born Abraham Abele, was a Russian educator and rabbi. He was born at Mitau, in Courland, on Sept. 20, 1837. In 1858 he began teaching Hebrew at Friedrichstadt's Jewish school. At Berlin he studied under Michael Sachs and taught Sachs's own children.

Ehrlich took his doctorate at Halle in 1868 after three years at Berlin University. Posts followed at Berlin and Neudenberg, then Tilsit. In 1876 the Russian government put him over Riga's Jewish school. He held that post for about twenty years. His writings include a Hebrew primer and a history of Riga's Jewish school, printed in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elephant-5561:
The elephant entry asks how the beast enters the Bible and later Jewish books. Scholars agree the animal is meant in a verse in First Kings. Solomon's fleet, the verse says, brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. The Hebrew word for ivory is a compound. Its first part means tooth, and its second part, most hold, means elephant. The entry traces the word through Assyrian and other tongues.

War elephants first reach Palestine in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes. Each beast bore a wooden tower on its back. Three to five men rode in the tower, with a guide called the Indian. Before a fight the beasts were given strong drink to madden them. The entry then turns to the Talmud and its lore. Noah stocked vine leaves for the elephant, its favorite food. Its time of bearing young is given as three years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-engel-gabor-gab: Gabor Engel was a Hungarian doctor and surgeon. He was born at Maros-Vasarhely in Hungary in 1852. He trained at Budapest and at Leipsic in his youth. In 1880 he became assistant surgeon at Klausenburg hospital. A year later he taught the art of childbirth there. In 1887 he took charge of the state hospital. In 1893 he rose to assistant professor at the school. His essays went to journals in Germany, Austria, and Hungary. They treat his field of women's medicine in the main.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esperial-samuel: Samuel Esperial was a physician of Cordova, Spain, and the entry gives only a few facts about him. He wrote a treatise on surgery for David of Jaen. The work was written in Spanish, but in Hebrew characters. It survives as Vatican manuscript number 372. No dates for his birth, death, or practice are given. The entry rests on three cited sources: Wolf's Bibliotheca Hebraea, Steinschneider on Jewish literature, and Kayserling's bibliography of Spanish and Portuguese Jews. That brief record is the whole of the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezer-5961: Ezer, in the short body that follows a long site index in the hosted text, is a son of Seir and one of the princes of Edom. The line cites Genesis chapter thirty-six and First Chronicles chapter one. Nothing else is stated about him: no acts, no place, and no dates appear in the entry's own text. A reader gets one firm fact, his Edomite princely descent from Seir, and no story around it. Any fuller account would need a source this entry does not give.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feld-julius-606: Julius Feld was a Rumanian artist born at Botuschany on June 21, 1871. He went young to France and studied at the Ecole des Beaux Arts under Delaunay, Bonnat, and Gerome. He made his name fast as a portrait painter. Zadoc Kahn and Prince Kalimaki sat for him. He also won fame as a decorator. For the Paris Exposition of 1900 he painted four panels for the Palais de la Femme, named for champagne, beer, chocolate, and liqueur. Other canvases show Cleopatra's death and Rebecca giving Eliezer a drink.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fraga-6261:
Fraga is a city in Aragon. In 1328 Alfonso IV confirmed all the rights the Moncadas had granted to its Jews. Four years later he let his second wife Leonora admit six Jewish families to Fraga. She had received Huesca and Fraga as a gift. The Jews are said to have been persecuted there in 1389 and 1391.

In 1438 the community was still as large as that of Jaca. Like it, Fraga paid 200 sueldos a year in taxes. The city was the birthplace of a baptized physician. Isaac Arama also served there as preacher for several years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedberg-berna:
Bernard Friedberg was an Austrian Hebraist born at Cracow on December 19, 1876. Besides many pieces in Hebrew and other periodicals, he has printed a shelf of books, most of them in Hebrew. The first treats Rabbi Joseph Karo, in 1895. Next came the grave stones of the Jewish cemetery at Cracow, with life sketches, in 1897.

A second edition of that work appeared in 1903. He wrote on the family of Abraham Braude and on two noted rabbis of old. Two books of 1900 treat Hebrew printing at Cracow and at Lublin. A history of the Schorr family followed in 1901. His latest named book treats the rabbis of Raszow, in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaffarel-gaffar: Jacob Gaffarel, a French Christian scholar of rabbinic lore born at Mannes in Provence in 1601, died at Sigonce in 1681. He gave his study to mystic thought, above all to Hebrew cabalistic works. His own books in that field are called unreliable in the entry. He wrote on the end of the world in 1629 and a list of cabalistic manuscripts in 1651. At Paris in 1637 he printed Leon Modena history of Hebrew rites without the author leave.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geiger-lazarus-:
Lazarus Geiger, a German scholar of language born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on May 21, 1829, died there on August 29, 1870. He was a nephew of Abraham Geiger. After years as a bookseller trainee, he turned to study and took gymnasium and university training. From 1851 he lived at Frankfort and gave his life to speech and reason.

His chief work treats the origin and growth of human speech and reason. Its first volume came out in 1868. The second came out after his death, in parts, in 1872. Geiger held that speech is not decay but growth. Reason, he argued, grew out of speech. Even before Darwin he saw growth by stages as a law of all nature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gibeah-hill-666:
Gibeah is the name of several hill towns, and the record is hard to sort out. Geba and Gibeah swap places in some verses. The Gibeah of Saul stood near Ramah, about thirty furlongs from Jerusalem. Most scholars match it with Tulail al-Ful. Joshua xviii lists both Geba and Gibeah among the towns of Benjamin.

A second set of verses points to the present Jeba instead. That town fits Judges xx and First Samuel passages on the ravine fight. Some verses under either name may in fact mean Gibeon. The entry sorts the cases verse by verse and marks which matches look firm and which stay in doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldschmidt-mei:
Meïr Aaron Goldschmidt was a Danish political writer. He was born at Vordingborg on Oct. 26, 1819. He died at Copenhagen on Aug. 15, 1887. Danish church rules barred him, as a Jew, from a degree in 1836. So he gave up medicine and started a political weekly in 1837. Fines and a year of censorship followed at once.

His next paper, the "Corsaren" of 1840, attacked the crown boldly. It cost him prison on bread and water and lasting censorship. Yet it made his name and sold his novels. From 1862 he left politics for literature alone. The entry praises his style and his deep portraits of Jewish character. His novel "En Jöde" (1845) spread across Europe in translation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gratz-college-p:
Gratz College is a Jewish school of higher learning in Philadelphia. Hyman Gratz set it up in a deed of trust in December 1856. The trust took effect in 1893. Congregation Mickveh Israel then named trustees to run it. The deed called for a college for Jews of the city and county. The trustees chose to train teachers above all.

Lectures came first, in 1895, by scholars such as S. Schechter and Joseph Jacobs. Regular teaching began in 1898 with three teachers. Twenty-seven pupils attended, and nine graduates had earned teachers' certificates. The college also ran a course feeding into the Jewish Theological Seminary. Moses A. Dropsie presided over the board from the start.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gutmann-moses-6:
Moses Gutmann was a Bavarian rabbi. He was born in Baiersdorf in 1805 and died at Redwitz on Feb. 1, 1862. His father was Yom-Ṭob Gutmann. He studied at Erlangen University. At twenty-two he was elected district rabbi of Redwitz. He held that post for thirty-five years. He was Bavaria's first rabbi with both a university education and full Talmudic training to back Reform. His essays and responsa show that stance.

He published a fresh German translation of the Apocrypha with notes at Altona in 1841. His Josephus translation, with a learned Latin commentary, stayed in manuscript. The entry names the journals that carried his Reform writings, among them Geiger's journal of Jewish theology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hair-7061:
Hair among the ancient Hebrews was generally black, and black hair marked youth against the white hair of age. Herod dyed his gray hair black to look younger. Thick, long hair stood for strength and life: Samson's seven braids tied his strength to his vow, and Absalom's heavy hair was cut just once a year. A bald head drew mockery.

The entry follows hair through custom and law. Men cut their hair often but shaved only on set occasions; priests might neither shave nor let it grow like Nazarites. Women's long hair was a beauty, cut only in mourning or shame. Mourners shaved part of the head, a heathen-seeming rite the Law banned yet prophets show in use. Later pages turn to dyes, wigs, and counts of Jewish hair color in modern lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamul-7161: Hamul was the younger son of Pharez, Judah's son by Tamar. He heads the family of the Hamulites. The entry is a single line. It rests on Genesis xlvi. 12, Numbers xxvi. 21, and I Chronicles ii. 5. No deeds, dates, or children of Hamul himself are named here; he is recorded only by his birth order, his father and grandfather, and the family line that carried his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harland-henry-p: Henry Harland was an American author born at St. Petersburg in March 1861. He studied at the College of the City of New York and at Harvard. After a few years in a New York law office, he moved to London. There he edited the "Yellow Book," a noted literary magazine. Writing as Sydney Luska, he produced novels on Jewish subjects. The entry names "Mrs. Peixada," "As It Was Written," and "The Yoke of the Thorah," dated 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-standard: The Hebrew Standard was a weekly paper founded in New York city by J. P. Solomon. Its first issue came out on Sept. 23, 1881. Solomon stayed its sole editor and owner. In religion the paper was strongly conservative, with Orthodox leanings. In politics it stood firmly with the Democratic party. The entry credits it as the first try at a cheap, popular Jewish newspaper in English. No word is given on how long it ran or how widely it sold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henle-friedrich:
Friedrich Gustav Jacob Henle, born at Fürth, Bavaria, on July 19, 1809, was a German anatomist. He and his parents were baptized. He studied medicine at Bonn, took part in student politics, and was detained after suspension. Pardoned, he graduated as a doctor at Heidelberg in 1832.

Henle taught at Berlin, Zurich, Heidelberg, and finally Göttingen, where he stayed until his death on May 13, 1885. His discoveries covered intestinal tissue, hair structure, the cornea, blood vessels, liver cells, and kidney loops. His systematic anatomy handbook was his main work. He also founded a medical journal with Pfeuffer in 1844.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hexateuch-7661: Hexateuch names the first six books of the Bible, the Pentateuch plus Joshua taken as one linked work. The entry gives two reasons for the link. A history of the land promise seems to need the conquest story, not a stop at Moses' death. Also, the sources of the Pentateuch seem to run into Joshua. The entry then argues back. The Pentateuch stands complete on its own, it says. Tradition never joined Torah with Joshua in that way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirschfelder-so: Solomon Hirschfelder, born May 16, 1832, at Dettensee, near Horb, was a German genre painter. He studied at the Academy in Munich and settled in that city in 1853. The entry lists five of his genre paintings by title. They include a campaign scene of 1871, a prison scene, and a sweetheart's letter scene. No training details beyond the academy, no family facts, and no account of his style are given. He died at Munich on May 10, 1903, days before his seventy-first birthday, by the dates shown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huzpa-7961:
Huzpa is an Aramaic word meaning impudence. The Bible uses only the verb, twice in Daniel, where it means to be strict or urgent. Talmudic writing uses both verb and noun in legal sayings and moral lines. Courts presume, for one, that no man would brazenly pick fruit from a tree not his own.

Other rules turn on the same idea. A son's bare signature in his father's name fails, since no son would dare use it as a shield against forgery. A father cannot make a marriage contract as his son's agent, for a son would not be so bold. Proverbs add that impudence will grow in the days before the Messiah. The word lives on as chutzpah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-igel-lazar-elia: Lazar Elias Igel was an Austrian rabbi born on February 28, 1825, at Lemberg, where his father sold second-hand books. He died at Czernowitz on March 26, 1892. At fifteen he went to Padua and studied at the rabbinical seminary under Luzzatto, graduating in 1849. Back home he taught religion and held a post in Semitic tongues at Lemberg University. In 1854 he became district rabbi at Czernowitz and later chief rabbi of Bukowina. He wrote a Syriac guide and many essays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-the-blind:
Isaac the Blind, or Isaac ben Abraham of Posquières, was a French cabalist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The entry treats him as the founder of the Cabala. More exactly, it says, he reshaped the mysticism of the Geonim into the Cabala's present form. Bahya b. Asher therefore called him Father of the Cabala. Other cabalists told how the science passed from person to person, from Mount Sinai down to Isaac.

Among his pupils was Azriel ben Menahem of Gerona. Isaac gave the ten Sefirot their names, and he was the first to take up the idea of metempsychosis, the passing of souls. Recanati wrote that Isaac could tell whether a man's soul was new or old. He is generally supposed to have written a commentary on the "Sefer Yezirah." Later scholars also credit him with the Bahir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isidorus-hispal: Isidorus Hispalensis was archbishop of Seville in the sixth and seventh centuries. He presided over the fourth Council of Toledo, called by the Visigothic king Sisenand in 633. There he voiced the principle that Jews ought not to be forced into the Christian Church. To win Jews over by argument instead, he wrote "Contra Judaeos," a two-volume work defending Christianity's claims from the Old Testament. Whether Spanish Jews answered him in controversy, in Latin as Grätz thought, the entry leaves an open question.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehoiada-8561:
Jehoiada was high priest under Ahaziah, Athaliah, and Jehoash of Judah. By marriage to the princess Jehosheba he became brother-in-law to King Ahaziah. After Ahaziah died, Athaliah killed the royal family, but Jehoiada and his wife hid the child Jehoash in the Temple for six years and kept him safe.

In the seventh year of Athaliah's reign, Jehoiada brought the boy out before a great Temple crowd, which hailed him as rightful king. Under his lead the people broke with Baal worship and tore down its altar and temple. He died at the age of 130 and was buried among the kings in the city of David.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-nathan:
Jonathan, often paired with the name Nathan, was a teacher of the second century who is rarely quoted apart from his schoolfellow Josiah. The two were trained together at the academy of Ishmael ben Elisha and learned his way of reasoning, set against Akiba's school. Jonathan all but won over a fellow student of Akiba to that system, and the man cried out his regret at not having studied with Ishmael.

Pressed by the Hadrian attacks on their faith, Jonathan set out to leave Palestine with other scholars. Love of the Holy Land would not let him stay abroad, and he came home. With Josiah he gave his sharp mind to working out laws from the Bible texts themselves. Only one saying of his stands in the Mishnah: who keeps the Law in poverty will keep it in wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-meir: Joseph ben Meir was a liturgical poet of the thirteenth century, perhaps an uncle of Meir of Rothenburg. He wrote a lament that opens with words the entry leaves in Hebrew. The poem is thought to mark the burning of the Talmud at Paris. Joseph may be the same man as Joseph ben Meir of Saulieu. Meir of Rothenburg cites that Joseph as having been his own teacher. The short entry rests on Zunz and on Fuenn's Keneset Yisrael and gives no other facts of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-of-arima:
Joseph of Arimathaea was a wealthy Jew who, out of sympathy with Jesus, gave him burial in a rock-cut tomb near Jerusalem. All the Gospels tell the story, most simply Mark. There Joseph is a member of the Sanhedrin who waited for the kingdom of God. The entry reads him as likely an Essene. Luke adds that he gave no consent when the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus.

Later accounts widen the tale. Matthew makes the tomb Joseph's own new tomb, and John joins Nicodemus to him at the burial. A later gospel tells of his prison escape, and legend sends him to Britain with a staff that grew into a thorn tree. Another legend ties him to the Holy Grail, the cup said to have caught drops of Jesus' blood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-or-juda-a:
Judah, or Juda, was an American family whose members settled in Newport, New York, Charleston, Richmond, Philadelphia, Montreal, Jamaica, and Surinam. The entry lists those known to have lived in America in alphabetical order, drawn from the Publications of the American Jewish Historical Society.

Names run from Abigail Judah of Richmond, born in 1742, to men who signed petitions, served in militias, and helped found congregations. Baruch Judah asked New York for cemetery ground in 1728 and died in 1774 aged ninety-five. Joseph Judah was among Newport's earliest settlers in 1658. Later names reach the Civil War and a Surinam writer on finance in 1869-70. The list is a record of names, dates, and town ties more than a family story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalisz-german-k:
Kalisz is a city in Russian Poland. In German its name is Kalisch. It stands on the River Prosna, near the Prussian border. Its Jewish community is one of the oldest in Poland. In 1264 Boleslaw the Pious gave its Jews a charter of rights. Later rulers used that charter as a model for their own.

The entry traces the community through hard centuries. Mob attacks came in the fourteenth century, with false charges of well poisoning. Troops killed 600 members of the community in 1666. An anti-Jewish riot broke out on June 23, 1878. The mob wrecked the synagogue and the rabbi's house. The article lists the town's known rabbis across the ages. It ends with a count from 1897. Jews then numbered 8,026 in a city of 21,680 people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kedushshah-lit-:
Ḳedushshah means "holiness." In common speech it names a set part of the 'Amidah prayer. The reader says it aloud, and the congregation answers. There are at least three fixed answers. The first is the "Holy, holy, holy" of Isaiah. Others come from Ezekiel and the Psalms. On Sabbaths and festivals two more answers are added.

The entry gives the full weekday form in English. It then gives the fuller forms for Sabbaths and festivals. German and Sephardic rites differ in their lead-in lines. The article argues that the spoken form is very old. No Talmud passage names the answers, yet no later age could have added them without a fight on record. A Talmud saying is quoted: since the Temple fell, the world is upheld by the Ḳedushshah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klaczko-julian-:
Julian Klaczko was a French publicist, born in Wilna on Nov. 6, 1825. His father taught him Hebrew and Polish. A Hebrew song from his bar miẓwah year was printed in 1838. He studied at Heidelberg and at Königsberg, taking his Ph.D. in 1846. Settling in Paris in 1849, he wrote steadily for the "Revue des Deux Mondes."

Austria's premier, Count Beust, called him to Vienna in 1869. Klaczko became Aulic Councilor in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He also sat in the Galician Landtag. There he urged Austria to take France's part against Prussia. Failing in that purpose, he left for Italy in 1870. He returned to Vienna in 1875. The entry calls him a foremost voice of Polish thought in western Europe. It notes that he severed his connection with Judaism early in his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-koplik-henry-94: Henry Koplik, an American physician born at New York on Oct. 28, 1858, took his medical degree in 1881 after study at the College of the City of New York. Postgraduate work took him to Leipsic, Prague, and Vienna. Back home from 1883 he worked at Bellevue Hospital and other city institutions, and from 1899 he taught pediatrics at Bellevue Medical College. He was first to describe an early sign of measles, still called Koplik's spots. He also found the bacillus of whooping cough and began free delivery of pasteurized milk to the poor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lattes-lattas-9:
Lattes, or Lattas, is a family name taken from a small town near Béziers in France. Its members include many scholars across Provence, Italy, and Rome. Abraham ben Isaac Lattes of Venice, born in 1809, led his community from 1839 and served it through the cholera siege of 1848.

Elijah Lattes, his son, born at Venice in 1843, taught Greek and Roman antiquities at Milan and wrote on land credit. Isaac ben Jacob Lattes wrote a Provence chronicle in 1340. Isaac ben Judah, a Talmudist and physician at Perpignan in 1303, signed both sides of the science ban fight. Moses Lattes of Venice died by accident in 1883.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leon-joseph-of-: Joseph of Carcassonne, called Leon Joseph, was a physician. He lived at the end of the fourteenth century and the start of the fifteenth. He spent his work turning medical books from Latin into Hebrew. Many of his versions are now lost. Three still survive in manuscript. One is a commentary by Gerard de Solo on Razi's ninth book, on pathology. One is a manual of medicine by Gerard de Solo. One is a chapter ascribed to Hippocrates. It treats how the stars relate to medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lieben-adolf-99: Adolf Lieben, an Austrian chemist, was born at Vienna on Dec. 3, 1836. He studied at Vienna, Heidelberg, and Paris and took his Ph.D. in 1856. He taught at Vienna from 1861. He then held chairs at Palermo in 1863, Turin in 1867, and Prague in 1871. Since 1875 he has held the chair of general and drug chemistry at Vienna. He belongs to the Vienna Academy of Sciences. His many essays, in the chief journals of his field, treat aldehydes, milk sugar, and formaldehyde.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-judah-ben-j: Judah ben Joshua Löb was a Bohemian scholar who lived at Prague in the middle of the seventeenth century. He served as secretary to Simon Spira, chief rabbi of Prague. He published an account of the siege of Prague by the Swedes in 1648 and of Jewish suffering at that time. The account was first printed at Prague. It was later reprinted with a Latin translation and again in a Hebrew journal. The entry lists several catalog sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowy-albert-101:
Albert Löwy (born 1816) was an English rabbi and communal worker born at Aussee in Moravia, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind gives his career. He studied Hebrew and Arabic at Vienna, then became a minister of the Reform Synagogue in London. He served there for fifty years, retiring in 1892.

Working with Professor Marks, Löwy helped compile the congregation’s prayer book, and he helped found the Anglo-Jewish Association, serving as its secretary from 1871 to 1889. The article stresses his scholarship: he catalogued Samaritan manuscripts, printed the first specimen of an Aramaic dialect spoken by Jews of Urmia, and catalogued the City of London’s Hebrew books. St. Andrews gave him an honorary doctorate in 1893. The entry shows a minister whose learning served both his synagogue and wider Jewish scholarship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manetho-greek-m:
Manetho, the Greco-Egyptian priest who wrote Egypt's history, is treated in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. He was high priest of Sebennytus in the Delta and lived under the first two Ptolemies. His history was written after 271 before the common era. Its value rests on his direct use of hieroglyphic sources.

The article explains how his work reaches us. Josephus is the only writer who gives connected extracts from it. Later chronologers copied out his tables of dynasties and kings. The writers warn that Josephus's extracts are full of confusion, above all on the Exodus. Some errors are Josephus's own. The Hyksos material holds real information, but tying those kings to Israel fails. Once blunders are corrected, the Exodus tale seems built from the Bible plus Egyptian folk stories. The entry teaches readers to use a priceless source with open eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maskil-plural-m:
“Maskil” is a Hebrew word with two very different lives. Joseph Jacobs, Peter Wiernik, and Gotthard Deutsch explain it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. In its older use the word was a title of honor. It meant a scholar or enlightened man. In parts of Italy it belonged to rabbinical students, while in the East it could name the overseers of the poor.

The second half of the article follows the word eastward: among the Jews of the Slavonic lands, a maskil was a self-taught Hebrew scholar. He was drawn to the Haskalah, the Jewish enlightenment that spread from the circle of Mendelssohn. Such men worked mostly as teachers and writers. They taught a generation of Russian Jews to read Hebrew and built the new Hebrew literature. Yet each generation of them had to be recruited fresh from Orthodox ranks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meinek-moses-sa:
Moses Säkel Meinek was a German scholar, editor, and probably printer at Offenbach in the early eighteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Almost everything known of him is three dated imprints: in 1715 he published, under his own name, “Teutsche Apothek” by Naphtali Pappenheim. In 1717 he issued a riddle in Judaeo-German verse by an anonymous author. Schudt reprinted it with a German transcription in his “Jüdische Merckwürdigkeiten,” calling Meinek a printer.

In 1722 he edited an anonymous guide for the reader of the Law. It is the “Siyyumah ha-Parashiyyot meha-Torah,” which the entry judges he probably wrote himself. That is the whole record. The editors assemble it from the bibliographies of Steinschneider and Wolf. Small as it is, the notice preserves a figure of the German-Jewish book trade, whose men rarely left any trace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelsohn-mart:
Martin Mendelsohn was a Berlin physician. He belonged to the generation that made nursing a science. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Posen in 1860. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1885. He spent a postgraduate year in Paris. He rose through the first medical clinic and the Charité. He reached a privat-docentship in 1895. He reached the title of professor in 1899.

His cause was the care of the sick as a discipline in itself. From 1894 he edited the "Zeitschrift für Krankenpflege," the journal of nursing. His books circle the bedside. They treat opium and the comfort of the patient. They treat medical art versus medical science. One, in 1896, treats the influence of cycling on the human organism. About a hundred journal essays complete the count. They mark a busy clinical career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-rachel-10:
Rachel Meyer, a German novelist born in Danzig on March 11, 1806, is remembered in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson, published in 1906. She married her late sister Frederika's husband and, while raising and teaching children and giving to charity, kept up her own self-education. Noted men were guests in her home.

Her first book, Zwei Schwestern, appeared at Berlin in 1853 and praised love's triumph over self within marriage. In Vienna she wrote a sketch of city life and a novel about the great actress Rachel, published in 1859. Her last novel, In Banden Frei of 1869, studied her friend Lina Davidson. Practical under her idealism, she even sketched the inventor Stephenson to stir a nephew's practical spirit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montelimar-hebr:
Montélimar, capital of the Drôme in France, held a large and comparatively prosperous Jewish community from the early fourteenth century, as Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Jews had a synagogue on the Rue de la Juiverie, a school by the Porte Saint-Martin, a cemetery, and a slaughter-house whose privilege the Dauphin Louis confirmed in 1455.

Scholarship passed through: in 1339 Samuel ben Judah of Marseilles revised there his Hebrew version of Alexander Aphrodisius on the soul. The turn came in 1439, when the lords imposed the Jewish badge the town's consuls had long spared them; in 1453 the Jews were ordered to attend Christian preaching. The entry names the community's leading men across two centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musa-of-tiflis-:
Musa of Tiflis, a native of Za'faran in Persia, was a Karaite who founded a sect of his own in the early ninth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His followers were called Abu Imranites, Meshwites, or Tiflisites. The Karaites themselves counted him an apostate.

Musa kept several Karaite rules, such as counting the fifty days from a Sunday. But his chief teachings broke away: he held that God, after creating the world, left it to run itself. He also denied the resurrection of the dead. His month began when the old moon vanished, not when the new one showed. The entry also weighs whether he is the Moses ben Amram quoted by Ibn Ezra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nabon-or-navon-:
Nabon, or Navon, is the name of a Turkish family that produced rabbinical writers from the seventeenth century on. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. One branch sat at Jerusalem and another at Constantinople. The earliest known member is Hanun Nabon, whose sermons the bibliographer Azulai saw in manuscript.

The article gives short lives of eight Nabons. Jonah Nabon of Jerusalem taught the great Azulai and left responsa and a work on divorce. Judah Nabon wrote notes on Maimonides' code, and Ephraim Nabon gathered responsa at Constantinople. Two later Nabons became chief rabbis of Jerusalem. Jonah Moses, in 1836, was the first to bear the title Rishon le-Ziyyon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-jose:
Nathan ben Joseph Official was a French rabbi famed for debate. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Sens in the later thirteenth century. His son called him the prince of polemists. Nathan argued in public with church leaders and baptized Jews.

He debated bishops from many French towns, one by one. He also faced the king's confessor and Paris bishop Guillaume d'Auvergne. In 1273 he debated Pope Gregory X on a Bible verse. Nathan spoke with striking freedom in these contests. No book of his survives today. His notes on Bible verses are quoted in later works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-ben-mose:
