Nissim ben Moses of Marseilles was a French philosopher. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. About 1306 he wrote on the Pentateuch. His age was split by a war over philosophy.

Orthodox Jews and philosophy's friends fought hard then. Nissim still gave reasoned readings of the miracles. Sodom's fall, he said, was a volcanic eruption. He pointed to Ischia's eruption of 1302 as its like. His commentary survives in several manuscript copies. It goes under three titles in those copies. They are Ma'aseh Nissim, Sefer ha-Nissim, and 'Ikre ha-Dat. Schorr also credits him with a homily on Ruth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oedenburg-sopro:
Oedenburg, also called Sopron, is a city in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and Miksa Pollak wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish group counts among the oldest in Hungary. A text of 1526 traces it to the tenth century. Fire gutted the town in the year 1317.

King Charles Robert asked Jews to settle there in 1324. They lived in peace for thirty years of that age. Then Louis the Great cast them out in 1354. Most went to Wiener-Neustadt, in Austria. A few years on, they were let back in. By 1379 the group numbered eighty souls in all. By the close of the next age it reached 400. Kings at times shielded them from town attacks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-organ-11761:
The organ is a wind instrument with pipes and keys. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jewish sages say it was one of the Temple's tools of music. The link rests on a verse in Psalm 150. That verse names stringed tools and organs in English.

Scholars think those two terms may be swapped in place. The true word for organ may be the first, not the last. In new Hebrew, one word serves for organ and piano. The Temple tool was the magrefa, by Talmud accounts. It had ten pipes, each pipe with ten holes. So one hundred notes could be got from it in all. An older tale gives it a square ell of size. It gives it pipes for a full one thousand tones.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palagyi-melchio:
Melchior Palágyi was a Hungarian writer born at Paks. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there on December 26, 1859. His first name at birth was Silberstein, as was his brother's. His father gave him his first school lessons at home.

Melchior then went to high schools at Temesvar and Kassa. In 1877 he went to the trade school at Budapest. In 1881 he passed his tests as a school teacher. His fields were the science of sums and of nature. Five years on, he was a professor at a trade school. As a pupil he wrote a treatise on sums in 1880. The Academy of Sciences put that work out in print. He then turned to deep thought as his main field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paz-duarte-de-1:
Duarte de Paz was a Portuguese Marrano who lobbied at Rome. He acted as agent for Portugal's New Christians, the forced converts. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died about 1541, after years of double dealing.

Duarte had won King John the Third's trust in war. He lost an eye fighting in the African war. Sent on a mission, he went to Rome instead. There his gifts and speeches swayed the cardinals. In 1532 the pope voided the bull that set up the Inquisition. Masked men later stabbed Duarte, but hidden armor saved him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peshitta-or-pes:
The Peshitta is the oldest Syriac version of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means the simple one. It covers both the Old Testament and the New. Syriac Christians still use it as their Bible.

No single translator made the whole version. The work grew over several centuries of labor. Tradition ties its start to King Izates of Adiabene. The Pentateuch may date to the first century. By the fourth century the full Bible stood in Syriac. Church fathers quoted it widely by then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pine-pnie-samso:
Samson Pine was a German Jewish translator of the 1300s. Gotthard Deutsch and A. M. Friedenberg wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was likely born at Peine, in Hanover. He later lived and worked at Strasburg. Such teamwork across faiths was rare in that age.

Two Christian poets preserve his name for us. In 1336 they continued Wolfram's great poem Parzival. Pine rendered the French text into German for them. He also invented rhymes for their verses. Their manuscript thanks him twice in ten lines. Both times it names him plainly as a Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-primo-samuel-12:
Samuel Primo was a follower of the false messiah Shabbethai Zebi. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jerusalem in the seventeenth century. He died, in all likelihood, at Constantinople. He was one of the first men to join Zebi's cause.

Primo served Zebi as his private secretary. He did so on the trip from Jerusalem to Smyrna in 1665. He lent the false messiah an air of state and honor. From Smyrna he spread the news through foreign lands. The messiah had come at last, he told the Jews. With a few close friends he planned a bold step. They would do away with rabbinic Judaism itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quetsch-solomon:
Solomon Quetsch was an Austrian rabbi and Talmud scholar of Nikolsburg. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in 1798. He died there in 1856. He learned at the yeshivah of his home town. His teacher was Mordecai Benet, whose dearest pupil he was.

Quetsch served as rabbi at Piesling and then at Leipnik. Last he served at Nikolsburg, his own home town. There he came after Samson Raphael Hirsch in the post. He held it for a few months only at the end. He was a rabbi of the old school in all things. Yet he stood out from that school in clear ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-randar-or-arend:
A randar was a tenant who leased farms, mills, or taverns. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word was used in Poland, Lithuania, and nearby lands. Whole villages could be held under such a lease.

The article notes that Jews leased most of these taverns. The Jewish tavern keeper became a stock figure in Polish writing. In Pan Tadeusz he appears as Jankiel, a loyal helper. He gives advice and even plays the cymbals well. The entry also notes many Russian rules on Jewish taverns. It shows how one job shaped both daily life and literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reif-abraham-12:
Abraham Reif was a Galician poet born at Mosciska in 1802. Isidore Singer and M. Margel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died in 1859. Early on he followed the Me'assefim school of Hebrew writing.

The article says he later broke away from that movement. Tobias Feder's sharp satire deeply shaped his work. Alexander Langbank introduced him to secular sciences. Reif's ready wit made traditionalists fear him, they say. He opened a school for Bible and Hebrew in his town. That school produced leading Hebraists. His dramas picture Galician Jewish life in vivid scenes. Too poor to print them, he gave copies to pupils. His language stayed pure Biblical Hebrew throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rime-12761:
Rime is the matching of sounds at the ends of words. Crawford Howell Toy and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some writers credited the early Hebrews with knowing rime. Judah Provencal even called Hebrew poetry mother of all poetries.

The article says Samuel Archevolti found rime in the Bible. He thought it existed but was not fully developed. Moses ibn Habib claimed it for other early Hebrew verse. Modern writers like Reuss gave rime a large role too. Yet most agree rime was no formal rule in the Old Testament. Matching line ends arise from grammar, they argue. Such echoes are not an organic part of composition. The entry separates chance sound likeness from true poetic form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-david:
David Rosenthal was a Polish physician born at Tarnogrod, in the Lublin region, in 1808. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father was a district physician on the Polish army staff.

Rosenthal studied at Vienna and was sent to fight cholera in 1831. He served Warsaw's Jewish hospital for decades, as chief physician from 1844 to 1879. He also taught hygiene at the Marymont institute near Warsaw. His account of an 1847 typhus outbreak described what was later called recurrent fever. He wrote as well on glanders in human beings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sambari-cattawi:
Joseph ben Isaac Sambari was an Egyptian chronicler of the seventeenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Franco wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Of lowly origin, he worked for a rabbi at Alexandria in Egypt.

Sambari spent his leisure on history, using a famous rabbi's great library. He knew Arabic, Hebrew, and Spanish, though his Hebrew is faulty. His first chronicle, a general history from Abraham onward, is lost. The second, Dibre Yosef, survives in two copies, at Oxford and Paris. It covers Egypt's Fatimite califs, Spain's Abbassids, and the Ottoman Turks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-francisco-1:
Cyrus Adler and Jacob Voorsanger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on San Francisco. The city was California's chief port and trade center on the Pacific coast. The village of Yerba Buena took the name San Francisco in 1847. Jews likely lived there early, though records are thin. The gold rush of 1849 changed everything.

That year large numbers of Jews reached the city. Some came on the first Pacific mail steamer in February. Others crossed overland or sailed from Europe and Australia. In autumn 1849 over one hundred Jews were in town. About fifty gathered for the Day of Atonement in a room above a store. In the summer of 1850 the two main congregations formed. One drew German and American Jews. The other drew Polish and English Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scheuer-jacob-m:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Jacob Moses David Scheuer, called Tebele. He was a German Talmudist. Scheuer was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main early in the eighteenth century. He died at Mayence in 1782. He ranked among the foremost pupils of Jacob Cohen, Frankfort's rabbi.

Scheuer served as a judge at Frankfort under the author of Pene Yehoshua'. In 1759, at an advanced age, he became rabbi of Bamberg. There he mediated a long dispute between Jews and gentry. His work produced the ceremonial agreement of 1760. A baptized Jew then slandered him to the prince-bishop. Bamberg became impossible for him. In 1767 he accepted the district rabbinate of Mayence. He stayed there until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sfej-abraham-13:
Abraham Sfej was a rabbinic author born at Tunis early in the eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He left Tunis and settled in Jerusalem, pausing at Constantinople on the way. He died at Amsterdam in 1784.

Sfej died while raising funds for the Jerusalem community. His book Ene Abraham comments on Maimonides' great code, the Yad ha-Hazakah. It was printed at Amsterdam in the year of his death. The entry is brief, but it keeps the name of a North African scholar who crossed the Jewish world for learning and duty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemoneh-esreh-:
Shemoneh Esreh is the set of blessings at the heart of daily Jewish prayer. Cyrus Adler and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name literally means eighteen, for its blessing count. Jews say it morning, afternoon, and evening each day.

An extra service on Sabbaths and holy days includes it too. As the prayer itself, it is called the Tefillah. Sephardic Jews call it the Amidah, the standing prayer. Worshipers must recite it while standing on their feet. In fixed form the blessings actually number nineteen. They group into praise, petitions, and closing thanks. The entry maps the prayer that structures Jewish worship every single day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-henry-n:
Henry Naphtali Solomon was an English Hebraist and educationist born in 1796. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London and schooled by his father. His father kept a school at Brixton in London. Henry became head master of the Jews' Free School in 1817.

In 1822 he opened his own school in Queen's square. It later moved to Hammersmith and then to Edmonton. He taught at Edmonton for more than forty years. He helped found a Jewish literary and scientific institution. He also preached for years in the St Albans Synagogue. He translated the Jewish prayer-book and wrote very widely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spingarn-joel-e:
Joel Elias Spingarn was an American educator born in New York in 1875. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in New York city on May 17. He graduated from Columbia University in 1895 with honors. He took postgraduate courses at Harvard and Columbia as well.

He earned his doctor's degree in 1899 at Columbia. That year he became a tutor at his alma mater. In 1900 he rose to adjunct professor of comparative literature. His chief book traced literary criticism in the Renaissance. It appeared in 1899 and was translated into Italian. He also wrote The New Hesperides and American Scholarship, both in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synagogue-archi:
Synagogue architecture covers how Jews have housed worship through the ages. Joseph Jacobs and A. W. Brunner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Ancient Jewish art survives mainly in the Temple's remains. Judea's place and history discouraged a lasting art tradition. Old synagogue ruins give builders only meager guidance today.

The Kafr Bir'im synagogue is the best preserved ancient example. Its front held three doorways with carved frames. The central door bore a rounded, enriched arch. Inside, the plan ran rectangular with a columned portico. The door faced west and the Ark stood east. The reading platform sat near the center. Men filled the side spaces while women used a gallery. The entry weighs what ruins can teach modern builders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tashlik-14261:
Tashlik is a rite of casting sins away at New Year. Isidore Singer and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its name comes from a passage in Micah. Micah says God will cast sins into the sea's depths. Jews gather by running water to act that verse out.

On the afternoon of New-Year's Day the congregation assembles. They recite Micah's closing verses beside the stream. Penitential prayers and hymns follow the reading. When and where the custom began is uncertain. One view links it to a decree in Josephus. That decree let Jews pray by the sea at Halicarnassus. The Zohar hints that what falls into the deep is lost. Talmud and early codes never mention the custom, though. The entry weighs hints against a long silence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodotion-1436:
Theodotion, a Greek translator of the Old Testament, is treated through his Daniel. Crawford Howell Toy and Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His version of Daniel replaced the Septuagint in church use. Only one Greek manuscript kept the older Daniel text.

Origen placed the Septuagint in his Hexapla but quoted Theodotion instead. Jerome blamed the Septuagint's faults for its rejection. Earlier fathers had already favored Theodotion's wording. Yet he did not translate straight from the Hebrew-Aramaic text. The additions to Daniel were Greek in origin, scholars argue. An Aramaic version of them adapts the Greek, not the reverse. The article untangles a tricky textual puzzle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toul-hebr-or-za:
Toul, a French town in Meurthe-et-Moselle, had Jews from the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. R. Eliezer of Toul, a tosafot author, once lived there. His brother Abraham studied under Isaac the Elder of Dampierre. Meir Abulafia addressed learned letters to Abraham's circle.

In 1708 the Bishop of Toul sought to expel Jewish bankers. His petition against the Levy family failed. Duke Leopold let 180 Jewish families stay in 1721. They could worship and trade without molestation. Leon Cohen represented Toul at Napoleon's Paris assembly in 1806. The Nancy consistory governed the small community. By 1905 it held forty or fifty families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ugolino-blaisio:
Blaisio Ugolino was an Italian scholar who gathered a vast treasury of Jewish antiquities. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Venice around 1700, he knew Talmudic literature deeply. He was said to be a Jewish convert. His Thesaurus ran to thirty-four Latin volumes.

The set appeared at Venice between 1744 and 1769. It reprinted most seventeenth-century treatises on Jewish antiquities. Bochart, Buxtorf, Selden, and Reland all stand inside it. Topics run from festivals to burial customs. Priests, Temple, Talmud, and law each fill several volumes. Ugolino translated many tractates himself from Hebrew. Menahot and Zebahim were his own renderings. Full indexes close the thirty-fourth volume.

Philipp Veit was a German painter of portraits and religious scenes. He was born in Berlin on February 13, 1793. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. His mother was a daughter of Moses Mendelssohn. His stepfather, Friedrich von Schlegel, had him baptized as a boy.

Veit studied art at Dresden and Vienna. In 1813 he joined the army and fought Napoleon. He won the Iron Cross for bravery. From 1815 he worked in Rome with the neo German school. He painted frescoes there with Cornelius and Overbeck. Later he directed the Staedel Institute at Frankfort. His large canvas Germania became his best known work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wallich-11161:
Wallich was a German family rich in doctors. Joseph Jacobs, Gotthard Deutsch, and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name may come from the Hebrew form of Falk. Its earliest known members lived at Worms. Joseph ben Meir and Moses Joshua Wallich practiced there in the fifteen hundreds.

A 1615 document lists many family physicians at once. Fathers and sons signed it together as doctors. In the seventeen hundreds, Wallich doctors practiced across Germany. Abraham ben Isaac studied medicine at Padua. He settled at Frankfort in 1657. His Hebrew medical book argued that body and soul ail alike. The entry traces the family's long medical line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weltsch-samuel-:
Samuel Weltsch was an Austrian cantor. He was born at Prague on September 12, 1835. Isidore Singer and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Prague on August 5, 1901. Cantors filled his family line. He sang at Prague's Meisel synagogue while still young. Prague's conservatory gave him his music training.

In 1865 Weltsch took a post in New York. He served Ahawath Chesed congregation until 1880. He worked to improve American synagogue music. He helped compile the first volumes of Zimrat Yah. That song collection serves all seasons of the year. It is still widely used today. He also led charities and schools in Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-ben-ishm:
Yannai ben Ishmael was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Zeera and Abba bar Kahana. A few of his rules of law live on in his name.

One rule treats a line of the set prayer of each day. A query on that same prayer came to him from Zeera. A rule on the cutting rite for slaves is told in his name. His tales have lived on as well as his rules. One tale treats the meet of Adam with the angels. One is a parting speech built on a verse in Judges. In a sick spell Zeera and Abba came to his bed side. There they fell to a debate on the groves of Solomon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamzam-15161:
Zamzam is a holy well in the mosque at Mecca in Arabia. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Muslim lore ties it to the spring of Hagar and Ishmael. That spring is named in the Book of Genesis as well.

Some Arab minds read the name as fill, fill in tongue. Hagar bid her son fill the jar at that spring. One mind read it as stay, stay in the Egyptian tongue. Hagar bid her son cease his road at that well. The spring is held to be a work of pure grace. Its water is prized for drink and for wash rites. Men ship it to far lands for the sick and the devout. The fast of the holy month is oft broken with it. Men wet their eyes with it to make sight more keen.
kardec-le-livre-des-mediums-1861:
Allan Kardec trains the seer in Le Livre des mediums, his French guide of 1861. The name means the book on mediums. Kardec had set out his faith's creed in his prior book. Rules, types, and warns fill the guide in calm prose. His faith took it as its chief hand book at once. In French, it is the school text of a world faith. Its order is its strength.

Ask what you can do for your country, the famous line concludes. Kennedy pledges strength for liberty's defense anywhere on the globe. He calls foes to talks and friends to shared, bold ventures. levi-clef-des-grands-mysteres-1861:
Eliphas Levi drew his whole creed into one book in La Clef des grands mysteres, out in 1861. The title means the key to the great riddles. He links the lore of the Jews, the cards of the tarot, and a bright force he calls the Astral Light.

lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's March 1875 number opens with an escape from Siberia. Australian scenes and adventures begin alongside it. Charlotte F. Bates offers a poem called Forecast. Ita Aniol Prokop's Matchless One concludes its tale of American society.

Trollope recalls the Tuscan court under Grand Duke Leopold. Munich as a pest-city and Mitchell's scientific life add nonfiction. Recollections of the Tuscan court continue across this number too.
macaulay-history-england-vol-5-1861:
Volume 5 of Macaulay's History of England from the Accession of James II appeared in 1861, after Thomas Babington Macaulay's death. Friends prepared the unfinished volume from his papers. It carries his story of William III's reign toward the end of the seventeenth century.

War with France, plots against the king, and fights over taxes and trade fill the chapters. Macaulay kept his vivid style, painting scenes and judging men with confidence. maine-ancient-law-1861:
Sir Henry Sumner Maine published Ancient Law in 1861. Maine, a law professor who later served in India, compared the oldest legal records of Rome, India, and other lands. He asked how law itself began and how it changed as societies grew.

Maine's famous summary runs from status to contract: early law fixes each person's place by birth, while modern law lets persons make their own bargains. He traced property, wills, and crime from family rule toward individual right. The phrase and the book founded comparative legal history and the sociology of law. Later research corrected many details, but Maine's questions still organize the study of early law.

Volume two of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter nine, in 1695. Harlay, Archbishop of Paris, died of epilepsy at Conflans that August. He had lost favor with the King and Madame de Maintenon.

He had stood against the word of her marriage to the King. Envious clergy took joy in his fall from high place. Gardeners raked out his footprints as he walked with the Duchesse de Lesdiguieres. mill-representative-government-1861:

Mill gives the first strong case for fair shares of seats by votes cast. He calls this plan a great step forward. He also weighs town rule, unions of states, and rule over subject lands. On that last point, later readers fault him. Students still read the book beside On Liberty.

Mill answered the charge that the theory is a pig philosophy by ranking pleasures of mind above those of body. He argued for liberty, justice, and rules that protect the weak as parts of happiness itself. The essay is short, clear, and argued with care against named critics. It remains the canonical statement of utilitarian ethics, the first text most students read on the subject.
morin-astrologia-gallica-1661:
Jean-Baptiste Morin was a French royal astrologer and professor whose Astrologia Gallica appeared in 1661, after his death. The work runs to twenty-six books in Latin, the fruit of a lifetime at the art. It is the last great Latin system of judicial astrology.

Morin rebuilds the judgment of nativities on strict rules for a planet's state, place, and aspects within the whole chart. njals-saga-dasent-1861:

oe-epistola-alexandri-cockayne-1861:

Glute growth needs a multifactor approach, the author concludes, and prescription should be individualized rather than crown a single winner.
openalex-w7221053161:
Lara Figueredo Santos, Luana Araújo Macedo Scalia, and Renata Rodrigues Batista Carneiro reviewed nursing care for breast inflammation in the weeks after childbirth, publishing in 2026. Their focus is first-time mothers, for whom pain, swelling, nipple injury, and mastitis can break breastfeeding within the first weeks.

The studies group into physical complications, clinical and teaching work by nurses, and the social setting that pushes early weaning. Nurses adjust the baby's latch and position, and newer care such as low-level laser therapy eases pain and heals nipple wounds. Weak family support and early return to work still undo progress, so the authors call for systematic nursing protocols in primary care.
pasteur-corpuscules-organises-1861:
Louis Pasteur read this memoir in French in 1861, on the tiny bodies that float in the air. It deals head on with the claim that life can spring from dead stuff. The work grew from his prize clash with Pouchet and his school.

His famed swan neck flasks let air in but trapped dust in the bent neck. Broth in such flasks stayed pure for months, while dust let life bloom at once. The clear proof, shown in a famed talk of the time, brought the long debate to an end.
plos-pbio-0020261:
Carsten Schnatwinkel, Savvas Christoforidis, and their team studied cargo intake in cells for PLOS Biology in 2004. Cells pull in material by endocytosis, pinching off small sacs from the surface. A protein called Rab5 manages early steps, and its partner Rabankyrin-5 helps run more than one intake route.

The study shows Rabankyrin-5 coordinates distinct mechanisms rather than serving just one. That makes it a hub in the intake system. Hubs are where a cell can tune traffic up or down with a single change. Knowing them helps explain how cells feed, sense their surroundings, and take in signals. It also matters for diseases where viruses or toxins hijack entry routes.
plos-pone-0000061:
Andrey Rzhetsky, Tian Zheng, and Chani Weinreb tackled the errors in biology's own maps in a 2006 paper. A molecular pathway map charts how genes and proteins interact, step by step. Such maps are drawn from thousands of papers, and they contain mistakes that later work then inherits.

Their answer was self-correcting maps: pathway charts built to detect and repair their own inconsistencies as new data arrives. A map that heals itself would give systems biology, the field that simulates whole cells, a firmer base to build on. The idea treats a scientific database less like a printed atlas and more like a living document that keeps checking its facts.
plos-pone-0000161:
Robert J. Greenstein, Liya Su, Vahram Haroutunian, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests how two long-used drugs, methotrexate and 6-mercaptopurine, act on Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis. This bacterium causes Johne's disease in cattle and has been debated as a factor in Crohn's disease.

Both drugs are used in inflammatory bowel disease, where benefit was often credited to immune suppression. The authors examine the drugs' direct action on the bacterium itself. If the drugs also kill or slow this microbe, the standard story of how they help bowel patients may need revision.
plos-pone-0000261:
A. Townsend Peterson, Brett W. Benz, and Monica Papeş published this avian flu risk paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks how highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza could enter North America through bird migration. The authors model the pathways that migrating birds might carry the virus along.

H5N1 had spread across Asia and Europe, and North America was watching its flyways. Mapping likely entry routes tells surveillance teams where to sample birds first. The paper is a risk assessment, using migration ecology to aim limited testing resources at the most probable doors.
plos-pone-0000361:
Faridabano Nato, Armelle Phalipon, Lan Phuong Thi Nguyen, and colleagues published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Shigella flexneri 2a is a bacterium that causes dysentery, a severe diarrheal disease. The authors present a dipstick test for rapid diagnosis of this strain directly in stool. The strip gives an answer at the bedside or in the field.

Dysentery outbreaks strike where labs are scarce, so a stool dipstick that needs no equipment is valuable. The authors report the test's performance on real samples. Fast identification guides treatment and outbreak control for a disease that kills many children in poor regions.
plos-pone-0000461:
Matthew N. Van Ert and colleagues traced the family structure of the anthrax bacterium worldwide, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax, a disease of animals and people and a feared bioweapon. The team analyzed its global genetic population structure, how its strains group and spread across regions.

Anthrax spores travel with livestock, wool, and soil, so strain patterns record both natural spread and human trade. A global structure map helps investigators match an outbreak sample to its likely origin. That matters for disease control. It also matters for forensic work after deliberate releases. It also shows how a bacterium with little genetic variety is organized across the planet.
plos-pone-0000561:
Lyubomir G. Nashev and colleagues studied an enzyme that tunes hormone strength inside cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase modulates how 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 handles certain steroids, including 7-keto- and 7β-hydroxy-neurosteroids. The type 1 enzyme activates cortisone-like signals and is a drug target in metabolic disease.

A modulator enzyme matters because it decides how much active hormone a tissue actually sees, whatever the blood level says. Neurosteroids act in the brain, so the partnership may shape mood and cognition as well. Fine-grained control points like this are where selective drugs try to act.
plos-pone-0000661:
Fabien Lacaille, Makoto Hiroi, Robert Twele and colleagues found that a fruit fly sex signal tastes bitter to males, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sexual behavior requires animals to tell the sexes apart and respond correctly to each. In Drosophila melanogaster, as in many insects, chemicals on the body surface called cuticular hydrocarbons are thought to carry sex recognition.

Direct neural proof of their role had been missing. The title names an inhibitory sex pheromone, a signal that discourages male mating attempts, and says males taste it as bitter. A taste pathway for a stop signal is a neat piece of sensory design, linking flavor to courtship decisions.
plos-pone-0000761:
Jing Tang, Jewn Giew Park, Charles B. Millard and colleagues used computer-aided design to improve a blocker of the botulinum toxin enzyme. Botulinum neurotoxin serotype A is among the most potent toxins known. Its zinc endopeptidase is the part that cuts proteins inside nerve cells. Optimizing a selective small-molecule inhibitor is a formidable challenge, because the enzyme-substrate interface is unusually large and the enzyme itself is big and complex.

Computer-aided lead optimization refines a starting inhibitor in silico before costly lab rounds. A better blocker could serve as an antidote after exposure, a long-standing biodefense goal. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study reports the improved inhibitor and the design path that produced it.
plos-pone-0000861:
Zohar Mor, Charlotte K. Kent, Robert P. Kohn and colleagues documented a paradox in HIV prevention, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Recent experimental evidence had demonstrated the benefits of male circumcision for preventing HIV infection. Studies had also shown circumcision is cost-effective and reduces risk for certain ulcerative sexually transmitted diseases. Few preventive measures arrive with that strength of trial evidence behind them.

Yet their title reports declining rates of male circumcision amid that increasing evidence of public health benefit. A proven intervention spreading more slowly than the science invites questions about culture, cost, and health system habit. The authors document the trend so policy can answer those questions with data.
plos-pone-0000961:
Tasneem Khanam, Carsten Raabe, Martin Kiefmann and colleagues tested whether repeated DNA elements can guide messages to dendrites, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Nerve cells send some RNA messages out into their dendrites, the branches that receive signals. Placement depends on signals within the RNA and on factors that read them.

A small RNA called BC1 is thought to tune protein building in dendrite zones. The team ask whether ID repetitive elements, common repeated stretches in rodent genes, can act as targeting signals themselves. They test the idea in living systems. The answer bears on how neurons place the right proteins at the right branch.
plos-pone-0001061:
Caitlin Conboy, Christiana Spyrou, Natalie Thorne and colleagues showed that cell cycle genes are the conserved targets of one factor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Resting cells are held in a quiet state partly by a protein complex called DREAM. In human cells the factor E2F4 directs that complex to its targets.

The team found E2F4 binds a highly overlapping set of genes across contexts, and those targets are cell cycle genes. Conservation of the target set suggests the quiet state is guarded by an old, stable program. When that program fails, cells divide when they should rest, a step toward cancer. The work names the guarded genes.
plos-pone-0001161:
Blood vessel lining cells survive in part because a growth factor called VEGF blocks their self-destruction. Ling Wang and co-authors mapped part of that survival signal in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on neuropilin-1, a partner protein for VEGF, and on p53 and the caspases, proteins that drive programmed cell death.

The authors report that neuropilin-1 modulates the p53 and caspase axis to promote endothelial cell survival. In plain terms, it tips a life-or-death switch inside vessel cells toward life. That pathway matters wherever new vessels grow, from healing wounds to tumors.
plos-pone-0001261:
Hospitals keep huge archives of tissue samples fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin. These archives are a goldmine for molecular studies, if the RNA inside them can be read. Silke von Ahlfen and colleagues investigated what determines RNA quality from such FFPE samples, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Fixation and storage damage RNA, but the adverse effects of standard pathology practice were incompletely documented.

The authors set out to pin down which steps of collection and processing hurt RNA most. Their guidance helps researchers judge which archived blocks can support gene expression profiling and which cannot. The archives' value depends on exactly this kind of quality map.
plos-pone-0001361:
Obesity is a major health problem with substantial heritability, yet the genetic mechanisms predisposing to it were poorly understood in 2007. Anke Hinney and colleagues performed a genome wide association study for early onset extreme obesity, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used a genome-wide SNP array covering the genome's common variation.

The authors report that the study supports the role of variants in the fat mass and obesity associated gene, FTO. FTO was the first gene robustly tied to common obesity, and this study extended the evidence to children with extreme, early onset obesity. The finding helped establish FTO as a cornerstone of obesity genetics.
plos-pone-0001461:
Sigal Saar and Partha Mitra wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on how birdsong rhythms grow. Brain rhythms in young birds build up over time scales from split seconds to years. Reading that growth poses hard math problems. The team focused on song, where rhythm change can be heard and timed with care.

They offer a way to track how song rhythm takes shape as a bird matures. The method splits rhythm into layers and charts each layer's growth. Tools like this help labs link brain change to learned skill. They may also serve work on how human speech rhythms form in the young.
plos-pone-0001561:
Moisés Santillán and Michael Mackey wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE model of how body segments form in embryos. The classic clock and wavefront model had gained strong backing from fresh gene finds. Genes that pulse in the tail bud form the clock. A moving front sets where each segment locks in. The pair asked how clock and front talk to each other.

Their model sets out a way the two could mesh to lay segments at a steady pace. A clear mesh lets labs test which gene faults break the rhythm. Segment faults cause spine ills in people, so the stakes are real. The paper gives those tests a firm frame.
plos-pone-0001661:
Robert-Jan Palstra and co-authors tested whether far-apart pieces of DNA stay in contact when transcription stops, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. DNA folds inside the nucleus so that distant genes and their switches can touch. Many thought active transcription by RNA polymerase II was what held that folded layout in place.

Using 3C and 4C methods, which capture which DNA pieces sit near each other, the team blocked ongoing transcription and rechecked the contacts. The full text gives the contact maps before and after the block. Their results bear on a basic question. Is the genome's 3D layout a stable scaffold that gene activity uses, rather than a shape activity must keep rebuilding?
plos-pone-0001761:
Jianzhong Yu, John Poulton, Yi-Chun Huang, and their co-authors studied two signaling pathways in fruit fly eggs in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Setting the head-to-tail axis of a Drosophila oocyte requires talk between germ-line cells and the surrounding follicle cells. Notch signaling is one of the pathways involved in forming oocyte polarity.

The team reports that the Hippo pathway promotes Notch signaling, and together they regulate cell differentiation, proliferation, and oocyte polarity. The full text gives the fly genetics and the egg chamber images. Pathway partnerships like this are a general theme in development. Organs are built by committees of signals, not single switches, and fly eggs are where many such partnerships are first mapped.
plos-pone-0001861:
Matthew Siegel, Pavel Strnad, R. Edward Watts, and their co-authors measured the activity state of a wound-healing enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Transglutaminase 2, or TG2, is a mammal protein with many jobs, including transamidase and signaling roles. Using chosen TG2 inhibitors and tagged amine targets, the team probed the enzyme outside cells.

They show most TG2 outside cells is inactive under normal conditions in the body, but is briefly switched on upon tissue injury. The full text gives the activity readings in tissues. An enzyme that wakes only at wounds is a safe drug target in principle: blocking it should spare normal tissue while touching healing and fibrosis.
plos-pone-0001961:
Lydia Jimenez-Diaz and co-authors studied how pain fibers make their own proteins on site, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Nerve cells are long, and the far tips that sense pain sit far from the cell body where most proteins are made. Recent work had shown that local protein synthesis at the tips matters for how nerves adapt.

The team focused on the mTOR path, a known driver of local synthesis, in primary afferent fibers, the fibers that carry pain signals inward. They report that local translation in those fibers regulates nociception, the sensing of harm. That puts a local factory on the map of pain control.
plos-pone-0002061:
Roberta Schulte and co-authors shrank a classic protein test down to single beads, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pull-down tests check whether two proteins bind by fishing one out and seeing what comes with it. Their miniaturized method uses standard affinity reagents, the same beads and columns labs already own.

Proteins are color-coded with quantum dots, tiny glowing crystals, so binding events can be seen on single beads under a scope. The name is SINBAD, for single bead affinity detection. Seeing single binding events can reveal weak or rare pairings that bulk tests wash out.
plos-pone-0002161:
Maya Dinur-Mills, Merav Tal, and Ophry Pines studied proteins that work in two places at once inside cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In complex cells, the very same protein can end up in different compartments, a trait called dual targeting. The team split a reference set of mitochondrial proteins into those that are dual targeted and those found only in mitochondria.

They compared the targeting signals that guide each group to its place. Dual targeted proteins showed lower signal scores and a lower total charge on their guide pieces. The contrast helps explain how one protein can be sent to two addresses by a weaker, more flexible signal.
plos-pone-0002261:
Michiya Kawaguchi and co-authors mapped a region of a cell-surface protein that helps cells stick together, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is called Bves, short for blood vessel epicardial substance. It gives cells adhesive properties, but how it does so at the molecular level was unknown. Its sequence shows no known functional motifs outside its membrane span.

The team found a new interaction domain inside the cell that is essential for Bves to work. Partners binding that domain likely switch its adhesive role. Finding the working part of an obscure protein is the first step to learning what it does in the heart and beyond.
plos-pone-0002361:
Mathias Streitz and co-authors dissected the T cell response in one patient with virus-linked heart inflammation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Parvovirus B19 is the virus most often found in heart muscle biopsies from patients with inflammatory cardiomyopathy, a disease where the heart muscle weakens. T cells are central to antiviral defense, yet their role against this virus in the heart was little known.

The team characterized B19V-specific CD8 T cells aimed at the viral NS1 protein. These cells showed effector function and a dominant receptor pattern in the patient. A close look at one case guides the search for immune markers in a murky disease.
plos-pone-0002461:
Giri and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Pramod K. Giri, Jeffrey S. Schorey, among others. Its subject is exosomes Derived from M. Bovis BCG Infected Macrophages Activate Antigen-Specific CD4 +. The rest of the title points to CD8 + T Cells In Vitro and In Vivo. Activation of both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells is required for an effective immune response to an M.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002561:
Dechartres and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Agnes Dechartres, Isabelle Boutron, Remy Nizard, among others. Its subject is knee Arthroplasty: Disabilities in Comparison to the General Population and to Hip Arthroplasty Using a French National Longitudinal Survey. Knee arthroplasty is increasing exponentially due to the aging of the population and to the broadening of indications.

We aimed to compare physical disability and its evolution over two years in people with knee arthroplasty to that in the general population. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002661:
In 2008, Amanda Ross and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about modelling the epidemiological impact of intermittent preventive treatment against malaria in infants. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Amanda Ross, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Trials of intermittent preventive treatment against malaria in infants (IPTi) using sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) have shown a positive, albeit variable. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002761:
David Kaplan and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of sample size and precision in NIH peer review. The catalog record names David Kaplan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The Working Group on Peer Review of the Advisory Committee to the Director of NIH has recommended that at least 4 reviewers should be. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002861:
In 2008, Toby Leslie and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was a randomised trial of an Eight-Week, once weekly primaquine regimen to prevent relapse of plasmodium vivax in northwest frontier province, pakistan. Authorship is credited in the record to Toby Leslie and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Vivax malaria remains a major cause of morbidity in the subtropics. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002961:
Adriano Boasso, Andrew Hardy, Stephanie Anderson and co-authors linked interferon, tryptophan breakdown, and T cell failure in HIV in 2008. HIV infection shows chronic activation of T cells alongside poor function, and the causes were largely unexplained. Type I interferon is a first-line signal that fights viruses.

The team cultured blood cells from uninfected donors in lab setups that copy parts of HIV infection. Their title reports that interferon and tryptophan breakdown together drive T cell dysfunction despite activation. Published in PLOS ONE, this process helps explain a central paradox of HIV immune defense. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003061:
Daniela Pignatta, Brian Dilkes, Tadeusz Wroblewski and co-authors tested gene silencing across ploidy levels in 2008. Whole genome duplication, which creates polyploidy, is common in plant populations and recurs in flowering plant evolution. It can change gene expression and epigenetic stability.

Transgene-induced silencing was not affected by a change in ploidy level, the title reports. That steadiness is useful news for plant breeding, where doubling genomes is routine. Published in PLOS ONE, the result separates one epigenetic process from the genome-size upheaval around it. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003161:
Jorieke H. Peters, Frank W. Preijers, Rob Woestenenk and colleagues describe a clinical grade method for preparing regulatory T cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Therapy based on these cells interests many groups as a way to promote tolerance in autoimmunity and transplantation. For trials, teams need an isolation protocol that meets Good Manufacturing Practice rules and yields enough cells.

The authors cover GMP isolation, improving purity by removing CD127 positive cells, expanding the cells, and freezing them for storage. Readers get a full practical pipeline, not just a lab result. That kind of protocol is what lets a cell idea move toward real patient trials.
plos-pone-0003261:
Walter Jetz, Robert P. Freckleton and Andrew E. McKechnie examine metabolic rate in birds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Basal metabolic rate represents the minimum maintenance energy requirement of a warm-blooded animal and has far-reaching consequences for interactions between animals and their environments. Avian metabolic rate exhibits considerable variation independent of body mass, and some long-distance migrants differ notably.

The authors test the roles of environment, migratory tendency, and phylogeny, or family history, in that variation. Readers see three explanations weighed against each other. Separating history from habitat helps predict how bird energy needs may shift with climate.
plos-pone-0003361:
Laura H. Tsang, James E. Cassat, Lindsey N. Shaw and colleagues study biofilm failure in staph mutants in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mutation of sarA in Staphylococcus aureus results in reduced capacity to form a biofilm, but the mechanistic basis for this remains unknown. Previous transcriptional profiling experiments identified a number of genes differentially expressed both in a biofilm and in mutant strains.

The authors assess factors contributing to the biofilm-deficient phenotype of sarA mutants. Readers learn how one regulator controls the communal surface growth that makes staph infections hard to clear. Biofilms protect bacteria on implants and wounds, so their control genes are clinical targets.
plos-pone-0003461:
Lorenza S. Colzato, Wery P. M. van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel measured blink rates in cocaine users in 2008. Long cocaine use lowers a class of dopamine receptors in the brain. Dopamine is a chemical tied to reward and self-control. Even casual use had been linked to weaker cognitive control.

Spontaneous blink rate is a rough gauge of dopamine activity. Recreational users blinked less often than non-users in this study. That pattern fits sluggish dopamine function, called hypoactivity. A simple eye measure may thus flag drug effects on brain control systems.
plos-pone-0003561:
Wiriya Rutvisuttinunt, Peter R. Meyer, and Walter A. Scott probed HIV's copying enzyme in this 2008 paper. Reverse transcriptase turns the virus's RNA into DNA. It binds tightly at fixed spots on a primer-template pair. Those stable complexes are the enzyme's working state.

The team examined contacts between the enzyme and the downstream template strand. Such contacts guide the enzyme as it copies. Fine detail on this grip exposes weak points in the machine. HIV drugs aim to jam this very enzyme. Each new grip detail gives drug design one more place to aim.
plos-pone-0003661:
Yongliang Yang, Lakshmanan K. Iyer, S. James Adelstein, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Doctors favor blood tests for finding cancer early, since blood is easy to draw and test. The team mined combined genomic data for signs of cancer that reach the blood.

Their search aimed at markers that could flag cancer before symptoms appear, when treatment works best. By pooling data across studies, they could spot signals too weak to see in one set alone. The work offers leads for blood tests aimed at early diagnosis rather than late confirmation.
plos-pone-0003761:
Charlotte Labalette, Yann Nouët, Florence Levillayer, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. FHL2 is a small protein tied to several pathways that control cell growth and tissue balance. The group had shown it regulates cyclin D1, a driver of cell division.

Here they show FHL2 mediates transformation driven by Ras, a classic cancer gene. It acts through the cyclin D1 and p53 pathways together. The finding flips a normal growth regulator into a cancer accomplice, and names routes by which it helps cells turn malignant.
plos-pone-0003861:
Arie Baratt, Sergey N. Arkhipov, and Ivan V. Maly published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Killer T cells destroy infected and cancerous cells with precision. To strike, a T cell positions its centrosome near the contact point with its target, the immunological synapse. How microtubules help set that polarity was controversial.

Combining experiments with computation, the team studied the effects of microtubule stabilization on T-cell polarity. Their results clarify the cytoskeletal choreography behind the immune system's precision strikes, and which parts of it depend on stable microtubules. Aim matters, since a missed aim wastes the cell's one strong strike.
plos-pone-0003961:
Pavel Krejci, Lisa Salazar, Tamara A. Kashiwada, and co-authors tested a growth receptor's signal in cartilage in 2008. Mutations that overactivate FGFR3 cause several human skeletal dysplasias. Those disorders stunt bone growth in the limbs. Many believed the transcription factor STAT1 carried the harmful signal.

Their PLOS ONE article tested six FGFR3 mutants for STAT1 activation. The results undermine the idea that STAT1 dominates the signal in cartilage. If STAT1 is not the main route, other paths must explain stunted growth. The work redirects the search for treatments for these dysplasias. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004061:
Qingzhong Xiao, Shu Ye, Friedrich Oberhollenzer, and co-authors drew on the Bruneck population study in 2008. SDF1 is a signal that guides progenitor cells to where they are needed. Its receptor, CXCR4, helps cells home, mobilize, and mature. Such repair cells in blood are called endothelial progenitor cells.

Their PLOS ONE article links a variant in the SDF1 gene to blood levels. The variant also tracked with counts of endothelial progenitor cells. Inherited differences may set how much repair capacity a person carries. That could matter for recovery after artery injury. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004161:
Hannes Drexler published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells under stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, their protein-folding compartment, pause most protein production while switching on protective genes. Part of this response works by disabling a key translation factor by tagging it with phosphate.

Drexler tested the phosphatase inhibitor salubrinal together with proteasome inhibitors, drugs that block the cell's protein shredder, on leukaemic cells. He reports that the two drug types work together, inducing far more cell death than either alone. The pairing suggests a strategy for pushing stressed cancer cells past the point of recovery.
plos-pone-0004261:
Lisa Ng and colleagues published this outbreak study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Little was known about how chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne virus, damages the body. During the first Singaporean chikungunya fever outbreak in early 2008, the team analysed immune mediators and growth factors circulating in patients' blood. The outbreak gave them a rare, well-defined group of patients to study.

Their goal was to establish biomarkers, measurable signs, associated with infection severity. They report that IL-1β, IL-6, and RANTES stand out as biomarkers of chikungunya severity. Such markers could help doctors spot, early on, which fever patients will become seriously ill.
plos-pone-0004361:
Jing Xiang and colleagues published this drug discovery study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cyclin-dependent kinases, or CDKs, control the cell cycle. Cancers often show too much of them, or switch them on wrongly. As a result, these kinases have become extensively studied targets for anti-cancer drugs. That is why drug hunters prize them.

The team combined combinatorial chemistry, which generates many candidate compounds, with zebrafish assays to identify tumour cell growth inhibitors. Testing candidates in living fish embryos filters for compounds that work in a whole animal, not just a dish. The pipeline hunts for kinase blockers with real potential.
plos-pone-0004461:
A remedy drawn from a plant may help repair hearts hurt by heart attack, report Lei Cheng, Hao Chen, Xinsheng Yao, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart attack, caused by blocked arteries, remains one of the top causes of early death. Dead heart muscle is normally replaced by scar, not by new working muscle.

True repair would mean regrowing heart tissue, either from the body's own progenitor cells or from stem cells brought in from outside. The team tested a plant-derived remedy toward that ideal. Their work asks whether a natural compound can push the heart toward real regeneration rather than scar. Even small steps matter here, because any gain in working muscle after an attack can add years of life.
plos-pone-0004561:
A signaling protein in the gut lining is essential to protect the bowel during chemical injury, show Jae-Young Kim, Rie Kajino-Sakamoto, Emily Omori, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is TAK1. Earlier, the team had shown that mice lacking TAK1 only in the intestinal epithelium suffer severe inflammation and die as newborns, because a death signal called TNF kills their gut cells.

Removing the TNF receptor largely rescued those newborns. This study follows the story into chemically induced colitis, inflammation of the colon, in older animals. TAK1 signaling from the epithelium proved essential for cytoprotection, the defense of cells against injury. The work maps a pathway that gut-healing drugs for colitis might aim to support.
plos-pone-0004661:
A computer model of virus sensing predicts new features of a key immune pathway, present Mohamed Helmy, Jin Gohda, Jun-ichiro Inoue, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The sensor is Toll-like receptor 3, which plays a critical role in the innate immune response against viral attacks. It recognizes double-stranded RNA, a hallmark of many viruses, or a synthetic mimic of it.

Recognition leads to activation of MAP kinases and NF-kappaB, switches that launch antiviral defenses in macrophages. The team modeled TLR3 signaling in these immune cells to predict novel features of the pathway. Predictions from a model can be tested in the lab, turning guesswork into a checklist. That speeds the search for points where immunity to viruses fails.
plos-pone-0004761:
Diana Rigola and colleagues presented a high output method to find induced and natural DNA changes, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reverse genetics starts from a gene change and asks what trait it causes. That needs fast screens that can spot single letter changes in pooled DNA from many plants or animals.

Older screens for such changes were slow and labor heavy. The KeyPoint method pools samples and uses deep sequencing to find rare changes. Faster finds speed up gene function studies and crop breeding. Breeders can locate useful variants in large populations with less work. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004861:
Lina Cheng and colleagues showed PP1 gamma2 and PPP1R11 form a multimeric complex in developing testicular germ cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mice lacking protein phosphatase 1 gamma isoforms are male sterile due to defective germ cell morphogenesis and apoptosis. Deficiency causes no obvious abnormality in other tissues, and a biochemical approach examined how output varies and partners interact during sperm cell growth.

Steady state levels of partners are reciprocally related. Complex balance controls germ cell maturation. Disruption explains tissue specific sterility. Male fertility depends on precise phosphatase control. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004961:
Tumors can wake sleeping cancer genes. One route is stripping methyl tags off a gene's promoter. Ian Smith and colleagues hunted for such cases in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used an integrative method on primary head and neck cancers. They also examined lung cancers. The targets were candidate proto-oncogenes and cancer testes antigens.

The team found the two groups switching on together. Promoter demethylation coordinated their activation across both tumor types. Such coordinated waking reveals a shared program in these cancers. The reawakened genes matter beyond basic biology. They are candidate targets for drugs and for immune-based therapies.
plos-pone-0005061:
K-Ras mutations drive many lung cancers. They occur almost exclusively in smokers. Courtney Granville and colleagues studied the immune setting of these tumors. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on regulatory T cells marked by Foxp3. These cells calm immune attacks.

The regulatory cells played a central role in K-Ras-driven tumor growth. The tumors benefit from their own immune suppressors. Peacekeeper cells, meant to prevent autoimmunity, shield the cancer instead. Blocking those suppressors could help fight these lung cancers. The finding matters for immunotherapy design. It suggests which brake to release for this common tumor type. Smokers' lung cancers may need exactly that release.
plos-pone-0005161:
Sleep fills about a third of human life. The genes that regulate it are barely known. Christopher Winrow and colleagues mapped them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied multiple sleep-wake traits in mice. Genome-wide association studies in humans had given few answers. Model organisms offer another route to the genes.

The study uncovered parts of the genetic landscape for sleep. Different traits mapped to different gene regions. Sleep is not one trait but many. Each may have its own genetic levers. The map opens the hunt for sleep genes. It also frames new questions about how the traits relate. Insomnia and other disorders may trace to these regions.
plos-pone-0005261:
Crops grown for biofuel promise cleaner energy, but a fuel crop that escapes could become an invasive weed. Buddenhagen and colleagues noted in PLOS ONE in 2009 that no one had yet quantified that invasion risk. Their case study set out to measure it.

The authors assessed how invasive proposed biofuel crops are likely to be. Weighing energy gains against weed risk gives growers and regulators a reality check before planting at scale. Once an invasive plant is loose, removal is costly or impossible, so early assessment matters. A crop checked in this way can be grown with more trust, and a crop that fails the check can be kept off the land while there is still time.
plos-pone-0005361:
Betulin comes from birch bark and is the precursor of betulinic acid, a compound studied for anti-tumor effects. Far less was known about betulin itself. Mullauer and colleagues tested it on tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2009 and found it potent.

Betulin induced apoptosis, the self-destruct program, by a mechanism similar to its acid cousin. Cholesterol enhanced the anti-tumor effect, as the title states. A cheap, abundant bark compound with a boostable effect is an interesting lead for drug development. Birch bark is waste from wood mills in the north, so a drug lead drawn from it would start from a cheap and rich source. Not from a rare plant that must be farmed.
plos-pone-0005461:
Gerardo Suzán and colleagues linked rodent variety to virus spread in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Many new diseases jump from animals to people, and changes made by humans can raise that risk. The team asked whether losing kinds of rodents changes how common hantavirus is among those that remain.

In field tests where rodent variety was lowered, the share of rodents carrying the virus went up. Fewer kinds meant the remaining hosts met the virus more often. The result warns that harming wild variety can raise disease risk for people living nearby.
plos-pone-0005561:
Sujit Suchindran, Emily Brouwer, and Annelies Van Rie reviewed studies on HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Tuberculosis is a major cause of suffering and death worldwide. Forms that resist standard drugs have become a threat to disease control, alongside HIV.

The authors gathered the published evidence on whether HIV infection raises the risk of drug-resistant tuberculosis. A careful review weighs weak and strong studies together before drawing a verdict. The answer guides testing and treatment policy where both diseases are common. The review method also shows where the record is too thin to settle the question, marking what to study next.
plos-pone-0005661:
A Whitman Miller and co-authors studied oyster larvae in more acidic water in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Human activity has raised the carbon dioxide in the air, and the oceans absorb much of it. That makes seawater more acidic and changes the chemistry shellfish need to build shells.

The team raised oyster larvae in estuary water at different acidity levels. Larvae in more acidic water built shells more slowly and grew less. The results warn that oyster beds, and the fisheries on them, face a hard future as the oceans change.
plos-pone-0005761:
Mark Romanish and co-authors found in 2009 that a human gene carries its own built-in promoters made from ancient viral-like scraps. The gene, NAIP, helps guard nerve cells from death and also serves innate immunity. Scraps called Alu elements litter the human genome by the million.

Some of those scraps inside NAIP act as start switches for a new, shorter form of the protein. That variant may do a different job than the full-length form. The find shows how junk DNA can be recycled into working controls. It adds a case study in how genomes invent new protein forms cheaply.
plos-pone-0005861:
Hon Cheng Muh, Joo Chuan Tong, and Martti Tammi built a program in 2009 to judge whether a protein might trigger allergy. Allergy is a growing problem in industrialized countries. With more engineered food crops arriving, their proteins need safety checks before entering the food chain.

Their system, AllerHunter, pairs machine learning with pairwise sequence comparison to flag allergen risk and cross-reactivity. Older bioinformatics tools did well, but a sharper screen catches more hazards. Regulators and breeders can run new proteins through it early. The goal is food innovation without surprise allergies.
plos-pone-0005961:
Inside a plant cell, mitochondria move along tracks made of actin, hauled by myosin motors. Maozhong Zheng, Martina Beck, Jens Müller and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the tracks themselves must keep changing for the cargo to move. Their PLOS ONE study uses root hairs of Arabidopsis, a small plant favored in labs.

Actin tracks are rebuilt without pause as their building blocks swap in and out. The title states the finding: that turnover is required for the myosin-driven motion of mitochondria. A still track, it seems, will not do. The result adds a rule to the plant cell's transport system, where track upkeep and cargo motion are tied together.
plos-pone-0006061:
Some genes are so vital that a bacterium cannot grow without them, yet how much of each one is enough? Shan Goh, Jaroslaw Boberek, Nobutaka Nakashima and colleagues measured that strictness in E. coli in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs growth rates with transcript counts as essential genes are dialed down, revealing how much slack each gene allows.

The pairing exposes gene stringency, a property that lists of essential genes alone cannot show. A gene that tolerates little slack is a tempting antibiotic target, since a drug need only dent it. The work turns a static gene list into a ranked map of bacterial weak points.
plos-pone-0006161:
A tiny RNA can tune the making of the heart by holding down a single helper protein. Gene Kim, Sadhana Samant, Judy Earley and colleagues traced that tuning in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies microRNA-130a and FOG-2, a transcriptional co-factor the team had shown to be critical for cardiac development, in cardiomyocytes, the heart's muscle cells.

MicroRNA-130a controls FOG-2 production at the translation step, the title reports, so the gene is read but its protein is rationed. Few microRNAs had been tied to heart development when this work ran. Each one named gives medicine a finer dial for a process where small timing errors become birth defects of the heart.
plos-pone-0006261:
Blood fats differ in people with high blood pressure, beyond the usual cholesterol story. Juergen Graessler and colleagues profiled the plasma lipidome of hypertensive patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE study, using a top-down approach. Obesity and insulin resistance often travel with hypertension, so the team sought effects specific to blood pressure itself.

The survey found a deficiency of ether lipids in the patients' blood plasma. Ether lipids are a less-studied fat family with roles in membranes and signalling. A specific shortfall could become a marker for hypertension risk. It may also hint at mechanisms that standard fat tests overlook.
plos-pone-0006361:
Breast cancer spreads to preferred organs, and the stiffness of tissue may help decide where. Ana Kostic, Christopher Lynch, and Michael Sheetz compared breast cancer cell lines in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Metastasis to lung, brain, bone, and liver is a leading cause of death in breast cancer patients.

Cell lines responded differently to matrix rigidity, and those responses correlated with tissue tropism, the organs each line favours. Sensing stiffness could steer circulating cells toward matching tissues. The mechanical view of metastasis complements the chemical one. It suggests blocking stiffness sensing as a future strategy.
plos-pone-0006461:
Michelle Millington and co-authors refined gene delivery into blood stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood-forming stem cells, especially those drawn from peripheral blood, are attractive targets for cell and gene therapy. Getting new genes into them with lentiviruses can work well. The catch is doing so without harming their ability to renew themselves and make all blood cell types.

The team worked toward a transduction protocol fit for clinical use. Their focus was primary human CD34 positive stem and progenitor cells. A clinic-ready protocol must be both efficient and gentle. Progress here brings gene therapy for blood diseases closer to routine care.
plos-pone-0006561:
Bruno Sainz, Naina Barretto, and Susan Uprichard compared liver cell lines for hepatitis C work in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 2005, the first robust hepatitis C virus infectious cell culture system was developed. It was based on a genotype 2a clone called JFH-1 and Huh7 human hepatoma cells. Different Huh7 cell lines vary in phenotype, though.

The team studied HCV infection in phenotypically distinct Huh7 cell lines. Line choice can change experimental outcomes, so documenting differences matters. Their comparison helps labs pick the right line and interpret past results. Good cell models underpin all drug testing for this virus.
plos-pone-0006661:
J. David Stiffler, Minhhuyen Nguyen, Ji Sohn, and colleagues mapped hepatitis C virus in infected livers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis C virus is a plus-strand RNA virus that replicates by amplification of genomic RNA from minus strands. That leads to accumulation of many copies per cell. The team examined the focal distribution of hepatitis C virus RNA in infected livers.

Focal means the virus concentrates in patches rather than spreading evenly. Patchiness affects biopsy accuracy and treatment expectations. A small sample may miss infected zones. Mapping the distribution explains why liver samples can disagree with blood tests.
plos-pone-0006761:
Ville-Petri Friman and his team tested how hunters shape the strength of germs in PLOS ONE in 2009. A germ's strength is called its virulence. Textbooks treat virulence as a duel between germ and host. Real hosts live in webs of many species. Other species can tilt that duel in round-about ways. Hunters that eat sick hosts are one such force.

The team let predation act at more than one level of the food web. Germ strength evolved in a new way when hunters were present. A germ may grow milder or stronger when its host faces hungry hunters. The work says the full web, not just the pair, sets how germs evolve. Germ science should study hosts in their real webs, not in pairs alone.
plos-pone-0006861:
Arian D. Wallach and colleagues examined lethal control of dingoes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The dingo is Australia's top-order predator. It is also a socially complex animal. Controlling socially complex species can have deep ecological effects. Those effects stay invisible if only head counts are considered.

Killing dingoes disrupts their social stability, the authors argue. Broken social structure can change hunting, breeding, and movement. Surviving animals may behave in ways that worsen livestock conflicts. The work urges managers to count social costs, not just animals removed. It reframes predator control as an ecological intervention with hidden side effects.
plos-pone-0006961:
Vlada Melekhin, Bryan Shepherd, Samuel Stinnette, and colleagues studied HIV treatment timing in pregnancy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pregnancy had been linked with slower HIV disease progress in the modern therapy era. What remained untested was how treatment timing around pregnancy affects the mother. The team compared women starting antiretroviral therapy before, during, or after pregnancy.

They tracked viral, immune, and clinical responses in each group. The question matters for the many women who first reach care while pregnant. Their results help clinicians decide when starting therapy gives mothers the strongest benefit.
plos-pone-0007061:
Chang-Yi Wu, Janet Steffen, and David Eide studied zinc hunger in yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. Zinc deficiency stresses many organisms with harmful oxidation. In baker's yeast, a defender protein called Tsa1 was known to help in low zinc. It destroys hydrogen peroxide, a damaging oxidant. The team asked what another defender, the enzyme SOD1, contributes.

They found cytosolic SOD1 is critical for tolerating low zinc stress. Without it, yeast coped far worse with the oxidation. Two defenders divide the work of clearing different oxidants. The result refines the picture of how cells survive mineral shortage.
plos-pone-0007161: Elena Grigor'eva, Alexander Shevchenko, Nina Mazurok, and colleagues derived trophoblast stem cells from the common vole in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method worked without FGF4, the growth factor normally required to grow such cells. Trophoblast stem cells build the placenta's exchange tissue. A line that grows without the standard factor gives researchers a new way to study early placental development in this rodent.
plos-pone-0007261:
Sha Liu, Zhi Li, and Jian-Fang Gui studied a duplicated fish gene and body left-right patterning in 2009. Gene duplication can supply raw material for new functions. Fish carry a duplicated gene called dmrt2b, copied from dmrt2a, but its function had remained unclear for years after its discovery.

The authors reduce Dmrt2b activity in zebrafish embryos. They link the gene to the Hedgehog signaling pathway. They report that dmrt2b contributes a divergent function while still helping establish left-right asymmetry. Their work shows how a copied gene can split old duties and gain new ones.
plos-pone-0007361:
Anirban Banerji and Indira Ghosh revisited ideas about protein interiors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A robust marker for mass, water-avoidance, and polarizability patterns could help decode protein structure. Each of those distributions is uneven inside a protein, so any useful marker must be sensitive to complex patterns rather than simple averages.

The authors study proteins using fractal dimensions for mass, hydrophobicity, and polarizability. Fractals capture self-similar patterns across scales. Their analysis challenges myths about protein interiors. Better interior measures can improve predictions of how proteins fold and remain stable.
plos-pone-0007461:
Atsushi Oyagi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 creating a new research tool for brain science. Growth factors and immune signals have been linked to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression. One growth factor, HB-EGF, also nourishes developing brain cells. Studying it has been hard because removing it everywhere at once distorts development. The team built a more precise option.

They engineered mice in which the HB-EGF gene can be switched off only in chosen tissues or at chosen times. Such conditional knockout mice let researchers isolate where the factor truly matters. The tool can now be used to test HB-EGF's role in brain development and mental illness. The paper reports both the construction of the mice and their first characterization.
plos-pone-0007561:
Zi-An Fang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a yeast called Kluyveromyces lactis responds to oxygen. Baker's yeast has an unusual, fermentation-loving lifestyle. That lifestyle may stem from an ancient doubling of its whole genome. K. lactis never had that doubling, which makes it a useful comparison. The team measured its gene responses as oxygen availability changed.

Genes tied to oxygen response showed notable patterns in the unduplicated yeast. Comparing them with baker's yeast reveals what the genome doubling changed. The oxygen-responding system was rewired along the way. Such comparisons are how evolution's experiments get read. One yeast kept the older wiring; the other rebuilt it after doubling. The study uses that contrast to trace how a metabolic lifestyle was born.
plos-pone-0007661:
Xiaomin Zheng and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the famous chromosome swap behind Philadelphia-chromosome leukemias. The swap between chromosomes 9 and 22 creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, a known leukemia driver. Being a balanced swap, it also creates the reciprocal fusion, ABL-BCR, on the other chromosome. That second product was largely ignored. The team tested its power to cause leukemia and its effects on B cell development.

The reciprocal fusion protein has leukemogenic potential of its own. It also altered how B cells commit to their lineage. So both products of one swap can push blood cells toward cancer. That doubles the list of suspects in these leukemias. It may matter for therapy, since drugs target the famous fusion alone. The study restores the swap's forgotten half to the story.
plos-pone-0007761:
Christopher Rex and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It hunts the source of a brain wave pattern called the sharp wave. Sharp waves start in one part of the hippocampus, CA3, and spread through the region. They appear when animals rest awake or during sleep.

The hippocampus is central to memory, and sharp waves may help store it. The team used slices of rat hippocampus to find what starts these waves.
