Backes and her colleagues classified acts such as sitting, strolling, and climbing stairs from the insole's signals. Good accuracy from the feet alone matters because insoles need no wristband or phone and work all day unnoticed. Doctors tracking recovery, and researchers studying real-world activity, need measures people will actually wear. A shoe-based sensor people forget they are wearing fits that need well.
plos-pone-0358261:
Thanh Huyen Nguyen and three colleagues measured jaw bone in patients with severe underbite, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In skeletal Class III malocclusion, the thin bone holding the lower front teeth limits how far orthodontics can safely move them. The team used three-dimensional CBCT scans to study that bone housing and the tilt of the teeth within it.

Nguyen's measurements show orthodontists how much room they truly have. Moving a tooth beyond its bone housing risks gum and root damage that cannot be undone. Precise 3D data from untreated patients give a baseline for planning treatment and surgery. The study serves a common clinical decision with uncommon care.
plos-pone-0358361:
Yuanzhi Yu, Margaret Banker, Jennifer Sherr, and Denise Scholtens published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It develops empirical modeling for continuous glucose monitoring data, the stream of sugar readings worn sensors produce for people with diabetes. The focus is transition probabilities, the chances of moving from one glucose state to another.

Modeling how readings evolve from moment to moment underpins alarms and automated insulin systems. Empirical probabilities drawn from real sensor traces reflect patients' actual lives better than tidy theory. Diabetes technology researchers building prediction tools are the readers who build on transition models like this one.
plos-pone-0358561:
Shan Xu leads a team of eight testing a protein destroying drug against bladder cancer in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug, a peptide based chimera the group developed earlier, does not merely block its target, a growth promoting kinase called PAK4; it tags the protein for disposal by the cell. First the team confirmed the kinase runs high in bladder tumor tissue, then compared cancer cells genetically stripped of it with cells treated by the drug, in dishes and in animals.

Both routes told the same story. Without the kinase, a key growth pathway went quiet, cells stalled before copying their DNA, and a self destruct program switched on. Tumors grew significantly more slowly in mice under both the knockout and the drug. Because a degrader removes the whole protein rather than one activity, the authors argue it may outflank resistance that defeats ordinary kinase blockers.
plos-pone-0358761:
Ryoga Hayashi, Hayato Kawaji, and Satoru Kojima check whether ultrasound can reliably measure a knee gap that matters for injury assessment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a sideways force stresses the knee, the inner joint space widens slightly. Therapists would like to measure that widening without an X-ray. Seventeen healthy men offered thirty-four knees. Two physical therapists of different experience measured each knee resting and under a standard stress load, on separate days.

Stress widened the space by roughly a millimeter and a third, a consistent and significant shift. Agreement within each therapist across days, and between the two therapists, both rated good. The smallest change the method can certify sat well under a millimeter, and error analysis found only random noise, no systematic drift. The authors conclude ultrasound is trustworthy enough for tracking this measurement in clinics and injury studies.
plos-pone-0359161:
Xuedong Bai and six colleagues test a liver targeted drug against artery disease in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Atherosclerosis grows from a mix of blood fats and vessel wall inflammation, and few drugs press both levers at once. Resmetirom switches on a thyroid hormone receptor mainly in the liver and is known for improving fat metabolism. Whether it also calms inflamed vessels was the open question.

Mice bred to develop the disease ate a high fat diet, then received the drug at two doses or a dummy treatment for eight weeks. Treated mice carried less plaque in the aorta, showed healthier blood fat patterns, and had quieter activity in a key inflammation switch inside vessel tissue, with stronger effects at the higher dose. The results support wider testing of the drug's vessel benefits beyond the liver.
plos-pone-0359961:
Rongrong Wang and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about Fanjing Mountain in China, a protected peak known for rich wildlife. The authors track vegetation cover change there and divide the mountain into zones based on classification. Their tool is Google Earth Engine, a platform for analyzing satellite images at scale.

Satellite records let the team watch forest and scrub expand or shrink across years without walking every slope. Zonation then turns that picture into management areas with different rules. Park managers use exactly this pairing of change maps and zones to target patrols, restoration planting, and visitor limits.
pmc-10657161:
Haein Lee, Bo Gyeong Lee, and In Seo La sorted lifestyle patterns in Korean women in 2023. Healthy habits after menopause help prevent chronic disease. Patterns of habits may differ by income level. The team used a national health and nutrition survey. They scored nine habits, from smoking and drinking to walking and sleep. A grouping method sorted women into hidden pattern classes. Income split the sample into lower and higher halves. Models were run separately for each income side.

Three pattern classes best fit each income group. A relatively healthy class was largest on both sides. Other classes mixed low activity with poor fruit intake. Risky drinking appeared in classes on both sides too. Low-income patterns stacked more unhealthy traits together. High-income patterns looked somewhat cleaner overall. The authors urge habit programs tailored to income group. One standard message will misfit many women, they argue.
pmc-10662161:
Jang and three co-authors scan the brain's salt hub in hurt folks with low blood salt in this twenty twenty-three study. Hard head blows can leave folks in dim states for long spans. Low salt can spring from harm to that hub in such cases.

Inside, hurt folks split by salt grade took wave-track scans of the hub. Low-salt folks showed loose hub webs and high spread marks there. They also stayed in care long and left with low wake grades. Wake gains shrank as salt lack grew in the same group. The team reads hub harm as the link tween blow and salt.
pmc-10689761:
Kelsea Best and a team of co-authors study who risks being cut off by sea level rise in the United States, in two thousand twenty-three. Rising seas will flood coastal land, but a quieter harm is isolation. Roads under water can block access to key services even where homes stay dry.

The team joined population data with a measure of isolation under sea rise from one to ten feet. Black and Hispanic communities faced a higher risk of isolation once rise reached about four feet. Areas with more renters and older adults also faced higher risk across scenarios. The authors argue that adaptation plans should weigh this hidden burden and its uneven spread.
pmc-10691261:
Rasim Barutcu, Michael Black, and Andy Nong re-mine public gene data to find dose-sensitive toxicity pathways. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, reworks data on forty-four test chemicals. Human breast cells in the original study were dosed and their gene activity read. The new pipeline takes an unbiased, whole-system route instead.

Steps run from gene changes to pathway enrichment to dose modeling. Network maps highlight pathways hit across many chemicals. Dose points from pathways match those from whole-animal endpoints. The authors argue this strengthens next-generation risk assessment. Chemical safety could lean less on animal tests. Public data reuse is the engine of the gain.
pmc-10696061:
Wang and a team of colleagues uncovered in twenty twenty-three how a protein called CPA4 calms a fiery form of cell death in liver cancer cells. The death mode, pyroptosis, is inflammatory. A lab-made antibody, HGS-ETR1/2, binds death receptors on cancer cells and was known to trigger quiet cell death.

Using microscopy, fluorescent staining, and protein blots, the team showed the antibody also triggers pyroptosis through a pore-forming protein, GSDME. Blocking the AKT signaling pathway or silencing CPA4 boosted this death, while extra CPA4 suppressed it. CPA4 and AKT reinforce each other in a feedback loop: CPA4 tunes a phosphatase that controls AKT, and AKT in turn sustains CPA4 production. The authors say the mechanism could guide future cancer immunotherapy design.
pmc-10696761:
Youngha Song, Liana Luzzi, and David Brennan model how mind, social life, and dentist relationships shape oral quality of life. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses South Australian survey data. Thousands of adults were sampled randomly for questionnaires. The hypothesised model runs from distant factors to near ones.

Nearly four thousand usable responses entered the final analysis. Wellbeing, social support, and health confidence formed one domain. Trust, satisfaction, and dental fear formed the relationship domain. A standard oral impact profile measured the outcome. Structural equation modelling tested the whole chain at once. Two-step estimation checked measurement quality before structure. Dental care is partly a relationship business, the model suggests.
pmc-10701861:
Pragya Kesarwani, Dhvani Vora, and Durai Sundar build a model to predict stray cuts by a gene-editing tool. Their twenty twenty-three article deals with CRISPR-Cpf1, which edits DNA at a guide-chosen site. The same system can cut at near-match sites, called off-targets, and that risk blocks clinical use.

Their pipeline first finds candidate off-target sites across the human genome. A multilayer perceptron then predicts how strongly each site would be cut, trained on sequence traits and binding energy features for two Cpf1 variants. The team also maps which bases help or hurt at each position. Thymine near the anchor motif was shunned, while guanine was favored at strong sites.
pmc-10710961: Golshani and five co-authors reported in twenty twenty-three a COVID-19 patient with a tangled heart course. The illness combined pericarditis, inflammation of the heart's outer sac, with a heart attack, and a clot then formed inside the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber. The authors stress that clotting problems can arise even when COVID-19 symptoms are nonspecific, so patients with odd cardiac signs should still be screened for the virus.
pmc-10714461:
Chaoyue Ruan and co-authors checked in 2023 why some patients develop persistent neck and shoulder pain, called axial symptoms, after an operation for a squeezed cervical spinal cord. The surgery, posterior open-door laminoplasty, widens the spinal canal from behind while keeping motion. And it reliably relieves cord squeezing, yet a share of patients are left with this complication. Knowing who is at risk would help surgeons counsel and follow patients.

The single-center retrospective study gathered over two hundred sixty patients treated over four years. All received the same operation across the five cervical levels. The study split them into those who developed axial symptoms and those who did not. The authors weighed the groups across personal factors such as age, sex, disease duration, and early rehabilitation. They weighed surgical factors. These included operating time, blood loss, and damage to facet joints or muscle attachments.
pmc-10719361:
Alejandro Jiménez-Meléndez and five colleagues read gene activity in gut cells infected by a cattle virus, a parasite, or both, in a twenty twenty-three study. The virus and the parasite both cause calf diarrhea and often strike together, with worse illness. Human gut cells were infected in the lab and sampled at one and three days. Gene reads compared each pattern.

At three days, virus and mixed infections changed more than six thousand genes. The parasite alone changed only fifty-two. Changed genes clustered in immune and cell-death paths. Over eight hundred genes moved only in the mixed infection, hinting at unique co-infection markers. The authors say the virus drives most of the response.
pmc-10730361: Max Levenson and co-authors lay out a protocol for reading single nuclei in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans in two thousand twenty-three. Many worm tissues fuse cells together, so cell-by-cell reading blurs the picture, while nuclei can be read one by one. The protocol walks through freeing intact nuclei from adult worms and readying them for single-nucleus RNA sequencing. A worked use case maps how the worm's tissues answer alcohol exposure. The authors point to a companion study for full execution detail.
pmc-10733861:
Joanna Nicholas and Sara Grafenauer surveyed pre-pro dance students in 2023. Dance demands extreme body effort daily. Looks-based pressure adds mental strain too. Health status was set down first at one school. Prevention knowledge was gauged with it. Long careers were the deeper concern.

Energy shortage risks stood out strongly. Awareness of it was low among practitioners. Dancers need aimed health teaching early. Programs should build prevention into training. Culture in dance needs deep change. Keeping dancers well takes effort from the whole field. Teachers and doctors share that duty. Starting data now guide those plans. Student voices shaped the advice.
pmc-10735661:
Ladan Ghazi-Saidi and Miechelle McKelvey wrote this conference paper, published in 2023. It describes a hands-on program that pairs speech-language pathology graduate students with older adults in the community, to build job readiness through real contact across generations.

Speech therapy students often find their core courses heavy and get few chances to practice on real clients. In this program, students give thinking-skills sessions to older adults by video call, as part of two core courses. Surveys before and after measured how competent students felt. Alumni and their internship supervisors were also asked how well prepared the graduates were. Students reported easier use of class material, stronger ownership of their learning, and fresh motivation. The authors present the bonding across ages as both enjoyable and a direct path to career skills.
pmc-10736061:
Brian Beach and Hugo Westerlund introduce, in twenty twenty-three, a symposium on who works longer in later life, and how working life expectancy varies across countries. As populations age, policy makers push longer working lives for tax and pension reasons. Workers gain income and social benefits too. But many factors drive early exit, and blanket rules ignore real differences. Life expectancy alone misses subgroup gaps and the stop-start paths many take near retirement. Scholars now use working life expectancy, the years a person can expect to spend in work.

The symposium draws on the IDEAR network and longitudinal aging studies in Europe. Results from Sweden and England use multi-state models, which, unlike older methods, allow moves back and forth between work and non-work.
pmc-10738261:
Barbara Delacourt and co-authors test an app that helps people with dementia and their caregivers keep talking in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Speech breaks down as the disease grows, and late-stage breakdowns leave both sides cut off. Few tools target this problem.

The app, COMPAS, shows short clips made for each person, with sights and sounds that spark warm exchanges. Seventeen pairs in two care centers used it in daily routines for eight weeks. Caregivers felt more achieved at work. Interviews told of better talks within pairs and a kinder style of care. The authors call the app a handy, natural way to reopen talks.
pmc-10738861:
Jennifer Beatty and Patrick Hill shared a 2023 study of how people take a hard message: that they showed bias against a group. Owning bias is the first step to shedding it. People may defend themselves when the message lands. Older adults may defend more, if entrenched views are hard to shift. The team built a new measure to read that defensiveness.

Over three hundred white adults in the United States took the measure. Ages ran from young adulthood to over eighty. People were more defensive about bias feedback than about feedback on the rest of the self. The defensiveness was weaker in people with a firm sense of identity. Age on its own told no story. With one subgroup in view, a modest age effect appeared. The conclusion: not all older adults defend. Sense of identity is the lever.
pmc-10739261:
Robert Tennyson and four co-authors checked how stable blood markers of inflammation are in older adults, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Such markers are often used to sum up a person's inflammatory state. Yet it was unclear how much they shift over a short span in later life.

Blood was drawn twice, about two weeks apart, from over two hundred adults. Resting markers proved fairly stable, and a combined resting score was highly stable. Markers measured after a lab trigger varied much more. People who rated their own health as low showed the most swing in the triggered response. The authors suggest that such swings may signal poorer health.
pmc-10741861:
Mohamed, Mohamed, and Kim review wearable EEG devices for sleep monitoring at home in twenty twenty-three. Sleep quality shapes mental health and daily wellbeing. Lab polysomnography is the gold standard but is bulky, costly, and expert dependent. Brain wave sensing offers the key signals for staging sleep outside the lab.

The review surveys recent wearable systems that capture EEG during sleep. It compares their designs, shapes, materials, and staging methods. Headbands and ear based sensors feature among the form factors. The authors aim to guide development of friendly home assessment tools. Better home monitoring could widen access to sleep disorder screening. The survey frames EEG wearables as the practical path forward.
pmc-10742261:
Anali del Milagro Bernabe Garnique and Glaucia Maria Machado-Santelli build 3D balls of lung cancer cells in the lab. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, mimics the mix of cells around a real tumor. That mix holds support cells and immune cells that shape how cancer grows. Flat lab cultures miss much of that context.

The team grew cancer cells alone and with skin support cells or immune cells. The mixed balls formed faster, while pure cancer balls grew larger. They checked shape, cell life, and movement under the microscope. They then dosed the balls with cancer drugs and other compounds. The model can help screen drugs in a setting closer to a real tumor.
pmc-10742961:
Anny M S Cheng and a large team review imaging for macular atrophy in late age-related macular degeneration. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. This eye disease is a top cause of blindness. In its late stage, the centre of the retina wastes away, in both its dry and wet forms, and sight falls hard. No proven cure for the waste is on hand.

Early spotting is thus key. The review walks through the scan and photo tools that can find and track the waste: dye tests, auto-glow views, infrared views, and layered scans of the retina and its vessels. Each tool shows a part of the harm, and a mix gives the best read.
pmc-10743361:
Farci and Piano wrote a reply in twenty twenty-three to a letter from Bharat and colleagues about the outer covering of a hardy bacterium. The bacterium, Deinococcus radiodurans, wraps itself in a layered envelope built from several protein complexes. The dispute turns on how parts of that covering connect.

The authors argue the two groups' findings fit together rather than clash. Bharat's group studied patches of one outer part, while Farci and Piano studied intact envelope patches. They present microscope maps showing a central complex ringed by six units of two other types. They also question older methods that used harsh chemicals, which may have changed the proteins before study.
pmc-10744061:
Eight authors wrote a review in two thousand twenty-three on a signaling molecule's role in gum disease. The molecule, CCL5, is a chemokine, a chemical call that summons immune cells. It is made by T cells and drives inflammation. In periodontitis, lasting inflammation against bacterial film destroys the soft and hard tissue around teeth.

No full review of CCL5 in this disease existed, a gap the authors set out to fill. They sum up its part in how the disease starts and advances. They also weigh its links to risk factors such as aging, smoking, diabetes, and obesity, and argue that drugs aimed at it deserve attention.
pmc-10744761:
Elisabeth Entfellner and a team of co-authors traced why one algae toxin family comes in so many forms. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with aeruginosins, four part peptides that block enzymes. Bloom forming cyanobacteria of one genus make them. Their shape spread is huge, but the gene ground was dim. The team set one hundred twenty-four strains from many fresh waters side by side.

They read the genes that build these peptides in each strain. Shape spread traced to swap events in those genes, most of all gains of helper enzymes. Readers in water safety learn how a toxin kit reshuffles in the wild. That bears on which forms a bloom watch must test for.
pmc-10745661:
Rosario Tavera-Hernández and four co-authors review chia seed as a help in diabetes care. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Chia is a crop from Mexico, grown since before Spanish rule, and now a common food in many lands. It is rich in omega-3 fats and fibre.

It also blocks two enzymes that break down starch, which slows sugar uptake. These acts may cut heart risk as well. The seed's wide use and low cost add to its draw as a care aid.
pmc-10755561:
Zohreh Hosseini Marznaki and colleagues surveyed older heart attack survivors at a hospital in Amol, Iran, for a study published in two thousand twenty-three. After a heart attack, older patients often face physical and emotional changes that lower quality of life. The team asked whether spiritual well-being connects to life satisfaction and daily quality of life.

Hundreds of patients answered questions about faith, sense of purpose, health history, and well-being. Strong spiritual well-being linked to higher self-rated quality in some areas, but not directly to overall life satisfaction. Care teams learn that spiritual life matters to recovery, though it does not by itself explain how satisfied patients feel.
pmc-10832661:
Geskin and seven co-authors share expert views on maintenance therapy for a skin lymphoma, in work dated twenty twenty-three. The disease is mycosis fungoides, a slow cancer of immune cells in the skin. When first treatment works, upkeep therapy may keep it away.

No firm guides cover when or how to give upkeep, the authors note. They focus on a chlormethine gel applied to skin, which patients can use at home and combine with other care. Experts debate how long a good response must last before upkeep starts. Their shared clinical experience offers practical steps until formal trials settle the open questions.
pmc-11037861:
Coheley and ten co-authors run a randomized trial of whole egg eating on bone growth in healthy children, in a trial from twenty twenty-three. Eggs carry quality nutrients and compounds thought to help bones. Children aged nine to thirteen eat egg-based or control foods for nine months. Bone content, density, and strength are measured by two scanning methods.

No significant intervention effect appears for any bone outcome overall. One spine measure approaches significance favoring eggs over gelatin control. Most shin bone measures grow over time in all groups equally. Eight to ten eggs weekly yields only small bone responses. Eggs remain nutritious, but bone claims need tempering.
pmc-11045361:
Antonio Lazzarino and six co-authors map unfair gaps in mental health care for young people in Northwest London. Care places are scarce, so use should at least match need. The team read linked health records for more than three quarters of a million people aged five to twenty-four. About two in each hundred had a mental health appointment in the study year.

Across the region, poorer areas used more care, as need would suggest. But in some boroughs that pattern broke down, and use looked oddly low. There, the illness of poor youth may be passing unseen. The paper flags those boroughs as places where records of use cannot be trusted to show need.
pmc-11536961:
Guan and four colleagues pool trials of ketorolac for pain after lumbar spine surgery in twenty twenty-four. The pain drug is common after back operations, alone or mixed with others. Thirteen trials with over nine hundred patients met the bar. Pain scores, morphine use, hospital stay, and side effects were weighed.

Pain fell most in the first six hours, past the line for a felt difference. Later gains stayed real but smaller. Morphine needs dropped sharply, though trials disagreed a lot there. Stays shortened by about half a day. The authors back the drug as a useful part of post surgery pain care.
pmc-11547561:
Olga Khromova, Vladimir Larionov, and four co-authors steer a classic reaction by swapping one ion in a copper catalyst. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, studies the Henry reaction, which joins nitro compounds to aldehydes. Their chiral copper complex is built from store-bought parts. With one base, the reaction gives chiral nitroalcohols in high yield and good purity. With another, it gives nitrostyrenes instead, also in strong yield. The aldehyde's own shape also sways the outcome. Two copper variants were compared side by side. Such a switch could simplify making either product family on demand.
pmc-11558261:
Filiz Namdar Pekiner and colleagues published a 2024 dental imaging study. They examined bone loss around upper back teeth. Scans came from several hundred consecutive patients. All patients were adults. The team sorted each defect by its shape. They also compared patterns by age and by sex.

Each molar was checked on four surfaces. Defects were classed as flat or as walled craters. Some teeth showed combined gum and root problems. Women showed one pattern more often than men. Age also shaped the damage seen. Such maps help dentists plan gum treatment. They show which defects need surgery and which need cleaning.
pmc-11577861:
Tianjie Lai and four co-authors trace smoking's link to leftover cholesterol in a 2024 paper. That cholesterol fraction is a growing heart risk factor, and what drives it is not fully known. Using two decades of a national health survey, they related a nicotine breakdown marker in blood to the cholesterol measure in thousands of adults. Statistical models handled the survey design and many side factors.

Heavy exposure came with clearly higher cholesterol, especially in women. The link bent into an N shape, peaking at a middle exposure level. Inflammation markers carried part of the effect, with white blood cells doing most of that carrying.
pmc-11580361:
Yoshiko Nakano, Ian Burns, Liana Nobre, and a large team detect childhood brain tumors from spinal fluid in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Central nervous system germ cell tumors strike adolescents, respond to treatment, but leave deficits, and biopsy carries risk. The team asked whether tumor DNA in cerebrospinal fluid could serve as a biomarker. They collected twenty-nine fluid samples from twenty-one patients and ran low-pass whole genome sequencing, reading copy-number alterations as measurable residual disease, alongside imaging and tumor markers.

At diagnosis, copy-number alterations were detected in samples from seventeen of nineteen patients, eighty-nine percent, including eight whose tumors were marker-negative by conventional tests. The authors argue spinal fluid tumor DNA offers a high-yield, less invasive window on these tumors, guiding biopsy decisions and radiotherapy adaptation.
pmc-11584661:
Kexin Chen and co-authors published a 2024 study of health poverty in rural towns of north-west China, measured on many dimensions at once. Health poverty is one face of the broad poverty that rural work still fights. The team studied the state of over nine thousand rural residents in one region, in two years set three years apart.

A dual-cutoff method set who counts as health-poor, on dimensions of health, care access, and spending and security. At the set cutoff, the share fell from over a fifth to over one in thirteen across the span. The combined index fell by nearly two in three. Women bore more of it than men. Chronic diseases were a chief dimension. Sex, age, education, state aid, family size, housing, and the digital gap all fed the index. Remote towns need the most attention still, the conclusion runs.
pmc-11589161:
Oluwamayokun Oshinowo and a large team show that self-attack antibodies change platelet squeeze force and flag bleed risk in kids. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The ill at issue, ITP, is a platelet ill driven by such antibodies, with no sound bleed risk mark. The team built a gel chip that lets one platelet's pull be taped under a plain scope.

In fifty-three child patients, low single platelet pull alone flagged bleed with high truth. Lab probes showed antibodies can raise or cut cell force by lock of grip parts in distinct shapes. The team names this force shift immuno-mechanical modulation. It may serve tests and cures past this ill.
pmc-11589961:
Mohamad Mohty and Bipin Savani share a personal view on social media in medicine, in two thousand twenty-four. Doctors once met face to face or in journals to swap knowledge. Platforms now let them share findings, join forces across borders, and reach patients faster than older channels allowed.

The editorial also weighs the downsides of that speed. Short posts can flatten nuance and spark misunderstanding. Constant alerts can break deep work and thin out real relationships. The authors close with best practice tips, starting with managing expectations for oneself and others. Their aim is a balance that keeps the gains of social media while limiting its costs.
pmc-11590261:
Deena Jalal and five co-authors look for early warning signs of relapse in Wilms tumor, the most common kidney cancer of childhood. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Most children survive, but about fifteen percent relapse, and then survival falls hard.

The team compared tumor tissue from nine children who relapsed with nine who stayed in remission, all at early stages. Genome-wide scans of chemical tags on DNA showed clear patterns. Fourteen tag sites marked the groups apart, with looser tagging in gene-free regions among remission cases. A combined gene, INS-IGF2, ran higher in relapse tumors. The authors suggest these markers could guide closer watching and tailored treatment, while noting the sample was small.
pmc-11600861:
Erfan Kashani and eight colleagues published a combined analysis in two thousand twenty-four on a blood ratio and a sudden eye stroke. The condition, called NAION, cuts blood flow to the optic nerve without artery inflammation. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is a cheap inflammation marker from a routine blood count.

The team pooled six studies comparing patients with healthy controls. Patients' ratios ran clearly higher on average. The marker's accuracy was modest: it caught about seven in ten cases while clearing about six in ten healthy people. The authors suggest the ratio may help flag the condition and hints that inflammation plays a part. They stop short of calling it a stand-alone test.
pmc-11602261:
Rahmah Javed and five co-authors report a rare eye disease that struck a woman's healthy eye after surgery on the other. Strong steroids failed, but a second drug, methotrexate, calmed the inflammation and restored much of her sight. The authors note the case as the first of its kind reported from Pakistan and urge fast treatment.
pmc-11603961:
Zhihao Liang and co-authors published a 2024 retrospective study of two back-side operations for a neck hyperextension injury in older patients with a narrow spinal canal at several levels. The injury often comes with a central cord syndrome and an unstable spine. The operation must free the cord and hold the neck stable. Both operations work from the back.

Records gave pain and nerve scores, operation time, blood loss, hospital stay, and complications. Nerve scores rose in both groups after surgery, with no firm gap by group. pmc-11604761:

The gauges proved grade at the million scale. They mapped how the ring spreads too. Free space plans let in wide beams and many side paths, not like chip guides. The team also set one sheet of tungsten diselenide in the pit. That joins the sharp light mode to a flat chip like stuff. The 2024 step opens free space stages for sense work and light stuff tests.
pmc-11604961:
James Orr and colleagues argue that the messy variety of ecosystem responses to disturbance is not noise but a signal, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Diversity measures and broad functions, such as total biomass, systematically moved in opposite directions. With geometry, simulations, and theory, they show this pattern is predictable. Better, it can be read backward: the way measures covary reveals which species carry which functions, and how each population answers disturbance. Variability, reframed, becomes a measuring tool.
pmc-11605561:
Yamashita and colleagues report a hospital study from twenty twenty-four on a field therapy for glioblastoma. The therapy uses a shifting electric field in the brain to slow tumor growth. The team looked back at nineteen patients treated at their hospital since twenty nineteen. They focused on the seven patients who quit the therapy within three months.

Patients who quit early had worse survival than those who stayed on the therapy. Early quitters more often had tumors on the left side of the brain. They also tended to start with lower daily function scores. The study says early dropout is a key poor sign. It urges staff to build patient drive to keep using the therapy.
pmc-11607461:
Matthew Barthet and five co-authors share GameVibe, a set of game clips with feel marks for use in feel tech work. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Feel work now leans on rich mixed sets, yet good seen-heard sets are scarce. The set holds clips from open game runs of thirty games, picked for wide game kinds and clean sound and sight.

Each clip bears in-game act reads plus marks from folks who watched and traced how drawn-in they felt, beat by beat. How well the marks agree folk to folk is read and told in full. The team offer the set as shared ground for mixed feel reads.
pmc-11607961:
Lorenzo Antonetti and eight colleagues published a gut study in two thousand twenty-four on common gut protozoa in Côte d'Ivoire. Blastocystis is a single-celled gut dweller whose effect on health is debated. Most past work covered sick people in rich countries, so healthy carriers in Africa add missing evidence.

Their mix held less Bacteroides and more Prevotella than non-carriers. One health-linked bacterium, Faecalibacterium, also ran higher in carriers. The authors treat the pattern as a sign these protozoa may sit well with a healthy gut.
pmc-11612161:
Hao Jiang, Zhenxi Li, Wei Xu, and Jianru Xiao trace why one breast cancer type homes to bone. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, covers luminal breast cancer, which often returns in bone. pmc-11621561:
Elisa Damiani and a large team watch lung tissue change under different ventilator settings in pigs. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses live microscopy through a small chest opening. Effects were stronger in upper, non-dependent lung regions. Higher end pressure alone did not change those dimensions. Pure oxygen widened the small vessels instead. The imaging method lets doctors see ventilation effects directly in living lung.
pmc-11621861:
Zhenxing Li and co-authors test blocking a checkpoint protein in spinal cord injury from lost blood flow, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Rats had the main body artery clamped to mimic the injury. The protein ran high in injured cord tissue.

Blocking it eased tissue damage, cell death, and swelling in the cord. The blocker also shifted spinal immune cells from an attack mode toward a repair mode. Like effects appeared in immune cells stressed in a dish. The authors back the antibody as a candidate care for this injury type.
pmc-11623461:

Six trials took in more than sixteen hundred sick folk split twixt the two ways. Come-back of the fault did not split  twixt the groups. The no-fix group told of less pain six months in the wake of knife work. Back-to-norm acts, rate of deep ills, and rate of fluid pools showed no firm splits. Checks by subgroup and by how firm finds are checked the strength of the finds. The team ends that a skip of the fix step seems safe. It cuts long-term pain  in the wake of it.
pmc-11624661:

Videos of fifty prospects were broken down by movement parts. Stats tests linked parts to jump height scaled for size. Links to first year pro value were also checked. No one part alone guessed jump height well. Top and low jump groups used distinct styles of move. The full model for height was strong and clear. Rookie year success was a second focus.
pmc-11629461:

pmc-11630561:

Women were affected more than men. People with the condition more often showed mild cognitive impairment. pmc-11635461:

The joint response did not match the simple product of the two single responses. The gases lean on each other inside the sensor, so methane readouts can be skewed when carbon monoxide is near. pmc-11636261:

Built-in fields swept charges apart efficiently, lifting efficiency to a notable level for this material. The authors present the tuning route as a general tool for such films.
pmc-11638261:
Marcela Mendoza-Suárez and three co-authors study helpful soil bacteria and faba beans in this twenty twenty-four paper. pmc-11638461:
Mátyás Vajda and six co-authors published a registry study in twenty twenty-four on children's elbow fractures treated with surgery in Hungary. Supracondylar humerus fractures are common in children and can damage nerves and blood flow when severe. pmc-11641361:

Physical activity, sex, age, schooling, sitting time, and diet also mattered. Heavy drinking did not. The results give clinics a short list of habits to ask about when judging eye risk.
pmc-11642561:
Renuka M. Chaphalkar and colleagues published an eye research study in 2024 on glaucoma damage in rodents. Glaucoma slowly kills the nerve cells that carry sight signals. High eye pressure is the main known risk factor. A peptide called endothelin-1 can also drive this damage in animals.

The team tested how that peptide affects the cells' energy centers. Treated cells made less energy and breathed more weakly. Damaged energy centers should normally be cleared by a cleanup process. Instead, that cleanup process fell after a day of treatment. The team also used a rat model of high eye pressure. Their work links failed cell cleanup with glaucoma-like nerve loss.
pmc-11644361:
Claudia Beatrice Bagnato and a large team run a trial of lifestyle change for fatty liver disease tied to metabolism. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The disease is common and links to obesity and stress hormone cortisol, which feeds liver fat and insulin trouble. They ask if diet and exercise can cut both.

Patients split by chance into three arms: diet advice alone, diet plus steady aerobic work, or diet plus hard interval training. Over four months, cortisol falls in both exercise arms, most in the interval arm. Liver fat eases in all arms, most in the aerobic arm, and in some patients it clears in full. Waist size also shrinks.
pmc-11644861:
Liao and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-four on how alkali choice shapes zinc oxide gas sensors. The team grow zinc oxide crystals with four distinct alkali sources in hot water. Crystal shape and sensing skill differ sharply by source. Checks confirm the samples are pure, with clear shape traits. Deeper probes map crystal structure and surface chemistry. Theory sums track charge transfer and flag the crystal faces most alert to ethanol. Tests span wide ethanol levels and heat ranges.

Three alkali routes yield sensors that respond even at modest heat. The ammonia route needs far higher heat to respond. All samples recover well at low ethanol levels at mid heat. The authors tie sensing skill to crystal face design.
pmc-11646461:
Li and seven co-authors study a kidney disease sign called crescents in work from twenty twenty-four. The disease is primary membranous nephropathy, where immune harm thickens the kidney filters. Crescents are scar like half moon growths in the filters, and their effect on outlook was unclear.

The team used records from a hospital in Zhanjiang, China, over about six years. Patients with crescents on biopsy were compared with more than a hundred patients without them. Clinical traits, tissue traits, and outcomes were set side by side. The test was whether crescents alone predict faster decline, which would change how closely such patients are watched.
pmc-11649761:
Moyer and Sisson test whether protecting liposuction port sites cuts local complications, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Liposuction is the most common cosmetic surgery in the United States. Port sites can scar, split open, or infect, yet protection had never been studied. The team reviews sixty consecutive cosmetic and fat transfer cases.

The first thirty cases use no protection, and the next thirty use a tubing shield. Groups match on demographics and surgical measures. Complications hit a third of unprotected patients versus a small share of protected ones. Wound splitting drives most of the gap. Protected patients need less wound care and fewer revisions. Simple protection looks well worth its minor cost.
pmc-11650761:
Julio Álvarez-Valle and five co-workers report a one pot gold led act that builds hard ring sets from chromones. Chromones are plain frames in goods from nature and in drugs. Their way adds a propargyl group with propargylsilanes and gold as the lead. Both parts wake each other. The gold wakes the silane, and the silicon part that forms wakes the chromone. The act hits one carbon spot and no next.

One shape form comes out, and models show why that one wins. The team then chained a next, distinct gold led step to the first. The chain makes fine three ring compounds in one run. The 2024 work gives lab staff a neat short cut to builds that would else take a great many split steps.
pmc-11652461:
Kokandi and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a five-year review of corneal tissue examined at a Saudi tertiary eye center. Corneal disease is a leading reversible cause of vision loss worldwide. The team collected every corneal specimen sent for lab examination over five years. Three hundred forty-seven patients were included with their diagnoses and surgery reasons. Full-thickness corneal buttons were the most common specimen type. Partial grafts and inner layer samples followed in frequency.

Keratoconus, a cone-shaped distortion of the cornea, was the top reason for grafting. Swollen corneas, failed prior grafts, and ulcers followed behind. Patients receiving full or partial grafts were significantly younger than others. Some sampling procedures differed by patient sex in the data. The authors say keratoconus is a major treatable burden in Saudi Arabia. They suggest screening and genetic studies for prevention.
pmc-11654161:
Chenyu Jiang and colleagues mine a national US health survey for a link between plant compounds in food and constipation, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The compounds are flavonoids, found in fruit, tea, cocoa, and many vegetables. The team drew on survey years twenty oh seven to twenty ten, pairing diet records with stool reports.

Across the board, people who ate more flavonoids reported less constipation. The pattern held for most subclasses, from isoflavones to flavones. It held most firmly for anthocyanidins, the pigments that color berries and red cabbage. For that subclass the link bent into an upside-down U, with benefit growing once intake passed a low threshold. The authors are careful: a snapshot survey cannot prove cause. Still, they suggest that flavonoid-rich food deserves a place in diet advice for a common gut complaint.
pmc-11655061:
Bruno Bockorny leads a large team building a protein atlas of blood-borne vesicles for pancreatic cancer detection, in a resource paper from two thousand twenty-four. Pancreatic cancer has the worst prognosis of common tumors, largely because diagnosis comes late. Liquid biopsies from extracellular vesicles hold out a chance of an early signal.

The test is to split cancer vesicles from those shed in benign disease. Chronic pancreatitis and precancerous cysts make hard controls that are of real use. A high-efficiency isolation method called EVtrap harvested vesicles from plasma for the team. Deep proteomics set out the cargo they carry in a catalog. The resource is meant for biomarker discovery across the field, and earlier detection is the hope that rides on it.
pmc-11656361:
Wai Hin Lee and David Haddleton print water-hating meshes with a light-based printer and compare ways to boost oil-water split, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Mesh resins were altered with fluorinated or silicone add-ins, and pore size was varied by design. Water beading and split skill were measured for each route.

A small dose of either add-in cut water wetting to a flat floor. Larger pores raised water hate on their own. The base resin at its best pore size already split oil and water well. Silicone add-ins helped more, while the fluorinated route added little. Readers learn pore design can spare harsh chemicals in such meshes.
pmc-11656861:
Elham Zarenezhad and co-authors synthesize new nitroimidazole compounds and test them against drug resistant bacteria, in work from twenty twenty-four. Resistance and biofilm growth make many infections hard to clear. The team made fifteen compounds by a copper aided coupling route.

Tests covered resistant staph and drug strong gut bacteria from standard and patient strains. One compound beat a classic drug by wide margins on several strains at very low doses. Others topped the classic drug against the resistant gut types. Ten compounds also fought biofilms. Computer docking checks backed the lab results. The authors call for animal and clinical follow up before any medical use.
pmc-11663761:
Junya Sato and colleagues teach an AI system to find abnormalities in abdominal CT scans using only the words radiologists already wrote. AI detection could reduce radiologists' workload, but development has been hampered by the shortage of large expert-annotated datasets. Instead of manual labels, the team mined free-text radiology reports from routine practice across multiple institutions.

The pipeline detects abnormalities in five organs: liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys. A segmentation model isolates each organ's images while an information extraction schema pulls disease information from reports. These paired data train a multiple-instance learning model for anomaly detection. Training and internal testing used three institutions' data; external testing used six others, the honest test of generalization. Performance was measured by discrimination and accuracy metrics. Annotation-free training turns every archive into potential training data; the bottleneck shifts from labeling to governance.
pmc-11666561:
Tengfei Niu and co-authors build a model to predict anxiety risk in older adults in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The group of interest is Chinese elders with abdominal obesity, where early warning could prompt early help. The data come from a large national longevity survey.

From more than two thousand participants, about ten percent had anxiety symptoms. A selection method narrowed forty-six candidate factors to nine key ones. A boosting model using those factors predicted risk well. An explanation tool ranked looking on the bright side as the strongest factor. The authors say the model can flag high-risk elders for targeted support, with clear reasons for each forecast.
pmc-11671161:
Frank Jorge Valdez Baez and co-authors study wrong dosing of blood thinners in 2024 in the Dominican Republic. These drugs, called DOACs, prevent strokes in people with a common heart rhythm fault. Too low a dose leaves clots possible, and too high a dose risks bleeding. Data from low-income countries were scarce.

The team reviewed close to four hundred outpatients at a cardiology institute. Over a quarter were dosed wrongly, split between under- and overdosing. The wrongly dosed patients were older, with weaker kidneys and more vessel disease and anemia. Age, vessel disease, and a kidney blood marker each predicted wrong dosing. The authors urge dose checks tuned to kidney function.
pmc-11672961:
Ching Sin Siau leads a team that built a shorter test of mental strain, reported in twenty twenty-four. The long form has forty questions and is used to gauge risk of suicide and mental illness. A shorter form would be quicker to give in busy settings.

The team used survey data from three groups in China: students, office staff, and hospital staff. They kept the five best questions from each part of the scale, making a twenty-question form. Checks on a held-back share of the data showed the short form still hung together well and matched the long form's structure. The paper offers a faster tool for screening strain.
pmc-11673961:
Laumann and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a study of whether a stress-like chemical ages immune cells in the lab. Chronic stress links to cancer risk, aging diseases, and weak immunity. The team repeatedly treated resting human immune cells with isoproterenol. That drug mimics adrenaline, a stress hormone. They then checked a panel of well-established aging markers. Several changes matched a senescence-like state in the treated cells.

DNA breaks increased and telomeres, the chromosome caps, shortened. Treated cells failed to multiply when stimulated. A classic aging enzyme marker rose, while some death enzymes fell. A sticky cell protein rose strongly, raising cell adhesion. The authors say the pattern suggests stress chemicals can drive immune aging. The work adds molecular detail to how stress may wear down immunity.
pmc-11675761:
Matko Glunčić and a team of co-authors study repeating DNA patterns in humans and other primates, in two thousand twenty-four. The patterns sit in a gene family tied to brain growth and thinking skill. Humans carry far more copies of the single units than great apes do.

The team scanned the full genomes of humans, chimpanzees, gorillas, and orangutans with a repeat-mapping tool. Humans held many more of the units arranged in neat triple groups placed end to end. Gorillas held a few, and the other apes held none in that form. The authors argue that this neat grouping, not just copy count, may help explain part of the human edge in thinking.
pmc-11676461:
David Vrech and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on how male scorpions' fertility fades across a breeding season. The species lives in the hills of Argentina. Early season males are fresh; late ones have aged and mated. The team gauges testis mass, sperm counts, and sperm life at each stage. They ask if age or effort drives the fade.

Early males held more testis mass and better sperm. The fade looks like aging, not spent effort. Males kept alone stored more sperm with no loss of life, a hint of a guard trick. Males in fine shape made more sperm yet lost its life faster late in the season. That trade frames the cost of early wins.
pmc-11676861:
Mousa Sha'at and seven co-authors design a single tablet carrying two diabetes drugs at different release speeds, in a two thousand twenty-four pharmaceutical study. The tablet pairs metformin, the standard first-line drug, with honokiol, a bioactive plant compound.

Hydrophilic polymers form a gel matrix that meters both drugs. Metformin released fast, reaching eighty percent within four to seven hours, while honokiol took nine to ten hours and responded more strongly to polymer levels. Classical kinetic models fit early release, but fractal and multifractal models captured the later, time-dependent behavior. Higher polymer content slowed release by thickening the gel barrier. Mechanical and stability testing supported extended-release use.
pmc-11677661:
Grace Fu and co-authors map how losing a folate enzyme rewires liver chemistry around two amino acids, in work from twenty twenty-four. The enzyme helps recycle a key carrier in one carbon metabolism. Its loss is common in cancers and favors tumor growth.

Earlier work showed knockout mice had shifted liver profiles, with glycine and serine among the changes. The team profiled liver and blood from knockout and normal mice of both sexes without targeting set compounds. Pathways tied to glycine and serine shifted broadly after the loss. Amino acid handling, antioxidant defense, fat burning, and vitamin pathways all moved. The authors read the pattern as support for building blocks and defense, and urge diet studies next.
pmc-11677761:
Jessica Hunter and colleagues examine associations between knowing health risks of sugary drinks and how much adults in the United States consume. Their 2024 cross-sectional study uses a twenty twenty-one national survey of over four thousand adults.

About thirty percent drank sugary beverages at least twice daily. Most adults knew these drinks relate to weight gain, diabetes, and cavities. Far fewer recognised links to some cancers, high cholesterol, heart disease, or high blood pressure. Knowledge levels varied by sociodemographic group. Surprisingly, knowing any listed health condition was not significantly associated with high consumption compared with non-consumers. The authors suggest other factors may drive intake more than knowledge.
pmc-11678561:
Shusuke Ueda and six co-authors dose human tendon cells with vitamin C to see whether the high dose protects them from oxidative degeneration, in a two thousand twenty-four cell study. Tendinopathy is an aging, overuse disease, and vitamin C is a popular remedy of unclear dosing.

Hydrogen peroxide injured the cells; a standard micromolar dose and a two-hundred-fold higher dose were compared. Both doses cut cell death and oxidative stress and suppressed the aging marker p16. Only the high dose, however, preserved the actin cytoskeleton's structure. Mitochondrial and collagen gene expression rose with treatment. The authors nominate high-dose vitamin C as a candidate therapy for tendon degeneration.
pmc-11678961:
Juan Tang and co-authors probe how bisphenol A harms rat livers through a stress-response pathway in two thousand twenty-four. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is a plastic chemical found widely in the environment and tied to liver lesions. How it wounds the liver was still murky.

Rats got corn oil or one of three BPA doses by mouth for thirty days. Liver and kidney tissue were read by staining and fine microscopy, and stress markers in liver and blood were gauged. Gene reads tracked the pathway's key names. Treated rats showed shrunken liver and adrenal weights, clear tissue changes, and raised levels of a liver enzyme and a swelling signal in blood. Stress damage signs rose as well, tying the pathway to the harm.
pmc-11679261:
Jiawei Cai and his team build a machine-run flagging tool for odd points in Chinese satellite data. Their study from twenty twenty-four aims at the BeiDou guide system and its broadcast ephemeris. Those orbit data sit under sharp place fixes for all who use the system. Ionosphere weather, sun press, and clock drift can mar them.

Their model turns the data into many-track rows that shift with time. A lone-point method and a memory network work as one in it. Checks for wholeness and for trends that hold steady guard the chain. Advance calls of orbit values grew far more exact. Clock calls for mid-orbit craft rose most of all. Unlike satellite kinds act in unlike ways and need handling apart. Machine checks beat hand review for this flood of data.
pmc-11679661:
Danjie Pan and seven co-authors published a 2024 review of therapeutic cancer vaccines. Unlike preventive vaccines, these aim to treat existing tumours by training the immune system to attack them and remember the attack. Tumours fight back by suppressing immunity, which has limited success so far.

The review surveys the main obstacles: weak targets, suppressive tumour surroundings, and resistance that grows during treatment. It then highlights a newer direction, in-situ vaccines made from anonymous antigens, where treatment releases the tumour’s own material in place to teach the immune system. Progress in that area is summarized in detail. The authors intend the review as a reference for the next round of vaccine design.
pmc-11683661:
Hisham Hamad and nine colleagues review three years of groin artery surgery at a Welsh hospital, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The operation, common femoral endarterectomy with profundoplasty, cleans out the main artery at the top of the leg and widens the deep branch, restoring flow for patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia.

The retrospective study covers seventy-seven patients treated at Glan Clwyd Hospital, excluding those whose surgery formed part of a bypass. Some also received treatment on the iliac artery above. The group averaged about seventy-three years of age, and roughly three in five were men. The authors evaluate how well the operation worked, what complications arose, and which factors predicted lasting success. Endarterectomy at this site is an old, durable operation competing with stents. Single-center outcome audits like this one tell surgeons what results their own practice actually delivers.
pmc-11686461:
Yu and five co-authors built printed foam-like filters in twenty twenty-four to catch tiny bits in fast air flow. Foam filters catch spray bits well but are hard to tune by shape. Their prints use neat cell shapes that can be swapped and sized at will.

They made four cell shapes and checked them with X-ray scans and a spray of one-micron beads. Shapes with more skin per cell caught more bits from the air. One shape was then made at a range of hole shares to test the rule. Catch rates ran from low to near full across speeds, with bits caught by hits and charge.
pmc-11691261:
Edward Miller, Elizabeth Simpson, and Sara Karon report a study of how the rates a public health plan pays nursing homes stack up against the true cost of care. Their set of talks is from two thousand twenty-four.

The plan is the top payer for such homes, and pays for about two in three of their guests. Those guests tend to stay long and need daily help, from loss of thought or of body. Till of late, scant facts tied the plan's rates to the cost for this group. The team used the plan's pay and cost files to draw that link. Such facts are key to talks on how to lift the safety and quality of home care.
pmc-11692061:
Sofia Mildrum Chana and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on social media use among Hispanic and Latinx family caregivers of people living with dementia. These caregivers experience elevated stress that can harm their health. They are prone to loneliness and isolation, and rely on social media to maintain ties, seek support, or cope with stress.

The study drew on a project with forty-five caregivers, most of them women with an average age of about fifty-six. Participants spent roughly two and a half hours a day on social media, with Facebook and Instagram the most used platforms. More time on social media was associated with greater distress from the behavioral symptoms of dementia and more depressive symptoms. Passive use, scrolling without posting or responding, showed the strongest links to distress, stress, and depressive symptoms. Active use showed no association with any mood measure.
pmc-11714461:
Alissa Kurzman and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on schooling, home size, and thinking scores among Latino adults in Southern California. Latino communities in the United States carry a heavy share of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.

The team used starting data from the SERVE OC trial, with two hundred fifty-four adults who took a standard thinking test in English or Spanish. Most had eight years of schooling or less. Among adults aged fifty and older, low schooling went with much lower test scores. Home size, used as a rough sign of social support, showed only a weak trend. The authors note that the test already adds a point for low schooling. They argue that more care is needed when the test is used in groups with low average schooling.
pmc-11715561:
Beny Spira re-evaluates mask effectiveness through an evidence-based medicine lens. His analysis from twenty twenty-four revisits pandemic-era claims. Masks were mandated widely on laboratory filtration evidence. Observational studies supported benefits, but trial evidence is thinner.

Meta-analyses including more randomised trials estimate smaller effects. Lab success often fails to repeat in real-world trials, he notes. Drugs show the same pattern during development regularly. Context, fit, and behaviour all dilute mask performance outside labs. The author argues for honest grading of the evidence layers. Policy should distinguish filtration facts from population effects. The piece invites calmer reassessment rather than slogans.
pmc-11723661:
Paola Spitalieri and colleagues studied stem cells in a rapid ageing syndrome in 2024. MDPL syndrome speeds up ageing features. Jaw, hearing, and fat problems combine. One gene fault causes the condition. Patient stem cells were grown and watched. The team asked when damage appears.

Ageing hallmarks showed up surprisingly early. They appeared during early development stages. Harmful oxygen species built up inside mitochondria. Stem cell function suffered as a result. Early signs may warn of progression. Mechanism work could guide drug timing. Earlier treatment might soften the phenotype. Rare ageing diseases may share lessons.
pmc-11799261:
Anas Al-okaily and Abdelghani Tbakhi present a new lossless compression method, using genome data as the test case, in two thousand twenty-four. Lossless methods shrink data with no loss on recovery, and demand grows as data piles up daily. Genome files, from tiny to huge, make a hard benchmark.

Their method scans the whole file, groups like stretches together, and compresses each group on its own. That divide-and-group plan differs from standard entropy, dictionary, or prediction methods. On a benchmark of seventeen genomes, it beat leading tools and saved meaningful space. The authors say the same plan can serve text, numbers, images, audio, and video.
pmc-11812061:
Yanquan Liu and seven colleagues published a case report in two thousand twenty-four on a rare and dangerous pairing of diseases. Severe acute pancreatitis inflames the pancreas and can fail several organs. In this case the stomach lining also tore away, causing massive bleeding.

The report follows one patient's course in intensive care. It walks through how the team spotted the bleeding, which treatments they used, and how the patient fared. Such combined cases are easy to miss because the pancreas disease hides the stomach injury. The authors want the report to sharpen doctors' watchfulness. They offer it as a reference for intensive care teams facing the same rare emergency.
pmc-11814461:
Miguel Berenguel and colleagues validated gene-splicing variants in immune patients in this study from twenty twenty-four. Splicing errors cause a large share of inherited disease, but not all are easy to judge. Among one hundred eighty-seven patients with inborn immune errors, twenty-three carried splicing variants. The team checked each variant's effect with a lab assay on the RNA message.

Twenty-one variants were analyzed, about half of them new to the literature. Most sat at the classic splice sites, where harm is predictable. Variants elsewhere, or in confusing genes, needed the lab proof. The authors propose an algorithm for when validation is required. It aims to spare labs work where the verdict is already clear.
pmc-11888661:
Revathi KT, Reena Rajan, S Mathavi, and Raghavendra Rao compare urinary tract infections from drug proof bacteria in catheterized versus plain patients at a city hospital in Salem, Tamil Nadu. Quick spotting of proof strains guides care. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Over six months, gram negative samples from both groups were tested for drug response, kill levels, and proof making genes by gene copy tests. Over half the isolates made the proof enzymes, more from catheter cases. Gene checks on a subset found one gene most often, with some strains holding several at once. The authors urge steady watch and firm drug policy.
pmc-11888761:
Syed Wali Peeran and five colleagues published a lab study in two thousand twenty-four on rose extract against gum disease bacteria. Damask rose compounds were tested on two bacteria that drive periodontitis. The team also modelled how a rose compound docks onto bacterial virulence proteins.

Methanol extracts outperformed ethanol ones in disc tests, clearing zones of roughly thirteen to sixteen millimetres. A dose of four hundred micrograms per millilitre stopped growth in broth. Extracts also cut how well the bacteria stuck to glass surfaces, an early biofilm step. Computer docking showed the compound myricetin binding a bacterial adhesion protein. The authors present the rose as a candidate natural adjunct for gum care.
pmc-12082661:
Moradeyo, Akinyemi, and Yusuf track how fast Nigerian wives have their first child in this two thousand twenty-four study. The gap from wedding to first birth sets the pace for later births when birth control is not used. The authors pooled four national health surveys, from nineteen ninety to twenty thirteen, and used survival models on women who wed with no child and no pregnancy.

The median wait shrank from two years to one year across the period. A first birth soon after the wedding was more likely for women with only primary schooling. It was also more likely for those who knew about birth control or their fertile days, those who wed after age nineteen, and those in the South East and South West. Community effects showed up too. The authors urge policy that backs more schooling for girls and wider family planning reach.
pmc-12118161:
Aleksandar Cirovic and others looked again at newborn hepatitis B shots in two thousand twenty-three. The authors read past work on aluminum in vaccines. They also weighed reasons for very early shots. In high-risk regions, early shots prevent mother-to-child spread. Many mothers carrying the virus live in such areas. Risk of infection at birth there is serious.

Low-risk countries give shots early too, they note. Very few newborns there face real contact, though. The authors claim aluminum adjuvants pose nerve-harming risk. They argue such vaccines should pause until children walk. They propose calcium or other helpers instead. That view is their own case, stated as their own finding.
pmc-12672161:
Rojan Abdollahzadeh Mirali and five co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-five on surgery for clots in the aorta tied to COVID-19 and to a vaccine linked clotting illness. The virus can spark a clot prone state, and a clot in the main artery is rare but dire. The vaccine illness adds low platelets to the clot risk, a hard mix for surgery.

Care turns on clot load and patient state. Open clot removal and bypass suit heavy loads; scope routes suit frail patients. Death rates stay high, and clots can return or limbs be lost. In the vaccine illness, non-heparin blood thinners and close blood watch are key. Late finds and wrong thinners worsen odds.
pmc-12692661:
Cong Danh Nguyen and colleagues test whether turning up a sugar-splitting gene in rice all the time would raise grain yield, in a twenty twenty-five study. Genes of this family set up sugar gradients between leaves, which make food, and grains, which store it. The team built rice plants that kept the gene OsCIN1 switched on in all tissues, driven by a strong viral switch.

The boosted plants broke down sugar faster, yet their leaves were nearly drained of table sugar at flowering. Extra simple sugars and starch piled up in the wrong places instead. In field trials the plants grew about half as many side shoots and lighter grains, so output fell. The work shows that where and when this gene acts matters more than raw strength.
pmc-12693961:
Yuting Wu and colleagues report a 2025 advance in laser design using colloidal quantum dots, tiny crystals suspended in liquid. Quantum dots can emit laser light, but until now only at low power, which blocked real uses. The team set out to break that limit with a new setup.

They paired the dots with a seed-and-amplifier layout, where a small laser beam is boosted in stages. Careful light tests showed why these dots perform so well: a narrow beam color and strong energy binding inside the dots. A special cavity let the beam color be tuned across a range. The boosted output reached peak power in the megawatt range, with a steady, focused beam. The team even used it to drive light-based research tasks. High-power dot lasers could widen what cheap, printable materials can do.
pmc-12698661:
Yang, Lei, Ren, Qin, and Xia review epigenetic control of the lung cancer environment, in work from twenty twenty-five. Lung cancer has among the highest incidence and death rates worldwide. Late detection, spread, and drug resistance drive its toll.

The tumor microenvironment, the mix of immune cells, vessels, and stroma around a tumor, helps sustain and advance it. Epigenetic changes, chemical marks on DNA and its packaging proteins, regulate that environment. The review covers mechanisms and therapeutic prospects. Drugs that reset epigenetic marks could make the environment hostile to the tumor instead of helpful.
pmc-12699561:
Emilie van der Valk Bouman and a Dutch team lay out a trial to test whether music calms patients waking from electroconvulsive therapy. Their protocol was published in twenty twenty-five. Agitation after the induced seizure is common, and the drugs used against it carry unwanted effects.

The open multicentre trial aims to enroll ninety-two patients at two centers in Rotterdam. Patients are assigned at random to music or standard care. The music group hears recorded music for half an hour before and twelve minutes after each of the first six sessions. The team will measure agitation, plus anxiety before treatment and thinking problems after. If music works, it would offer a gentle, drug-free way to ease recovery. The protocol is a plan; results will come later.
pmc-12700861:
Dale Hughes, Daniel Dundas, Phuong Mai Dinh, Paul-Gerhard Reinhard, and Eric Suraud study how nitrogen molecules respond to a flash of extreme ultraviolet light in two thousand twenty-five. Past work found that the molecule's electric response can grow unstable after such a flash. The flash flips the usual balance of electron states, and the instability follows from that flip.

Computer runs track the molecule in real time on a spatial grid. Pulses lasting a single femtosecond were varied in strength, and the team charted growth rate, charge loss, and the size of the flip. Past a point, stronger pulses made the growth rate fall, a new twist on the effect. The pattern held across distinct ways of modeling the ion cores.
pmc-12702261:
Adan, Hirsi Snr, and Jayte reported a case in twenty twenty-five of a Ugandan woman whose rheumatoid arthritis had scarred her lungs, a serious complication called interstitial lung disease. Diagnosing and treating it is hard where advanced scans and tests are scarce.

The patient, aged forty, had lived with arthritis for six years. She arrived with three months of worsening cough, breathlessness, and chest pain, and her oxygen level was dangerously low. Basic imaging showed widespread lung shadowing and fibrotic change. Two key confirmatory tests simply did not exist at her facility. Doctors treated her with oxygen, steroids, and an arthritis drug, plus rehabilitation and lifestyle changes. Two months later her symptoms had eased markedly. The authors use the case to argue for stronger diagnostic capacity in low-resource hospitals.
pmc-12705461:
Briana Applewhite and four colleagues published a combined analysis in two thousand twenty-five on arts therapies for trauma in young people. Post-traumatic stress is rising among youth, and standard treatments help unevenly. Music, dance, art, and drama therapies are gaining ground as complements.

Thirty-three trials and quasi-experiments with over four thousand five hundred participants were pooled. Arts interventions cut symptoms substantially overall. Effects were strong in diagnosed cases and in general trauma groups. West African and Middle Eastern samples showed large gains. Western samples showed no significant effect, a gap the authors flag for study. They call the arts a culturally fitting tool, above all outside the West.
pmc-12706961:
Seyhan Çerçi and Ülkü Baykal build a scale for how health workers feel about quality work, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Quality programs lift patient and staff satisfaction. No trusted tool measured staff views on them. Over a thousand Istanbul hospital workers took part.

The team drafted items, took expert views, and ran a pilot. Factor tests split the scale into three parts. Forty-two items survived the checks. Scores for internal consistency were very high. Fit tests backed the final shape. The authors call the scale valid and reliable. Hospitals can now gauge staff buy-in before quality drives. That helps plan changes people will accept.
pmc-12711561:
Zierer and a large team boost cassava yields by tuning how the plant moves potassium, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Cassava feeds many small farms in the tropics, but yields stay low. Drought, poor soil, and disease all cut the harvest. The team placed a tweaked plant gene for potassium flow into the plant veins.

The changed plants moved sugars from leaves to roots faster. They also used light and carbon at higher rates. Storage root yield rose in glasshouse tests and in a multi-year field trial. The plants also stood up better to drought with no extra fertilizer. The work offers a path to stronger harvests in harsh climates.
pmc-12714761:
Ping Qin and three co-authors study how knowing a water tariff affects household conservation, in work from twenty twenty-five. Residential water use is growing faster than other sectors as cities and incomes grow. That demand threatens freshwater supplies worldwide.

Governments respond by redesigning tariffs and raising prices. A seven year dataset of daily household water use from several Chinese counties gave the evidence. Reforms that changed structure and price together produced only short lived savings before use rebounded. The title states the remedy: familiarity with the tariff sustains conservation. Policy design thus needs user understanding, not just price signals.
pmc-12718561:
Rosa Ferrer Tarrés and six colleagues report the case of a sixty-five-year-old man with a rare autoimmune brain disease, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The disease, tied to antibodies against a brain receptor called GABA-B, usually causes seizures and memory loss. It often appears alongside a type of lung cancer. The man arrived with nonstop seizures, and tests found the antibodies in his blood and spinal fluid.

Strong steroid treatment helped him improve, yet he died suddenly during recovery. An autopsy found the expected immune attack in his brain and a hidden lung tumor. It also found immune cells inside his heart muscle, a sign of heart inflammation. The authors suggest heart checks may be wise for patients with this disease.
pmc-12732361:
Pauline Jubin and colleagues published a pain study in 2025. They explored blood proteins during acute muscle pain. Salty fluid injected into muscle safely models pain. Healthy volunteers joined two linked study cohorts. Blood was sampled before, during, and after pain. Protein and cytokine profiles were tracked over time. A second group mapped spreading touch sensitivity carefully. Sensitivity spread across the same-side limb during pain. The other limb showed no such sensitivity gain.

Many blood proteins changed with acute pain onset. Changes pointed to metabolism and immune pathways broadly. Pain seems to trigger body-wide molecular responses quickly. Local sensitivity spread stayed on the treated side though. Systemic signals and local sensitivity may diverge mechanistically. The dataset opens new questions about pain biology.
pmc-12736461:
Eun Jin Kim and co-authors build a packed air filter system in this 2025 paper. The system uses loose filter balls that can be rearranged as needed. One ball type targets fine dust particles. Another targets formaldehyde, a common indoor pollutant. Both need to work without blocking air flow.

Dust balls were made from etched sponge and glass fiber with magnesium and silicon added. They removed 97.4 percent of fine particles at low pressure drop. The formaldehyde balls cleared the gas fully within one minute. A half and half mix did both jobs at once, with the same low pressure drop. Performance held over 50 reuse cycles. The design suits homes and offices that need flexible cleaning.
pmc-12738561:
Tariq Alqubaysi and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study on stronger, greener road concrete. Cement making drives a large share of world carbon emissions. Recycled concrete aggregate can replace natural stone, but weak old mortar limits its strength.

The team treated recycled aggregate with metakaolin slurry and added silica fume at several doses. Mixes used recycled aggregate at four replacement levels, up to full replacement. Tests showed clear gains in strength and durability, backed by statistical checks. Machine learning helped tune the mix. Road builders get evidence that treated recycled material can serve in rigid pavements.
pmc-12740061:
Deskins and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a quality improvement report on children returning after tonsil removal surgery. Tonsillectomy is one of the most common outpatient operations in children. Their hospital found seven-day revisit rates above national peers in early twenty twenty-five. Pain and dehydration looked like the main drivers of returns. A multidisciplinary team built a bundle to prevent both. It standardized fluids and pain medicines during surgery and recovery.

Discharge packets added a two-day hydration checklist and a medication calendar. Planned family check-ins aligned expectations after going home. Three improvement cycles ran under a unit-based safety program. Early revisit rates fell from about three point eight to two point two percent. The team judged the bundle feasible in daily practice. Longer monitoring will test whether the gains hold.
pmc-12742461:
