Leo Biggs and seven colleagues use citizen science to compare the diets of two Australian coastal raptors, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The Eastern Osprey and the White-bellied Sea-Eagle share shoreline hunting grounds. Whether they compete for the same prey or divide it was hard to test.

Traditional diet studies demand huge effort and skew toward nesting birds. Photos and videos posted on social media offered a shortcut. The team mined that material to measure dietary breadth, diversity, and overlap between the species. Citizen records cover wide areas and non-breeding birds alike. The approach tests whether public wildlife media can answer real ecological questions about predator competition.
pmc-12747661:
Andres Parga and co-authors review teledermatology for skin cancer in rural areas in this 2025 paper. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States. Rural patients face late diagnosis due to distance and a shortage of skin doctors. Remote review of skin images could close that gap.

The review searched four databases for studies from 2015 to March 2025. It covered diagnostic accuracy, time to diagnosis, and patient satisfaction. It also covered barriers to rollout and equity effects. Rural programs must handle weak connectivity, licensing rules, and uneven access to devices. The authors weigh whether remote care truly narrows the rural gap. Their synthesis can guide clinics planning services for underserved areas.
pmc-12751661:
Alison El Ayadi, Nadia Diamond-Smith, Mia Schuman, and Laura Weil ask how folks in group care for the unborn use web apps by their own pick. The work came out in 2025. Group care, through the Centering Pregnancy plan, builds face-to-face aid while a child grows. It stops at birth, just when lone days can sink in deep.

The team asked if sick folks and their mates fill that gap with their phones now. They polled past folks in a plan at the San Francisco school of the state. Health files and mail were used to reach them. The asks mapped which apps folks use and what they use them for. They asked if phone aid feels of use while a child grows and past birth. Aid from peers is a real health input for new mums and dads.
pmc-12766761: Burlew and six co-authors collected practical tips for trauma surgeons from a twenty twenty-four certification course session. The article gathers experience-driven advice on four topics. They are preperitoneal pelvic packing for pelvic bleeding, and trauma video review for team improvement. Also covered are camera-assisted chest surgery for retained blood in the chest, and keyhole exploration of the common bile duct. The authors frame the shared aim as sharper technique, better team performance, and better patient outcomes through deliberate, refined practice.
pmc-12770561:
Qiqi Yang and colleagues studied drug resistance in a childhood muscle cancer in 2025. The cancer is called rhabdomyosarcoma. A two-drug pairing is now in clinical trials for it. Resistance to that pairing has appeared in other cancers. The team grew human tumors in mice and treated them. The pairing shrank tumors at first. Over half later resisted treatment and grew again. Resistant tumors changed gene activity without new shared mutations.

Most resistant models switched on one growth pathway. That pathway woke a stress protein and its target genes. Those genes build pumps that push drugs out of cells. A drug blocking the pathway made resistant cells sensitive again. The triple pairing also killed cells that resisted standard chemotherapy. It curbed tumor growth in the mouse models too. The authors name this pathway as a common escape route. They propose blocking it as a strategy against resistant disease.
pmc-12772961:
Dawson Cooper and a large team of co-authors ask whether the side of a brain bleed shapes mood and pain afterward. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Bleeding inside the brain is a severe stroke type, and its non-physical effects are often overlooked.

The work reuses data from a large international trial of surgery plus clot-dissolving treatment. About four hundred ninety-three patients were assessed at one month, six months, and one year. Those with right-side bleeds reported more pain and discomfort at every check. They also reported more anxiety and depression early on. Standard function scores were tracked beside the mood measures. The authors argue recovery care should weigh bleed side when watching for pain and mood problems.
pmc-12774961:
Zi-Jing Zhang, Ziyue Liu, Xinran Chen, and Lutz Ackermann report iron-catalysed alkene reactions driven by mechanochemistry. Their chemistry paper from twenty twenty-five joins indoles with alkenes. Such products matter for bioactive molecules and drug candidates. Older methods needed harsh reagents and struggled with simple alkenes.

Grinding-based chemistry replaces much solvent use in the new method. An iron catalyst with a carbene ligand directs the bond formation. Swapping the ligand flips which product form dominates for aryl alkenes. Magnesium metal cleanly generates the active iron species. Lab tests and computer studies explain how the catalyst works. Data analysis also pinpointed which ligand features control the product choice.
pmc-12780461:
Stephan Möller, Sophia Cole, Anna Möller, and Jan Adriaan Graw hunt for what makes some heart-bypass patients need a breath machine for long. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, reads one year of cases at a large center.

Long breath aid brings grave risks, such as lung infection, and lifts death rates. The team took all who had lone bypass surgery and care in the joint unit that year. Most were off the machine in a day, at a mid time of half a day and a bit. The rest form the group to explain. The aim is to name fresh risk marks for the long-need state.
pmc-12784661:
Hansun Fang and co-authors test a fish drug on young zebrafish, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Eggs were placed in water with the drug from four hours after laying to four days. Doses ranged from trace levels found in nature to very high ones.

At high doses, many cells died by a self-kill path, and genes for that path switched on. Brain growth genes rose in an odd way at the same doses. Genes that place chemical marks on DNA fell in turn. The results warn that heavy use of the drug in fish farming could harm young fish and waters.
pmc-12787761:
Emine Hozdić and Elvis Hozdić test how print settings and oil shape the strength of 3D-printed plastic parts. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses plain PLA and a carbon-fiber blend. Parts were printed with three inner patterns at three densities. A week in mineral oil followed, to mimic work fluids.

For plain plastic, a sparse straight pattern gave the top tensile strength. A honeycomb pattern stretched the most before breaking. Oil slightly softened the plain plastic but made it far more stretchy. The fiber blend grew stronger with density and even gained from oil. Pore size shrank after oil in the blend, which the images confirm.
pmc-12788261:
Qisheng Xu and co-authors gauge the light-bending power of tiny hollow silica capsules with sound-like light modes in two thousand twenty-five. The capsules are uniform, porous, and hollow, with uses that hinge on how light moves through their walls. That trait, the refractive index, is hard to pin down for such spongy shells.

Capsules dyed with Rhodamine B trap light in whispering gallery modes, rings of light that circle the shell. The glow spectrum shows evenly spaced peaks, and a math transform reads the gap. One capsule size gave an index of about one point one six. Two standard mix models then implied a porosity near sixty-three percent, matching gas-based pore tests. The optical route checks single particles without harm.
pmc-12812661:
Xianbin Wang, Sijie Sun, Yan Chen, and four colleagues test magnetic brain stimulation for stroke walking recovery in this two thousand twenty-six trial, run at random with a sham arm. Sixty-three stroke patients were split evenly into three groups: sham stimulation, stimulation of the affected leg's motor cortex alone, or dual-target stimulation adding the opposite cerebellum. Everyone also received standard rehabilitation, with daily stimulation at eighty percent intensity for twenty-one days. Outcomes combined function and balance scales, three-dimensional gait analysis, and near-infrared brain imaging.

After treatment, the dual-target group improved much more than both other groups in lower limb motor function and balance scores. Gait measures, including step length, improved most in that group, and brain network measures were tracked. The authors conclude stimulating both together beats either standard care with sham or single-target stimulation for restoring gait after stroke.
pmc-12816261:
Alina Petrica and colleagues surveyed health workers and technology professionals in two thousand twenty-six about using artificial intelligence to sort emergency patients. Sorting, called triage, decides who is seen first, and trust may matter as much as smart software. Their online survey used standard attitude scales and grouped answers into patterns.

Three outlooks emerged: cautious critics, keen optimists, and a larger balanced group in the middle. About two-thirds fell outside the keen group, showing adoption will need care. Hospital planners learn that staff views differ sharply by background, and rollout plans must earn trust across both clinical and technical teams.
pmc-12820361:
Bin Yang, Shihang Zhang, and Xiaoguo Wang map soil carbon across China and split the picture by dry versus wet zones. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Soil carbon stores matter for China's pledge to reach net-zero carbon by twenty sixty. Yet how dry and wet zones store and shift carbon was still unclear.

A random forest model drew fine maps from a large soil data set and read most of the spread well. Wet zones held more soil carbon than dry zones at both depths checked. Rain and heat drove dry-zone stores most, while heat, rain, and height drove wet zones. Next-era scenes show dry stores falling and wet stores rising.
pmc-12821261:
Zhao and co-authors link early pregnancy uric acid to later gestational diabetes risk. The cohort sat in Xi'an, China, from 2018 to 2023. Women joined in their first trimester of pregnancy. Diabetes risk rose across uric acid quartiles in step. The top quartile carried a risk ratio of 1.46.

Uric acid ranked as the top predictor after body mass. Risk climbed once body mass passed 18.5 in their models. The high acid plus high body mass pairing held the most risk. The second quartile already showed a small rise, at 1.15. The authors flag acid as a marker worth causal study.
pmc-12822061:
Humphreys and coauthors probe flaws in vaccine studies that use health records. Record-based studies give fast, real-world vaccine proof. Records can misclassify cases and hide key patient traits, though. Both flaws can bend the vaccine effect that studies report.

The team checked a large European COVID vaccine study. Records spanned up to 18.7 million people in many states. A control outcome, deaths not tied to COVID, flagged hidden bias. Shifts from data pull timing were also checked in full. Two time spans, in late 2023 and early 2024, were used. Fixes may lift trust in record-based proof.
pmc-12827261:
Chang and four co-authors compared gut germs in twenty twenty-five among autistic folks, their well siblings, and a control group. Sibling checks help spot marks of a trait while kin share much of life and genes. The groups held more than four hundred young folks in all.

Well siblings had the most wide range of germ kinds, and autistic folks had a set that set them apart. Some kinds were more rich in controls, and a few ruled in siblings. Germ mix tied to trait signs and gut signs in the autistic group. One kind went with less social strain and fewer inner woes.
pmc-12828861:
Ramnarain, Hosking, and Gibbs report a rare form of inherited transthyretin amyloidosis in a 54-year-old Australian woman. A single change in the gene, written p.Asp58Val, makes a faulty blood protein. That protein builds up and harms organs over time.

Repeated fainting was her main early symptom, well before the cause was found. Care then drew on a team of specialists to keep her function as high as possible. The authors also compare her case with prior reports. They note that nerve damage followed by heart muscle disease may mark this rare variant.
pmc-12829061:
Paulina Olgemöller and co-authors lay out a trial protocol in 2025 for brain training in advanced Parkinson's disease. Thinking problems are common in Parkinson's, and most patients face dementia over time. Drug options are few, so training the mind by computer is a hopeful path, but it has rarely been tried at advanced stages.

The trial will enroll one hundred forty patients. Half will get five weeks of structured digital training at home, plus short videos on brain health. Half will get usual care. The team will test thinking, movement, mood, and quality of life before, after, and three months later. Training diaries will show whether the program is workable and welcome at this stage.
pmc-12830061:
Vallabhan and co-authors survey gum conditions around crooked teeth in orthodontic patients in Tamil Nadu, India. Gum deformities often gather near poorly aligned teeth. They can raise the risk of attachment loss during brace treatment. A full gum check before treatment helps prevent that harm. Patient awareness also eases fear of corrective steps. The study measured how common these conditions are by bite type.

Questionnaires captured what patients knew about their own gums. Quality of life tied to oral health was scored as well. The team compared groups by Angle's class of bite fault. Results can shape pre-treatment counseling in orthodontic clinics.
pmc-12845261:
Maria Coanda and co-authors design new hybrid drug molecules in this 2025 paper. Their scaffold joins quinazolinone, a ring system with wide biological activity, to hydrazone linkers. Six compounds were made by a green microwave method from varied aldehydes. Standard spectroscopy and mass checks confirmed each structure.

Computer models and docking simulations predicted how the molecules might act. Lab assays then tested antioxidant strength, microbe killing, and cancer cell toxicity. A brine shrimp test gave early safety signals. Joining two proven pharmacophores can yield multi use agents in one molecule. The series offers starting points for drugs that fight infection and oxidation together. Further work must separate the most potent from the merely active.
pmc-12847961:
Soyoung Kwak and eight colleagues tested whether alpha-lipoic acid protects the brain after a stroke-like injury in mice. When blood flow returns after a blockage, the reperfusion itself triggers oxidative stress, inflammation, and barrier damage. The hippocampus is especially vulnerable. The twenty twenty-five study used a mouse model where both neck arteries were briefly blocked. A cell culture model of oxygen and glucose deprivation provided a second test bed.

Treated mice showed better spatial memory without changes in movement. The acid restored barrier proteins and antioxidant enzymes in the hippocampus. In cells, it lowered reactive oxygen species, improved survival, and reduced cell death signals. Synaptic proteins were not restored, so the authors suggest protection works through other routes, chiefly barrier stabilization and oxidative stress control.
pmc-12852761:
Ruoqian Xie and nine co-authors tag gene bricks at a set spot with a light-plus-copper trick. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Tagged bricks serve in ill finds, cures, and nano work, but old ways need pre-set bricks or fail with fat tags. Their way joins bricks and chains to fat-tag roots through a light and copper pair that cuts a gas part free.

The join is plain and straight, and works late on whole chains as well as lone bricks. Wide roots can feed it. The team pitch it for drug and life work where such tags count.
pmc-12853661:
Chacón and four co-authors tour rust math in worn-out cells in this twenty twenty-six review. Worn cells stop growth and leak signs that age the flesh round them. Rust marks are a core trait of that worn state in cells.

Inside, brew scans of man skin cells map how rust paths re-set. One shield brew path stands at the heart of that re-set. The worn leak set ties back to those rust shifts at each turn. Rust acts also keep the worn state firm once it forms. The tour shows which paths ask for deep reads next.
pmc-12853761:
Arezoo Solati and six co-authors test stem-cell products for maturing eggs in a 2025 paper. They used fluid the cells grew in, and the tiny vesicles those cells shed, both from umbilical cord tissue stem cells. Immature eggs came from normal mice and from mice given a drug-induced version of a common hormone disorder. Eggs were matured in dishes with plain medium or medium plus one of the products. Staining picked out promising eggs first.

Both products raised maturation rates compared with plain medium. Eggs from disorder-model mice matured poorly and degenerated more, but treatment rescued much of that loss. Gene activity shifts in key cell-cycle regulators matched the improvement.
pmc-12859861:
Kihwan Kim and three colleagues published a biofuel study in two thousand twenty-five on reworking a plant's wood chemistry. Woody biomass resists breakdown because lignin shields its sugars. Cutting lignin helps, but too little weakens the plant.

Using a model plant, the team knocked out two lignin-building genes and boosted a wall-building switch gene at the same time. The engineered plants had about a third less lignin. At the same time their cellulose rose by about a quarter and another wall sugar rose by half. Sugar release during breakdown improved over both normal and knockout-only plants. Yeast then turned the extra sugar into more ethanol. The authors call it a balanced design.
pmc-12860461:
Mahtab Zargham and five co-authors report long-term results in two thousand twenty-five for a double sling surgery. The patients were women with severe front vaginal wall prolapse plus stress urinary incontinence that had not responded to conservative care. Their repair used a four-arm mesh made of PVDF, a plastic with good tissue tolerance.

Thirty-eight women had the combined surgery and were followed for at least two years, on average over five. Scores for vaginal symptoms and incontinence improved clearly at two years. The anatomical success rate was eighty-three percent. Two mesh exposures appeared after four years, with no other severe mesh problems. The authors call the procedure safe and convenient for this selected group.
pmc-12866561:
Mahamadou Sagara, Abderrahim Majjad, Laila Taoubane, and Ahmed Bezza gauged low mood in patients with painful knee osteoarthritis in twenty twenty-five. The joint disease is a major health burden in Morocco, but its tie to mental health is little charted in the region. The study took in four hundred ten patients, scored their joint symptoms with a standard index, and screened mood with a hospital scale.

Nearly thirty-two percent met the bar for clear low mood, and most of them were women. Low mood tracked being female, a higher body mass index, worse pain, worse function, other ills, and being inactive. The X-ray grade of joint damage, by contrast, showed no tie to low mood. The authors say care for knee osteoarthritis should screen for low mood and treat the traits that feed it.
pmc-12907761:
Qudus Lawal and a large team sum up a research conference in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The twenty twenty-five African Voices for Research Virtual Conference gathered cross-field work on Africa's public health problems. The authors summed up all submitted abstracts in narrative form, using an AI tool to help spot patterns and themes, with the team checking results. Themes were grouped into broader classes of problems and fixes.

The summary showed health care access, schooling, environmental justice, gender equity, and innovation meeting around universal coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. Through social determinants and One Health lenses, infrastructure gaps, money barriers, and low health literacy emerged as drivers of unequal results. Case studies on maternal health and environmental exposures showed how socioeconomic inequality and structural violence shape health. The paper argues African public health needs joined responses across fields rather than single-sector fixes.
pmc-13080261:
Six authors report a case dated two thousand twenty-six of a rare cancer spread. A woman aged eighty-one came to hospital after a fall and signs of a stroke. Scans done for another problem found a large mass in her uterus and a small lesion in her pancreas. Tests pointed to a uterine muscle cancer called leiomyosarcoma.

A biopsy of the pancreas lesion showed the same cancer had spread there, with no other spread found. Spread to the pancreas alone is very rare for this cancer, which more often goes to the lungs or liver. Given her other health problems, the patient chose hospice care after full advice from the care team.
pmc-13117361:
De Salvatore and a team of colleagues compared recovery pathways after scoliosis surgery in adolescents in twenty twenty-six. Posterior spinal fusion corrects the curved spine but brings a hard recovery. Structured Enhanced Recovery pathways, here combined with a nerve-numbing erector spinae plane block, promise faster, less painful recovery, yet pediatric evidence is thin.

At one center, thirty-four patients treated before June twenty twenty-five under standard care were compared with thirty-five treated after, under the new pathway. Pain at rest on the day of surgery was far lower in the pathway group, and pain during standing was lower on later days and at two weeks. Nausea was less common on some days. Hospital stay shrank from about eight nights to about five and a half. The authors call for prospective multicenter confirmation.
pmc-13132661:
Daisuke Fukuyama and four co-authors studied how a fuel molecule breaks into ions in a corona discharge. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, deals with n-heptane at air pressure. They read which ions form when the molecule is charged this way. The plain molecule ion and a hydride stripped ion come from known paths: tunnel charging in a strong field, and hydride grab reactions.

Other ions lose two, three, or five hydrogen atoms. The team puts forth that those come from loss of single hydrogens off the stripped ion. They also map the shapes and electron states of the ions. This is part one of a series. Readers in mass spectrometry get a step map of a plain fuel's ion paths.
pmc-13143161:
Jiyeon Yu, Angelica de Antonio, and Elena Villalba-Mora segment older adults by lifestyle for smart home design in this 2026 paper. Spain has a fast growing older population. Smart homes can support safety, health, and independence at home. Older adults differ widely in lifestyle, health, and tech experience, so one design will not fit all.

The survey groups respondents by how they live at home. Each group gets a profile of needs and readiness for smart home tools. Functions covered include environment control, safety monitoring, and communication aids. Matching features to real and perceived needs should raise adoption. The work helps companies and care planners target the right tools to the right households.
pmc-13151661:
Vergouwen, Ramos-Pachon, and a large panel set out a European guideline for bleeding in the brain from a burst aneurysm. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Such a bleed kills a large share of patients, and many who live face lasting harm to thought, body, or mood.

The guide grades proof from trials, reviews, and large cohorts. Firm advice backs one drug by mouth and favours coiling over clipping when both suit a patient in good shape. It rules out a set of drugs with no gain. A run of expert points adds care in a specialist unit and repair of the burst within a day. For many steps, proof is too weak for firm rules.
pmc-13154661:
Xuan Zhou leads a team of eight authors finding a lethal dependency in prostate cancers that have lost the ATM repair gene, a common event in advanced disease. An unbiased drug screen searched for compounds that kill ATM-deficient cells selectively. Blocking PARG, the enzyme that dismantles poly(ADP-ribose) chains, emerged as the hit, confirmed across cell lines and reversed when ATM was restored.

In the deficient cells, PARG blockade let those chains pile up persistently, not through the usual double-strand-break alarm but through ribonucleotides wrongly built into DNA. Mouse xenografts lacking ATM tested the strategy in vivo. The work runs from mechanism to therapeutic pitch: a synthetic-lethal target for a cancer subtype that badly needs one.
pmc-13171361:
Kurt Eggers and Sharon Millard ask what shapes the burden of stuttering in school children in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. How hard stuttering hits a child may depend on temperament and mood, not just speech severity. Past results on severity alone have been mixed.

The study covered three hundred six children aged nine to fourteen seen at a specialist center. A standard scale measured each child's lived impact of stuttering. Bolder temperament predicted lower impact. Higher negative affect, more anxiety and depression signs, older age, and worse overt stuttering each predicted higher impact. Self-control and sex did not matter. The authors call for models that add more factors.
pmc-13181161:
Palma and co-authors build a joint frame that ties sway in health marks to end times. Marks read through time can sway, and that sway may flag ill pace. Plain per-host spreads miss how sway shifts through time. They also bend risk marks when fed as traits in end fits. Their joint frame sets the tie through the sway term straight. A place-scale form reads the marks, their sway, and their ties.

End time takes a share-risk form with a bent base line. Facts from the marks pass to the end form through hid parts. The tie is set in terms of each host's own sway. That set-up lets sway grade be read in clean terms. The frame is Bayes in build, with odds drawn from the pool. It serves more than one mark read at once in hosts.
pmc-13182761:
Kugler and a team of colleagues surveyed patients with ventricular assist devices in twenty twenty-six about traumatic stress. These pumps support a failing heart, and living with one can be hard psychologically. The team asked how common traumatic experiences and stress symptoms are in this group.

The multicenter study gathered two hundred sixty-five patients, mostly men, with an average age of fifty-nine. About forty-three percent reported some traumatizing life event, split evenly between heart-related and other events. Heart surgery was the most cited event. Yet measured stress symptom rates were low, under four percent. Patients reporting trauma showed no worse anxiety, depression, or quality of life. Women faced higher depression risk. The authors still urge routine screening after implantation.
pmc-13194361:
Kaden and co-authors test a bile acid on inflamed gut tissue grown in a chip system. Inflammatory bowel disease has many causes and no curative treatment yet. Past work found that fecal bile acid levels shift with gut microbes and inflammation in this disease.

Lithocholic acid, a secondary bile acid, drops sharply during active disease. Yet it seems to help the gut lining when present. The team applied it in a human intestine-on-chip model with colitis-like inflammation. The acid eased the inflammation in this system, backing its promise as a lead for new gut therapies.
pmc-13196961:
Brent D Mishler and colleagues introduce a 2026 method for mapping where rare lineages live. Endemism means a lineage lives in just one small area. Scientists sort it as new, old, or in between, based on branch length on the family tree of life.

Their method compares each branch on a range-weighted tree with the same branch set to equal length. The gap shows which branches add most to local rarity. It adds a middle class for lineages that are range-bound but neither very young nor very old. They show the method on Acacia plants across Australia. It can pinpoint branches behind rarity hotspots, which may sharpen protection plans.
pmc-13197261:
Alexandru Guranda and colleagues published a 2026 study on brain bleed shape and patient outcome. A deep brain bleed with spread into inner fluid spaces is hard to forecast. The standard ICH Score uses bleed size and clinical signs, so the team asked whether bleed shape adds more signal.

They studied fifty patients with deep bleeds and inner spread. Software outlines yielded shape measures such as roundness and surface area. Bleed roundness forecast in-hospital death about as well as bleed size did. Lower roundness still linked to death once the standard score was counted, while size lost its edge. Shape traits of the inner spread showed no link. Roundness may refine forecasts beside the score.
pmc-13197361:
Nawin Ngampoopun and colleagues present a 2026 case study of a coronal hole edge on the Sun. Coronal holes are dark, open-field regions in the Sun's outer air that release the solar wind. Their edges, where open and closed magnetic fields meet, host key reshaping events.

The team studied one large low-latitude hole, mapping plasma traits and edge roughness. The leading edge was slightly hotter, with a stronger and more one-sided magnetic field, and had a smoother line. The trailing edge was rougher and more mixed. They link the contrast to nearby loop shapes: large neat loops at the front, small scattered loops behind. Local field layout, they argue, shapes edge traits.
pmc-13198061:
Alfonso Valenzuela Hurtado and colleagues compared costs of robotic bowel surgery with and without a care pathway in 2026. A clinical pathway is a standard step-by-step care plan meant to cut variation and waste. Whether it saves money in robotic colorectal surgery was unknown.

The team costed care for sixty-three patients in detail, counting supplies, staff, and complication care. Twenty-one patients followed the pathway and forty-two did not. Mean cost per patient ran higher in the pathway group, though the gap was not firm proof of a real rise. Supplies and staff drove costs in both groups. Robot use level swung yearly costs a lot. A pathway alone did not cut the bill here.
pmc-13200361:
Mariano Esperatti and colleagues review steroid use in acute respiratory distress syndrome in a 2026 article. ARDS is severe lung failure with high death rates. Inflammation drives the damage, so steroids, which calm inflammation, have long been a plausible therapy, yet practice still varies worldwide.

Trials over decades tested varied drugs, doses, and start times, with COVID-19 adding proof for virus-driven cases. A new wider definition now covers patients on noninvasive support, raising questions about older evidence. The authors propose a practical framework: start early, within one to two days, at solid doses for at least seven days, matched to cause and patient traits. Subtype-specific proof remains a research need.
pmc-13200961:
Hatice Ağir, Aydin Çifçi, Turgut Kültür, and six colleagues study, published in 2026, fibromyalgia in dialysis patients at two Turkish centers. The widespread pain condition is common in kidney failure yet often missed. One hundred twenty-six patients were split by standard criteria: sixty-six with fibromyalgia, sixty without. The team compared quality of life scores, pain impact surveys, and blood measures of oxidative balance built around thiol compounds. The study ran across the second half of 2024.

Patients with fibromyalgia scored worse on every quality of life domain and on the pain impact survey. The balance ratios between the compounds did not shift. Links between the blood values and the survey scores were weak. Total thiol stayed tied to fibromyalgia after adjustment, but explained little. The authors advise caution: the condition clearly burdens life on dialysis, while its chemistry stays murky.
pmc-13202061:
Pain beliefs may shape how back muscles respond to therapy, and a 2026 prospective cohort analysis authored by Ryan Lebens studies that connection in chronic low back pain. The research article uses registry data from patients completing an eight to ten week supervised, training-based physical therapy program.

Participants filled in psychosocial surveys before treatment, and technicians measured lumbar extensor strength with an isokinetic dynamometer. Strength, pain, and disability all improved on average during the program, though strength gains did not track symptom gains. Greater improvement was linked to lower fear avoidance, and stronger muscles were linked to higher confidence in managing pain, suggesting coping support belongs inside rehabilitation.
pmc-13205361:
Jun Huang and four co-authors published a randomized crossover trial in twenty twenty-six on whether a smaller dose works for the urea breath test that detects Helicobacter pylori. The stomach bacterium drives ulcers and cancer risk, and breath testing is the gentle way to find it. Four hundred thirty-one adults took both the standard and low-dose tests on the same day.

Agreement between the forty-five and seventy-five milligram versions was substantial, above ninety percent at thirty minutes. Sampling at thirty minutes beat fifteen minutes for both doses. The low dose's accuracy was statistically non-inferior to the standard. Younger and leaner participants did especially well on it. A cheaper, lighter test looks viable for routine diagnosis.
pmc-13210561:
Smart ankle prostheses cost too much for most amputees, and a 2026 engineering study led by Zhanar Bigaliyeva builds a cheaper prototype. The article presents a microprocessor-controlled ankle driven by a ball-screw and stepper motor, governed by an ESP32 chip with an inertial sensor and a wireless control interface.

Bench tests without load showed the joint moving through its programmed step range with repeatable angles and a reliable homing routine. The design actively bends the ankle up and down, while a passive side-tilt mechanism adds adaptability to uneven ground in the structure. The authors frame the device as a feasibility platform awaiting load and walking trials.
pmc-13212661:
Vincent van de Ven and colleagues report in 2026 on how familiarity with a setting changes the way people cross event boundaries. Normally, a shift in context slows responses, because the brain must update its model of what is happening.

Volunteers viewed picture lists while sound backgrounds changed after every three pictures, with one sound repeated several extra times. Responses at boundaries grew faster with each repetition of the familiar sound, compared with fresh contexts. Ratings of how well pictures fit the sounds showed no such effect, and later memory for picture order was unchanged. Familiarity seems to ease boundary processing without strengthening event memory itself.
pmc-13213161:
Fathi Yasin Yusuf and Abdiwali Mohamed Hussein argue in 2026 that artificial intelligence could strengthen how Somali nursing schools test whether graduates are truly competent. Nursing education there has expanded fast, but standards, licensing checks, and rural access have not kept pace.

Their commentary maps promising tools, including adaptive learning platforms, AI-supported simulation, and automated feedback on practice tasks, against the system's real constraints. Tools must run on low bandwidth, stay under teacher supervision, and follow clear ethical rules, they say. Introduced in phases and aimed at known gaps in standardisation and feedback, such systems could raise graduate competence more fairly across city and countryside.
pmc-13215461:
Huimin Jiang and thirteen co-authors identify the protein SPARC as a driver of kidney scarring through an epigenetic relay, in a two thousand twenty-six nephrology paper. Tubulointerstitial fibrosis is the common final pathway as chronic kidney disease advances to failure.

SPARC levels tracked fibrosis severity in human biopsies and two mouse injury models, and deleting the gene markedly reduced scarring. Mechanistically, SPARC stabilizes the enzyme DOT1L, boosting a histone mark that switches on fibrotic programs in tubule cells. The acetyltransferase CBP controls DOT1L's stability through MEK-ERK signaling. Blocking any link in the SPARC-CBP-DOT1L chain, the authors argue, could slow fibrotic progression where few treatments exist.
pmc-13216661:
Mujtaba Bala and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review of family-level risk factors for noma. This gangrenous infection destroys the faces of young children in sub-Saharan Africa and kills most of its victims. Medicine usually blames malnutrition and infection; this review asks what household life adds.

Thirty-five studies met the criteria, spanning noma case series and wider child health literature. Eleven family themes emerged, from family size, income, and structure to caregiver quality, marital conflict, and separation. Poverty, large families, stretched caregiving, and household instability interlocked to raise children's vulnerability. The authors recommend prevention that works through families: economic support, caregiver education, birth spacing, and community outreach alongside medical measures.
pmc-13216861:
Muhammad Raza and co-authors present a 2026 environmental chemistry study turning banana peels into a sponge for Congo red dye, a stubborn pollutant in textile wastewater. The peels were tested raw and after loading with zinc oxide nanoparticles.

In batch experiments, each form had its best conditions: raw peel powder at pH 6 and the treated material at pH 5.8, both at a dose of 1.2 grams. Equilibrium data fitted the Temkin model best for the raw peel and Langmuir for the treated one, while uptake over time followed pseudo-second-order kinetics closely for both. Thermodynamic values indicated the process is spontaneous and releases heat. The authors offer the composite as a cheap, waste-derived option for dye removal.
pmc-13217261:
Vaez and co-authors weigh two kinds of genetic risk for psychiatric disorders together. Their 2026 study uses the Danish iPSYCH2015 case-cohort, covering 140,116 people drawn from national birth records, including over 92,000 with hospital diagnoses such as depression, autism, ADHD, and schizophrenia. The team examined recurrent copy number variants, rare deletions or duplications of DNA chunks, alongside polygenic scores, which sum many small common-variant effects.

The authors estimated absolute risks from each factor alone and in combination. They also asked what share of the population carries a polygenic burden matching a copy number variant's risk. They also compared polygenic profiles between variant carriers and non-carriers to probe whether cases arise through different routes. The study is designed to give clinically interpretable risk numbers rather than relative measures alone, across several disorders in one population sample.
pmc-13218161:
Rumanveer Singh Duley and colleagues review the part community pharmacies can play in preventing heart and vessel disease among minority ethnic groups in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 mixed-methods systematic review. Pharmacies are easy to reach and run screening and support services, which could help close prevention gaps for minority groups. Barriers to using those services, and what makes them work, needed mapping.

Searches across five databases plus grey literature, with citation tracking, yielded twenty-three matching studies. Using thematic synthesis, the reviewers found five themes: trust, systemic barriers, language fitted to culture, faith and cultural influences, and family and social networks. Pharmacies most often screened for heart risk and supported diabetes care, with smaller roles in quitting smoking, weight and cholesterol control, and helping patients stick with treatment. Language barriers, cultural beliefs, mistrust of providers, and time pressure limited engagement, while tailored services and language support helped.
pmc-13219361:
Herrera reviews how brains of late preterm infants wire up differently in this 2026 mini-review. Babies born at 34 to 36 weeks were long treated as nearly full term. Evidence now shows they face real risks for learning problems at school age.

The review gathers recent studies on brain connectivity in this group. It links altered connections to the cognitive weaknesses seen later. Herrera also flags where the evidence is thin and which brain-behavior ties need testing. The goal is practical: sharpen research questions and guide early intervention while the brain is most plastic. Late preterm birth is common, so even small risks affect many children.
pmc-13219461:
Andre Jatmiko Wijaya, Aleksandar Anžel, and Georges Hattab evaluate ensemble machine learning for spotting transferred genes in bacterial genomes in a 2026 study. Bacteria swap DNA through horizontal transfer, and the swapped blocks, called genomic islands, are a vehicle for spreading antibiotic resistance. Detecting them by computer would strengthen surveillance, and combining representations in one ensemble helps in other genomics tasks.

The team used a two-stage selection process to find the combination of representations for a classifier. Ensembles built from weakly correlated representations recalled more true islands than any single one, but the gain was not statistically significant. When the task shifted from classifying whole sequences to locating where islands sit inside them, the ensemble did no better than its parts. The authors read this as a cross-task generalization problem and suggest the field needs to rethink how island detection is posed before ensembles can deliver their advantage.
pmc-13220661:
Andreas Siebert and colleagues measure which ions crowd the surface of a calcium chloride solution in a 2025 study. Sea spray aerosols carry these salts into the atmosphere, where their surface chemistry steers cloud formation and ozone reactions, so knowing the surface composition matters for climate models. Bulk concentrations are easy; the outermost nanometer of liquid is not.

The team aimed X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy at a flat sheet of liquid and paired the measurements with molecular dynamics simulations, adding the first measurements of their kind to correct for electron scattering. Calcium ions turned out to be depleted at the water-vapor boundary relative to the liquid's interior, while chloride ions were enriched, so the layer carries a higher chloride-to-calcium ratio than the bulk. Simulations reproduced the pattern and showed the solvation behind it. The authors offer the profiles as firmer ground for modeling atmospheric reactions on surfaces.
pmc-13221661:
Zuquan Yao and ten co-authors described three new fungi that live on bamboo in southwest China, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The specimens belong to the family Cainiaceae and were gathered in the south of the country. The team judged them with close study of their form and with family trees built from two gene regions.

Two of the finds are new species of Amphibambusa, named fangchenggangensis and yunnanensis for their home areas. The third is a new species of Arecophila, named viscosa. The paper gives full accounts of each, with micrographs and a family tree that places them among their kin. The authors note that bamboo forests hold a rich store of fungal life that is still being charted.
pmc-13222561:
Vycke Yunivita and co-authors pool trials on adding an antimalarial pair to standard prevention in HIV-positive pregnancy, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Three studies with 1,353 participants met the criteria after screening nearly four hundred records. Mothers received sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim with or without dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine given three times.

Adding the antimalarial showed a non-significant trend toward fewer malaria infections in mothers and placentas. Maternal side effects overall were significantly fewer in the added-drug group, including stomach and gut complaints. Fetal events and birth outcomes, such as low birth weight and early delivery, did not differ significantly. The combination appears safe on these data, with malaria benefit still unproven.
pmc-13223961:
Minh Quang Pham and colleagues present a 2026 engineering method for estimating the working traits of thermoelectric modules without costly laboratory tests. Such modules convert heat into electricity, and their material traits shift with temperature. The team infers equivalent values from a module's measured output, using two modelling routes.

One route uses thermal resistance calculations, while the other uses full numerical simulation. Sensitivity checks and tests across different modules supported both routes, and predicted voltage and power stayed within a few percent of maker data. Because the simpler route matched the heavier simulation, the authors argue it can stand in for large system studies and save computing effort.
pmc-13224061:
Jiahui Jiang and colleagues built a moving nanoparticle gel for cancer treatment in 2026. Gels can carry anti-tumour drugs, but high pressure and dense tissue inside tumours block deep penetration. Their injectable gel contains two-faced polydopamine motors designed to push drug cargo deeper while supporting two light-based therapies at once.

Heat therapy and light-activated therapy were combined in the one system. The motors also eased low-oxygen conditions inside the tumour, which strengthens light-activated treatment. Tumour growth was strongly suppressed in tests, and spread was effectively held back. The authors present the gel as an advanced platform for combined cancer therapy worth further development.
pmc-13224361:
Hanqiao Li and co-authors report a 2026 Chinese cohort study of allergy patients who caught COVID-19 after lockdowns ended. Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, congestion, and a runny nose, and its only treatment that changes the disease course is allergen-specific immunotherapy, a long course of controlled allergen doses. The question was whether that immune training also softened a later coronavirus infection.

Patients receiving immunotherapy faced lower risk of smell loss and sore throat once infected. Their whole-body symptoms also ended sooner, and their quality of life scored better than that of comparable patients. The authors read the pattern as a first signal that this immune modulation may extend protection beyond the original allergy.
pmc-13227761:
Jiali Yang and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to their randomised study of dapagliflozin, a diabetes drug, in patients who had coronary heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Those patients were treated with a stent procedure. The original single-centre trial asked whether the drug improved cardiorespiratory fitness after the procedure. The correction concerns numbers printed in the trial's baseline and results tables, which the authors state were wrong.

Three fixes are itemised for the baseline table: a medication percentage in the drug group, a nitrates percentage in the comparison group, and a decimal slip in a body-mass-index p-value. Corrected versions of both affected tables are republished in full with the notice. Readers using the trial's data should work from these replacement tables rather than the originals.
pmc-13229261:
Megan L. Sweet and co-authors follow a 2026 study of what happens to cells that suddenly double their whole genome, becoming tetraploid, an event seen in thirty to forty percent of human tumours. Freshly doubled cells were tracked in living animals and in culture under stresses typical of tumours, including oxygen-radical exposure and nutrient shortage, to see which conditions help or hinder them.

New tetraploid cells grew at a disadvantage when nutrients ran low. Even so, a small surviving population sufficed to recruit tumour-supporting stromal cells around them. Inside animals, doubled cells were also prone to duplicating their centrosomes, the cell's division organisers, possibly driven by the reactive oxygen species common in tumour surroundings. Genome doubling and tumour environment thus feed each other.
pmc-13229861:
Ali Özkaya and three co-authors study how school students link space-related words to school subjects, in a paper published in twenty twenty-six. Tests of spatial skill usually score performance, but they say little about how learners sort ideas in their minds. The team used word association to fill that gap.

Over four hundred middle school students in Türkiye gave more than sixteen thousand responses. Each response was sorted as leaning toward math, geography, both, or neither. Words like slope, scale, and area leaned to math. Coordinate, location, and graph bridged both fields. Environment and distance floated free of either subject. Results also differed by sex and by how students travel to school. The authors say the method widens how spatial thinking can be studied.
pmc-13232261:
Jaime Iranzo and colleagues ask in 2026 why mobile DNA parasites inside bacteria so often carry defense systems of their own. Viruses, plasmids, and jumping genes move between cells and drive much bacterial evolution. Many carry tools that block rival parasites, sometimes more often than the host chromosome does.

Their math model points to rivalry between the mobile elements themselves as the key force. Mild rivals carry cheap defenses that also shield the host cell from worse attackers. Fierce rivals carry costly weapons that help them replace competitors, even while harming the host and the wider population. Host cells may still gain in the long run, because rough new defenses can later be polished into cheap, useful ones.
pmc-13233661:
Fatemeh Jafarabadi, Meenal Datta, and Maria A Holland published a 2026 review of computational models of inflammation after traumatic brain injury. A blow to the head causes immediate mechanical damage, then a slower secondary injury driven by swelling and immune responses that can unfold for days. The review gathers the hallmarks of that inflammatory phase and surveys how researchers have simulated it.

Models range across scales and methods, each capturing part of a complicated timeline involving immune cells, fluid buildup, and tissue deformation. The authors weigh what current approaches do well and where they fall short for clinical translation. They close with directions for making simulations more realistic and useful, aiming at tools that could eventually help predict a patient's course and test treatments in silico.
pmc-13233861:
Emmanuel K. Teye and colleagues published a 2026 correction to their 2021 Scientific Reports article on the protein PIGN and its control of the spindle assembly checkpoint in leukemia. The correction discloses that several immunoblot and cell synchronization panels in the article came from the same experimental films and flow cytometry datasets as the group's earlier work. That reuse, as reference data for the mechanism analysis, was not disclosed in the original figure legends.

Amended legends for the first three figures now state the reuse openly and describe how cells were synchronized at different cell cycle stages for the blots and gene measurements. The correction leaves the article's scientific claims in place while repairing the record on data provenance. Such disclosures let later readers judge how much of the evidence is new and how much is shared reference material.
pmc-13234461:
Karjalainen and a large team image calcium deposits in human knee meniscus tissue in twenty twenty-six. Such deposits link to meniscus decay and osteoarthritis. Two main mineral types occur, and they may form in unlike ways. The team used micro computed tomography to map the deposits in three dimensions.

Samples came from patients with knee osteoarthritis and from deceased donors. A light based method confirmed which mineral type each sample held. One type sat at tissue borders and inside tears, with a porous structure. The other formed rod like strands between collagen bundles inside the tissue. It also built up much more volume and larger particles. The imaging method could help track disease and find new markers.
pmc-13236561:
Janelle Posey and a large team study interferon gene dose in Down syndrome lung and platelet troubles. Their study from twenty twenty-six ties one extra gene copy to inflammation. People with Down syndrome face high rates of lung ills. Pulmonary hypertension stands as a grave one of them.

One extra interferon receptor gene lifts immune signals from birth. Platelets may turn that signal into inflammation that harms lung vessels. Blood tests set platelet switch-on in people with the syndrome beside those without it. A mouse model then singled out the interferon path at work. Low oxygen tests showed effects that turned on gene dose in the model. Easing interferon signals might shield lungs in this group.
pmc-13236661:
Mohammed S. Abdulrahman and a large team made in 2026 a two-metal nanoparticle using potato peel extract and tested it against a drug-resistant hospital bacterium. The carriers combined zinc oxide with manganese oxide and measured only tens of nanometres across. Standard instruments confirmed their size, crystal structure, and the plant chemicals coating them. Lab tests covered bacteria killing, biofilm disruption, and teamwork with a common antibiotic.

Growth of resistant Acinetobacter isolates stopped at moderate particle amounts in the assays. Biofilms, the slimy shields bacteria build, were cut by nearly two thirds at the strongest treatment. Bacteria died quickly as their proteins leaked through damaged membranes in large amounts. Adding the antibiotic cefotaxime strengthened the killing effect beyond either agent alone. Cancer cell lines were also quite sensitive, while normal cells tolerated higher doses in comparison.
pmc-13236861:
Bingxue Zhang and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how the airway lining helps drive asthma, a disease affecting more than 260 million people. Older accounts blamed immune cells alone, yet that view cannot explain why asthma persists, returns during quiet periods, or resists treatment in some patients. The review places damaged airway epithelium at the center.

Barrier leaks let alarm signals escape from the lining, which wakes immune cells and starts type 2 inflammation. Exposures and inflammation also leave lasting chemical marks on the lining cells' DNA packaging, a memory that survives after attacks settle. The authors survey drug ideas aimed at this memory, from enzyme blockers to newer antibody treatments. They note that low-type-2 asthma still needs far more study.
pmc-13237261:
Bin Jiang and colleagues compared two keyhole operations for benign liver growths called hepatic hemangiomas in a 2026 hospital study. One operation shells the growth out of the liver, while the other removes a section of liver with it. Records covered 100 patients treated between 2019 and 2023, and statistical matching built 34 balanced pairs to compare fairly.

Shelling out the growth won on several measures: far less blood loss, far fewer transfusions, and a hospital stay about two days shorter. Operating time and complication rates did not differ, and no patient died within thirty days in either group. The authors counsel caution because the study looked backward and the matching itself has limits. Still, enucleation looks gentler when it is technically possible.
pmc-13238261:
A Martin and colleagues stress-tested 43 Salmonella enterica isolates in 2026, comparing strains tied to foodborne outbreaks with strains that were not. The bacteria came from five major serovars and faced heat shock, two sanitizers, and attachment tests that predict biofilm formation. Genome checks ran alongside the bench work.

Most isolates carried at least one drug resistance gene, and nearly half resisted important antibiotics in genes or in practice. All isolates survived at least fifteen minutes at 56 degrees, and three survived beyond an hour. Sanitizer tolerance and strong surface attachment appeared in both outbreak and non-outbreak groups, with no clean pattern by serovar. The authors suggest particular tolerance profiles, rather than outbreak labels, may explain why some strains cause trouble.
pmc-13239361:
Ibrahim Msuya and colleagues present a 2026 study of long-term lung and airway diseases in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The researchers asked whether damp, flood-prone ground and household conditions help explain where these illnesses cluster across the city.

They linked satellite-based wetness measures for 1,533 households in fifteen neighbourhoods with reported disease rates. Wetter locations carried higher risk, and homes in the most flood-prone spots faced far greater odds of illness. Larger households and shared communal rubbish bins also raised risk, while air conditioning lowered it. Neighbourhood income showed no direct link once other factors were counted, suggesting poverty works through living conditions.
pmc-13239661:
Inês Silva and colleagues tackle a practical design question for wildlife tracking in a 2026 methods paper. Tagging studies must decide how many animals to follow, for how long, and how often to record locations, and poor choices waste money or produce biased estimates of home range and speed.

The authors propose a workflow that weighs those three choices together and carries uncertainty through to population-level conclusions. Simulations guided by real data show how the trade-offs play out, and extra factors such as failed fixes and device faults can be folded in. The workflow is built into a free app called movedesign so field teams can test plans before spending.
pmc-13240061:
Katherine Antel and a large team present a blood test approach for spotting lymphoma where tuberculosis is common in a 2026 study. Swollen lymph nodes in South Africa often turn out to be TB rather than cancer, and biopsy services are scarce, so diagnosis is frequently delayed.

Their platform reads fragments of DNA floating in blood plasma, combining shallow whole-genome data with very deep targeted sequencing. In 124 patients, lymphoma samples carried more DNA fragments, more tumour signal, and more mutations than benign cases. A machine learning classifier separated malignant from benign swelling with high sensitivity and good overall accuracy. The authors propose it as a minimally invasive aid for similar settings.
pmc-13240261:
Songjun Shao and his team show that an acid drawn from plants cuts lung scars by a hold on an enzyme that shifts the main scar protein. Their 2026 study names the good as a drug that fights scars. It aims at the cross-links that make scar flesh stiff.

The enzyme was marked high in cells of the lung wall and in scar cells in the scar ill. When it was made still, scar protein make was cut in the wake of a growth sign. The plant good brought the grades of the enzyme down. It eased scar-based re-shape in a clear way, brought lung build back, and cut scar protein piles. Acts took in blocks on two shifts of cell state and on a growth sign path. The team puts forth a block on this enzyme by drugs as a bright route to fight lung scar ill.
pmc-13240361:
Sarah M Greene and Lucy A Savitz introduce a thematic journal issue on artificial intelligence in health services research in a 2026 editorial. Conversational tools launched in 2022 spread through health care at unusual speed, and the editors invited the field's professional community to document what the wave is actually doing.

Contributions to the issue span prediction models for at-risk groups, huge record networks for training systems, and warnings about bias baked into older datasets. Other pieces show algorithms supporting community health worker screening and evidence searches that answer clinicians at the point of care. The editors frame the collection as a snapshot of a transformation still under way.
pmc-13240761:
Asep Santoso and colleagues report a 2026 orthopedic case involving a large shin bone defect in a 22-year-old man. His earlier bone transport treatment had stopped early, and the lengthened bone hardened while a gap remained. Infection and a skin defect added to the problem.

Surgeons first covered the area with a flap of tissue from the other leg. They then cut the previously lengthened bone again and restarted gradual bone transport. New bone of good quality formed, and the entire defect eventually closed. Total length gained across both rounds reached a substantial span. The case suggests that even consolidated transported bone can be lengthened again successfully.
pmc-13240861:
Worku's team in Gondar tracked malaria mosquitoes and insecticide resistance across two seasons in northwest Ethiopia. Larvae from Maksegnit and Gendawuha were reared and tested under World Health Organization rules. Adults from houses near breeding sites joined the sampling. The team checked species and knockdown-resistance mutations by PCR.

Bioassays on 776 mosquitoes confirmed resistance to deltamethrin, worst after the rains. Anopheles arabiensis made up over nine in ten samples. The L1014F mutation dominated, mainly among those that lived through spraying, while its sibling variant stayed rare. Anopheles stephensi appeared in Gendawuha for the first time, raising a new control concern.
pmc-13240961:
Mohammad Soheilypour and co-authors publish a 2026 computer modeling study of how two yeast proteins interact during messenger RNA quality control. Cells must block faulty RNA messages from leaving the nucleus. One protein, Mlp1, checks messages by binding partners such as Nab2.

Earlier work singled out one amino acid in Nab2 as vital for binding. Simulations here suggest that this spot works indirectly, by holding Nab2 helices in a compact shape. Swapping in a smaller building block loosened that shape and weakened binding, while a bulkier swap strengthened it. The flexible tail of Mlp1 appears to adapt around its partner. The authors propose this flexibility as a general inspection strategy at the nuclear gate.
pmc-13241461:
Haas's team at Eawag read a Karelian lake's mud for a century of farming and abandonment. Lake Lavijärvi saw heavy farming from about 1900, then postwar emptying. Mud chemistry, magnetism, and leaf-wax carbon dating tracked the catchment's soil shifts. Erosion and nutrient runoff left layered marks.

Farming decades brought peak erosion, old soil carbon washing in, and algae-rich layered mud. After abandonment, soils settled and the lake cleared toward its earlier lean state. Low oxygen in deep water persists today all the same. Haas warns that land-use marks haunt lakes for ages. The mud core spans a full century.
pmc-13241961:
Rui Guo and a large team report a 2026 multi-centre study of an artificial intelligence tool that judges blood vessel invasion in pancreatic cancer scans. Whether tumor has entered nearby vessels decides if surgery can help, and human reads of scans vary. Their system, called CRVIA, was built to mimic how clinicians reason.

Training used over a thousand cases, with validation in internal and external groups drawn from five centres. The tool beat nine comparison approaches, from classic radiomics to foundation models. Its performance stayed steady across stages and vessel types. In reader studies, the tool surpassed senior radiologists and lifted junior radiologists to expert level, while agreement between readers rose. The code is openly shared for other teams.
pmc-13243161:
Dominic Sagoe, Maarten Cruyff, and Razieh Chegeni pooled studies that estimate doping in sport without asking athletes directly. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in Sports Medicine - Open in 2026. Indirect estimation methods let respondents admit banned behavior while keeping their answers hidden, which should yield honester numbers than surveys. The team searched records up to March 2025 and modeled lifetime and past-year rates by athlete type.

Forty-six records fed the review, and thirty entered the pooled analysis, mostly from Europe. About one in five competitive athletes in multi-sport samples admitted doping at some point in their lives. Among recreational single-sport participants, about one in six admitted doping in the past year. Competitive multi-sport athletes showed higher rates than their single-sport peers, while the recreational pattern ran the other way. The authors say indirect methods reveal a doping problem larger than testing statistics suggest.
pmc-13243761:
Alaa Alresheq and colleagues report a rare pairing of complications after a difficult feeding tube placement in a critically ill woman. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Gastrointestinal Medicine in 2026. The forty-year-old patient, burdened by several illnesses, received a camera-guided Kangaroo tube threaded through the nose into the intestine. Scans afterward showed air in the bile ducts, called pneumobilia, and inflammation of the pancreas.

Pinning down the cause proved tricky. She was also in heart-driven shock, had recently started captopril, and showed inflamed colon on imaging, all of which can injure the pancreas and bowel through poor blood flow. Extra air blown in during the placement plausibly explains the biliary air better than the pancreatitis, which the authors call multifactorial. They found no published case. Their practical advice: go gently with air insufflation and think hard before deploying tube technology in unstable patients.
pmc-13244061:
Han Ki Park comments in 2026 on a fresh clue for choosing heart repair in babies with borderline left hearts. Some newborns have a small left side of the heart plus a narrowed or broken aortic arch. Surgeons must guess whether the left side can grow enough for a two-chamber repair.

Size scores alone predict that growth poorly, Park notes. He discusses a study of 161 infants where pressure across a hole between the upper chambers tracked later growth of the mitral valve. Flow-based signs like this one may sharpen choices that size alone cannot settle. Better prediction matters because a failed two-chamber repair often ends badly.
pmc-13245061:
Luana Conte Nunes and co-authors mapped thirty years of patents for antimicrobial surface coatings, asking whether the innovation keeps pace with safety proof. Their patent review appeared in Future Science OA in 2026. Healthcare infections, worsened by drug-resistant germs, drive the market for self-disinfecting surfaces. Searching the Espacenet database under PRISMA rules, the team analyzed forty-nine patents filed between 1995 and 2024.

Filing surged after 2015, led by private companies, concentrated in the United States, Canada, and China. Synthetic chemicals, above all quaternary ammonium compounds, dominate the formulations, with natural and hybrid approaches in the minority. The gap the authors stress is validation: while many patents claim green credentials, fewer than half disclose how the coating works, and only about a third report toxicology data. Their call is for life-cycle assessment and tougher safety testing before these surfaces scale.
pmc-13245561:
Kate Dupont Phillips and co-authors share lessons from Healthy Communities Delaware in a 2026 account of place-based health work. The network joins community groups and funders to improve the basic conditions that health rests on. Housing, learning, work, transport, and belonging all count among those conditions.

Since 2020 the network has invested over nine million dollars in 18 communities with the poorest outcomes. Stories from Laurel, the Route 9 Corridor, and West Side Wilmington ground the account. Three tenets held up across the sites: stay invested for the long term, partner across sectors, and tailor support to each place. Resident-led projects drove the deepest change, the authors report.
pmc-13245761:
Al-Haddad and colleagues examined the tiny blood vessels of the retina in children with amblyopia, or lazy eye, in this 2026 PLOS One study. Using a scanning method that maps retinal blood flow without dye, they compared the amblyopic eye, the fellow eye, and the eyes of healthy controls in seventy-eight children around ten years old.

Amblyopic eyes showed denser small vessels and stronger perfusion across the outer and full macula than control eyes, and a smaller vessel-free zone at the center than their fellow eyes. The optic disc looked much the same across groups. The authors treat the findings as early evidence that lazy eye involves subtle retinal changes, needing larger studies.
pmc-13246461:
Takefuji, Komagamine, and Ota report a severe infection case in this 2026 Clinical Case Reports article. A thirty-seven-year-old woman arrived with fever and abdominal pain and was first treated for gastroenteritis. Within days she developed diarrhea, vomiting, and falling blood pressure, along with a widespread rash, eye inflammation, and a bright red, bumpy strawberry tongue.

The picture pointed to streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, a dangerous toxin-driven reaction, and she was moved to intensive care on several antibiotics. The authors note that strawberry tongue is a recognized clue to this syndrome, and they report, for the first time, the tongue's surface peeling as she recovered. They urge clinicians to weigh the diagnosis in shocked patients showing the sign.
pmc-13247061:
Ghallab, Shaheen, and Elkorany compared error-correcting radio schemes for smart power grids in this 2026 Scientific Reports paper. Smart grids must move monitoring and control data reliably over noisy, bandwidth-limited links spread across wide areas. The authors set out the mathematics of trellis coded modulation, which merges coding with multi-level signaling to gain reliability without extra bandwidth, and of its turbo extension, which adds iterative decoding.

Simulations under plain noise and fading channels tested both against uncoded transmission. The simpler trellis scheme delivered the highest data rates in several settings, including multi-antenna channels, while the turbo variant emphasized robustness. The authors discuss adding artificial intelligence driven adaptive coding and fifth-generation grid networks, arguing dependable communication underpins the modern energy system.
pmc-13248961:
Li, Huang, and Li examined transfusion crises in pregnant patients with thalassemia, in a 2026 article. People with this inherited blood disorder need regular transfusions, and pregnancy raises the demand. Repeated transfusions can train the immune system to attack donor blood, or even the patient's own blood, and such reactions are easily mistaken for ordinary pregnancy changes.

The authors analyze three cases where transfusions stopped working as expected. From those cases and current guidelines they build a step-by-step pathway. At the first sign of trouble, teams should screen for antibodies and run a direct antiglobulin test. That separates immune causes early, so treatment can target the right one, protecting both mother and fetus.
pmc-13249061:
Armstrong and colleagues lay out a trial protocol for virtual reality pain relief in children, published in 2026. Laser treatments help many skin conditions but hurt, and eye protection limits ordinary distraction tricks. The planned crossover trial enrolls forty young patients who need at least two outpatient laser sessions at a Midwestern children's hospital.

Each child will play an immersive game during one session and wear a darkened headset during the other, with the order assigned randomly. Pain, anxiety, and medicine use will be compared between the two visits, alongside sickness symptoms from the headset. Enrollment finished with forty children completing both visits, and results are expected in mid 2026.
pmc-13249761:
Marseglia and colleagues update the practical handling of severe allergy attacks in children, in a 2026 European Journal of Pediatrics review. Searching guidelines and studies from 2020 onward, the authors cover anaphylaxis, the fast, whole-body reaction that can kill. Food remains the top trigger in childhood, with drugs, bee stings, and exercise-related cofactors gaining weight as children age.

Adrenaline injected into muscle stays the only life-saving first step, yet it is still given too late outside hospitals. A needle-free nasal spray version is coming, easing needle fear, though pediatric evidence is still thin. Newer long-term options, an antibody drug and gradual food exposure therapy, lower everyday risk without replacing emergency readiness. Discharge planning and family training close the authors' checklist.
pmc-13250261:
Indranill Basu-Ray and Partha Narayan Dey offer a 2026 editorial on yoga as a treatment for metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is the cluster of high blood sugar, abnormal blood fats, and excess weight that raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease. The authors ask whether an old mind-body practice belongs in standard care now that drug options have multiplied.

The editorial reviews two decades of trials and finds that the research has grown stronger, with larger randomized studies and careful systematic reviews. In type 2 diabetes, trials show that yoga practice can improve blood sugar control and related measures over time. The authors argue that the evidence is now hard to ignore, even though drug treatment remains central to care. They present yoga and its linked lifestyle changes as a serious partner to medicine rather than a soft extra.
pmc-13250561:
Marc W. Cadotte argues in a 2026 opinion piece that politics is closing doors that science spent decades opening. Boycotts and broken partnerships, triggered by wars and diplomatic fights, are pushing research back behind national borders. He accepts that the wish to show solidarity is understandable, yet calls the long-term cost too high.

Cadotte traces limits on scholarly exchange from ancient travel bans to Cold War restrictions that still shape the field. He points to joint work such as the International Space Station as proof that rivals can cooperate on shared problems. The piece warns that cutting ties slows the flow of people, data, and ideas that global crises demand. His plea is for universities and governments to resist reflexive bans and keep collaboration open.
pmc-13250861:
Zeng and colleagues track mouth bacteria inside jaw cysts to predict how well bone will regrow after treatment. Their 2026 Journal of Oral Microbiology study follows patients treated by marsupialization, where a tooth-related jaw lesion is opened and left to shrink slowly. Bone regrowth after this gentle surgery is slow and hard to predict.

Samples from saliva, tissue, fluid, and swabs across treatment showed that the closed lesions held a distinct bacterial community rich in Fusobacterium and Clostridia. Opening the lesion let ordinary saliva bacteria take over, and later a different community settled in. A swab signature at three months predicted twelve-month bone regrowth with high accuracy. Lingering early bacteria meant poorer healing, giving doctors a possible early warning tool.
pmc-13251061:
Tyler E. Ball and co-authors describe a 2026 method for growing polymer brushes directly from nylon surfaces. Nylon is strong and widely used, but its surface resists water and collects protein fouling, which limits medical and industrial uses. Earlier ways to attach controlled polymer layers needed harsh steps or long preparations.

The new method uses light and a catalyst called thioxanthone to pull hydrogen atoms from the nylon surface, starting polymer chains right where they will stay. Those chains are then capped by a sulfur-based control agent, giving tidy, well-defined brushes under mild conditions. The process works with common acrylic monomers and several commercial nylons, and masking lets the team print brush patterns. Hydrophilic brushes measurably cut the sticking of a test protein, which points to fouling-resistant coatings.
pmc-13251761:
Durbhakula and colleagues ask why some knee replacement patients hurt long after surgery while others recover cleanly. Their 2026 Journal of Pain Research analysis covers fifty-eight adults having a first total knee replacement. Blood inflammation markers were drawn before surgery, and oxidative stress was measured during the operation itself.

Patients starting with higher inflammatory cytokines showed a tighter link between surgical oxidative stress and pain six months later. At low cytokine levels, oxidative stress showed no relationship with later pain at all. The authors call the pairing a biological double hit that primes lasting pain after surgery. Because the analysis was exploratory and small, they stress the findings are hypotheses for larger cohorts to test.
pmc-13251861:
Byunggul Lim and co-authors watch hunger and blood sugar in daily life in this 2026 study. Adults with overweight or obesity, even without diabetes, can show unstable sugar control, and real-time hunger might foreshadow the swings.

Eighty-four adults wore continuous sugar monitors for 14 days and answered phone prompts about hunger six times a day. Hunger reports came with lower sugar at that moment and half an hour later. Over the next three hours, though, sugar climbed, and the odds of a sharp post-food spike rose by about a quarter in the first hour after hunger. The authors suggest hunger alerts could time just-in-time support.
pmc-13253661:
Geoffrey Kaye and co-authors report a 2026 study of smooth pursuit, the eye movement that tracks a moving target. People tracked a target while doing mental math on digit streams they saw, heard, or both. The team also checked whether working memory, the mind's short-term store, changed the results.

Tracking stayed steady when focus went to visual input but grew shaky when focus went to sound. When heard digits clashed with seen digits, math errors rose while eye tracking did not worsen. People with stronger working memory tracked a bit more steadily under hard sound tasks, which the authors link to shared brain circuits.
pmc-13253761:
Fauve van Veen and colleagues explore family choices in a 2026 interview study on genodermatoses, inherited skin diseases. They spoke with 30 people aged 16 and older who had such a disease and wanted children now or later. The talks covered how the disease shaped that wish, what options they knew, and what advice they got.

Most wanted to avoid passing the disease to a child, a wish shaped by fear from their own hard years. Two main themes and nine subthemes came out of the talks. Many said doctors did not offer counsel on reproductive options as routine care, which the authors urge clinics to fix.
pmc-13254561:
Naoko Higuchi and colleagues chart how human milk sugars change over the first months of nursing in Japanese mothers in a 2026 longitudinal study. Human milk oligosaccharides, the third most abundant solid in milk, feed infant gut microbes and tutor the immune system. Their recipe depends on the mother's Secretor and Lewis blood group related genes, which sort mothers into four milk groups.

Samples came from 270 mothers in a Chiba birth cohort, collected as colostrum and again at one and four months, giving 570 samples in total. Fifteen major milk sugars were measured in each. The commonest milk group, positive for both traits, covered about seventy-one percent of mothers.
