Sugars typical of secretor mothers, including the well-known 2'-fucosyllactose, declined as lactation progressed, while 3-fucosyllactose rose in every group. The authors describe the work as the first comprehensive longitudinal map of its kind for Japan.
pmc-13254861:
Nguyen Thanh Nguyen and a large team build machine learning models to predict severe drug skin reactions in Vietnamese patients in a 2026 study. Carbamazepine and allopurinol, two widely used medicines, can trigger life-threatening cutaneous reactions, and the known genetic warning flags, two HLA variants, catch only a fraction of cases. The team sequenced the exomes of 249 patients and controls to search wider.

Eight prediction models were trained separately for each drug. For allopurinol reactions, random forest and extra trees models reached an average accuracy of 99.67 percent across ten independent tests. For carbamazepine, a linear support vector classifier performed best, with an accuracy-curve score of eighty-six percent on held-out data. The authors say the models capture genomic risk beyond the two classic HLA flags. Clinically, they propose assessing high-risk HLA carriers with the model before the first dose.
pmc-13254961:
Montacer Hafsi and co-authors present a 2026 case report about vasa previa, a pregnancy complication where fetal blood vessels cross the cervix without protection. Their patient was a 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. Scans at 32 weeks showed the vessels alongside a two-lobed placenta and a cord that inserted into the membranes.

Transvaginal ultrasound with color Doppler confirmed the diagnosis after she moved care from Bordeaux. Doctors scheduled a cesarean birth at 36 weeks and 5 days, before labor could rupture the exposed vessels. The baby girl was born healthy with strong Apgar scores. The authors stress that finding vasa previa before birth turns a dangerous condition into a manageable one.
pmc-13255061:
Risi Chen and co-authors report a 2026 study of how dim light at night harms the developing heart. Artificial night light reaches most of the world's people and has been tied to cardiovascular disease. The team used zebrafish embryos to find mechanisms, then checked their findings in mice.

Embryos raised under dim night light developed fluid swelling around the heart and weaker blood flow. Gene activity pointed to disturbed inflammation and stress pathways, plus a sharp drop in a chloride-channel helper protein called zclca1. Blocking that protein reproduced the damage, while the diuretic bumetanide, which shifts chloride balance, reversed it in both species. The authors propose chloride control as a possible way to blunt light pollution's effect on the heart.
pmc-13255661:
Mamokoma Cathrine Modiba and colleagues report a 2026 genome scan of four South African beef cattle breeds: Bonsmara, Nguni, Simmental, and Angus. Each breed carries a different history, from locally adapted Sanga cattle to imported European stock, and those histories leave marks in DNA. The team used dense genetic marker data to find regions shaped by recent selection.

The scan uncovered both breed-specific selected regions and regions shared across breeds. Several candidate genes in the selected regions relate to reproduction traits. Indigenous breeds like the Nguni reflect long adaptation to African conditions, while the Bonsmara blends local and British ancestry by design. The authors say the mapped regions can guide breeding programs that aim to lift fertility and resilience without losing local adaptation.
pmc-13256161:
Amna Abu Na'aim and colleagues wrote a 2026 review sorting out leptin's confusing role in making new fat cells. Leptin is best known as the hormone that reports fat stores to the brain and curbs appetite. Oddly, studies disagree on whether leptin helps or hinders adipogenesis, the process that turns stem cells into fat-storing cells.

Some experiments show leptin promoting fat cell formation, others show it blocking the process, and some find no effect. The review argues the contradictions follow the experimental setup: leptin dose, timing of exposure, cell type, fat depot, and species all flip the answer. The authors map the molecular pathways involved and name the knowledge gaps that matter most. Their goal is a context-aware picture useful for obesity and metabolic disease research.
pmc-13256861:
Chen Yang and co-authors sprayed a helpful germ on peach trees in 2026 and measured what changed in soil, microbes, and fruit. The germ Bacillus velezensis is used as a living treatment in orchards, but its pre-harvest effects across peach varieties were not well understood. Three cultivars received either the bacterial treatment or sterile water under field conditions. The team then sequenced the bacterial and fungal groups living around the roots.

Treated plots showed lower soil acidity and shifts in several nutrient measures. The root-zone microbial groups changed in composition for both germs and fungi. The research staff also assessed the fruit's nutritional and working parts, antioxidant capacity, and electronic sensory traits tied to flavor. If a microbial spray boosts fruit quality while changing form soil life favorably, growers gain a substitute for purely chemical inputs.
pmc-13257261:
Ernest O. N. Phillips and a large team describe a 2026 mouse model of radiation skin injury combined with a wound. Such combined injuries could follow nuclear accidents or attacks, and few countermeasures exist. Thoracic X-ray exposure was paired with an immediate experimental wound.

Radiation clearly slowed wound closure, while the wound itself did not worsen skin inflammation from radiation. A soy compound, genistein, given a day before exposure sped early closure and eased dermatitis. Treated skin showed better structure with less inflammation and scarring under the microscope. A cell-aging marker fell, a scarring marker fell, and skin stem cells were preserved. Disaster medicine researchers gain both a working model and a candidate preventive. Human use would require far more testing for dose and timing.
pmc-13257961:
Koji Mizukoshi and colleagues present a 2026 study asking whether sharper face images change how attractive a face looks. High-resolution photos of 180 Japanese female models were taken with an 8K camera system. Blurred low-resolution versions were made from the same photos by pixelation, meaning breaking the image into coarse blocks. Both versions were shown on an 8K display, and each viewer rated every face on a six-point scale.

Faces in high resolution got slightly higher attractiveness ratings than the same faces in low resolution. The boost was strongest for faces already rated as more attractive at the start. Ratings fell with the model's age in both versions. The authors suggest extra visual detail can strengthen the cues people use when judging attractiveness, even if the effect is small.
pmc-13258061:
Charles E Hoogland leads a 2026 secondary analysis comparing in-person and online recruitment to a smoking cessation trial for adults facing food insecurity. Food insecurity means lacking steady access to enough food. Eligible adults had used food aid in the past thirty days, smoked at least five cigarettes a day, and were willing to try quitting within seven days. Baseline surveys were done on tablets in person or on personal devices after online adverts.

Online recruits reported deeper food insecurity, more schooling, and higher income, but lower motivation and confidence to quit, plus more loneliness and depressive symptoms. Online enrollment ran much faster, at 64.8 people per month against 7.7 in person, with 324 online enrollees against 178 in person. Eligible online recruits were also more likely to enroll, at seventy-one percent against forty-nine percent.
pmc-13259361:
Deniz Dudukcu and co-authors survey what happens when blockchains guard software-defined networks. Software-defined networking centralizes control, which is handy but paints a target on the controller. Their 2026 unified survey organizes a scattered literature on blockchain-backed defenses.

Six territories structure the tour: industry uses, security mechanisms, defense plans, attack-specific shields, artificial intelligence, and performance. Prototypes blunted denial-of-service floods, man-in-the-middle tricks, and spoofing across internet-of-things, vehicle, and smart-grid settings. Consensus delays and scaling limits still bite hard in big deployments. The authors close on missing standards that keep these designs out of production.
pmc-13259861:
Rui Gu and co-authors investigated in 2026 whether copper levels and copper-linked cell death can reveal when a traumatic brain injury happened. Forensic doctors often lack steady markers for dating such injuries. The team paired tests on human postmortem brain tissue with experiments in injured mice.

Copper built up in the bruised area of human brains over the 30 days after injury, rising in step with time. Mouse tissue showed signs of cuproptosis, a copper-driven form of cell death, in the same region. Certain genes, among them FDX1, DLD, and SLC31A1, tracked the early stage after injury. Other genes, LIAS and SLC31A1, fit the later stage better. The authors propose these measures as candidate tools for estimating injury timing.
pmc-13259961:
Marina Mello Villalba and colleagues wrote a 2026 controlled intervention study of co-contraction training in older adults. In co-contraction training, opposing muscles are tightened against each other at the same time, so no weights or machines are needed. Thirty-four physically active adults aged sixty to eighty-five were assigned by chance to co-contraction training, traditional machine training, or a control group. Both training programs ran twice a week for eight weeks.

Muscle size grew in both training groups, by up to ten percent with co-contraction and fifteen percent with machines. Strength, however, improved only in the traditional group, while the co-contraction group showed a small reduction in one strength measure. All groups improved on functional capacity tests like sit-to-stand and walking, with no differences between groups. The authors call co-contraction a workable low-cost option where machines are unavailable.
pmc-13260161:
Shoichiro Amari, Masato Eto, and Hiroshi Oyama present a 2026 feasibility study of a standalone virtual reality system for neonatal resuscitation training. Neonatal resuscitation is the emergency care that helps newborn babies breathe. Repeated practice is needed, but mannequin training is limited by cost, space, and instructor time. Thirty-two already-certified perinatal professionals, including eleven physicians, fourteen nurses, and seven midwives, tried an app focused on positive-pressure ventilation.

All thirty-two finished the session, a completion rate of one hundred percent, with no one stopping over side effects. Median usefulness and willingness to recommend both scored five out of five. A standard usability score came to 65.0, which the authors call moderate. Simulator sickness was low, and three people reported mild symptoms that cleared within ten minutes. Realism and involvement ratings need improvement, the authors say.
pmc-13260461:
Domenico Del Turco leads a 2026 mouse study of a protein called synaptopodin in brain cells involved in learning. Synaptopodin sits inside dendritic spines, the tiny receiving knobs on nerve cells, and is required to build the spine apparatus, a small calcium store inside the spine. The team engineered mice whose dentate granule cells made about three times the normal amount of the protein, then examined spine structure and electrical activity.

In the engineered mice, the protein appeared in twice as many spines as normal. The number of spine apparatuses rose about threefold, while spine density and head size did not change significantly. Electrical recordings showed about a 3.5-fold increase in the frequency of small excitatory currents, indicating more active synapses. The authors suggest extra synaptopodin enlarges the pool of synapses available for strengthening during learning.
pmc-13262161:
Zhao-Ming Lin and co-authors examined in 2026 how pulsed electric fields change the muscle proteins of abalone, a prized seafood. The treatment zaps food with short high-voltage bursts to slow spoilage without cooking it. Their team treated the myofibrillar protein at settings from ten to thirty kilovolts.

Higher voltage steadily raised protein solubility, fragmentation, and oxidation markers while enzyme activity tied to freshness fell. Several qualities peaked at the gentlest setting, including clinging groups, surface water-shyness, and charge. The protein's size distribution stayed untouched, showing the backbone was not chopped. Internal structure shifted toward more helix and more sulfur crosslinks. The authors say the gentlest setting best balances preservation gains against protein damage, giving processors a tuning guide for abalone handling.
pmc-13262861:
Nigus Telele and colleagues compare two self-sampling methods for human papillomavirus testing in a 2026 journal article. The virus can cause cervical cancer, and self-sampling could widen screening where clinics are scarce. Girls and women aged 15 to 25 in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan provided both a self-collected vaginal swab and a first-void urine sample.

Paired samples from 753 people were tested the same way for high-risk virus types. Rates for 14 high-risk types were 8.6 percent by swab and 7.2 percent by urine, and rates for vaccine-covered types were close. Each method caught some types the other missed, and samples with less virus were more likely to disagree. Overall agreement stayed high, supporting either method for large surveys.
pmc-13263561:
Sui-Yong Du and colleagues compared in 2026 two operations for a single pinched neck nerve: a two-portal endoscopic approach from behind and the standard front fusion. That operation relieves pain reliably but stiffens the segment. Their single-center study matched thirty-eight patients per group on background traits, covering treatment years 2020 to 2024.

Both operations relieved pain and disability well. Five days after surgery, the endoscopy group reported lower pain and disability scores, though the gap closed by twelve months. Neck movement stayed clearly better in the endoscopy group at both later checks. The endoscopic route took longer in the operating room, yet patients left hospital sooner and returned to work faster. The authors present it as a motion-keeping option for suitable patients, pending randomized proof.
pmc-13263761:
Louise Heyzer and colleagues ask which kinds of frailty make walking while thinking so costly for older adults. Dual-task cost, the slowdown when mind and legs work together, signals vulnerability. Their 2026 Singapore study examines two hundred eighty-one community dwellers across physical, social, and oral frailty.

Participants walked while counting backward or naming animals, taxing two mental systems. Frontal executive function, measured by a bedside battery, predicted cost in both tasks most strongly. Social and oral frailty seemed relevant to the arithmetic task until cognition entered the model, where their effects faded. Sharpening executive function, they propose, is the promising intervention target.
pmc-13264061:
Alejandro Fabrega Gerbaud and colleagues set out a 2026 framework for adding artificial intelligence and automation to health care without losing trust. Tools often fail in clinics because of safety worries, unclear reasoning, poor data and legal questions. Patients fear harm and distance from doctors, while clinicians worry about opaque algorithms and accountability when something goes wrong.

The understand, transform and sustain framework comes from a quality academy at Mayo Clinic. First teams map workflows and find the real problem, then they test changes with feedback while checking data for bias. Lasting value comes from monitoring outcomes and standard routines. The article argues that fixing processes first makes later automation safer and more welcome for staff and patients alike.
pmc-13264161:
Manjae Kwon and colleagues test two home brain stimulation methods for alcohol craving in a 2026 randomized study. Sixty adults with subclinical alcohol use were assigned to light-based stimulation through the skull, ear-based vagus nerve stimulation, or both together. Participants used portable devices at home for short sessions five times a week over five weeks, with craving change as the main outcome.

Light stimulation alone and the combined approach cut craving and drinking scores clearly more than ear stimulation alone. Odds of responding were notably higher in the light and combined groups. The authors suggest light-based treatment, alone or paired, deserves larger trials. Ear stimulation by itself showed weaker effects in this small sample.
pmc-13264261:
Man Qian and colleagues build explainable prediction models for poor outcomes in diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 study. One hundred eighty biopsy-confirmed patients were followed for a combined outcome of death, dialysis start or transplant. Eight machine learning models were trained on clinical and laboratory data, then checked in an independent outside group to test whether performance held beyond the original hospital sample.

One simple probabilistic model reached the best internal accuracy, and several models shared top discrimination scores. Outside validation performed even slightly better. Explanation analysis ranked kidney filtration rate, albumin, a complement protein, creatinine and red cells in urine as strongest drivers. Two less traditional markers gained value through non-linear patterns. Transparent models may support more personal follow-up planning.
pmc-13264361:
Samar El Sherbiny and colleagues systematically review blood metabolites linking diet to frailty in older adults in a 2026 article. Frailty, a state of low reserve and high vulnerability, is partly shaped by nutrition, and metabolomics can reveal chemical fingerprints of dietary exposure in the body. Mediating molecules may come from food itself or from gut microbes transforming it, and many sit on several pathways at once, reflecting tangled biology.

Sex may change which metabolites predict frailty, so pooled cutoffs could mislead. The authors argue that metabolite-guided dietary advice could tailor prevention for aging adults better than generic guidance. Biomarker discovery remains an active need, since frailty definitions and diet measures vary widely across existing studies in this literature.
pmc-13264761:
Marius N Stan and John J Schmitz assess new devices for thyroid ablation in a 2026 review. Most thyroid nodules are harmless findings, but toxic nodules that overproduce hormone and compressive nodules that press on the throat need action. Surgery long dominated, yet needle-based heat ablation now handles many benign problem nodules in their practice, rivaling radioactive iodine for toxic cases without its whole-gland fallout and early swelling concerns.

Newer gadgets promise better control, safety or reach for these procedures. The authors weigh what each advance truly adds over established radiofrequency and related methods, including learning curves and cost. Careful patient selection remains the foundation: malignant nodules still belong to surgery in most cases. Device enthusiasm should follow outcome evidence, not marketing.
pmc-13264861:
Sara Nsibirwa and six co-authors trace care-seeking by liver cancer patients in Uganda in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The cancer is often found late there. The team asked how patients moved through the health system before diagnosis, and whether delay cost lives.

Of six hundred fifty-one patients, nearly all had sought care for their symptoms, most of them repeatedly. Visits mixed public clinics, private providers, and traditional healers. Median time to diagnosis was ninety days. Being male, having hepatitis B or HIV, or more schooling sped diagnosis. Older age and hopping between facilities slowed it. Delay itself did not predict survival in this cohort. The authors urge faster referral paths and surveillance of high-risk people.
pmc-13265161:
Xufeng Shu and his team bring to light a catch point on the face of cells as a mark that can tell how stomach tumours will fare. Their 2026 study weighs LAIR1, a catch point that sets the self-attack kit. Its role in this ill was not set in the past.

Store checks linked use of the catch point to how sick folk fared. Then one hundred seventy-seven sick-bay tests backed the maps. The catch point was marked high in tumour flesh. It was tied to poor cell form, late stage, spread to lymph nodes, and short life span. When it was cut out, tumour cells grew, moved, and pushed in at a slow pace in lab tests. When it was added, those acts rose. Beast models with more than one spread route backed acts on tumour growth and spread.
pmc-13265261:
Jiangchen Ma and the team compare swallow rehab plans for elderly patients in China, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Muscle loss can weaken swallowing, a condition called sarcopenic dysphagia. Standard therapy and electric pulses each help somewhat. Whether adding step-up strength work improves results was tested.

Ninety-six patients, with a mean age near eighty-two years, got one of three plans over six weeks. All groups improved on swallow scores. The combined plan with resistance training improved most on standard scales and food intake scales. Weight and food signs were also tracked. The authors support combined training for this growing old-age problem.
pmc-13265861:
Grace Kitunzi Mulyowa and colleagues describe a chronic shin skin condition in southwestern Uganda, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The condition, shortened to DCPA, causes pustules and thinning skin. It is little recognised in Uganda. Skin clinics at two regional hospitals collected data and photos.

A total of 405 participants were studied between late 2022 and early 2024. Most were young, with a mean age near twenty-two, and women formed the large majority. Students and young pupils were the biggest groups. Petroleum jelly was the most common skin application. The authors link oily products as one contributing factor among several.
pmc-13266161:
Wenli Li, Brianna Murphy, and Anna Larsen study calf caecum responses to dosing with adult cow rumen fluid, published in 2026. Most cattle nutrition work focuses on the rumen, leaving the lower gut unexplored. Eight calves received live or sterilised rumen content. Caecum gene activity and microbes were then compared.

Nearly two thousand genes changed with treatment, mostly dialled down. Immune and inflammation pathways dominated the changes. Microbe-linked genes also centred on immunity. The same dosing retained differently across gut sites. The authors argue the hindgut responds robustly and that tissue-specific study is required for full understanding.
pmc-13266761:
Haddouga, Sidayne, Ouachaou, Aicha, El Khettab, and Zarrouki report a case of many brain abscesses tied to a severe chest infection. Their report is from two thousand twenty-six. Brain abscess is a rare but grave infection. It can start when germs spread through the blood or from a near site, and lung disease can be one source.

The patient was a woman aged fifty with type two diabetes. She came in with lung failure from severe bronchiectasis and acute respiratory distress. Tests found pneumococcus and influenza A, though blood cultures stayed clear. She first got better on drugs, then had seizures on day five. Brain scans showed many abscesses on both sides. In spite of stronger drugs and full intensive care, she died.
pmc-13266861:
Hassan Saleh, Firas Amil, and Luke Domaleski appraise in 2026 the STORM-PE trial of early clot removal for intermediate-high risk lung blood clots. These patients have stable blood pressure but a strained right heart, leaving doctors unsure whether blood thinners alone suffice. STORM-PE was the first randomized trial to test adding a catheter thrombectomy procedure.

The commentators praise the team for randomizing in a fast-moving emergency, yet they note that 767 patients were screened to enroll one hundred. That funnel means results come from selected patients at experienced centers with dedicated clot teams. Confusing wording about cancer during screening also needs clearing up, they argue, since cancer patients form a large share of real clot cases.
pmc-13267561:
Yangpeng Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of optical mapping, a method for filming the heart's electrical waves. Special dyes make heart tissue glow as signals pass, giving films with fine detail in space and time. The review covers how the method is used to judge drugs meant to fix irregular heartbeats.

Optical mapping can track many electrical measures at once and can be paired with other methods. The authors list drugs already tested this way and show how the films reveal how rhythm problems start. They also note limits, including the gap between lab hearts and patients. The review aims to give a full framework for using the method in drug work and to guide its move toward clinical use.
pmc-13267761:
Izadian Bidgoli and Gomez Veliz report a case of IgA multiple myeloma that hid behind a more common problem. A 50-year-old man had repeated bleeding from the gut and severe anemia that needed transfusion. Care first focused on acute blood loss as the likely cause.

Lasting low blood counts and very high total protein, with normal albumin, pointed to a deeper illness. Further lab work revealed IgA multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells. Unusual bone disease without the lytic lesions doctors often expect added to the delay. The case warns against missing such clues.
pmc-13268161:
Yi-De Tai and colleagues present a 2026 study of wireless power for brain interfaces placed inside blood vessels. Such devices record or stimulate the brain without open surgery, but current versions trail long wires through vessels to the chest. Wires raise infection and clot risks. Removing them means beaming power through skull and tissue within safety limits.

The team designed coil pairs shaped for vessel use and tested them in computer models, on the bench, in sheep tissue, and in living sheep. Power crossed at useful depths: peak transfer reached about 11 percent at shallow depth and about 2 percent at double that depth, still delivering meaningful power under safety limits. One coil pair won at short range; a ferrite-core design won farther out and forgave misalignment better. The authors call wireless powering of these implants feasible.
pmc-13268261:
Brian E Bunnell and colleagues report a 2026 feasibility trial of virtual reality therapy for specific phobias. Exposure therapy works, and VR can stage feared situations at home, but therapist and client had never been shown sharing one remote VR session. Adults afraid of dogs, snakes, or spiders were randomized to twelve weekly sessions by standard video care or by a multiuser VR platform.

The trial enrolled 54 people, well above its target of 30. Follow-up data collection beat every benchmark, and rated treatment fidelity reached 90 percent. Fear outcomes did not differ between groups in this small sample. Client satisfaction, though, improved significantly more with VR. The authors calculate a full trial needs about 160 participants and say the approach is ready for that test.
pmc-13268361:
Ramazan Kerim Yılmaz and colleagues present a 2026 image-based case report on emphysematous pyelonephritis, a dangerous kidney infection. Gas-forming bacteria destroy kidney tissue, and diabetes is the main risk factor. Their patient had diabetes and high blood pressure and arrived with flank pain and fever. CT scans showed a swollen left kidney with pockets of gas in its lower part.

Blood cultures grew a drug-resistant strain of E. coli. Strong intravenous antibiotics were given, and after two weeks the patient improved enough to go home, keeping the kidney. The report contrasts older aggressive surgery with today's more conservative drainage-plus-drugs approach. Its images show the trapped gas that marks this emergency, where quick recognition and antibiotics can prevent kidney loss or death.
pmc-13269561:
Willinton Hernan Pinchao Pinchao and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on zinc oxide nanoparticles given to Santa Inês ewes around lambing. Tiny zinc particles may be absorbed better than standard zinc. Thirty-three ewes received no supplement, nano zinc, or standard zinc particles, at 300 milligrams a day from late pregnancy to weaning.

Body weight, parasite egg counts, and most blood and immune measures did not differ between groups. The nano group showed higher counts of one white cell type and higher albumin than the standard particle group. Several protective antioxidant enzymes, which guard cells against damage, also responded clearly in the nano group. The authors conclude that nano zinc improved antioxidant response with no signs of poisoning at that dose.
pmc-13269961:
Linfa Chen and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a woman in her late 50s who arrived with sudden speech trouble. Brain scans showed many calcium deposits inside the skull plus a fresh stroke in the left front of the brain. Gene sequencing found a new frameshift variant, a spelling shift that truncates the protein, in a gene called SLC20A2.

The same variant appeared in her son and eldest daughter, who both showed brain calcification on scans. Her second daughter lacked the variant and had clean scans. The variant was classed as likely disease-causing under standard guidelines. The authors say the case widens the known range of faults behind primary brain calcification and supports genetic testing and counseling.
pmc-13270261:
Te-du Yang and co-authors propose in 2026 treating dry eye disease and depression as one intertwined condition rather than two separate clinic problems. Each disorder raises the odds of the other, and patients carry a double burden that single-specialty care handles badly. Eye doctors rarely screen for psychological distress, while mental health clinicians often overlook the eye discomfort feeding low mood.

The authors trace shared roots: nerve-driven inflammation, stress hormone axis disturbance, and an eye-brain connection, plus the way symptom perception amplifies both illnesses. Their framework sorts patients by combined eye and mood profiles, then climbs a stepwise treatment ladder whose order is tuned over time to the two-way interaction. The goal is precise, whole-person care that improves long-term outcomes for both organs of suffering.
pmc-13270661:
Christian Kempny is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a broad survey of a new field, on how large language models are used in qualitative research. Qualitative research works with words, interviews, and themes, and its reporting guides say little about documenting model use.

Searching five databases for studies from January 2020 to May 2025, the team screened thousands of records and kept 75 studies. OpenAI GPT models appeared in 93 percent of them. Help with coding data and finding themes were the most common uses. Reporting of basic technical settings was patchy: only 13 studies gave temperature settings, and only four gave another key setting, top_p.
pmc-13271061:
Chenlan Li and coauthors present in 2026 a set of dichroic dyes that can flip the handedness of glowing light in liquid crystal materials. Most natural chiral compounds come in only one mirror form, which limits circularly polarized luminescence, the twisting light used in advanced displays. The dyes use a proton-shift structure to work around that limit.

Placed inside natural cholesteric liquid crystals, the dyes produced mirror-image light across the full color range, including white light. The work widens what natural chiral materials can do in polarized light devices. It also offers a more sustainable route toward flexible optical displays and secure communication tools.
pmc-13271961:
Jing Zhao and coauthors pool in 2026 trials of electrical stimulation at acupuncture points for nausea after breast surgery. Nausea and vomiting after anesthesia remain common and distressing in this setting. The needle-free method, called TEAS, is used as an add-on in surgical care, but breast surgery evidence was scattered.

Fifteen randomized trials with 1,752 patients were combined, comparing stimulation with sham treatment or routine care. Stimulation cut the overall risk of nausea and vomiting by about two fifths, with consistent results across trials. Patients also reported less pain, needed fewer rescue drugs, and rated early recovery higher.
pmc-13272061:
Mutassim M Abdelrahman and coauthors feed in 2026 graded amounts of artificial saliva to growing lambs and track effects on the rumen and body. Artificial saliva acts as a buffer, steadying acidity in the first stomach where microbes ferment feed. The team tested whether more buffer always helps or whether excess backfires.

Forty-five lambs received diets with zero to six percent artificial saliva. Moderate levels steadied rumen acidity and raised useful fermentation acids, while the highest level cut fermentation output and disturbed blood measures. Mineral levels in rumen fluid rose with dose. Meat acidity also climbed at the top dose, warning that dosing needs balance.
pmc-13272161:
Lisa Feinstein presents in 2026 a case series of four teenage girls who died of mucinous ovarian carcinoma, a rare ovarian cancer that tends to strike younger women. Reports in teenagers are scarce, and recent gene research links combined TP53 and KRAS mutations to worse outcomes at younger ages. The series was assembled through an online patient community, with mothers supplying medical records.

The girls were diagnosed between ages fourteen and nineteen over the last four years, each presenting with abdominal pain and a large ovarian cyst. Most were first operated on by gynecologists who did not suspect this cancer type. The author argues younger patients need more targeted treatment research.
pmc-13272261:
Carolyn Ten Holter and Mira Wolf-Bauwens wrote a 2026 journal article on dual-use quantum technologies in defence, technologies that can serve civilian and military ends at once. New technologies never develop in a moral or political vacuum, they argue, so funding, use cases, and context shape how quantum tools should be judged.

The authors argue the label dual-use is inadequate for moral judgement because it mixes a plain description with an ethical verdict and misses context and process. They propose building Responsible Innovation frameworks into quantum development, enabling case-sensitive ethical assessment and practical guidance. Their way forward engages critics of military quantum uses while respecting current geopolitical realities.
pmc-13272561:
Elliott Rogers and a large team described an open diagnostic reader in a 2026 hardware article. Rapid tests are cheap and common, yet reading faint lines by eye can give wrong results, and lines fade within minutes. Their reader aims to give steady images and measured results at very low cost.

The device is modular and 3D printed, with trays shaped for cholera tests, hepatitis E tests, and agar plates. Parts cost only a few pounds for trays and under fifty pounds for a full imaging rig with its own light. Designs are shared under an open license. The authors link the reader to machine learning analysis, so field teams can record tests in a standard way.
pmc-13273161:
Katarzyna Czarzasta leads a 2026 study in rats of how offspring recover from maternal depression around birth, focusing on brain chemicals by sex. Maternal stress during pregnancy and nursing had earlier caused depression-like and anxious behavior in young offspring, more in females, but not in adults. The team measured signal chemicals in three brain regions of adult offspring.

Female offspring of stressed mothers showed the biggest changes, with lower levels of a dopamine breakdown product and of protective amino acids in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. Male offspring showed only lower serine in the frontal cortex. The authors suggest these sex-dependent changes may underlie recovery in adult offspring.
pmc-13273261:
Tam Duc Mai and Jonathan Gershenzon wrote a 2026 commentary on two part plant defenses, prompted by a new study of common ivy. Plants that store toxins must avoid poisoning themselves. Many keep the toxin inactive with a sugar attached, then release it when tissue is chewed and an enzyme cuts the sugar off.

The ivy study they discuss tracked two related saponins, soap like toxins in the leaves. After damage, the stored three sugar form fell while the two sugar active form rose quickly. The active form burst red blood cells and harmed plant cells far more strongly. Rebuilding the pair in a test plant confirmed the switch. Mai and Gershenzon present the work as a clear case of this defense design.
pmc-13273461:
Trang Thi Minh Nguyen and co-authors used genome guidance to find antibiotic activity in a soil bacterium in a 2026 study. Multidrug resistant Staphylococcus aureus is a major treatment problem, and soil Streptomyces species are classic antibiotic makers. Their strain, called THA-960, came from Streptomyces virginiae.

Screening showed the strain killed clinical resistant isolates at low doses, beating familiar producer strains, and electron images showed rapid cell wall damage. Its full genome held thirty-one clusters for making specialized compounds. Comparing hundreds of Streptomyces genomes mapped where the cluster for amycomicin, a known active compound, is conserved. Chemical analysis then detected a feature matching amycomicin in the strain. The authors offer this as a roadmap for targeted strain hunting.
pmc-13274161:
Mengmeng Jie, Qiushi Liao, and Cheng Liu wrote a 2026 review article on circular RNAs in inflammatory bowel disease. This long-term gut inflammation covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and present drugs help only partly. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped genetic messages that fine-tune cell behavior and show altered patterns in patients.

The review maps how these rings interact with classic signaling routes inside gut cells, including the JAK-STAT and NF-kappa-B pathways that drive inflammation. Several rings already look promising as blood or tissue markers for spotting and staging the disease. Others might become drug targets. The authors note the field is young, with clinical use still to be proven.
pmc-13274761:
Yu-Ting Wei and colleagues report a 2026 journal article testing whether acupuncture changes how brain signals flow in Alzheimer's disease. Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the standard drug donepezil alone, or donepezil plus acupuncture, for six weeks. Resting brain scans were analyzed for the frontoparietal network, a system for attention and control, before and after treatment.

Both groups improved on a standard thinking test, with larger gains in the acupuncture group. Patients' frontoparietal wiring looked scrambled yet partly rebuilt compared with seven healthy adults. After treatment, the acupuncture group showed its own pattern of changed connections, including paths from the right insula and the precuneus into a left temporal region. The drug-only group's changes followed a different route.
pmc-13275061: Dongyue Jiao and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their 2024 eLife article on a signaling pathway that sustains protein production in cancer cells. During a self-review, the authors found that representative microscope panels in Figure 4F, showing cell invasion and migration assays, had been inadvertently duplicated. Similar-looking raw images were mixed up during figure assembly. The notice stresses the error touches only those specific images, not the captions, the measured data, or the paper's conclusions. A corrected figure is supplied, and the authors apologize for the oversight.
pmc-13275561:
Cristina Bridi and a large team present a 2026 journal article testing the weedkiller 2,4-D on the earliest life stages of a South American frog, Physalaemus gracilis. The chemical is widespread in surface waters, and this frog is known to be sensitive. They compared the pure active ingredient with two shop-bought formulations at five low doses matching Brazilian freshwater limits.

Every version harmed the young frogs at all tested doses, cutting survival and altering swimming. The pure ingredient raised a cell-damage marker at low doses and weakened an antioxidant enzyme at high doses. The two products diverged on heart rate, one slowing it at higher doses, the other speeding it at every dose. Effects differed in size and direction by compound, complicating simple safety claims.
pmc-13275661:
Gunjan Kumar and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of probiotics for saliva, mouth microbes, and gut health. Probiotics are live microbes taken to support health, and earlier work hints they can suppress harmful mouth bacteria. The review asks how strong the evidence is across these linked systems.

Randomised trials in humans were gathered from five major databases, and bias was checked with a standard tool. Probiotic use improved some saliva measures and reduced Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium tied to tooth decay. Gut microbe balance and stomach symptoms also tended to improve. Effects varied by strain, and mixed study quality keeps overall certainty modest.
pmc-13275961:
Marios Platon Dimopoulos and co-authors report a 2026 case series on a rare, severe narrowing of the aorta, the body's main artery. Nicknamed coral reef aorta, the condition fills the vessel with hard, jagged calcium. Open surgery is the standard fix but is risky for frail patients.

The team treated three patients with intravascular lithotripsy, a method that sends soft sound pulses through the vessel to crack the calcium. A pressure-based measure, called FFR, tracked blood flow before and after. All three procedures worked, and flow improved clearly in each case. One patient developed a tear in the vessel wall, fixed with a stent. The others needed no stent. At checks up to a year later, all three still felt better with open vessels.
pmc-13277161:
Meiying Lei and seven co-authors studied how family life links to obsessive-compulsive disorder in teens, in twenty twenty-six. One hundred thirteen teens with the disorder were scored for symptoms, family setting, parenting style, obsessive beliefs, and anxiety. A smaller set of parents and of teens without the disorder filled the same scales for comparison.

Strained family settings, harsh parenting, obsessive beliefs, and anxious traits all rose with symptom severity. When the paths were teased apart, obsessive beliefs fully carried the link from family factors to symptoms. Anxiety traits added no separate path once beliefs were counted. Parents of teens with the disorder also scored high on beliefs and anxiety, which hints these traits run in families. The authors say family-based care should aim squarely at obsessive beliefs.
pmc-13277761:
Aleksandra Janiszewska leads a 2026 study of louse flies, blood-feeding parasites of birds, across migrating species in Central Europe. The team screened more than 100,000 birds from 157 species caught during autumn migration. They then used family-tree-aware models to ask which host traits track with parasite rates.

Seven louse fly species turned up, with two dominating the sample. Most host species carried the parasites, but only about two in a hundred individual birds were infected at the median. Body size, rainfall in the breeding range, habitat, diet niche, and migration distance all shaped rates. The two common fly species responded to host traits in opposite ways, warning against one-size predictions as climate shifts migration.
pmc-13278061:
Debra R Milamed and John Hedley-Whyte wrote a 2026 biographical reflection on Sir Benjamin William Rycroft, an ophthalmologist who shaped Hedley-Whyte's early education. Rycroft led eye care at a military hospital at Musgrave Park outside Belfast in 1940 to 1942, where he also taught the young Hedley-Whyte and became godfather to his brother.

Born in Yorkshire in 1902, Rycroft trained in medicine, moved into eye surgery, and served with distinction in the Mediterranean during the war. Afterward he advanced burn reconstruction, corneal grafting, and tissue banking in Britain. The piece also recalls his organ playing, gardening, and royal connections, and his 1964 memorial lecture in Belfast on plastic surgery and ophthalmology.
pmc-13278961:
Ashley Lu and a large team map microglial cell states in ageing human brains in a 2026 Alzheimer study. Dementia is not inevitable even when amyloid and tau proteins accumulate. Brain tissue came from octogenarians with and without dementia, plus cognitively intact centenarians carrying similar amyloid loads.

Spatial and single-nucleus gene profiling charted six tissue zones forming a disease continuum. A turning point appeared where amyloid-linked inflammation gave way to tau-linked programmes. Microglia shifted there from early inflammatory states to later antigen-presenting ones. People without dementia lacked the late programme, while centenarians showed it detached from tau build-up. The transition is proposed as a resilience lever for therapy.
pmc-13279561:
Zia Ullah and colleagues report a 2026 case of brucellosis that inflamed both sacroiliac joints. Brucellosis is a germ illness caught from farm animals or raw milk. It often hits one sacroiliac joint, the joint that joins spine to pelvis. Two sided joint harm is less typical and can mimic tuberculosis or joint swelling diseases. Their patient was a nineteen year old man.

He had one month of buttock pain that spread to the legs, plus two weeks of fever, chills and sweats. He drank unpasteurized milk, a classic risk. Blood tests showed high swelling marks, and a standard test found Brucella antibodies, germ fighter proteins. MRI scans proved two sided joint swelling with bone wear and fluid in the bone. Care began with two antibiotics, doxycycline and co-trimoxazole. Two sided pain with fever in raw milk users should prompt this test.
pmc-13279661:
Phumzile Mkhize and colleagues published a 2026 review asking whether boosting the protective chemistry of medicinal plants leads to stronger immune effects in people. Plants make compounds such as flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids, many active against inflammation in lab tests. Growers can raise those compounds with genetic methods, chemical elicitors, and biostimulants. Few studies, though, connect higher plant levels to real immune outcomes in humans.

Elicitor and biostimulant methods reliably raise compound levels in the plant, the authors find. The chain then weakens. Uptake in the gut, chemical stability, and dose decide whether a richer plant means a stronger effect in a patient, and proof there is thin. The review sets out a framework that links plant changes to uptake testing and then to immune endpoints. Each step is checked rather than assumed. The work is aimed at researchers designing plant-based immune treatments.
pmc-13280461:
Yuntao Hao and team report a 2026 gene study of familial ovarian immature teratoma, a rare ovary germ cell tumour. Past work by the team found a germline fault in BMP15 as a risk factor in one family. Yet not all female carriers in that family had the tumour. The team ask if a second gene acts with BMP15 to cause disease. Subjects came from two three generation families.

Whole exome sequencing, a full protein gene read, was done, and candidate variants were checked by Sanger sequencing. Unlike the two unaffected sisters, both affected second generation members held a germline fault in CDHR2 as well. It was a truncating fault, which cuts the protein short. Harm was predicted by standard gene tools and graded by gene guidelines. Lab tests of CDHR2 levels used PCR, protein blots and fluorescence microscopy. Two hits may explain why just some carriers fall ill.
pmc-13280661:
Yuh-Shan Ho and colleagues mapped thirty years of research on false teeth and mouth repair in a 2026 study. They counted and sorted papers from 1991 to 2024 in a large science database. More than thirty-eight thousand papers fit their search. They grouped the work by words in titles, short summaries, and keywords.

Implants, tooth materials, and digital tools led the field across all three decades. The team found four broad themes, from implant-based repair to function-focused care. Three newer themes grew fast in the last period. They were three-dimensional printing, checks on digital accuracy, and the use of smart software. The map shows a field moving from hand craft toward digital work.
pmc-13281361:
Anaisa Cajigas Gandia and colleagues published a 2026 population genetics study of Oophaga vicentei, an endangered poison frog found only in central Panama, where habitat fragmentation and mining press on its range. Almost nothing was known about how its populations are structured. Instead of a genome project, the team mined RNA sequencing data for thousands of gene-region markers, a cheaper route to genome-wide diversity estimates.

Two main genetic clusters appeared: a western group spanning three localities and an eastern group at La Ceiba, the most genetically distinct population of all. The western cluster showed hints of further splitting. Population size reconstructions traced a peak around the last interglacial warm period and decline after the last glacial maximum, with La Ceiba shrinking most steeply. The authors present the results as a genomic baseline for conservation: every known population carries distinct heritage and all deserve protection.
pmc-13281561:
Ahmed Adly and colleagues tested how tooth caps are made in a 2026 lab study. Partial caps cover part of a tooth rather than the whole crown. A cap must fit tight at its edge, or decay can creep in. The team used forty-eight sound human upper premolars. Teeth were shaped in two designs, a thin classic cut and a wide cut that spans all faces. Each design was copied three ways: a putty mold, and two mouth scanners.

All caps were glued in and cycled through hot and cold baths to mimic the mouth. Fine microscopes then measured the edge gap of each cap. One scanner gave the tightest fit in both designs. Its wide-design caps beat the putty mold by a clear mark. Most clear wins in the study traced to that scanner. The authors say scanner choice shapes fit as much as tooth design.
pmc-13281761:
Jacquelin I Cordero and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of why men rarely get the HPV vaccine, reading the problem through stigma. Men account for the majority of HPV-related throat cancers, yet they were left out of vaccine research and campaigns, and uptake lags. The researchers reanalyzed group interviews from 2021 with thirteen vaccine-eligible men aged 18 to 35 in El Paso, Texas, using critical discourse analysis guided by a health stigma framework.

Four themes traced stigma from the inside out. At the personal level, masculine norms cast male sexual health as shameful and framed HPV as a women's issue, leaving men feeling unaffected rather than unprotected. Within families, silence and moralizing kept the topic closed. At the system level, policy and clinic practices reinforced it. The authors argue vaccination programs built only on information will keep missing men; interventions must work at the individual, family, and structural levels.
pmc-13281861:
Khalid Abdukadir Osman and colleagues set size norms for testicles in Somali men in a 2026 study. Testicle size is a basic sign of male hormone and fertility health. Norms differ by population, yet Somalia had no sound-scan norms of its own. Doctors there leaned on foreign charts that can mislabel healthy men. The team read scans of two hundred twelve men with normal findings in Mogadishu. The men, aged eighteen to eighty-four, were scanned from 2022 to 2025.

Size averaged about ten milliliters on the right and a shade less on the left. The healthy range ran from roughly five to eighteen milliliters. The right side was reliably the larger one. Size did not track with age. Somali values differed clearly from European, West African, and Asian charts. The authors give a cutoff for when a side gap counts as real. They urge local use of these first Somali norms.
pmc-13282161:
Yan-li Chen and Jin-hua Wang present a 2026 case report built around working backwards from an ultrasound clue to a hidden narrowing of the aorta. The aorta is the body's main artery. A birth narrowing, called coarctation, can drive high blood pressure and stroke yet stay missed in adults. Their patient was a thirty-two-year-old man admitted with sudden right-side weakness and slurred speech, after ten years of uncontrolled high blood pressure.

Ultrasound of his kidney arteries showed a slow, delayed waveform pattern on both sides, known as parvus et tardus. That downstream clue prompted scans upstream, which found a severe narrowing at the start of the descending aorta. Blood pressure in his arms was far higher than in his legs. Later dye scans confirmed the tight segment. The authors argue this cheap clue can trigger early screening in young patients.
pmc-13282461:
Mehdi Karimi and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on coffee, caffeine, and breast cancer risk. Coffee carries antioxidants and bioactive compounds, yet individual studies have disagreed for decades. Searching the literature through February 2026, the team pooled thirty-one prospective cohort studies of regular coffee, decaffeinated coffee, and caffeine, with subgroups by menopausal status, follow-up, and hormone receptor subtype.

Regular coffee drinking was associated with a small reduction in breast cancer risk, a pooled hazard ratio of 0.95, and the association concentrated in postmenopausal women. Caffeine intake alone showed no association, with a hazard ratio of 0.99, and decaffeinated coffee likewise sat at a null 1.00, with subgroups flat for both. That pattern suggests any protection comes from coffee's non-caffeine chemistry, not the stimulant. The authors keep the claim modest: an inverse association in one subgroup of drinkers, awaiting larger prospective work and a mechanism before dietary advice changes.
pmc-13282861:
Sugar handling in the fungus Nakaseomyces glabratus is the subject of a 2026 laboratory study led by Jolien Vreys. The fungus lives in host sites where sugar levels rise and fall. The team asked how its sugar kinases, the enzymes that first process sugars, control entry into energy pathways.

Laboratory tests covered five predicted kinases. Only three processed glucose, fructose, or mannose, and each had a distinct role. One kinase worked best when sugar was scarce, while others handled larger amounts. A compound tied to trehalose storage blocked two kinases and slowed sugar uptake. The results show layered control that helps the fungus grow when food is limited.
pmc-13282961:
What does a rare muscle disease cost American health plans each year? Amanda A Hill and associates answer with 2026 claims work. The disease weakens face, shoulder, and arm muscles over time. Its cost to health plans had not been measured before in this country.

Claims from 2018 to 2021 covered 383 patients and 1,915 matched controls. Yearly medical costs per patient were far higher for patients than controls in both plan types. Drug claim costs were also higher, even for patients without other conditions. Stroke-related disease and ear problems were more common in patients. The authors call the totals a cautious first estimate of direct medical cost.
pmc-13283161:
Airway cells washed from ventilated COVID-19 patients sort into sparse and dense profiles in Franklin Pereira Araujo's 2026 analysis. The virus can drive intense lung inflammation and cell change. The team studied cells drawn from the windpipe of patients on breathing machines.

Samples came from 48 draws in 28 patients with severe disease. Cell counts split samples into sparse and dense profiles for comparison. Dense samples showed more basal cells, young cells, and lung lining cells with odd shapes. They also held more active immune cells and more virus spike signal. Dense profiles arose more often in patients who died. A surface marker called EpCAM rose on lining cells in dense samples.
pmc-13283961:
Fazheng Zhao and colleagues surveyed views in 2026 on a pricing reform for traditional Chinese medicine services in Northeast China. New national guidelines issued in 2025 push these services toward value-based pricing. The survey gathered 399 valid replies from Jilin and Liaoning provinces: 250 health professionals, 125 patients, and 24 administrators.

Among professionals, higher job title and tighter insurance payment limits tied to lower satisfaction with pricing and payment, while management support raised satisfaction. Patients knew little of the billing changes directly, yet split between wanting lower prices and accepting moderate rises for better quality, and many backed tiered pricing. Administrators flagged complex cost accounting and weak links between pricing and insurance payment. The authors call the reform a system coordination problem.
pmc-13284461:
Elizabeth Anne Breen writes a 2026 commentary on RNA treatments for Alzheimer disease and related tau disorders. A recent review by Rajbanshi and colleagues surveyed new RNA tools, hurdles in translation, and trials now under way. Breen notes strong skill at hitting molecular targets, yet patient benefit has stayed hard to prove.

The commentary argues that target contact alone will not be enough. Immune dysfunction in the brain, wide differences between patients, and disease stage all shape whether a drug can help. Future success, Breen suggests, will need precise tau control plus proof of lasting gains in thinking and daily function, with trial designs that match patient biology and timing.
pmc-13285361:
Live X-ray guidance during front-approach hip replacement ties to a slightly lower early redo rate in Dutch registry data analyzed by Marije C. Vink and co-authors in 2026. Guidance may help place parts well, but proof of better results was thin. The study covered 49,878 first hip replacements done from 2022 to 2024.

Raw redo rates at two and a half years sat close in both groups, near two percent in the figures reported here. After adjustment for body size, past surgery, and fixation, the guided group showed a lower redo risk. No clear gaps appeared for redo due to bad alignment or breaks near the implant. The authors note gains are small.
pmc-13285661:
Joyce Esposito and twelve co-authors grow 3D muscle balls from stem cells to model Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a muscle wasting disease. Flat cell cultures model the diseased muscle niche poorly. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

In this disease, stem cells that rebuild muscle bear inner flaws, and scar tissue blocks repair. The team grew balls from gene matched healthy and diseased stem cells, plus patient cells, and compared them with flat cultures. Gene and protein reads tracked growth and maturity marks. The 3D balls raised a key stem mark but lowered several growth marks, which suggests a distinct state worth study.
pmc-13286061:
NAOKO KAWASHITA and fellow researchers studied how community nurses in Japan decide which new mothers and babies need continued home support. Their 2026 qualitative study draws on focus groups with 17 mother-child nurses at three local health centers. Nurses must judge family circumstances and a mother's mental health quickly during postnatal visits.

The nurses' assessments sorted into eleven categories covering the mother's body, emotions, finances, social support, and behavior, plus the child's physical state. The range shows how wide their checks run during a short visit. Picking up these signals early can help prevent abuse and postpartum depression. Seamless support after the first visit, the authors stress, matters for both mother and child.
pmc-13286361:
Anna Mertens and colleagues map the grip system that moves a cell convoy in living zebrafish in a 2026 developmental study. A cell cluster called the lateral line primordium crawls along the embryo's flank, and its grip on the sheet beneath mixes several related anchor proteins. Knocking out anchors singly and in stacks let the team see which ones truly share the work.

Two anchor types sat in overlapping zones of the cluster and covered for each other. Only stacked losses broke the shared anchor hub, sped up stray protrusions, and slowed the march. A sheet protein, laminin alpha5, guarded the floor's soundness but not motion by itself. Pairing its loss with one anchor loss stalled migration outright and sprouted invasion-like fingers, proof the convoy runs on backup grips.
pmc-13286761:
Ana Carolina Dias, Ana Rita da Cruz, and Carolina Dall'Antonia da Motta review how brain stimulation with magnetic pulses has been used with people involved in the justice system. Their 2026 scoping review searched Portuguese, Spanish, French, and English literature. Criminal behavior has been tied to brain dysfunction in moral and self-control circuits, which makes a tool that can probe those circuits attractive.

Only three studies qualified. Those studies suggest the method can reveal functional deficits linked with antisocial behavior, such as weak response control. Using stimulation as a treatment in forensic groups remains almost untouched. The authors call for larger, more varied samples before any forensic service adopts the approach.
pmc-13286961:
Weihua Hu and colleagues test whether pairing rice husk biochar with a helpful bacterium repairs acidified tobacco soil in southern China. The 2026 field study set five plots: a plain control, biochar alone, and biochar with three doses of Bacillus subtilis fertilizer. Acid soil limits fertility and leaf quality across the region's tobacco farms.

Combined treatment reshaped the soil bacterial community and raised its diversity, while moderate microbe doses strengthened nitrogen cycling potential. Soil chemistry and enzyme activity improved alongside. Multi-method scoring placed two combined doses at the top for fertility, and leaf quality rankings favored the middle and high microbe doses. The middle combination won overall. Path modeling showed enzymes carrying much of the benefit from soil to leaf.
pmc-13287061:
Chiara Bonfanti and colleagues created educational leaflets to help parents of premature babies take part in early intervention inside the neonatal intensive care unit. The 2026 project sits inside a clinical program for families of infants born between twenty-four and nearly thirty-three weeks of pregnancy. Prematurity stresses babies and parents alike, and involved parents protect development.

Seven bilingual leaflets, in Italian and English, explain infant behavioral cues, calming together, gentle sensory experiences such as voice and massage, and the move home. Drafts were refined through focus groups with unit staff and informal parent feedback. Materials reached 104 families, who valued them strongly. Staff reported smoother delivery of the program and better collaboration with parents.
pmc-13288161:
Touqeer Rehman and co-authors report in 2026 a baby aged four months. The baby arrived with seizures, a rash around body openings, and hair loss. Dangerous blood acidity first looked like blood infection. Urine chemistry showed a pattern pointing to a rare, treatable fault in how the body uses the vitamin biotin.

Firm proof tests were not available at their centre, so the diagnosis stayed unconfirmed. Even so, starting biotin at ten milligrams a day brought fast clinical and chemical recovery. Combined with a review of earlier cases, the report urges doctors to weigh this vitamin fault in infants with the same trio of signs.
pmc-13288361:
Zahid Ahmad Paul and co-authors profiled yarrow plants gathered in Kashmir in 2026, testing alcohol extracts and two separated fractions for antioxidant and germ-fighting strength. The herb has a long folk history for wounds, fever, and pain, and the team used chemical fingerprinting to name its active parts.

The ethyl acetate fraction fought oxidation most strongly and also hit a bacterium and a fungus hardest in dish tests. Fingerprinting named diosmin, pelargonin, and epicatechin as key compounds. Computer docking showed diosmin gripping a bacterial growth protein most tightly. The authors propose guided separation of the active parts as leads against drug-resistant germs.
pmc-13288561:
Jolly Lapat and colleagues compare pregnancy outcomes for teenage and adult mothers in northern Uganda. Their retrospective study from twenty twenty-six reviews deliveries at Anaka General Hospital. Teenage pregnancy carries known risks for mothers and babies. Local evidence comparing the two groups was still limited.

Charts covered three years of deliveries at the hospital. Teenagers accounted for more than a quarter of all deliveries. The team sampled equal groups of teenage and adult mothers for comparison. Teenage mothers showed a lower rate of HIV infection. Other maternal and newborn outcomes were compared with adjusted models. The results give local staff a firmer base for targeting care to young mothers.
pmc-13288861:
Dennis A Eichenauer leads a large expert panel writing 2026 European Hematology Association guidelines for Hodgkin lymphoma, a B-cell cancer that often strikes young adults. Staging rests on PET and CT scans plus risk factors, and the document walks through diagnosis, treatment by stage and age, salvage care, and follow-up.

Early favorable disease usually gets two cycles of ABVD chemotherapy followed by low-dose targeted radiotherapy, with stronger or gentler variants for unfavorable early disease depending on scan response and age. Advanced disease options include the BrECADD combination or nivolumab with AVD, again adjusted by interim scans. Relapsed patients are steered toward checkpoint inhibitor salvage, high-dose chemotherapy, and stem cell transplant when eligible.
pmc-13289261:
Nina Mitterbauer and co-authors ask why health promotion programs miss men and how to draw them in, in work from twenty twenty-six. Men die younger than women on average and take more health risks. Yet many feel that health programs are not made for them and stay away.

The rapid review drew on twenty-one studies of boys and men aged twelve to seventy-nine, plus health staff views. Gender norms stood out as a top barrier to joining. Programs set in sport clubs, workshops, or workplaces drew more men, and peer support helped change stick. Plain, action based words beat clinical or shaming terms. The authors urge programs built inside settings men already trust.
pmc-13289661:
Luis Felipe Ensina and colleagues review a 2026 set of options for chronic spontaneous urticaria that resists omalizumab. Urticaria means recurring itchy hives driven by mast cells, harming quality of life. Omalizumab helps many who fail high-dose antihistamines, yet some respond partly or not at all, and sorting true resistance from missed diagnosis matters first.

Validated scores over seven days and control tests should judge response, the authors advise. Blood markers can hint at subtype: high IgE favors allergy-driven disease with better drug response, while low IgE and autoimmune signs favor a harder subtype. Cyclosporine remains a proven next step. Newer targeted drugs, including dupilumab and kinase blockers, are widening choices toward tailored care.
pmc-13289761: Editors and the publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy issued a 2026 retraction notice for a 2019 article on Atractylodes polysaccharides and colorectal cancer by Feng and coauthors. A third party raised integrity concerns in 2025 about Figure 3, and the authors themselves asked for retraction in March 2026. Checks found Western blot overlaps with papers from related and unrelated groups representing different samples. The notice lists the suspect figures but presents no replacement science, so its content stays narrow.
pmc-13290461:
Robotic surgery for gallbladder cancer matches open surgery on cancer outcomes and beats it on several recovery measures, a 2026 meta-analysis by Piyun Zhang and colleagues concludes. Robotic removal has spread in recent years, but doubts about safety and cancer control have lingered.

Searching five databases, the authors found five propensity-matched studies covering 629 patients, 202 robotic and 427 open. The robotic group had fewer major complications, less blood loss, lower pain scores, and a shorter hospital stay. Mortality, overall complications, operating time, lymph node counts, clear-margin rates, and three- and five-year survival all came out statistically alike. Zhang and colleagues call robotic surgery a safe option while asking for randomized trials to confirm the recovery edge.
pmc-13290561:
Patience, treated as a resource teams can hold, gets a measuring stick in a 2026 study by Risheng Qiao and colleagues. Their subject is patient capital, a concept usually tracked with money metrics, here rebuilt from interviews and surveys in organizational settings.

Starting with grounded-theory coding, the team distilled five dimensions: self-control and patience, steady persistence, long-term goal drive, emotional and social skill, and adaptability. Factor analyses supported a second-order model with those five parts, and large surveys confirmed the scale measured reliably. A multilevel model then showed patient capital carrying part of the effect of transformational leadership onto team innovation performance. Qiao and colleagues offer the validated tool to managers who want to grow long-horizon strength in teams.
pmc-13290661:
Semen quality in Emirati men wobbled over a decade while sperm movement slid steadily, Temidayo Omolaoye and colleagues report in a retrospective study from 2026 from a UAE fertility center. Middle Eastern data are scarce in the global debate over falling sperm counts.

The team analyzed 13,276 samples from 2,730 men seen between 2012 and 2022. Every measure stayed above World Health Organization reference limits, but volume, concentration, and total count dipped sharply in 2016 before partly recovering. Motility told a cleaner story: both progressive and total motility fell year after year, by 6% to 17% annually in the reported estimates. Men over 35 showed lower volume and motility, and higher body mass tracked with poorer quality. The authors call for studies that add environment and lifestyle to the picture.
pmc-13290861:
Small tested nudges lifted survey recruitment among Muslim immigrants in Indianapolis, Olanrewaju Onigbogi and colleagues report in a quality improvement study from 2026. Recruiting underrepresented groups into community research stalls on mistrust and access barriers, and standard community-engagement playbooks rarely say how to adjust tactics mid-course.

Within a health survey of African and Middle Eastern Muslim immigrants, the team ran three phases over 32 weeks. First came standard recruitment. Then an agile nudge phase used an eight-step cycle of designing, testing, and refining behavioral prompts. Then came observation. Weekly completions rose from a mean of 20.9 to 30.0 during the nudge phase, then settled at 25.9, still above baseline, with 709 surveys completed overall. Run charts showed the shift was not random drift. Onigbogi and colleagues offer the cycle as a practical upgrade for community studies.
pmc-13290961:
Akiyuki Okamoto and co-authors present a 2026 case report on early rehabilitation started inside an intensive care unit during a myasthenic crisis. Their patient was a 67-year-old woman newly diagnosed with myasthenia gravis who developed breathing failure and needed a ventilator.

Exercise began on hospital day 3, with the team watching vital signs and muscle tiredness as the load rose step by step. Standing practice started on day 12, and walking practice followed on day 17 while ventilation continued, with no adverse events reported. She left the ventilator on day 24, walked on her own with a cane by day 64, and went home on day 78.
pmc-13291061:
Swallowing trouble after head and neck cancer treatment may be getting missed in routine follow-up, argue Sinead Rothrie, Grainne Brady, and Justin Roe in a 2026 service evaluation. Surveillance visits usually hunt for returning cancer, while lasting problems with eating, drinking, and daily life receive far less attention in their tertiary center.

Notes from 52 patients showed documented checks for swallowing harm in only a small share of cases, and just one referral to speech and language therapy followed. A separate group of 74 patients screened with a concerns inventory found that most reported at least one unmet quality-of-life need. The authors press clinics to ask about swallowing and wider concerns directly, rather than waiting for patients to raise them.
pmc-13291161:
Telling schizophrenia from bipolar disorder is hard, and Zefeng Wang leads a 2026 study using brain scans to help. The two illnesses share many symptoms. Mistakes in diagnosis are common. A light-based brain scan during a word task may offer a fairer test.

The team built a learning model called TimeMIL for these time-based scans. It took data from 52 healthy people, 50 with schizophrenia, and 67 with bipolar disorder. The model finds key time segments on its own. It sorts the three groups with high accuracy in tests. Added tools show which brain areas drive each call. That openness may help doctors trust the output.
pmc-13291261:
Bangqin Cheng and colleagues study how to steady a jet engine compressor under twisted intake flow, in 2026. Curved, buried intakes on fighter jets swirl the air before it reaches the compressor. That paired swirl can trigger stall, a breakdown of smooth airflow. The team combined computer simulation with rig experiments on a high-speed axial compressor. They traced stall to a tip leakage vortex that swells and blocks the passage.

A casing treatment, grooves in the wall above the blades, curbed the vortex's growth. Stall margin rose by about 53 percent in simulation and about 50 percent in experiments. Peak efficiency barely moved, dipping only a tenth of a point or less. The treatment also reshaped radial flow and lifted the total pressure ratio. The authors present casing treatment as a practical stability upgrade for engines fed by stealthy curved intakes. Flight safety gains follow from the wider stall margin.
pmc-13291361:
Ancient DNA may cling to cave walls and paintings. Alba Bossoms Mesa leads a 2026 study testing that bold idea. Past DNA work used bones, dirt, and tools from cave floors. Painted walls are a direct mark of human hands.

Samples came from 24 art panels in 11 caves. Sites spanned Spain and Portugal. Marks ranged from plain signs to hand stencils and figures. Human DNA traces turned up in one crust sample. The cave was Escoural in Portugal. No animal DNA joined those traces. A bare wall sample from the same cave also held human DNA. Such finds could one day link art to its makers.
pmc-13291661:
Ocean eddies feed tiny plants in barren subtropical seas. Alexandra E. Jones-Kellett leads a 2026 study of these swirling refuges. Gyre waters hold few nutrients on average. Yet many plant plankton types coexist there.

Eddies stir deep nutrients up into sunlit water. Eukaryotic plankton bloom inside those swirls. Outside eddies, two water regimes split sharply. Still, unmixed waters starve eukaryotes for months. Freshly mixed waters hold eddy-like plankton counts. Horizontal mixing thus spreads the eddy benefit wide. Diversity rests on motion, not calm. The carbon food web gains from that churn.
pmc-13292061:
Zehao Wei and co-authors review a 2026 question: how far can artificial intelligence push pancreatic cancer care, from detection to immunotherapy? Pancreatic cancer kills at high rates, is usually found late, and resists immune treatment because of its dense, suppressive surroundings. The review gathers recent work on AI tools across that whole arc.

Covered uses include characterizing the tumor immune environment, predicting mutation profiles, designing nanomedicines, and tracking how patients respond over time. The authors describe how AI can fuse single-cell sequencing with multi-omics data to attack immunotherapy bottlenecks. They also weigh technical hurdles still blocking routine clinical use. Their aim is a practical foundation for precision immunotherapy in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13292261:
Keli An and co-authors design a 2026 cancer drug that wakes up only where tumors run low on oxygen. Their molecule, hrFP-E, is a PROTAC carrying two warheads: one destroys focal adhesion kinase, a protein tied to stiff tissue and invasion, and the other blocks EGFR growth signaling. A nitroreductase-sensitive switch keeps it inert until it reaches hypoxic zones.

In lung cancer models, the activated drug wiped out roughly 96 to 99 percent of the target kinase and suppressed EGFR signaling by about 88 percent of its starting level. Combined effects slowed cell movement and growth in flat and 3D cultures. In animals, tumors shrank by about 66 percent of expected growth without obvious toxicity, and tissue grew softer and less collagen-dense. The authors pitch the design as a modular mechano-chemical platform.
pmc-13292561:
Eunji Park and Juwhan Song build an early warning system for dead chicks on broiler farms, in a 2026 study. A dead bird looks much like a deeply resting one in a single camera frame. Their pipeline instead measures how long stillness lasts. Ceiling cameras filmed a commercial flock of about thirty thousand young birds. A detector located each chick, and a sequence classifier labeled eight-frame clips as stationary or moving.

Stillness durations from over ninety-three thousand normal observations set candidate alarm thresholds. Stricter thresholds traded a little speed for far fewer false alarms. A conservative cutoff flagged deaths with precision near ninety percent on a fresh month of data. Alarms fired roughly eight hours before workers would remove the birds by hand. The authors argue death detection is a timing problem, not a shape problem. Farms could adopt the approach to speed carcass removal and cut disease spread.
pmc-13292661:
Cristine Joy Yap and colleagues compile chemistry data for Canada's underground salt formations in a 2026 data report. Salt beds sit two hundred to two thousand meters down in onshore sedimentary basins. The compilation merges new project analyses, published results, and public provincial and national databases. Samples come mostly from drill cores cut for oil, gas, potash, and salt cavern work. Three thousand one hundred forty-seven samples anchor the set.

Four data families are reported, led by whole-rock chemistry from acid digestion and plasma instruments. Brined core samples simulate the fluids that solution mining would produce. A small set of real industrial brines joins them, plus X-ray diffraction mineral data. Much rock chemistry covers the non-salt beds hugging the deposits, like marls and anhydrites. New analyses targeted critical minerals such as lithium and rare earths. The authors aim the compilation at government research and industry users.
pmc-13293061:
