Charles Egloff and colleagues study, in 2026, whether a mother's cytomegalovirus load in early pregnancy predicts infection in her baby. The virus can pass to the fetus after a first infection, and a drug called valacyclovir may cut that risk.

Records from two centers covered 133 women with confirmed first infection near conception or in the first trimester, of whom 90 took the drug. No baby was infected when the mother's blood test was negative at diagnosis. With measurable high load, treated mothers passed the virus less often than untreated mothers. Treated loads also fell faster over time. Load testing may help target care.
pmc-13293561:
Hongxia Pan, Jialin Liu, and Siru Liu propose, in a 2026 viewpoint, a framework to keep doctors resilient when working with generative artificial intelligence. These tools aid diagnosis and planning, yet they can invent facts, sound sure when wrong, and add checking work that dulls skills.

The framework rests on three linked domains: shaping mental workload, governing who holds clinical authority, and setting safety duties at the organization level. Tools include risk-based triggers for checks, bounded handover of tasks, and team review. The authors warn of workflow friction and alert fatigue, and call for ongoing tuning so safeguards help rather than hinder care.
pmc-13293661:
Peter U Amadi and a large team test, in a 2026 study, whether blood levels of a protein called SOS1 can forecast worsening chronic liver disease. No dependable blood marker yet tracks the march from scarring to liver cancer in a single patient.

A cohort of 556 people across disease stages was followed for up to 36 months with repeated SOS1 measures. Levels rose step by step with stage and tracked standard scarring scores closely. Higher starting levels predicted death and beat two standard markers at sorting risk. Blocking SOS1 in scarring cells and a mouse model reduced scarring genes and tissue scarring, linking marker to mechanism.
pmc-13293761:
Sangmin Lee and co-authors engineer, in a 2026 study, tissue scaffolds that use ball-shaped cell clusters to grow blood vessel networks. Getting vessels into thick lab-grown tissue is a core hurdle for regenerative medicine, since cells deep inside starve without flow.

Clusters of vessel and fat stem cells sat in gel inside printed frames with set spacing and linked pores. Clustered cells sprouted and migrated together better than loose cells, with higher vessel and matrix gene activity. Spacing between clusters tuned how networks formed, and more linked pores let host vessels grow in better in animals. Host vessels lined up along frame strands, guiding design.
pmc-13294161:
Liang Liu and David A. Liberles warn that studies of evolution can pick the wrong kind of complexity, in a 2026 essay on phylogenomics. Analysts often choose a substitution model, a recipe for how DNA letters change, while assuming all sites share one family tree. Genome-scale data break that idea, since genes in one set often carry truly unlike histories.

New work shows that unmodeled splits among gene trees can look like extra substitution complexity. Analysts then pick rich models even when the true process is simple. The pair trace how that mix-up can warp species trees, date estimates, and the meaning read into model settings. They urge readers to treat a hunger for complexity as a warning sign of broken assumptions.
pmc-13294261:
Yating Jin and colleagues test whether brain stimulation over visual or parietal areas changes perceptual learning in a 2026 experiment. Training sharpens a practiced task but gains often fail to spread. Forty-one volunteers trained on contour detection over several sessions while getting high-frequency random noise stimulation at the back of the head, the side parietal area, or a sham version.

Both real stimulations beat sham on total learning. Parietal input sped early gains and alone improved transfer to new curvature cases, while occipital input kept late gains going. The split fits a layered view where sensory zones lock in detail and parietal zones carry flexible generalization.
pmc-13294361:
Samah A M Abou-alfitooh and coauthors test new green-made flooding chemicals for squeezing more oil from mature reservoirs in a 2026 study. Three bis oxalamide compounds were made in ethanol at room temperature and checked with quantum calculations and infrared spectra for surface activity. Lab tests measured oil-water tension, rock wetting shifts, and flooding through real rock cores under reservoir heat and pressure.

The best compound cut tension from 27 to 5 in the reported units and flipped rock preference toward water. Flooding recovered more oil as dose rose, reaching 34.12% of remaining oil at the highest strength in the reported series. Favorable economics were calculated for field use.
pmc-13294461:
Bettina Arca-Tschudi and colleagues challenge routine cuffed tracheostomy tubes in a 2026 retrospective study from a Swiss neuro rehabilitation clinic. Guidelines warn against cuffless tubes when swallowing spills threaten the lungs, yet proof that cuffs protect is missing. Records covered 124 non-ventilated patients from January 2019 to December 2022, nearly all arriving with cuffed tubes.

Everyone switched to cuffless tubes within seven days, even severe aspirators. Suspected and confirmed aspiration counts fell after the switch, and pneumonia plunged from 112 documented patients before to 14 afterward in the reported tallies. Speaking valves and caps were tolerated at once by most, suction needs dropped, and secretions thinned.
pmc-13294561:
Koji Hasegawa and coauthors appraise a failed heart drug trial in a 2026 viewpoint on non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The phase III ODYSSEY-HCM trial tested mavacamten, a cardiac myosin blocker, in symptomatic patients whose thick hearts lack outflow blockage. Symptom scores and peak oxygen use did not improve significantly, the primary goals.

Blood strain markers fell clearly and ultrasound measures of filling and atrial function improved, showing real biological action. At the same time, pumping strength declined in a substantial share of treated patients, which may have canceled gains and could raise rhythm risks. Better patient picking, endpoints, and dosing are the lessons drawn.
pmc-13294761:
Juan Jesús Muñoz García and colleagues test a questionnaire called MOLDES in people with psychotic disorders in a 2026 study. Long illness and long hospital stays can limit daily functioning in ways that symptom scores alone do not explain. The questionnaire instead measures stable thinking and emotional styles linked to adaptation.

Eighty-three clinically stable men in long-term psychiatric care completed the measures used for checking the tool. Scores for the full scale and its three parts showed acceptable consistency, with alpha values from 0.70 to 0.77 across the parts. Links with stigma and quality of life, but not symptom severity, support the tool as a useful extra assessment in rehabilitation care.
pmc-13294961:
Myeongsu Shin and Youngjoo Byun report controlled syntheses of two natural fatty compounds in a 2026 chemistry article. Both compounds come from linoleic acid through enzyme action and act as signalling lipids in the body. Their exact three-dimensional shapes matter for activity, yet modified versions for drug work remain little explored.

Step-by-step routes were developed that set each chiral centre as intended for 9(S)-HODE and a triple-alcohol relative. Having reliable access to these exact forms opens the door to making close variants for testing. Such analogues could clarify roles in inflammation, pain sensing, skin barrier function, and other pathways where these lipids act.
pmc-13295661:
Gudambe Nellithaya Spoorthi and colleagues map what aural rehabilitation should offer Kannada-speaking adults with hearing loss in India, in a 2026 focus group study. Hearing aids alone rarely meet the full need, and programs built for Western settings may not fit local life. Fifteen people took part: audiologists, adults with hearing loss, and their close family members.

The audiologists backed four parts drawn from past work: sensory management, facts-based counseling, hearing training, and personal adjustment support. Family voices, little heard in Indian work on this topic, stressed how deeply hearing loss shapes daily life and how few options families know about. Most adults and relatives saw hearing aids as the whole answer. The authors call for a full program shaped to this group.
pmc-13295861:
Hideaki Takahashi sets out a 2026 hypothesis review on why premium Japanese native chicken, sold as Jidori, tastes richer than standard broiler meat. Fat, and one fatty acid in particular, has often been credited, yet that molecule is unlikely to reach taste buds directly.

Takahashi proposes a two-step account: handling and cooking first turn meat fats into small compounds that dissolve in juices, and those compounds then stretch and strengthen taste signals in savoury food. On this view, keeping or removing fat and the cooking method change flavour a lot. The piece aims to guide lab tests linking cooked-meat chemistry to taste.
pmc-13295961:
Xinxin Chen and co-authors devote their 2026 review to daidzein, a plant compound from legumes noted for calming inflammation and mopping up harmful oxygen species. Earlier reviews covered related compounds broadly, so the team focus on this molecule's twin actions.

Daidzein is reported to tune immune cells, block central inflammatory pathways and switch on the body's own antioxidant defences. Lab evidence links those effects to protection in cancer, heart disease and sudden kidney injury. Because the body absorbs daidzein poorly, the review also covers tiny carrier systems designed to deliver more of it to diseased tissue.
pmc-13296061:
Domenico Schillaci and colleagues build a library of new compounds meant to stop Staphylococcus aureus from forming biofilms, in a 2026 study. Biofilms are slimy cities of bacteria that shrug off standard drugs, and no anti-biofilm drug has yet reached the clinic. The team made twenty-one compounds that join two ring systems and tested them on two germs, in dishes and in wax moth larvae.

Five compounds blocked biofilm growth in the staph germ at low doses. The set was also checked for wiping out set biofilms in staph and in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Two leaders went into the larvae for safety and anti-infective tests, and one, coded 9u, guarded the larvae well in the early stage of infection. The authors offer the family as a lead for biofilm care.
pmc-13296461:
Catherine C. Y. Chang and colleagues report, in a 2026 cell study, that part of a protein called caveolin-1 sits with a second protein inside one zone of the cell's inner membrane system. The second protein, ACAT1, turns free cholesterol into a stored form. Whether the two proteins meet, and what that would mean for how cells handle cholesterol, was not clear.

Pull-down tests, membrane sorting, and fine microscopy all pointed to the pair sharing the same small zone. Mouse cells that lacked caveolin-1 turned more cholesterol from blood fats into the stored form. The pattern hints that caveolin-1 holds ACAT1 back. The finding adds a control point for how cells spread cholesterol among their membranes.
pmc-13296861:
Zhiyuan Bian and co-authors clarify, in 2026, the job of a heat-shock-related gene in thale cress defence against a bacterial leaf pathogen. Plants missing the gene caught disease more easily, while plants with extra copies resisted better, and the gene switched on after attack or defence signals.

Gene-wide reading showed the mutant mis-set defence and hormone response genes. The protein partners with an enzyme that tunes the defence hormone salicylic acid, moving toward the nucleus during attack through tube-like extensions from chloroplasts. Plants missing both partners held less hormone and fared worst. The authors map a positive defence role.
pmc-13297161:
Hongbiao Shi and colleagues map where a gene-switching tool acts in the mouse testis and use it to test one chromatin protein in a 2026 study. The tool, PR-Cre, was known from female reproduction work but never charted in males. Leydig cells, the testis hormone factories, were the focus.

The tool proved active in several testis cell types, including Leydig cell precursors and sperm cells. Deleting the chromatin protein BRG1 from adult Leydig cells produced no visible defect in development, sperm production, or fertility. Two other deletion methods gave the same quiet result. BRG1 looks dispensable in these cells, and the tool's map should help future male fertility studies.
pmc-13297361:
Serfling gives a self tale of two NFAT switch parts in guard cells. The parts, NFATc1 and NFATc2, are the top lime-tied switches there. They steer scores of genes when guard cells wake in hosts. Much of their build and work looks the same at first read. Yet their pace and force split wide by cell type. Forty years of lab work ground the tale in the text. One gene wakes hard on cell wake, the next hums at a low hum.

The woke gene makes a short form with a lone head bit. That short form lacks a long tail bit its kin bear. The hum gene backs cell death, dull states, and worn states. The short woke form points the other way in his reads. Serfling sets that split next to growth birth in the close.
pmc-13297561:
Ahmed Ismail and colleagues ask whether a low lymphocyte count before immunotherapy marks cancer patients headed for worse outcomes, in a 2026 study of health records. Lymphocytes are the white cells that immune checkpoint drugs unleash against tumours. The team used a large United States record network and matched patients with low counts to similar patients with normal counts.

Patients starting treatment with low counts lived shorter lives across tumour types. They also needed more hospital care soon after starting and may have suffered more serious infections. Immune side effects, though, showed no clear rise. A cheap, routine blood test could thus flag patients who need closer watching and support during treatment.
pmc-13298061:
Kim Ma leads a large Canadian expert group issuing a 2026 consensus statement on folate receptor alpha testing in ovarian cancer. The protein appears at high levels on most epithelial ovarian cancer cells, making it a drug target. A recently approved targeted medicine benefits patients whose tumours show high levels of the receptor.

The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada statement recommends timely testing access for all Canadians with this cancer type. Testing guides treatment decisions and opens access to a life-prolonging option in a disease with poor survival among gynaecological cancers. Readers get the group's shared position rather than a single centre's practice.
pmc-13298461:
Beibei Wang and colleagues design a bone repair scaffold that releases different agents in sequence, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Early healing needs antibacterial action, while later stages need blood vessel growth and bone formation signals. Their composite pairs a drug-filled hydrogel with a 3D-printed plastic framework.

Arginine-derived carbon dots leave the hydrogel quickly, giving antibacterial effects and control of reactive oxygen species. Glass nanoparticles on the framework release chondroitin sulfate plus calcium and phosphorus ions slowly, supporting long-term bone induction. Cell tests showed combined gains in proliferation and bone differentiation. The authors propose timed release as a strategy for reconstructing bone defects.
pmc-13299961:
J Yamamoto leads a team asking which comes first after acute heart failure with atrial fibrillation: major bleeding or stroke, in a 2026 competing-risk study. Anticoagulation choices are hard because early paths diverge sharply. The authors tested whether combining anaemia with poor kidney function flags patients whose bleeding risk dominates.

First events were bleeding more often than stroke, and death without either event was commonest of all. The combined flag independently predicted bleeding-first and sharply raised one-year bleeding incidence compared with patients lacking it. Adding the flag to a standard bleeding score improved prediction meaningfully. Safety-first tailoring, including gentler anticoagulation, is advised for flagged patients.
pmc-13301161:
S Kwok and co-authors review twenty years of epicardial defibrillator implants in children at one Asian tertiary center, in a 2026 retrospective study. Small bodies and growing anatomy make these systems hard to place and keep working. Nine children, implanted at a median age of four and a half years between 2005 and 2025, were followed a median of about nine years, tracking coil position and system survival.

No child died, and six received appropriate therapy, the earliest within a year. Trouble came from the hardware's life inside a growing body: two thirds needed late revision at a median of about six years, mostly for sensing lead failure. Coil placement mattered. Coils that migrated or sat under the skin or on the diaphragm failed testing, while coils tucked into the back of the pericardial space or its transverse sinus stayed stable. The authors give placement guidance grounded in that contrast.
pmc-13302761:
S Gerrits and co-authors build, in a 2026 modelling study, a patient-specific computer heart to test which resynchronization strategy fits one complex case best. The patient had internal conduction disease plus scar on the side wall, a combination where bundle branch pacing may disappoint. Imaging supplied the geometry and scar map for the simulation.

The calibrated model reproduced the real ECG closely, and its fitting suggested widespread slowing of the natural wiring. Simulated activation was fastest under a combined strategy that paced the bundle area and the free wall together. Ordinary two-site pacing came second, while bundle pacing alone performed worst in this scarred heart. The authors offer the workflow as a planning aid for difficult cases.
pmc-13303361:
Two mango cultivars answer a heat wave with different chemistry, Wenju Luo and colleagues dissect in a 2026 multi-omics study from southern China. Seedlings under acute heat stress underwent metabolome profiling and RNA sequencing across thirty-six samples, with co-expression networks tying genes to compounds. Oxidative stress damage framed the physiological backdrop.

Over twelve thousand genes changed expression, touching photosynthesis, stomatal control, and hormone pathways. Amino acid derivatives, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and lignans responded most among metabolites. Three hub genes stood out, copper chaperone, cytochrome c, and the energy sensor AMPK, which linked broadly to lipids and flavonoids. The network map, the authors say, hands breeders concrete targets for heat-tolerant mango.
pmc-13303461:
Won-Young Cho and co-authors develop, in a 2026 study, a chemical fingerprinting method for safflower-based injections used in Korean medicine. Such herbal products vary with plant origin and harvest, which threatens consistent dosing. Two formulas were compared: safflower alone, and safflower combined with deer antler.

Gas-based separation paired with mass readings tracked four fatty acids in both products, tuned to tell look-alike molecules apart. Linoleic acid dominated both formulas, and only oleic acid differed clearly in simple tests. Pattern analysis still separated the two products cleanly, with the top parts holding nearly all the spread. The authors present the multi-marker approach as a practical quality check for making herbal injections.
pmc-13303961:
Aurora I. Flores and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how genetic engineering can sharpen the microbes that help crops grow and clean polluted land. Friendly plant microbes already fix nitrogen, free up phosphorus, and fight crop diseases. Editing their genomes could push each talent further.

Strategies surveyed include random mutation, precise CRISPR editing, gene overproduction, genome shuffling, and rebuilt metabolic pathways. Reported gains span stronger biocontrol, better stress tolerance, and improved breakdown of contaminants. The authors insist that edits must stay safe for the wider soil community, farm animals, and people, and they compare how different countries regulate release. The review positions engineered microbes as partners for cutting fertiliser dependence.
pmc-13304661:
Renata R. Silva leads a 2026 study pairing silver nanoparticles with a yeast-made soap-like compound for germ control. Drug-resistant microbes push the search for greener options, and plant or microbe soaps can steady silver particles while attacking cell walls.

The soap came from Candida glabrata grown on farm waste, cutting cost and waste together. It held steady across wide heat, acidity, and salt ranges. Silver particles made with it slowed bacteria and fungi in lab tests, though less than standard antibiotics. Harm to normal cells stayed low, supporting use as a helper treatment.
pmc-13305861:
Matteo Gelardi sets out a 2026 proposal that nasal cytology should serve as a local marker of airway inflammation. Blood tests dominate current practice, yet they only hint at what happens inside the nasal lining. Examining cells taken from the nose is simple, non-invasive, and repeatable.

Gelardi argues that eosinophils reflect longer-lasting inflammation while mast cells mark more active phases of disease. When both cell types appear together, disease may be more severe. Adding cytology results to a combined clinical grading system could sharpen patient grouping, especially in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. The proposal is framed as testable in ordinary clinics and research settings, rather than as settled practice.
pmc-13306761:
Zilin Zhao compared pre-surgery treatments for muscle-invasive bladder cancer in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Fourteen studies with 2234 patients weighed combined chemo-immunotherapy against chemotherapy alone and immune therapy alone before bladder surgery.

Full tumour clearance at surgery was highest for the combined route at 0.41 in pooled figures, ahead of immune therapy at 0.26 and chemotherapy at 0.15 in the reported rates. Network odds strongly favoured the combination over chemotherapy alone. Severe side effects ran highest in the chemotherapy group in early results, shaping the efficacy and safety trade-off. Care teams can use the trade off to pick a plan that fits each case.
pmc-13307661:
Anna De Filippis and co-authors report in 2026 on the ninth yearly meeting of the Italian Society for Virology, held in Turin from June 22 to 24, 2025. More than 400 people from Italy and abroad joined talks under the theme of One Virology and One Health.

Sessions ranged over new virus threats, gene sequencing, virus and host links, vaccines, and viruses in food, farms, and wild species. Talks also covered virus based tools for gene therapy and drug design work. Joint panels and mentor events linked senior and junior staff. The report ends with calls for stronger joint watch systems and shared data tools across human, animal, and nature health.
pmc-13308961:
Changjian He and co-authors describe in 2026 a clash between two leadless pacemakers in the heart of a man aged 91 years, fixed by settings alone. His first Micra unit lost battery charge early at 28 months, so a second unit was placed beside the spent one in the right ventricle.

The pair rubbed in a way that fooled the sensor and paused pacing at odd times during the implant run. Raising the sense threshold calmed the false reads, since his own heart signal stayed strong at 7.4 millivolts in the checks. No pull out or shift was needed on the day. Piled up units still add load that later care must weigh.
pmc-13309261:
Joyce May Sum Leung, Ho Ming Cheung, and Kwok Sing Ng search in 2026 for survival predictors among Chinese lung cancer patients in Hong Kong who chose supportive care alone. Patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2024 had full staging scans yet received no surgery, radiation, or drug therapy. Records covered fitness, tumour size and uptake, fluid around organs, and reasons for the choice.

Four factors independently predicted survival: sex, performance status, tumour diameter, and fluid around the lung or heart. Larger tumours, worse fitness, and fluid collections all pointed to shorter survival in the analysis. Fear of side effects led the reasons patients gave for declining treatment, followed by advanced age and poor fitness. The authors intend the factors to guide honest conversations and care planning. Their cohort shows supportive care is often a considered choice, not simply a default.
pmc-13310761:
Long Zhao and colleagues test a potassium channel opener in mice with drug induced high blood pressure in a 2026 study. Long pressure harms the heart by thickening and scarring its walls, which can lead to heart failure. Channels that help blood vessels relax were lower in sick hearts, so the team asked if boosting them would protect the heart.

Mice got a pressure raising drug for four weeks, with or without the channel opener. Treated mice showed lower pressure, less scarring, and less cell stress. In lab immune cells, the opener calmed a signal chain that drives swelling. Results point to a new target for pressure related heart harm.
pmc-13311161:
Jing Nan and colleagues solve in 2026 the atomic structure of GTR1, the plant transporter that moves glucosinolates, the sulphur-rich defence chemicals of cabbage-family plants. Seeds cannot make these compounds and import them through such transporters, which creates a breeding dilemma: low-toxin seeds usually mean defenceless leaves. Electron microscopy captured the transporter empty and loaded with one glucosinolate.

Both structures, taken at two acidity levels, showed the transporter in an inward-open shape. The cargo sits in a central cavity where the protein's two halves meet. GTR1 grips the shared glucosinolate scaffold firmly while tolerating wide variation in the side chain, which explains how one transporter hauls many variants. Knowing the grip points could let breeders or engineers block seed loading specifically. Defence chemistry would then stay in leaves while meal from the seeds turns safer for livestock.
pmc-13311461:
Bobby G Warren and co-authors compare two ways of hunting fungi in hospital spaces in a 2026 study. Germ growth on plates is slow and misses much, while a DNA test may catch more.

From September 2023 to June 2024 the team sampled air, bathroom floors, vents, bedrails, and linen stores monthly on three wards. Of 742 samples, 64 percent tested positive by the DNA method and 29 percent by culture in this study. Culture still found a wider range of fungi. The pair of methods may work best together for watching hospital contamination. Both methods were run on the same collected samples.
pmc-13311661:
Stephanie M Topp and colleagues introduce a 2026 supplement of papers from the eighth Global Symposium on Health Systems Research, held in Nagasaki in 2024. Health systems worldwide face pressures that overlap: unstable world politics, economic shocks, climate change, and shifting populations. The editors frame the set around a practical question. How is change actually worked out on the ground, and when does it advance justice and lasting reform rather than undermine them?

The papers examine settings as varied as informal city settlements, reforms that push power to local levels, economies under sanctions, and places facing environmental harm. Across them, the editors stress that ministries and frontline services do not change systems alone. Professional bodies, local groups, charities, and private firms all shape outcomes. Readers get a map of where formal policy meets daily practice. The editors argue research should track adaptation while it happens, not only failures after the fact.
pmc-13311861:
Saarang Patel and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether sex shapes outcomes for kidney failure patients who receive clot removal treatment for acute ischemic stroke. Mechanical thrombectomy has improved stroke care, yet patients with renal failure face higher risks, and sex differences in this specific group were little documented. The team analyzed the National Inpatient Sample from 2019 to 2022 and adjusted for demographic, clinical, and hospital factors.

The cohort held 3,280 hospitalizations, split between 1,675 men and 1,605 women. After adjustment, women had notably higher odds of a non-routine discharge, meaning transfer or care beyond going home, with an odds ratio of 1.536 in the model. Death in hospital, by contrast, showed no significant sex difference. Age and certain other illnesses raised the odds of both outcomes. The authors support equal access to thrombectomy while urging discharge planning that accounts for sex.
pmc-13311961:
Beth Dorrans and co-authors offer a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on physical disease rates in people who have been imprisoned, compared with the general population in rich countries. Non-communicable diseases drive much sickness and death overall.

Searches found 32 studies giving 341 data points on illness and death from such diseases. Pooled results showed higher death risk from several major diseases in the formerly imprisoned group, on the review's account. Methods mixed meta-analysis with direction-of-effect counting, plus checks for what drives spread between studies. The findings press prison and community services to plan chronic disease care.
pmc-13312161:
Jens C. Thimm and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, two Norwegian self-report surveys that measure narrative identity, the story people tell about their own lives. Identity was long judged by trained raters coding life stories, so brief surveys promise a cheaper route, provided they hold up under testing and connect to personality problems in sensible ways.

A sample of 330 adults completed both surveys plus measures of personality function and problem traits. Both scales hung together well, and early analyses backed their planned structures even where stricter tests were mixed. Disturbance scores on the self-evaluation scale tracked strongly with poorer personality functioning and more pathological traits. The authors conclude the Norwegian versions are sound and useful, and relevant to newer models of personality disorder.
pmc-13312261:
Bhoomija Chauhan and co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 before-and-after study, whether training helps dentists connect oral cancer risk factors with the mouth changes those factors produce. Early detection leans on this link, yet dentists in places with few cancer cases and little specialist training may get little practice at it.

General dental practitioners from several regions of Indonesia completed questionnaires before and after an oral cancer education program, with 177 responses beforehand and 144 afterward. The correlation between correctly named risk factors and correctly matched pathological changes rose slightly, from 0.464 before the program to 0.485 after it, but the shift was not statistically significant. The authors suggest education may help modestly and call for stronger designs to test whether better-targeted training moves diagnostic awareness further.
pmc-13312761:
Su and ten co-authors scan the brains of kids with fresh blood cancer for fluid-path marks in this twenty twenty-six study. A brain wash path clears waste and moves fluid, and its state in sick kids was not known. The team used scan marks tied to that path in place of direct tests.

Inside, seventy-two sick kids were matched with seventy-two sound kids of like age and sex. Sick kids showed less brain bulk and low marks on all the wash-path scans used. One blood type also showed less white bulk and more brain fluid than sound kids. A low wash mark went with high risk grade and worse sleep in that group. The team calls for more work on what the marks mean.
pmc-13313261:
Albert Osterhaus tells the story of his own career in virology in a 2026 memoir that starts with a boyhood love of animals in Amsterdam in the 1950s and 1960s. That pull led him to study veterinary medicine at Utrecht University, where a placement in the new virology lab of Marian Horzinek taught him the craft.

After his degree in 1974 he worked as a vet and saw at first hand how viral outbreaks hit wild and farm animals, which deepened his drive for vaccine work. Horzinek then offered him a PhD post with wide freedom to hunt new animal viruses. Among his early finds was the first papillomavirus seen in a non-mammal, which caused skin growths on finches. He also built a vaccine against a new cat coronavirus, work he calls a turning point in his growth as a scientist.
pmc-13313761:
Jielan Zhou, Hao Liu, and Rong Luo use, in a 2026 Mendelian randomization study, genetics to probe what in childhood, or in parents, might feed into children's psychiatric disorders. Candidate influences included childhood obesity, childhood absence epilepsy, and intelligence on the child's side. On the parents' side they included longevity, Alzheimer disease, and severe depression. Outcome data for conduct problems, ADHD, autism, and other disorders came from genome consortia and the FinnGen resource.

Out of the grid of tests, only one signal stood out. Liability to childhood obesity associated with raised odds of autism, at an odds ratio of 1.06 in the analysis. For ADHD the figure was 1.09. Neither survived correction for multiple testing. No other trait showed a strong effect, and bias checks came back clean. The authors present the obesity findings as suggestive rather than settled. A child's health trajectory, they argue, deserves a place in explanations of these disorders.
pmc-13314261:
Abdulkarem Al-Shabebi and co-authors map, in a 2026 study, where the protein osteopontin appears in the dromedary camel's tract during the breeding season. Osteopontin shows up in many body fluids and is suspected of helping sperm travel and function, but camel data were lacking. The team sampled the vas deferens at three points, two regions of the prostate, and the bulbourethral glands from twelve adult males. They measured the protein with tissue staining and its message with quantitative PCR.

The methods agreed. Staining burned brightest in the ampullary end of the vas deferens and in the prostate tissue. It ran moderate in the prostate and the vas sections, and faintest in the bulbourethral gland. Gene expression ranked the regions in that order, with significant gaps. The authors suggest osteopontin in semen may ease sperm passage and performance in the female tract, making it a marker for breeding selection.
pmc-13315361:
Carla Lanca, Ian Morgan, and Andrzej Grzybowski argue, in a 2026 commentary, that the predicted global myopia epidemic will not arrive in Europe on schedule. Influential projections assume most of the world will follow East Asia's trajectory toward near-universal short sight. Reviewing recent European data, including reviews, the authors find young adult rates holding around 20 to 30 percent, nowhere near the 70 to 90 percent reported in East Asian cohorts.

They credit real differences, in schooling systems, lifestyles, and time outdoors, but also measurement artifacts. Much child data uses refraction without dilating drops, which inflates rates, and shifting age mixes exaggerate trends. Restricting comparisons to like ages and properly dilated measurements makes Europe's supposed surge look inconsistent. The authors propose pairing school screening with standard dilated tests for honest monitoring, and present Europe as the test case proving an epidemic is a possibility shaped by environment, not a destiny.
pmc-13315561:
Ana-Maria Imbrea and co-authors used a lab model of chicken gut contents in 2026 to test an organic acid blend called AuraShield. Such blends are sought as antibiotic stand-ins that can curb germs and shape gut microbes, and the team used a low dose that does not fully block growth.

At 0.125 percent, the blend raised growth of a helpful gut germ and its butyrate output in whole caeca kept for 24 hours. Adding that germ lowered Salmonella and Campylobacter loads, and the blend strengthened the effect. Signals for gut inflammation and oxidative stress also fell, and related gene activity rose with dose.
pmc-13315761:
A Jantine van Voorden and colleagues used human placental organoids in 2026 to test how two inflammatory cytokines affect the cells that burrow into the womb wall. Extravillous trophoblasts must invade the decidua and reshape spiral arteries, and failure links to preeclampsia and poor fetal growth, which are more common in inflammatory disease.

Both interferon-alpha and tumor necrosis factor-alpha cut invasion while leaving cell growth steps intact. Imaging of untreated organoid and decidua co-cultures showed deep invasion into tissue and arteries, sharply reduced after cytokine exposure, most clearly with interferon-alpha. Gene profiles shifted in several invasion-linked pathways. This block may be one cause of poor growth in some babies.
pmc-13315961:
Bo Ma and a large team built a nerve repair tube in 2026 that shrinks to fit, needs no stitches, and answers magnetic signals to speed regrowth. Standard tubes often mismatch nerve width, demand fiddly suturing, and support only slow fiber growth, leaving repair results weak.

Inspired by heat-shrink tubing, their conduit contracts under infrared light through a heat effect in its carbon nanotube and iron oxide blend, while a sticky inner layer grips the nerve stumps. The layers mix Pluronic gels, alginate, and polydopamine-treated particles. Size adaptation, stitch-free fixing, and electrical responsiveness are combined in one device.
pmc-13316161:
Connor D. Martz and a large team asked in 2026 whether living near deadly gun violence speeds biological aging in teenagers. The sample held 1,781 fifteen-year-olds from the Future of Families and Child Well-being Study, with data from 2014 to 2017 and wide social diversity.

Exposure counted fatal shootings within about one mile of home in the prior year. Aging was scored by combining three epigenetic clocks, GrimAge, PhenoAge, and DunedinPACE. Matching balanced exposed and unexposed teens on race, family economics, and area crime, and weighted models then estimated the aging gap tied to nearby lethal violence.
pmc-13316761:
Xiujun Zhang and co-authors test, in a 2026 cell study, whether vitamin D can calm brain immune cells after a bleed inside the brain. Using hemin to mimic hemorrhage around microglia, they tracked how the cells swing between attack and repair modes.

Vitamin D boosted cell growth, lowered attack markers, and raised repair markers in the dish. It also cut several inflammatory signals while lifting others tied to calming, and it dialed down two pathway proteins, P2X7R and NLRP3, that drive the attack mode. A drug blocking P2X7R matched the vitamin's effect, and combining them worked still better. The pathway gives a concrete lead for easing bleed-related brain injury.
pmc-13316961:
Ryoh Funatsu and colleagues follow, in a 2026 case report, a man in his forties with central serous chorioretinopathy. The fluid blister under his central retina refused to settle for eighteen months. Laser spots closed two leaks, yet fluid stayed, and he declined the stronger light therapy offered.

Vision in the affected eye slipped from 20/25 at first visit to 20/200 by month eighteen in the recorded checks. The light-sensing layer thinned steadily, its outer nuclear layer shrinking from 86 to 46 micrometers, and bright specks appeared inside the retina late on. The case warns that stubborn fluid can damage sight faster than the usual slow course, pressing for timely, decisive treatment.
pmc-13317361:
Ziyang Yu and nine co-authors describe a new imaging platform in two thousand twenty-six for watching germs bind to live cells. To understand infection, researchers need to see the first steps of binding and uptake. They also need to track how cell surface receptors gather at the binding site.

The platform pairs holotomography, which builds three-dimensional images from refractive index, with fluorescence microscopy. It can rebuild volumes and track single particles and bacteria over time. The team used it on Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria meeting live human cells in culture. Both channels ran at once and were aligned, giving a synced record of binding and receptor movement. The tool could suit other receptor-ligand systems as well.
pmc-13318761:
Emily F. Craven and colleagues present a 2026 study of mood signs in freshly calved dairy cows. Qualitative behavioural assessment judges a whole animal's posture and behaviour. It usually rates herds, not individuals. The team tested whether daily scoring could track single cows over time.

Thirty-five cows were assessed after calving, for a mean of 12 days each. Scores were gathered in group settings and individually. Statistical patterns split into an agitated dimension and a playful, inquisitive one. Both shifted as days in milk increased. One pattern fell with a slope of −0.22 per day in their model. Twenty cows clustered into stable or shifting profile types. The authors suggest individual scoring could flag welfare changes, even with less frequent checks.
pmc-13318861:
Haipeng Xie and Wenling Li review, in 2026, the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus as a hub in epilepsy. This thalamic region supports working memory, cognitive control, and emotional integration. It is not one uniform structure but several specialised subregions. Evidence links it closely to seizure networks.

In epilepsy patients, the nucleus shows shrinkage and abnormal connections. Its activity is recruited early during seizures, aiding spread and generalisation. Brain stimulation aimed at it gives mixed results so far. The authors blame poor knowledge of subregion functions and pathways. They call for causal studies at subregional level. Future therapies should target specific seizure pathways within thalamocortical circuits, they argue, rather than the nucleus as a whole.
pmc-13319261:
Jennifer Hanson and Penelope E. Bonnen review the gene basis of a rare inherited illness in a 2026 article on cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis. Faults in both copies of one gene block a step in making bile acids. Harmful fats then build up in the body, causing lasting loose stools, early eye clouding, lumps on tendons, and nerve harm that grows worse over time.

More than 200 fault types in the gene are now known, and large gene banks help show how often each one occurs and where cases get missed. Faults that shut the gene off tend to cause worse illness than faults that only weaken it. New blood tests and baby checks could catch cases early, when drug care still helps most.
pmc-13320261:
Zeng Lin and co-authors show that stretch training boosts stem cell parcels for cartilage repair in a 2026 study. Cartilage heals poorly on its own, and stem cell care gives only modest gains so far. Rhythmic stretch was used to prime stem cells before gathering the tiny parcels they shed, which carry gene scraps that steer other cells.

Stretched cells shed parcels rich in one key gene scrap, and those parcels revived worn cartilage cells in lab tests. The scrap restored clean up of worn cell power houses through a named gene path, which cut cell death, aging, and filler breakdown. In rats with cartilage holes, primed parcels sped true repair. Stretch priming may lift cell free care for joints.
pmc-13320461:
Shriganesh Devaru Bhat and Premjith B․ present a labeled word set from an early Ayurvedic text for Sanskrit language tools in a 2026 data article. Sanskrit joins words into compounds that machines must split to read sense, yet labeled sets for that task in medical Sanskrit were lacking. Pages of a famed old healing text were scanned, read by machine, proofed by experts, and split into single words for labeling.

The set holds 31179 words in all, split between plain words and compound words, each tagged with a zero or one label in the script of the source. Source lessons come from the first part and a later part of the text, across hundreds of pages. The set can train compound spotters and also serve class teaching on compound types.
pmc-13321261:
Francis Dalisay, Jay Hmielowski, and Young-Rock Hong study disaster news on social media and substance use in a 2026 article. People hit directly by disasters face higher distress and drug or alcohol use, but heavy viewing of disaster content may act as indirect exposure. Two surveys were analysed, one after Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024 and one after Los Angeles wildfires in 2025.

In both surveys, more disaster content viewing and more depressive symptoms each went with more alcohol and cannabis use. Viewing linked to depressive symptoms only in the wildfire survey, where symptoms also formed a path from viewing to substance use. The authors warn that news seeking after a disaster may carry hidden costs.
pmc-13321461:
Shaoyue Chen and co-authors sort new art college students by mental health profile in a 2026 study from Anhui Province, China. A total of 1685 first year students at an art vocational college completed a national screening scale for college mental health. The team used latent profile analysis to find natural groups rather than a single average.

Three groups emerged: a high stressors with low symptoms group at 41.8 percent, a moderate group at 43.5 percent, and a low stressors with high symptoms group at 14.7 percent of students in the study. All 22 health dimensions differed clearly across groups. Background traits were then tested for group membership, giving colleges a base for targeted support.
pmc-13322461:
Catarina Domingues, Maria Ferreira and Rosa Pinho review, in 2026, weight and metabolic drugs for people with severe mental illness. Antipsychotic medicines often cause weight gain, insulin resistance and abnormal lipids, driving early death from heart and metabolic disease. Monitoring alone has not solved the problem.

Their structured search covered trials and syntheses from 2015 to 2025, yielding nine studies of GLP-1 receptor agonists, the drug class widely used for diabetes and obesity. Liraglutide and semaglutide reliably reduced weight and improved blood sugar control, with no sign of worsening psychiatric symptoms. Exenatide showed no extra weight loss over placebo. Gut side effects were the commonest problems and were usually mild to moderate. Small samples and short follow-up limit certainty, the authors caution.
pmc-13323061:
Ziad Obermeyer and co-authors train deep learning on electrocardiograms to flag sudden cardiac death risk, in a 2026 study linking all ECGs in a Swedish region to death records. The standard marker, left ventricular ejection fraction, misses most such deaths and flags many low-risk people.

Their model marked a small high-risk group, given as 2.2 percent of the sample, whose yearly rate of sudden cardiac death beat that of the low ejection fraction group. Most model-flagged patients were not flagged by ejection fraction at all. Checks in a United States health system and a Taiwanese registry supported the signal. A paired generative model made the waveform pattern visible for study.
pmc-13323161:
Peng-Cheng Yao leads a study of device closure of the left atrial appendage in persistent atrial fibrillation, published in 2026, asking whether electrical isolation of the appendage improves sealing. Remaining patency after closure is a key driver of later stroke risk.

Of 686 patients who had combined ablation and closure, 469 were matched by propensity methods, split between isolation and no isolation. Just over half showed complete closure at three-month CT scanning in the matched set. Patency ran lower in the isolation group, and isolation stayed protective after adjustment in their models. The largest appendage diameter also predicted leaks, guiding which patients may need closer follow-up imaging.
pmc-13324561:
Katharina Schun and co-authors showed how shedding of the iron importer transferrin receptor 1 protects cells from iron overload. Their 2026 study addresses a tight control problem: cells must take up enough iron without tipping into ferroptosis, an iron-dependent death now eyed as a cancer therapy target. Surface levels of transferrin receptor 1 set the pace of uptake, and its soluble form already serves as a clinical marker for anemia types.

The team identified iRhoms, regulators of the surface protease ADAM17, as platforms that bind the receptor and enable its release. The receptor favored pro-inflammatory iRhom2 over iRhom1, and both ADAM17 and ADAM10 proved able to shed it in endothelial cells and human lung slices. Shedding cut excessive iron uptake and protected cells against ferroptosis in live imaging, while mice with reduced ADAM17 showed higher serum iron. The authors frame receptor shedding as a systemic safeguard for iron balance.
pmc-13325461:
Paul Schweng and colleagues make light-active porous polymers from cheap building blocks for splitting water into hydrogen in a 2026 study. Many polymer photocatalysts need costly monomers and palladium chemistry, which prices them out of wide use.

Their hypercrosslinked polymers embed a sulfone-bearing thiophene unit that absorbs light. The best mix, at a 2 to 1 ratio of the two monomers, evolved hydrogen at 249 micromoles per hour per gram. The materials faded under working conditions, but adding a radical scavenger steadied them and lifted output to 275 micromoles per hour per gram. No noble metals were needed at any step.
pmc-13325861:
Rylie E. O. Pelton, Fabian Bernal, and Tim Kurt map greenhouse gas emissions from United States dairy products by region in a 2026 study. The industry aims for net neutrality by 2050, but no full farm-to-processing account existed.

The life cycle covered 12 regions holding 99.96 percent of national production. Total emissions for 2020 came to 163.3 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent across the chain. Raw milk production drove an average of 81 percent of that total. Processing emissions varied by region with product mix, energy use, grid makeup, and hauling distance. Cutting emissions will take action on farms and in plants together.
pmc-13326561:
Ivor Popovich models why tiny blood vessels fail in septic shock even when blood pressure recovers in a 2026 theoretical study. Patchy capillary flow beside normal big-vessel numbers, called hemodynamic incoherence, lacked a unifying explanation.

His simulation ran one million parallel small arteries with realistic size spreads. Each vessel aimed at a sensed shear target, and total heart output had to cover the summed demand. Even mild widening of all vessels sent the needed output soaring, since demand grows with vessel radius cubed. When the heart cannot pay, low-flow vessels drop out and flow turns patchy. The model predicts that easing vessel widening could restore even flow.
pmc-13327661:
Courtney Barnes and a large team assess early effects of Australia's social media age law in a 2026 observational study. The 2024 Act set a national minimum age of 16 for holding accounts on named platforms, a world first. Researchers surveyed adolescents aged 12 to under 17 just before the rules began and again about three months later.

Of 436 teens recruited at the start, 408 gave follow-up data, covering daily use, time spent, age-check experiences, workarounds, and any shift to other activities. A sharp cutoff design compared teens just either side of the age line to gauge the law's effect. Early evidence like this helps other countries weigh similar bans.
pmc-13328261:
Abebe Wirtu and co-authors profile drug-resistant E. coli in young broiler chickens in central Ethiopia in a 2026 study. Heavy antimicrobial use on intensive farms breeds resistance that fecal bacteria carry onward. The team took 485 cloacal swabs from 52 commercial farms and tested 163 isolates against fifteen drugs, sequencing twenty genomes.

Over half the swabs, 53 percent, yielded E. coli, and resistance ran highest to tetracycline at 84 percent, nalidixic acid at 74 percent, and ciprofloxacin at 72 percent among the isolates, while no resistance appeared to four key last-line drugs. Multidrug resistance hit 77 percent of isolates, a heavy baseline burden that farm programs must cut before it reaches people.
pmc-13329561:
John-Henry Dean and team reviewed guarding against hardening-linked heart artery disease in tactical athletes. Their 2026 state-of-the-art review covers military members, firefighters, and law officers, whose hard jobs make sudden collapse a public safety issue and a personal one. Old risk factors such as high blood pressure, obesity, insulin resistance, and sleep trouble are rife and often undertreated in these groups. Job stressors add heat, breathed-in hazards, and performance drugs.

Despite strong base fitness, tactical athletes bear an outsized hardening-linked disease load, and sudden heart death is the top cause of duty-linked deaths. Fitness can hide large heart-metabolic risk, so guarding should move from symptom-led checks to system-wide risk spotting, firm risk control, and picked noninvasive hardening scans. The review sums up proof on risk factor spread, heart artery disease, screening, and care choices for this group.
pmc-13330061:
Samat Amat and colleagues map microbes living on cattle eyes and test whether friendly ones can block pinkeye germs in a 2026 study. Pinkeye keeps rising in North American beef herds despite vaccines and antibiotics. Eye swabs came from 143 cattle in North Dakota before treatment, with 102 sick and 41 healthy animals.

Culture work found 351 isolates across 61 genera, led by Bacillus and Streptococcus groups in the reported counts. Gene sequencing of a subset showed clear community gaps between sick and healthy eyes. Eight species were richer in healthy eyes. Lab screens then tested 52 friendly isolates against Moraxella germs, with five taken to deeper checks. The work supports probiotic ideas for eye health.
pmc-13331061:
Kim Alipio and colleagues test whether early-life data can predict multiple long-term conditions at midlife in a 2026 study. Data came from the 1970 British Cohort Study, covering 5,007 people at age 46. Records from birth and age 5 were tested as predictors of having two or more lasting conditions that limit daily roles.

In total, 11.9 percent of the group reported limiting multiple conditions in the reported outcome counts. Four models varied by data timing and outcome type. The best model, joining birth and age 5 data, still sorted risk only modestly, with an accuracy score of 0.66 in the given results. Kept predictors spanned shots, behaviour, asthma, and mother traits. Later childhood data may predict better.
pmc-13331161:
Gilbert Dechambenoit writes a 2026 letter on what a Danish spine registry teaches about surgery timing and choice. The DaneSpine registry holds over 115,000 procedures from 16 sites since 2009, about 80 percent of national activity, with patient scores tracked for years after surgery. The letter sums backward-looking reports from 2012 to 2024.

Lumbar work forms about 80 percent of cases, led by spinal narrowing and disc herniation in the figures given. Disability and leg pain scores improved a lot by one year for both groups. Gains ran larger when symptoms before surgery were shorter. Long sick leave cut return-to-work chances sharply. Early referral matters, the letter argues.
pmc-13332461:
Sambuu Ganchuluun and co-authors surveyed Japanese nurses nationwide in 2026 on whether personal resilience protects professional autonomy after the pandemic. Nurses rated their independent judgment lower when caring for COVID-19 patients, and the study asked if resilience cushions that drop.

From June to September 2024, 483 nurses at 18 hospitals scored their autonomy for COVID and non-COVID care on a 28-item scale and resilience on a 10-item scale. Autonomy was significantly lower in the COVID setting across all five factors, yet higher resilience went with higher autonomy in both settings. For COVID care, resilience still predicted three higher-order factors, performance, abstract judgment, and independent judgment, even after accounting for non-COVID autonomy. The authors suggest building nurses' resilience may defend self-directed practice in both routine and high-demand care.
pmc-13333461:
Chao Chen and colleagues chart a diagnostic trap in a 2026 retrospective study: neurological disease that first shows up looking like a psychiatric illness. Patients whose brain infection, stroke, or autoimmune flare opens with strange behavior often land in psychiatry wards first, losing time.

The tertiary neurology department screened 16,473 admissions from 2019 to 2023 and confirmed 76 such cases. Most arrived suddenly with vague behaviour change, and almost a third showed no neurological signs at all. Central nervous system infections led the list at 55.3 percent, mainly viral encephalitis at 40.8 percent, followed by cerebrovascular disease and autoimmune encephalitis. Poor outcomes, disability beyond mild at discharge, hit 42.1 percent. Low blood sodium at admission, viral encephalitis itself, and intensive care admission predicted those outcomes. A three-item score split patients from 7.1 percent poor outcomes at zero points to 100 percent at three. The authors urge fast scans, spinal fluid checks, and routine sodium testing in such cases.
pmc-13334061:
D. Diane Zheng and colleagues test 2026 whether plasma blood markers plus thinking challenge tests predict daily-life decline in older adults with thinking problems. Plasma biomarkers have emerged as promising, less invasive indicators of Alzheimer disease signs, yet biomarkers alone cannot show whether clinical symptoms are present or progressing. Paired with specific thinking deficits on brief novel Cognitive Challenge Tests, plasma markers show excellent hit rate for underlying Alzheimer disease signs in pre-symptom and early stages. Data have been lacking on how well the pair predicts over-time daily-life decline in the earliest impairment stages.

The study evaluated whether plasma blood markers and challenge tests, alone and jointly, predict start and over-time changes on the Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes scale. Older adults aged 54 to 98 diagnosed with thinking problems without dementia, 159 at baseline, were followed over time.
pmc-13335561:
Ayed Askar and colleagues report a 2026 newborn case of inborn superior lumbar hernia with face, limb, and rib anomalies. Inborn superior lumbar hernia, also called Grynfeltt-Lesshaft hernia, is a very uncommon flaw in the rear belly wall of newborns, often linked to other birth anomalies. The patient was a one-month-old girl with a right-sided lumbar swelling present since birth.

Examination revealed a large, pushable mass measuring 8 by 10 cm in the superior lumbar triangle. Linked anomalies were a full right-sided cleft lip, right thumb undergrowth with radial bend, and absence of the lower right chest ribs. Belly scan showed bowel loops inside the hernial sac with no signs of blockage or pinching. The patient underwent successful open tension-free mesh hernia repair, with uneventful recovery, good healing, and no return at one-month follow-up.
pmc-13335961:
Ben Wang and colleagues present 2026 PhosSight, a unified deep learning framework boosting and accelerating phospho-protein finding to enable biological discoveries. Protein phospho-tagging is a key control of cell signals, with mass spectrometry based phospho-protein work serving as the top tech for its analysis. Phospho-tagging scans, however, are blocked by acquisition biases: DDA suffers from random gaps and missing values, while DIA faces computing logjams and waste from vast spectral lists.

PhosSight is a unified deep learning framework designed to boost finding depth and accelerate search speed. PhosSight features PhosDetect, a model that clearly encodes phospho traits to well predict peptide finding. For DDA, PhosSight uses predicted hold time, fragment strength, and finding to refine site finding and re-scoring, recovering borderline, low-level spectra. For DIA, PhosSight uses finding-guided list trimming to remove useless spectra.
pmc-13336361:
Takuya Tanaka and co-authors used computing to learn how molecular shape governs light-driven energy loss in glowing stilbene compounds in a 2026 light-physics study. These clumping-induced glow compounds shine when clustered, and conical intersections, the funnels where excited molecules dump energy without light, decide how bright they get.

Quantum chemical analysis of 30 asymmetric donor-acceptor variants showed that side-group patterns shift the energy gap between the freshly excited geometry and the conical intersection, predicting which molecules go dark fastest. The team made key compounds, including DCBS[6], DCBS[7], and two DPB variants, plus references. Their lab behavior mostly tracked the computed trends. The design rules connect bridge flexibility and donor-acceptor imbalance to brightness, guiding brighter probes and glowing materials.
pmc-13336561:
Shang Wang and many co-authors report a 2026 mouse study on endometriosis, where womb-like tissue grows outside the womb and causes pain and fertility problems. Their two-color mouse model lets them watch endometrial cells enter the blood in real time. The colors show whether cells came from the womb or from outside growths.

Both cell types entered the blood, rose during womb-lining breakdown, and reached distant organs such as the lungs. Levels peaked three times a day and moved with prolactin, a hormone in the blood. The results support spread through the bloodstream and hint that daily hormone rhythms shape it, which could matter for testing and treatment.
pmc-13336661:
Jessica K Niblo and colleagues studied in 2026 how floppy protein segments interact with folded parts in multi domain proteins. These flexible regions, joined to structured domains, give proteins unusual shapes and jobs, but their effect on overall structure has stayed unclear. The team focused on ubiquilins, proteins that carry damaged cargo to the cell recycling machinery.

Using biophysical tests and computer models, starting with the yeast version called Dsk2, they measured contacts between disordered tails and folded domains. The contacts shape how ubiquilins fold, move, and bind cargo. The findings help explain protein quality control and why its failure can harm cells, with lessons for diseases tied to faulty protein disposal.
pmc-13336861:
Bohao Ding and colleagues merge two memory styles in one tiny device for brain-like computing in a 2026 study. Their nanoporous silica memristor can hold a state briefly or keep it long-term, switched simply by tuning the current limit. Clear ion paths inside the pores let filaments form and dissolve in a controlled way.

Used as a physical reservoir, the fleeting states processed signals while stable states served as readout weights. The system reached 93.7% accuracy on handwritten digit recognition in benchmark tests and over 88% accuracy when sorting normal from abnormal heartbeat patterns in ECG tests. One CMOS-friendly material doing both jobs could shrink low-power smart hardware.
pmc-13336961:
Qinhua Gan and a large team build a heat-switched plug-in chassis in a marine microalga in a 2026 study. Algae make valuable oils and nutrients from light, but always-on production traits weaken the grower. Two heat-triggered promoters found by gene profiling act as thermal switches in Nannochloropsis oceanica.

Heat switches on a fat-making gene that raises storage oil and eicosapentaenoic acid, while warming also quiets a wall-building gene to soften walls only when wanted. Combined strains release lipids without grinding and keep growing normally when cool. Surprisingly, the thermal programs also worked inside mammalian hosts. A chassis that separates growth from production on command could serve biomanufacturing and synthetic biology broadly.
pmc-13337361:
Yue Bao, Jun Ma, and Lei Li report a rare heart procedure complication in a 2026 case study. During a coronary intervention on a 71-year-old man, the artery perforated in the most severe Ellis type III pattern. Such tears usually flood the sac around the heart and crush it, but this case behaved differently.

Imaging found a giant blood pocket under the heart's outer surface on the right ventricle, with only a little fluid in the sac. The hidden pocket mimicked tamponade and could easily be misread. Emergency bypass surgery plus pocket drainage rescued the patient. The report reminds intervention teams that post-perforation bleeding can hide beneath the epicardium rather than filling the sac.
pmc-13337661:
Yupeng Guo and Xuanwei Dong wrote a 2026 narrative review of drug treatment for sudden one-sided facial weakness. The condition, often called Bell's palsy, recovers on its own for many people. Others are left with weak movement, linked movements, or lasting social strain.

Evidence from trials and prior reviews supports starting steroid drugs within 72 hours of onset as the core treatment. Steroids raise the chance of full recovery and lower long-term problems. Antiviral drugs alone showed no clear gain, though adding them may help older patients or severe cases. The review also covers extra therapies, rehab, and future care matched more closely to each patient.
pmc-13338161:
Fatemeh Sadat Fatemi and three colleagues develop a greener method for measuring fungicide residues in food and water, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Triazole fungicides protect crops, but they linger as contaminants in food and water. To detect a range of them at once, at trace levels, takes sensitive sample preparation.

Their extraction solvent is a hydrophobic deep eutectic mixture of diphenylamine and benzophenone in equal parts. Dispersed as fine droplets in the sample, it grabs the fungicides from grain and water. Centrifugation then splits the phases apart. Detection limits came in below one nanogram per milliliter. Enrichment factors ran into the hundreds and past them. Precision held up within days and between days. It replaces harsher solvents and keeps the sensitivity regulators demand.
pmc-13338861:
Rula Ghandour and colleagues surveyed well being in 2026 among 3,000 adults in West Bank refugee camps and nearby towns living under prolonged occupation. Using the WHO Five Well Being Index, they tested how deprivation, political violence, and rights violations relate to mental well being. Nearly three quarters of respondents, 73.8 percent, reported poor well being.

Material deprivation showed the strongest link: low or moderate deprivation carried 1.7 and 2.4 fold higher odds of poor well being. Household exposure to political violence also raised the odds. The findings tie population mental health to living conditions and rights, with clear implications for aid and health policy.
pmc-13340661:
A parasitic cyst hiding in the abdominal wall is the surprise finding in a 2026 case report by Soukayna Bourabaa and Yahia Zain-Al-Abidine Khedid. The patient had a growing, painful lump in the right abdominal wall, and imaging showed a cyst inside the muscle with no spread into the abdomen.

Nothing pointed to a parasitic cause before surgery. Complete removal followed, and tissue analysis unexpectedly confirmed a hydatid cyst, after which albendazole was given and recovery stayed smooth. Because such cysts imitate harmless lumps or soft tissue tumors, the authors urge clinicians in endemic areas to keep hydatid disease in mind.
pmc-13341461:
Grip strength tracks belly fat and muscle loss in a 2026 study by Dingliu He and colleagues. Health checkup data from Yancheng First People's Hospital, gathered March 2023 to November 2024, let the team relate handgrip strength to visceral obesity and low limb muscle mass in Chinese adults.

Adults in the strongest grip quartile had far lower odds of visceral obesity (OR 0.14), low muscle mass (OR 0.10), and both together (OR 0.09) than the weakest group. Grip predicted low muscle mass with an AUC of 0.88 and visceral obesity at 0.93. A simple squeeze test could thus flag two hidden risks at once.
pmc-13341661:
Emphysema changes the outlook of COPD flare-ups in unexpected ways, in a 2026 prospective study by Jiaqi Pu and colleagues. The multicenter registry enrolled patients hospitalized with mild-to-moderate exacerbations who had chest CT within a day of admission; emphysema showed in 4,558 of 5,713 patients, or 79.8% of all cases.

After matching 2,258 patients, the emphysema group arrived sicker, with respiratory failure in 12.1% of patients versus 3.4% of the others, and longer stays. Yet their three-year death rate ran lower, at 24.8% for the emphysema group versus 30.2% for the comparison group. The non-emphysema group instead carried heavier heart disease burdens. Scan-defined subtype, the authors argue, belongs in prognosis talks even for moderate flare-ups.
pmc-13342261:
Lin Han and co-authors review, in 2026, a host protein called NMI and its shifting role in the body's first defense against viruses. Rather than always helping or always harming, NMI seems to act as a switch whose effect depends on its partners, its place in the cell, and the stage of infection.

In some RNA virus models NMI weakens interferon signaling and helps the virus copy itself. Against foamy virus it traps a viral activator in the cytoplasm and blocks viral gene reading, while in cytomegalovirus infection a viral protein attacks the NMI pathway to mute defense. Outside cells, NMI can also act as a danger signal that fuels inflammation.
pmc-13342861:
Akin Nihat and co-authors describe, in 2026, a dividing cell line that can grow and measure human sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease prions. Drug hunting for prion diseases has long stalled because the infectious agent would not spread in dividing lab cells, forcing slow animal tests and stand-in screens.

Their EKV cells keep the core strain traits of the human pathogen and allow direct infectivity counts with sensitivity close to mouse bioassays. Because the line is scalable, labs can test whether a treatment truly clears authentic human prion infection rather than a surrogate. The platform gives researchers a faster route to study human prion biology and screen candidate drugs.
pmc-13343461:
Wei-Jung Yen and co-authors report a family of iridium-silver nanoclusters in 2026 whose shapes and glow shift with their outer ligands. Each cluster holds one iridium hydride unit inside twenty silver atoms wrapped by twelve sulfur or selenium donor ligands, forming an eight-electron superatom system made in one pot.

Swapping ligands mid-synthesis moved capping atoms around, giving forms with symmetry from none to threefold, including the first selenium-guarded iridium-silver superatom. All four clusters glowed in the near-infrared as solids, with quantum yields up to 10 percent. The brightest carried the most lopsided ligand shell, suggesting that deliberate core distortion can raise emission for future light-based materials.
pmc-13343561:
Sujata Balasubramanian and colleagues survey flea-borne zoonotic agents in fleas taken from domestic cats in Texas's Rio Grande Valley. Their 2026 study investigates the ecology of Rickettsia and Bartonella pathogens amid rising human concern.

One hundred sixty-seven mostly stray cats were examined, and over eighty percent carried fleas. Seven hundred twenty-one fleas were collected, overwhelmingly the common cat flea. Flea burden significantly predicted Rickettsia infection in fleas. One candidate Rickettsia species appeared in a fifth of flea pools, while the murine typhus agent appeared in a small share. Cat blood and some tissues were also tested for infections, completing the ecological picture.
pmc-13344261:
Elsa Parra and co-authors survey United States maternal-fetal medicine fellows about bedside ultrasound on mothers in 2026. Point-of-care scans of the heart, lungs, and abdomen guide care for critically ill patients, yet how often high-risk pregnancy trainees use them on mothers, rather than fetuses, had never been counted.

Responses came from 215 of 382 fellows contacted, and 60.0 percent had performed a maternal scan at least once in training. Time in an obstetric intensive care unit made no difference, but feeling adequately trained raised the odds of scanning nearly twentyfold, and merely watching one helped greatly too. Nearly every respondent, 96.7 percent, wanted more training, a clear mandate for fellowship programs.
pmc-13345861:
Olga Kuvaldina and co-authors build and validate questionnaires for judging how crises shake Olympic preparation in 2026. Working from the PEST frame of political, economic, socio-cultural, and technological forces, the team drafted two tools for Ukraine's Olympic team, one framed on Tokyo 2020 and one on Paris 2024.

Seven sport science experts from four countries rated 55 items for clarity, relevance, and fit, and weak items were rewritten after cognitive interviews. Every item then cleared the content validity bar, with average scores from 0.80 to a perfect 1.00 and tight agreement across raters. The validated tools now stand ready for long-term studies of national sport systems under instability.
pmc-13347361:
Alexander Stüber and co-authors build a small copper complex that mimics a methane-burning enzyme site, in a chemistry study from 2026. A zeolite catalyst called Cu/ZSM-5 is thought to turn methane into methanol at a paired copper-oxygen core. So the team made a discrete molecule with that same core and tested it on oily carbon-hydrogen bonds.

The complex drove single-oxygen addition to bonds as strong as 82 kcal per mol in the reported range, a notable reach for a bench molecule. Calculations then showed an energy path for breaking those bonds that closely matched the zeolite catalyst, supporting the paired-core idea. Such models help clarify how nature handles methane at mild conditions.
pmc-13348161:
Ludovico Aloisio and a large team grow tiny conducting fibres inside living cells to restore cell-to-cell electric talk, in a 2026 study. Gap links normally carry signals between cells, and their loss feeds heart, nerve, wound, and tumour trouble. So a small molecule called DTTO was let to self-build into fibres that can span neighbouring cells without gene edits.

Paired electrode records showed signals crossing again even when native gap links were drugged shut. Control checks ruled out simple membrane holes as the cause in the reported tests. Fibre networks carried charge with ion and surface effects shaping flow, opening a built-in route to repair bioelectric links.
pmc-13348561:
Seven authors present a proof-of-concept study dated two thousand twenty-six on predicting heart-related death in people with prediabetes. Participants had excess weight, established heart disease, and blood sugar in the prediabetes range. Their risk of fatal heart events is raised, yet standard risk tools were not built for this group.

The team aimed for a simple model that doctors can explain. Over five thousand six hundred participants took part, with one hundred eighty-two heart deaths over an average of about two years. A logistic regression model was trained and checked in rotating splits. Its risk estimates were calibrated and judged on how well they separated outcomes.
pmc-13348661:
Madeline Pan and Jennifer McCracken told in 2026 of a case in which sarcoidosis posed as severe asthma. This mix-up has real costs. Both ills cause breathlessness, chest tightness, and dry cough. Sarcoidosis can be missed as asthma when standard therapy fails.

A 59-year-old man with severe asthma kept getting worse despite high-dose inhaled steroids, long-acting bronchodilators, antimuscarinics, and biologic therapy. Lung function shifted from reversible blockage toward a restrictive pattern. This shift sparked a rethink. The case urges clinicians to revisit the diagnosis when asthma resists maximal therapy. Sarcoidosis needs a distinct workup and therapy, and delay prolongs breathlessness that might else improve.
pmc-13349961:
Keli Hu and colleagues proposed a new image model in 2026 for outlining polyps in colonoscopy pictures. Finding and removing polyps during screening prevents bowel cancer. But polyps vary greatly in shape. Their edges are often blurred, which defeats automatic tools.

Their model, PAC-P2T, starts with a transformer encoder that reads wide context. Added layers then sample features at several spacings to catch different sizes. An attention step stresses the most useful channels. Tests addressed the shape variety and edge problems that limit clinic use of earlier networks. Cleaner automatic outlines could help doctors measure and remove polyps more fully.
pmc-13350061:
Muhammad Wajid Javed and colleagues tested gentler ways to weaken green peach aphids on canola in a 2026 study. The aphid cuts canola yield by 35 to 60 percent. It harms plants by sucking sap and by spreading viruses. Heavy insecticide use is ecologically unwelcome.

Leaf sprays of salicylic or citric acid were tested. So were silicon and ammonium sulphate fed through soil. Soil additions such as elemental sulphur, bio sulphur, and compost were also tried. Each was scored for aphid growth, breeding, and survival. A strong salicylic spray cut fitness measures most. Silicon and a sulphur mix also performed well. Such plant-strengthening tactics could anchor greener aphid control.
pmc-13350261:
Huajun Xu and co-authors tested in 2026 musculoskeletal ultrasound for gauging fat build-up in the supraspinatus muscle of patients with tendon tears. Fatty swap weakens the rotator cuff and affects surgery outcomes. Yet most studies have leaned on MRI, not bedside ultrasound.

Looking back at 154 patients whose tears were confirmed by arthroscopy, the team graded fat build-up semi-quantitatively by ultrasound. They added shear wave elastography and weighed both against MRI as the reference standard. Agreement and diagnostic accuracy were tallied, with links to build-up degree. The results back ultrasound as a workable, easy alternative for grading fatty muscle change before shoulder surgery.
pmc-13350461:
Hao Chen and a large team compared gut microbes and inflammation between men and women with kidney stones in a 2026 cross-sectional study of 60 patients, 40 men and 20 women. Stones are far commoner in men, but differences within patient groups are rarely examined.

Blood tests showed men carrying higher levels of several inflammatory messengers. Overall gut microbe communities looked similar between sexes, though two bacterial groups were enriched in women and one in men. Routine blood chemistry barely differed. Sex-aware reading of inflammation and gut profiles could eventually tailor stone prevention, which today is largely one-size-fits-all.
pmc-13350961:
Rice farmers in northwest Bangladesh face a shifting climate, and Md Shohidul Islam, Bikash Chandra Ghosh, and Apurba Adhikary study how they adapt, not one tactic at a time but in bundles. Surveying four hundred and ninety-eight farmers, they modeled five tactics together: moving planting dates, managing pests as a system, planting hardy or improved rice types, and mulching with straw.

Experience, credit access, and membership in farmer groups all shaped who adapted. The tactics leaned on each other: farmers who took up one tended to take up the rest, so bundles beat single fixes.
