The authors urge policy that backs whole bundles, fitted to local ground, rather than pushing one practice at a time.
pmc-13351761:
Jinhyoung Lee and co-authors showed in 2026 a designable van der Waals crystal that mimics an artificial nerve cell, bridging light control and bio-inspired computing. Light control of neurons gives rare precision for studying learning and memory. Yet device-scale mimics of nerve behaviour remain hard.

The crystal exploits build likeness between ion channels in biological membranes and layered van der Waals lattices, realised through nano-crystallisation. Sequential carrier transport shifts in the crystal reproduce nerve-like replies to light cues at device scale. The work gives a materials platform for engineering data handling that borrows nerve principles with no need for living cells, opening routes to neuromorphic devices.
pmc-13351961:
Alison Ma and co-authors present a 2026 case series on a system that turns 2D endoscope views into 3D during spine surgery. Flat views remove depth sense and steepen the learning curve, while true 3D scopes are wider and can disrupt work. Fourteen patients with worn spine conditions had surgery using live conversion software, mostly through one portal.

Judgement covered sight, tool handling, bleeding control, teaching value, workflow, and comfort. Depth and orientation gains were seen in all cases, and tool handling improved in all 10 decompression cases. Bleeding cues improved in 6 of 10 cases. Workflow broke down in 4 cases, and mild dizziness or double vision occurred in 6, so gains come with trade-offs.
pmc-13352061:
Filippo Murina leads a 2026 pilot trial of a topical resiniferatoxin cream for vestibulodynia, the most common form of vulvodynia. The condition causes lasting pain at the vulvar vestibule when touched, and nerve overgrowth and receptor excess are thought to drive it. Standard care often gives partial relief or whole-body side effects.

Premenopausal women aged 18 years or older with at least 3 months of illness applied 10 mcg/mL cream once daily for 4 weeks with a measured dispenser. Pain scores, tolerability, and nerve measures were tracked. Resiniferatoxin strongly activates the TRPV1 receptor and can quiet pain fibres for a long stretch, so a local cream may target pain at its source.
pmc-13352761:
Alexander D Gibson and others studied unreliable data behind medical forecast models, gave their warning in 2026. Forecast tools are often built from large routinely gathered banks, and sound decisions depend on those data being sound and clearly sourced. The team focused on two widely reused Kaggle banks, on stroke and diabetes, whose origins were unclear.

Exploratory checks studied the banks for quality problems and reporting gaps, and the authors traced how often peer-surveyed forecast studies had relied on them. The work shows how weak provenance can quietly spread through issued models. It urges teams and editors to verify a dataset's history before building or trusting a medical forecast tool.
pmc-13353061:
Christian Werner leads a 2026 hunt for ring-shaped peptides that block assembly of the CK2 kinase holoenzyme. CK2 is raised in many tumours and helps them survive, yet most blockers fight for the ATP pocket. A screen of 67,000 compounds with a fluorescence displacement test sought molecules that pry the catalytic alpha units off the beta dimer instead.

A family of decorated cyclic pentapeptides hit the beta binding site on CK2 alpha and its twin form alpha-prime. New energy-transfer assays were built and vetted to confirm the blocking action. The peptides bound more strongly in follow-up checks, opening a non-classic route to weaken a cancer-linked enzyme without touching its active site.
pmc-13354161:
Qi Wang leads a 2026 interpretive synthesis building a framework for putting health-system guidance into practice. Evidence-informed policy needs more than good guidance on paper. Eleven databases plus grey sources were searched, and documents were screened for relevance and quality before interpretive analysis.

Twenty-one documents from 2004 to 2024 qualified, with 15 empirical and six non-empirical works. The framework lists 10 facilitators, 10 barriers, nine mixed factors, and 11 strategies. Factors span six levels, from the political system and health system down through communities, organisations, providers, and patients. Shaped into a practical tool, the framework could support rollout across many topics and settings.
pmc-13355261:
Nisan Korkmaz and co-authors created a 2026 digital model of the human kidney's collecting system, complete with kidney stones, for training and computer vision work. No open, highly realistic model of this kind existed before. The team built the model from CT scans, with careful shape fixes and painted textures, and made stones of two common types.

Fifteen urologists rated the model, giving the collecting system a median realism score of four out of five. Uric acid stones looked more real than the other stone type in both texture and shape. The authors say the model can support simulated stone surgery training, while some inner surfaces still need polish.
pmc-13355461:
Mariko Hattori and three co-authors published a prosthodontics case report in twenty twenty-six. Their patient needed a new upper jaw prosthesis after the jaw was rebuilt with a tissue flap. Taking impressions in such mouths is risky and fiddly. Their shortcut started from the patient's own well-worn prosthesis.

The old device was scanned, and its data printed as a bite record base that already fit. Jaw relations were recorded on it, teeth were arranged, and a functional impression was taken at the try-in stage. The final prosthesis was then made in standard heat-cured acrylic. Fit was accurate and post-delivery adjustments shrank. The method suits clinics without advanced digital laboratories.
pmc-13355861:
Chai Li Tay and co-authors tested a short questionnaire in 2026 for spotting possible sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle strength, in older Malaysians. The SARC-F form asks about strength and daily tasks, but its accuracy in this group was unclear. Across eleven clinics, 578 adults aged 60 and over took the questionnaire and a hand grip strength test.

People flagged as high risk did grip far more weakly, yet the form missed many weak-grip cases, catching only about a third. It was strong when positive, ruling in risk with fair accuracy. The authors advise a two-step plan: screen with the form, then confirm with a grip test in primary care.
pmc-13356461:
Amos Grünebaum and Frank A Chervenak write a 2026 ethics commentary on freebirth, the planned choice to give birth with no trained attendant present. The movement is growing worldwide, and a recent editorial urged respectful outreach to women weighing out-of-hospital birth. The authors warn against blurring attended home birth with unassisted birth, which carry distinct duties for clinicians.

Respect for a woman's choices, they argue, does not mean staying neutral when preventable harm to a baby is likely. Honest, complete counseling with a clear recommendation against unassisted birth is part of informed consent, not coercion. After viability, the fetus also counts as a patient owed care, a duty unassisted birth removes entirely.
pmc-13357061:
Christina T Muijs and Gursah Kats-Ugurlu ask in a 2026 commentary whether cancer staging rules need an update for throat-tube cancer treated with chemo and radiation before surgery. How well the tumor shrinks strongly shapes outlook, so a post-treatment stage group was added in the eighth edition rules. Yet survival curves still cross between stages, blurring the groups.

A new system by Park and co-authors sorted patients into four stages with cleaner survival splits and better accuracy scores. The commentary notes the rules ignore tumor type, though response rates and outcomes differ by type. Finer, type-specific staging could sharpen prognosis after pre-surgery treatment.
pmc-13359761:
Stefano Restaino and co-authors compare guidelines for a common womb condition in a 2026 review. Endometrial hyperplasia, an overgrowth of the womb lining, is seen in everyday practice and can precede cancer. Yet the major medical societies do not fully agree on how to diagnose, treat, watch, or manage it in women who still hope to bear children.

The authors line up the recommendations side by side, marking where they agree, where they split, and where proof is simply missing. From that map they draft a practical, evidence-based path for clinicians. The review also lists the research gaps whose answers would let future guidelines speak with one voice.
pmc-13360961:
Amr S Abouzied and co-authors tested the essential oil of an edible herb for cancer-fighting promise in a 2026 study. The herb, Anisosciadium orientale, is used in traditional medicine but barely studied. The team drew oil from its above-ground parts and mapped its chemistry with a standard scanning method. Sixty compounds were found in the oil.

The oil was tested for antioxidant power and for effects on several cancer cell lines. Flow tools tracked how the oil pushed cancer cells toward programmed death, and computer docking tested how its compounds fit cancer targets. Plant oils with proven cell effects are a hunting ground for new drug leads. The authors present the combined lab and computer proof as a case for deeper study of this herb.
pmc-13361761:
Hui Li and co-authors report a 2026 forensic case on trafficked fish parts. Police seized 1,777 fish maws, the prized swim bladders sold as food, and 18,170 shark fins. Naming the species behind such goods is key to fighting illegal wildlife trade, but dried parts defy the eye. The team turned to DNA barcoding, which reads short gene stretches as species tags.

They sampled 325 items at random, 197 maws and 128 fins, across the eye-sorted groups. Two gene markers were read and matched against large public databases. Family trees built from the sequences confirmed the calls, and the sample results were scaled up to estimate the whole seizure. Such forensic proof gives courts hard evidence and shows which protected species the trade targets.
pmc-13363761:
Nanting Huang and colleagues present a 2026 study on a hybrid classical-quantum network for spotting autism spectrum disorder in brain scans. Autism seems to mix local activity quirks with whole-brain wiring faults, so their design reads both at once. A wide residual network reads local activity maps. A small quantum circuit reads the connectivity matrix, using quantum state space to catch long-range patterns with few settings.

Trained and tested on resting brain scans, the fused model reached about 68 percent accuracy, ahead of ten rival methods they compared. Its readouts also flagged core disease hubs on a standard brain atlas. The authors present the tool as decision support for scan-based diagnosis. The team tested shortened human RD3 forms in those mice. Short forms still calmed the enzyme and saved rods from dying, but the enzyme never reached the outer segment. Extending RD3 to a later point restored delivery and light responses. One short stretch of RD3, it seems, links the cargo to the cell transport system.
pmc-13400461:
Felipe Machado Mota and colleagues study, in 2026, why donated corneas lose quality while stored cold in an eye bank. Corneas are graded by microscope on 13 features, from excellent to unacceptable. A fall in grade can mean a lost chance for a transplant that restores sight.

Records covered 422 donors and 844 corneas assessed twice between 2022 and early 2024. No donor trait, handling factor or storage fluid showed a clear link with decline. The two fluids compared performed almost identically, perhaps because rechecking came within four days. Still, scores tended to creep upward, meaning slightly worse quality, at the second look, so the authors urge attention to storage time and handling.
pmc-13400661:
Kyle B Christy and co-authors report, in 2026, outcomes of donor bone grafting for contained socket defects during revision shoulder replacement. When a reverse shoulder implant must be redone, the shoulder blade socket often lacks bone to hold the new base. Filling a central, contained defect with shaped donor bone is one fix.

Thirteen patients received a femoral head donor graft, carved to match a mold of the defect and impacted in before a long-post baseplate was fitted. They were followed for at least two years with X-rays, movement measures and pain and function scores. The series examines graft healing, implant shift and loosening, and forward arm lift before and after surgery.
pmc-13400761:
Priya Vart argues, in 2026, that age subgroup analyses in chronic kidney disease drug trials deserve a closer look than they usually get. Five major trials between 2019 and 2024 established three drug classes that protect kidneys. Each split results at age 65 and reported no clear age interaction, suggesting benefits hold across ages.

Vart notes problems beyond the usual low statistical power. The trials main outcomes mix two very different events: kidney deterioration and cardiovascular death. A single subgroup number blends them, so a drug could help one outcome with age and hurt the other without the analysis showing it. Finer age splits exist only in later dedicated papers. Interpretation, the author urges, should match that complexity.
pmc-13401061:
George-Paul O Byrne and co-authors propose, in 2026, an enhanced recovery framework for the phase after traumatic brain injury. It draws on surgical recovery programs that bundle proven care steps. Brain injury causes heavy death and disability worldwide. Yet recovery-phase care stays fragmented and poorly pulled together compared with acute treatment.

The review covers rehab strategies, patient traits and prior conditions as drivers of later outcomes. Early, intensive rehab from a full care team linked to better recovery. Gains showed in nerve function, independence and quality of life. Hospital stays shrank too, with no added deaths. New tools like virtual reality and remote rehab showed promise. Their studies, though, are small and varied.
pmc-13401561:
Jiwon Lee and many colleagues report 2026 results from the KOSMOS trials, where patients with advanced cancers received treatments matched to their tumours' molecular profiles. Their focus is the drug pair erlotinib plus bevacizumab in tumours with amplified EGFR, a growth receptor whose value as a drug target has been disputed.

Patients whose cancers had progressed after standard therapy were treated on central molecular tumour board advice between February 2021 and April 2024. Only those with an EGFR copy number of at least three qualified, giving 25 patients with a median copy number near nine. Colorectal cancer was most common with 14 cases, followed by glioblastoma with five. Four patients had partial responses and seven had stable disease. Clinical benefit rate was the main endpoint, with response rate, survival measures, and safety also tracked.
pmc-13402261:
Alessia Marzanni and team investigated pink discolouration on the walls of an alpine chapel in South Tyrol, at about 1,000 meters altitude. Their 2026 work compares rosy biofilms on the north wall of St. Cyprian Chapel, where salt efflorescence is present, with the south wall, where it is absent. Salt crystallization is often blamed for pink biofilms, yet high-elevation cases had been poorly explored.

Despite similar stone mineralogy, the north wall showed distinct salt-related surface chemistry, stronger discolouration, and clear bacterioruberin pigment detection. The south wall hosted carotenoid-producing bacteria, including Rubrobacter and Pontibacter, though pigment signals were weak, and no photosynthetic organisms appeared on either wall. Microbial communities differed markedly between walls. The work shows salt modulates, but does not solely explain, alpine pink biofilms, guiding conservation choices.
pmc-13402361:
Yuxuan Lin and Dongyan Cao report two young women, aged 22 and 23, treated for ovarian anaplastic carcinoma with surgery that spared their fertility. They also review five published cases in the same situation. The cancer is rare, strikes mostly older women, and grows aggressively. Keeping the womb and one ovary matters deeply to patients this young, yet safety data are thin.

Across the reviewed cases, average age at onset was 22.8 years, and nearly all tumors were stage IA. One stage IIIC patient died six months after fertility-sparing surgery; two stage IA patients stayed disease-free at a median of 49.5 months, while two others died after far longer courses. Stage, the authors conclude, drives outlook more than any other factor. They advise sparing fertility only in carefully picked young patients, adding molecular testing where possible, and gathering longer follow-up before the approach can be called safe.
pmc-13402761:
Fadlilah and colleagues map how body problems and stress feed each other in type 2 diabetes, using data from 1,815 adults across Indonesian provinces. Quality of life suffers in diabetes, but the mechanics of weight, blood pressure, blood sugar, and stress are rarely modeled together. Their 2026 study measures quality of life obstacles and stress with tools. It then tests single effects, combined effects, and which factors carry others' influence.

Each problem, excess weight, advanced systolic hypertension, and high fasting glucose, predicted high stress on its own. Stacked together they multiplied the odds beyond simple addition. Quality of life obstacles tracked both the body problems and stress, peaking in people with several problems. Path analysis put fasting glucose and stress at the center of the web, with stress the strongest effect. Care that treats sugar and stress as one problem, the authors argue, should clear more than either fix alone.
pmc-13402861:
Carmicheal and colleagues review a strategy for breaking radiation resistance in tumors. The strategy forces cancer cells into ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and rust like damage to membranes. Radiation pushes cells partway there, raising oxygen and freeing iron, but tumors answer by switching on antioxidant shields that block the pathway. Their 2026 review maps the wiring between radiation and ferroptosis and weighs evidence on drugs that strip the shields.

Two shield proteins take center stage. One imports material for the cell's main antioxidant. One detoxifies membrane damage. Both switch on through a stress pathway radiation activates. Ferroptosis inducing drugs that block these defenses restored radiation kill in preclinical studies. The review closes with problems: which tumors depend on the shields, how to time the combination, and how to spare tissue. Pairing an old workhorse with a death pathway, the authors argue, deserves clinical trials.
pmc-13403561:
Zlatan Zvizdic and co-authors reported in 2026 a young boy with repeated painless bleeding from the bladder and no clear cause. Step-by-step tests ruled out kidney, infection, shape, and whole-body causes for the 5-year-old. A bladder scope showed broad lining swelling with bleeding patches near the bladder neck.

Treatment aimed to rebuild the bladder's protective coat with hyaluronic acid placed inside the bladder. Gross bleeding stopped after the first dose. Later scopes showed steady healing, and he stayed free of symptoms for 12 months. The case suggests a weak bladder coat can drive such bleeding in children.
pmc-13403661:
Viviam Solangeli Bermúdez Paiva and team studied SPARK, a scenario-based activity that brings out moral tensions in AI-aided precision medicine teaching. Their 2026 work takes on a training gap: precision medicine is often taught as tech novelty, while fairness, duty, and governance get less airtime. Structured talk formats could help students probe doubt and rival values.

Across two Norwegian university workshops with medicine and bioethics students, structured scenarios, info cards, and prompts steered small-group policy talks. Students began framing precision medicine in tech, solo terms, then widened to fairness, duty, and resource shares, spelling out trade-offs without always settling them. The authors conclude that making tensions plain, rather than settling them, is the activity's teaching value.
pmc-13404361:
Yanping Wang and colleagues built risk tools in 2026 to sort chronic liver patients by their chance of cirrhosis, the late scarring stage. Their set held 344 patients, split into a build group of 241 and a check group of 103. Routine labs, scar markers, and a liver stiffness scan fed the search for predictors.

Six factors stood alone as predictors, among them age, platelet count, and liver stiffness. A forest-style learning model edged out two rivals on accuracy. Its scores held up at a fair level in the check group. A paper chart version offers a simple bedside form of the same math. Outside groups must test it next.
pmc-13404861:
Annemijn H Jonkman and Gaetano Scaramuzzo comment in 2026 on a proposed breathing index drawn from electrical impedance tomography, a bedside lung imaging method. Zhang and others suggested the flow index could predict failure of breathing trials and reintubation within 48 hours of tube removal. Continuous maps of air movement during weaning appeal to both commentators.

Their concern is method detail: how the impedance signal is cleaned and turned into the index is thinly described. Filter types and cut-off values go unreported, which blocks replication by other teams. Validation steps also need strengthening before the score can guide extubation choices. The letter asks for fuller reporting so the index can be judged on its merits.
pmc-13405061:
Xiaohong Liu and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol for personalised lifestyle advice in sarcopenic obesity. The condition mixes muscle loss with excess fat, and one-size advice fits patients poorly. A knowledge graph, a structured web of health facts, will generate tailored recommendations.

The trial will recruit 208 patients and assign them evenly for 24 weeks. One group uses the Sarcopenic Obesity-Knowledge Graph Care System alongside routine guidance, while the other receives routine education alone. The main outcome is skeletal muscle mass, with strength and physical function also tracked. Results should show whether graph-driven personalisation beats standard lifestyle advice for this group.
pmc-13405361:
Roberto Rodriguez-Ramirez and co-authors present a 2026 clinical case of a giant fatty tumour in a woman's thumb pad. Lipomas are common benign growths, but in the tight space of the hand a large one can squeeze structures and weaken grip. The patient, aged 73, had lived with the mass for six years.

Pain on thumb movement, weakness and reduced pinch strength brought her to clinic. Scans showed a clean-edged fatty lesion of 5 by 3 centimetres with no sign of cancer. Surgeons removed it through the palm mound and found a neat capsule under the thumb muscle, sparing nerves and tendons. Tissue checks confirmed a lipoma and her recovery was smooth.
pmc-13405961:
Anca Daniela Raiciu, Mihaela Carmen Eremia and Amalia Stefaniu review how inulin fibres and plant polyphenols interact, in a 2026 survey. Inulin feeds helpful gut bacteria, while polyphenols rank among the main natural antioxidants in food. Together they may protect or release each other in useful ways.

Literature from 2000 to 2026 across three databases grounds the review. Studies link inulin levels with antioxidant test scores including DPPH, FRAP and enzyme activities. Binding between plant cell wall fibres and polyphenols changes stability and how fast compounds free up during digestion. The authors sketch functional food formulas pairing inulin-rich extracts with polyphenol sources for stronger health effects.
pmc-13406761:
Yasin Taşkın and colleagues test a blood inflammation index as an early death predictor after emergency skull surgery for major stroke, in a 2026 study. Removing part of the skull relieves pressure in malignant middle cerebral artery infarction, yet many patients still die in hospital. A cheap admission marker could flag the highest risk.

The systemic immune-inflammation index, built from routine blood counts, independently predicted in-hospital death in the reported analysis. It beat the simpler neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, reaching an AUC of 0.833 in the reported curve analysis. Older age, higher creatinine, hypertension and prior blood-thinner use also raised risk. The authors propose adding the index to preoperative assessment.
pmc-13407561:
Yun Wang and co-authors review, in 2026, engineered materials designed to mend spinal cord injury, a devastating condition that strips feeling for good and movement below the damage site. Existing treatments fall short, so attention has turned to substances that might protect surviving tissue, invite regrowth, and rebuild connections.

The survey sorts the field into four families: polymer, inorganic, biologically active, and composites mixing several kinds. Across studies, these materials show varied helpful functions, from scaffolding regrowing fibres to delivering supportive chemistry, with promising performance in early research. Still, the authors stress that most evidence sits at the early stage. More follow-on work is needed before material-based repair becomes routine care for injured patients.
pmc-13407861:
Michelle L. Harrison and a large team report, in 2026, a year of surveillance for suspected infection in newborns at Manila's Philippine General Hospital. Most knowledge about newborn sepsis comes from wealthy countries. The team enrolled every intensive-care baby with a suspected infection. Enrolment ran from November 2023 to November 2024. The tally was 799 babies and 1,024 episodes.

The diagnostic gap was stark. Only 1 percent of suspected early infections, appearing in the first two days of life, grew anything from blood culture. Fifteen percent of the babies died, including 53 percent of those with lab-confirmed infection and 12 percent of those without. Gram-negative bacteria dominated confirmed cases per the study's framing. The authors urge better case definitions and testing capacity, partly to curb antibiotic overuse driven by uncertainty.
pmc-13407961:
Krishna Salil and colleagues tested whether gum thickness relates to plaque buildup on baby molars in preschool children. Their 2026 cross-sectional study examines 360 caries-free deciduous molars from healthy children aged 3 to 5, measuring marginal gingival thickness by transgingival probing and plaque by a standard index. Gum thickness may influence plaque retention, yet its effect in young children had been underexplored.

No significant differences in thickness or plaque appeared between left and right molars, upper or lower, first or second. A moderately strong positive correlation between thickness and plaque appeared in most teeth, with weak to very weak correlations in others. The authors note that primary dentition generally shows a thinner gum phenotype with less plaque overall. The paper suggests thickness-aware hygiene guidance, while cross-sectional data cannot prove causation.
pmc-13408161:
Nozomi Asaoka, Diane Pagano, and Yasunori Hayashi report a 2026 mouse study on how habits form in the brain. Habits begin as deliberate, motivation-driven choices and later run more automatically. Their puzzle was why the amount of a habit, its frequency and duration, stays steady even as the underlying decision strategy changes.

Using a task that produced habits within a set time window in male mice, the team traced the two features to plasticity in separate cortical pathways. Erasing one pathway's plasticity changed decision strategy but left execution untouched, while erasing the other did the reverse. Readers gain a two-part model of habit control, with separate levers for choosing and for doing, which may help explain compulsive and addictive behaviour.
pmc-13408361:
Praveen K Bali and colleagues compared virtual reality and binaural noise as distractions for anxious children during dental care. Their 2026 in vivo study enrolls 44 healthy children aged 5 to 8 with mild to moderate anxiety, each experiencing control, binaural noise, and virtual reality on separate visits. Dental anxiety can worsen pain perception, yet non-drug distraction options had not been directly compared in this design.

Both virtual reality and binaural noise significantly reduced anxiety versus control, with virtual reality showing the largest drops in pulse rate and visual anxiety scores. Binaural noise gave moderate relief, while control children showed a significant anxiety rise after local anesthesia. The authors attribute virtual reality's edge to immersive, multisensory distraction. The paper supports virtual reality as the stronger non-drug option for anxious pediatric dental patients.
pmc-13408661:
Hensen and a large Dutch trial team report in 2026 the first placebo-controlled test of seeding healthy volunteers with a harmless strain of Clostridioides difficile. The toxic form of this germ causes serious hospital infections. Seeding the gut with its harmless cousin is a candidate way to block it. Sixty-nine healthy adults aged eighteen to forty-five swallowed capsules for five days, at low or high dose.

The capsules proved safe. Dose made no difference to whether seeding took hold. Antibiotic prep mattered most. Almost nobody was seeded without it. A third took hold after one day of vancomycin, and most after five days. Some volunteers picked up wild strains from the world around them before dosing. That shows how common the germ is. Gut profiling showed variety drops after antibiotics. Trial designers gain a workable human model.
pmc-13408761:
Li Lin and a large team map in 2026 how autism-related disorganisation is laid out in space inside developing brain tissue. Autism has hundreds of genetic contributors and wide clinical variety, yet how its biology first takes shape was unclear. The team grew prenatal cortex organoids from genetically diverse patients and read gene activity cell by cell and place by place.

Healthy zoning between progenitor and neuron regions broke down, leaving local patches of disorganised neurons whose placement differed from patient to patient. The disorder persisted as neurons matured and pointed to weakened adhesion between progenitor cells. Because each patient's mosaic pattern is different, the authors propose that scattered spatial abnormalities arising before birth could explain why symptoms and brain structure vary so much across the spectrum.
pmc-13408861:
KT Shivakumara and nine co-authors tune adult diet and mating time to boost mass rearing of a predatory lacewing used to eat crop pests. The lacewing hunts well and bears spray well, but farm scale output lags demand. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team paired larva feeding tests with adult diet and mate time trials. Older larvae ate the most eggs of a moth prey, in the hundreds per larva. A diet of water, honey, protein powder, and pollen gave the top egg counts per female. Keeping a male with the female for five days gave the highest egg counts of all.
pmc-13410761:
Ekin Beşiroğlu-Turgut, Gökçe Aykol-Şahin, and Yiğit Cem Öğretmen test in 2026 whether finger length ratios predict how well adults clean their teeth. The ratio of index to ring finger length reflects hormone exposure before birth, which some link to behavior. Whether it touches oral hygiene was unknown.

The study enrolled 126 adults at a dental clinic in Istanbul, measured fingers, and scored plaque and gum state before and after one week of standard cleaning instruction. Teaching improved scores for everyone. Finger ratio, though, showed no reliable link to plaque or gum change. Left-handed people kept lower plaque scores at both checks, and some brushing habits varied by ratio without showing in the clinical scores.
pmc-13410861:
Xindan Meng, Qing Wang, and Yixia Zhang report in 2026 a mismatch between blood flow and nerve signals in children with lazy eye from unequal focusing power. One eye sees poorly because the two eyes need very different lenses. Brain effects are known, yet retinal blood flow changes were less clear.

Sixty-eight untreated children aged 4 to 14 had the weaker eye compared with its healthy fellow. Scans showed thinner blood flow in the central retina and a wider vessel-free zone in lazy eyes. Electrical tests showed slower, weaker signals traveling from eye to brain. Flow and signal measures moved together, and nerve layer thickness helped predict sight level. Paired eye and brain markers may sharpen tracking.
pmc-13415261:
Vincenza Gianfredi and colleagues tested whether food insecurity predicts death among older English adults in a 2026 study of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Food insecurity already tracks with chronic disease and frailty, yet its direct link to dying had been little tested, so the team followed 8686 people aged 50 and older from 2004 onward.

After full adjustment, food insecurity came with a 41 percent higher risk of death overall and a 126 percent higher risk of early death. The paper argues that food support for older adults may be a life-saving health measure, not merely a welfare one.
pmc-13415461:
Tatiana Rodideal and co-authors compare scented oils and their leftover waters, called hydrosols, across three skullcap species grown in Moldova, in 2026. Twenty oils and twenty waters came from varied plant parts by steam. Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry sorted the makeup into eleven classes of plant goods.

One species, Scutellaria altissima, led with linalool in both oils and hydrosols. Scutellaria baicalensis oils were rich in two sesquiterpenes, beta-caryophyllene and germacrene D. The third species mixed those same compounds with spathulenol in its oils. Grouping split oils from waters cleanly and gave each species its own scent mark. Above ground parts, often discarded, clearly hold value.
pmc-13415561:
Fangfang Liu and colleagues test how background noise levels affect attention in students. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses a number grid search task. Noise usually counts as a distraction at work and study. Some people, though, focus better with moderate background sound.

Thirty-eight healthy students worked under three noise bands. Brain blood flow was measured with a light-based scanner. Faces and heart signals were recorded during the tasks. The middle noise band gave the strongest brain connectivity. That band also showed the highest heart rate readings. Emotional expressions peaked under the same middle condition. A moderate sound level may be a focus sweet spot.
pmc-13416661:
Sadaki Mitsuzawa and colleagues present a 2026 study of shoulder muscle measured by scans taken before reverse shoulder replacement surgery. An artificial intelligence tool split the muscles on computed tomography images automatically. The team then linked muscle size and makeup to how well patients could lift the arm after surgery.

Only 13 patients with 14 shoulders were followed for at least one year, so the work is exploratory. More healthy muscle in the supraspinatus tracked with better forward lifting, while more fat in two muscles tracked with worse lifting. No clear link appeared for outward rotation. Readers get a careful early test of automated muscle measurement before joint surgery.
pmc-13416761:
Nadia Kebaïli and co-authors test a cleaning step for tooth enamel before bonding orthodontic brackets, in a 2026 laboratory study. They use human bicuspid teeth and a self etching primer, which etches and primes in one step. Pretreatment with sodium hypochlorite removes protein from enamel and may help the bracket grip.

Seventy eight teeth were split into three groups of 26. The pretreated group reached bond strength close to the standard acid etch method, and both beat primer alone. Microscopy showed resin went deepest after standard etching, though. Extra teeth were used for that imaging part. The step offers a faster route to strong bonds.
pmc-13417161:
Ningning Du and co-authors survey flu vaccination among older adults in Suzhou, China, in a 2026 comparative study. Flu hits older people hard, yet uptake in the city lags behind rich countries. Face to face interviews ran from April to August 2024 in six districts, covering the prior flu season.

Valid replies came from 4,622 adults aged 60 or more, split between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups. Vaccinated adults knew more about flu and vaccines and felt at higher risk. Knowing a vaccine existed was the strongest single link to getting it. Health sites informed the vaccinated more, while television reached the unvaccinated more, suggesting channels for outreach.
pmc-13417661:
Kouchi and colleagues report a 2026 study of a visual teaching system for diabetes self-care in Japan. The Diabetes Card System lays out care topics on structured cards for outpatient lessons. The team reviewed 141 type 2 diabetes patients given card-based lessons at one clinic, tracking distress and blood sugar over six months.

Both measures improved clearly over the six months: scores on a diabetes distress scale fell, and HbA1c, the long-term blood sugar marker, dropped too. Only the starting distress score predicted how much distress improved. Sugar improvement linked to starting sugar level and diabetes duration, among other factors. Structured visual teaching thus eased the mental burden of diabetes, not just its numbers, a gain that routine care often fails to measure.
pmc-13418161:
Libang Liu and colleagues build a model that finds objects in satellite images from a written description, in a 2026 computer vision study. Descriptions mix what the target is, how it relates to neighbours, and where it sits, which older models blur together. Their system first splits the description into those three roles, then reasons over a graph of candidate objects.

Stepwise mask refinement keeps the language guidance alive through decoding. On a standard benchmark the model beat the prior best by about four points on the main overlap score, with a large gain at a strict threshold. A second benchmark confirmed competitive results.
pmc-13420061:
Dorna Derakhshan and colleagues report a 6-year-old girl carrying two rare problems at once: a genetic loose-skin disorder and severe backward flow of urine toward both kidneys. Her skin condition stems from a gene fault that weakens connective tissue across the body. She came to care after repeated fevers from urinary infections, a warning sign that the urinary tract was in trouble.

Scans showed the highest grade of urine reflux on both sides, with the left kidney already small and scarred. Nuclear scans confirmed lasting kidney damage from the backflow. She also showed developmental delay, part of the wider picture her gene condition can bring. The pairing matters because kidney damage can advance quietly while attention stays on the visible skin signs.
pmc-13420161:
Michela Marchetti and colleagues review how a World Health Organization talk therapy has fared when rolled out in humanitarian crises. Problem management plus is a brief, lay-deliverable program for people hit by conflict, disaster, or displacement, where distress runs high and services are scarce. The review searched four databases for work published through June 2025.

Screening 2093 records left 23 studies with 5377 participants across varied crisis settings in the final set. Feasibility was judged in 70 percent of studies and acceptability in 65 percent in the shares reported, with mostly positive findings on joining, staying, and cultural fit. Adherence to the manuals rated high where it was checked. The record supports wider rollout while flagging outcome types that studies still skip.
pmc-13420361:
Baumann and colleagues compared in 2026 two ways to rebuild a torn hip labrum using donor meniscus tissue. The labrum is a ring of cartilage that seals the hip joint, and some tears cannot be repaired. Patients had either open surgery or arthroscopic surgery, which works through small cuts with a camera. The team tracked pain and function scores for one year in 32 patients.

Both groups improved clearly on hip function and general health scores by one year. All 22 open cases and nine of ten arthroscopic cases were judged successful. Pain, however, fell clearly only in the open group, whose pain scores were lower at every check. Arthroscopic patients reported more pain at three, six, and twelve months than open patients. The authors say both methods restore function well at one year.
pmc-13420661:
Omar Toubat and colleagues report two 2026 cases where a blocked left subclavian artery starved bypass grafts and caused heart attacks. Both patients depended on a mammary artery graft fed through that vessel, one arresting after esophagus surgery and the other suffering a heart attack after colonoscopy.

Covered stents reopened the subclavian artery in both cases, restoring graft flow and easing ischemia without open thrombectomy. Surgeons gain a reminder that graft-dependent patients can infarct from upstream blockage, and that stenting offers a workable rescue and for teams planning redo bypass care.
pmc-13420861:
Murat Altan and colleagues study young women to untangle how social media use, eating behavior, and depression move together, using machine learning beside standard statistics. The survey gathered body mass index, media habits, a standard depression inventory, and a scale for media effects on eating. Tangled, non-linear links among the three are exactly what tree-based models handle well.

Random Forest modeled both the eating scale and the depression scores best in held-out tests, with a gradient boosting rival close behind. Overall, media use tracked with both eating-related behavior and depressive symptoms in the group. Association is not cause, and the authors keep that line. Still, models that rank which habits matter most can guide campus screening toward the heaviest-risk patterns first.
pmc-13421661:
Marwa S. Hassan leads a seven-author team building, in a 2026 paper, a decision tool for choosing replacements for plastic drinking straws. Climate evidence lives in research papers while user experience lives in online reviews, and buyers rarely see both together, which is the gap the workflow fills.

Their system combines a per-use greenhouse-gas score drawn from the literature with features mined from customer reviews by language processing, inside a transparent scoring scheme run under four priority scenarios. Among five shortlisted materials, silicone won every scenario, pairing low emissions per use with the happiest users. Paper ranked last, with the highest emissions figure and middling reviews. The authors stress the ranking holds within their dataset and assumptions.
pmc-13421761:
Chen and colleagues present a 2026 engineering paper on restoring power quickly after faults in local distribution networks.  The authors propose a load transfer method that joins expert rules with virtual power plants, which coordinate many small energy sources as one unit. A learning system makes the switching choices.

The method maps the network as a graph, with buses as nodes and switches as edges the system can flip. A two-level decision structure sits on top: an upper agent, guided by expert knowledge, picks the type of restoration task. Lower actions rewire the network and call on the virtual power plant's sources.  The design aims at fast restoration using local clean power.
pmc-13422661:
Aslak E Lyster leads an eleven-author team testing, in a 2026 trial, whether eating less protein — without eating fewer calories — can itself slim men with overweight or obesity. In lean men, protein reduction raises the hormone FGF21 and energy needs; whether that translates into weight loss at stable calories was unknown.

Seventeen men spent five weeks on tightly controlled diets holding calories equal: protein at under half the habitual level, swapped for carbohydrate, versus normal protein. The low-protein group lost about two kilograms, and their FGF21 rose, with bigger hormone rises tracking bigger weight losses. Fat mass fell significantly while lean mass only tended downward. Muscle energy machinery and fat-tissue FGF21 signalling stayed unchanged, leaving the mechanism partly mysterious.
pmc-13422861:
Fahimeh Alsadat Hosseini, Kimia Bahman, Maryam Shaygan and Shahrazad Yektatalab test, in a 2026 mixed-methods trial, whether delivering positive psychotherapy through virtual reality changes its effect on major depression. Positive psychotherapy builds wellbeing rather than only fighting symptoms, and immersive headsets offer a new delivery room that earlier depression research had mostly filled with cognitive-behavioural content.

Seventy-eight patients were randomised between headset delivery and the same three sessions face to face. Mood, life satisfaction and suicidal thinking were measured around each session. Outcomes improved significantly across sessions in the combined analysis, with within-group effect sizes reported for each arm. Interviews with the headset group afterwards helped interpret the numbers. The authors present the study as a first test of this pairing.
pmc-13423161:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of gentle electrical stimulation through the skin at acupuncture points, aimed at gut problems after keyhole urological surgery. Sluggish gut after surgery is among the most common setbacks for these patients. The trial will enroll 112 patients and assign them at random to real or sham stimulation.

Each patient gets two 30-minute sessions, one before surgery and one in the recovery room afterward. Stimulation targets three point pairs, at the wrist, below the knee, and on the lower back, set to the strongest level each patient can bear. The team will compare gut recovery and side effects between groups. If the method works, it offers a drug-free way to speed gut recovery after common operations, with a sham design that keeps the test honest.
pmc-13423361:
Petrecca and colleagues pooled studies in 2026 on stitches coated with antimicrobial agents in plastic surgery. Such coated sutures aim to cut surgical site infections, a common problem that slows healing and raises costs. Together they covered 1,553 patients, roughly half treated with coated stitches and half with plain ones.

Coated stitches were tied to a clear drop in infections, with risk about a third lower overall. The benefit was strong in abdominal surgery but not proven in breast surgery, where the data were weaker. Coated stitches also gave better cosmetic results and fewer poor healing outcomes in the pooled data. Rates of wounds splitting open did not differ between groups. The authors support coated sutures in plastic surgery but call for randomised trials to compare agents and body areas.
pmc-13423561:
Hohmuth and Möller surveyed male patients at a urology practice about cycling-related genital complaints. The complaints included perineal pressure pain, penile numbness, and urination problems. They then tested whether a bicycle saddle sized to a rider's prostate volume lowers pressure on the perineum. They also built an exploratory formula to estimate prostate volume without internal examination.

One group rode on the adapted saddle, and a control group used a conventional saddle. The prostate-adapted saddle cut central perineal pressure by about 88 percent. pmc-13447661:
Hala Kerbage and coauthors review a 2026 bounce-back-focused roundup of post-trauma stress illness from early childhood through late teen years, an illness still missed despite growth harm. The story review covers stopping, age-tuned spotting, complex PTSD after chronic between-people trauma, and multi-part healing.

Trauma-focused thought habit therapy stands as the gold standard, with EMDR and story facing as strong options, while single-session debrief is warned off. No drug is cleared for child PTSD, leaving talk therapy first-line. Healing needs rebuilding safety, bonds, and agency across family, school, and local systems.
pmc-13447861:
Lin Ji and coauthors review a 2026 roundup of oxytocin therapy for dark symptoms of schizophrenia, the drive and outward gaps that resist current drugs. Grounded in a scale-based symptom model, the review traces oxytocin multi-circuit actions on reward, drive, emotion, and motor output.

Future work should fuse genes, imaging, and conduct to find oxytocin-tuned kinds, tune dosing, and pair drugs with habit therapy toward pinpoint mind care.
pmc-13449661:
Amina Karray and colleagues describe in 2026 a rare pediatric case: a hydatid cyst growing in the kidney of a fourteen-year-old girl, with no disease elsewhere. Hydatid infection, caused by a tapeworm larva, usually settles in liver or lungs, and isolated kidney involvement in children is uncommon and hard to recognize. The girl, previously healthy, reported three months of left-sided back pain, and examination found a smooth, painless flank mass; her mother had undergone liver hydatid surgery a year earlier.

Ultrasound showed two cystic lesions in her left kidney, one of them multilocular, with no spread to other abdominal organs. Surgeons performed a partial pericystectomy, removing the cyst walls while sparing kidney tissue, and she recovered without incident. The family received counseling on preventing spread. Screening relatives then found a lung hydatid cyst in her nine-year-old brother, underlining the value of household checks.
pmc-13450861:
Vojko Pjanovic and co-authors model in 2026 how the brain keeps a steady sense of head direction while its signals stay noisy. Brain cells that track heading form a stable bump of activity, yet the bump wobbles more when cues turn unreliable. The team built a spiking network that weds two ideas: pull toward a stable state, plus flicker that stands for doubt.

In their model, a cell group races among likely headings while holding the broad direction firm, so wobble itself carries news about doubt. The work yields testable signs, such as shared voltage flickers under the firing line and set patterns in how the bump drifts. The authors offer the design as a shared trick for noisy brain circuits.
pmc-13451261:
Peipei Jin and others ran four experiments in 2026 on how money changes acceptance of unfair splits in the ultimatum game. Responders often reject unfair splits, but prior studies disagreed on when monetary incentives soften that rejection. The team varied incentive realism, gain span, task setup, and participant background.

Hypothetical questionnaires and real-money tests showed fairness and gain effects but no interaction at first. Expanding the gain range in a repeated virtual game showed gain effects grew stronger under very unfair offers. A final test under a fixed very unfair offer found steeper gain effects among students than working adults. The pattern shows fairness and money interact only under certain contexts, a nuance for bargaining research.
pmc-13452161:
Dararat Sirimongkol and co-authors scan in 2026 the germ load of rats and shrews caught at Bangkok Port, a world cargo hub. Small mammals that live beside people can carry germs that jump to humans, yet port zones are little checked. Gene shotgun reads of tissue from animals caught in mid 2025 were stripped of host DNA and sorted by kind.

The reads flagged names of concern, among them the plague germ and a fever germ, plus germs tied to drug resistance. Harm and resistance genes sat in some of the finds. The plague germ showed in rats, shrews, and their fleas alike. The team urges steady watch of port mammals to catch cross-border germ traffic early.
pmc-13452461:
Angela Muscettola and thirteen co-authors gather first person accounts of paranoia, from mild mistrust to fixed beliefs of persecution. Their 2026 review draws on 36 studies that used interviews and other first person methods, drawn from six databases. The team sorted the studies into core cases, where paranoia sat at the center, and side cases, where it formed part of a wider picture.

Three broad themes came out of the accounts. People described a slide from watchfulness toward a world that felt set against them, a self marked by shame and past harm, and efforts to win back safety and meaning. Mild accounts stayed local and open to doubt, while severe ones felt total and body deep. The authors urge clinicians to ask what a belief means to the person, not just whether it is true.
pmc-13452561:
Yang Yang and ten co-authors test whether enzymes can speed up the release of carbon dioxide caught by a common scrubbing liquid. That liquid, monoethanolamine or MEA, soaks up carbon dioxide from factory exhaust, but boiling it free again eats most of the energy in carbon capture. Their 2026 study mined gene data for amidase enzymes, natural proteins that cut certain carbon bonds.

One enzyme from a heat loving microbe stood out, staying stable near 70 degrees and cutting the bond that holds carbon dioxide in the used liquid. At a small dose, it raised the first release rate by about 20 percent. The time needed to free 80 percent of the caught gas fell by about half next to liquid with no enzyme. The team frames the find as a first step toward cheaper, cooler carbon capture.
pmc-13452961:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a dual-probe system for detecting polystyrene nanoplastics, plastic particles too small to see, at trace levels in food.  One probe uses magnetic particles dressed with peptides that specifically grab polystyrene; the other is a long-glow luminescent particle that reports the catch without background glow from the food itself.

Magnets pull the captured particles out of the mixture, and a pH trick that flips surface charge helps binding and release. Long-glow signaling avoids the autofluorescence that blinds ordinary fluorescent tests in food. The optimized system reached high sensitivity and selectivity for this one plastic type in complex samples. Regulators cannot limit what they cannot measure, so sensitive food tests are the enabling step for nanoplastic safety rules.
pmc-13453461:
Hiroshi Ito and others examined loneliness and health in Japan in 2026, using a nationwide survey of 25,014 adults aged eighteen to seventy-nine. Loneliness is increasingly linked to death and heart disease, but most evidence came from Western countries with varied measures. The team used the standardized UCLA three-item loneliness scale.

Weighted models adjusted for demographic, economic, health, and distress factors tested links to poor self-rated health and high symptom burden. Lonely participants reported worse health and more symptoms in the reported patterns, with distress explaining part but not all of the links. Japanese health planners gain East Asian evidence that loneliness is a health risk worth addressing through social and clinical routes.
pmc-13453661:
Naoyuki Iwahashi and others mapped ovary spread from bowel cancer in 2026, from tumor DNA in blood. Ovary spread from bowel cancer is rare but grim, and hard to treat, with some sites reacting unlike others to drugs. The DNA traits of this rare spread were poorly known.

Blood samples were read by deep gene scans, to find bad gene changes and gene-copy shifts. Most patients bore bad changes, with classic bowel drivers TP53, KRAS, and APC at rates like those in big gene banks. Extra copies of growth genes EGFR, MET, and ERBB2 turned up again and again. Cancer doctors gain a gene sketch to steer drugs for this rare spread site.
pmc-13454061:
David Dickerson and five co-authors pilot an AI workflow that watches spinal cord stimulator use and flags patients who may need a therapy tweak. Stimulators treat chronic pain, yet needs shift between visits and patients do not always call. Their 2026 pilot feeds device interaction data into a neural model, whose daily shortlist goes to a human care team for review and outreach.

Model training used 747 implanted patients, where true reprogramming days were rare at 0.77 percent per patient day. At a strict threshold the model hit a 28.8 percent precision, about 37 times richer than chance. Across 91 working days the team reviewed 188 cases, and 80.9 percent of patients answered within three tries. Two thirds of reviewed cases proved therapy related, and pain scores fell after outreach where follow up scores existed.
pmc-13454761:
Qianqian Zhang, Meifang Lei, Hong Li, Gui Yi, and Dong Li report, in 2026, a rare case of brain inflammation in a child caused by the bacterium Rickettsia felis. The germ lives inside cells and is usually tied to flea exposure. Reports of it reaching the brain are scarce, above all in children.

The patient was a healthy nine-year-old boy who arrived with fever and headache, then grew very hot and drowsy. Brain scans showed a lesion in the left temporal lobe with lining swelling, and a brain wave test ran slow. Gene sequencing of spinal fluid found abundant Rickettsia felis material, while autoimmune tests came back negative. Treatment paired doxycycline with steroids, immune globulin, and pressure care. The child recovered fully. The authors urge doctors to consider this germ in unexplained encephalitis and to sequence early.
pmc-13455261:
Adesh Kadambi and colleagues published a 2026 study of how therapists judge home video of hand use after nerve injury. The work covers outpatient rehab for people recovering from stroke or spinal cord injury, where hand skill often decides how much daily life a person can manage alone. Five patient and therapist pairs took part, with patients filming daily tasks on head-worn cameras at home.

Therapists reviewed dashboards built from that footage and then gave interviews and scored questionnaires. They valued watching real movement far more than bare numbers, and said home scenes revealed habits a clinic visit could never show. That detail could shape therapy around tasks people truly do each day, though time pressure and added work for patients stood in the way. Ease of use scored high, at a mean of 80.0 on the study scale, and therapists said they would trust and reuse such a tool.
pmc-13456561:
Yi-Yun Zeng and six colleagues explore, in a 2026 interview study, the stalled recoveries of patients whose leg veins were stented for a compression problem. A stent should restore flow where an artery squeezes the iliac vein, yet some patients stay unwell. Earlier work charted general recovery, not the stuck minority. The team used a phenomenological approach, listening closely to lived experience.

Patients described distress turned inward, spoken through the body rather than in words. Silence and delayed requests for help quietly blocked their care. Regret about choosing the procedure pushed some to skip follow-up visits altogether. The authors urge care that reaches past physical checks: emotional screening, culturally attuned conversation, and follow-up that assumes hesitation rather than blaming it. Personal tools for tracking well-being, they suggest, could help patients voice what they now carry quietly.
pmc-13456661:
Adrien Lavalley and four colleagues build, in a 2026 study, an air-powered tremor gauge that works inside an MRI scanner during focused ultrasound treatment. Essential tremor therapy aims sound waves at a brain spot, and doctors must verify the aim by watching the tremor fade. Electronic sensors can clash with the scanner's magnets.

Their gauge is a standard breathing cuff held in the patient's hand. Shaking squeezes the cuff, and the pressure pulses travel by tube outside the room to be recorded. Software turns them into a live tremor reading synced with each ultrasound burst. In ten patients, tremor fell by an average of 86 percent right after the test burst, confirming the target in nine. One target was moved after sensory side effects. The authors stress the device's low cost and easy setup.
pmc-13457261:
Supraja Ganeshan and colleagues compare two seed extracts with a standard mouthwash ingredient against Streptococcus mutans, the bacterium most closely tied to tooth decay. Interest in plant-based antimicrobials grows as synthetic agents bring side effects and resistance concerns. Their 2026 laboratory study prepared water extracts of chia seeds and fennel seeds by cold maceration and set them, at full, half, and quarter strength, against 0.2 percent chlorhexidine in agar wells seeded with the bacterium.

Both extracts slowed the bacterium, judged by the clear zones around each well and by minimum inhibitory concentrations. Fennel clearly outperformed chia, a difference that reached statistical significance, while chlorhexidine served as the benchmark treatment. The authors read the results as early evidence that familiar culinary seeds carry genuine antibacterial activity worth developing. Because the work is in vitro, they note that testing in people comes next, before any dental product claims.
pmc-13457461:
Qian Lv and colleagues ask what a long-standing bad bite does to the brain, using rats fitted with one-sided crossbite. Misaligned teeth change sensory input from the jaw, and human studies hint at brain effects, though pain and medication muddy those data. Their 2026 study placed a left-sided anterior crossbite in seven female rats at six weeks, kept seven sham controls, and scanned all fourteen with resting-state functional MRI at 26 weeks.

Crossbite rats showed altered activity in the right ventral posteromedial thalamus and primary somatosensory cortex, opposite the dental change, plus abnormal activity in the right amygdala. Whole-brain analysis found higher clustering and small-worldness in the crossbite group, a locally cliquish organization. One strengthened subnetwork centered on the right amygdala held the most changed connections. The authors read this as evidence that persistent abnormal bite input reorganizes networks, reaching beyond touch circuits into emotion.
pmc-13457861:
Amanuel Berhanu Bonso and colleagues ask whether adapting to climate change also frees rural women in Ethiopia's East Shewa Zone. Their 2026 study sampled 446 households across four districts, mixing surveys with focus groups and interviews, and scored empowerment with a purpose-built index spanning social, economic, political, and farm dimensions.

Farmers reported 22 adaptation strategies, led by mixed cropping at 91 percent and shifting the crop calendar at 89 percent. Adopting households scored higher on decision-making, livelihood control, and leadership than non-adopters. Modeling showed empowerment for male-headed households rising with schooling, livestock, extension contact, income, training, and membership, and falling with distance to market. For women-headed households, cooperatives and irrigation access also helped, while crop failure dragged scores down. The authors recommend gender-responsive adaptation policy tied to several global development goals.
pmc-13458161:
Najla Sassi and Wassim Jaziri build a knowledge graph system for explainable online assessment feedback in a 2026 study. Online courses often return only a score and a generic comment, leaving tutors blind to why a learner struggles. The authors model outcomes, tasks, learner traits and feedback strategies in a reusable ontology. It is instantiated as a knowledge graph updated with learner activity, with rules and queries flagging at-risk learners and generating tailored feedback tied to evidence.

Queries on about 4.2 million triples ran under one second. Institutions gain a transparent, near-real-time feedback foundation, though results rest on one dataset and expert judgement.
pmc-13458261:
Qiao-Qiao Zhou and Ling Peng published this 2026 review on one of oncology's harder judgement calls: whether to restart immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs after they have injured a patient's kidneys. These cancer drugs can cause acute kidney injury, and guidelines allow restarting in selected patients, but no tool predicts whose kidneys will fail again. Reported recurrence rates run from 16.5 to 44 percent across the studies the authors reviewed.

Candidate markers include a urine chemokine ratio with a proposed cut-off, a blood receptor level, and a gene variant in the PCCA gene. Each tier comes with advice on restarting, monitoring and preventive steroids. The authors warn the biomarker cut-offs come from other studies, so they are hypotheses for recurrence prediction until trials test them.
pmc-13458361:

Removing other PRC1 parts did not reproduce the tumors; the protective role sits outside the canonical complex. pmc-13458761:
Jinho Kim and co-authors tested whether repeated mild stress early in life leaves a lasting mark on brain support cells and on a blood protein. Their 2026 study used mice exposed to layered mild stressors: prenatal stress, separation from the mother, and social defeat during development. The mice were later sorted into susceptible and resilient groups by social behavior. The team examined astrocytes, star-shaped support cells, in the prefrontal cortex, a region involved in mood control.

Susceptible mice showed anxious and depressed behavior, alongside reduced astrocyte marker proteins in that brain region. A protein called S100B, released by astrocytes, ran high in the blood of the stressed mice. The same rise appeared in blood from drug free young adult patients with major depression, and higher levels tracked with worse symptoms. The authors propose blood S100B as a candidate marker for depression tied to early life stress.
pmc-13459161:
Dumura Jeneral Alfin and colleagues report in 2026 the case of a seven-year-old girl in Nigeria whose spinal cord swelling turned out to be schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection. She arrived with four days of severe back pain, weak legs, and loss of bladder and bowel control. Scans showed a swollen conus medullaris, the tapered end of the spinal cord, holding a mass that looked like a tumor.

Surgeons removed the mass through a small opening in the spine, and tissue study revealed eggs of Schistosoma haematobium inside an inflamed lesion. Treatment with praziquantel and steroids followed. Her pain resolved fully, and leg strength recovered substantially. The authors urge clinicians in endemic regions to suspect this rare cause before assuming cancer.
pmc-13459261:
Hilal Ahmad Tantray examines the women medical missionaries who built much of Kashmir's early modern healthcare between the late 1800s and early 1900s. His 2026 historical study draws on missionary memoirs, institutional reports, travelers' accounts, and official records to reconstruct how they worked around gender norms to reach female patients.

Tantray argues the missionaries did far more than import Western medicine. They created new channels for public health work through dispensaries and prenatal care, plus nursing services and medical schooling for local women. Their zenana work, visiting women in their segregated quarters, opened care to patients otherwise unreachable. The paper restores these women to a regional medical history that has largely overlooked their role.
pmc-13459461:
Zhengkang Bai and co-authors built a combined scoring system to measure how different landscapes restore mental health, testing nine scene types from city streets to mountain fields. The streams were fused into a single Cross-Modal Restorative Index for healthy-city research.

Mountain and field scenes combined relaxed brain activity, stronger calming heart signals, and clear mood gains, with subjective tension in mountain scenes falling from 18.6 to 12.3 on the scale used. Built landscapes restored only in fragments, and road scenes showed a split pattern, drawing visual attention without calming the body. The index can rank urban green-space designs by measured restorative value, the authors say.
pmc-13460161:
Rui Zhou and co-authors describe in 2026 a keyhole approach for removing tumors at the front of the chest cavity. Tumors ranged widely in size, averaging a little over three centimeters across, and patients averaged about fifty-three years old.

Every operation finished without major bleeding, conversion to open surgery, or injury to the phrenic nerve, and no severe complications followed. Operating time averaged around one hundred minutes with modest blood loss, and patients stayed about five to six days. The authors judge the method safe for capsule-intact tumors up to five centimeters that show no obvious invasion.
pmc-13461261:
Joon Pio Hong reflects in a 2026 essay on what a true legacy means for a surgeon, writing as editor emeritus of a plastic surgery journal. He traces the word from its Latin roots in envoys sent with a commission, through its medieval sense of property left at death. From there it reaches today's broader meaning of reputation, values, and lasting influence. Aging, he notes, sharpens everyone's concern with being remembered.

It lives in the people touched directly: family, friends, trainees, colleagues, and patients. Their memories carry a life forward longer than any textbook will.
pmc-13461561:
Benhur Sirvan Cetin and colleagues audited live vaccine coverage in children awaiting solid organ transplants at their centre. Live vaccines cannot be given after transplant, when immunity is suppressed, so protection must be finished beforehand.

At transplant, about 19.2 percent were under-vaccinated for chickenpox and 21.6 percent for measles, with infants worst off. Some children even slipped from fully to partly vaccinated during the wait, tied to faster listing after evaluation. pmc-13461761:

The pan genome contained a substantial strain specific fraction indicating niche adaptation. Most notably, both strains carry unique clusters for making nisin Z and sactipeptides, molecules that plausibly underpin immune effects. Genes for short chain fatty acid metabolism were also present.
pmc-13462061:

Parkinson's care rests on symptom relief, with no treatment that slows the disease itself. The drugs can reach the brain and, in early studies, calm inflammation, ease cell stress, and improve insulin response. The team searched two databases for work joining the two topics up to April 2026.

Hot topics included oxidative stress, insulin resistance, the clumping protein alpha-synuclein, the blood-brain barrier, and one drug of the class. Rising themes included mild memory problems and dual-action drugs. The authors say the map shows a field shifting toward multi-target ideas linking body metabolism with brain disease.
pmc-13462561:
Pei Tao and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study, an enzyme called caspase-4 in lung wash fluid from children with acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure condition. Faulty inflammation drives the syndrome, yet this enzyme's role in children was unmapped. The study included 28 children with the syndrome, half tied to gram-negative infection and half to viruses, plus 17 uninfected controls.

Levels tracked a clotting breakdown marker and showed a link to oxygen measures. Blood markers, by contrast, tied inconsistently to severity. pmc-13462761:
Yufei Huang and a large team report, in a 2026 mouse study, that an overactive brain circuit dulls mental flexibility early in Alzheimer's disease, before memory fails. Signals from cortex to one striatal cell class ran stronger. A second class of striatal cells, which release the chemical acetylcholine, was more strongly hushed, fired less, and released less of its chemical. The authors name early circuit overactivity, not cell loss alone, as a driver worth targeting while treatment can preserve thinking.
pmc-13463761:

A candidate named JSKN033 shows such a mix can work at high strength. Success will hinge on each molecule, so the authors call for case-by-case testing across design, formulation, and trials before skin delivery becomes routine.
pmc-13463961:
Gudra and co-authors tested in 2026 whether superglue can clean skin well enough for sampling microbes inside hair follicles. Surface contamination is the core problem in such sampling. The glue treatment cut the microbial load in biopsies by nearly fourfold against untreated skin. Treated biopsies also yielded far fewer stray bacterial types. pmc-13464461:

pmc-13465161:

Some spread deposits held only non-16 high-risk types, which first-biopsy typing would miss. Over a fifth of detections fell outside current vaccine coverage. Type maps may steer immune therapy choices in advanced disease, the authors suggest.
pmc-13465661:

A path model tested the links, with resampling checks for the chain effects.

The full sequence, mindfulness to reframing to resilience to play, was real but modest in size. That pattern fits a multi-stage self-control process rather than a single switch. The authors suggest staged training that builds reframing and bounce-back strength on a mindful base, rather than drilling sport skills alone.
pmc-13465961:

pmc-13467061:

The current fix, an injection behind the knee joint, can be awkward to perform.

pmc-13467461:

pmc-13467761:

His tumour carried a gene change that can favour chemotherapy response.

He was treated gently. Low-dose daily temozolomide was given. This is a chemotherapy drug. Valproic acid was added. It is normally an epilepsy medicine. The regimen caused no serious side effects. Scans showed stable disease at three months. His functional scores improved markedly. The authors offer this as a palliative option for similar patients. Larger studies are still pending.
pmc-13468761:
Zhou and colleagues introduce BiasFormer in this 2026 computer vision paper. The task is temporal action segmentation, splitting a video into its successive actions, such as pouring or opening. BiasFormer adds structural guidance at two levels: statistical estimates of likely actions steer how video features are weighted, and a segment-based decoding head enforces plausible durations and transitions. Tested on four public video collections, including Breakfast and EPIC-KITCHENS, it beat the FACT model on most segment-level measures. The gains showed up as cleaner, more coherent action segments rather than scattered short pieces.
pmc-13469061:
Olivier Perrin and a French multicenter team stretch a scarce imaging tracer further in 2026 by splitting commercial single-vial kits and double-eluting radioactive generators. Every approach passed full pharmacopoeial quality control. Economics were tallied as well. pmc-13469361:
Jianming Wen sets out a theory paper in 2026 on a light based sensing method that rebuilds an interference pattern from one fixed detector. In the setup, called time reversed Young interferometry, the pattern comes from how often each of two light sources fires. Wen recasts the method in Bayesian terms, treating the chosen firing rates as prior beliefs that can be engineered before the light travels.

Because the prior is set in advance, it shapes which outcomes the detector actually records. Wen shows the useful signal lies in how strongly outcomes favor one explanation over another, not in brightness alone. A two source code can turn a tiny disturbance into a clear imbalance between the sources. The paper closes with design rules and a tabletop double slit test using weak phase and loss changes.
pmc-13469461:
Jianjun Rui and colleagues present in 2026 a tracking method for maneuvering targets that a radar hopes to follow without being noticed. Such low probability of intercept operation limits how often the radar can measure. Misspecified motion models and slow switching between them add further error.

Their screened method pairs a classic multi model filter with a recurrent neural network. Its outputs are checked against a smooth path built from recent measurements, and estimates that clash with local motion are rejected. During silent periods, a classifier guesses the target motion mode and guides the next prediction round. Within the tested settings, accuracy improved while the model structure stayed readable. The radar also needed fewer active measurements to hold the same accuracy.
pmc-13469661:
Yang, Lindahl, and Robben test whether patterns in T cell receptor genes can predict type 1 diabetes. The disease is autoimmune: the body attacks its own insulin-making cells. A person's genetic background shaped which features mattered most. That points toward personal risk markers rather than one universal test. The same signals could also be pulled from ordinary RNA sequencing data, a cheaper measurement. This raises the prospect of a fast, accessible blood test for children at risk.
pmc-13470061:
Wanxin Pan and colleagues showed in 2026 that crack density in overlying rock, not just rock strength, governs mining subsidence in China's Ordos coalfield. Strength analogies proved reliable only when crack densities matched, and denser cracking lowered the width-to-depth ratio needed for full subsidence, explaining delayed sinking. Mine planners must thus map fracture density before forecasting surface damage.
pmc-13471461:
Kai Zhao and co-authors build in 2026 a prediction model that sorts thymus tumors by risk before surgery using only plain CT scans. Thymomas are graded into low and high risk types, but scan features overlap between them, so surgeons often learn the grade only after removal. Records of 436 patients with proven thymomas, gathered over thirteen years, were split into training and validation sets.

The team extracted hundreds of texture features from each tumor outline and narrowed them to eleven that separated the risk groups best. Two ordinary clinical imaging features joined them in a combined scoring chart. That chart outperformed every single model at telling low risk tumors from high risk ones. The authors propose the tool for planning how aggressive surgery should be before the chest is opened.
pmc-13471661:
Xueyan Liu, Zhaotai Wang, and Yingjuan Cao map in 2026 the symptom web linking depression, poor sleep, and thinking problems among older adults with type 2 diabetes living in rural areas. The three burdens cluster in this group, yet which symptoms hold the web together was unknown. Abstraction and calculation trouble, together with feelings of helplessness, sat most centrally in the network. Abstraction ability, perceived memory problems, and concentration trouble acted as bridges carrying influence between the three domains. Repeat analyses supported the structure, and men and women showed no meaningful difference in connection strengths. The authors suggest that targeting bridge symptoms could loosen the whole cluster at once.
pmc-13471961:
Abby Bronson and colleagues interview in 2026 adults and adolescents living with Becker muscular dystrophy to test whether standard surveys truly capture their experience. One pain survey item and three domains of a broad outcome system were understood well and judged relevant. An upper limb survey from another system missed the mark conceptually. The authors conclude the validated pieces can support trials, while the weak one needs replacement or rework.
pmc-13472161:
Sousa and colleagues study hybrid drug-delivery bubbles in this 2026 biophysics paper. Earlier work judged such hybrids by biological performance, but the physical consequences of mixing were poorly explored, so the team varied the lipid-to-protein ratio and measured the membranes directly.
