Positively charged hybrids showed stronger fusion-like interaction signals in calorimetry tests, suggesting they merge with other membranes more readily. The authors frame these measurements as design parameters for building sturdier biomimetic delivery systems.
pmc-13472961:
Giuseppe Valerio Aurucci and co-authors present a 2026 trial of virtual reality paired with nerve stimulation for arm recovery after stroke. Thirty-four people with long-term stroke effects joined a small pilot phase and a main trial phase that lasted about a month. One group used the combined system, called MultiSensy, while the other group had standard rehab care. The team tracked arm movement, hand use, and sense of body position.

Scores for arm movement and hand tasks rose more in the combined group than in the standard care group. The system also gathered motion data during each session to give firm measures of progress. Readers see how pairing a virtual world with timed stimulation may support stroke rehab. The authors treat the work as a first step that needs larger trials.
pmc-13473961:
Xu Sun and co-authors design a smart particle in 2026 that attacks tumors with heat and chemistry at once. Careful measures linked each design choice to the gain in effect. The work offers a recipe for building multi-action cancer tools with intent, not trial and error.
pmc-13474161: Wang and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their earlier study of HPV vaccination intent among medical students. That study drew on the health belief model and vaccine hesitancy theory. The notice fixes the affiliation for all authors to the School of Public Health at Xuzhou Medical University, replacing the Graduate School. It also swaps the author contributions statement for a shorter, correct version, and records that Wang and Zhao share first authorship as equal contributors.
pmc-13474661:
Rohit B Ponnada and colleagues track United States deaths tied to both pancreatic cancer and heart disease from 1999 to 2020 in a 2026 study. Federal death data held just under one hundred ninety thousand such deaths. Rates were age-adjusted and split by race, sex, and city versus rural living. Trend software measured yearly change for each group.

The joint death rate rose from about twenty-six to about thirty-one per million people over the span. Men stayed above women throughout, and both rose at a similar pace. White patients had higher raw rates, while Black patients showed a faster relative climb. Rural areas carried higher rates than metro areas across the years.
pmc-13474761:
Danqing Hu and co-authors pool studies in 2026 on whether women wait longer than men before reaching care for a heart attack. Bias checks and pooled odds gave the headline results.

Women faced higher odds of long delay on both measures, with the patient part showing the stronger gap. The pattern held across heart attack types and after adjusting for other factors. Mixed results in past single studies settle into a clear pooled answer. Faster public response for women could save heart muscle and lives.
pmc-13474961:
Lemmerer and colleagues test a new way to fix the shape of 1,3-diols. These units appear in many natural products. Their shape can be hard to set during a build. That step flipped the centre into the wanted shape.

Some matched diols gave a single mirror form with very high purity. Others gave both syn and anti forms in high purity from a mixed start. Tests on how the catalyst acts tie these results into one clear picture.
pmc-13475961:
Yeaeun Kim, Jihoon Lee, and Jongho Park study whether elderly patients outside South Korea's capital kept traveling there for hospital care during the pandemic. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Care in Korea clusters in the capital area, a long-standing policy concern. Sick elders traveling far during COVID-19 raised both access and infection questions.

Using a national discharge survey covering millions of weighted cases, they compared the two years before the pandemic with its first two years. The capital share of admissions held steady overall. Beneath that calm, some age groups and diagnoses shifted significantly. Regression work profiled who still traveled during the crisis. The authors argue the delivery system needs regional strengthening so elders can be treated nearer home. The study gives planners a before-and-during snapshot.
pmc-13476161:
Lihao Qin and six co-authors track liver cancer patients' blood immune markers across treatment cycles to see which trajectories predict survival. The patients had hepatitis B-related, unresectable tumors treated with the modern triple combination: artery-directed chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint inhibitors plus vessel-targeting drugs. Blood was drawn at baseline, cycle two, and cycle four, with tumor response judged at the end of cycle four.

Both the static marker levels and their changes between cycles were fed into selection models against overall survival, progression-free survival, and response rates. The retrospective single-center design covers patients treated from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-four. The premise is that immunity in motion, not just at baseline, carries the prognosis.
pmc-13478061:

On MIT degradation data for lithium iron phosphate-graphite cells, the hybrid beat both base models, with mean relative error of 3.45 cycles, root-mean-square error of 4.75 cycles, and near-perfect fit. The authors offer the model for battery health tracking, predictive maintenance, and real-time management systems.
pmc-13479461:
Chia-Hung Wu and coauthors published a 2026 brain imaging study of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, a condition where brain vessels narrow for a time and cause sudden, crushing head pain. The team asked how blood-brain barrier leakiness relates to brain activity patterns. Patients seen at a large Taipei headache center between 2016 and 2023 were compared with matched healthy controls.

Resting brain scans yielded an entropy measure, a gauge of signal messiness, compared between patients with and without barrier leaks. Contrast scans measured barrier leak in hard numbers, and ultrasound added vessel data. The design links a leak measure with an activity pattern measure in the same patients. Findings aim to clarify why this passing condition sometimes leaves lasting brain effects.
pmc-13479561:
Desalegn and colleagues measured moral distress in 2026 among nurses in public hospitals in Ethiopia's West Arsi Zone. It drains staff and can lower the quality of care, yet data from Ethiopia were scarce.

Nurses unhappy with their jobs had almost eight times the odds of high distress, and those in poor work settings had about four times the odds. The authors urge hospital leaders to raise job satisfaction and build more supportive wards as the surest route to relief.
pmc-13479661:
Jekaterina Strelčenko and coauthors published a 2026 forensic study of sharp-object injuries across different suicide cases in Lithuania. Suicide by cutting or stabbing is uncommon, and self-inflicted wounds can be mistaken for assault or accident, which makes careful pattern analysis essential for investigators. The retrospective analysis covered ninety-eight cases from 2019 to 2024 with anonymized records. Injury locations, counts, and types were compared against the additional methods used in each case. The team looked for correlations that help pathologists distinguish self-inflicted patterns from inflicted ones. Findings feed directly into medico-legal practice where the manner of death must be certified.
pmc-13481561:
Ju-Wei Hsu and co-authors describe a 2026 study of inflammation and thinking control in young people with major mood disorders. Current suicidal thinking was graded by a depression scale item, past attempts were recorded, blood was tested for an inflammation marker, and a card sorting test probed flexible thinking.

Young people with strong current suicidal thinking showed the highest inflammation levels and the most slips of a type tied to lapses in attention. Mild thinking sat in between. A different error type, rigid repeats, rose only in those with a past attempt. The pattern splits signs of present crisis from signs of lasting trait, which could sharpen risk checks in youth clinics.
pmc-13482361:
Yang and colleagues track two decades of plant growth in China's Gaoligong Mountains in 2026, asking how extreme weather has helped or hurt the region's greenery. Productivity climbed overall across the 23 years, rising at a trend slope of 1.5 units per year in the team's model, with the sharpest monthly gain in January. pmc-13483161:

pmc-13486761:

pmc-13487261:

Statistical mediation showed that this connection accounted for the link between caudate drive signal loss and motor gravity. pmc-13487361:

pmc-13487961:
Shizuko Angerhofer and co-authors survey married, employed, childless Japanese women in their thirties about planning for children in a 2026 questionnaire study. About a third of participants worked forty hours or more each week, and the average desired family size was under two children. The authors propose support that joins reproductive planning with career planning.
pmc-13488561:
Hui Chen and Baidi Fu survey parents of school-age children with asthma at a Chinese children's hospital in a 2026 cross-sectional study. pmc-13489561:

pmc-13490261:
Suelen Maria Parizotto Furlan and colleagues test progesterone blood levels as a predictor of embryo transfer success in a 2026 study in Brazil. The work adds a caution against one-number rules in fertility care.
pmc-13490361:
Wang and co-authors used provincial health surveillance data from Henan, China, to test whether smoking lowers vitamin D in adults, and whether blood fats change that relationship. pmc-13490561:

pmc-13491061:

Healthy habit adherence, however, moved in mixed directions across behaviors, and at-risk groups underused proven follow-up drugs. Care quality also varied unevenly despite wider access. pmc-13491661:
Zhao and team surveyed Chinese anesthesia doctors on whether they know and follow the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign advice on fluid revival care, the first-line treatment for sepsis. Knowledge of specific 2021 updates lagged the general claims, and junior doctors showed the largest gaps. Single traits predicted know-how more than hospital traits did. Zhao urges targeted schooling rather than blanket campaigns.
pmc-13491861:

pmc-13493961:

The activated protein partners with a transcription factor to order production of TGFBI, a secreted factor that drives endothelial cells to build tubes and migrate. Screening then found hesperidin, a citrus flavonoid, binding the secreted factor tightly enough to cancel the vessel growth and slow tumors in animals, a candidate precision therapy.
pmc-13494361:
Otsuka and colleagues examined what happens to the deep fascia when a leg nerve is cut, in a 2026 mouse study. The fascia is the dense connective sheet wrapping muscles and transmitting their force. Muscle wasting after denervation is documented, but the fascia's response was unknown. Rehabilitation after nerve injury must reckon with a stiffening fascial envelope, not the shrinking muscle inside it.
pmc-13495161:

The team gathered data from nineteen regions on start dates, delivery models, and hospital and intensive care admissions. Northern and central regions began early with few snags and saw falls in RSV admissions, over eighty percent in one region. Southern and smaller regions started late amid shortages and red tape, and gains were smaller. Intensive care trends matched. Set beside early results from France, Spain, and Luxembourg, the lesson is plain: an early start, steady supply, and organization decide how much good the shot does.
pmc-13495261:

It also tied far more strongly to a standard jump quality score, and the tie held up when jump height was counted, where the raw tie flipped sign. Switching to the scaled index moved nearly half the athletes by ten or more ranking places. The authors say the index should sit beside, not replace, standard jump measures.
pmc-13495361:
Shidan Wang and a large team present MicNet in a 2026 article, a deep learning method that joins tissue images with spatial gene data. The authors offer MicNet as a way to let photos and gene maps explain each other, which may sharpen how pathologists and biologists read tumor and organ structure.
pmc-13495461:

Coating the particles with silica shells shifted the resonances toward redder wavelengths and blocked charge-transfer coupling between nearby particles. Pairs showed bonding-like and antibonding-like modes that turned on their orientation and the light's polarization, while weakly coupled pairs kept mostly independent responses. Tests matched the simulations closely, giving design rules for building localized optical fields.
pmc-13496061:

Their results place sterile stamens at the base of a petal-free lineage, later lost, reduced, or made petal-like in many branches. Readers gain a clear claim: these flowers lack true petals.
pmc-13497761:

Surgery took notably less time with the on-top method, and pain on the first day was lower, while hospital stay was much the same.
pmc-13499361:
Lakshya Motwani, Vijay Kumar Doddapaneni, and Erin L Heuring describe in 2026 a rare blistering skin reaction linked to pembrolizumab, an immune therapy drug used against lung cancer. pmc-13499761:
Brian Hanley and a large team of co-authors build a ranking of the greatest runners of all time in this 2026 paper. The pool covers medal winners at the Olympics and World Championships since 1896. World record setters since 1912 are also included. Sprint, hurdles, and distance events all count.

The system awards points by medal type and event level. Olympic gold and world records earn the most points. Bonus points reward records that stood for a long time or were set in Olympic finals. pmc-13500461:

Peak concentrations for most elements also sat significantly below drinking water limits at every stage of the pilot. The authors read the pattern as evidence that groundwater pollution risk from this storage method is likely minimal, at least under Jizan conditions.
pmc-13500561:
Zhongxing Zhang and colleagues upgrade in 2026 an object detection algorithm for finding defects in solar panels from near-infrared images. Ablation tests, where parts are removed one at a time, and comparisons with rival detectors each supported the design choices. Field relevance spans factory quality control and maintenance scanning of installed arrays.
pmc-13501561:
Abubaker Rom Deng Ayuiel leads a nine-author team with a 2026 qualitative study of seasonal malaria chemoprevention delivery in Northern Bahr el Ghazal, South Sudan. pmc-13501661:

Correlation checks supplied evidence that the scale relates to outside criteria as expected. The three-factor structure held up with sound reliability and validity. pmc-13501761:

pmc-13502161:

Fifty healthy adults, twenty-five of each sex, swallowed on command with two cubic centimetres of thin liquid and also swallowed saliva uncued. Deliberate swallows generated far higher pressures in the velopharynx, tongue base, and the segment below the upper oesophageal sphincter after it closed. Sex influenced none of the swallowing measures despite neck size differences.
pmc-13502561:
Barry Halliwell writes a 2026 review asking why iron-removing drugs keep disappointing in brain disease despite a rationale. Iron accumulates in the regions that degenerate in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and related conditions. Free ions catalyse oxidative attack on DNA, proteins, and fats through chemistry such as the Fenton reaction. Chelators, which bind iron, should starve that damage. Yet trials of chelating agents have delivered unimpressive results, and in cases patients fared worse.

Halliwell argues the explanation sits in redox chemistry that trial design has neglected. A chelator can hold iron in a form that stays reactive, shuffle it between compartments, or strip iron from enzymes that need it, so binding is not the same as silencing. The review weighs where in the body and cell a chelator reaches, which iron pools matter, and what measurements prove engagement. Chelation is not abandoned, but it is put on probation pending chemically sound trials.
pmc-13503061:
Sulaiman Abubakar Musa reviews how sampling in epidemiology has changed over time. His narrative review came out in 2026. How samples are picked shapes validity, efficiency, and how far results for a whole group can be spread.

The new sources are digital health data, electronic health records, and online cohorts. Musa tracks new routes that use artificial intelligence to draw in subjects. He also tracks active learning and adaptive sampling. He backs hybrid frames that keep statistical rigour but use the power of algorithms to adapt. Risks tied to ethics get close care. So do the effects for low- and middle-income countries.
pmc-13503761:
Kakeru Matsukuma leads a chemistry team that found a controlled way to break tough carbon-halogen bonds, in a 2026 paper. Such bonds in haloarenes need extreme push from electrons, past what one flash of light can give. Two-flash methods make strong reducers, but the active forms drift off and react at random.

Their plan first pairs the partners into ordered complexes that act as tiny reaction pockets. A first flash builds a charged scaffold that grabs and holds the target in place. A second flash then fires its stored energy right at the bond. The setup blocks side paths and works even with air present. The team shows the method opens a wide range of changes for late-stage work on complex compounds.
pmc-13504361:
Gallican Rwibasira leads a team of eleven authors mining Rwanda's national HIV surveillance system for what predicts viral suppression in teenagers and young adults on treatment. This age group suppresses the virus less reliably than older adults across the region, and Rwanda lacked national evidence on why. The study followed patients aged fifteen to twenty-four who started therapy between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-five.

Over four thousand participants at more than four hundred fifty facilities were included. Most were female and aged twenty to twenty-four; nearly all received a dolutegravir-based regimen and showed good recorded adherence. Suppression meant a viral load at or below one thousand copies. Regression with facility clustering and imputed missing data estimated which demographic and clinical factors tracked with success.
pmc-13504961:
Minjian Kong leads a team comparing two chest openings for a combined valve and aorta operation, in a 2026 study. The Wheat procedure replaces the aortic valve and the rising aorta in one sitting. A small side cut between ribs offers a less invasive route than sawing the breastbone, but proof for this operation pairing was thin.

Of 163 patients treated over three years, 59 had the small-cut route. Matched groups of 43 each had like starting profiles. The small-cut group spent longer on the heart-lung machine yet lost less blood. No one died in hospital in either group, and no small-cut case needed rescue conversion. New rhythm trouble struck far fewer small-cut patients, who also reported less pain and left sooner.
pmc-13505761:
Richard B. Warren and others report one-year results for icotrokinra in high-impact site scaly skin. In 2026, the phase 3 ICONIC-TOTAL trial randomized people aged twelve or older with at least modest scalp, genital, or hand and foot scaly skin two-to-one. They ranged 67 to 70 percent overall, 72 to 78 percent for scalp, 85 to 90 percent for genital, and 54 to 62 percent for hand and foot disease. pmc-13507061:
Heehyeon Sim and colleagues report 2026 lab work on how serpentine, a water-rich mineral in sinking ocean plates, carries water deep into Earth. Samples held about 13 percent water by weight and faced high pressure and heat along two cold sinking paths. Extra water in the setup varied widely, and X-ray and sound tools tracked new minerals as they formed.

With plenty of extra water on the coldest path, samples took up even more water and formed new water-rich phases past about 280 kilometers deep. With little extra water, change occurred without water loss. On a warmer cold path, samples instead released water. Slabs may carry far more water than once thought.
pmc-13507261:
Guo Yaqin leads a 2026 team that assesses mercury emissions unit by unit across the world's coal power fleet. Mercury builds up through food chains and harms health, and coal plants rank among its top human sources. Standard pollution gear already traps much mercury as a side benefit, yet plants differ hugely in size, efficiency, and controls.

A minority of units, dubbed super emitters, release outsized shares and clustered in emerging economies by 2020. Retiring those units first and upgrading controls elsewhere offers large, cheap near-term cuts. Deeper cuts later need mercury-specific gear such as activated carbon injection. Country-tailored, staged plans follow from the unit-level map.
pmc-13507661:
Remi Luschei and Werner Brannath published a statistics paper in 2026. They study error control in multi-population clinical trials. Some trials test treatments in overlapping patient groups. Each group may receive its own tailored policy. False positive claims could then harm several groups. Trials usually control the family-wise error rate. That rate is the chance of any false rejection. Standard adjustments assume equal null effects everywhere. The authors show that assumption can fail badly.

When opposite effects cancel across groups, control breaks. Tests may reject true null claims too often. The standard method no longer protects the error rate. Alternative procedures are proposed and compared directly. Power and error control are weighed for each option. Trial designers should check the cancelling case carefully. Safer methods exist for overlapping population designs.
pmc-13507861:

pmc-13508261:
Sibin Wang and six co-authors test two ultrasound measures of the heart's upper left chamber as warnings that a rhythm disorder will return after treatment, in 2026 work. Before treatment, scans measured how much the chamber stretches as it fills, and how fast blood flows through a small side pouch. Follow-up ran a median of about 17 months.

Sixty-eight patients, just over a quarter, saw the rhythm problem return after the early healing window. Both measures ran lower in patients whose problem returned. Each held up as an independent predictor after full adjustment. Higher stretch and faster pouch flow each meant lower risk of return. The authors argue that pairing the two measures gives a fuller picture of chamber health, and could help doctors tailor follow-up intensity.
pmc-13508361:

Blood homocysteine was measured, brain scans gave cortical thickness, and memory tests scored performance. Homocysteine ran high in patients, highest in the resistant group. Within that group, more homocysteine meant worse memory by a moderate margin. The authors frame these paths as leads for new studies, not settled mechanisms, given the single-time-point design.
pmc-13514161:
Marcella Chagas-Sena and four co-authors review damage to the blood-brain barrier and brain blood vessels in COVID-19 and its long form, in 2026 work. The review follows topics such as viral receptor presence on vessel cells and downstream injury patterns. pmc-13514661:
Kurose and colleagues report in 2026 on adding Gosha-jinki-gan, a traditional Japanese herbal formula, for men whose nighttime urination persisted despite desmopressin treatment. The retrospective study included forty men aged sixty or older with nocturnal polyuria, meaning most urine is made at night. After adding the herbal formula, nightly voids fell from 3.38 to 2.60 episodes per night, and hours of undisturbed sleep rose from 116 to 186 minutes at four weeks, a gain of about seventy minutes past the three-hour mark linked to meaningful benefit. Insomnia scores improved, and no serious adverse events appeared. Without a control group, the authors call the findings preliminary.
pmc-13516161:
Ying Xiang leads a ten-author team hunting a compact gut-microbe signature for necrotizing enterocolitis, a gut emergency of preterm babies, in a 2026 study. Certain shifts recurred: opportunist genera such as Enterobacter, Klebsiella, and Serratia rose, while friendly Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus fell. In the fresh samples the signature kept its direction but discriminated only modestly.
pmc-13516261:

pmc-13516961:

pmc-13517061:

pmc-13518861:

pmc-13518961:

pmc-13519061:

Worse insomnia severity and poorer sleep quality tracked with lower vessel reactivity, and insomnia past the clinical cutoff linked to a drop of about 0.94 index units. pmc-13520161:

Host change plus geographic isolation, Ganbold and colleagues argue, is driving the pair apart.
pmc-13520361:
Himanshi Rathnasekara and Ruwan Jayathilaka analyse in 2026 two decades of data on deaths before age five across 45 African countries. Child survival tracks national progress, so the study tests which economic, health, social and environmental factors move together with mortality over time.

pmc-13521361:
Stogios and five colleagues lay out a brain scan study of antipsychotic drugs and brain insulin action in women in twenty twenty-six. These drugs can trigger diabetes, and women bear the brunt. pmc-13521861:

pmc-13521961:

Call-back rates, hit rates and find types fill the result tables. The team also tracked if fertility care went on during workup. Clinic flow grounds the screening advice in real practice.
pmc-13522461:
Lu and colleagues report a cleaner way to make N-phenylhydroxylamine, a building block used in drug manufacturing, by reducing nitrobenzene with electricity in water during 2026 research on green chemistry. Their electrodeposited silver catalyst, called CV-Ag, then ran at ampere-level current while reaching selectivity of nearly 99.6 percent toward the desired product across the run. It also kept producing steadily at gram scale, delivering batches of 5.85 grams each without losing that selectivity.
pmc-13523261:

pmc-13523461:
Ah-Hyun Yoo, Hak Seung Lee, and Kyung-Hee Kim present a 2026 case series on tracking artificial intelligence electrocardiogram scores over time during heart failure treatment. pmc-13523761:
Qiu and colleagues reviewed fluorescent probes modeled on green fluorescent protein, the glowing jellyfish protein that transformed cell biology, in a 2026 perspective. pmc-13526461:

The authors argue that gentle, response-guided dosing can work for frail older patients who cannot face harsher chemotherapy regimens.
pmc-13526861:

Tagging matters because it shields oxygen groups and adds silicon handles used to build complex molecules. The authors frame the solvent itself as the enabler, opening cleaner routes to shielded building blocks. Readers get a practical advance for synthesis labs, with solvent green credentials still to weigh.
pmc-13527061:
Haniyeh Azadi and colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial testing yoga, an omega-3 rich seed powder, and their combination in women with type 2 diabetes. Camelina sativa powder supplies plant omega-3 fats, and yoga adds gentle structured activity. The authors report a favorable combined effect.
pmc-13528061:
Sarah Jameel and eight colleagues study virtual health care for people with disabilities in India in a 2026 paper. The team ran twenty in-depth interviews and five group talks. Participants had vision, hearing, physical, or intellectual disabilities. Caregivers joined too. Regions across India were covered, and themes were drawn from the talks.

Staff rarely had disability-specific training. The public platform eSanjeevani was little known and hard to use. The authors recommend staff training, access audits of platforms, and policy that cuts costs. Awareness campaigns for public services are also needed. Inclusion must be designed in, they argue.
pmc-13528161:
Mette Møller Handrup and four colleagues pool survival data for a rare nerve sheath cancer in a 2026 review. The cancer, shortened to MPNST, is an aggressive sarcoma. It can arise alone or in people with neurofibromatosis type 1, an inherited tumor condition. The review searched to October 2024. It screened over four thousand records and kept thirty-six studies.

Eight studies fed the pooled comparison. Having NF1 raised the risk of death in that analysis. Fifteen studies reported clearly worse survival for NF1-linked tumors. Four favored the sporadic form, none firmly. Five-year survival stayed poor across the board. The authors note NF1 tumors often grow larger and harder to remove. That size gap may drive much of the survival gap. They call for studies that separate the gene effect from the size effect.
pmc-13529361:
Eleonora Gariazzo and co-authors study whether re-testing tumours at progression improves care for lung cancer patients whose EGFR-mutant disease has stopped responding to osimertinib. Their 2026 multicentre retrospective study, called Rebiopsy on Osi, uses an Italian registry of patients on this first-line targeted drug.

Of 457 patients who progressed, 206 had a rebiopsy, mostly tissue sampling. A resistance mechanism was found in 38.8 percent of those tested, with tissue testing detecting far more than blood testing, and MET amplification was the commonest actionable finding. Among patients receiving second-line therapy, those given treatment matched to their rebiopsy result lived longer without progression and overall than patients rebiopsied without adaptation or not rebiopsied at all. Median survival reached 14.1 months with adaptive therapy against 8.2 months without rebiopsy. The authors support routine rebiopsy at progression.
pmc-13529661:
Pravin Khope and seven colleagues build a learning framework that helps factories trade smartly with the power grid in a 2026 paper. Prices, weather, and machine states all shift at once. Most control algorithms flatten that richness. Their five-stage pipeline keeps it. A graph stage merges price, weather, and process data over time. A replay stage imagines counterfactual runs for safe judging.

Later stages balance cost against carbon under uncertainty. A calibrator keeps bids inside market rules. A safety layer guards live adjustments. In their tests the system cut energy bills by fifteen percent. Carbon fell twelve percent and peak demand twenty percent. Output stayed intact through the cuts. The authors pitch the design for plants joining smart grids. Real plant trials remain the proving step.
pmc-13530161:
Sijie Lou and colleagues pool evidence in 2026 on machine learning models that forecast sports injuries. Predicting who gets hurt remains hard, yet data-driven models promise earlier warnings for coaches and clinicians. Five databases yielded ten studies with ten separate models for combined analysis.

Pooled results showed moderate skill at spotting future injuries and at clearing those who stayed healthy. Wide differences in methods across studies limited how far performance could rise. The authors advise handling uneven data in small samples, using repeated cross-checks, and adding time-based signals. Larger studies must confirm whether those steps truly sharpen forecasts.
pmc-13530261:
Yinfeng Zhao and colleagues test in 2026 how plant scenery restores people under different weather and seasonal growth stages. Brain-wave recording joined with mood surveys measured recovery across blooming and fading landscapes and several plant types. Personal traits, including how tense or outgoing people are, entered the design as possible modifiers.

Blooming scenery lifted both body and mind recovery in every weather condition, while fading scenery helped or hurt depending on plant type. Traits shaped recovery most strongly, outweighing weather preference and gender. One trait showed a curved pattern, helping at moderate levels yet hindering at extremes. Planners gain evidence for healing city green space.
pmc-13531861:
Anmol Desai and colleagues lay out a 2026 trial protocol testing Stress First Aid for substance use outreach workers across the south-central United States. These frontline workers face burnout and moral strain while serving people who use drugs. About 500 workers from roughly 90 organizations in ten regions will be randomized by cluster.

The program pairs a two-hour virtual training with monthly half-hour learning sessions. Surveys at start, two months, and six months track support, burnout, coping, and turnover plans. Interviews add reach and upkeep evidence. Results will feed a national rollout plan for workforce wellbeing.
pmc-13533061:
Güliz Ak and colleagues built a nasal barrier ointment from chitosan particles carrying plant extracts. Published in 2026, the formulation study loaded thyme oil and olive leaf extract into chitosan microparticles made by ionic gelation and spray drying, then mixed them into a glycerin-starch ointment. Plant antimicrobials attract interest as antibiotic resistance grows, but volatile oils need stable carriers.

Particles averaged about 1.8 micrometers with solid phenolic content, and the ointment's acidity sat within a nose-friendly range. Mouse tests showed time-dependent drops in microbial viability after nasal dosing. The authors present the system as a supportive antibacterial barrier for the nose, with human safety and efficacy trials still ahead. Readers get a formulation story from particle to animal test.
pmc-13534561:
Hajer Fraj A Alhawiti and colleagues make in 2026 zinc oxide nanoparticles using Teucrium polium plant material and test many possible uses. Plant-made particles avoid harsh chemicals and can carry several actions at once. Standard tools confirmed particle formation and shape before a battery of lab tests.

Particles scavenged harmful radicals in a dose-linked way and blocked four test bacteria, with the strongest zone against one lung pathogen. Breast cancer cells died more as dose rose, with stress signals and cell death markers present. The particles also broke down a dye under light and killed mosquito larvae.
pmc-13534861:
Sangjin Han and colleagues report in 2026 the first record of the fly genus Protopiophila in South Korea, a group tied to late-stage body decomposition. Korean skipper fly fauna lacked full form and gene data, which limits forensic work. Five male specimens were collected and identified by body traits as one known species.

Detailed drawings describe male internal parts that were poorly documented before, and a new key covers all four Korean species in the family. DNA barcodes placed the Korean specimens in a distinct, well-supported branch apart from close relatives, aiding future forensic identification.
pmc-13536861:
Luis Felipe Dias Lopes and colleagues develop a scale for why people eat out in Brazil in a 2026 validation study. Eating away from home shapes diet quality, yet Brazil lacked a full validated tool covering money, behavior, and experience together. A total of 426 adults who ate out at least weekly answered an online survey. Statistical modeling checked reliability, validity, links among dimensions, and consistency across groups.

Five dimensions held up well, covering cost, convenience, habits and tastes, social and shared experience, and perceived food quality. Cost sat at the center, lifting convenience and habits while lowering social and shared experience scores. Convenience and social experience each lifted perceived quality. Scores behaved consistently across sex, marital status, and region. The authors offer the scale for research and food policy work.
pmc-13536961:
Charles Dharmani and colleagues assess a safety program for a joint tumor drug with liver risk in a 2026 survey series from 2020 to 2024. Pexidartinib treats a rare joint lining tumor yet can seriously harm the liver, so use requires enrollment, teaching, and regular liver checks. Four voluntary survey waves asked patients and caregivers about liver risk knowledge and monitoring duties, drawing 239 completed replies in total.

Single knowledge items scored high throughout. Understanding of liver harm stayed at or above the preset success level in each wave, while understanding of monitoring improved over time and reached a perfect share in one wave. Combined understanding of both messages dipped below the level in three waves. The authors conclude that knowledge stayed broadly steady and supports program effectiveness.
pmc-13537761:
Laura Bohorquez and five co-authors test whether the grip gap between single and paired forms of the MinD protein is key to its gradient in Bacillus subtilis, a rod shaped bacterium. The Min system stops division at cell poles, which avoids tiny cells. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

In a cousin germ, MinD swings pole to pole with a partner protein. This species lacks that partner and holds a still gradient with a membrane anchor at poles and division sites. The team finds both forms of MinD grip the membrane about alike here. MinD meets its anchor as a pair, which reshapes how the gradient model should be built.
pmc-13538161:
Bailey Keith and four colleagues measure how much joint cartilage a trendy foot fracture screw destroys on its way in. Intramedullary screws fix broken metatarsals through a small incision, but the screw crosses the toe joint's cartilage. In fourteen cadaver feet, fifty-six lesser metatarsals received the standard retrograde screw.

Cartilage damage averaged about ten percent of the joint surface in the second metatarsal, rising to over seventeen percent in the fifth. Screws consistently landed in the middle band of the joint. Whether that damage causes arthritis is unknown. The authors map the cost side of a technique whose benefit side, faster recovery, still needs clinical outcome studies.
pmc-13538661:
Sonja Blasche and colleagues test how common food and drug chemicals reshape gut bacteria responses to low-calorie sweeteners in a 2026 lab study. Twenty-five diverse gut strains met thirty-nine commercial sweeteners, alone and paired with four frequent co-consumed compounds including caffeine and an antidepressant. Protein, metabolite, and genetic analyses probed one strong pairing, and a synthetic gut community tested wider effects.

Three quarters of sweeteners altered growth of at least one strain, and over one hundred interactions appeared with the partner compounds. One sweetener component plus the antidepressant jointly suppressed two gut species tied to glucose control and healthy flora, apparently by altering small molecule transport. The pairing also shifted community metabolism, raising toxicity to human cell lines and changing inflammatory signals. The authors urge deeper study of such everyday mixtures.
pmc-13540861:
Tongxuan Wang and colleagues run a randomised trial in 2026. They tested whether lidocaine given into a vein cuts sedative needs. The procedure was endoscopic ultrasound. Propofol alone often depresses breathing and circulation in this setting. Lidocaine is a familiar local anaesthetic.

Eighty patients split evenly into two groups. One group got lidocaine as a bolus, then as an infusion. The other group got saline instead. Propofol rules stayed identical in both arms. The lidocaine group used less propofol in total. Oxygen drops were fewer, and blood pressure was steadier. Patients woke faster and reported less pain later. Both patients and doctors rated satisfaction higher.
pmc-13540961:
E Nicole Teal and colleagues pilot a safety bundle in a 2026 study. The bundle targets severe high blood pressure in pregnancy. It moves hospital routines into outpatient clinics. Many severe cases first appear in those clinics. Three federally qualified health centres took part. The work ran from late 2021 to mid-2022.

Nineteen care teams trained on the adapted bundle. Each team rehearsed with a patient actor. The actor showed severe hypertension at a prenatal visit. Observers scored how faithfully teams followed the steps. They also scored how respectful the care felt. Scores rose after training. Every team finished training and both simulations.
pmc-13542661:
Atere and colleagues compared blood markers in 2026 between fifty patients with type 2 diabetes and thirty matched controls at a federal medical center in Owo, Nigeria. They centered on ceruloplasmin, the blood's main copper-carrying protein and a suspected marker of metabolic dysfunction. The team measured blood sugar, the full lipid panel, ceruloplasmin, a damage marker called malondialdehyde, and total antioxidant status with standard assays.

The diabetes group differed significantly on sugar, ceruloplasmin, most lipid measures, and the damage marker, while total antioxidant status fell markedly, a pattern of stronger oxidative stress with weaker defense. Obese participants showed the worst lipid and stress profiles. Ceruloplasmin rose alongside the lipid measures, while the damage marker moved against antioxidant status. The authors propose ceruloplasmin as an early flag for the biochemical slide toward diabetes complications, worth adding to monitoring in similar clinics.
pmc-13543561:
Nir Tsur and colleagues reported in 2026 on how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped surgery and resident training in a children's ear, nose, and throat department in Israel. Fifteen residents rotated through the department between 2019 and 2021. The team reviewed all 1,992 operations across the pre-pandemic year and the two pandemic years, comparing total volume, urgency, and case mix.

Volume swung oddly: 614 operations in 2019, a rise to 874 in 2020, then a fall to 504 in 2021. Urgent work grew steadily as a share, reaching about a fifth of cases by 2021, and foreign-body operations also increased that year. Operations per resident dropped from the sixties to about forty, though the change missed statistical significance in this small sample. Training programmes, the authors argue, need flexible designs that protect operative experience when a crisis rearranges the caseload.
pmc-13545261:
Waad A. Aljohani headed a 2026 computer-based effort to design a vaccine against Eyach virus, a tick-borne virus linked to brain inflammation for which no specific treatment exists. Working entirely in software, the team picked promising fragments from two viral proteins, checking that each fragment looked antigenic yet unlikely to trigger allergy or toxicity. The chosen pieces were stitched into a single construct of 256 amino acids with an added immune booster.

Simulations suggested the construct was stable, water-friendly, and able to dock with two immune sensors, TLR3 and TLR4. A simulated three-dose course produced strong antibody and memory cell responses. The authors stress that laboratory and animal testing must come before any claims about real protection.
pmc-13545361:
Jue Lin and colleagues examined in 2026 how two features of the aging eye, cone photoreceptor density and choroidal thickness, change together across adulthood. Sixty-eight volunteers aged 20 to 70 received full eye examinations, including adaptive optics photography, which counts individual cone cells, and OCT scans that map the choroid, the blood-rich layer beneath the retina.

Older age groups showed fewer cones at several distances from the center of vision, and their choroids were thinner than those of the youngest group. Cone density tracked choroidal thickness at every measured position. The authors read the pattern as linked aging of the eye's blood supply and its light-sensing cells, relevant to understanding age-related visual loss.
pmc-13546561:
Lunjian Xia and colleagues developed in 2026 a model that predicts which patients with newly metastatic cancer of the gastroesophageal junction will die of their cancer within six months. That early window shapes decisions about tolerating first-line treatment and starting palliative conversations. Records came from a national registry and covered 6,564 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2021, most of them men with an average age of 64.

Six machine learning approaches were compared, and a gradient boosting model won out. Tested on patients from later years, it sorted people into low, medium, and high risk groups whose six-month death rates were about 20, 32, and 80 percent. The authors also show which factors drive each prediction, keeping the model interpretable for clinicians.
pmc-13547461:
Jia Zhang, Huaiwei Zhang, Yan Peng, and Yubin Li culture the pus from children's appendicitis cases to guide antibiotic choice, in a two thousand twenty-six children's surgery paper. Empirical treatment is often started blind, while resistance patterns shift by region.

Seventy children in a row at one hospital provided intraoperative specimens; nearly eighty-nine percent grew pathogens. Gram-negative bacteria led almost fully, led by Escherichia coli at about seventy-four percent, then Pseudomonas. Over forty percent of the Escherichia coli made extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, making common antibiotics fail, though amikacin and imipenem remained reliable. The authors use the local spectrum to argue for evidence-based empirical treatment plans in children's appendicitis.
pmc-13549961:
Onur Tunca and a large Turkish study group search kidney biopsy features that foretell decline in membranous nephropathy, in a 2026 registry study. In this disease the kidney's filters thicken under immune attack, and outcomes vary widely. The team analyzed 322 patients from a national glomerular disease registry, scoring several tissue features, most notably the share of filters already scarred solid, called the global sclerotic glomeruli ratio.

Over a median five years, about one patient in eleven suffered the combined bad outcome of halved kidney function, kidney failure, dialysis, or transplant. A scarred-filter share above roughly sixteen percent marked a dramatic split, with event rates near thirty-five percent versus barely one percent below it. That ratio, inflammatory exudative changes, and response to immune-suppressing treatment each predicted outcomes independently, holding across treatment groups.
pmc-13550261:
Samuel Tschudi and colleagues compare two plates used to fix corrective bone cuts near the knee in children, in a 2026 retrospective study from Zurich. Surgeons cut the thigh bone to straighten bowed or twisted legs, then hold it with a plate while it heals. The PediLoc blade plate was designed for hip work, but surgeons used it off-label at the knee for multi-direction corrections. The team checked whether its semi-rigid build heals bone faster than a standard locking plate.

Across 111 operations, early healing signs at six weeks appeared in thirty-nine percent of blade plate cases versus six percent with the comparison plate. By three months, consolidation reached ninety-one percent against seventy percent. Complication rates did not rise. Because the gap showed in only some scoring systems, the authors call for randomized trials to test whether the faster pictures mean faster recovery.
pmc-13550661: Christopher J Borgert, for a large group of co-authors, issued a 2026 correction to a forum article on glyphosate safety. The notice is a correction only. It asks the journal to drop one cited article from three pages of text and from the reference list. The citation details were wrong, the notice says. The item also added nothing beyond other press sources already cited. The dropped item was a Retraction Watch report on the safety article's retraction. No new data or claims appear in the notice.
pmc-13551161:
Fatih Şahin and Özlem Ulaşoğlu published a 2026 phenomenological study of digital care in psychiatric nursing at a state hospital in eastern Turkey. Electronic records and digital documentation are spreading, and the authors asked how nurses and patients experience that shift. Sixteen nurses and fourteen patients gave semi-structured interviews, analyzed through Colaizzi's seven-step method.

Three shared themes emerged: professional identity being quietly rewritten under digital pressure, a fragile therapeutic relationship in screen-mediated care, and a trust paradox around privacy and surveillance. Participants credited digital tools with efficiency and visibility, yet felt care grew more technical and empathy harder to sustain. Talk of artificial intelligence reflected expectations, the authors note, not routine use in that hospital.
pmc-13551761:
Priya Giri and Rakesh Kumar Saroj published a 2026 plan for a review of early risk calls in womb cancer. Womb cancer is rising as populations age and gain weight. Standard staging and grading miss some early return risk. New tools use biomarkers and machine learning to sharpen the call. No review had yet weighed those tools against standard methods.

The planned search covers four databases from 2010 to 2025. Two reviewers will screen and extract data on their own. A third will settle disputes. Studies must build or test a risk model in human patients. The team will judge the models on accuracy and fit. Set tools will rate bias risk and the strength of proof.
pmc-13551961:
Zeng Qiaoqian, Wu Qing, Li Bowen, Wei Qijiao, and Wang Na published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of tumor markers repurposed to detect lung scarring in rheumatoid arthritis. Interstitial lung disease is a leading killer in this arthritis, and blood markers could complement imaging. The team searched six databases to April 2025 for studies comparing marker levels between arthritis patients with and without lung disease, rating quality with a standard scale.

Thirty-six studies with 7,300 patients entered the synthesis. Eight markers, including CA125, CA199, and CEA, ran significantly higher in lung disease in the pooled results reported, and two markers, KL-6 and CYFRA21-1, discriminated the condition best. Evidence came mainly from Chinese cohorts, so the authors propose a multi-marker panel pending wider validation.
pmc-13554161:
Peerapat Lertwiram leads a seven-author team testing whether shoulder arthritis seen before surgery predicts results after rotator cuff repair in a 2026 study. One hundred fifty patients had keyhole repair between 2018 and 2023, with at least two years of follow-up. Two readers graded arthritis on MRI scans with a standard severity score, agreeing closely. Patients rated shoulder outcome on three standard scales.

Worse arthritis grades tied to modestly lower scores on two of the three scales. Damage around the tendon and lip of the socket tied to lower scores on all three scales. Biceps tendon trouble stood out as an independent drag on outcome. A cutoff score meant to flag failure sorted patients poorly. The authors say arthritis matters, but no single grade should bar repair.
pmc-13554261:
Nilofar Akbarzadeh and three colleagues make zinc oxide nanoparticles with a wormwood plant extract and test them on stomach cancer cells in a 2026 study. Stomach cancer kills many people worldwide, driving hunts for fresh treatments. The plant-based route avoids harsh chemicals while forming tiny round to many-sided particles. Tests measured killing power, cell suicide, movement, and gene activity in cancer and healthy kidney cells.

Cancer cells died at far lower doses than healthy cells, though the safety margin stayed modest. At the strongest dose, more than three fifths of cancer cells entered programmed death. Migration of cancer cells slowed sharply as well. Death-path genes switched on strongly, pointing to an inner mitochondrial route driven by the guard protein p53.
pmc-13554361:
Vellone and co-authors explored a 2026 link between apathy in mild behavioural impairment and a blood marker of Alzheimer's disease. Mild behavioural impairment means new, persistent behaviour symptoms emerging later in life, and its apathy domain may flag early dementia risk. Blood phosphorylated tau is far easier to measure than spinal fluid markers.

Using Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, the team grouped older adults as apathy type, other symptoms, or no symptoms by persistence over a year. Sixty-nine people fell in the apathy group, 112 in other symptoms, and 215 with no symptoms at all. Vellone found apathy linked to about a quarter higher blood tau levels at baseline in adjusted models. The gap persisted and grew slightly over two and three years of follow-up, while other symptom groups showed no such link.
pmc-13555161:
Wei Du leads a five-author team reviewing how age-related blood clones interact with CAR T cell therapy in a 2026 paper. With age, some blood stem cells gain mutations and expand into clones, a state called clonal hematopoiesis. This state links to inflammation and blood cancers. CAR T therapy retools a patient's own T cells to hunt cancer, and many recipients are older adults likely to carry such clones.

The review covers how common these clones are in treated patients and how they shift after therapy. It weighs their ties to inflammatory side effects and to later marrow cancers from treatment. Different mutations may steer blood growth, immune function, and how long engineered cells persist. The authors map questions for patient selection and tailored care.
pmc-13555261:
Rae-Kwon Kim, working alone, asks whether a DNA-replication protein also sustains the stem-like cells that make breast cancer dangerous. MCM2 runs high in breast tumors and predicts poor prognosis. In a triple-negative breast cancer cell line, silencing it with targeted RNA changed the cells' character across the board.

Stem cell markers fell, sphere-forming ability collapsed, and the cells regained the adhesion protein E-cadherin while losing the molecular machinery of the mesenchymal, invasive state. Migration and invasion both dropped sharply. Kim concludes that MCM2 helps maintain both cancer stemness and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, nominating it as a target against the most treatment-resistant breast cancer cells.
pmc-13555961:
Marc Kouadio N'goran leads an eight-author team evaluating story-based peer support groups for teens living with HIV in Côte d'Ivoire in a 2026 study. Many such teens struggle to accept their status and keep up daily treatment. Six facilities in Abidjan ran groups built on a ten-topic course where stories, real or invented, made lessons relatable. Forty-five interviews gathered views from teens, peer leaders, and health workers.

Groups were prized across all three audiences. Teens shared personal experiences more freely and trusted each other more deeply. Peer leaders stood as living proof that daily medicine works. Health workers reported warmer communication with their young patients. Scheduling clashes and transport costs remained the chief barriers to attendance.
pmc-13556061:
Yina Hu and ten colleagues studied in 2026 whether breathing ozone-heavy air relates to lower ovarian reserve in women seeking fertility care. Their cross-sectional study covered 8,233 women aged 20 to 45 at a reproductive medicine centre in Jiangxi between 2021 and 2023. Home addresses were matched to daily ozone maps, blood hormone levels measured the egg supply, and blood lipids were tested as a possible middle step.

Higher ozone during one key window of follicle development linked to measurably lower hormone levels, with the drop clearer in younger women than in women over 35. Cholesterol measures carried part of the association in mediation analysis, suggesting that air pollution may act partly through lipid changes. Other exposure windows showed no clear link. The authors call for cleaner air as part of protecting reproductive health.
pmc-13556561:
Tol and colleagues pooled studies on whether prolactin-raising antipsychotics raise breast cancer risk in women. Many older antipsychotics lift prolactin, a hormone tied to breast tissue growth. Other drugs in the class spare it. No guideline yet splits first drug choices by sex, so the question matters.

Fourteen studies from eight countries covered nearly three million women. Cohort studies linked prolactin-raising drugs to a risk rise of over half. Case-control studies put the rise closer to a fifth. Both designs pointed the same way. The authors say the hormone profile of a drug should weigh in prescribing for women. They call for care, not alarm, since the studies track association rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13557861:
Zihan Wang and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, a rare lung cancer whose jelly-like growth often looks like pneumonia on scans. Its vague symptoms and spread to many spots make it hard to spot early. It can be mistaken for an infection or for several distinct tumours. The review gathers what is known about its course, its scans, its tissue look, its gene changes, and how it responds to treatment.

Next to the usual form of this cancer, this type carries more KRAS gene changes and certain gene fusions. The classic EGFR changes are rarer in it. Spread through air spaces inside the lung needs care, and doctors need large tissue samples with full gene testing. Surgery serves early disease well. Drug therapy for late disease stays hard, and the role of immune therapy is unclear. The authors call for studies built for this type alone.
pmc-13558561:
Ramona Kasra Kermanshahi and four colleagues tested in 2026 whether thymoquinone, the active compound of black seed oil, can protect rat testes from a common fungicide. Chemicals in the environment link more and more often to male infertility through hormone and oxidation damage. Adult rats received the fungicide tricyclazole, thymoquinone, both, or neither for 58 days. The team measured hormones and tissue structure. They also tracked sperm production indices, gene activity by development stage, and sperm motion by computer.

The fungicide lowered testosterone, raised oxidative damage, thinned the sperm-producing lining, and stalled sperm development stages, while leaving the earliest stem cell recovery index largely intact. Adding thymoquinone countered much of that harm across the measured endpoints. The authors present the compound as a shield for the sperm-producing tissue, while noting that animal protection does not yet prove a human treatment.
pmc-13558761:
Fitri Fareez Ramli and six colleagues ran in 2026 a small randomised trial of ebselen, a compound mimicking a protective enzyme, added to standard antidepressants in patients who had not responded adequately. Earlier work in healthy volunteers showed the drug brightens emotional processing and shifts brain chemistry. Thirty participants, as designed, took ebselen or placebo twice daily for seven days while brain scans at rest mapped how strongly brain regions fluctuate together.

One connection, between a frontal control region and the cerebellum, moved more under ebselen than placebo before statistical corrections, and effects inside visual networks appeared as well. None of the changes survived correction for the many comparisons performed. The authors report the short course as producing no significant connectivity change. They blame the brief duration and the small, mixed sample for the weak signal. Longer trials remain the open question.
pmc-13559561:
Huan Liu and colleagues profile HMGA1, a chromatin protein that switches genes on, across many cancers, with deep focus on pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Their 2026 study merges public transcriptomic, genetic, methylation, and single-cell data, then tests the protein in pancreatic cancer cells. HMGA1 has been tied to tumor spread and stem-like behavior, yet its wider pattern stayed unclear.

The protein ran high in most tumor types, and high levels matched worse survival in several cancers. Inside pancreatic tumors it concentrated in malignant epithelial cells and rose as cells moved along a path scored for stemness. Silencing HMGA1 in the lab cut the cells' migration and invasion sharply. Low methylation at the gene's promoter tracked with its activation. The authors build an association-based model linking this activation to a remodeled, suppressive tumor environment, supported by their cell experiments.
pmc-13559661:
Long and colleagues published a 2026 study on a blood score that forecasts chemo success in breast cancer. The HALP score mixes blood counts and a nutrition protein into one number. It reflects immunity, nutrition, and inflammation in a single cheap index. The team studied 314 patients who had chemo before surgery.

After balancing the groups, 226 patients fed the main model checks. Low HALP scores halved the odds of full tumor clearance at surgery. A hormone-related tumor trait, HER2, raised clearance odds fivefold instead. Higher scores also tracked with longer survival without disease return. Their chart tool may help tailor treatment plans before chemo starts. Outside hospitals must still test the chart before wide use.
pmc-13560261:
Ahmad Sani Nurulhuda and colleagues ran a randomized trial testing whether a week of eye-mask and earplug use improves glucose levels in sleep-deprived pregnant women. Their 2026 trial enrolled 240 women at a Malaysian university hospital between July 2021 and August 2022, all sleeping seven hours or less nightly. Half received the sleep aids for the week before their routine diabetes screening test.

Wrist actigraphs tracked actual sleep while glucose was measured fasting and two hours after the test drink. Neither glucose reading differed meaningfully between the groups. Total night sleep also matched almost exactly, at about 347 minutes against 349 in the reported means. Secondary measures of waking after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, and self-rated quality likewise showed no significant gaps. The authors conclude that one week of these aids neither lengthens measured sleep nor lowers glucose in this population.
pmc-13560761:
Jackson Woodrow and seven co-authors compare lower limb soft tissue injury and repeat surgery rates in patients with anorexia or bulimia versus matched controls. The data came from a nameless claims database. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Tens of thousands of patients with each eating disorder were matched to like controls by propensity scores. Primary and repeat surgeries for knee and ankle ligament work and meniscus care were tracked by procedure codes. Patients over forty or with short follow up were left out. Bulimia patients showed higher risk for several injuries, among them knee ligament tears and ankle sprains, the authors report.
pmc-13561161:
Adam Lu, Seyed Ourang, and Jeffrey Moore study rhythm control in the rodent brain in a 2026 paper. Rats sweep their whiskers to feel their surroundings, adjusting the sweep range to the task. Whisking is driven by a brainstem rhythm circuit that is linked to breathing. How the sweep size is set was unknown. Their idea borrows from coupled oscillators in engineering.

Re-analysis of rat behavior data showed whisking signatures of amplification through locking with sniffing, the fast breathing mode. A network model then showed sweep size can be set by shifting the rhythm's own frequency relative to sniffing, a detuning effect. The authors propose detuning as a general gain control trick in nervous systems.
pmc-13561661:
Koichi Kodama, Kosei Katayama, and Takuji Hirose test a chemical helper for sorting mirror-image forms of acids, in two thousand twenty-six. Many drug-like acids come as two mirror forms that must be separated. One common trick forms salts with a helper, since the two salts dissolve at unlike rates.

Their helper failed for some acid families, including a well-known one. It worked well for others, such as tropic acid and a set of halogen-bearing acids. Its strengths filled gaps left by a close cousin helper with a flipped shape. Crystal studies of the less soluble salts showed the bonding patterns and packing behind the sorting.
pmc-13562061:
Ragavendirane and colleagues fuse multi-focus photos into one sharp image with fuzzy logic. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-six addresses a common photography problem. Different shots focus at different depths, leaving parts blurred. Border zones between sharp and blurred areas are genuinely uncertain.

Their method converts images into an intuitionistic fuzzy form first. That form tracks both belonging and non-belonging degrees. A block-based rule then assembles the sharpest regions. Scores for detail, gradient, and spatial frequency beat rival methods. The optimised partitioning handles focus transitions more gracefully. Microscopes, phones, and inspection cameras all face this fusion task. Cleaner fused images help both humans and algorithms.
pmc-13562261:
Marije Harmsen and three colleagues collect user needs for an emotion-aware robot meant for long-term care. Their 2026 study runs thirteen focus groups and twenty interviews with care receivers, family caregivers, and staff, in two rounds. The group held people with dementia and people with learning disabilities.

Needs grouped into basics such as sturdiness and ease of use, wished-for jobs like company and backing for independence, and look-and-feel wishes favoring personal tweaks and simple controls. The robot was greeted as a source of structure and company for residents. Worries held on about losing warm human contact and about trust when the machine acts alone. Take-up that works, people said, needs honest talk, focused training, and a phased rollout. The authors frame a core tension between support that boosts self-rule and the human warmth care is meant to carry.
pmc-13564361:

pmc-13567061:
He Huang and three colleagues published a methods study in two thousand twenty-six on machine learning for rubber-modified asphalt. pmc-13569461:
Svitlana V. Bach and colleagues characterize, in a 2026 study of human brain tissue and cultured nerve cells, two newly found genes sitting beside BDNF, a gene central to neuron growth and learning. pmc-13572361:

pmc-13572461:
Canan Aydınlıoğlu, with nine colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of wild strawberry tree fruit in Hatay Province, Türkiye. pmc-13572761:

pmc-13574761:
Shabana S and Sumit Kumar Jindal present a 2026 design study for a micro pressure sensor that touches down twice as pressure climbs. pmc-13576261:
Zhao and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction model for a danger sign in colon cancer using spectral CT scans. Five dynamic measures differed between patients with and without vein invasion and stayed independent predictors in the final model. The nomogram discriminated well, with accuracy scores high in training and internal test groups and solid in the external group. pmc-13578761:
Claire Short and Rebecca Calisi tested horse-assisted activities with teenagers in two thousand twenty-six. Animal interaction programs aim to lift emotional wellbeing. pmc-13578861:

pmc-13579561:
Jingchen Shi and colleagues thread ring shaped sugar molecules onto plastic chains at factory scale, in a 2026 study. The rings, spun from starch, can lock along a chain like beads, and the threaded bundles make plastics tougher and easier to blend. pmc-13580361:
Hye Been Kim, Eun Su Kang, Dong Chan Son, Ju Eun Jang, and Hee-Young Gil publish the full chloroplast genome of a Korean island plant, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13580461:
Khaled Abu-Amero, Shereen Abualkhair, Hajar AlOtaibi, and Gorka Sesma published an updated review in twenty twenty-six on the genetics of primary open-angle glaucoma, the commonest glaucoma type. pmc-13581861:
Zhihong Li and co-authors pull as one, in a meta-analysis, past work on how leadership styles shape safety performance in workplaces where risk is high. Their 2026 study draws on past results that did not agree, and that had not been reviewed in a counted way.

The frame took in one hundred two studies. They held more than one hundred thousand people in all, and came out before 2025. The team puts the work forth as the first check to join twenty-one leadership styles as one.
pmc-13583061:
Huang and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-six on a ginger compound that fights acute myeloid leukemia. Computer docking points to two proteins as likely targets.

pmc-13584561:
Dilyara Sagandykova and colleagues review what can go wrong underground when carbon dioxide is pumped in for storage. Storing captured CO2 deep in rock is a key climate plan, yet the rock itself can be damaged in ways that slow injection and threaten the seal. Acid formed by the gas can eat minerals loose, clays can swell, and microbes can gum up flow paths. The second half of the review weighs lab tests, computer models, and new watching tools for spotting damage early. The authors say long studies under real conditions are still badly needed.
pmc-13585161:
Laura W. D. Knijff and colleagues study donated kidneys that start work slowly after transplant in this 2026 paper. All the kidneys came from donors whose hearts had stopped, a group prone to delayed graft function, where the new organ needs support for days or weeks. pmc-13585861:
Jiming Jiang wrote a 2026 review on chromosome painting in plants, a method that lights up whole chromosomes in color. The method began in mammals nearly forty years ago. There it became a core tool for naming chromosomes and tracing how genomes change over time.

pmc-13586461:

pmc-13586761:

pmc-13587561:

pmc-13588161:

pmc-13590161:

pmc-13590461:

pmc-13591661:

pmc-13591961:

pmc-13592561:

pmc-13592661:

pmc-13595161:

pmc-13595761:

pmc-13597061:

pmc-13598561:

pmc-13599561:

pmc-13600061:

pmc-13601061:

pmc-13604761:

pmc-13605061:

pmc-13605661:

pmc-13606461:

pmc-13610261:

pmc-13610761:

pmc-13611061:
Szilárd László Takács, Konrád Kajdy, and Emanuel Puschita study how well autoencoders spot oddities in FM radio spectrum recordings. Monitoring the crowded airwaves means scanning waterfall images of frequency against time for rare anomalies. Their autoencoders learned only from normal broadcasts in the 87.5 to 108 megahertz band, so anything they failed to reconstruct could be flagged. The team varied the whole pipeline: normalization, image resolution, network depth, latent size, symmetry, and scoring.

More complex networks did not detect better. The best development setup reached an F1 score of 91.4 percent on labeled development data. On a held-out test set, performance dropped and the ranking of setups changed, warning against crowning a winner from development numbers. A controlled ablation showed the scoring formula itself changes how distinct oddities look. The study is pipeline-level guidance: preprocessing and scoring choices deserve the same respect as architecture.
pmc-13611361:
Chen, Wu, Chen, and Lin present a wearable rehabilitation system based on edge computing, in work from twenty twenty-six. A Colles fracture is a wrist break from falling on an outstretched hand. After surgery, patients need long self rehabilitation to restore wrist function.

Traditional rehab relies on medical staff and lacks real time feedback or progress tracking. Poor home practice can even worsen the condition. Their wearable system processes data on the device itself, which improves portability and response speed. Guided, tracked home rehab could raise recovery quality while cutting clinic visits.
pmc-13611661:
He Huang and three colleagues published a computing study in two thousand twenty-six on laser scanning in bad weather. Self-driving systems use LiDAR, which maps scenes with laser pulses. Rain, snow, and fog scatter those pulses and confuse scene labelling.

Their system, WeatherMamba, learns from clear-weather data yet aims to work in unseen storms. It judges how trusty each laser point looks, using signal strength and nearby point density. Points judged shaky get smaller corrections, without needing any weather report at run time. On standard test sets the system ranked near the top while using fewer resources than a rival design. Ablated versions scored worse, which supports the value of each added part.
pmc-13612061:
Neslihan Ölmez and seven co-authors pool trials of organic acids in feed for broiler chickens hit by coccidiosis. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Coccidiosis is a gut disease of poultry that cuts growth. Feed acids are one low-drug way to blunt it.

They pool eleven controlled studies. Acids show no firm gain in weight growth or feed efficiency, and spread across studies is wide. Gut lesion scores are lower with acids, and shed parasite eggs drop too. Subgroup hints vary by acid kind, worm species, and trial span, but rest on few studies. Proof grade is rated very low for all outcomes, so firm claims must wait for better trials.
pmc-13612861:
Yaghoubi Naei and six co-authors reviewed in twenty twenty-six whether tumor cells found in the blood could guide the use of antibody-drug conjugates, precision medicines that deliver poison straight to cancer cells. These drugs only work when the tumor wears the target the antibody seeks, and targets vary and shift over time.

A needle biopsy samples one spot once, while blood draws can be repeated and catch cells shed from many sites. The review weighs trial evidence for steering several cancer treatments by these circulating cells. It also examines how artificial intelligence sharpens the hunt for the rare cells and might one day recommend treatments. The authors are candid that direct proof for guiding this drug class is still thin. They propose practical frameworks for clinics to use the tests now, while calling for proper prospective trials.
pmc-13614661:
Carlo Guastamacchia and colleagues study how the arrangement of muscle fibres shapes the beating of a mouse heart in computer models. Heart muscle fibres run in organised sheets, and their direction decides how electric signals and squeezing forces spread. Doctors cannot measure fibre direction in a living heart, so model makers usually fake it with rule-based patterns. This team built a detailed two-chamber model using real fibre maps captured with fine optical imaging.

A smoothing trick let them separate the broad sweep of fibre direction from small local tangles, called disarray. Comparing the true map, the smoothed map, and a rule-based map shows which features of a heartbeat come from gross anatomy and which from fine disorder. The lesson guides builders of human heart models, where only rough fibre guesses are ever available.
pmc-13616361:
Zhejun Hong and colleagues review how ultrathin sheets of post-transition metals can be grown on the surface of liquid metals. The chemistry at that liquid skin decides the crystal quality of the result. A liquid metal's surface is atomically smooth and forms a self-limiting skin, offering a clean birthplace for two-dimensional materials wanted in sensors, optics, and catalysts. Growth there is governed by tangled factors: redox reactions, alloy balance, atom migration, and the gases above the melt.

Those factors set the sheet's phase, its exact recipe, and its burden of defects, from missing atoms to torn patches. The review sorts which conditions breed which flaws and which uses tolerate them. Growers of two-dimensional materials gain a map from melt conditions to final quality, instead of discovering defects after the sheet is made.
pmc-13617061:
Li and six co-authors link cord blood traits to first gut germs in small-born babes in this twenty twenty-six study. Such babes face high risks at birth and life-long fuel ills past it. How womb growth, blood traits, and first germs tie was not yet mapped.

Inside, more than one hundred term babes split into small and fair size groups at birth. Small babes held far less of a key growth scent in their cord blood. That scent rose with birth weight and length in the checks the team ran. Their blood trait maps split clean from fair babes, with fat traits thinned. First stool germs split too, with two foe types high in small babes.
pmc-13617261:
Somayeh Haji Ahmadi and three colleagues review machine learning and deep learning tools that automatically outline cervical cancer on MRI scans. Doctors rely on MRI for staging and treatment planning, yet drawing tumor boundaries by hand is slow and varies between readers. The reviewers searched six databases through December 2025 and judged study quality with standard diagnostic accuracy tools.

Thirty studies qualified, covering tumors, high-risk treatment volumes, and organs at risk. Deep learning models, especially U-Net variants, ordinary convolutional networks, and newer transformer designs, performed best. Their overlap scores ranged from roughly six tenths to over nine tenths depending on target and scan protocol. Risk of bias raised some concerns, mainly over patient selection and weak outside testing, and overall certainty was rated low. The authors call for multicenter studies with shared protocols before routine clinical use.
pmc-13617361:
Siting Yang and six colleagues review botanical extracts as skin-lightening agents, sorting the findings by how plant compounds change skin color. Skin color is set by melanin production, pigment transfer between cells, oxidative stress, sun exposure, and skin renewal, so plant ingredients can act at several points. The review weighs how well they work, how they act, and how safe they are across published studies.

Six pathways structure the findings: shielding against ultraviolet and environmental damage, tuning a master pigment switch called MITF, blocking the enzyme tyrosinase, slowing pigment transfer, adjusting redox chemistry, and speeding epidermal turnover. Polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, and alkaloids recur as the active families. Much evidence still comes from cell and animal work rather than human trials, and safety worries include killing pigment cells and patchy lightening. The authors call for standardized extracts, testing by mechanism, and proper trials in people.
pmc-13617761:
Na Zhang and eleven colleagues copy the skin of the loach, a slippery bottom-dwelling fish, to cut underwater drag on vehicles and ships. Their surface combines V-shaped microgrooves with microbubbles, aiming to hold a stable gas film between hull and water so the craft slides on air rather than dragging against liquid. Computer simulations explored how bubble size and concentration affect the effect.

Simulations found drag reduction near thirty percent at the best bubble settings, mostly by lowering pressure drag. The team then fabricated a flexible, strongly water-repelling version of the surface, on which water beads at a very high contact angle, and tested it in a flow channel. There it achieved about thirty-one percent drag reduction at roughly four and a half meters per second. The authors present the groove-and-bubble pairing as a practical strategy for saving energy in underwater transport.
pmc-13618061:
Steve Keyrane Kuida Tchikapa and six colleagues recycle oyster shell waste into porous phosphate-based geopolymers, cement-like binders made here from volcanic slag. Calcined shells supply calcium and promote pore formation, replacing part of the slag at levels from zero to fifteen percent by weight, with phosphoric acid as activator. The team tracked phases, microstructure, and strength with diffraction, spectroscopy, microscopy, and physical testing.

Acid strength and calcium availability jointly steered the chemistry: calcium from shells precipitated mainly as monetite, a calcium phosphate, while acid activation built the continuous binding matrix around it. Five percent shell content struck the best balance, giving an even pore structure while holding compressive strength close to the shell-free reference at about twenty-two megapascals. Higher shell shares brought patchier structure, surface efflorescence, and strength loss.
