The authors frame the route as waste valorization that turns two problem materials into functional porous products.
pmc-13618261:
DongHwan Oh and colleagues report a catalyst study, published in 2026. It removes the need for platinum in making propylene from propane. Propylene is a core feedstock for chemicals. A gallia-alumina catalyst splits the first bonds well. Leftover hydrogen atoms join into hydrogen gas too slowly, though. Platinum is usually added despite its cost and wear problems.

Adding magnesium into the catalyst created active oxygen sites. They sit in the crystal lattice. They let hydrogen form directly on the oxide surface. Light-based tests, isotope tests, and maths all showed faster hydrogen release. Surface hydrogen drained away quickly in heat-light readings. The bottleneck was removed without precious metal.
pmc-13618461:
Yurim Lee and five colleagues review wearable thermoelectric devices, solid-state gadgets that can cool or warm the body directly and can also harvest electricity from the temperature gap between skin and air. The catch is mechanical: conventional devices are built from rigid parts that cannot follow the body's curves and motion, opening gaps at the skin and peeling apart. That wrecks both thermal and electrical performance.

The review surveys structural and material strategies that make devices compliant and skin-conformal, then turns to performance boosters such as better electrical contacts and deliberate heat-flow design. Applications span personal thermal management, energy harvesting for small electronics, and sensing. The authors frame these devices as body-integrated systems rather than isolated generators, arguing that skin contact, stretch, interfaces, and heat paths deserve the same engineering attention as the thermoelectric materials themselves.
pmc-13619061:
Dieter Riemann and seven colleagues review the risks of benzodiazepine sleeping pills taken for more than three months, in a 2026 analysis with meta-analyses where data allowed. Guidelines warn against use beyond four weeks because of dependence and side effects. Yet long prescriptions remain common. Twenty-seven studies from 1987 to 2023 met their criteria, and five outcomes, insomnia severity, sleep quality, falls, depression, and anxiety, could be pooled.

Long-term users slept worse than healthy sleepers but better than unmedicated insomnia patients, a pattern reflecting who gets prescribed these drugs. Fall risk did not differ between users and non-users. Depression and anxiety ran higher in users than in healthy sleepers. The reviewers stress how few such studies exist. The available evidence suggests extended use may erode sleep, mental health, and quality of life. Their conclusion backs guideline advice: keep courses short, with behavioral therapy and safer alternatives first.
pmc-13619161:
Giulia Gaglianone Lemos and ten colleagues describe an unusual feeding site for biting midges found during bird rescue work in southern Brazil. Teams from a beach monitoring project examined weakened kelp gulls and cormorants brought in from two coastal towns. Inside the birds' airways they found midges of the species Leptoconops floridensis, along with a few Culicoides, feeding within the respiratory system itself.

About eighteen percent of the kelp gulls and sixteen percent of the cormorants carried the insects internally. Kelp gulls made up most of the affected birds, and the windpipe, air sacs, and lungs were the sites hit most often. The authors present the finding as the first record of these blood-feeding flies living and feeding inside a bird's breathing passages, a detail that matters for judging disease risk in coastal wildlife.
pmc-13620161:
Jie Li and eleven colleagues uncovered a chain of signals that explains why teeth erupt late in a genetic bone disorder. People missing one working copy of the RUNX2 gene develop cleidocranial dysplasia, whose signs include delayed tooth eruption. Working through the gum line requires bone-eating cells, called osteoclasts, to clear a path through the jaw.

Mice with one faulty copy showed weak osteoclast formation, less jaw bone removal, and late molar eruption, matching the human picture. The team traced the fault to a long non-coding RNA that RUNX2 switches on. That RNA ties up a second protein and thereby protects a receptor message the osteoclasts need. Mice lacking the RNA copied the eruption defect, while lowering the tied-up protein rescued bone cell formation even in a bone-loss model. The authors name the RNA a possible drug target for jaw remodeling problems.
pmc-13620261:
Yinbo Jiang and four colleagues tested a virus-vectored vaccine against the syphilis bacterium in mice and rabbits. No vaccine exists to stop syphilis passing from mother to fetus, which causes stillbirths and newborn deaths worldwide. Their vaccine makes the body produce antibodies against one outer membrane protein of Treponema pallidum, the spiral bacterium behind the disease.

Vaccinated animals mounted strong antibody responses plus a helper-cell response of the antibody-supporting type. Those antibodies blocked the bacterium from sticking to cells, helped scavenger cells eat it, and killed it directly. Challenged rabbits developed milder sores and carried far fewer bacteria in their tissues. Tissue moved from treated rabbits failed to start infection in fresh animals, a classic test of real protection. The authors back the candidate for further development toward preventing congenital syphilis.
pmc-13620861:
Md Fuad Al Fidah, Sayeda Sumaiya Efa, Md Ridwan Islam, and Md Abdullah Saeed Khan pooled research on whether people in South Asia would pay for health insurance. Care in the region runs mostly on out-of-pocket spending, which pushes families into poverty when illness strikes. The team gathered seventeen studies from five countries and assessed their quality before combining the results.

Across the pooled studies, about seventy-two percent of participants said they were willing to pay for insurance. Bangladeshi studies reported higher willingness than Indian ones. Willingness tracked a familiar set of traits: age, sex, schooling, family size, income and social position, occupation, and how much a household already used and spent on care. Results varied enormously between studies, so the authors warn the single number hides real differences and call for stronger local research.
pmc-13621661:
Jiahao Gao and seven colleagues compared two pelvic bone surgeries for children born with dislocated, poorly socketed hips, in 2026. The Salter and Pemberton osteotomies both reshape the pelvis to cover the thigh bone's head, and both work, yet complications still occur. The team reviewed seventy-two patients operated between 2011 and 2018, following them at least five years, and introduced a congruity index: how much of the ball the socket covers.

Sixty-five children completed follow-up. Salter patients ended with a higher congruity index and better satisfactory rates on both X-ray appearance and clinical function grading, roughly nine in ten against roughly eight in ten. The congruity index itself carried prognostic weight: poorer coverage predicted both blood-supply damage to the femoral head and worse functional grades. The authors conclude both operations serve children well, and the coverage percentage can warn surgeons which hips need closest watching afterward.
pmc-13623061:
Peter J Gianaros wrote a 2026 Scientific Spotlight asking whether strong blood pressure reactions to stress can, over a lifetime, damage the brain. Some people respond to mental stress with large, lasting rises in blood pressure. Those reactions are known to raise the risk of hypertension and heart disease, and the essay explores a further path into stroke and dementia.

Gianaros pulls together early evidence linking stress reactivity to white matter lesions, stroke risk, and blood vessel traits tied to dementia. He frames the proposed route as interoceptive, meaning the brain senses signals rising from the body, and names the idea the Neurovascular Burden of Stress hypothesis. Repeated pressure surges might slowly injure the brain's small vessels, which then undermines thinking in old age. The piece is a call for a new wave of studies to test the pathway and find points where intervention could protect brain health.
pmc-13623361:
Alinne de Santo Nascimento and colleagues test the link between thyroid hormones and anaemia in a large Brazilian adult cohort. Anaemia means having too little haemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in blood, and thyroid trouble has long been suspected of lowering it. The data come from the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Adult Health, gathered between 2008 and 2010 across six sites.

After exclusions, 13,247 civil servants aged thirty-five to seventy-four were analysed. Higher levels of free thyroxine, one of the two main thyroid hormones, went with steadily lower odds of anaemia across most of the hormone range. The pattern held for men and women alike. The other hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone, showed no link with anaemia at all. The authors say the results single out thyroxine rather than the stimulating hormone, and they hold after accounting for social and clinical differences between participants.
pmc-13623761:
Mehdi Duyan and co-authors published a 2026 study of how women new to fitness change in mind and identity as they train. Gym memberships have grown in recent years, yet women take part in sports at rates that lag behind men. Studies of the whole arc of a woman just starting out were few. The team set out to fill that gap with close reading.

The group was sixteen women at women-only gyms in one city, each training for two months or more. Three in four had trained for a year or less. Their accounts were collected in written form, not on tape, for privacy. Four themes came out: what drove the start, a shift in how body and self are seen, the two faces of the people around them, and change made real in daily life. Training, the team finds, means far more than physical work.
pmc-13625361:
Cunxin Lin leads a large team, publishing in 2026, that watches brain rhythms flicker in people with migraine. Using magnetoencephalography, a sensitive magnetic scan of brain activity, they compared patients whose attacks come in episodes, patients whose migraine turned chronic, and healthy controls. A modeling method sorted the signals into six recurring brain modes, spanning vision, hearing, movement, and the resting default networks, during rest and during touch stimulation.

Episodic patients held the vision mode longer and switched modes less often than controls at rest, while chronic patients switched the vision mode faster than episodic ones. The hearing mode behaved differently again, and longer illness tracked with quicker hearing-mode turnover under stimulation. Such timing signatures may reveal how occasional attacks harden into daily disease.
pmc-13625461:
Kathleen Grueter and co-authors try to sharpen engineered immune cells against head and neck cancer. Their T-cells carry a receptor aimed at EGFRvIII, a tumor-only variant of a growth receptor, yet that target appears sparsely and unevenly on these tumors, blunting the attack. Full-length EGFR is plentiful on the same tumors but also sits on healthy tissue, so it cannot trigger killing safely. The team added a second, silent receptor that merely grips EGFR without firing.

In dish tests, killer cells bearing both receptors destroyed more tumor cells in several combinations, with the biggest boost where the firing receptor alone had been weakest. Microscope work watched the immune contact point form between cell and target. Extra grip without extra signal, the results hint, may rescue target-poor tumors for cell therapy.
pmc-13626361:
Sahar Khademioore leads a team setting out the plan for a review of eye scans that might forecast sight after macular hole surgery. A full-thickness macular hole tears the center of the retina, blurring and warping central vision, and surgery closes most holes, yet how well patients see afterward varies widely. Their protocol will search four databases for studies linking pre-surgery features on optical coherence tomography, a layered retina scan, to vision at three to twenty-four months.

Planned pooling uses random-effects models, and the certainty of the findings will be graded by the GRADE system. The goal is practical: sharper counseling before surgery, and matching technique to the scan pattern each eye presents. As a protocol, the report promises a map of what is known rather than new answers, and it registers the methods before results can bias them.
pmc-13627961:
Sammy Eden and four colleagues interviewed twenty people with bipolar disorder about how caffeine affects their moods. Bipolar disorder is a long-term condition that swings between low and high mood states, and caffeine is a daily habit that might help or harm that balance.

Using a method that studies personal experience in depth, the team found one theme running through most accounts: caffeine use is a balancing act. Participants described coffee as a small helper during low moods, yet also linked it to racing thoughts and poor concentration when their mood ran high. The authors argue that patients and clinicians both need clearer knowledge about these trade-offs.
pmc-13629161:
Lubna Shawar, Thomas Piper, and John Eiler measure isotope patterns inside steroid fragments. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-six uses Orbitrap mass spectrometry. Standard steroid testing gives one average isotope value per compound. That average can be inconclusive when values overlap natural ranges.

Anti-doping labs face exactly that overlap problem. The new method reads isotope values for several fragments separately. Volunteers received known androgen doses for controlled comparison. Fragment patterns revealed responses hidden in the bulk average. Some fragments changed over time in distinct ways. Those shifts may reflect changing metabolic routes in the body. Multi-part fingerprints could sharpen doping tests for urinary steroids.
pmc-13629261:
C. Walters and two colleagues mapped a decade of research on moral distress among emergency department nurses, the anguish of knowing the right action while being blocked from taking it. Their 2026 scoping review searched four databases for studies from 2015 to 2025 and organised the findings thematically.

Four themes organised the literature: what contributes to the distress, the situations that trigger it, its impact, and the support strategies tried. Organisational constraints and impersonal, rushed care recurred as causes, with effects on well-being, job satisfaction, and care quality. Most studies merely described the problem; few tested interventions, and none followed nurses over time. The authors call for intervention trials and longitudinal work to guide leaders trying to stem emergency nurse attrition.
pmc-13629761:
Bohua Zhang and four colleagues reviewed 123 dialysis patients whose tunneled chest catheters had failed because the large central veins had blocked, a severe complication of long-term catheter use. Treated between 2017 and 2025, the patients received either a catheter exchange or a new catheter at a different site, often combined with balloon widening or stenting of the vein.

The commonest blockage sat in the brachiocephalic vein, followed by the vena cava. Treated catheters lasted a median of about two years, though nearly four in ten patients needed another intervention. Clots in the heart's upper chamber and protein sheaths around the catheter predicted shorter survival. The authors judge exchange plus vessel treatment safe and effective, with direct vena cava puncture as a salvage route.
pmc-13630861:
Selvi Ince and colleagues linked disrupted TIE-2 signalling to leaky brain vessels and Alzheimer's damage. Poor brain blood flow and vessel leakiness track cognitive decline and amyloid and tau spread, yet human vessel-signal evidence was thin. Their 2026 study measured TIE-1 and TIE-2 in spinal fluid, blood, and postmortem parietal cortex across control, Alzheimer's, and vascular dementia groups.

Soluble TIE-2 ran high in spinal fluid from Alzheimer's-marker-positive people, tracking tau, leakiness, injury, and inflammation. Brain-tissue TIE-2 fell in early-intermediate tangle stages and further in vessel-rich fractions at end stage, tracking poor perfusion and leakiness. Ince and colleagues describe a mirror pattern: fluid TIE-2 up, tissue TIE-2 down.
pmc-13630961:
Jordan E Jackson and five colleagues asked what is lost when surgeons skip sentinel lymph node biopsy in early breast cancer. Their study appeared in 2026. Skipping the procedure spares women surgical side effects. Recent trials support skipping it. Yet node results also gate access to modern add-on drugs and partial breast radiation. So the study checked 1,194 women who would have qualified for skipping.

About eleven percent in fact held positive nodes. The yield climbed steeply in younger women. It also climbed with larger tumours and higher grades. It fell to roughly two percent in women over sixty with small, low-grade cancers. The authors argue for a risk-adapted policy. Skipping looks safe in carefully chosen older patients. It looks costly in younger ones.
pmc-13631061:
Yanshu Li and nine co-authors report a light driven way to attach a trifluoroacetyl group to nitrogen ring compounds that lack electrons, a long hard task in chemistry. The free radical involved is unstable and its charge clashes with such targets. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Under visible light, the new method needs no pre work on the target, no pricey catalyst, no transition metals, and no extra additives. It worked across a range of ring types, from pyridine to chromone, and bore many side groups well. The authors frame it as a fit for late stage tweaks of active drug like molecules, in line with green chemistry aims.
pmc-13631361:
Rachel D Flynn and six colleagues describe wheat plants that tolerate a major insect pest so well that being attacked raised their harvest, published in 2026. Hessian fly larvae usually kill or stunt wheat, and breeding has chased outright resistance, which pests eventually evolve around. Tolerance, letting the plant shrug off feeding, is the understudied alternative.

In two elite durum cultivars, most larvae survived feeding, yet infested plants yielded about fourteen percent more than uninfested ones, driven by survival of the attacked stems themselves. The plants sat physiologically between resistant and susceptible types, and higher caffeic acid levels tracked the tolerance. The authors offer the first integrated portrait of the trait, arguing it could protect yields without pressuring the pest to adapt.
pmc-13631561:
Miao Sun, Dengju Li, and Jia Wei review drugs that block Bruton's tyrosine kinase, a switch inside B cells. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. The switch relays signals from many receptors and steers B cell growth, movement, and inflammation.

Blocking it has reshaped care for B cell cancers. The drug family now spans several designs: firm-binding, loose-binding, dual-target, and degrader types. The review covers how the switch works, how the drugs are classed, and how cancers escape them. It also weighs pairings with cell therapy, checkpoint drugs, and other targeted agents, plus stem cell transplant. Uses beyond cancer are charted too. The authors draw the whole arc into one reference.
pmc-13632661:
Hamid Abbasi and four colleagues examined whether the sources of protein building blocks in food relate to epilepsy in Iran. Amino acids come from both animal and plant foods, and their role in epilepsy is unclear. The team used a large Iranian cohort based in Sabzevar. They compared one hundred twelve people who had epilepsy with nearly four thousand who did not, using detailed food questionnaires to sort eating patterns.

Statistical sorting produced two patterns, one dominated by animal sources and one by plant sources. People with epilepsy ate less of every amino acid measured. The plant pattern told the strongest story, since those following it most closely had far lower odds of having epilepsy. The animal pattern showed no clear link once other factors were counted. Because everyone was measured once, the authors caution that only follow-up studies can show whether diet itself changes epilepsy risk.
pmc-13633161:
Arwa Hosni and five co-authors run a trial on jaw fracture repair in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Breaks at the angle of the lower jaw are common and tricky to fix. One group of patients received a custom 3D plate, planned on a computer and placed with a patient-specific guide. The other group received the standard Champy technique, a long-used plating method. Twenty-four patients were split between the groups by chance.

The team judged how exact the guided method was and how well chewing function returned. Virtual planning let the plate fit the bone before surgery began. Surgery through the mouth also leaves no skin scar. The trial weighs precision tools against a trusted classic. Oral surgeons planning fracture care are the main readers.
pmc-13633961:
Ayse Tugba Eminsoy Avci and colleagues tested root canal cleaning in two thousand twenty-six. Calcium hydroxide paste must leave canals before filling. Residue hides in hard-to-reach grooves. Extracted human teeth provided the test setup. Grooves were cut and filled under standard conditions. Two rinse solutions and three activation methods competed.

Sound and laser activation were compared with plain needles. One disinfectant solution clearly outperformed the classic partner. Ultrasound activation plus that solution cleaned best overall. Differences between groups were strongly significant. The winning pair beat needle rinsing with the same solution. Dentists gain a concrete protocol upgrade. Cleaner canals should heal more predictably.
pmc-13634461:
Hritul Karim and five co-authors test two scores that predict survival after a heart stops inside a hospital. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such forecasts guide hard conversations about whether resuscitation should be attempted at all.

Swedish registry data covered six hundred forty-seven arrests across three hospitals; five hundred one cases qualified. Twenty-eight percent survived with good brain function. The PIHCA score discriminated slightly better than GO-FAR 2, though the gap was not significant. Calibration told the reverse story, with GO-FAR 2 tracking real rates more faithfully. The authors conclude neither score dominates, and decision aids should report both discrimination and calibration honestly.
pmc-13634561:
Isaac Rodríguez-Rovira led a 2026 mouse study that untangles how two elastic fiber proteins shape heart and vessel disease when both are faulty at once. Marfan syndrome, tied to fibrillin-1, widens the aortic root, while Williams-Beuren syndrome, tied to elastin loss, narrows the aorta above the valve. The team crossed mice carrying each single defect to make double-heterozygous animals, then tracked growth, aortic size, blood pressure, and heart function.

The double-mutant mice developed aortic root widening matching Marfan mice, with a thicker vessel wall and thinner elastic fibers like the Williams-Beuren model. They also developed the hypertension seen in the elastin model but not in Marfan mice, while heart pumping was equally reduced in all three mutant groups. Several stress markers that rose in single mutants normalized in double mutants.
pmc-13637361:
Fang Wei led a 2026 survey of what heart failure patients know, feel, and do about cardiac rehabilitation, a structured exercise and support program with strong evidence behind it. Participation remains low worldwide, and the team wanted to know where the chain breaks. They surveyed 589 patients at a hospital affiliated with Guizhou Medical University in late 2025, scoring knowledge, attitudes, and practices, then modeled how those pieces connect.

Average knowledge was moderate, attitudes were generally positive, and practices were relatively active. Modeling showed knowledge lifting attitudes, attitudes lifting practice, and knowledge reaching practice mainly through attitudes, with a surprising direct negative link from knowledge to practice once attitudes were accounted for. The authors read this as proof that information alone does not change behavior. Program designers get a practical steer: pair education with work on attitudes and real-life barriers, or knowledge gains may stall before they become action.
pmc-13643161:
Jens Hainmueller and David D Laitin present a meta-analysis of whether gaining citizenship raises immigrants' earnings, the so-called naturalization premium. People who naturalize differ from those who do not, so separating citizenship's own effect from self-selection is the core problem.

Across sixty preferred estimates from thirty-one studies, the average premium sat near ten percent. Credibility varied sharply by design: the randomized lottery study found almost no effect, a cutoff-based study found a clear gain, and instrumental-variable studies gave the largest, unstable numbers. The authors warn that observational averages should not be sold to policymakers as causal forecasts.
pmc-13643261:
Anando Sen and five colleagues present a study that builds machine learning models to predict death from any cause in people who have both type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. That combination multiplies risk, yet accurate forecasting tools are limited.

The team used national survey data from 1999 to 2018 linked with death records through 2019, covering 2,428 adults. During roughly seven years of typical follow-up, 719 participants died. A random forest model beat four rivals on discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness, leaning on age, race, kidney disease, body mass index, and a kidney blood marker. The authors offer it for risk sorting in clinics.
pmc-13643561:
Karim Hoyek and co-authors describe a heart finding in six patients in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The finding is forward blood flow through the lung valve late in the heart cycle. It is well known after repair of a birth defect, but its meaning in carcinoid heart disease, where tumors harm the valves, is less clear.

All six patients were sent for surgery and had scans around the operation. The scans showed the late flow starting after the upper chambers squeezed and before the lower chambers beat. All had both the lung and the three-leaflet valve replaced, with more work as needed. The authors link the flow to stiff chamber walls and leaky valves, and warn it can hide how bad the leak is.
pmc-13645761:
Zhaoyang Yu and nine colleagues map how the chemotherapy drug cyclophosphamide damages ovaries and can cause early ovarian failure, a major threat to fertility after cancer treatment. Their approach combines network toxicology, gene and metabolite profiling, and a rat model of the injury. Machine learning ranked candidate target genes, and genetic methods tested whether those links might be causal. Tissue checks in rats confirmed the main patterns.

Six candidate targets emerged, with two signals, named CXCL1 and COL4A4, contributing most to the prediction model. The injury signature combined stalled cell division, faulty DNA repair, rising cell death, and suppressed energy and vitamin pathways. Computer tests on single cells suggested the two lead signals act through inflammation and tissue scaffolding changes. The study gives fertility researchers a systems-level picture of the damage and a short list of targets for protective drugs.
pmc-13646161:
Xiang Sun, Yuanyuan Zhu, and Wen Wang measure rubella immunity in 1,196 pregnant women in Jiangsu Province, China, looking for gaps left in the vaccine era. Rubella infection in pregnancy can cause severe birth defects, so immunity in mothers matters greatly. Blood tests measured protective antibodies, and results were compared across ages and birth cohorts. Overall patterns and factors tied to lacking immunity were modeled.

Only about six in ten women tested positive for protective antibodies. Immunity rose steeply with age, from under two fifths in the youngest women to about three quarters in those over thirty. Younger birth cohorts consistently carried lower antibody levels, which marks a concentrated gap in women just entering childbearing years. The authors urge immunity monitoring in mothers alongside childhood vaccination and checks before pregnancy, so elimination gains are not lost.
pmc-13647461:
Jianbo Feng and nine colleagues review smart gel platforms that adapt to the hostile environment of an infected bone defect and help rebuild bone. Such defects combine stubborn bacterial films, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, immune imbalance, and poor blood supply, which is why standard cleaning, antibiotics, and grafting often fall short. Gels can be injected, fill the defect, stay put, and release cargo on cue. The review sorts designs by the signals they answer, from acidity and enzymes to applied light.

The strongest platforms stack several jobs: killing bacteria and films, calming immune cells, growing vessels, and driving new bone. The authors insist these jobs overlap in time rather than marching in fixed stages, shifting with the wound's state. They separate evidence gathered in truly infected defects from work borrowed from cleaner models. Their map aims to guide engineers toward gels that read the wound and respond as it changes.
pmc-13647961:
Helvis L. S. Fontoura and six colleagues compare two instruments for the DPPH test, a workhorse assay that rates how well substances neutralize free radicals. Labs usually read the test by light absorption, while a magnetic method called EPR watches the radicals directly. Measuring the same samples both ways at once, the team found the light method systematically underrates scavenging power. Leftover color from spent reagent and breakdown products fools the light reading.

Three correction procedures were designed and shown to erase the statistical gap between the two methods. The fixes held for standard phenolic compounds and for deeply pigmented samples, including a purple fruit juice rich in anthocyanins. Pigment still disturbs very concentrated readings, yet the key potency values come out right after correction. The authors offer the corrections as a path to standardizing a test that food and natural product labs run every day.
pmc-13649461:
Ziheng Wang and seven colleagues read the full genome of a drug-resistant bacterium taken from a patient after surgery. The germ, Raoultella ornithinolytica, is a gut relative that can infect people with weak defences. It carried two plasmids, small DNA rings that can jump between germs, loaded with resistance genes.

In all, the strain held 14 resistance genes, among them genes that defeat last-resort drugs and a broken copy of a gene tied to one more drug class. Both key plasmids proved able to transfer to other germs in the lab. The strain also bore traits for sticking to tissue, grabbing iron, and tolerating bile. It killed wax moth larvae at a moderate rate. The authors urge watch lists to include this species.
pmc-13649661:
Yi-Chih Chang and three colleagues asked how body type and metabolic health, split by sex and age, link to stiff arteries in adults who came for routine health checks. Their group held 9,981 Chinese adults sorted into four types, from lean and healthy to heavy with poor metabolic health.

Stiff arteries, read by a pulse speed test at the arm and ankle, showed in about one in thirteen people. Two types stood out in every sex and age band: people of normal weight with poor metabolic health, and heavy people with poor metabolic health. Heavy people with good metabolic health showed no clear excess. The authors say a weight score alone misses risk, while metabolic health adds real signal.
pmc-13650361:
Unni Olsen and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, ask which patients with hand osteoarthritis actually respond to recommended care, and whether the care experience itself matters. Their analysis reuses data from a randomized trial in specialist services, where patients received education, medication, guided hand exercises, and, for thumb-base arthritis, a thumb support.

Of 340 participants, most of them women around retirement age, only about a quarter met the standard responder definition after six months. Milder thumb-base damage nearly doubled the odds of responding, and higher starting pain also predicted a better response. Trust in professionals' competence and feeling that treatment helped both raised the odds. Surprisingly, feeling very well informed about the diagnosis lowered them, which the authors link to dampened hope. They recommend earlier, individualized care and a thoughtful balance in how much detail patients receive.
pmc-13650561:
Nilasree Kannadoss and one co-author review how artificial intelligence is changing cervical cancer diagnosis, a disease that kills heavily where screening is scarce. Smear tests and virus testing remain limited by access, accuracy, and scale, which has pushed researchers toward learning algorithms that read cell images straight.

The review covers deep networks built for cervical images, hybrid systems, and combined ensembles, judging them on detection accuracy and workflow gains. Lasting obstacles include lopsided datasets with few abnormal examples, patient privacy, and models that cannot explain themselves. Proposed fixes include a synthetic oversampling method paired with noise cleaning to balance training data, and federated learning, which trains models across hospitals without moving records. The authors align the agenda with the World Health Organization's 2030 elimination goals and call for real-world validation before clinical trust.
pmc-13650761:
Merna Elsharawy and three colleagues report the removal of a large fatty tumor from a 67-year-old woman's palm. The growth had invaded two tight tunnels that carry the hand's main nerves. The tumor type, an atypical lipomatous tumor, grows locally without spreading unless it changes character, yet its size and position made nerve damage the central surgical risk.

Magnetic resonance imaging measured the mass and showed internal partitions that raised suspicion of a low-grade cancer of fat. After a sarcoma team planned the approach, surgeons entered from the palm side and used microsurgical dissection to peel the tumor away from the digital nerves. They freed it from around the ulnar bundle and off the median nerve, and removed it in one piece. Tissue study confirmed the diagnosis, and the patient went home the same day with function preserved. The authors stress imaging and team planning.
pmc-13652061:
Anchao Song and five colleagues review how machine learning is being used to turn wastewater testing into an early warning system for infectious disease. Sewage collects biological traces from whole communities, yet the raw signals are messy and hard to interpret. The authors sorted published work by method and by task, from forecasting outbreaks to spotting unusual changes and cleaning up inconsistent data.

Most of the solid evidence still comes from SARS-CoV-2, and the strongest early-warning results came from simpler statistical methods rather than deep learning. Reported accuracy varied widely with local conditions, and many proposed uses remain untested. The review closes with priorities for the field, including shared standards, better data fusion, and honest measures of uncertainty before such systems guide public decisions.
pmc-13654361:
Palwasha Anwari and seven colleagues announce a new regional working group for immunization research in the World Health Organization's Eastern Mediterranean Region. The region spans twenty-two countries and territories, from Morocco to Pakistan, with about three quarters of a billion people and sharply different health systems and disease patterns. The authors argue that vaccine policy there needs evidence produced within the region rather than borrowed from elsewhere.

The launch piece lays out why coordinated research matters for equity, since countries facing conflict, weak infrastructure, or vaccine hesitancy cannot close coverage gaps on imported data alone. A standing working group can set shared priorities, connect national teams, and speed the path from study results to program decisions. The article serves as both an announcement and a case for regional scientific cooperation in public health.
pmc-13664661:
Ben Saunders argues that bioethicists can hold a fair place in democratic choice on health policy. His paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Calls for more direct rule, by vote of all or by lot-picked panels, seem to leave no room for the expert voice. He says that room is no threat to democracy.

First, those wide paths have their own gaps: they can shut out groups with no vote, such as children and the unborn of later years. Second, democracy is not bare rule by the most hands; it splits power to guard the few. Bioethicists can serve that guard role, most when they speak for those shut-out groups.
pmc-13689461: Nakabori and Maeda reported the full genome of a soil bacterium in twenty twenty-six. The strain, called PKM581, belongs to Methylobacillus glycogenes. It can grow only on methanol, a simple one-carbon food. Methanol is cheap and can be made from carbon dioxide or plant waste, so microbes that use it well interest green industry. The genome is one round chromosome of about three point four million base pairs, giving researchers the strain's full set of instructions.
pmc-2736161:
Damschroder, Aron, Keith, and co-authors build a consolidated framework for implementation science. Health studies often prove a treatment works, yet that success fails to reach routine patient care in many settings. Researchers increasingly judge not only final outcomes but also how change happens along the way.

Their framework gathers the many factors that help or block new practices, from leadership to local culture. It gives teams a shared language for planning and judging rollouts. Hospitals and clinics use it to find why a proven practice stalls in one place and thrives in another.
pmc-2984261:
Reuter and Mathews describe RNAstructure, software for predicting and analysing RNA secondary structure. To understand how an RNA sequence works, its folded structure must be known. Structure also matters when designing small interfering RNAs and antisense tools that target a specific RNA.

The software predicts folding using thermodynamics, estimating which pairing pattern is most stable. Predictions guide experiments before costly lab tests begin. RNAstructure gave researchers a shared, tested workbench for RNA folding, used in basic studies and in designing RNA-targeting therapies and research tools.  Designers of gene-silencing tools use its folds to avoid self-pairing traps inside constructs.
pmc-3375761:
Scallan, Hoekstra, Angulo, and co-authors estimate foodborne illness from major pathogens in the United States. Their figures attribute millions of episodes each year to a set of thirty-one known pathogens. Those illnesses lead to tens of thousands of hospital stays and more than a thousand deaths annually.

Counting the burden pathogen by pathogen shows which germs cause most harm. That ranking guides food safety rules, inspection effort, and outbreak response. The estimates became the standard reference for United States foodborne disease, cited whenever agencies weigh new controls on farms and processors.
pmc-4204661:
Cruz-Jentoft, Landi, Schneider, and their colleagues reviewed sarcopenia in 2014 for the International Sarcopenia Initiative. Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with aging. The review asked how common it is and what nutrition and exercise can do about it.

The authors gathered clinical studies that used the agreed European definition of the condition. They examined both prevalence figures and trials of food and training interventions. Such pooled evidence helps doctors spot the condition early and act before frailty sets in. The report gave health systems a shared base for care of older adults losing muscle.
pmc-4352761:
Nott, Petsalaki, Farber, and their team reported in 2015 on a protein that forms droplets inside cells. Cells keep molecules apart in compartments to control their reactions. Besides membrane-bound parts, cells also build membraneless organelles, such as stress granules, from protein and RNA.

The team studied a disordered protein from nuage, a germ cell structure. It can shift phase and form droplets that respond to their surroundings. That behavior shows how cells create order without membranes, on demand. Such droplets are now a major topic, since their failure is linked to diseases of the brain and muscle.
pmc-6602461:
Uku Raudvere, Liis Kolberg, Ivan Kuzmin, and coauthors described g:Profiler in its 2019 form. Gene lists pour out of modern experiments, and each list needs interpretation. g:Profiler tests which biological categories appear more than chance would predict.

It also converts between gene identifier systems and maps genes to their counterparts in other species. Data sources are refreshed often so results reflect current knowledge. Care is taken to use sound statistics that correct for testing many categories. The tool is a staple for turning raw gene lists into readable biology. A public server handles lists of many thousands of genes within seconds.
pmc-7759461:
Charles Harris and many co-authors introduced in 2020 the ideas behind NumPy, the array programming library at the heart of scientific computing in Python. Array programming lets a user describe operations on whole grids of numbers at once, in compact and readable code. NumPy supplies that machinery for vectors, matrices, and arrays of higher dimensions.

The authors explain the design choices that made the library fast, flexible, and easy to build on. They also describe the large community and ecosystem that grew around it, from physics and biology to machine learning. Few papers describe a tool so many scientists use daily without thinking about it, which makes this account a useful piece of computing history as well.
pmc-9287161:
Felix Teufel and co-authors introduced SignalP 6.0 in 2022, a predictor for signal peptides, the short tags that direct proteins to be secreted or moved across cell membranes. Every living organism uses these tags to route its proteins. Earlier prediction programs could not detect all five known types of signal peptide, leaving gaps in genome annotation.

SignalP 6.0 is built on protein language models, systems trained on huge numbers of protein sequences that learn the patterns of the code. The authors show it recognizing all five peptide types in one tool. Correctly spotting these tags matters because a protein's destination shapes its function, and annotation pipelines process millions of sequences that no human will inspect.
pmc-9997061:
Justas Dauparas and co-authors described ProteinMPNN in 2022, a deep learning method that designs protein sequences to fold into a chosen shape. Predicting structure from sequence had just been transformed by deep learning. Designing the reverse, a sequence for a desired structure, still relied mostly on physics based tools such as Rosetta, which produced nearly all proven experimental designs.

ProteinMPNN takes the backbone shape as input and proposes sequences likely to fold into it. The authors show its designs solving in the laboratory at strong rates. A fast, reliable design method widens the door to custom proteins built for medicine, materials, and research, rather than only borrowed from nature.
rodwell-koran-1861:
John Medows Rodwell, an English cleric and friend of Darwin, made this English Koran in 1861. The text here is from the second print of 1876. Rodwell was a sound Arabic scholar, and his aim was a clear, true text for the English reader.

His new step was the order: he sets the surahs, the parts of the Koran, by the time they were first given out. That order lets a reader trace how the word of the Prophet grew with the years of his life. The book is the Koran re-set by time, a first of its kind in English.
romeo-and-juliet-pg2261: Editorial notes, not the play named in this record's title, fill the opening pages shown. Michael S. Hart explains that old printers' spelling has been kept, and quotes the first lines of Hamlet to prove it. Printers, he says, packed type into cliches and swapped letters when sorts ran short. Scholars, he adds, prize many such errors as canon. The notes end by announcing the text that follows as Shakespeare's First Part of Henry the Sixth. No line of Romeo and Juliet appears here.
rousseau-inequality-1761:
Rousseau was born at Geneva on June 28, 1712, a watchmaker's son, a note up front records. His schooling was patchy, and he tried engraving, music, and teaching before fame found him. A prize essay for the Academy of Dijon first made his name.

The discourse printed here asks where human inequality began and what grounds it. Rousseau argues that private property and civil life warped a free and equal nature. The note calls the work unsound in places yet mighty in effect. It fed the zeal for liberty, fraternity, and equality that drove the French Revolution, and it still provokes debate.
rousseau-julie-kenrick-1761:
Julie and Saint-Preux trade letters across a Swiss lake in Rousseau's Julie, the novel William Kenrick Englished in 1761. That first English version, titled The New Eloisa, carried a bestseller across the Channel. A tutor loves his pupil, and duty, rank, and marriage stand between them for six long volumes.

Europe wept over Julie, and the book taught a generation to feel in a new key. Love, nature, and virtue argue in every letter, with the Alps watching over all. As a founding text of Romanticism in fiction, it shaped the novel of feeling for a century.
sanderson-abominable-snowmen-legend-come:
Ivan Sanderson took up the hairy man question for English readers in 1961. Abominable Snowmen: Legend Come to Life is the first major English survey of yeti and sasquatch reports. Sanderson was a trained zoologist and a famed teller of animal tales.

Fourteen chapters gather case reports from five continents, from the high Himalayas to the woods of the Pacific coast. Appendices take up footprint casts and the wild life of the snow ranges in close detail. Sanderson argues the reports point to real, unlisted primates. His book brought the snowman debate to a wide and eager public.
schaaffhausen-busk-crania-ancient-races-:
Hermann Schaaffhausen first described the Neanderthal skull in German in 1858. George Busk's English translation, with his own remarks, appeared in 1861. The skull had been found in the Neander Valley in 1856 by quarry workers.

Schaaffhausen measured the brow ridge, skull shape, and limb bones in detail. Johann Fuhlrott, who first recognized the find, gives his own account here. The paper treats the bones as remains of an ancient human race. Scholars now regard it as the founding document of paleoanthropology, the study of fossil humans. Busk's notes connect the skull to other ancient remains known then.
semmelweis-aetiologie-kindbettfieber-186:
Ignaz Semmelweis was a Hungarian doctor who worked in a Vienna birth clinic. In 1861 he set out his findings in German in a long, hard-fought book on childbed fever. He had seen far too many young mothers die after giving birth.

Semmelweis showed that doctors carried the fever from dead bodies to healthy women. He proved that washing hands in a chlorine mix cut deaths at once. Most doctors of his day mocked him, and he died in disgrace. His book now stands as the first great work on clean hands and safe care.
silius-italicus-punica-english-1661:
Silius Italicus, a Roman consul and rich patron of poets, spent his last years writing the Punica, an epic on the Second Punic War. At seventeen books it is the longest Latin epic that survives. Thomas Ross turned it into English verse in 1661, the first time the poem had appeared in the language.

Hannibal crosses the Alps, wins at Cannae, and slowly loses the war to Roman patience and to Scipio. Silius follows Livy for the facts and Virgil for the music, with gods and omens at work above the armies. Ross's version is a landmark of translation history. The poem itself is Rome's last full epic of its own past.
spencer-education-1861:
Herbert Spencer published Education in 1861, a set of essays on how children should be taught. His famous question opens the work: what knowledge is of most worth? His answer is science, in all its forms, for health, work, parenting, and citizenship. Classical languages, the pride of old schools, rank low by that test.

Spencer urges lessons that follow the child's own growth and curiosity. He opposes rote learning, harsh punishment, and cramming for exams. The essays helped found the science-based side of modern pedagogy. Teachers still quote his central question. The book reads as fresh common sense even where later practice moved on.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-l: The American Phrenological Journal and Life Illustrated, 1861. The illustrated repository. This book preserves that periodical. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Paris and Holland, the opening part of The Eternal Quest in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows Arthur Machen's English version of the 1894 London edition, with chapters found by Arthur Symons. The part's own heading numbers it Volume 2a, although the parts that follow it are numbered 3b onward; the mismatch stands as printed. Chapter One opens in March 1757, when a handsome young Venetian arrives with a letter from Madame Manzoni.

The visitor is Count Tiretta of Treviso, and he brings back Casanova's manuscripts in a small box. Tiretta asks for friendship, protection, and perhaps a purse. He confesses that, as a young keeper of the Mont de Piete, he and his companions borrowed from the till after carnival expenses. They hoped to replace the money before balancing day, in vain. Readers see the escaped prisoner turned patron of another man's flight.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Loch Goil Head in Argyllshire, residence of the poet Thomas Campbell, fills the Mirror's No. 377, dated Saturday, June 27, 1829. The village sits at the end of Loch Goil under Alpine sublimity, and Campbell's retreat appears at the engraving's left. The author of The Pleasures of Hope is called one of the most celebrated of British poets. His romantic position, the article suggests, has likely inspired many of his soul-stirring compositions.

The parish holds Carrick Castle, said to be Danish-built, once sea-girt on its rock. Ben Cruachan rises 3,300 feet nearby, and the Duke of Argyll's castle at Inveraray rears amid nature's sublimities. Loch Lomond and Ben Lomond lie in the same vicinity, with Glencoe's massacre associations not far off. Readers tour a poet's address through an entire Highland landscape. The magazine sells scenery by association, one famous resident at a time.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-06:
Motley's sixth volume covers 1560 and 1561. Chapter two summarizes agitation across the Netherlands. Ancient charters rise as barriers against government measures. The joyous entrance of Brabant heads those charters. The constitution of Holland stands beside it in the list. Granvelle's growing unpopularity dominates the summary's middle. Orange and Egmont oppose the new bishoprics with other nobles.

Crowds rage at the foreign soldiers still quartered there. Orange resigns his legion command in protest. The troops are recalled to Spain at last. Philip attends personally to details of persecution meanwhile. Perrenot becomes Cardinal Granvelle with all power in hand. Old friendship cools toward enmity between the two men. Constitutional language and personal rivalry advance together here now.
the-sable-cloud-a-southern-tale-with-nor: The Sable Cloud was printed in Boston by Ticknor and Fields in 1861. The author is named only as the author of A South-Side View of Slavery. An epigraph from Milton's Comus supplies the title image. The pages at hand stop after the title matter and contents, so the tale itself is absent. The contents open with the death and burial of a slave's infant. Northern comments on southern life follow. Later chapters treat a morbid northern conscience and resolutions for a convention.
the-treasure-pg5161:
Selma Lagerlöf's Treasure opens in the days when Frederik the Second of Denmark ruled Bohuslen, then under the Danish crown though now Swedish. At Marstrand dwelt Torarin, a poor fish hawker with a palsied arm that kept him from fishing boats and oars. He earned his living on the road, selling salted and dried fish from village to village, seldom spending many days at home. One February day at dusk he drove toward Solberga parsonage along a lonely, deserted road.

Beside him on the sledge rode his trusty friend, Grim, a little black shaggy dog who answered all conversation by blinking. The contents promise the quays, a messenger, moonlight, haunting, flight over the ice, and the roar of the waves. Lagerlöf, Sweden's Nobel laureate, builds a tale of murder and conscience from this humble travelling salesman and his dog.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-: Gilbert Parker's Weavers, a tale of England and Egypt of fifty years ago, is split in the library into single-volume records beside a complete-edition record. This record carries the novel's title and a contents segment for book three, so the story text does not appear. Two dozen chapters appear here, beginning with The Red Slayer Retaliates. Egypt settings dominate: a village at noon, the council of the notables, jehad, and a game played at El Wasta. Later headings promise Mohammed's rage.
tob-0161:
C. G. Jung published Psychology of the Unconscious in German in 1912, and Beatrice M. Hinkle's 1916 translation, the first of Jung's books in English, brought it to America. The long study of a patient's fantasies marks Jung's public break with Freud. Libido, for Jung, is general life energy, not sexuality alone, and myths are the psyche's own language.

Symbols from world mythology are read as stages of an inner transformation, a method Jung would expand into analytical psychology. Hinkle, herself an early American analyst, renders the dense argument faithfully. Readers watch a founder declare independence in real time, with consequences for a century of psychotherapy and literary criticism.
tob-10261:
Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit scholar in Rome, published Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae, the Great Art of Light and Shadow, in 1646. He wrote on nearly every subject of his age, and optics gave him rich ground. Fine engravings fill the large volume.

Kircher treats lenses, mirrors, sundials, and light thrown through colored glass to cast pictures on walls. One device he describes stands close to the magic lantern, the ancestor of the film projector. His science mixes sound tests with wonders and errors, yet the book shows how Baroque scholars pictured light and made a show of knowing it.
tob-10361:
Johann Weyer, a Dutch physician, issued the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum in 1563 as part of his work on demons and witchcraft. Weyer doubted that accused witches had real powers. Yet he still catalogued the spirit world his age believed in.

His list names sixty-nine demons, with their ranks, forms, legions, and the hours when they may be called. Later grimoires, above all the Goetia, borrowed the list and its order. The catalogue is a master index of Renaissance demon belief, and Weyer's doubt about witch trials gives the strange book a humane core.
tob-4161:
Edward Burnett Tylor published Primitive Culture in 1871, the book that founded anthropology as a science in English. Tylor, a Quaker who never held a university post when he wrote it, worked from travelers' reports worldwide. The copy here follows the 1920 edition, in two volumes.

He defines culture, traces the doctrine of souls he calls animism, and treats magic, myth, and ritual as stages in one human development. Tylor's famous definition of culture, the complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, and custom, opens the work. The science of man begins in these volumes, complete, and every later anthropologist has argued with them.
two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-catara: Volume two of Richard F. Burton's Two Trips to Gorilla Land, printed at London in 1876, carries a contents list headed Contents of Vol. I, a mismatch with its own title page. The listed chapters sail from Fernando Po up the Congo River to Boma and Banza Nokki, then reach the Yellala falls. An appendix promises plants collected by Consul Burton. Only the title page and this mismatched contents list are present here, so the second volume's journeys do not appear.
un-ga-res-161:
Congo's crisis deepened into blood in February 1961, and the vote filed here as Resolution 161 answered it. The text is in fact a Security Council vote, passed on 21 February 1961 by ten votes to one. Word had come of the killing of Congo's chiefs: Patrice Lumumba, Maurice Mpolo, and Joseph Okito. Grave fallout from those crimes, and the risk of wide civil war, hang over the text.

The UN is urged to act at once with all fit steps to bar civil war in the Congo. Truces must be set, all armed moves halted, and clashes barred, with force used if need be as a last resort. All Belgian and other foreign armed men must leave the land at once. The vote marks the UN's deepest plunge into the Congo fight.
un-ga-res-57-161:
Guatemala's peace entered its last UN phase under Resolution 57/161, passed in December 2002. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2002 by a vote of the year before. The state had restated its pledge to put the peace deals into full force. Yet core parts of those deals, the text stresses again, still waited to be done.

The follow-up team's timetable for the work now ran through 2004. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's thirteenth report on human rights is weighed in the text. So is the seventh report on the checking of the peace deals, and the truth report on the war's crimes.
un-ga-res-a-69-61:
Women belong at the center of disarmament work, argues Resolution A/69/61, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Charter itself states the equal rights of women and men. The text recalls votes of 2010 and 2012 on women and arms. It also recalls Security Council calls of 2013. Those calls seek a full part for women in the fight against the illicit spread of small arms.

Equal, full, and real roles for women and men alike are named as a core need for lasting peace. The work of women in hands-on disarmament is praised: at local, state, and regional levels, they help cut armed strife and gun deaths. The vote presses states to open that work wide.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 57/161, adopted on 16 December 2002, extends the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala through 2003, near the end of the timetable agreed for completing the country's peace accords. The Assembly acts on the mission's verification reporting and on Guatemala's own request for the extension.

The mandate runs from 1 January to 31 December 2003, and the Secretary-General is asked to recommend how the mission should continue afterward. The resolution welcomes steps such as the agreement to create a National Reparations Commission for victims of the armed conflict and urges both sides to sustain and deepen compliance with the accords. With the end of the implementation timetable in sight, the extension kept the settlement's final phase under international observation.

Resolution 69/61 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, deals with women, disarmament, non-proliferation and arms control. It urges states to promote equal opportunities for women to be represented in decision-making on disarmament and arms control. It supports collecting data broken down by sex and age on the impact of armed violence. It notes the role of UN-Women and the Arms Trade Treaty's reference to gender-based violence. That keeps women's participation a standing part of disarmament policy.
un-sc-res-1361: A seat on the International Court of Justice fell vacant in 2001. Judge Mohammed Bedjaoui had resigned, with effect from 30 September 2001. On 5 July 2001 the Security Council fixed the date to fill his place. The election would be held on 12 October 2001. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its fifty-sixth session. The whole resolution performs that single scheduling act.
un-sc-res-1461: Holding number 1461 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1973 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1561:
By Resolution 1561, adopted unanimously on 17 September 2004, the Council acted on Liberia. The peace mission there had helped end a long civil war. Disarming fighters had gone well so far. Elections were due by October 2005, and ex-fighters still needed jobs and training.

The Council extends the mission, called UNMIL, until 19 September 2005. All Liberian parties are called to back the peace process in full. They must work together so the polls are free, fair, and open. Donors are asked to fund the return of ex-fighters to civil life. Past pledges from the February rebuild talks should be paid.
un-sc-res-161:
Resolution 161 reacts to grave news from the Congo. Congolese leaders Patrice Lumumba, Maurice Mpolo, and Joseph Okito had been killed. The Council adopted the text on 21 February 1961. It said it learned of the killings with deep regret. Reports also pointed to a civil war taking shape.

The Council urges the UN to act at once. The aim is to stop civil war in the Congo. Steps could include cease-fires and a halt to all fighting. Force could be used if needed, as a last resort. The text also urges the removal of foreign troops and advisers. They must not serve outside UN command. Mercenaries must leave as well. States are asked to stop such people from leaving for the Congo.
un-sc-res-1661: Resolution 1661, adopted in 2006, is a Security Council act preserved through English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. The Council's resolutions are how peacekeeping missions live and die, sanctions rise and fall, and demands reach governments. This entry holds one complete instance of that machinery, in the members' own formal language.
un-sc-res-1761: Adopted in 2007, Resolution 1761 is a Security Council decision preserved in official-record form. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Inside the act, the members cite their earlier texts the way courts cite precedent, then extend the line of action one step further. The entry preserves that step in its full legal dress.
un-sc-res-1861:
Chad and the Central African Republic are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1861, adopted on 14 January 2009. Darfur's war kept spilling across their borders. Refugees and displaced families crowded camps in the east of Chad. A European Union force guarding those areas was due to leave in March.

The Council extends the United Nations mission, called MINURCAT, until 15 March 2010. A military wing of up to 5,200 troops joins its 300 police. It takes over from the European force on 15 March 2009. Under Chapter VII it may use force to guard civilians in danger and keep aid moving. A special Chadian police unit keeps order inside the camps.
un-sc-res-2361: Resolution 2361, from 2017, is a Security Council decision preserved in this collection through a transcription of the official record. Its form matches acts decades older in the same series: the institution changes slowly on paper. The entry preserves the full text at its number, so its demands can be read in the members' own durable format.
un-sc-res-261:
Encouraging news from Cyprus reached the Council in December 1968, along with a familiar warning. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 4 December, noted recent progress on the island. It still held that the peacekeeping force was needed to maintain peace. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond 15 December. Resolution 261 was adopted unanimously on 10 December 1968.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They had to make good use of the favorable climate and press on with their joint efforts. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1969. The pattern was by then well set. Each renewal kept the peacekeepers in Cyprus for a few more months, while the search for a final settlement went on.
un-sc-res-361:
Cyprus's displaced people were the Council's focus on 30 August 1974. The summer's fighting had uprooted large numbers across the island. The Secretary-General's report on the crisis was before the Council. The United Nations refugee chief had already been named coordinator of relief for Cyprus.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General for bringing the two communities' leaders into talks. It called on them to press the talks forward for the sake of all Cypriots. All parties had to ease human suffering, honor basic human rights, and avoid acts that could worsen the crisis. Grave concern was voiced for the refugees and displaced. The parties were urged to seek peaceful answers with the Secretary-General, give relief, and let those who wished return home in safety. He owed the Council a full report on the refugees at the earliest chance, and emergency aid was to continue.
un-sc-res-461:
Iran's holding of United States hostages brought the Council to the edge of sanctions on 31 December 1979. The seizure of the embassy staff broke international law and fed rising tension. The World Court had ordered Iran on 15 December to free every hostage without exception. The Secretary-General reported on 22 December, and resolution 457 (1979) had already demanded release.

The Council restated resolution 457 in all its parts. It deplored the continued detention of the hostages against its decisions and the Court's order. Iran was urgently called once again to free them and let them leave the country. The Secretary-General was asked to lend his good offices and to report on them before the Council met again. The Council fixed that meeting for 7 January 1980. It would review the crisis and, if Iran still refused, adopt measures under the Charter to enforce its decisions.
un-sc-res-61:
The Palestine truce was collapsing in the autumn of 1948. Fighting had broken out again in the south in October. On 4 November 1948 the Security Council reminded the parties of its earlier rulings. No side could break the truce as a reprisal. No side could gain land or advantage by breaking it. The acting mediator had asked both governments on 26 October to pull back.

The Council now calls on them to withdraw forces that had pushed past their 14 October positions. They also had to open armistice talks at once. Talks could run through the mediator or directly. The aim was a lasting armistice across Palestine. Those talks began on Rhodes weeks later and produced the 1949 agreements.
un-sc-res-661: Numbered 661 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1990 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1361, passed unanimously on 5 July 2001, deals with a vacancy on the International Court of Justice, the UN's highest court in The Hague. Judge Mohammed Bedjaoui had resigned, with his departure taking effect on 30 September 2001, leaving his seat empty for the rest of his term.

Because the Court's statute leaves the scheduling to the Council, the members fixed the election for the vacant seat on 12 October 2001. Judges are chosen jointly, so the vote would happen both in the Security Council and in the General Assembly, which was then holding its fifty-sixth session. The whole text is short and purely procedural.

At Lebanon's request, UNIFIL is renewed for six months on 30 January 2003. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's January report, including its advice to extend the mandate. The force's main remaining task was restoring peace and security in the south of the country.

The mandate now runs until 31 July 2003. All violence is condemned, and grave concern is voiced over serious breaches of the withdrawal line by air, sea, and land. The parties are urged to end those violations and to respect the safety of United Nations staff. UNIFIL is to keep full freedom of movement throughout its area of operations.

Liberia was climbing out of a savage civil war in 2004. Resolution 1561, adopted unanimously on 17 September 2004, extended the UN mission there, UNMIL. West African states and the African Union backed the peace effort. Ex-fighters were handing in weapons. The Secretary-General's report of 10 September 2004 guided the decision.

UNMIL's mandate now ran to 19 September 2005. Members told Liberian parties to prove their commitment to peace. Free and fair elections had to happen by October 2005. The text also appeals for money to reabsorb former fighters into civilian life. Donors were reminded of pledges made at a February 2004 rebuilding conference.

News that Congo's first prime minister and two fellow leaders had been murdered drives this text of 21 February 1961. A serious civil war was building in the Congo, and widespread bloodshed and a threat to world peace were feared.

The United Nations is urged to act at once to prevent civil war, including arranging ceasefires, halting military operations, and using force if needed as a last resort. The withdrawal of all Belgian and other foreign military and political advisers and mercenaries not under United Nations command is demanded. All states are called on to stop such people leaving for the Congo from their soil.

Just one month is granted to UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, on 14 March 2006, until 15 April 2006. Eritrea had placed heavy restrictions on the mission, and border demarcation was still blocked. The short renewal signalled frustration while the mission's future was weighed.

Both parties are demanded to comply fully with resolution 1640, including lifting the restrictions on UNMEE and reversing Eritrean limits on its movement. Lasting peace, it is repeated, requires full demarcation of the border under the Boundary Commission's final and binding ruling. Both governments are told to give the mission the access, help, and protection it needs to do its work.

Côte d'Ivoire's Group of Experts is extended until 31 October 2007 on 20 June 2007. The group's final report under its previous term had just reached the Council. The experts track how the arms embargo and the targeted travel and financial measures on the country are applied and where they are broken.

Acting under Chapter VII, the group stays working alongside the renewed sanctions. A written update, through the sanctions committee, is asked for before 15 October 2007. That update is to cover enforcement of the measures and offer recommendations. The aim is current evidence in hand when the sanctions themselves come up for renewal at the end of October.

Chad and the Central African Republic get a UN military follow-on to the EU force in Resolution 1861, adopted on 14 January 2009. Darfur's violence spilled across the borders, and EUFOR Chad/CAR was due to end on 15 March 2009. Both governments asked for a UN military component to succeed it.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, MINURCAT, until 15 March 2010. It authorizes 5,200 military personnel, 300 police, and 25 military liaison officers, taking over from EUFOR on 15 March 2009. Acting under Chapter VII, MINURCAT may use all necessary measures in eastern Chad to protect civilians in danger, especially refugees and displaced persons, and to secure aid delivery. In the north-eastern Central African Republic it keeps a presence at Birao and may extract endangered civilians and aid workers. It trains the Chadian camp police, the Détachement intégré de sécurité.

Liberia's remaining sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1961, adopted on 17 December 2010. Timber and diamond measures had ended years earlier, the forestry reform law and Kimberley Process controls were in place, and Liberia was cooperating on weapons marking. The Panel of Experts still found too little progress toward the conditions for ending the arms and travel measures, and none on the asset freeze.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and the travel ban for 12 months. It confirms the Resolution 1532 (2004) asset freeze stays in force, demanding Liberia meet its obligations under it. The Committee must keep the public reasons for each listing updated. The Panel of Experts is extended to 16 December 2011 to check compliance, judge how the freeze is working, and assess Kimberley controls. It must report midway by 1 June 2011 and finally by 1 December 2011.

The United Nations force that watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria is the subject of Resolution 2361, adopted in 2017. The force is called UNDOF, and it works on the Golan Heights. Syria's civil war had spilled into the force's area. Heavy weapons were being used near its positions.

The Council renewed UNDOF's mandate for six months, until 31 December 2017. It stressed that both sides must respect the Disengagement of Forces Agreement of 1974. No armed forces other than UNDOF's own were to stay in the area of separation. Armed groups were told to leave UNDOF positions and return vehicles and weapons they had taken. The Council also welcomed the first peacekeepers returning to Camp Faouar.

Encouraging news from Cyprus reached New York late in 1968. On 10 December, the Council adopted Resolution 261 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the peace force was still needed. He also noted welcome recent gains on the island. Cyprus agreed to the force staying past mid-December.

The text restates the by-now long list of Cyprus decisions. It urges restraint and joint effort in the hopeful climate of the day. It then extends the posting to 15 June 1969. The standing hope returns at the end. Enough progress might soon let the force shrink or head home. That formula stayed with the mission through this era.

Resolution 361, adopted unanimously on 30 August 1974, turns from battle lines to human suffering in Cyprus. Weeks of fighting after the July coup and the Turkish intervention had displaced a large share of the island's people, who were in dire need of help. The UN refugee chief had already been named coordinator of humanitarian assistance for Cyprus.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General for bringing the two communities' leaders into talks and warmly welcomed the start of that dialogue. It called on all parties to do everything possible to relieve suffering, to secure respect for basic human rights for everyone, and to hold back from anything that might worsen the crisis. Relief work, in short, was declared a duty of the combatants.

Resolution 461, adopted on 31 December 1979 by eleven votes to none with four abstentions, returns to the Tehran hostages as the year ends. The Council recalled its December demand for the Americans' release and the appeals its president made in November. The World Court had ordered Iran on 15 December to free every hostage without exception, and Iran's foreign minister had sent letters setting out his government's grievances.

The Council again urgently called for the immediate release of all the hostages and for their safe departure. It took note of the Secretary-General's view that the crisis threatened international peace. And it decided to meet again in January to review the situation and consider steps, sanctions included, if the hostages were still held.

Truce lines in Palestine had to be drawn in the fall of 1948. Both sides had gained ground since 14 October. The stand-in mediator had asked them to pull back on 26 October. The Council weighed its past truce texts. Resolution 61 passed on 4 November 1948 by nine votes to one. The Ukrainian team said no. The Soviet team held back.

Troops that had moved past the 14 October lines had to quit them. The mediator would draw stop lines no one could cross. Set truce lines and bare zones would come next, by talks or by his word. A team of the five big powers, plus Belgium and Colombia, would coach him. If a side balked, the team would weigh hard steps under the Charter's teeth. The war's end game was taking shape in these lines.

Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the Council answered with sanctions four days later. Resolution 660 had ordered Iraq to withdraw, and Iraq had ignored it. The invasion and occupation continued, with more loss of life and more destruction. Resolution 661 was adopted on 6 August 1990.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council imposed wide sanctions. Their purpose was to force Iraq to comply and to restore Kuwait's government. All states had to block imports of goods from Iraq and from occupied Kuwait. Their nationals could not promote exports from those places either. Iraq was also to be denied funds and economic resources. A sanctions committee, made up of all Council members, was created to watch enforcement. The text affirmed Kuwait's right of self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter.
uslaw-usc-t2-s161: Section 161 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the tax treatment of gifts to the Library of Congress. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. The rule is a single sentence. Gifts, bequests, and devises to or for the gain of the Library, and the income from them, are free of tax. The freedom covers gifts to the board of the Library as well. It runs to all federal taxes and to taxes laid by the District of Columbia.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2261: Section 2261 of Title 2 of the United States Code gives the sense of a term, transfer date. It sits in Chapter 31, on the Capitol Visitor Center, in a part on the move of a set of staff. The term means the first day of the first pay round for the staff moved under a named section. That pay round must fall on or after 30 days past 20 October 2008. The section is a short sense clause for use in its subchapter.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5561: Section 5561 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers reporters for the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 55 of that title, on House officers and administration, in the part on the Clerk. The rule is a single sentence and states a bar on hiring. No person may be employed as a reporter for the House without the approval of the Speaker. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: The record here shows a Project Gutenberg header only, with Widger's Montaigne quotations not present. The source is The Essays of Montaigne, in the fuller header form Michel de Montaigne. The set is number 12 in David Widger's Quotations series. It was released in January 2003 as etext number 3661. The first posting date is July 8, 2001, and the edition is number 10. The rest is the usual Gutenberg header matter on law, giving, and the archive.
wundt-vnd-leibartznei-die-gantze-chirurg: Pages present here show the title page and contents of a German surgery book printed at Frankfurt in 1561. The title promises treatment of wounds and bodily ills, hidden and open sores, and the so-called French disease. It also names material drawn from Paracelsus and a section on the fifth essence credited to Raimundus Lullius. The contents list wound inspection and healing in old German type. No clear narrative text appears in these pages.
